consensus_answer:
Not clear on how the Marines still get the foxhole TEM. A12.15 A unit forced back to an entrenchment/shellhole Location can derive no TEM benefit therefrom vs any ensuing Defensive First Fire, although it can for any Defensive Final Fire or subsequent attacks.

This is an interesting observation, but my best guess is this is not fixed for the Journal 16 changes. I could be wrong here, though. Per q&a, 
12.15 & B27.4 An American squad is in a Foxhole in Open Ground adjacent to a Concealed German unit in Woods. During the MPh:
(1) The American squad uses non-Assault Movement to exit the Foxhole for 1 MF and then attempts to enter the Woods.
(2) The American squad uses non-Assault Movement to exit the Foxhole for 1 MF, then attempts Smoke Grenade placement for 1 MF, and then attempts to enter the Woods.
(3) The American squad makes one combined expenditure of MF using Assault Movement to exit the Foxhole and enter the Woods.
In all cases the American squad is forced back into its initial hex via A12.15. In the above cases, is the American squad under the Foxhole for Defensive Final Fire?
A. Case 3 only.
If the answer to any of the above is yes, can the American squad—on returning to its initial hex—decline being placed back in the Foxhole?
A. No option exists.

Not unless there was already residual in the hex. The residual is placed after any attack. The unit would make its expenditure in an attempt to enter, be bounced back and be considered in the hex it attempted to leave. It would then be subject to DFF in that hex if not disallowed per B27.4, and residual would be placed as a result of said DFF. The unit would not be attacked by residual from an attack made against it unless it made another expenditure.

Defensive First Fire Attacks [EXC: Residual-FP/OBA (if pinned/broken by such the unit remains in the foxhole hex above the foxhole); FFMO can apply] in the foxhole Location." The rule in A12.15 may be another EXC, but as currently written the unit pushed back by A12.15 when using combined foxhole-exit-next-hex-entry MF would not be subject to DFF in the foxhole hex, and so would only be eligible for attack during DFPh, and so eligible for the +2 TEM.IMO these two situations are very different.

B27.4 is dealing with normal movement from one hex to the next, and it's telling us that using Assault Movement to exit a Foxhole as you leave its hex shields you from taking Defensive First Fire in that hex.

A12.15 is entirely different: it talks about thwarted movement and it says, when you're bounced back, you ARE exposed to Defensive First Fire attacks in the Location you were attempting to leave. And it explicitly says no Foxhole TEM applies during Defensive First Fire. (So FFMO is a possibility.)

I can't see how B27.4 would overrule A12.15: they cover two distinctly different events--especially as A12.15 explicitly addresses entrenchments.

title: A8.3 Subsequent First Fire MF "Expended in that Location"
question:
Am a little embarrassed to ask about this, but we're not totally certain we've been playing the illustrated situation correctly:

Rule A8.3 SUBSEQUENT FIRST FIRE states in part that "The same unit/weapon can never fire on a moving unit in the same Location more times than the number of MF/MP expended... in that Location during that MPh."   In our game, the German SQ in J9, having totally missed with his Defensive First Fire at F10 (w/ DRM -2 for FFMO & FFNAM), wishes to follow up immediately by using Subsequent First Fire, also into F10.  Can he do so?

The Americans did expend 3 MF to get to hex F10, but given that 2 of those MF were expended crossing the bocage, are they or are they not considered to have expended all 3MF in the F10 Location?  If they didn't expend the extra 2 MF in that Location, then my understanding is that no immediate Subsequent First Fire back into F10 should be allowed.
author: A2SimGamer
consensus_answer:
Am a little embarrassed to ask about this, but we're not totally certain we've been playing the illustrated situation correctly:

Rule A8.3 SUBSEQUENT FIRST FIRE states in part that "The same unit/weapon can never fire on a moving unit in the same Location more times than the number of MF/MP expended... in that Location during that MPh."   In our game, the German SQ in J9, having totally missed with his Defensive First Fire at F10 (w/ DRM -2 for FFMO & FFNAM), wishes to follow up immediately by using Subsequent First Fire, also into F10.  Can he do so?

The Americans did expend 3 MF to get to hex F10, but given that 2 of those MF were expended crossing the bocage, are they or are they not considered to have expended all 3MF in the F10 Location?  If they didn't expend the extra 2 MF in that Location, then my understanding is that no immediate Subsequent First Fire back into F10 should be allowed.
The cost to cross a wall/hedge is an addition to the COT [B9.4], resulting in an increased MF cost for that expenditure. That addition is not made as a separate expenditure (unlike, say, exiting a foxhole or placing a DC/smoke grenade), so the unit performs its move then receives DFF for all MF spent in that expenditure at any point to which the LOS can be traced. Similarly extra MF for entering SMOKE add to the COT for the expenditure and are not separate expenditures. Once the movement action is complete the unit may be fired on as many times as the unit spent MF in that expenditure.

As a slightly different example an infantry unit spending two MF in bypass, say in H10 when there is SMOKE present, can be fired on two times at any of the two or three vertices that are used by that bypass. The unit does not spend one MF at each vertex for a single-hexside bypass nor expend two-thirds of a MF at each vertex for a two-hexside bypass. The firing unit could fire at different vertices if it wanted (e.g. it turns out that LOS to one vertex was blocked, and the DEFENDER wanted to try LOS to a different vertex), but it is not required to switch the vertex for a single expenditure.

"8.22 RESTRICTIONS: ......

A unit can be attacked by Residual FP only once per Location [EXC: if, since that first Residual FP attack, the Residual FP has increased in strength or the unit is subject to more-negative-DRM/less-positive-DRM, it will be attacked again by that Residual FP upon further MF/MP expenditure]. However:
MF/MP expended "simultaneously" (e.g., two MF to enter a building, two MF to cross a wall and enter Open Ground, eight MP for a truck to ascend a Crest Line, etc.) do not cause multiple Residual FP attacks. Expending MF/MP for separate activities (e.g., one MF to enter a hex plus one MF to place SMOKE grenades) is never considered a "simultaneous" expenditure (8.1).

Residual FP does not attack until any activity that a MF/MP expenditure allowed is completed (e.g., placing SMOKE grenades, SW Recovery, Searching, firing a Smoke Dispenser, etc.) [EXC: entering a vehicle; (un)hooking; D5.43].  An attack vs a pillbox never leaves Residual FP in the pillbox Location, nor in the non-pillbox Location of that hex unless the attack could affect the entire hex (e.g., Spraying Fire, Area Target Type, etc.)."

author: jrvjrv
consensus_answer:
I like the consistency in the Perry Sez answer: when Infantry are changing hexes, they're moving and can be seen through gaps in a wall. This aligns well with note B in the A12.121 Concealment Loss/Gain Table.
One reason I had my doubts is A.3, which says that says the term "move" is used only for the MPh, and rules which want to address more than that use "move/Advance." But when the original question arose I looked at A.3 more carefully, and it says
Whenever a rule refers to a non-vehicular unit's inability to move, it refers only to movement in the MPh. If a unit's advance capability during the APh is also restricted, the rule will specifically prohibit both movement and advance.
When I reviewed the rule in the context of the original question I realized that A.3 covered a very specific subset of rules and was not the general-purpose rule I had imagined it to be. That said it does raise the point that in the ASLRB the word "move" may or may not be restricted to translation in the MPh. There is no formal definition of, "move," as being "all counter translation" or just "counter translation during the MPh." Because of this ambiguity one can come to have doubts about the specific use of "move" that is intended in a given context.

One reason I had my doubts is A.3, which says that says the term "move" is used only for the MPh, and rules which want to address more than that use "move/Advance." But when the original question arose I looked at A.3 more carefully, and it says
Whenever a rule refers to a non-vehicular unit's inability to move, it refers only to movement in the MPh. If a unit's advance capability during the APh is also restricted, the rule will specifically prohibit both movement and advance.
When I reviewed the rule in the context of the original question I realized that A.3 covered a very specific subset of rules and was not the general-purpose rule I had imagined it to be. That said it does raise the point that in the ASLRB the word "move" may or may not be restricted to translation in the MPh. There is no formal definition of, "move," as being "all counter translation" or just "counter translation during the MPh." Because of this ambiguity one can come to have doubts about the specific use of "move" that is intended in a given context.

title: Shellholes and TEM
question:
Hi all,

I'm making an effort to move from ASLSK to full ASL. Pulled out my old Paratrooper and giving it a go. Figuring I'll have lots of questions. 

So, shellholes. Does the TEM always apply regardless of the MF spent?  My understanding is that if you pay 1 MF, you could be subject to FFMO but would still get the +1 TEM. The benefit to paying 2 MF isn't for the TEM, it just negates suffering FFMO.  Sound right?

If not, and only those infantry that spend 2 MF benefit from the TEM, how does one mark such units so you'd know?

Again, my understanding is that the TEM applies in both cases, it's the FFMO that is the sole benefit to spending 2 MF versus 1. 

Thanks in advance.
author: Baetis
consensus_answer:
For the most part the nuance would never matter. Per B2.1 with Journal 11 errata installed, other terrain in the hex no longer exists when shellholes are placed. As far as I know geomorphic maps don't have terrain other than open ground with shellholes. When there are shellholes they tend to be in places where there is no lower level from which to move into them. Sword & Flame broke this by having shellholes in terrain other than open ground, and also by having hexes where you could easily move/advance up a level into foxholes.
Such is the nature of a living set of rules!

Thanks again

replies.body:
So, shellholes. Does the TEM always apply regardless of the MF spent?  My understanding is that if you pay 1 MF, you could be subject to FFMO but would still get the +1 TEM. The benefit to paying 2 MF isn't for the TEM, it just negates suffering FFMO.  Sound right?

No. During DFF moving Infantry must spend two MF to benefit from the shellhole TEM. If it benefited from the shellhole TEM it would not be subject to FFMO.

If not, and only those infantry that spend 2 MF benefit from the TEM, how does one mark such units so you'd know?

It's not necessary to mark the unit unless you have a very, very short memory. The unit moves with MF expenditure announced so both players know whether the shellhole TEM applies or not. The DEFENDER can now announce DFF. Once the MPh ends the unit "falls into" the shellhole and gets the TEM. This is not like foxholes where the unit has to explicitly enter (and exit) the entrenchment.

title: Concealed firer unit against dummy target
question:
Hello,
A concealed unit fires at a dummy target with no result. Does the firer lose their concealment ?
author: runrun
consensus_answer:
Hello,
A concealed unit fires at a dummy target with no result. Does the firer lose their concealment ?
A12.14 "If the only Good Order enemy ground unit in LOS is itself concealed when a concealed friendly unit makes a concealment-loss action (other than breaking or being Reduced/Wounded), that enemy unit must completely forfeit its "?" momentarily (without revealing its possessions, to prove that it is not a Dummy) if it opts to force the friendly unit to lose his; the viewing unit's momentary forfeiture of concealment is instantly regained."

If the enemy refuses to reveal momentarily a (real, with Good Order implied by the fact that it has concealment) unit with LOS, concealment is retained by the firing unit.

title: Residual fire attack

author: JTV656

Yes.
A player is subject to Sniper attack during
any PFPh, MPh, DFPh or AFPh whenever he makes a TH, MC, TC, non-
OBA IFT, or Entrenching, Original DR [EXC: those made for Prisoners]
equal to the enemy SAN. Any such DR that can yield no game result other
than a SAN is not made [EXC: the DR required for an attack negated by
blocked LOS (6.11) is made].

As for the rules weigh-in, there is this:
A.1 DICE: The rules often require use of a colored die to differentiate
it from the other die in use. A set of four dice of different colors is included
in ASL Module 1: BEYOND VALOR. A white die and one of the colored
dice are rolled simultaneously and summed normally for most purposes, but
occasionally the colored dr will take on added significance either by itself or in
comparison to the white dr. Players may also find it beneficial to get in the habit of
rolling three dice, and using the third colored die as an automatic “subsequent dr”

title: Having trouble making sense of Journal 16 changes for Assault Move INTO foxholes
question:
This is the Journal 16 debriefing change:
B27.4: line 7, after "RtPh" add "or when using Assault Movement to enter/exit a foxhole". At the end of the last sentence add "and Defensive First Fire attacks [EXC: Residual-FP/OBA (if pinned/broken by such the unit remains in the foxhole hex above the foxhole); FFMO can apply] in the foxhole Location".

This is B27.4 with these changes applied:
B27.4 The cost of entering a hex containing a foxhole is equal to the COT of the hex entered. However, Infantry moving beneath an existing foxhole counter or from beneath a foxhole counter must pay one additional MF separately after payment of the COT to enter the hex and after suffering any Defensive First Fire that MF expenditure may have enticed. Note, however, that the cost to enter/exit a foxhole/pillbox during the RtPh or when using Assault Movement to enter/exit a foxhole may be combined with the entrance cost of the next hex—thereby escaping Interdiction in the foxhole/pillbox Location (27.41) and Defensive First Fire Attacks [EXC: Residual-FP/OBA (if pinned/broken by such the unit remains in the foxhole hex above the foxhole); FFMO can apply] in the foxhole Location.

Assuming that we are looking at the MPh and that Residual-FP/OBA is not of concern at the moment, this reduces to:
B27.4 The cost of entering a hex containing a foxhole is equal to the COT of the hex entered. However, Infantry moving beneath an existing foxhole counter or from beneath a foxhole counter must pay one additional MF separately after payment of the COT to enter the hex and after suffering any Defensive First Fire that MF expenditure may have enticed. Note, however, that the cost to enter/exit a foxhole/pillbox ...when using Assault Movement to enter/exit a foxhole may be combined with the entrance cost of the next hex—thereby escaping ... Defensive First Fire Attacks ... in the foxhole Location.

I have bolded a bit to which I want to draw attention for this discussion.

This is a situation Bill Kohler suggests on gamesquad.com:

He says the 4-6-7 makes a combined Assault Move from O3 to N3 for two MF. He says that the moving unit can be attacked twice, presumably using DFF, for the two MF spent. The attack would not be subject to FFMO. In the next post Perry agrees with this statement.

This is kind of what I would expect, but the way the change to B27.4 is written, it asserts the unit should escape "Defensive First Fire Attacks ... in the foxhole Location." So by my reading of B27.4 the 4-6-7 could not be attacked using Defensive First Fire for this move. The MF would be spent in N3, N3 is a foxhole Location, and by the changes added in J16 a unit using Assault Move cannot be attacked in the foxhole Location, here N3, by "Defensive First Fire Attacks." Any attack would have to wait for the DFPh.

Given that Perry agrees with Bill's assertion in the next post, my interpretation probably can't be correct. I have several possible resolutions to this:
1) I have misquoted or misapplied the J16 debriefing change. I have double- and triple-checked everything, and I don't see it, but maybe I've done something hilariously wrong.
2) I have applied the change correctly but have misparsed the new rule.
3) The snippet, "thereby escaping ... Defensive First Fire Attacks ... in the foxhole Location," is badly worded and should say something like, "thereby escaping ... Defensive First Fire Attacks ... in the foxhole Location outside the foxhole." I suspect this is the needed correction.
4) The MF are not spent in the foxhole Location but for this situation in the entry Location. This goes against every movement rule to date, and I expect it is not the case here.
5) My reading of the B27.4 debriefing change is correct. When the unit moves from O3 into the foxhole in N3 it is not subject to DFF. Both Bill and Perry are wrong on gamesquad. This seems unlikely.

Can anyone spot a problem with my reading of this change to B27.4?

consensus_answer:
Not really seeing what issue there is with these two - can you elaborate perhaps?Prior to J16:
--If an A11.4 Ambush occurred in CC, then the A11.4 Ambush DRM would apply but the A11.8 Street Fighting Ambush DRM could not apply.
--If no A11.4 Ambush occurred in CC and the requirements for Street Fighting were met, then the A11.8 Street Fighting Ambush DRM would apply.
The word "Ambush" was overloaded: it could mean normal Ambush, or it could mean Street Fighting Ambush, but the two were mutually exclusive so it sort of worked.

Now we have a rule change and the two Ambushes can potentially occur together. This creates an ambiguity that previously was avoided (because previously the two were mutually exclusive).

D7.21 CC REACTION FIRE: Each Infantry/Cavalry DEFENDER unit that is unbroken, unpinned and neither Unarmed (A20.5) nor in Melee may attempt CC Reaction Fire, using the CC-vs-vehicle rules (A11.5, etc.; see also 7.211-.213) [EXC: Ambush is NA unless using Street Fighting; 7.211].
The EXC, as written, can be read as saying that (a) if "Street Fighting" conditions are met, then ordinary Ambush is also possible;
or it can be read as saying that (b) ordinary Ambush DRM is always impossible but the Street Fighting Ambush DRM may be possible.

ASOP 8.12B: Resolve Ambush if advance into CC (not Melee) was into woods/building/jungle/bamboo/kunai (A11.4; G.6) and/or by/vs “?” (automatic ATTACKER Ambush for Street Fighting; A11.8) {night Ambush dr; E1.77}.
Here, "automatic ATTACKER Ambush for Street Fighting" likewise now has two potential meanings: (a) that whenever Street Fighting conditions are met, the ATTACKER also automatically qualifies for ordinary Ambush DRM, or (b) that ordinary Ambush may or may not occur, but the Street Fighting Ambush DRM can separately apply.

I recommend that the wording be improved to avoid this kind of confusion.
--The EXC could read: A11.4 Ambush is NA but Street Fighting is permissible; 7.211.
--The ASOP parenthetical could simply read: Street Fighting; A11.8.

I know what these two phrases mean and how to interpret them, but that's only because I know the history of how Street Fighting previously worked. I also know that these two phrases were originally worded to describe the old mechanic, but I think they were allowed to remain as they are because, if you squint, they still sort of work.

A new player will not have that history, and IMO may be quite confused. I sure would be.

title: Where did this counter come from?
question: I found this single counter by itself on the driveway leading up to the shop the other day. Its not one of mine. It looks to be older generation SL,  which I never owned, and found in a spot where I would have never  taken my kit.  Can anyone recognize what module its from? Truly a mystery.
author: Fly by Night
consensus_answer:
So yellow (sunlight) and green make blue😆
It's just crazy for being where I found it. I had an unpunched Partisan years ago. 
CMYK is a subtractive color system, that is colors are taken away from white. To generate green (for Axis Minor) you would use cyan and yellow. If the yellow ink faded and no longer subtracted, that would leave only the cyan ink, which is a kind of blue. Mixed with more white from the faded yellow areas that might produce a light blue.

It would take a long time for such fading to take place, I would think. I don't think sitting out in the parking lot for a day or two would be long enough, and you'd expect a cardboard counter to have water damage if it spent a long time outdoors. Perhaps it was sitting in a car under the windshield for a long time and finally got dislodged.
And thats the crazy part.  I had Partisans module quite a few years ago.  Never punched it since I then got the newer updated module when I was first getting into ASL from SK.  There is no reason for that one counter to be in the center of the driveway leading up to our shop.  It had to have been recent because there is no water damage as you say.   Maybe a bird picked up elsewheres and dropped it as it flew overhead.  No idea.

replies.body:
Can a MMC in P5 bypass  O5/O6 for 1 MF and then bypass N5/O6 for 1 MF or does the hedge block that move?
An infantry bypass move of 2 hexsides in the same hex (O6 in your example) only costs 1 MF (not 2 MF).  An infantry bypass move in a hex costs 2 MF only if 3 hexsides are bypassed in the hex.  

And NO, the hedge does not block that move for infantry (it could block that move for a vehicle using VBM if the gap between the hedge and the obstacle is less than a counter width).

[Side note:  For VBM, when I play SASL and Deluxe SASL I actually 1) consult a data source on the width of the vehicle in question 2) convert that dimension to the scale of the hex {to come up with a specific dimension in millimeters that slightly exceeds the to scale dimension of the vehicle ... by 0.5 meters or so} 3) and measure the actual gap using a scale graduated in millimeters to determine if VBM is possible.  But that is just me being OCD about my SASL play.]

Can a MMC in P5 bypass  O5/O6 for 1 MF and then bypass N5/O6 for 1 MF or does the hedge block that move?
You would need to designate hex O5 as the hex entered for the O5/O6 bypass move (1 MF); from there (in O5 and at the O5/N5/O6 focal point), you could designate an N5 entry as a Bypass along N5/O6 (1 MF) for the 2nd MF expended, placing you then in N5 and at the N5/N6/O6 focal point.

See also the A4.31 EX on p A7, col 2 bottom, of the ASLRB

Units in bypass are always in the hex of the obstacle bypassed.
A bypassing unit moving from/to another hex always crosses the hexside separating them.
So hexside obstacles (hedge, wall, bocage) only affect bypass movement to/from the bypassed obstacle hex if they separate the obstacle hex from the hex entered or left.

And here is the usual off topic pedantic remark: Hedges/walls/bocage hexsides otherwise affect bypass if they touch (for infantry) or leave a too narrow space (for vehicles) between them and the obstacle.
I would ask what is you bypassed hexed route, not hexsides?  Looks like O5, N5, M6, M7, N7?

1MF: O6/O5
1MF:N5/O6 and N5/N6
The bypassed hex must be specified.
Your example works if bypassing the O5 woods.

I would ask what is you bypassed hexed route, not hexsides?  Looks like O5, N5, M6, M7, N7?

title: Moving into a road hex with one wreck?
question:
If a CE fully track AFV moves into a road hex with one wreck, does it cost 4½ MP (2 MP for the AFV and 2 MP for the wreck + ½ MP for road moving )?

Can the CE fully track AFV enter the road as open ground, paying only (1 MP for AFV and 1 MP for wreck and 1 MP for open ground= 3MP)?
author: Nslcole
consensus_answer:
The question is not about moving "across a road" hexside, but about using the road rate or not.
A vehicle may enter a hex across a road hexside, but not using the road rate: the cost would be COT+1 (Note that "All MP penalties for entering a hex containing a wreck/vehicle, and/or for changing a VCA across a non-road hexside, are doubled while in a woods hex" B13.41).
Works well for tracked vehicles.

If a CE fully track AFV moves into a road hex with one wreck, does it cost 4½ MP (2 MP for the AFV and 2 MP for the wreck + ½ MP for road moving )?

Can the CE fully track AFV enter the road as open ground, paying only (1 MP for AFV and 1 MP for wreck and 1 MP for open ground= 3MP)?

A CE fully tracked AFV moving along a road into an adjoining road hex that contains a wreck/other vehicle spends 2 1/2 MP (1/2 MP to enter the hex, +2 MP for the wreck/vehicle).

A CE fully tracked AFV entering open ground NOT ACROSS a road hexside with a wreck/vehicle in that hex would pay 2 MP (1 MP to enter the hex, +1 MP for the wreck/vehicle).

However, it seems that if you did so you should not be able to use roadrate when exiting that hex through a road hexside (but I'll let someone like JRV or Klas clarify that point).

title: Concealment
question: A  concealed squad moves into an open ground hex in the LOS of an enemy squad, but there's a hinderence hex between them. Does the moving squad lose concealment?
author: JTV656
consensus_answer:
A  concealed squad moves into an open ground hex in the LOS of an enemy squad, but there's a hinderence hex between them. Does the moving squad lose concealment?
The hindrance means the concealed squad is no subject to FFMO, and is therefore not moving in the open. Therefore, the concealed squad maintains concealment if it is an Assault Move, and loses concealment otherwise.

title: Rout question- broken versus berserk
question:
Situation has arisen in a current game of Jungle Fighters (J12)

Japanese berserk squad has entered the hex with a broken British unit in the movement phase.

Brits are marked DM and also a CC counter is placed in the hex.

Do the Brits get to attempt to rout out in the Rout Phase as they are not held in melee? If so the nearest hex they could rout to is woods in X10, but they would have to first move adjacent to the berserk squad. Would they be eliminated for failure to rout, or would they take an interdiction check and be forced to stop as a broken HS in W10 if they fail?

Given that berserk units don't take prisoners as per A 15.432 I'm not clear on how this should play out.
author: MagisterLudo
consensus_answer:
Do the Brits get to attempt to rout out in the Rout Phase as they are not held in melee? 

Correct.

If so the nearest hex they could rout to is woods in X10, but they would have to first move adjacent to the berserk squad. Would they be eliminated for failure to rout, or would they take an interdiction check and be forced to stop as a broken HS in W10 if they fail?

Because the Berserk unit is not Good Order, Surrender is not an option [A20.21]. The broken unit can rout from in-hex to ADJACENT, A10.51 "A routing unit may never move ADJACENT to a Known enemy unit, unless in doing so it is leaving that enemy unit's Location." Once in the ADJACENT hex they *could* be interdicted (Japanese player's option). If the Interdiction results in a pin, the unit would be Eliminated for Failure to Rout.

Yes they can move adjacent to an enemy unit as long as they are leaving that unit's hex.

Yes they will be interdicted.

title: Infantry OVR TC DRM for foxholes
question: An Infantry OVR requires a TC, to which a DRM for TEM applies [A4.15]. B27.3, "Any unit beneath a foxhole counter is entitled to a +4 TEM against any OVR [EXC: an OVR using only FT armament] or OBA attack, or a +2 TEM to any other type of attack." What is the DRM for the TC vs. a SMC in an foxhole, +2 or +4?
author: jrvjrv
consensus_answer:
I'm failing to communicate, apparently.

The Infantry OVR TC TEM modifier has nothing to do w/CC, per se -- like most any ASL TC, it is a test vs unit morale to answer an abstract Q, in this case, Willingness or not to move into [a place] occupied by a known enemy SMC.

Terrain affects that willingness, e.g., going into a wood building, say, would likely be more intimidating than vs a guy in a Foxhole in Open Ground.

Apply an Infantry OVR TC Foxhole TEM modifier?  Why?

I've given the plausible why not.
...perhaps you can cite/quote a rule.

A unit in an entrenchment gets either a +2 TEM or +4 TEM (unless attacked by a FT), so as far as I can see those are the only possible answers, i.e. the Infantry OVR NTC DRM against a unit in a foxhole is either two or four, unless you claim that *all* TEM is zero for CC and therefore the NTC DRM is zero for all terrain, foxholes or not.
I can see your logic.

You omit, however, the EXC re CC, in B27.3.

 Any unit beneath a foxhole counter is entitled to a +4 TEM against any
OVR [EXC: an OVR using only FT armament] or OBA attack, or a +2 TEM
to any other type of attack including on-board mortar fire [EXC: CC, FT]. A
foxhole TEM is not cumulative with that of other positive TEM in the same
hex but is applicable in combination with the negative TEM of an Air Burst
(13.3).

Arguably, an Infantry OVR is an "other type of attack."  It happens that one of is resolution mechanics is potential CC.

As you argue, CC is "always" resolved w/out TEM ... so, why the EXC re Foxhole TEM in B27.3, if not to address the corner case Infantry OVR TC DRM?

[Given the history of the Infantry OVR rule (as related in Footnote A3) I find it easy to believe a reference, from the B27.2 CC EXC, to A4.15 was maybe overlooked?]

 4.15 INFANTRY OVR: The inclusion of an Infantry OVR rule was a source of
heated debate among our playtesters—many of whom opposed it as an unnecessary
complication. Others pointed out the End Game problem of using SMC as unrealistic
sacrifices to “block” movement into hexes required for Victory Conditions. The result-
ing rule is an attempt to deal both with the artificial time constraints of the Game Turn
and to give lone SMC the option of giving way before overwhelming force rather than
risk sure elimination or capture.
It seems to me there was no intent to grant an Infantry OVR TC Foxhole TEM DRM advantage to an SMC facing a potential Infantry OVR.

As a corner case, this matter is seldom visited.  TBH, IDK the intent.  But I best-guess as per the evidence and my argument as given above.  YMMV.

I've nothing more.  Peace.

title: Question on concealment status if entering from offboard.
question:
Just setting up to play scenario J12 Jungle fighters, with both sides entering from off map on turn 1.

Can the first side to enter remain under concealment when entering as there are no enemy on map?

Will they remain concealed even if in the open?
author: MagisterLudo
consensus_answer:
If no enemy is in LOS, a unit only loses concealment (regardless of concealment terrain or not)...
"If it: becomes broken/Reduced/Wounded/fails a MC, is in a Location successfully Searched by the enemy, or is a Dummy in a building successfully Mopped Up by the enemy."

replies.body:
If no enemy is in LOS, a unit only loses concealment (regardless of concealment terrain or not)...
"If it: becomes broken/Reduced/Wounded/fails a MC, is in a Location successfully Searched by the enemy, or is a Dummy in a building successfully Mopped Up by the enemy."
The causes for concealment loss are given in the rules. If none of the conditions are met, the units remain concealed (unless they voluntarily give up concealment).
Yes they enter concealed, yes they will remain concealed even in OG. Someone needs to strip your concealment by seeing you or shooting you.

In short: units offboard are concealed. 
When moving on board, concealment loss (or preservation) applies normally.

title: Shellholes & MF costs
question:
I asked about shellhole MF costs related to , and the answer I got back changed my understanding of shellholes for all ASL. I had thought that the one MF or two MF cost to enter a shellhole hex was the COT, so entering a shellhole (to preserve concealment in the APh, for example) at a higher level would cost four MF to use the shellholes. But apparently the cost is treated like a wall, i.e. COT + 1 MF if using the shellholes.

In Sword and Fire shellholes are used in combination with various other types of terrain . Shellholes have a conditional MF cost [B2.4] of one MF if shellholes are not used or two MF if shellholes are used. When used in combination with woods, I believe it's clear the MF cost to enter would be cumulative if shellholes are used, i.e. the cost to enter a woods-shellhole hex would be four MF if shellholes are used. Would the cost for entering a woods-shellhole hex be three MF if shellholes are not used, i.e. the one MF cost for shellholes hex without entering shellholes? Or is the cost for entering a woods-shellhole hex be two MF if shellholes are not used, i.e. when entering a shellhole hex it is treated as Open Ground (i.e. not cumulative) when shellholes are not used?

Cost is 2 MF w/o using shellholes; 3 MF if using them.
....Perry 
MMP

Would the cost for shellholes be doubled for moving to a higher elevation when using shellholes, e.g. is the cost to move from 3D14 (a ground level hex) to 3C13 (a bridge ramp adjacent to a bridge and treated as a level one elevated road) three MF (one MF for open ground doubled for higher elevation plus one MF for using shellholes) or four MF (two MF for open ground using shellholes doubled)?

3 MF.
See the B2.4 EX.
....Perry

I filed away the use of uphill shellholes next to where I filed away the use of uphill smoke hexes.

title: 2.9 Set up limitation question
question:
Hello, I am just setting out on my ASL journey and going very slowly through the rule book.
So far, so good but the last sentence of 2.9 has puzzled me and so any clarity would be appreciated.
Does it mean that 90% of your units must be set up with a Leader ie an SMC ? 
Also the words “ if the nationality is capable of Deployment” - why are they in play if not?
I have been messing around with ASLSK and thought why not go for the real thing and work retrospectively? Perhaps it is just me, but this way has given me a better understanding of ASLSK now I can see the whole picture- and this is not a criticism of these rule books just the way I function
Thanks
Mike
author: major disaster
consensus_answer:
... the last sentence of 2.9 has puzzled me ...
Does it mean that 90% of your units must be set up with a Leader ie an SMC ? 
Also the words “ if the nationality is capable of Deployment” - why are they in play if not?

ASL rule 2.9"] Up to 10% (FRU) of the squads that set up on-board, and up to 10% (FRU) of the squads that enter in a given turn, may be freely Deployed (without leader/TC) prior to setup, if the nationality is capable of Deployment.

In ASL, Deployment means exchanging a full squad for two half squads of the same type.

Some nationalities cannot Deploy.  See rules sections A25 and G18.

Most can.

If you are playing one of the nationalities which can Deploy, and you start with 1 to 10 squads, one of them can be exchanged for two half squads when you are setting up.   You don't have to do this, but you can.

If you have 11 to 20 squads, you can exchange one or two squads for two or four half squads if you decide to Deploy.

And so on.

You can also do this with each turn's reinforcements if you like.

So rule A2.9 allows automatic Deployment upon setting up at start forces and reinforcements.

To Deploy during play, a squad needs to be stacked with a Leader and pass a Task Check during the Rally Phase of its player turn (A1.31).

The automatic Deployment on setup does not require the presence of a Leader or a Task Check.

title: Sustained Fire in Prep Fire Phase
question: This seems like a very basic question but I can't seem to find where it might be clarified in the rules. Can an MG marked with a Prep Fire marker (and so has failed to retain ROF) make one more attack using Sustained Fire penalties, or is Sustained Fire only available during Defensive Fire?
author: bnscott
consensus_answer:
This seems like a very basic question but I can't seem to find where it might be clarified in the rules. Can an MG marked with a Prep Fire marker (and so has failed to retain ROF) make one more attack using Sustained Fire penalties, or is Sustained Fire only available during Defensive Fire?
Sustained Fire is not an attack option. It is a penalty for certain attack options such as SFF, FPF or fire during the DFPh when marked with a First Fire counter [A9.3]. There is no attack option in the PFPh that has Sustained Fire as a penalty.

title: SMOKE
question: Does SMOKE cause blind hexes behind it from a squad in a higher elevation? I'm kinda confused by the example in the rules. I thought SMOKE caused a hinderence and not an obstacle?
author: JTV656
consensus_answer: See the E3.31 EX.

replies.body: In general, Smoke never causes blind hexes unless at +6 or greater combined Hindrance.  Smoke is always a Hindrance unless there is some SSR or something, as far as I know... (again, until >= +6 combined Hindrance).

Does SMOKE cause blind hexes behind it from a squad in a higher elevation? I'm kinda confused by the example in the rules. I thought SMOKE caused a hinderence and not an obstacle?
SMOKE is not like an (in-season) orchard, i.e. it is always a hindrance even when the LOS goes through it diagonally. The principle of "blind hexes" is used to determine whether the LOS goes through or *over* the SMOKE. A viewer at level three where the LOS goes across a hex with level two SMOKE (from level zero) at range three hexes will have two hexes behind that SMOKE at level zero that are hindered. Hexes along that LOS at ranges > two from the SMOKE will not be hindered. Of course if the total hindrance is six or more, LOS is blocked as normal.

title: Desperation Morale
question:
If 2 FP attacks a broken unit in a stone building and rolls a 2 resulting in a NMC which the unit then passes, is the broken unit now DM?

I ask this because if the attacker cowers, then there is not an opportunity for a NMC result on the 1 FP column.

10.62 DESPERATION MORALE (DM): DM is a condition
which afflicts any unit during the Player Turn it breaks (even if it
breaks voluntarily) or any already broken unit which is subsequently attacked by CC/WP, or enough FP (taking the possibility of Cowering into account) to possibly inflict at least a NMC result on the target
author: Bombadil929
consensus_answer:
Put another way, there are thirty-six possible DRs on the IFT. Write them all down. For all those DR combinations, write next to it the result you would have gotten on the IFT for this particular attack. For a given combination if cowering would have applied (because the attacking firegroup was susceptible) then write down the adjusted result. If any of the results you wrote was a NMC or better, the target is marked with DM. If all the results you wrote are PTC or NE, the broken target is not marked with DM.

If the firing comes from a fire group susceptible to cowering, does it have to be accounted for the different combinations or Random Selection, including rolling doubles in the RS? The rules of ASL should take this possibility into account, lest they are viewed as somewhat shaggy.
The random selection for marking the unit for cowering does not affect the FP for the attack, if that is what you are thinking. When the firegroup cowers the attack FP drops two columns if Inexperienced Personnel are participating, even if those units are not selected by any Random Selection. Otherwise the firegroup attack FP drops one column, again independent of who is selected by any Random Selection. There is no need to consider the Random Selection when looking at the possible results.

title: Bocage LOS a different level.
question:
Hi all.

Working through the Chef-du-Pont example, and reviewing point B9.52, I'd say I (perhaps) have a better understanding of the LOS at different levels through a Bocage hexside.

But I still have two questions: From the above, can we deduce that "normally" the bocage hexside and its "conversion" into a "Single-Story house" produces one more blind hex in addition to those an observer at a one higher level would normally have? For example, three blind hexes seven hexagons away? Or—as I think—does it only produce that one hex?

BTW, as I said I understand the issue of "converting to a Single-Story house", but I don't understand what it's meant to represent in the real world. What could it mean if, being at different heights, you could see the hex immediately after the bocage but not the next one?

Thanks in advance.
author: Pavlo
consensus_answer:
But I still have two questions: From the above, can we deduce that "normally" the bocage hexside and its "conversion" into a "Single-Story house" produces one more blind hex in addition to those an observer at a one higher level would normally have? For example, three blind hexes seven hexagons away? Or—as I think—does it only produce that one hex?

There should be no more blind hexes for bocage than for other obstacles. But perhaps what is meant by "range" is confusing? In any event here is a bocage and a building at seven-hex range from a second-level hill. 

LOS is clear from 00M5 to 00T3 & 00T5 because those are the obstacle hexes. 00U3 is the first blind hex for the building, and 00V3 is the second blind hex. Likewise 00U6 is the first blind hex from the bocage, and 00V5 is a second blind hex. All of hexrow W would be visible to a unit on the second-level hill of 00M5.

BTW, as I said I understand the issue of "converting to a Single-Story house", but I don't understand what it's meant to represent in the real world. What could it mean if, being at different heights, you could see the hex immediately after the bocage but not the next one?

Any units in 00T5 would be at the roots of the line of trees on top of the bocage. As the unit on the hill raised its eyes to look farther it would be looking through the branches and leaves of those trees to see beyond, so LOS would be blocked until it raised its eyes beyond the top of those trees. That gives a number of blind hexes, i.e. hexes where the LOS has to pass through the branches and leaves of trees planted on the bocage mound.

title: Basic question on Rout path
question:
I'm in the process of relearning ASL after many years away from it and I've reached the stage of starting to question basic things that I thought I knew thoroughly 😀.

My question is, when can a routing unit follow a path that is not the shortest in MF (with the intent of avoiding Interdiction) to reach its destination hex? I'm a little confused by the wording in 10.51 that says "[a unit] need not take the shortest route, but as long as it follows the shortest path in MF otherwise (my italics) it may enter a shellhole / entrenchment / pillbox to avoid Interdiction...". But can the unit enter other terrain to get to its destination hex if this causes it to not take the shortest route?

For example, I have a unit that must Rout and the only valid destination is a Woods hex two hexes away; the shortest path to the destination is 3MF, into an Open hex and then into the Woods, but it would be subject to Interdiction in the Open hex in this case. But it can also get to the Woods hex through a Grain hex, but that makes the total path cost 3.5MF. Can it go through the grain to void Interdiction?
author: bnscott
consensus_answer:
My question is, when can a routing unit follow a path that is not the shortest in MF (with the intent of avoiding Interdiction) to reach its destination hex? I'm a little confused by the wording in 10.51 that says "[a unit] need not take the shortest route, but as long as it follows the shortest path in MF otherwise (my italics) it may enter a shellhole / entrenchment / pillbox to avoid Interdiction...". But can the unit enter other terrain to get to its destination hex if this causes it to not take the shortest route?

For example, I have a unit that must Rout and the only valid destination is a Woods hex two hexes away; the shortest path to the destination is 3MF, into an Open hex and then into the Woods, but it would be subject to Interdiction in the Open hex in this case. But it can also get to the Woods hex through a Grain hex, but that makes the total path cost 3.5MF. Can it go through the grain to void Interdiction?
This will depend in a couple of ways. First the alternate rout path must be legal, e.g. it can't involve moving closer to known, armed enemy unit or ADJACENT to one. In your example if the path through open ground did not involve moving closer but the path through grain did, the path through grain could not be used. Second if not using shellholes/entrenchments and/or if using shellholes/entrenchments but not following the otherwise shortest path, the broken unit must reach its rout target. Continuing with your example if the broken unit has enough MF to reach the rout target through open ground but not through the grain then the path through grain could not be used. Because you have put the rout target so close that is not the case for your example unless the routing unit were a broken, wounded leader. In your example a broken wounded leader would be forced to use the open ground because that is the only way it could reach the woods. If both the open ground hex and the grain hex contained foxholes, the broken, wounded leader could rout into the foxhole in open ground even though that would prevent it from reaching the woods but it could not rout into the foxhole in the grain. A broken MMC could rout through the foxhole in either hex unless it was a walking-wounded MMC (a feature of some campaign games).

title: Pillbox squad fire against enemy squad pasing the hexside of you own hex in CA of pillbox
question:
A8.15 reads: "[EXC: A Snap Shot cannot be taken at a unit while entering
the firer’s hex]." and "Snap Shots are resolved as Area
Fire." 

B30.2 reads: "Fire
from inside a pillbox into its own hex is limited to CC, or SMOKE grenade
placement, or a Thrown DC (30.31), or to vertices of its CA, or to PBF vs units
currently crossing the CA hexsides of its own hex."

B30.2 don´t mention Snap Shot, so are the "PBF vs units
currently crossing the CA hexsides of its own hex" from B30.2 resolved as Area fire or not.

EX: A 447 fire out of a Pillbox vs and enemy squad entering the pillbox hex by passing a hexside in the Pillboxs CA. Does it fire with 8 FP or 4 FP?

title: Concealment - Sniper Attack
question: A stack contains only concealed units and dummy counters.  Sniper attack is a 1-2 and that hex is selected.  Regardless of which unit is selected by Random Selection, do all units lose concealment and elimination of dummies? OR does only the selected unit lose concealment?
author: Bombadil929
consensus_answer:
A stack contains only concealed units and dummy counters.  Sniper attack is a 1-2 and that hex is selected.  Regardless of which unit is selected by Random Selection, do all units lose concealment and elimination of dummies? OR does only the selected unit lose concealment? 

Only the unit attacked, but it must be in LOS of a Good Order enemy unit within 16 hexes.  

It's not clear from the RB itself but if you look at the Concealment Loss/Gain table, under Note A, you'll find  '...or is attacked by a Sniper dr (A14.3)....'

The table applies to individual units; the stack itself isn't attacked by the A14.3 dr (barring an unfortunate random selection roll), only a unit within it.

JR,
I could be misreading this, but per A14.23 if there are dummy counters and real, it would seem the dummies are eliminated and the real units are then subject to random selection, or am I missing something.  Here is the rule in question:

14.23 CONCEALED TARGETS: If the eligible possible targets include
both concealed and unconcealed units, treat the concealed stack as one pos-
sible target (regardless of how many units it actually contains) for Random
Selection purposes. Then, if a concealed stack is chosen as the sniper’s tar-
get (either per the above Random Selection or if all units are concealed), the
sniper player’s opponent must declare the number (only) of eligible possible
targets that stack contains. If it contains none (i.e., is a Dummy stack), it is
automatically eliminated. If it contains one, that unit is selected. If it contains
two or more, the player rolls for Random Selection accordingly.

Yeah, I do not think the Dummies are removed, unless it is only Dummies.
1. Concealed stack is chosen as Sniper target.
2. Number of targets announced. 
3. If zero targets, remove the Dummy stack. Otherwise, do nothing with the Dummies.
4. If at least one target, roll Random Selection on the targets.

title: DRMs for infantry vs. non-armored targets
question:
One of the many, many things in ASL I can’t get my hands around is infantry with small arms fire (non-ordnance) vs. an unarmored vehicle using the star row on the IFT. What DRMs, if any, come into play (e.g., terrain, hindrances, vehicle size, moving or not moving)?       

Thanks
author: jrv8374
consensus_answer:
One of the many, many things in ASL I can’t get my hands around is infantry with small arms fire (non-ordnance) vs. an unarmored vehicle using the star row on the IFT. What DRMs, if any, come into play (e.g., terrain, hindrances, vehicle size, moving or not moving)?       

Any DRM that appear on the IFT and apply to vehicles. This is perhaps not spelled out as directly as it could be, but A7.308 says that such attacks "are resolved on the ★ Vehicle line of the IFT using the same IFT DR (after any applicable modification) for any Personnel target in the same Location."

Some ways in which the IFT DRM differ from TH DR and also from IFT DRM vs. Infantry: FFMO & FFNAM to not apply (because those apply to Infantry only), an overstacking DRM does not apply [A5.132] and neither target size or moving are DRM for the IFT (nor affect FP). TEM generally applies, although for instance shellholes apply to Infantry only. Hindrances apply (always, I believe). 

Great answer, but also lends me an opportunity to wax philosophical regarding "rules."

In a few years, we will have progressed to the point where we realize that asking humans to read rules to play a game, especially very long and complex rulebooks, will be as outdated as the horse and carriage. Or as outdated as asking them to write a C++ or Java program to achive some goal. Yes, I said it. 

What's needed for ASL really is countless examples of play, saying what can be done, and which tables to use. And flowcharts, much like the great routing flowchart from Texas ASL.

In this case, you realize "I want to shoot at that jeep / truck with a unit riding in it, what are my options, and what do I do? And how are the effects adjudicated and applied?" You don't want to read rules. You want a clear example showing a number of options, and telling you how to resolve based on the options chosen.

Rules are for computers (just like programs are), not people.

You guys will see that in just a few years (especially with the advances in AI) I will be proven right.

Getting a ruleset as massive as ASL's "correct and complete and usable" is a nearly impossible and certainly gargantuan task. Especially the "usable" part.

I see the error in your statement. It becomes quite obvious when you realize that your question is "Should I shoot at etc etc".

title: Human Wave - Bypass Movement
question: Can a HW unit use bypass?
author: Bombadil929
consensus_answer:
Here is what D 14.31 says.  I added the bold.   Human wave says to use impulse movement and references D14.3

14.31 IMPULSE: When using Impulse Movement, the MPh of all participating
units is broken into a number of Impulses. During each Impulse each
participating unit may perform a maximum of one MF/MP expenditure (EX:
moving to a new Location; changing VCA one hexside; using VBM along
one hexside; exiting a Foxhole; using Infantry bypass along 1-4 hexsides).

Looks like it is specifically listed as allowed.

I like it because one certainly views a human wave as "washing over and around" stuff just like water would do. No time to go in through the front door and out through the back door of the building when you are rushing the enemy while yelling. In fact, you're liable to be executed as a coward if you take a tour of that house between you and the enemy.

title: Firing to CE AFVs, Wrecks and Trench in a wire hex.
question:
HI, all. Three questions I'd like confirmation on.

-Any CE or OT armored vehicle fired upon from a higher level reduces its armor def value by one for each level of height (to a minimum of zero). Of course, other possible modifiers such as LOS hindrances (orchards, for example) must be taken into account. Correct?

-When an AFV becomes a Wreck it immediately becomes a +1 hindrance (at same level LOS) and gives +1 Tem to any unit in its hex (including a burning wreck though in that case I'd add the smoke modification, a +2). Correct?

You can always place one trench in a barbed wire or roadblock hex, which allows infantry units to move freely through those obstacles, whether friendly or enemy troops (if they manage to enter the trench). Correct?

I'm reasonably sure about all of them, but I can't find the rules cross-references. 

Thanks for the help.
author: Pavlo
consensus_answer:
-Any CE or OT armored vehicle fired upon from a higher level reduces its armor def value by one for each level of height (to a minimum of zero). Of course, other possible modifiers such as LOS hindrances (orchards, for example) must be taken into account. Correct?

A mix of correct and incorrect. A CE, CT AFV is not affected by any elevation advantage an attacker might have. An OT AFV has its CE DRM reduced if the elevation advantage of the firer is > the range [D5.311].

-When an AFV becomes a Wreck it immediately becomes a +1 hindrance (at same level LOS) and gives +1 Tem to any unit in its hex (including a burning wreck though in that case I'd add the smoke modification, a +2). Correct?

As already mentioned, if the vehicle was a moving target [C.8] it is not a TEM until at the end of the following APh [D9.3] Also a burning wreck does not give a +1 TEM [D9.3]. The TEM of a non-burning wreck would be cumulative with SMOKE in the hex, but a burning wreck provides no TEM, only Smoke.

You can always place one trench in a barbed wire or roadblock hex, which allows infantry units to move freely through those obstacles, whether friendly or enemy troops (if they manage to enter the trench). Correct?

For this one trench is typically not enough. A trench in a wire hex allows a unit to move under the wire to under the trench if it is moving from trench-to-trench [B27.54], e.g. from under an adjacent trench, from a bunker or from a lower-level Location to a friendly-controlled trench [B27.6]. If the unit is not moving trench-to-trench it enters above the wire. Unless there is a bunker or a lower-level Location to a friendly-controlled trench, you need two trenches to enable trench-to-trench movement.

One could have two trenches, one on each side of a roadblock, to allow infantry to move "under" that roadblock without crossing the roadblock by moving trench-to-trench [B27.54]. A single trench is not enough.

replies.body:
According to D6.61 the passengers in a half-track are vulnerable to fire from a height greater than the range.
Burning wrecks don't give the TEM to infantry, just the smoke in D10.3.
Wire doesn't affect movement between connected trenches, B27.54.

Thanks a lot!

So in the first case I was missing the range consideration! 
And in the second case everything else is correct, including the +2 burning wreck smoke value (sorry if this is obvious, but I've learned that in ASL the old medieval saying "the devil is in the details" is very true).

And regarding the Roadblock (or a trench with a minefield, BTW)?

And a tactical consideration:
If I somehow manage to position my non-gyro Sherman adjacent to a stationary enemy AFV, it might be worth shooting at it even if I'm still moving (despite its terrible modifiers plus doubling the lowest die), as I can benefit from the -2 for stopped adjacent vehicle. I know that in ASL there are no absolute answers but, overall, to what extent might this be useful or is it more of a desperate measure?

Thanks again.

-When an AFV becomes a Wreck it immediately becomes a +1 hindrance (at same level LOS) and gives +1 Tem to any unit in its hex (including a burning wreck though in that case I'd add the smoke modification, a +2). Correct?

That is incorrect.

If the destroyed vehicle had been moving/in-motion during the Mph of the current player turn (C.8), then the wreck TEM/LOS Hindrance does not go into effect until AFTER the following AFph (i.e., the beginning of the Rout Phase).  See D9.3 and D9.4.  

There are exceptions to this for Armored Assault and PRC that are abandoning/unloading/bailing out (see applicable rules referenced in D9.3) .  Also, there is a subtle nuance as written such that if a motion vehicle is destroyed during Prep Fire it appears the wreck TEM/LOS Hindrance would go into effect immediately.

However, Smoke hindrance from a burning AFV goes into effect immediately.

That's true! Which makes it even worse. I imagine non stopped fire will be reserved for desperate situations, or perhaps a gun duel. 

Not sure it would be useful for a Gun Duel all that often, as the moving penalties would apply as firer-based DRM, making winning a Gun Duel very difficult. Perhaps vs. a Gun in woods/building that has to change CA.

Non-stopped fire is also practical if the vehicle has a gyro-stabilizer . You want to use any Motion attempt first [D2.401] because being marked with a defensive fire counter will prevent the Motion attempt. In general if an enemy vehicle might move in LOS, you want your vehicles stopped.

title: Gully and crest status
question: Making sure I have  crest side status TEM correct.The TEM for a  crest status unit in a gully hex is +2 for fire through the hex sides of the crest and zero for fire through the other hex sides?
author: JTV656
consensus_answer:
Why is the TEM for fire from the 6-4-8 in hex J4 zero? It seems that it should be no different than the TEM for fire from the 4-5-7 in F3.
Also, I am assuming the 2-4-8 in hex G2 is at a higher elevation, correct?
Unlike something like a foxhole, the protection a unit gets from crest status is directional. If the target is shot from the front (with some other conditions) it gets a +2 TEM. If attacked from the rear it gets no TEM [B20.92]. The crest counter (the brown counter under the 3-4-6) indicates which hexsides are protected and which are not. The 6-4-8 is attacking through an unprotected hexside. 

The 2-4-8 is one level higher than the crest level. Because it is at level one at range two from the depression, it has LOS INTO the depression [A6.3], which voids the protected hexside it is shooting through.

Correct.

author: Nslcole
consensus_answer:
M4A1 fires WP against X11 and gets a hit with a DR 4. WP is placed in the hex. 
1) Am I right when I think the 447 takes a MC, but not the 548, because WP is not inside the Pillbox?

Because the WP attack is through the pillbox NCA and the firer is not ADJACENT to the pillbox [B30.34], the 5-4-8 is immune to the WP NMC [B30.113]. If the attack had been through the pillbox CA it is possible that the 5-4-8 could take a WP NMC, but only on a critical hit [B30.34].

correct.

No because it is not in CA or ADJACENT [B30.34]. In the situation you give only the 4-4-7 could be hit by a CH.

If "the unit placing/firing the WP is ADJACENT-to/within-the-CA-of the pillbox" [B30.34] then the CH is possible against the contents of the pillbox and random selection would be used.

title: C5.2 Case B - ordnance firing in the AFPh
question:
5.2 CASE B; FIRE IN AFPh: All ordnance weapons firing during the AFPh which did not enter their current hex/hexside during that Player Turn, and are not using Opportunity Fire (A7.25), are subject to the Case B (+2) To Hit DRM—regardless of whether the Gun has pivoted or changed its CA while in that hex.

(emphasis added)

An ordnance weapon (which is not a LATW) moves into a new hex during the MPh, by being portaged (if it is SW ordnance) or pushed (if it is a Gun) by a MMC.

Case B does not seem to apply:  it applies to ordnance weapons which did not enter their current hex this turn.

Can the ordnance fire at all?  If so, does case B apply?  I feel like I am missing a rule which says "you can't do that".
author: Malcolm C
consensus_answer:
An ordnance weapon (which is not a LATW) moves into a new hex during the MPh, by being portaged (if it is SW ordnance) or pushed (if it is a Gun) by a MMC.

Case B does not seem to apply:  it applies to ordnance weapons which did not enter their current hex this turn.

As you have noted per A4.41 "heavy" SW can't fire after being moved. A Pushed Gun (or a towed Gun that has been unhooked) can't fire both for A4.41 and because the units Pushing Gun (or unhooking) the weapon are TI after the activity [C10.12; C10.3].

replies.body:
Define what you mean by "ordnance" (Ordnance is a way of firing - using the TH DR process - not a weapon type).
There are LATW that fire as Ordnance and which can fire in the AFPh after having moved.
A non vehicular Gun that moved may not fire during the AFPh.
A vehicular Gun may.
Ok - I found it:  A4.41 is the rule which I felt like I was missing, and which I have now found.  ☺️

An ordnance weapon (which is not a LATW) moves into a new hex during the MPh, by being portaged (if it is SW ordnance) or pushed (if it is a Gun) by a MMC.

Case B does not seem to apply:  it applies to ordnance weapons which did not enter their current hex this turn.

As you have noted per A4.41 "heavy" SW can't fire after being moved. A Pushed Gun (or a towed Gun that has been unhooked) can't fire both for A4.41 and because the units Pushing Gun (or unhooking) the weapon are TI after the activity [C10.12; C10.3].

I'll just add that the Case B penalty is really there because the AFPh fire represents quick shots when you have already been doing other things that turn (which is why you cannot intensive or sustain fire… time in the AFPh is short).

During the turn, a vehicle subject to Case B could have moved (in which case, it would be subject to Case B because of the clause in Case C which overrides the explicit statement in Case B about not moving).

It could also have prep fired, in which case it would have maintained ROF, allowing it to fire again.

It could have declined to do either, in which case the vehicle spent its turn searching for targets and not laying its gunsights (not as bad a penalty as B+C). It is usually better to prep fire, since even if you were waiting for a concealed defender to reveal itself with defensive fire, the penalty would have been the same either way.

A crewed field gun can opportunity fire, which avoids the Case B penalty entirely.
Just to be clear, keeping rate in the Prep Fire phase does not allow a unit to fire again in the Adv Fire phase.

title: Rule concerning Acquisition and Bounding First Fire/Bounding Fire
question:
I haven't played ASL in a few years and I can't remember the rule concerning target acquisition by an AFV using Bounding First Fire/Bounding Fire. You have found the rule for BFF. The Gun must be stabilized. For Bounding Fire (fire in the AFPh after having moved) acquisition is gained normally, i.e.  a stationary vehicle can gain acquisition, and a Motion vehicle can gain acquisition if it is stabilized.
consensus_answer:
There's also "C6.55 GYROSTABILIZER: Only a Stabilized Gun (D11.1) may claim/retain its Acquisition DRM for Motion/Bounding-First Fire TH attempts, and only if it retains its LOS to that target (as per 6.15) during its move. If having Area Acquisition on its target, it must transfer to a ½" Acquired counter before it can use that DRM for Motion/Bounding-First Fire (since use of the Area Target Type is NA for such fire; 3.33)."

So anything other than a Stabilized Gun may NOT claim/retain its Acquisition DRM for Motion/Bounding-First Fire TH attempts.

title: LOS at different levels
question:
Hello there!!!
Been playing RPT82: The Montiguidi Mambo, and we got confused a lot with the diferent LOS between units. So I took a picture of different examples that made us doubt about getting right the diferent LOS.
https://i.postimg.cc/J4QdCR6Q/LOS.jpg
Which units can the germans see; one at level 1 (F5) and the other in top of the hill (level 3 because the building first floor) and why?
Appreciate it!
author: MikeMacCrego
consensus_answer:
Similarly, from the first floor of G3 you would also see B0 (since the crest of C1 is only 4 hexes away).

Even if it were five hexes away (e.g. as you suggested above the building moved from G3-H3 to H3-I4) a unit at building level one (in H3, absolute level three) could see B0 over C1 because the number of blind hexes behind a crest line in reduced by one [B10.23] for being a crest line, and the viewer is two full levels above the obstacle [B6.42]. The full blind hex calculation is: C1 has one blind hex to level zero behind it (its top is one level higher than the target) plus one for range to obstacle from H3 [A6.41] minus one for being a crest line [B10.23] minus one for the viewer being two full levels above the obstacle height [B6.42], for a net zero blind hexes.

In contract if C1 were a woods at level zero and LOS were traced from level one G3 again, the calculation would be one blind hex not increased by range and decreased by extra full level to zero but always a minimum of one blind hex per B6.42.

I arrived late but that's what I wanted to say regarding the half level obstacles: "I understand why M6 is visible from H3: L5 has a height of 1.5 (because of the houses in the hex) while M6 is only level 1 but a half-level obstacle never creates blind hexes". Right? (I would like this to remain as a clear example for anyone who might see this thread later).
L5 is not a level one-and-a-half obstacle. It is only a level one obstacle [B23.21]. A building has to be multi-hex [B23.22], have a large white hex center [B31.3] or a steeple [B31.1] to be higher than level one. Though you are correct that if L5 were a level 1.5 obstacle it would still not block LOS from H3 to M6. As you say, relative to M6 a level one-and-a-half obstacle in L5 would only be a half level above M6, and that would not be a large enough difference to form a blind hex.

replies.body:
F5 only has a LOS to the 8-1 in D3. All other LOS are blocked by Level 1 (or higher terrain).

H3 has a LOS to D3. Possibly to L7 (depends on whether the LOS goes through any of the building depictions in K7), and M6.
LOS to B0 is blocked by building in G3. All other American units are in Blind hexes to H3.

H3 has LOS to D3 and M6. The building top in L5 being the same level or lower than H3 and M6 means it can't block LOS. The woods in K5 is lower than H3 so H3 can see past to lower levels. Relative to level one K5 is a level one obstacle so at this range it creates only one blind hex to a level one Location, which would mean that L5 level one would be blind (as well as L5 level zero). 

Other than non-cliff crest lines obstacles always have at least one blind hex behind them, so H3 could not see M2, L3, L7 (assuming the LOS hits the building in K7) or K5 no matter how high it was. In contrast a crest line can be reduced to zero blind hexes, so from H3 both E3 and E4 are reduced to zero blind hexes (-1 crest line, -1 two full levels advantage of higher unit), and F3 is reduced to one blind hex (-1 crest line).

There are some shortcuts that I think most experienced players take before they start thinking about the blind hex calculations. title: SMC Prisoners
question: Can SMC prisoners escape and re-arm? If yes do they become the same leader they used to be? If a prisoner Squad and leader kill their 1 squad guard in CC do they both get to re-arm from the 1 squad? If the leader escapes but is still unarmed how do we know where on the map he is? author: Neilyoung
consensus_answer:
Can SMC prisoners escape and re-arm? If yes do they become the same leader they used to be? If a prisoner Squad and leader kill their 1 squad guard in CC do they both get to re-arm from the 1 squad? If the leader escapes but is still unarmed how do we know where on the map he is? Do we still have to write it down?

SMC can escape. They are assumed to be rearmed once they successfully escape, A20.551, "Escaped SMC are always Armed." They return to their previous state, A20.5 "An unarmed SMC must be noted on a side record, but maintains its normal morale and leadership levels." There is no need for a leader to get weapons from an eliminated enemy unit; its counter is just put on board regardless of how it got away. For example if one is abandoned the counter is put on board.

title: Marked with a counter vs. being in a state
question:
This originally came to me via a direct message. Although the rules are fairly casual about it, being marked with a counter is not necessarily equivalent to being in a particular state. I was asked recently about a unit that fired its MG in the PFPh, kept ROF and didn't fire its inherent. If you follow the mechanics it is not marked with a Prep Fire counter. Can it move? Can it fire again in the AFPh? Per A4.1, "During his MPh, the ATTACKER may move all, some, or none of his Infantry units provided they did not fire during the PFPh." For game purposes the marking with the Prep Fire counter is a reminder, not a rule. Most players will mark such a unit with the appropriate counter anyway, just to avoid confusion. A7.1, "no unit can fire its inherent FP/SW/Gun in more than one fire phase (A.15) per Player Turn." A.15 allows a unit to fire in both the enemy MPh as DFF and in the friendly DFPh. So no fire in the AFPh, whether you choose to mark the unit or not.

A.12, "All counters printed on a white background can be used by any nationality and are often informational or memory devices only." The rules don't explain this in any more detail nor say which are purely memory devices only and which are not, but it is my belief that Prep Fire counters are among the memory devices. A unit that fires in the PFPh can't move not because it is marked with the counter, but because of A4.1. Many of the rules are written casually as if being marked with a particular counter is equivalent to its state, but it's not necessarily true. 

I don't know of any cases at the moment, but this sound like the kind of thing that gets messed up in the rules somewhere, i.e. there is a place where being marked with the counter *is* equivalent to being in the particular state. So consider this something to be aware of in reading the rules, not necessarily an absolute truth.

title: CC vs AFV and HS
question:
It's the American turn. A concealed US 747 squad advanced into an open ground hex with a stop German Pz 35R 731(f) and a 237 half squad and pass the PAATC

1) The 747 don´t lose concealment because it´s not an advanced into open ground because of the AFV, right? 

2) It´s scenario SM01, so the american have gammon bombs. 
The 747 wins ambush and get a gammon bomb. It´s CCV are 5 with -2(gammon bombs) - 1 ambush and +1 for escorting hs.
SO if the 747 DR is 4, the AFV is eliminated, but what with the 237?

3) if the 747 DR is 11 and nothing happens. How do the German AFV and HS attack back - one attack combined, to separated attacks or only the AFV?
author: Nslcole
consensus_answer:
As Kevin points out, the 747 would not retain concealment as an enemy AFV does not provide TEM.  Without concealment on the part of some unit present, unless another circumstance such as Streefighting applies, this isn't an ambush situation so no need to roll for it.  Therefore, no extra -1 to the US CC DR.  However, it is still sequential (A11.31) with the non-AFV side attacking first.  Note this initial attack doesn't have to be versus the AFV; in some situations you might want to go after the escorting infantry instead.

Kevin is also correct that the HS and the AFV can't combine for a single CC attack.  Normally a given unit may only be attacked once in the Close Combat Phase, but A11.12 has a specific exemption for situations involving an AFV, so presumably both units can take a crack at the 747 if it comes up empty on its own CC DR.

replies.body:
It's the American turn. A concealed US 747 squad advanced into an open ground hex with a stop German Pz 35R 731(f) and a 237 half squad and pass the PAATC

1) The 747 don´t lose concealment because it´s not an advanced into open ground because of the AFV, right? 

No.  Per D9.3, it has to be: "wreck/friendly-AFV/abandoned-enemy-AFV".  The German AFV is none of these, so does not count as a TEM.

2) It´s scenario SM01, so the american have gammon bombs. 
The 747 wins ambush and get a gammon bomb. It´s CCV are 5 with -2(gammon bombs) - 1 ambush and +1 for escorting hs.
SO if the 747 DR is 4, the AFV is eliminated, but what with the 237? 

CC is normally sequential in this case, so the US was only attacking the AFV.  Checking D.8B, I'd say its a specific collateral attack and would only effect vulnerable PRC... the HS is not one of these.

 3) if the 747 DR is 11 and nothing happens. How do the German AFV and HS attack back - one attack combined, to separated attacks or only the AFV?

I do not believe HS and AFVs can join in a CC attack, so the German player would get a CC attack with the HS using normal CC rules and, if the German AFV has CC-appropriate MGs or other aspects ... (per A11.62) a second CC attack, also versus the 747.
And perhaps the "ambush" did not occur because the US 747 lost concealment advancing into the hex?

1. An AFV grants cover only if friendly, so the 747 loses concealment.

2. As there is no ambush, the 747 CCV is 5 and the CC DRM is -1 (gammon bomb -2, escorting personal unit +1).
It attacks first (Sequential CC).
- Original DR = 6 (Final = 5, i.e. = CCV #) Pz35 is Immobilized ; 
- Orignal DR = 4 or 5 (Final = 3 or 4 i.e. < CCV #) Pz35 is eliminated ; 
- Original DR = 2 or 3 (Final = 1 or 2, i.e. = or less than half CCV # ), the Pz35 burns.
Whatever the result of the CC DR, the 237 is unaffected, as only the AFV is attacked.

3.  The AFV and the HS attack back separately.

The Pz 35 attacks with its 2 FP CMG vs the 747 CCV : 2 to 5 --> ratio 1 to 4 (CC# 3)
The 237 attacks with its IFP, same ratio.
For both, a 2 DR eliminates the 747 and a 3 DR Casualty Reduces the 747.
It the HS rolls a 2, it may Withdraw from CC due to Infiltration (A11.22).
If the Pz 35 or the 237 roll 12, the 747 can withdraw due to Infiltration (A11.22) – and the CMG of the Pz35R is malfunctioned.

Without concealment on the part of some unit present, unless another circumstance such as Streefighting applies, this isn't an ambush situation so no need to roll for it.  Therefore, no extra -1 to the US CC DR.  However, it is still sequential (A11.31) with the non-AFV side attacking first.  Note this initial attack doesn't have to be versus the AFV; in some situations you might want to go after the escorting infantry instead.

Kevin is also correct that the HS and the AFV can't combine for a single CC attack.  Normally a given unit may only be attacked once in the Close Combat Phase, but A11.12 has a specific exemption for situations involving an AFV, so presumably both units can take a crack at the 747 if it comes up empty on its own CC DR.

title: ASL vs ASLSK Scenarios
question:
How does one know whether a scenario is meant to be played using the full ASL rules or only those in ASLSK – there is no indication on the scenario card. Is it simply dependant on its origin (i.e, a scenario found in ASLSK #1 will obviously use ASLSK rules)? 

Also, would using the full ASL rules with ASLSK scenarios be a bad idea? Or, once I get BV and the rulebook there is no reason to play ASLSK scenarios (except to teach new players)?

Must all the ASL rules be applied simultaneously, or are they meant to be layered on? What can be included/excluded to maintain game balance?
author: Lt_Hornblower
consensus_answer:
One thing I noticed about using ASL rules to play starter kit scenarios, is that the balance can change substantially. This depends on the particular scenarios and the rules used. For example, using multiple-story ASL rules in ASLSK, can really give the defender an edge they didn't have before, as it can open up LOS on some boards.
Very important features that may affect a SK scenario played with full ASL rules are the Bypass movement, which strongly adds to the mobility of units ; and concealment (even though it is introduced in SK4).
With literally thousands of full ASL scenarios, trying to play SK scenarios with full rules is not the wisest idea.
Schwerpunkt produced two Rally Point scenario packs, with scenarios playable with both systems (but with necessary adaptations).

title: Street Fighting A11.8
question:
The second to last statement in A11.8 reads like this -

"Any vehicle in stationary Bypass or using VBM is also subject to Street Fighting rules from any Infantry in the Bypassed obstacle of their hex."  

Underline added for emphasis

I note the following about this sentence -
1.  "also" ... as "in addition to everything previously stated in A11.8"
2. The subject vehicle is NOT stated to be in a road hex straddled by buildings
3.  And the Infantry is not stated to be in a building (simply a "bypassed obstacle")

So, when I read this sentence, it implies to me that any Infantry in an obstacle bypassable by a vehicle (building/woods/light jungle/et. al.), even a single hex stand of woods out in the middle of an open field, can invoke "Street Fighting" to conduct "CC Reaction Fire" in its DFF and/or gain the "Street Fighting Ambush" drm in its CC phase against an enemy vehicle bypassing the hex it occupies (regardless of the presence of buildings/road).

What say the gurus?
