consensus_answer:
Why would the squad be frozen, JR? It doesn't say in 11.8 "...and following any CC attack returned to the same locations they came from."
"VBM Sleaze Freeze" is an action by the vehicle owner during his MPh. It refers to the tactic of moving a vehicle into a Location containing enemy units, which prevents the enemy units from using DFF outside the Location due to A7.212. After he has driven his vehicle in and ended its MPh in the Location, the enemy units are "frozen" i.e. they can't make DFF attacks outside their own Location. This can be done by entering the Location proper, but against enemy units in woods/buildings this is often done by entering the hex in Bypass. The vehicle is still in the same Location, invoking A7.212, but it doesn't have to pay the usually high MPs to enter the terrain and doesn't have to take a Bog check.

There are a number of counter-moves to VBM sleaze freeze. Obviously the units in the Location can use CC-RF, and if the vehicle has used Bypass the vehicle is subject to "street fighting ambush" even though it is not in a road Location with buildings on either side, the point of the comment on the matter. And my reply was that also CC-RF did benefit from the -1 street-fighting-ambush DRM, if the vehicle did not stop that DRM would be combined with the +2 non-stopped DRM. Another possible tactic is to fire at the vehicle (even if it is a BU, CT vehicle) before it enters the Location so as to leave Residual. Other ways to avoid VBM sleaze freeze include having some kind of ordnance or other AT capability in the to-be-frozen Location or nearby, e.g. PF, MOL, MG, a true A-T Gun, etc. Because a bypassing vehicle has a wider side armor facing these can often benefit from hitting the side armor and not the front. None of these countermeasures will guarantee that VBM sleaze freeze is ineffective, but they do give a risk to the maneuver. 

VBM sleaze freeze does not refer to the enemy entering the vehicle's Location using proper street fighting, which is when friendly infantry enter a road Location between two buildings.

title: Riders D6.2
question:
I don´t understand this in the D6.2 rule "Riders are limited to tanks (not tankettes),TD, SPA, SPAA, Carriers (limited capacity; 6.81), and Assault Guns"

Can a motorcycle be a tank, TD, SPA,SPAA, Carriers or Assault Gun? 
Can a Puma( PSW 234/2) not have riders because it is a AC, but a PSW234/4 can because it is a AC/TD?

I am sure i miss something, but need help to see it.
author: Nslcole
consensus_answer:
Per the index, "Rider (Personnel transported on the outside of an AFV, Cavalry, or a motorcycle)," and D6.2, "Riders are Personnel being transported on the outside of an AFV (or Cavalry or motorcyclists)." I think you have to take the sentence you quote from D6.2 as discussing Riders in the context of AFVs, i.e. it should be read, "Riders on AFVs are limited to tanks (not tankettes), TD, SPA, SPAA, Carriers (limited capacity; 6.81), and Assault Guns," and not other uses of Riders. 

Regarding the question of whether the PSW 234/4 allows for Riders, my personal belief is that the "AC" part would overrule the "TD" part of the vehicle type. You could submit for a clarification from Perry if it's important to your game.

replies.body:
At the beginning of D6.2 it says "AFV (or Cavalry or motorcyclists)", so the motorcycle is there. The rest of the rule is for AFV.

And yes, the AFV must be one of the listed types.

Per the index, "Rider (Personnel transported on the outside of an AFV, Cavalry, or a motorcycle)," and D6.2, "Riders are Personnel being transported on the outside of an AFV (or Cavalry or motorcyclists)." title: Bore sighted MMG
question:
If a 447 with a MMG that has Bore Sighted a hex fires as a FG, can it get the -2 DRM?
Or is it only the MMG that has Bore Sighted, and therefore the -2 DRM will not count if the squad used it inhernt firepower with the MMG as a FG.
author: Nslcole
consensus_answer:
If a 447 with a MMG that has Bore Sighted a hex fires as a FG, can it get the -2 DRM?
Or is it only the MMG that has Bore Sighted, and therefore the -2 DRM will not count if the squad used it inhernt firepower with the MMG as a FG.

No, per the rules  (C 6.44) all elements of the FG would need to have bore sighted the location (and the MMC can not bore sight its inherent FP).  Now if you had multiple MMG/HMG with the same hex bore sighted, then those MGs would be eligible to FG together with the -2 DRM (if situated in same/qualifying adjacent location).

title: Can I switch a fire mission from Smoke to HE?
question: I'm playing through my 1st RB CG. In my opening move, I dropped a Smoke fire mission on a location to good effect. The next time I use that fire mission, I wish to drop HE on the same target. Being a former soldier, this is not uncommon when using arty - we call a mixture of smoke and HE a "cocktail" - but the rules are not clear. Within the construct of ASL, is this allowable? Military logic is that all the observer is doing is asking the gunline to switch from smoke to HE and fire for effect, but logic and rules are not always in alignment. My opponent believes you can only engage in one type and to switch ammo natures would require a new fire mission from scratch, and we went with this to move the game on. Grateful for any clarity or thoughts on this and on whether, in the absence of rules clarity, anybody takes a house rules view on it?
author: ivorgardiner
consensus_answer: C1.7 FIRE MISSION: A Fire Mission consists of the entire time between Battery Access chit draws in which a FFE is on board. There are seven types of Fire Missions. The first is the HE Concentration and the second the SMOKE Concentration (1.71), the Blast Area for both of which is defined in 1.32. The other types are Harassing Fire (1.72), IR (E1.93), Barrage (E12.1), SMOKE Barrage (E12.51) and Creeping Barrage (E12.7). A Fire Mission cannot be of more than one type; e.g. if a battery uses a HE Concentration in its FFE:1 stage, it cannot switch to Harassing Fire or SMOKE, etc., in its FFE:2 stage.

Thank you, Mark. Don't know how I missed that, but it makes it very clear - as a rule, if not a reflection of reality.

Remember... game turns are what, only a couple of minutes?  So one could switch between Smoke and HE FFE in a span of < 5 minutes (TOT) in game terms.  Perhaps not /exactly/ what you're used to in your experience, but given that this is modeling behavior back in the 1940's, I can't believe it is actually that far off from what could be achieved...

Thank you, Mark. Don't know how I missed that, but it makes it very clear - as a rule, if not a reflection of reality. 
FWIW, different projectiles have different weights and require different powder charges.

Outside the scope of the game, p/o a fire mission is the battery crew adjusting the gun elevation for the firing solution and cutting the charges to match the projectile weight required.  Assuming good order, this cutting of charges all might happen before the first round of a rapid volley is fired.  A mid-mission change of munition could result in a projectile_weightcharge_size mismatch and that round landing =well= away from the intend POI.  This happening was Bad and could get your battery officer reprimanded or worse.

There is also the projectile flight time.  As the FFE1 is resolving the FFE2 could possibly already be in process.  The greater the range from battery, the longer the flight time and the more likely this is to be.  At most, there may be time to slightly adjust elevation/deflection.  ASL assumes this is always feasible.

The prohibition against mid-mission changes from concentration  harassing_fire likely reflects the need for differing firing solutions per tube and differing crew SOPs entirely.

Upshot:  the kinda crude ASL prohibition against changing between SMOKE and HE mid-mission kinda reflects the technology then.  You do get a bit of HE hindrance through the HE FFE hexes -- that likely represents explosion smoke, dust and the like.  Mixed missions (SMOKE + HE) were possible but likely always (?) involved two concurrent batteries/sections (one SMOKE, one HE) and (in ASL) two or more batteries to an OB for the capability to be a posibility.

question:
C.4 Ordnance Area Fire reads in part: "Ordnance Area Fire never halves the FP effect of any hit."

C3.33 Area Target Type reads in part: "[...] each hit is resolved with only half the FP of the firing ordnance [...]".

  I have always played that area fire (including all fire by mortars) is resolved with half the FP indicated on the IFT by the caliber size of the gun.

  It seems like C.4 is saying something that is distinct from C3.33, but I can't figure out what. What is the significance of C.4?

  My rules for these pages date from 1987 (on paper).

LQ
author: LesterQuaestor
consensus_answer:
If you are feeling lucky, Ordnance Are Fire can be entertaining. But there's no acquisition.
Ordnance Area Fire *may* result in acquisition. It depends on the cause for Area Fire and the target type. The most common cause of Area Fire is probably concealment, and if you use the Area Target Type or the attack strips concealment, acquisition is gained [C6.57]. Another example: Area Fire vs. Dash of an unconcealed unit will gain acquisition.
Okay, now you have got me. Thinking about acq markers sitting in the middle of the street because the dasher ran out of LoS.
The second step of a dash need not be out-of-LOS [A4.63]. It only needs to be not Open Ground. If it is out-of-LOS and the dash unit does not pin or break on some attack then of course the acquisition would remain in the street, but if the second step is in LOS and/or the dashing unit pins or breaks, the acquisition will be effective.

Perhaps obvious, but I've found you increase your odds of getting an answer by the following:
--Keep the question brief: one or two sentences if by any means possible.
--Include a picture if useful.
--Isolate the core question from irrelevant details.
--Include rule references.
--Phrase the question precisely, without ambiguity.
--Don't ask for the moon: keep the question as specific as possible. E.g., don't ask "are bridge Locations road Locations"--answering that requires a lot of research and cross-checking of the rules; instead ask "can a roadblock be set up in a bridge Location".
I would add: your question should lead to a yes/no answer.

title: Campaign Game Oddities
question:
Most of my friends here know I'm a CG aficionado and certified nut ... 

But I just got to thinking about two things in KG play that seem reasonable .... (I have my own thoughts about below, but I'll hold them for now)

Let's say we're playing KGP.

1. I build (or expend FPP) for a foxhole counter.  At some point a few CG dates later, can I replace the Foxhole with a Trench counter using my FPP during the interphase?  Why or why not?

2. I have dummy stacks and minefields unknown to the enemy.  Can I run my dummy stacks through the unknown minefields without subjecting my dummy stacks to the minefield attacks?  Again, why or why not?
author: Dr Brian
consensus_answer:
2) B12.11 "Before announcing any mine attacks exposed by the movement of a stack topped by a "?", the DEFENDER may force the ATTACKER to momentarily reveal a non-Dummy unit in that stack to show that an actual force exists there. If he cannot, or if the stack is friendly to the DEFENDER, the Dummy stack is removed."

First, when would such a stack (being moved) be friendly to the DEFENDER (the player not moving)?  I guess during the RtPh is possible, but the stack wouldn't be concealed.

Second, the situation being described by the OP would be during the ATTACKER's turn, A12.11 doesn't seem to apply, but B28.41 seems pretty clear (and Dummies are units):

Whenever a unit enters/leaves a minefield hex, the owning player must announce a minefield attack vs the unit (as per A12.11) on the IFT, revealing the minefield factors involved only when necessary to verify the IFT results [EXC: A-T mines do not attack Infantry/Cavalry; 28.5]

A good observation. I am guessing this B12.11 is written "sideways." I have always understood it as, "Before announcing any mine attacks exposed by the movement of a stack topped by a "?", the owner of the mines forces the ATTACKER to momentarily reveal a non-Dummy unit in that stack to show that an actual force exists there. If the ATTACKER cannot, or if the stack is friendly to the owner of the mines, the Dummy stack is removed." That may not be the intention, but it is how I have interpreted it.

author: igycrctl

A unit is held in Melee when it meets the conditions of A11.15. Units that have just advanced in are not in Melee, and so would not be encircled yet. If a Melee formed or they joined an existing one at the end of the CCPh then they would be encircled.

title: MG fire after being overrun
question: If a squad has first fired with its MG and thereafter are being overrun, can the MG then fire with a to hit against the overruning AFV?
author: Nslcole
consensus_answer:
If a squad has first fired with its MG and thereafter are being overrun, can the MG then fire with a to hit against the overruning AFV?
It depends on if the MG kept ROF. The attack could only be made "without any form of halved FP penalty imposed" [A9.62]. Halving for sustained fire would prevent using TH/TK.

title: Tank Riders
question: While the Soviets sorta pioneered the tactic, and Later the Germans and western allies followed suit what other nationalities used this tactic? I can find little evidence of other nationalities using this, and I'm looking for a specific evidence that the tactic was used in the Pacific.
author: Stonewall1126
consensus_answer:
If you choose between three options 1) Ride tanks into the face of enemy fire, 2) Advance in open order accompanied by tanks, or 3) Advance with partial shelter behind the tanks; clearly riding would be the most hazardous.

Generally true, but not always (see below).

It's certainly the least effective, since infantry clinging to a tank bounding across unpaved  terrain could hardly use their own weapons.

Least effective by what measure?  Crossing a couple thousand meters of steppe terrain on foot under artillery and mortar fire, not to mention small arms fire in enfilade, is pretty hazardous itself.  Riding on the engine deck of a T-34 is no picnic but reducing your time under fire is an offsetting factor.  

Also, your personal survival isn't the only factor in consideration - tactical success is a goal as well.  Unsupported armor struggles against a prepared position.  If your choices are advancing at the pace of dismounted infantry or carrying your escorts with you, the latter gets the nod especially if you have a loose tolerance for casualties.  

It's a pity there isn't more combat footage of Soviet attacks. I think there is close to zero actual combat footage from the eastern front.

Agreed - I'd be shocked if there's more than ten minutes total of the eastern front.

I have grave doubts about accounts of infantry riding tanks into enemy fire. It seems to require foolhardiness beyond the point of insanity.

The exterior of a tank is inimical to the survival of a human body. You are exposed, conspicuous, crowded and subject to enhanced ricochet effects. Put 10 men on a tank and fire from almost any direction is going to cause casualties.

But even more, infantry clinging to a moving tank will be utterly unable to do the one thing that they supposedly are there for: protect the tank from enemy infantry.

There are two things I don't doubt. First, that many riders where attacked by ambush. This would have been unintended, and I'm sure the consequences were devastating. Second, that lunatic commanders in the Soviet or Japanese armies were willing to order troops to ride tanks under enemy fire. As I have said, I can just about believe that the Japanese, with the suicide culture they encouraged, would be crazy enough to do it. I can't but believe that the Soviets would have baled out as soon as they felt in actual danger.

title: Smoke TH DRM at CAFP from adjacent Wreck Blaze while in Stationary Bypass
question:
There is no wind. The British tank is in stationary bypass of the woods hex Q8 (see image), and its TCA matches it VCA. There is a burning wreck in Q7, which is adjacent to the hex (Q8) being bypassed. The British tank wishes to fire at the German tank in V6. LOS is shown in the image.

The questions are: 1. Is a +3 (due to fire "out" of a +2 smoke/wreck blaze hex) DRM applicable to the TH DR? 2. Is any smoke based DRM applicable to the TH DR?

My opponent (as the Germans here) tried to argue that there was a +3 DRM to my TH attempt, attempting to argue that my CAFP was effectively "in" Q7. In response, I pointed out that the British tank is in bypass of hex Q8 not Q7, and as such, there is no smoke DRM at all. At the time, I found what I thought to be a determinative paragraph in the rule book (which I now cannot find) and my opponent graciously conceded the point. My TH roll was left unmodified by the smoke in the adjacent hex, and play continued.
author: BlitzkriegBeast
consensus_answer:
The unit is not in hex Q7. B.6 says that "mere entrance of the hex (even if only to trace a LOS to or through a vertex of such a hex) or a LOS exactly along one of its hexsides (A6.1) suffices." The LOS does not enter Q7. The LOS is traced to hex Q8 through hex R7. The fact that the vertex the LOS in Q8 is traced to is shared by Q7 does not change that. As I said previously if the unit had been in bypass around a hypothetical obstacle in Q7 then the hindrance would apply. In the same way a unit moving along the Q7-Q8 hexside bypassing in Q8 would not pay the extra one MF/MP for SMOKE but one moving along the Q7-Q8 hexside bypassing a hypothetical obstacle in Q7 would pay the extra one MF [A24.7]. Units in bypass or at a vertex are still only in one of the two or three hexes. They are not in some quantum state where they are in two or all three hexes equally. The two q&a are entirely consistent with B.6. 

I disagree.  You're looking at B.6 in isolation.  D2.32 states LOS to a vehicle in VBM is traced to the vertex itself, which brings B.6 into play.  I am fully in favor of the Q&A resolution but it represents an exception to the rules as written as opposed to an interpretation.

replies.body:
Smoke is in Q7.
The tank is in Q8.
Smoke doesn't affect the shot V6 nor to it.
And? Did you kill the tank?????  :)

The tank is in Q8, but LOS is traced to the Q7/Q8/R7 vertex.  The smoke from the Q7 blaze is an Inherent hindrance, which includes that vertex:

B.6 It is not necessary that a LOS actually cross such a symbol to be affectedV10 X10 mere entrance of the hex (even if only to trace a LOS to or through a vertex of such a hex) or a LOS exactly along one of its hexsides (A6.1) suffices.

A tank in VBM has all LOS traced to or from its CAFP:

D2.32 This vertex is called the Covered Arc Focal Point (CAFP) and is the point in the hex where all fire to and from the vehicle is traced while using VBM or Stationary Bypass in that hex.

I reckon the blaze hinders the shot, but am happy to be proven wrong.  Also, by a literal reading of the above, a shot from S8 would suffer the hindrance, which seems odd.

A vertex is part of each of its three adjacent hexsides, like a hexside is part of its two adjacent hexes.

It's not a question of "through, along, crossing". It's "out of".
A24.2 says "All direct fire and on-board mortar fire traced into, through, within, or out of a smoke location is affected by a Hindrance DRM''.
A vertex is part of each of its three adjacent hexsides, like a hexside is part of its two adjacent hexes.
If Smoke exists, as inherent terrain in one of those hexes, then according to B.6 it exists in the vertex; just as if the LOS was traced along the hexside.
In ASL the vertex both is a part of all three hexes, but the unit is in only exactly one of the three hexes. Among other things this is important for determining range. The vertex is a point to which LOS is traced, but it is not the Location of the unit. That is the hex. In the OP the unit is in hex Q8 and in no other. Per A6.7 a LOS has to be traced through a Location with a hindrance to have effect, and SMOKE extends that to into or out-of. In this case the LOS is not traced through Q7 (i.e. from one face of the hex and out another nor into Q7, since the unit is not in Q7. In this case the hindrance does not apply. If the LOS continued on past the vertex to another place on the map, the LOS would be through Q7, and the hindrance *would* apply. But because the LOS is traced to the vertex and no farther it does not.
Ok. Thank you!

If there were a bypassable obstacle in Q7 (and also SMOKE of some kind), and the vehicle were in bypass of Q7, then the hindrance *would* apply even though the LOS is traced to the same point on the map. Similarly if the hypothetical bypassable obstacle in Q7 were a building, an attack by a MTR would not be eligible for airburst, but if the unit was in Q8 as there it would be affected by airburst. The appearance of the map and the counters on it does not uniquely determine what rules apply, perhaps regrettably.

Yes. Meets the criteria.
4.63 Infantry may declare a Dash through a road Location if it declares a Dash move to a particular Location prior to moving, and then moves from a non-Open Ground Location on one side of the road directly into the road and then directly into a non-Open Ground Location on the other side of the road provided the normal MF expenditure for this two-hex move is ≤ the unit’s available MF.

Nope. Fails "on the other side of the road".
Does that mean the other side of the road depiction or the other side of the road Location?

Okay, fair question, since the rules don't define that. And the authors weren't even good enough to footnote the rule.

However, the entire point of "dash" is that roads are generally much narrower than the 40+ meters given them in the standard board depictions. Dashing (and Street Fighting) are efforts to combat this abstracted representation (first pointed out in the designer's notes in the original SL). Going from T10 to V10 is roughly 40 meters of open ground, possibly spending much of it going along the road. Note that you can go the same distance between the same obstacles through M10, and you can't dash that. It isn't because the road is that much smoother (all that can do is get you one extra MF from the road bonus).

But if you Dash from T10 to U9 (assuming there's non-clear terrain there), the game assumes that geometry has been warped a bit to give a nice depiction of the road in its own hex, and the distance between those two is less than 40 meters, and then you can Dash, spending so little time in the open that the enemy has to use Area Fire. (Note the other way to do that is with a snapshot.)

title: Bounding first fire from a stopped vehicle
question:
During the MPh, if an attacking vehicle receives a Motion Status (it entered a new hex/hexside during that Player Turn) but spends one MP to stop, does it immediately cancel the Motion status, hence the Case C⁴ Motion Firer DRM?
As from C 5.35 it seems so.

C 5.35 CASE C4; MOTION FIRER: A Motion/Non-Stopped vehicle which is moving and wishes to fire without stopping first, must add the applicable DRM of Case C⁴ to its To Hit DR.

However the confusing part comes from D 2.13

D 2.13 STOPPING: A vehicle must expend one additional MP in its current hex to stop movement...Even though stopped, the vehicle is considered a moving target if it entered a new hex/hexside during that Player Turn or began its MPh in Motion.

So the same vehicle would be considered as a stopped vehicle when firing, but as a moving target against a Defensive Fire? A stopped firer, but moving target?
author: poifpoif
consensus_answer:
During the MPh, if an attacking vehicle receives a Motion Status (it entered a new hex/hexside during that Player Turn) but spends one MP to stop, does it immediately cancel the Motion status, hence the Case C⁴ Motion Firer DRM?

"Motion status" [D2.4] is a technical term for a vehicle not during its MPh that has not expended a Stop MP since its last Start MP and has not become Bogged/Immobilized. It is a state the vehicle is in only outside its own MPh. So for instance a vehicle that begins its MPh stopped, expends a Start MP, moves one hex (for example), then expends a Stop MP is never in Motion status. Between when the Start MP is spent and when the Stop MP is spent it is "non-Stopped." If it uses BFF during its MPh it would use case C⁴ when non-Stopped and not use it when Stopped. When using BFF a vehicle is never in Motion because BFF occurs during its MPh. For your example you only mention states during the vehicle's MPh, and Motion status is not defined during that vehicle's MPh.

As from C 5.35 it seems so.

C 5.35 CASE C4; MOTION FIRER: A Motion/Non-Stopped vehicle which is moving and wishes to fire without stopping first, must add the applicable DRM of Case C⁴ to its To Hit DR.

However the confusing part comes from D 2.13

D 2.13 STOPPING: A vehicle must expend one additional MP in its current hex to stop movement...Even though stopped, the vehicle is considered a moving target if it entered a new hex/hexside during that Player Turn or began its MPh in Motion.

So the same vehicle would be considered as a stopped vehicle when firing, but as a moving target against a Defensive Fire? A stopped firer, but moving target?
Yes a vehicle that has expended a Stop MP would be considered a Stopped vehicle, i.e. one that C⁴ does not apply to. But BFF would still be  subject to the other case C DRM (C, C¹ or C², which then invoke case B). The vehicle might be a C.8 Moving Target while being a D3.3 Stopped firer.

There are at least four pairs of technical terms used in ASL for various aspects  "moving." First is "Motion"/"not in Motion".  This is something that is defined only outside the vehicle's MPh. Second is "Stopped"/"not Stopped". This is something that is defined only during the vehicle's MPh. Third is "Moving Target"/"not Moving Target". These are defined both in and not in the vehicle's MPh. Finally there is "moving"/"not moving". "Moving" in this sense is not formally defined but seems to mean something like, "currently conducting its MPh." These four pairs of "moving" terms are only somewhat interrelated, and it is possible for a unit to be in the movement-related state for one of them but not in the movement-related state for another. For example the example vehicle that I described above that spent a start MP,, moved a hex then spent a Stop MP would be a C.8 Moving Target until the beginning of the RtPh but would be a Stopped vehicle for the remainder of its MPh and a "not in Motion" vehicle after its MPh.

It is a mistake to try to relate the ASL technical terms to the non-technical meaning of those words. Doing so only leads to confusion. Within the context of the rules you have to stick to the defined (or in the case of "moving," undefined but implied) technical meaning.

replies.body: being a 'moving target' (i.e. the OTHER player firing at it must add the appropriate DRM (+2 or more, depending on # of MPs spent in LOS) is different than being a Motion/Non-Stopped vehicle.  The latter is, as you note, pertaining to the doubling of the lower die in the To Hit roll.  If you aren't gyrostabilizer equipped and don't spend the Stop MP, then you must double the lower die on the To Hit roll.  If you Stop, then you do not double the lower die.  However, in either case, you are still considered to have been a moving vehicle and add the appropriate Case B+C To Hit DRMs (generally +4 (+2 and another +2) for a turreted vehicle, etc.).

D 2.13 STOPPING: A vehicle must expend one additional MP in its current hex to stop movement...Even though stopped, the vehicle is considered a moving target if it entered a new hex/hexside during that Player Turn or began its MPh in Motion.

So the same vehicle would be considered as a stopped vehicle when firing, but as a moving target against a Defensive Fire? A stopped firer, but moving target?
Yes a vehicle that has expended a Stop MP would be considered a Stopped vehicle, i.e. one that C⁴ does not apply to. But BFF would still be  subject to the other case C DRM (C, C¹ or C², which then invoke case B). The vehicle might be a C.8 Moving Target while being a D3.3 Stopped firer.

There are at least four pairs of technical terms used in ASL for various aspects  "moving." First is "Motion"/"not in Motion".  This is something that is defined only outside the vehicle's MPh. Second is "Stopped"/"not Stopped". This is something that is defined only during the vehicle's MPh. Third is "Moving Target"/"not Moving Target". These are defined both in and not in the vehicle's MPh. Finally there is "moving"/"not moving". "Moving" in this sense is not formally defined but seems to mean something like, "currently conducting its MPh." These four pairs of "moving" terms are only somewhat interrelated, and it is possible for a unit to be in the movement-related state for one of them but not in the movement-related state for another. For example the example vehicle that I described above that spent a start MP,, moved a hex then spent a Stop MP would be a C.8 Moving Target until the beginning of the RtPh but would be a Stopped vehicle for the remainder of its MPh and a "not in Motion" vehicle after its MPh.

It is a mistake to try to relate the ASL technical terms to the non-technical meaning of those words. Doing so only leads to confusion. Within the context of the rules you have to stick to the defined (or in the case of "moving," undefined but implied) technical meaning.
Too many players use the term interchangeably. Motion/Moving

Too many players use the term interchangeably. Motion/Moving

This...

Too many players use the term interchangeably. Motion/Moving

This...
From the Jay Richardson tutorial. 

Moving: a vehicle that is currently executing its MPh.
Motion: a vehicle that is not moving and is not stopped. 
Non-stopped: a vehicle that is moving and not stopped. 
Moving target: a vehicle that is/has been in Motion and/or entered a new hex this Player Turn.

That is a very good explanation JR V.

Some simple mnemonics I use are:

+ You put the "Motion" counter on top of the vehicle only outside the vehicle's MPh. Hence "Motion/not in Motion" is outside MPh,

+ To get a vehicle moving during its MPh you need to spend a "start" MP and to stop spend a "stop" MP.  Hence, in its MPh the vehicle is "Stopped/not Stopped".

+ If you are considered a "moving target" someone is shooting at you, and a tactical tip you should always know is that if you spend a Start MP the opponent can shoot at you immediately before you become a "moving target".

+ There is a circumstance in which you need to use your memory. If a vehicle moves and then stops, in the DFPh you need to remember that it is still a "moving target". There are no markers for that ftf, but in Vassal it will still have the indicator of having moved.

+ If you are considered a "moving target" someone is shooting at you, and a tactical tip you should always know is that if you spend a Start MP the opponent can shoot at you immediately before you become a "moving target".

This is the most common case but there are situations where the vehicle might be a C.8 moving target anyway after expending a Start MP. If the vehicle begins its MPh in Motion and/or has entered a new hex during its MPh, it might stop then expend a Start MP, and it would be a C.8 moving target on that Start MP. Once a vehicle becomes a C.8 moving target it remains such until the end of the turn (effectively the end of the DFPh because enemy can't make any ordnance attacks after that).

title: Collateral attacks vs exposed crews
question:
From the rules:
D.8A SPECIFIC (Collateral Attacks) : When a vehicle is attacked (such that a DR is made on the IFT or a To Kill Table) as a predesignated target but not destroyed, etc., any Vulnerable PRC in/on it are subject to a full strength Specific Collateral Attack as per D.8 above.

1) Should the exposed crew be considered as a vulnerable PRC here? In other words, should a Collateral Attack be resolved as a separate attack vs the the crew of an opened AFV immediately subsequent to the resolution of the attack vs the same vehicle, using the same Original Effects DR that resolved the attack vs the vehicle? 

2) There's an EXCeption in D8 stating that No Collateral Attack occurs if the vehicle is destroyed outright (5.6). If the crew/Passenger(s) are/become shocked (C7.42) or stunned (5.34), a Collateral Attack applies only to the vehicle’s Riders (6.23). Does the exception applies to both types of collateral attacks, or only to general ones? 
Let's say an AFV targets with its main gun a hex occupied by infantry and an opened AFV. How to resolve the attack against the CE in the targeted hex? As a general collateral attack? Or does the exception here applies and exposed crews being considered as immune to general collateral attacks?
author: poifpoif
consensus_answer:
I was implying an ITT attack against the hex. Sorry about the lack of clarity. 

When firing on the ITT the vehicle is not specifically targeted, so any attack would be a general collateral attack. Even though the vehicle can't be affected [C3.32], if the vehicle is hit any PRC on the vehicle are attacked as a general collateral attack. But note that the vehicle has to be hit, and with different DRMs it may be the case that the vehicle is hit but the infantry not or vice versa or both are hit or neither.

NB: PRC may only be the target of a specific collateral attack if the « carrying » vehicle was targeted first, can we agree on this?
The vehicle would not only have to be targeted first, but it would also have to be specifically targeted. So for instance the ATT will attack an AFV (possibly killing it), but because the ATT does not specifically designate the vehicle the collateral would be a general collateral attack, i.e. PRC would potentially be affected but also non-PRC in the Location and also a second vehicle and its PRC if overstacked. 

Specific collateral attacks occur when one vehicle is specifically targeted (and other units in the Location/hex are not). The most common case would be using the VTT, but LATW using their own TH Table (e.g. BAZ, PF, PSK) may also be specifically targeting the vehicle, and FTs can specifically target an AFV [A22.6.12].

For the purposes of the effects the two different types of collateral are the same. The difference is which units are attacked and which units are not attacked.

Take it step by step. A vehicle can be part of all targets in a Location or be a specific target, with no other vehicles or units in the Location being targeted.
Whatever the target type, if the vehicle is destroyed outright, then PRC just roll for survival as normal. If the vehicle is not destroyed, but its Crew or Passengers are affected by the attack, then only its Riders received a Collateral Attack.

I do understand why you might think so but I'm not sure I would agree with this exactly. The collateral attack rules basically say that a type of attack that specifically affects one AFV (e.g. the VTT, a FT per A22.612 or similar) will, if it does not destroy that vehicle, potentially affect only PRC on that vehicle. Any attack that is not specifically required to designate one vehicle target will attack all vulnerable units in the Location, either directly or collaterally (PRC can only be attacked collaterally). I think this is "obvious" even if it needs to be spelled out in rules. Could the rules have been written better? Probably. But the ideas behind collateral attacks are not particularly unintuitive or complicated. They are attacks just like any other fire attack against infantry. Who gets attacked (general or specific collateral) depends on the type of attack. That's pretty much all there is.

The rules are fixed and do not adapt to what you want to understand. When you ask a question here we can construct the answer to your question, which a great advantage. We can filter out the bits that aren't important for you.

title: Basic rout question
question:
A squad is broken and marked with DM. It is currently in a woods hex which is on the edge of a large multi-hex woods area. It is not adjacent to an enemy. Can that unit rout to an interior woods hex (increasing distance to any known enemy unit)? Can it rout to the location of a leader, also increasing it's range to known enemy units? Or does it have to stay where it is since it is already in a woods hex and not forced to rout?

LQ
author: LesterQuaestor
consensus_answer:
This fixes the case where a unit begins its RtPh in a woods hex with no KEU. q&a:

No.

....Perry
MMP

     
    A broken unit begins its RtPh DM in a woods hex with no ADJACENT 
    woods/building hexes. There are no KEU in LOS. The broken unit must 
    choose its rout destination, which is "the nearest (in MF calculated at 
    the start of its RtPh) building or woods hex" [A10.51]. Since the 
    nearest woods hex is its own at zero MF, must it choose its own hex as 
    its target?

replies.body: As long as it is marked with a DM counter it may rout within that woods mass as long as it obeys the other general restrictions of routing.  It may leave the woods mass as long as the next hex entered is a woods or building hex.  This is the most important distinction between woods and buildings for routing purposes - a broken unit may exit a building in which it began the rout phase (subject to other routing constraints), even into open ground, but isolated woods are occasionally death traps (this is detailed in the last chunk of A10.51).

As per the previous answer, a broken unit marked with a DM counter at the start of its rout phase may always rout at least one hex if it is otherwise able, even if it begins the RtPh in a woods/building/pillbox/whatever. There are circumstances where it may not be otherwise able, e.g. it would be routing closer to a KEU, it is held in Melee, the only Locations it can rout to are forbidden (water obstacle, blaze), etc.

Basically, if you are DM you may route. Route means: leave where you are and go somewhere else. That somewhere else is typically (but not always) a woods or building hex that is within routing distance. You choose such a hex as a target. If more than one target is available, you have to choose the one that requires the smallest MF expenditure to reach. None of this says you have to stay in the isolated woods hex (though you may choose to), and none of it forbids you crossing open ground (and possibly facing interdiction) to get to a route target. Unless, of course, you are adjacent to an enemy unit to whom you would surrender (if No Quarter has not been invoked) if your only way of getting to your target would cause interdiction, or force low crawl.

title: Assault Movement
question:
There have been a number of posts I have read recently that suggest some players are misinformed about Assault Movement. Since Assault Movement is bread-and-butter ASL―it is not very common that you would play a scenario without using Assault Movement at some point—I thought it might be a good idea to go through the mechanics.

Mechanics
All movement is done by picking the unit or stack to move, declaring and executing an expenditure and waiting for the completion of DFF. After the completion of an expenditure, if the unit/stack can continue making expenditures and wants to, the player may repeat the process until no more expenditures are allowed or desired. This does not change with Assault Movement. Assault Movement adds a few restrictions. With Assault Movement the unit/stack cannot become or have been PRC, at most one of the MF expenditures can be for a change of Location (hex in ASLSK), and the total MF expended must be strictly less than than the unit's available MF, with bonuses such as road movement or leadership bonus included, but disallowing Double Time. The declaration for Assault Movement has to be done before expending any MF, and the effects (e.g. no FFNAM) remain in effect until the end of the move unless Assault Movement is voided, e.g. going berserk or breaking. Assault Movement cannot be cancelled voluntarily.

Some Observations
A unit using Assault Movement can make any number of MF expenditures in any order as long as it does not violate the restrictions for Assault Movement. For example it can recover SW, place DC or smoke grenades or enter/leave entrenchments, possibly in addition to changing Location.

The expenditures do not have to pre-designated. A unit can wait to see the result of the recovery dr before declaring it will place the DC it is trying to recover. Likewise a unit might move into one Location in a subsequent expenditure if it successfully places a smoke grenade but into a different one (or end its MPh) if it does not. In both cases the player could wait until he sees the results of the first expenditure before making (or not making) the second.

Costs for making an expenditure or the total move do not change when using Assault Movement. The MF spent in Assault Movement are *not* ALL, nor (automatically) one-less-than-all nor any fixed number.

Although changing Locations using Assault Movement does not cause concealment loss unless done in A10.531 Open Ground, declaring Assault Movement does not negate concealment loss caused by expenditures made for anything besides movement. Making an expenditure for smoke grenade placement, recovery or DC placement for example cause concealment loss even if done as part of Assault Movement.

A Quick Example
A MMC in a foxhole moving as a stack with an unwounded leader can expend one MF to recover a DC in its entrenchment (one MF), place smoke grenades in its own Location (one MF), exit its foxhole (one MF), enter the adjacent Open Ground hex (one MF) and enter the foxhole in it (one MF). Each expenditure would be done separately, and each would allow intervening DFF.

Last Observation
A unit can't declare Assault Movement then get one extra MF by declaring Late Double Time. Nice try.
author: jrvjrv
consensus_answer:
Does anyone who may be lurking have insight into why the ASL design team decided that it was beyond the capability of an unassisted American 1st line squad to toss smoke grenades into the adjacent street hex (2MF) and then move into that hex (2MF) as Assault Movement?
I'm guessing it was just a game design decision that made an interesting game mechanic. ASL is all about making tough decisions, all the time. If a lone MMC could place Smoke into an adjacent hex and still have 2 MF left using Assault Movement, we would see tons more Smoke attempts every turn. If you'd fail, you would still have 2 MF left to maybe move to an adjacent building location. As opposed to now, if you fail, now there's no Smoke in the street and you have 1 MF left... what are you going to do now then? Just stay in place? Risk it and Assault Move into the street anyway?

Reasonable. But let's not forget there's always a 1/6 chance of ending your movement phase immediately anyway if you roll the dreaded 6. (To my mind, just another rule to discourage making smoke all the time.)

If you had two squads and one has an 8 morale, and a decent smoke exponent, you could try:

1. declare assault move and move the 6-6-8 (or whatever) into the street for 1 MF
2. survive DFF at -1 FFMO (this is iffy, but not as iffy as -2 FFMO + FFNAM)
3. spend 1 MF to attempt to place smoke in your own (middle of the street) hex (possibly provoking SFF*)
4. don't roll a 6
5. if successful, whistle to the 6-6-6 squad you were originally stacked with to assault move into the street with you (2 MF), under cover of the smoke

* If the smoke grenade placement 1 MF expenditure provokes SFF and is successful, is the incoming SFF shot affected by the +2 Smoke DRM? (That is, does the SFF shot come before or after the smoke appears?) In either case, can the defender decide whether to fire only after seeing the result of the smoke grenade attempt?

question: If a unit routes away from an adjacent enemy unit such that the enemy unit is not in LOS, and on the next turn routes again, should it "remember" the enemy unit and thus it is "known"? consensus_answer:
A10.51 Direction?

Correct. Broken units have memory in a phase but not across phases. Berserk units, on the other hand, are like elephants.

title: D2.6 - Enemy AFV in hex
question: Do the provisions of D2.6 apply if the enemy AFV is immobilized and abandoned?
author: Bombadil929
consensus_answer:
"Immobilized" is not a factor. There is a q&a that could be applied here:
A7.4 & D5.4
Is an abandoned vehicle still a unit? If it is a unit, is a previously friendly vehicle which was abandoned still a friendly unit, thus preventing another friendly unit to fire on it? If it is not a unit, may an abandoned vehicle be fired upon?
A. An Abandoned vehicle is a unit, but it is neither friendly nor enemy and can be attacked by either side.

Since it is not an enemy unit, it would presumably not be an enemy AFV, and so D2.6 would not apply.

title: Moving to Bunker from Accessible Trench Hex
question:
Imagine two adjacent hexes, each with a Trench. There is a Pillbox in one hex, making it a Bunker (B30.8). A squad wants to move from the plain Trench hex into the Bunker in the adjacent hex. Can it move directly (either by regular movement or Assault Movement) into the Pillbox\Bunker, or must it spend a separate movement point in the Bunker's Trench first (potentially undergoing DFF in the Trench) before safely arriving in the Bunker (where, if the only defensive firers are outside the CA of the Pillbox, it would be immune to DFF)?

The uncertainty in my mind arises from the wording in B30.8 (even though B30.33 is quite clear that the MF expenditure to enter/exit the Pillbox is a separate expenditure), which applies to a Bunker even if only in an Accessible hex to a Trench. In that case, there could be a Trench hex adjacent to the Pillbox hex, and it would still be a Bunker and "a unit may move... between a bunker and such a trench as if the bunker were also a trench." If that implies a move between the adjacent trench hex and the Pillbox in one go, it seems weird that if the Pillbox also has a trench in its own hex, it's a separate expenditure.

The meta here is the annoying habit the ASL rules have of treating seemingly similar terrain features differently. Imagine explaining to a new player that, even though when he moves from an Open Ground hex to an adjacent hex containing a tiny single-story wooden house in the center, he is immediately in the wooden house for DFF purposes, but when he moves from a trench hex to an adjacent trench hex that also has a Pillbox in it, he must traverse another part of the hex (namely the trench) first before being "inside" the pillbox.
author: BlitzkriegBeast
consensus_answer:
Imagine Trench A (in hex A) is adjacent to Trench B (in hex B) and in the Trench B hex there is a Pillbox, which is then a Bunker. But now, imagine that there is an unpossessed SW in Trench B.

1. Can a squad in Trench A move directly into the Bunker in hex B using assault movement, without undergoing DFF in hex B except when already inside the Bunker? The consensus here seems to be: yes.

As above, yes.

2a. Can a non-CX 1st line squad in Trench A move into the Bunker in hex B using assault movement, while also spending 1 MF to pick up the SW in Trench B along the way? (It certainly has enough MF to do so: 1 + 1 + 1.)

2b. If yes to 2a, would the moving squad be subject to DFF in trench B?

No, the unit may not make such a move as Assault Move. There are a number of problems here. In order to recover the SW the moving unit would have to enter the trench Location [A4.44]. In your proposed move it would then move to the Pillbox/bunker, which is a second Location [B30.1] in the hex. That would not be possible using Assault Movement, which allows a change of at most one Location [A4.46].

This could be done as normal movement (and FFNAM does not apply for movement in a trench [B27.54]), but each of the moves (into the trench, recovery, into the pillbox) would be a separate MF expenditure. Each MF expenditure would allow DFF [A8.1]. 

Looking beyond what you are asking I think you may be under the impression that Assault Movement somehow fundamentally changes the way movement is conducted. The mechanics of movement do not change for Assault Movement; the unit makes separate MF expenditures and awaits DFF as normal. Assault Movement means that at most one of those MF expenditures can be for Location change. For example a squad stacked with a leader might use Assault Movement and expend one MF to place Smoke grenades in their own Location (expenditure one), expend one MF to leave a Foxhole (expenditure two), expend one MF to enter the ADJACENT Open Ground hex (expenditure three), attempt to recover a one PP SW in the new Location (expenditure four) and finally enter a Foxhole in the new hex (expenditure five). Each of these expenditures would be announced and performed separately and would allow DFF before the moving player continued. As far as movement mechanics are concerned, the only difference is that the unit can only make one MF expenditure to enter a new Location.

In the game, I was quite sure that 1 was correct (despite my not arguing the point too hard with my opponent). I also thought both 2a and 2b were true, and so I told my opponent (after discussing this possibility with him) that I wanted to move directly into the bunker, without stopping along the way to attempt to recover the SW. But, as stated elsewhere, my opponent did not agree with point 1, so even making the more conservative move, I never got into that bunker.

Per B30.8, "A Pillbox counter in the same hex with a trench and/or in a hex Accessible to a Trench counter's hex is considered a bunker. A bunker is treated as a pillbox in all respects except that a unit may move/rout/advance/Withdraw-from-CC between a bunker and such a trench as if the bunker were also a trench."  The trench in the same hex is "such a trench." The trench in the adjacent, presumably accessible, hex is also "such a trench." B30.8 allows movement between the pillbox/bunker and the two different trenches directly, without having to go through any intermediate Location and without reference to whether there is another trench that also makes the pillbox a bunker. The joining phrase "and/or" makes it clear that there can be both a trench in-hex and also in the adjacent hex. The rest of the rule says they are treated the same, as if the other did not exist.

title: 2 enemy squad in a hex
question:
Hello,
In APh, a concealed german Half Squad move in a hex occupied by a know enemy Squad.
In the CCPh the german decline the combat but the enemy attack with no result.
The 2 units are not held in melee (EXC of the rule 11.15).  In the next PFPh, the enemy Squad is not be mandatory to fire in his hex to the german  squad but in the next DFPh, if the german want to fire it must do it against the enemy squad in his hex ? I'm right ?
Thanks for Your answers
author: runrun
consensus_answer:
A concealed German squad advances into a Location occupied by an unconcealed US squad. The German chooses not to attack in CC, staying concealed. The US squad attacks in CC, no effect. 

It is now the next turn and the US MPh. If the US squad does not move from the Location, does this automatically remove the German squad’s concealment? 

I have an inkling that because the US squad legally ended its MPh in the same Location as the German squad, this strips concealment…as with a Berserk unit charging into an enemy’s Location, a vehicle in bypass, and possibly other cases. I tried to find a relevant rule, no joy.

You may be thinking of A8.312, where a unit is required to attack an enemy MMC that enters its Location during the MPh. In this case A8.312 does not apply because the German unit did not enter during the MPh. The loss of concealment is not inherently due to the entry but rather due to the required attack. If the only unit with LOS is, say, the Berserk unit performing a charge, concealment would not be lost because the Berserk unit is not Good Order and so can't force concealment loss. In your situation the German would remain concealed until something else  happened. 

The only time I can think of where the presence of an enemy unit strips concealment at the end of the MPh is a vehicle bypassing and ending its MPh in the hex [A12.42].

title: Armored Assault vs HIP Squad

I would appreciate some opinions from people who may have experience with this.

  There is an AFV and one squad using armored assault. Their last MF is spent moving into a woods-road hex that contains a HIP squad. What happens?

  If I understand the rules correctly, the AFV could enter the hex, but the squad cannot. The hidden unit must be revealed and the moving squad returned to the last hex where their movement ends.  The player does not want the AFV to enter the hex alone (MOL capability is in effect).

LQ
author: LesterQuaestor
consensus_answer:
There is an AFV and one squad using armored assault. Their last MF is spent moving into a woods-road hex that contains a HIP squad. What happens?

If I understand the rules correctly, the AFV could enter the hex, but the squad cannot. The hidden unit must be revealed and the moving squad returned to the last hex where their movement ends.  The player does not want the AFV to enter the hex alone (MOL capability is in effect). 
Are both AFV and squad returned to the previous hex? Or does the AFV have to move into the woods-road hex since movement was declared?

As you say the squad bounces back per A12.15 but A12,15 does not apply to vehicles and it enters as per the player's move.

If the HIP unit is a squad, note that it must use its inherent when attacking with MOL even when there's no vulnerable target, so there's no chance of firing with MOL & destroying the AFV then firing the inherent against the adjacent infantry, at least as first fire.

title: Mines Purchases

author: Stonewall1126
consensus_answer:
What is the cost of purchasing AT mines and AP Mines?  It's been ages since I have used mines and have forgotten and I didn't see the cost in the rules(likely overlooked).
In general you don't purchase mines. They are given in the scenario OB. If there are none listed on the scenario, you don't get any. If given mines A-P mine factors may be exchanged for A-T mine factors [B28.5]. A small number of scenarios will allow purchase by SSR. Mines can also be purchased in DYO per H1.6. In campaign games mines can often be purchases, but the exact mechanism and costs will depend on the CG.

title: Placing smoke with OBA, Ordnance
question: When placing smoke with OBA, Ordnance you only have to roll on the To Hit Table/Area (Mortar, SMOKE)-row with range up to the hex where you want to place it, correct? No further roll needed, I suppose?
author: neo.colpaert
consensus_answer:
With regard to DRM for firing SMOKE you are getting into an area where game mechanics meet reality. From a pure "reality" standpoint, there's no reason why a SMOKE round would be affected by a moving vehicle or a concealed unit in the area. The firing unit would decide that a SMOKE round is needed in a particular place and fire it. But from game perspective the "coincidental" fact that there is a concealed unit in that hex sounds suspiciously like the player is using his game knowledge (i.e. the existence of a large stack under a "?" counter) that the real life firing unit would not have. Likewise with a moving vehicle the fact that the game holds the counter in a hex for the enemy player turn means the player is using the game mechanics (i.e. the existence of player turns) to try to hobble a target unit for much longer than the few seconds that it would take the moving vehicle to drive through that SMOKE. There's no way for the rules to determine whether the real unit would have made those SMOKE placement attempts that the player made or not. Since this is a game and not a simulation the solution is to allow the attempts but penalize them by applying DRM for trying to hit units. The rules basically assume the player is up to no good and using his knowledge from the game mechanics that the real life firing unit would not be able to use.

You can compare, for instance, firing SMOKE at a hex with a concealed unit vs firing at a hex with a HIP unit. In the latter case the player's information matches that of the firing unit and there is no game penalty. In the former case it seems suspicious that the player has selected the hex with the concealed unit, and it is possible and perhaps likely that he is using information the real unit would not have.

Another place where game mechanics meet reality is OBA. The player has to make an extra chit draw when there is a reason the player would choose a hex for OBA but there is no reason the real observer would choose that hex [C1.21].

replies.body:
these are 2 different things

OBA uses the mechanics described in C1

Ordnance uses the To Hit mechanics described in C3, plus the Special Ammo rules in C8

In my case especially Ordnance then, Mark.

C3.331 Area Target Type

With regard to DRM for firing SMOKE you are getting into an area where game mechanics meet reality. From a pure "reality" standpoint, there's no reason why a SMOKE round would be affected by a moving vehicle or a concealed unit in the area. The firing unit would decide that a SMOKE round is needed in a particular place and fire it. But from game perspective the "coincidental" fact that there is a concealed unit in that hex sounds suspiciously like the player is using his game knowledge (i.e. the existence of a large stack under a "?" counter) that the real life firing unit would not have. Likewise with a moving vehicle the fact that the game holds the counter in a hex for the enemy player turn means the player is using the game mechanics (i.e. the existence of player turns) to try to hobble a target unit for much longer than the few seconds that it would take the moving vehicle to drive through that SMOKE. There's no way for the rules to determine whether the real unit would have made those SMOKE placement attempts that the player made or not. Since this is a game and not a simulation the solution is to allow the attempts but penalize them by applying DRM for trying to hit units. The rules basically assume the player is up to no good and using his knowledge from the game mechanics that the real life firing unit would not be able to use.

You can compare, for instance, firing SMOKE at a hex with a concealed unit vs firing at a hex with a HIP unit. In the latter case the player's information matches that of the firing unit and there is no game penalty. In the former case it seems suspicious that the player has selected the hex with the concealed unit, and it is possible and perhaps likely that he is using information the real unit would not have.

Another place where game mechanics meet reality is OBA. The player has to make an extra chit draw when there is a reason the player would choose a hex for OBA but there is no reason the real observer would choose that hex [C1.21].

title: Control Multihex Multilevel Buildings for VP Purposes
question:
At scenario start of Panzer Lehr Sanction, the British control building dB3.  However, after a quick firefight, the British infantry have all routed from dC4 leaving only German infantry present in the building.  

Per scenario victory conditions, the Germans need to Control Buildings, not hex locations, to win.  Being the sole infantry still present in multihex/multilevel building dB3, is that building already under the VP Control of the German player regardless of the fact that he's never Mopped Up nor moved through any locations of that building other than the ground floor of hex dB4?
author: A2SimGamer
consensus_answer:
As above mopping up is never necessary. Besides finding HIP units and removing dummies, one advantage of mopping up is that all Locations are controlled. If the VC are  Location control, mopping up can gain a whole bunch without having to move the unit through each individual Location. There aren't many scenarios that use Location control and for smaller buildings just moving through each Location is often better (not TI, no search casualties), so this benefit won't come up often. Even for finding potential HIP just moving through each Location is often better.

Another advantage of Mopping Up:  A12.153 "...all broken enemy units therein immediately surrender to units of the ATTACKER’s choice inside that building regardless of their proximity.". You can occasionally bag a nice haul of prisoners by Mopping Up.  Note the Mopping Up must be successful - a single SMC is enough to 'save' broken troops. Dummies are removed whether the Mopping Up is otherwise successful or not.

title: HoB - Surrender Question
question:
7-0 German Leader rolls a 12 for his HoB DR. However, there is a Berserk Russian in the same hex. What is the result? NQ has not been declared. It is the Russian MPh.

I “think” the 7-0 leader breaks and is disrupted and will rout in the next RtPh.
author: Bombadil929
consensus_answer:
I agree with JR V.

A.7 GOOD ORDER: This term refers to a Personnel unit/inherent crew which is not broken, berserk, captured, stunned, shocked, or held in Melee. ...

A15.5 SURRENDER: A Final Heat of Battle DR ≥ 12 causes the affected unit to become broken if it is not already, and Disrupted (19.12), and to Surrender immediately to any ADJACENT Known Good Order armed enemy Infantry/Cavalry as if they shared the same Location. If no such enemy unit is ADJACENT, the unit is only Disrupted instead [EXC: Units subject to No Quarter, Japanese, Gurkhas, Partisans, Fanatics, and Commissars never surrender by the RtPh method nor do SS vs Russians (20.21); nor do they become Disrupted whether thusly ADJACENT or not. They instead become berserk on a Final Heat of Battle DR ≥ 12].
Is the German leader SS?

A19.12 DISRUPTION: ... Unless rallied by a leader first, a Disrupted unit will surrender at the start of any RtPh it begins ADJACENT to, or during any phase it occupies the same Location as, a Good Order armed Known enemy Personnel unit not in Melee [EXC: No Quarter 20.3]. ...

A10.5 ROUTING: During the RtPh a broken unit not in Melee may not remain in the same Open Ground hex in the Normal Range (10.532) and LOS of a Known non-Melee enemy unit/its-SW/Gun, nor—regardless of terrain—may it end a RtPh ADJACENT to or in the same Location with a Known enemy unit that is both unbroken and armed [EXC: Night; E1.54]. ... Broken units must rout away (ATTACKER first—one unit at a time [EXC: Voluntary Rout; 10.711]) during that RtPh or be eliminated for Failure to Rout [EXC: Surrender; 20.21]. ...

A10.51 DIRECTION:  ... A routing unit may never move ADJACENT to a Known enemy unit, unless in doing so it is leaving that enemy unit’s Location. ...

A20.21 RtPh: Any broken Infantry unit during its RtPh that is both ADJACENT to Known, Good Order, armed enemy Infantry/Cavalry and unable to rout away from it or only able to rout while being subject to Interdiction or resorting to Low Crawl (regardless of how it actually routs or if the possible unconcealed Interdictor is Known to it), will surrender to that enemy unit as its prisoner instead, (captor’s choice of unit receiving surrender if more than one unit qualifies) after first abandoning all its SW [EXC: if pinned; 10.53 & G5.5]. A stack of broken units in a Location surrenders simultaneously and must be accepted or rejected (20.3) as a stack. If there are not enough Guards for all such surrendering units, the excess units (captor’s choice) are freed as Unarmed (20.5). Surrendering units are not subject to FFE or minefield attacks. If the only adjacent armed enemy unit is in-Melee/berserk/vehicular, the broken unit must rout away (even if Disrupted) or be eliminated for Failure to Rout—such elimination does not incur No Quarter penalties. If the broken unit is also Disrupted, Encircled, or surrendering due to a Heat of Battle DR (15.5), it will instead rout to that enemy unit as its prisoner even if it had a legal rout path not requiring Interdiction or Low Crawl. Partisans (25.24), Gurkhas (25.43), Commissars (25.22), SS troops facing Russians (25.11), Fanatics (10.8), Japanese and units faced with No Quarter (20.3) never surrender via the RtPh method; they always use Low Crawl or risk Interdiction to avoid surrender. If unable to do any of these, they are eliminated rather than surrender.

----------------------------------

BTW, I think A20.21 is written out of order, and can lead to wrong conclusions. The fifth sentence is meant to be read in opposition to the first sentence. And it appears that the fourth sentence can be negated by the fifth sentence, but I doubt that's intended. I believe this rule would be improved if written in this order:

A20.21 RtPh: Any broken Infantry unit during its RtPh that is both ADJACENT to Known, Good Order, armed enemy Infantry/Cavalry and unable to rout away from it or only able to rout while being subject to Interdiction or resorting to Low Crawl (regardless of how it actually routs or if the possible unconcealed Interdictor is Known to it), will surrender to that enemy unit as its prisoner instead, (captor’s choice of unit receiving surrender if more than one unit qualifies) after first abandoning all its SW [EXC: if pinned; 10.53 & G5.5]. If the broken unit is also Disrupted, Encircled, or surrendering due to a Heat of Battle DR (15.5), it will instead rout to that enemy unit as its prisoner even if it had a legal rout path not requiring Interdiction or Low Crawl.  if the only adjacent armed enemy unit is in-Melee/berserk/vehicular, the broken unit must rout away (even if Disrupted) or be eliminated for Failure to Rout—such elimination does not incur No Quarter penalties. Partisans (25.24), Gurkhas (25.43), Commissars (25.22), SS troops facing Russians (25.11), Fanatics (10.8), Japanese and units faced with No Quarter (20.3) never surrender via the RtPh method; they always use Low Crawl or risk Interdiction to avoid surrender. If unable to do any of these, they are eliminated rather than surrender. A stack of broken units in a Location surrenders simultaneously and must be accepted or rejected (20.3) as a stack. If there are not enough Guards for all such surrendering units, the excess units (captor’s choice) are freed as Unarmed (20.5). Surrendering units are not subject to FFE or minefield attacks.

For clarity, here is my reordered paragraph with subsidiary clauses removed:

A20.21 RtPh: Any broken Infantry unit that is ADJACENT to Known, Good Order, armed enemy Infantry/Cavalry and unable to rout away--or only able to rout while subject to Interdiction or resorting to Low Crawl--will surrender to that enemy unit. If the broken unit is also Disrupted, Encircled, or surrendering due to Heat of Battle, it will rout to that enemy unit even if it had a legal rout path. But if the only adjacent enemy unit is in-Melee/berserk/vehicular, the broken unit must rout away (even if Disrupted) or be eliminated for Failure to Rout.

A stack of broken units in a Location surrenders simultaneously and must be accepted or rejected (20.3) as a stack. If there are not enough Guards for all such surrendering units, the excess units (captor’s choice) are freed as Unarmed (20.5). Surrendering units are not subject to FFE or minefield attacks. If the only adjacent armed enemy unit is in-Melee/berserk/vehicular, the broken unit must rout away (even if Disrupted) or be eliminated for Failure to Rout—such elimination does not incur No Quarter penalties. If the broken unit is also Disrupted, Encircled, or surrendering due to a Heat of Battle DR (15.5), it will instead rout to that enemy unit as its prisoner even if it had a legal rout path not requiring Interdiction or Low Crawl. Partisans (25.24), Gurkhas (25.43), Commissars (25.22), SS troops facing Russians (25.11), Fanatics (10.8), Japanese and units faced with No Quarter (20.3) never surrender via the RtPh method; they always use Low Crawl or risk Interdiction to avoid surrender. If unable to do any of these, they are eliminated rather than surrender.

And it appears that the fourth sentence can be negated by the fifth sentence, but I doubt that's intended. I believe this rule would be improved if written in this order:

A20.21 RtPh: Any broken Infantry unit during its RtPh that is both ADJACENT to Known, Good Order, armed enemy Infantry/Cavalry and unable to rout away from it or only able to rout while being subject to Interdiction or resorting to Low Crawl (regardless of how it actually routs or if the possible unconcealed Interdictor is Known to it), will surrender to that enemy unit as its prisoner instead, (captor’s choice of unit receiving surrender if more than one unit qualifies) after first abandoning all its SW [EXC: if pinned; 10.53 & G5.5]. If the broken unit is also Disrupted, Encircled, or surrendering due to a Heat of Battle DR (15.5), it will instead rout to that enemy unit as its prisoner even if it had a legal rout path not requiring Interdiction or Low Crawl.  if the only adjacent armed enemy unit is in-Melee/berserk/vehicular, the broken unit must rout away (even if Disrupted) or be eliminated for Failure to Rout—such elimination does not incur No Quarter penalties. Partisans (25.24), Gurkhas (25.43), Commissars (25.22), SS troops facing Russians (25.11), Fanatics (10.8), Japanese and units faced with No Quarter (20.3) never surrender via the RtPh method; they always use Low Crawl or risk Interdiction to avoid surrender. If unable to do any of these, they are eliminated rather than surrender. A stack of broken units in a Location surrenders simultaneously and must be accepted or rejected (20.3) as a stack. If there are not enough Guards for all such surrendering units, the excess units (captor’s choice) are freed as Unarmed (20.5). Surrendering units are not subject to FFE or minefield attacks.

For clarity, here is my reordered paragraph with subsidiary clauses removed:

A20.21 RtPh: Any broken Infantry unit that is ADJACENT to Known, Good Order, armed enemy Infantry/Cavalry and unable to rout away--or only able to rout while subject to Interdiction or resorting to Low Crawl--will surrender to that enemy unit. If the broken unit is also Disrupted, Encircled, or surrendering due to Heat of Battle, it will rout to that enemy unit even if it had a legal rout path. But if the only adjacent enemy unit is in-Melee/berserk/vehicular, the broken unit must rout away (even if Disrupted) or be eliminated for Failure to Rout.

I agree with JR V.

title: Recall and bounding fire
question:
May a recalled AFV:

1) Try to repair it's MA in the RPh?
2) Fire as bounding fire with MA an BMG/CMG in the MPh as it moves offboard?
author: Nslcole
consensus_answer:
Because the vehicle must exit as soon as possible, it may need to go CE to use the road movement rate.
I would have thought that a recalled AFV cannot CE. D5.3441 says that Recall is treated the same as a stun (BU and may not regain CE status) and I did not see being CE as an exception to it further in the text. Can you confirm a recalled AFV can become CE?
As you say, D5.341 says the effects are the same as D5.34 with additions. D5.34 says, "Stunned AFV and its Passengers immediately become BU if CE, and may not regain CE status (even if BU when the Stun occurred) until able to do so as per 5.33 in a subsequent Player Turn." When the vehicle starts its Recall it would be able to regain CE per D5.33, and may be obliged to do so in order to exit in the greatest possible haste. If there are no roads around then of course it would not be obliged to go CE. Additionally per D1.322 a 1MT may not become CE during the Recall, and I did not mention that detail.

replies.body:
Yes to both, I think.
The AFV would not be allowed to stop, though, so its Bounding Fire capacities would be quite diminished.

Agree both actions are possible. Because the vehicle must exit as soon as possible, it may need to go CE to use the road movement rate. That in turn would make using turret-mounted weapons impossible on restricted-slow or single-man turrets. But in principle vehicles can fire as they attempt to exit.

title: Airfield/Boulevard "TEM" for concealment gain?
question:
We had a question that came up in our game with Boulevards (resolved as an Airfield).

A HS wanted to gain concealment on it, out of LOS of all enemy units.  They rolled a '3' ... which would normally be ok (+2 for HS), but the Boulevard has "-1 TEM for IFT" ...

Which led us to wonder ... does it gain Concealment or not?
author: kbernatz
consensus_answer: As I read the A12.222 drm for concealment gain, a negative TEM would be applied as a positive drm because the TEM is applied as "-Y", where "Y" is value of the TEM (& hindrance) of the Location. The answer for the situation would be, "no, the halfsquad does not gain concealment if it rolls a three on its concealment dr."

replies.body: That's a good question. I interpret the runway TEM as an additional modifier for IFT fire, but not a "real" TEM, as later it says it is considered Open Ground for all purposes. Maybe if instead of TEM they had used another word like an "special IFT drm" there would be no doubts. By using TEM, maybe it has to be interpreted as a TEM for all purposes.
Right... that was our confusion.  It confuses the issue by calling it a "TEM" for IFT/To Hit ...

The boulevard is not concealment terrain, so the TEM does not matter, I thought. But then I thought, a unit can try to conceal itself in a boulevard hex if it is out of LOS. Then I looked at the rule. It states "minus TEM", so "minus -1" won't help a unit conceal.

As I read the A12.222 drm for concealment gain, a negative TEM would be applied as a positive drm because the TEM is applied as "-Y", where "Y" is value of the TEM (& hindrance) of the Location. The answer for the situation would be, "no, the halfsquad does not gain concealment if it rolls a three on its concealment dr."

As JR V notes, the '-' of the TEM is applied as a '+' to the concealment roll, so the '3' would result in a final dr of '6' (+2 for HS, +1 for the negative -1 of the "TEM") ... IF the -1 is an actual TEM versus a special modifier for the IFT/To Hit, which is how the Runway wording reads...

7.3 Any unarmored unit in a runway hex receives a -1 TEM to all IFT fire 
resolved against it regardless of fire phase. This TEM is in addition to any
applicable DRM for FFMO/FFNAM and is cumulative with other (including 
hexside) TEM. A runway hex is considered Open Ground for all Interdiction 
purposes (barring the presence of any Artificial Terrain). 

Just looked at the TEC (lol, not sure why we didn't look earlier, lol) ... and it explicitly lists it at a TEM ... so, yes, this seems clear that the HS does NOT get concealment (which is how we ruled it, so at least we got it right 🙂 ).

title: Two doubts about sniper and forced stopped AFVs.
question:
Hi, there.

- If after the Random Location roll the sniper ends up off the map, where is it placed?

- If the only unit eligible for a sniper attack is already broken, what effect does that unit suffer?

- Even when a stun result (or bog check, etc.) forces an AFV to stop, it is still considered a moving target for the rest of the turn, correct?

Thanks.
author: Viqui S
consensus_answer:
Hi, there.

- If after the Random Location roll the sniper ends up off the map, where is it placed?

Place another board down, determine the location, and adjust to nearest as normal.  I.e. the world doesn't end for the cardboard soldiers at the end of the board :).

- If the only unit eligible for a sniper attack is already broken, what effect does that unit suffer? 

On a dr2 sniper, No effect other than into DM (if not already).  On a dr1 sniper, they'd suffer Casualty Reduction and go into DM.

- Even when a stun result (or bog check, etc.) forces an AFV to stop, it is still considered a moving target for the rest of the turn, correct? 

Assuming it has entered at least one new hex, I believe (or began in Motion).  See C.8:

 C.8 MOVING VEHICULAR TARGET: A vehicle is considered a 
moving target for To Hit/Effects purposes only if during the current Play-
er Turn it has entered a new hex, or used VBM (D2.3), or began its MPh in 
Motion (D2.4), or is currently in Motion. A Stopped (D2.13) vehicle is also 
treated as a moving target if during the current Player Turn it has entered 
a new hex, used VBM, or began its MPh in Motion. Thus a Non-Stopped 
vehicle is a moving, Mobile (D.7) vehicle that has not expended a Stop MP 
(D2.13) since its last Start MP (D2.12) expenditure. Expenditure of MP 
for other purposes (such as loading/unloading, Bog Removal attempts, or 
VCA changes) do not by themselves qualify a vehicle as a moving target 
although they too allow Defensive First Fire shots vs it.

title: WA in a situation with OVR?
question:
We had a US HS that had Wall Advantage (WA), but what then overrun by a German StuG and pinned (not broken).  The StuG then moved across the wall and stopped.  We weren't sure if the US unit loses WA due to the OVR and, if they did, whether the StuG then gains WA when it moves across because the US unit was Pinned and both units were able to attempt to claim WA.

Or if the OVR doesn't remove WA (or the Pin doesn't)?

Note: there is NO in-hex TEM for the US HS ...
author: kbernatz
consensus_answer:
We had a US HS that had Wall Advantage (WA), but what then overrun by a German StuG and pinned (not broken).  The StuG then moved across the wall and stopped.  We weren't sure if the US unit loses WA due to the OVR and, if they did, whether the StuG then gains WA when it moves across because the US unit was Pinned and both units were able to attempt to claim WA.

Or if the OVR doesn't remove WA (or the Pin doesn't)?

Note: there is NO in-hex TEM for the US HS ...
A unit cannot claim WA when it is "in a Location containing a non-hidden, non-prisoner enemy [EXC: "broken" vehicle (A12.1)] unit" [B9.32]. If it has WA when such an enemy unit enters its Location it must forfeit WA [B9.322]. When the StuG enters the Location neither unit can have WA for this same reason, OVR or not. The OVR is conducted and the DEFENDER becomes Pinned in the non-WA state. A Pinned unit may neither voluntarily claim nor forfeit WA [B9.322], but in this case WA is mandatory. When the StuG exits the hex the DEFENDER has first right to claim WA so the Pinned unit reclaims WA if otherwise allowed.  Even if the DEFENDER weren't Pinned, when the StuG exits the hex the DEFENDER cannot claim WA because it is not one of the five times that allow WA to be claimed by the DEFENDER. As it exited the StuG did not forfeit any WA, which would be the only way for the DEFENDER to claim it. On the other hand this being the StuG's MPh the StuG could claim WA as it enters the next hex assuming it is otherwise allowed.

replies.body:
Being pinned or broken does not force forfeiting the WA status. Also, if the case is for a mandatory WA, then they cannot forfeit it.
So the HS but be pinned but still have the WA, and the StuG not.
