title: Vehicle bogged and in cc
question:
May I enquire please. 
A Pz 4 with 3/5 MGs is bogged in a building and enters CC. 
What is the FP of this tank for cc? Would the hull MG be added? FP 8? 
Or would only the CMG of 3 is used?

Also, would the immobilised penalty of -1 be applied to bog vehicles?  
Thanks in advance.
author: alexisW
consensus_answer:
May I enquire please. 
A Pz 4 with 3/5 MGs is bogged in a building and enters CC. 
What is the FP of this tank for cc? Would the hull MG be added? FP 8? 
Or would only the CMG of 3 is used?

Also, would the immobilised penalty of -1 be applied to bog vehicles?  
Thanks in advance. 
The hull MG is never used to attack in CC although its presence will negate the "no usable MGs" CC DRM. Only the CMG, (manned) AAMG, RMG and/or IFE for weapon ≤ 15mm are usable to attack in CC [A11.62]. 

You are reading the vehicle MG factors wrong. They are BMG/CMG [D1.8]. The CMG of the Pz IV is five FP, not three FP. 

The -1 penalty is for an immobile vehicle. Per the index immobile is, "any vehicle which is Abandoned, Bogged, Immobilized, Shocked, or Stunned." Note that "immobile" and "immobilized" are not the same thing, although a vehicle that is immobilized is immobile.

You did not mention this but I will throw it in. When a vehicle attacks infantry its MGs and/or IFE are used in ratio against the infantry's CCV, not against the printed FP. This is different from how infantry attack each other. So if a Pz IV with a five FP CMG attacks a Soviet 6-2-8, the attack is at five (CMG FP) to five (squad CCV) i.e. 1:1, not five to six.

title: mines in single story building
question:
Am I right
A-P Mines attack in building(single story house) and in open ground(bypass area)?
AFV has to go into building to clear mines in bypass area?
author: Nslcole
consensus_answer:
Am I right
A-P Mines attack in building(single story house) and in open ground(bypass area)?
AFV has to go into building to clear mines in bypass area?

Mines don't apply in the building but since there's no way to enter/exit a single-hex building without going through the non-building part of the hex, that's irrelevant.

The only way to clear mines in the bypass area would be to completely clear the mines from the hex, i.e. by putting a trailbreak across all six hexsides [B24.74]. Otherwise a trailbreak across a hexside does not affect mine attacks for units in bypass of that hexside.

title: Line of Sight Question
question:
Can the Partisan unit in BB6 see the German unit in DD9? I'm not sure because the building touches the vertex that they need to shoot through.

Per A6.1, that LOS is clear because if you stretched a thread from hex BB6 to hex DD9 the building obstacle would not appear on both sides of the thread along hexside BB7/CC7.

Now if the BB6/CC7 hexside was hypothetically a rowhouse black bar hexside, then that would depend on how the artwork on the map is drawn.  Since rowhouse black bars block LOS (at other than rooftop levels).  And some rowhouse blackbar artwork is more intrusive into the vertex/adjacent hex than others, depending on the map in use and the LOS in question.  For example:  If a rowhouse black bar on the BB6/CC7 hexside protruded into BB7 such that the subject LOS of your question, when checked with a thread, showed rowhouse black bar on both sides of the thread along the BB7/CC7 hexside, then the LOS would be blocked.

title: Human Wave, HW Units, Pin & Heat of Battle
question:
The units participating in the HW are termed HW Units; they lose any concealment and are exempt from Heat of Battle, PAATC, and any pin results [EXC: Minimum Move (4.134), Wounded SMC (17.2), Collapsed huts (G5.5)] while they are part of the HW; for the remainder of that Player Turn they have their Morale Level increased by one [EXC: if broken] and are Lax (11.18).

 A unit remains a HW Unit (even if no longer adjacent to another HW Unit) until it is: eliminated; broken; out of MF at the end of an Impulse; at the start of an Impulse in a Location (or in a hex with a pillbox) containing an armed, Known enemy unit; or is a Guard due to capturing a SMC/Unarmed/Disrupted unit (25.234).

Does the quoted rules mean that during the HW the HW units cannot Pin or HoB, but at the end of the HW (whether out of MF or have entered Enemy Location), they can?
author: norev
consensus_answer: I believe the timing of the loss of 'HW unit' status is missed by a lot of players - many continue to apply the HW unit effects (no Pin/HoB/PAATC) during the DFPh which is clearly (IMO) incorrect. replies.body:
Does the quoted rules mean that during the HW the HW units cannot Pin or HoB, but at the end of the HW (whether out of MF or have entered Enemy Location), they can?
The rules in fact say a HW unit *can* Pin but only in unusual circumstances. To your question there are no "Human Wave units" once the Human Wave ends. There are only former Human Wave Units. The rules here become a bit vague, but I believe per D14.32 the Impulse does not end until all DFF is complete. If a DEFENDER wants to fire after the HW expends its last MF, it has two options. It can fire during the MPh on the MF expenditure for the last Impulse, which will allow FFNAM & FFMO, but will prevent Pin (for the most part) and HoB. Or it can wait until the DFPh, when Pin & HoB can happen, but of course FFMO & FFNAM no longer apply.

If a German attacker pins a Russian defender, when is that pin removed? At the end of the German CC phase or does it last through the upcoming Russian turn?
A7.8 "Remove all Pin counters at the end of the current Player Turn or if the unit subsequently breaks/goes-berserk/Battle-Hardens/becomes-heroic (whichever comes first)."

Information/status counters are supposed to be color-coded per A.12 (point-one-two, not twelve). Red-on-white counters are removed at the end of the CCPh.

ASL is not a linear map from time in the real world to time in the game and vice versa. A Pin that occurs in the first DR of the turn does not necessarily reflect two minutes spent keeping heads down. Trying to apply real world measures to game mechanics seems to me to be a somewhat misdirected way to view them. I second that as they mirror my thoughts on ASL as well.  And that is not developed in a void, if you study the various designer notes and footnotes and General/Journal articles, etc.  you will see that you have to look at that Game Turn (consisting of 2 player turns) as a total mish mash of random/player controlled occurences happening within a 2 minute time frame.  All of this can not be played out in real time/real world sequence in the realm of a cardboard game that is enjoyable to play.  The abstraction factor in time sequence is a real thing to understand when evaluating the cardboard game as an approximation of events occurring within a set time frame, but not actually played tit for tat second by second (which would be unmanageable and unplayable and definitely not fun in terms of a cardboard game).

If you want the real deal time frame stuff, then I suggest you try playing the Combat Mission series of PC games (such as Combat Mission: Normandy and Combat Mission: Fortress Italy ... there is a Russian Front and Late war version out of it as well).  The Combat Mission series of PC games was developed by some of the people who were working the concept of "ASL for computer" for Avalon Hill in the late 90s.  When AH dissolved, some of the developers of "ASL for computer" went on to create the "Close Combat" series of PC games, while other developers of "ASL for computer" went on to work on the "Combat Mission" series of PC games.  In my opinion, the "Combat Mission" series is much better than the "Close Combat" series, and captures "ASL for computer" in the best terms ... and it is NO boardgame.  It is real time sequence with 3D graphics and absolutely unforgiving to the player.  Example:  Attacking an immobilized Tiger with an American squad with a bazooka creeping along a stone wall in real time back and forth firing and a previously concealed/unknown German halftrack in the woods on the flank opens up on the American squad with a MG42 and they are nearly wiped out in an instant (half the squad KIA and the rest wounded or broken).  

My point being that it takes a PC game to put everything in timeline sequence ... to try to do so with a boardgame at ASL level of tactical would make an unplayable, not enjoyable monster of a mess.

If you’re interested in a “simultaneous movement” type WWII squad level game system, you may want to check out Storm Over Arnhem. 

It also offers a very interesting possibility to compare game design choices, when played next to ASL’s A Bridge too Far… :)

title: Flooded Stream
question:
Greetings, gentlemen!

I need your help with clarifying the rules. After reading all the rules related to Streams, Ponds, and checking the Terrain Chart, I couldn’t find any information about the movement cost for infantry for entering a flooded stream. We are currently playing the scenario "Dreil Team" (FCaC) and faced the issue of crossing a flooded stream. I read what people are saying on BGG, and opinions seem to be divided—some say the movement cost is 4 mp for infantry, while others say it's not passable at all. So, where is the truth?... 

Thank you for your attention and answers.
author: Gromstal
consensus_answer:
Greetings Danil.
Here is my take. B20.44 states that a flooded stream is treated as a flooded pond (one level higher than normal) and becomes a Water Obstacle (B21.1 states Water Obstacle is a body of water large enough to stop the normal movement of men and vehicles, which cannot enter without special assistance.). Section B21.4 states "Entrance of a Water Obstacle hex is usually limited to units on a bridge, boat, or amphibious vehicle. Otherwise, entrance is limited to swimming or fording by Personnel units." The Terrain Chart shows a Water Obstacle, for Infantry, as using ALL MF but only if fordable. Therefore, I believe Infantry will have to use boats or swim to cross a water obstacle w/o a bridge.

title: OVR versus Bog result versus OVR flowchart
question:
So an ENEMY AFV announces a combined woods entrance MP + OVR MP expenditure against FRIENDLY infantry in a woods hex as a combined MP expenditure.

Per D7.1,  - The OVR MP expenditure must be
announced as a combined expenditure with that for entrance of the hex as
the vehicle enters the OVR hex, unless that hex contains only unknown
enemy units (A12.41). An OVRing vehicle may not declare a Gun Duel
(C2.2401); instead, the OVR is resolved on the IFT immediately after the
MP expenditure [EXC: Bog DR, and defensive First Fire other than Reaction Fire (7.2), prompted by that MP expenditure (or by the MF expenditure of accompanying Infantry using Human Wave {A25.23} and Armored Assault {9.31}) are resolved first]

The ENEMY AFV Bogs.

Per D8.21, - If a Final Bog Check DR is ≥ 12, the vehicle bogs, is
marked with a Bog counter, and must end its MPh immediately. 

So my interpretation of that combination of D7.1 and D8.21 is that the ENEMY AFV's Mph ends immediately, and thus NO OVR attack occurs.

Is my interpretation correct?

The only thing giving me qualms about this is that the OVR flowchart does not tell you to STOP and move no further down the flowchart if the AFV Bogs (or falls through a cellar. etc.).

Also, using the OVR flowchart, it is hard to determine what the FRIENDLY infantry units occupying the OVR target hex have as DFF/DF options -

Are they limited to standard DFF/DF options separate from the OVR rules/flowchart since the OVR didn't occur?

Or do they have the options (and which options) for in hex DFF/Reaction Fire following further down the OVR chart (given that the ENEMY AFV did declare OVR MP as simultaneous expenditure ... or is all that completely negated by the Bog result?
author: Xenophobic_Luddite
consensus_answer:
Per D8.21, - If a Final Bog Check DR is ≥ 12, the vehicle bogs, is
marked with a Bog counter, and must end its MPh immediately. 

So my interpretation of that combination of D7.1 and D8.21 is that the ENEMY AFV's Mph ends immediately, and thus NO OVR attack occurs.

The ending of the unit's MPh should be interpreted as meaning the vehicle may not make any more expenditures. But the expenditure that led to the bog has to be fully resolved. So any residual attacks and/or OBA attacks and/or DFF attacks allowed by that expenditure are resolved. Likewise as was stated a previously-announced OVR attack is also resolved at half FP.

title: Let me guess, Heros are supposed to deal with subsequent wounds just like Leaders because A15 (HOB rules) are lower numbered than A17 (SMC Wounds)?
question:
So the rules for Heros in A15 state that a wounded Hero that fails a MC is eliminated.

However, the Wound rules in A17 state that a wounded SMC who is wounded again takes its wound severity dr with a +1 modifier (i.e., 50% chance to survive the second wound and keep operating as a wounded SMC).  And there is no mention in A17 of an exception for Heros.

Thus applying the "higher numbered/organized rules supersede lower numbered/organized rules" admonition toward the beginning of Chapter A, a wounded Hero that is wounded again should deal with it as specified in A17 (rather than being outright eliminated as stated in A15).

 Is that correct?  Or am I missing an official Q&A on this?

(And darn ... last turn on current game I outright eliminated my wounded Hero per instructions in A15 ... but then thought about it later that it didn't make sense that a Leader could theoretically be wounded a dozen times and keep on functioning, but a Hero has no such capability 😪 ... and then what about a wounded Heroic Leader? ... does A15, or rather A17, apply to that?)
author: Xenophobic_Luddite
consensus_answer: Per A15.2, "If a wounded hero fails a MC it is eliminated." It would not be wounded a second time for failing a MC while wounded, and so A17.11 does not apply. A *broken* leader is wounded for failing a MC because that is a CR [A10.3], but of course a hero can never be broken.

I think of it as a just payment for my opponents getting free use of a hero.

title: Area Target Type Critical Hit on a Gun and Crew.
question:
Can anyone help me with this situation?

A 50mm mortar fires at wooden building containing an enemy Gun with a crew and rolls a Critical Hit of 1,1.  It must use Area Target Type, so is not targeting the gun, it is targeting the hex.  The To Kill DR will be on the IFT Table, column 12, with a -2DRM.

Does C3.74 apply?  The wording is not clear: 

"Regardless of the number of targets in the a Location, struck by a CH, the special provisions of a CH only apply to the target(s) determined by Random Selection.  Attacks on other units hit in that Location ...."

As I understand it, a Gun can be a target, but it is not a unit.

So is it just the crew that gets hit (with no Random Selection), and the gun only takes a possible C11.6 (Gun Destruction Table) result?

Or does random selection apply, and either the gun or the crew gets the CH, the other getting a standard "2+2" attack?

That would seem odd, as C11.6  says a CH is N/A to a gun.  Meaning that if the gun is selected, the CH is wasted and the crew only take a FP 2 + 2 attack?  

As it happens, my TK DR was also a 1,1 so I think both the gun and the crew have been vaporised, but I would love someone to explain to me what the correct method should be.

Is this something that has come up many times before and I have just never seen it?  Or is it just very late and I'm not thinking straight.
author: tward3
consensus_answer:
See C11.4 (and see C3.71 for the same): "A CH automatically destroys both the Gun and its manning Infantry." You don't even need to roll for effect on the IFT, both are gone from this world.
I did read those, but because I was using ATT I didn't think it applied: I was not firing at the gun, but at the hex.  Which is why I fell into the "Random Selection" hole.
When you use ITT or ATT you are really firing at all eligible targets in the Location or Hex. For ITT in C3.32 it says that all PRC and non-AFV "in-LOS enemy units in that Location can be hit." Similarly C3.33 says, all "(including friendly) non-Aerial units in the target hex can be hit ." The text of the rules is somewhat casual about the difference between "firing at a hex," "firing at a Location" and firing at eligible targets in that hex or Location. They should be considered the same.

Similarly the rules are somewhat confusing about "firing at a Gun" and "firing at the crew manning a Gun." These again are equivalent, i.e. anything that attacks the Gun also attacks the crew of that Gun and vice-versa. For instance if inherent FP is fired at a manned Gun and its crew, if the result is a KIA then A9.74, RANDOM SW/GUN DESTRUCTION, will apply. As an aside this is also true of possessed SW, but there is no rule like C11.4 for possessed SW resulting in automatic destruction.

replies.body: You don't separate the crew from the Gun.

One way to think about it is that a Gun is a "very large support weapon" carried by the crew.  That is why the crew is located under the Gun, just like if manning a LMG or HMG, etc.  So the 'Gun' is not targetable any more than one could fire at the LMG counter or HMG counter...

title: Broken infantry after overrun
question: Hi, I'm struggling through Khamsin desert scenario and trying to learn the effects of overruns. I'm not sure what happens to an infantry unit that was broken due to overrun and the overrunning vehicle remained in the hex. Does the infantry unit survive the Rout Phase and stay in place? Does it fight in CC phase? Can someone explain, please?
author: Daath
consensus_answer:
Just apply A10.5 and A10.51.
A broken unit can get ADJACENT to a KEU only if it is leaving that KEU's Location. So the broken unit can rout away from the vehicle, notwithstanding other constraints of not getting nearer to other enemy units, etc. Note that if the broken unit ends its rout ADJACENT to the vehicle it will be eliminated for FtR, so Low Crawl is not an option. That means that the unit will be probably interdicted by other enemies, if able to.

This situation can happen with vehicles and also when berserk units or cavalry enter an enemy location during movement.

If by some situation at the start of the CCPh a broken unit is in the same Location as enemy units, the broken unit cannot fight and cannot escape. It has to wait for a Melee to be created and then it must Witdraw from Melee.

title: Fire Lanes
question:

The situation is a MMC has a MG and I don’t want to Cancel an existing fire lane.

1) If only the MG first fires and successfully puts down a fire lane, can the MMC first fire at another enemy unit without canceling the FL?
2) If the MMC has already first fired, can the MMC SFF at an enemy unit without cancelling the FL?

I believe the answer to both questions is, yes.

Please confirm and expand upon any other FL errata till your heart is content. Thank you.
author: Bombadil929

#1 - Yes.

A9.223:
"A MG may cancel its Fire Lane in order to gain freedom to fire elsewhere (/its manning Infantry may use Subsequent-First-Fire/FPF after establishing the Fire Lane) only if a TPBF/CC-Reaction-Fire situation occurs (8.312/D7.21)—in which case the Fire Lane must be cancelled"

title: Night Rules +1 Attack Modifier
question:
Is the +1 modifier for Night attacks applicable to Fortifications (Foxholes etc) on higher ground.
Height Advantage and the Night modifier are not both applied where a unit is outside any fortification but as the choice of Height Advantage still exists instead of use of the Foxhole modifier, I think the Night modifier would not be applied.
A Height Advantage modifier could be chosen instead of the foxhole but I've never found the situation where I wouldn't use it.
author: csonson
consensus_answer:
Height Advantage and the Night modifier are not both applied where a unit is outside any fortification but as the choice of Height Advantage still exists instead of use of the Foxhole modifier, I think the Night modifier would not be applied.
If a unit has height advantage [B10.31] or its possibility, that *usually* means the night LV DRM cannot apply. The unit is on terrain that is above the firer, and in most cases terrain that is one full level above the firer, which negates Night LV [E1.7]. Hillocks, where the target is ½ level above firer, explicitly denies height advantage [F6.51]. But the other case where a unit can be ½ level above the firer, rooftops, allows height advantage [B23.81]. So for rooftops it is possible to get both Night LV and Height Advantage.

But it is important to understand that Night LV denial is not keyed to the level of the *target unit*. It depends on the height of the *terrain*. The unit can be at any (legal of course) height in that terrain, and it will not affect whether Night LV applies or not. A unit in a level zero woods/orchard or the ground level of a building will not get the Night LV hindrance when fired on by an enemy unit also at level zero. The existence or absence of Fortifications and the target's status as in or out of any Fortification will not change whether Night LV applies, perhaps primarily because Fortifications do not increase the level of the terrain.

title: Abandoned bulldozers
question:
I recently played FT292, "Engineer Hill." It features an Abandoned, armored bulldozer. This is my attempt at a summary of the rules for such a thing.

The reason it is not obvious how such a thing should work in ASL is because bulldozers do not have crews; they have Inherent Drivers [G15.11]. Per D5.1 an Inherent Driver "never leaves the vehicle" [D5.1]. It is not possible to create an Abandoned Bulldozer by dismounting the Driver during the course of play if you start with a manned one. However per G15.111 an *unarmored* bulldozer can have its Inherent Driver killed (by small arms/MG fire), leaving it Abandoned. Presumably an armored bulldozer could have its Inherent Driver killed and become Abandoned by being attacked with sufficient elevation advantage so it is treated as unarmored [D5.311]. Abandoned bulldozers are possible, just not by using D5.4 (in general; see below about A21.21).

In this scenario the Americans start with two heroes in the same hex as the Abandoned bulldozer. The Japanese VC include CVP, a bulldozer is worth four CVP out of twenty needed for the scenario (eight CVP if captured), so the Americans would like to save the bulldozer if possible, and if not possible then to make sure it ends up destroyed. They might just attack it and be done, but there is a fair chance that they will want to insert one of the heroes as the new Driver.

Remanning a bulldozer (or other Abandoned vehicle which take an Inherent Driver)

D5.42 says, "An Infantry unit may enter an Abandoned vehicle to become its Inherent crew only if it occupies that vehicle's Location at the start of its MPh (not APh) and expends all of its MF to do so." But a bulldozer does not have an Inherent crew, only an Inherent Driver. Disregarding the reality argument that the two ought to be pretty much the same, it is not clear that D5.42 allows a unit to become (if a SMC) (or possibly install if a MMC) an Inherent Driver in the MPh. If it were allowed by D5.42, would the unit (which might be a MMC) be removed to become the Inherent Driver? Would a MMC instead re-crew the vehicle expending all its MF and not be able to move elsewhere? From what I read a unit can re-man a vehicle only if it becomes the Inherent crew, not the Inherent Driver. But that could easily be wrong.

Although I think these are questions that should have answers, in this particular scenario they are probably not important. The Japanese move first, and Abandoned vehicles can be "captured" (re-manned) in the CCPh [A21.2]. The Japanese do not have enough MF to enter the hex with the bulldozer, so in most playings it can be "captured" by one of the two American heroes in the Japanese first player turn CCPh. It will probably then attempt to drive away in the American player turn, which at least prevents it from being lost with double CVP. 

Attacking an Abandoned bulldozer

Per a q&a, "An Abandoned vehicle is a unit, but it is neither friendly nor enemy and can be attacked by either side." In case the Americans want to destroy the Abandoned instead of capturing/re-manning it they can.

Getting a SMC back out after putting it in as Inherent Driver.

If the Americans do decide to try to save the bulldozer by re-manning it, they may want to get the hero back out of it. A21.21 says, "If the vehicle was captured by a SMC, that SMC is removed until the vehicle takes on a new crew (D5.42) or is Abandoned." It is not clear if A21.21 allows all vehicles (including those with just inherent drivers) to be abandoned, apparently overriding D5.1, or it just says that new inherent driver can be installed for those vehicles that can be Abandoned and are. Likewise it says the SMC can be removed once a new crew is installed per D5.42, but one of the requirements for using D5.42 is that the vehicle is Abandoned. Perhaps A21.21 says D5.42 can also be used if the vehicle is not abandoned but rather has a SMC Temporary Driver. After a while of parsing and re-parsing these rules I think I will punt and say that a SMC Temporary Driver can Abandon a vehicle that only has an Inherent Driver despite D5.1, and can also leave the vehicle at the same time a MMC installs a new (permanent) Inherent Driver or a different SMC becomes Temporary Driver per A21.21.

These are my understandings of how Abandoned bulldozers should be handled. If anyone thinks I have misunderstood something or if I have missed some aspect, let me know.
author: jrvjrv
consensus_answer:
4 CVP for a bulldozer ? 
It's an Armored bulldozer. Much, much more valuable than an ordinary bulldozer. See G15.12.

Edit: Sub shots would be 8 factors with ROF 2, for completeness
author: kbernatz
consensus_answer:
So I've managed to pull off a nirvana situation where I have two heroes manning a MMG along with a 10-2 leader in the hex (and another MMC+MMG).  My understanding is that this gives us a 12 -4 (German MMGs with the MMC being a 4-6-7) out to 12 hexes, with a ROF 2.  But is there a restriction on the hero being able to apply his DRM if he is sharing manning a MG with another hero?

Edit: Sub shots would be 8 factors with ROF 2, for completeness
Twelve FP down four (plus any other DRM, e.g. TEM, hindrance, etc.) is correct for a MMG manned by two heros and a second MMG manned by a 4-6-7 directed by a -2 leader from range two out to range twelve. Range zero and range one would be more of course. Heroic DRM are cumulative, unlike leadership DRM, and one leadership DRM in addition to the heroic DRMs can also be added. The hero "firing" the MG (i.e. its possessor) and the hero "assisting" both use their heroic DRM out to the normal range of MG.

title: ESB / Mechanical Reliability / Motion Attempt
question:
I just want to make sure I interpret the rules correctly. Reading D2.5 (ESB) and D2.51 (MR), its seems these rules are for vehicles during IT's MPh. Motion Attempt (D2.401) is a rule for vehicles during IT's DFPh. Yes?

Scenario is BoF14: Cocktails For Molotov (I'm enjoying this one). The situation is: A stopped Russian BT-5 M34 (red MP) facing west on 51R5 and another stopped facing Northeast in 51S5. A stack of Polish 7-0/457 w/DC is in 51S7 with a burning Russian BA-6 in 51S6. It's the Polish MPh and is willing to attack the AFV in 51R5 going through the burning wreck and attack from it's rear. Both Russian AFV's have had the Polish stack in it's LOS. So in reading D2.401, neither AFV can make a Motion attempt in order to change it's VCA/TCA. Am I correct or am I missing something?

If the AFV's were allowed to make a Motion attempt, would an MR still be required?
author: dansp
consensus_answer:
I think this is the situation as you described it:

Getting warm in here

Yes, barring other information, a Motion Attempt would be the best option for the BTs, but since that's off the table they should turn their VCAs during Defensive First Fire to face the oncoming Polish infantry.  It will add another +1 DRM to your shot over just turning the turret, but the Poles will then suffer the +1 DRM for placing the DC through the front hull facing (C7.346).  

Also, it wasn't clear who possessed the DC, the leader or the squad.  Three reasons to give DCs to leaders are:

- Leaders have six MF, giving you a few more options when operating with a DC.

- Leaders are elite, so the DC doesn't suffer a lowered malfunction number (B23.2).  It's rarely an issue in my experience but this case is an exception - the DC TK is high enough that any roll eliminates the BT, assuming a successful placement (final DR of 8 or less), unless the DC malfunctions.  With the squad, that occurs on a ten or higher, but only on boxcars with the leader.

- Most importantly in this particular situation, leaders don't need to take a PAATC to place a DC on an enemy AFV, so that's one less DR you have to sweat.

There are also good reasons *not* to give a DC to a leader - placing a demo charge is dangerous work and your leaders usually have a host of other responsibilities as well.

Good luck!

title: SW MG Bore Sighting at Night vs NVR
question:
So I just ran into a complicated "analysis paralysis" inducing ASL rules quandary.  Usually I can "Sherlock Holmes" my way through the ASL rules to figure this stuff out, but this one is not quite showing me the solution.  While I am soloing my current scenario (KGP1) and could just "go with my gut," I can imagine that if I was in a face-to-face game this issue could raise an argument between players on rules interpretation, so I would like to see what some of the "expert gurus" think of this.

First off, just the facts -

A9.22 tells us that NVR does not affect the placement of a MG Fire Lane (i.e., a termination point for the MG Fire Lane at Night can be placed beyond NVR provided there would be a LOS not blocked by Obstacle during Daytime)

Nothing in the KGP1 SSRs or the overarching KG SSRs tell you that you can't Bore Sight, but KG CG SSR 12 reveals that the Design Intent is that no Bore Sighting is allowed in KGP with the EXCEPTION of SW MG in Night scenarios (thus my interpretation that the American Scenario Defenders in KGP1 should be able to Bore Sight their SW MMG/HMG).

E1.71 provides an EXCEPTION to Fire Lanes that I want to learn to exploit along the lines of a MMG/HMG may place a Fire Lane at Night (provided a starshell/IR has been fired during the scenario) without firing at a particular moving enemy unit TO a Bore Sighted location.

Chapter C Bore Sighting rules make no mentions of NVR or rule E1.71 and only refer to "LOS"

Now to my question/quandary -

In a nutshell, is Bore Sighting as described above limited by NVR?  or is NVR irrelevant to Bore Sighting in this situation given that Fire Lanes are allowed beyond NVR? 

What "my gut" tells me (and here comes the danger of a "realism argument") is that the Bore Sighted location can be beyond NVR because the defenses (historically in this scenario) were set up before Night fell.

Otherwise, what is the point of E1.71 Exception???

title: Halftrack passengers, STUN and disembark
question:
Assume the following situation during the German Movement Phase:
A SPW 251/1 with a 8-3-8 Passenger squad moves ADJACENT to a Russian 6-2-8+LMG using its 8th MP. The Russian squad fires 16FP, resulting in a 1MC versus the CE crew and Passenger.
The 8-3-8 passes the 1MC valiantly, but the SPW crew rolls an “8” and is stunned. 
Question 1: Is it correct to put the whole stack, including the 8-3-8, beneath a BU counter (as per D5.33-34)?
Question 2: Can the 8-3-8 disembark?
Question 3: Can the 8-3-8 take the LMG of the SPW (D6.631)?
Question 4: Will the 8-3-8 be attacked by a 6FP Residual?
Question 5: Does the 8-3-8 have 2MF in total because the stun result vs. the SPW crew stops the AFV without the need to spend a MP to stop (D5.34)?
Question 6: At the end of the turn, the Stun marker will be flipped to the +1 side. But the BU counter remains in place, correct?
author: Lebenslicht
consensus_answer:
This strikes me as in violation of the whole rationale behind a vehicle needing to "expend" all of its MP if it moves at all in a MPh. The expenditure of delay MP represents the inevitable ticking of the clock since the vehicle's whereabouts need to be known and its status accounted for in any given time slice. If a vehicle moves and uses half of its MP and is then stunned (and forced to stop), it makes no sense under that stated rationale that the remaining MP would not be "considered spent" in Delay, for Defensive Fire purposes (as the original poster asked). If it's the way you state here JRV, then there is a space-time discontinuity, which does not happen in our universe (except maybe in a black hole).
Although a vehicle *usually* has to expend all its MP, there are cases where it does not. D2.4, "A vehicle may end its MPh in Motion without expending all of its MP only if it has insufficient MP remaining to enter the next hex it wishes to enter." So if a vehicle is currently not stopped and has, say, four MP left, and the next hex it wants to enter is up a hill (four MP plus COT), it may end in Motion without expending the last four MP. Although this appears to conflict with D2.1, "A vehicle which ends its MPh with MP remaining is assumed to use all those MP in that hex," there is a q&a:

D2.1 & D2.4
Assume the AFV enters the bypass Location from B2 and announces a MP expenditure of 2. As it does so, presume it has MPs remaining. May the AFV declare a desire to enter into D2 for more MPs than it has left, remain in C2 and place a Motion Counter?
A. No.
Assume the AFV has less than Half its MPs left. May it declare a desire to enter into D1, have insufficient MPs left, remain in C2 and place a motion counter?
A. No.
Follow up, to enter D1, it would have to continue to bypass around to the C2/D2 hexside. Assuming it has done so and now has less than half MPs left, may it now declare a desire to enter D1 without bypass and stay in C2 with a motion counter in accordance with D2.4?
A. Not if it has enough MP to enter in bypass. 
Is an AFV required to enter a new hex/hexside if it is able to before falling back on D2.4?
A. It must be unable to enter the hex in its VCA (or RVCA if moving in reverse) it desires to enter.
Does D2.4 only kick in if the AFV has no movement options left that do not require ESB?
A. No; see above.
When you say “It must be unable to enter the hex in its VCA (or RVCA if moving in reverse) it desires to enter” what happens to the remaining MPs?
A. Those MP disappear (D2.4).

Also when a vehicle Bogs it "must end its MPh immediately" [D8.21]. There is a q&a that says it is still subject to DFF, but it is not clarified whether this is just for the expenditure that caused the Bog, or whether it is considered to also be liable for DFF for MP that remain beyond that. I would be interested in seeing a q&a that clarified this, but only out of curiosity right now. If a vehicle moves into LOS for one MP but Bogs, can the defender wait for four MP in LOS and fire in that MPh, or must it wait for the DFPh?

It has never been clear to me what the purpose is for trying to account for all vehicle MP most of the time but not all. It is possible that it was done to make it harder to VBM freeze, forcing the vehicle either to stop so it can spend delay MPs or enter with no MPs left to exit, i.e. to commit to the VBM freeze rather than allowing it to see what happens and possibly move on. Or it may be to cover the case when a HIP Gun pops out and fires on the expenditure, missing but keeping ROF; the moving vehicle can't terminate its vulnerability to further attacks just by declaring its MPh at end, which is in contrast to what infantry may do. Anyway it doesn't seem to be a desire to perform simulation of physical reality; MP available disappear in some cases, just as MF are always allowed to do.

On  thinking on this more, I suspect my second guess is the reason that vehicles have to continue their MPh to its termination (usually). If an AT Gun has executed a perfect ambush but missed with its first shot, the vehicle can't get out of the hole it is in by immediately terminating its MPh and having other units perform their MPh in a way that saves the ambushed vehicle. That's a play purpose, not a literal simulation purpose. This does not always work out, so if the ambush is sprung on the last MP then of course other units can now try to rescue the ambushed vehicle, but it is a nice compromise between the game mechanics and what would happen in reality. And the fact that MP can be made to "disappear" will only rarely be of use to a vehicle caught in an AT ambush.

In contrast infantry can decide to drop to ground, so allowing infantry to end its MPh without spending more MF and without being attacked again is not so wrong an implementation of how things would work in reality.

But I was not present at the design discussions, so all this is just guess. Still I think a plausible guess.

title: Residual FP and placement of DC
question:
A 8.22, 2nd bullet point states: "Residual FP does not attack until any activity that a MF/MP expenditure allowed is completed (e.g., placing SMOKE grenades, SW Recovery, Searching, firing a Smoke Dispenser, etc.) [EXC: entering a vehicle; (un)hooking; D5.43]."

Assume a squad equipped with a DC enters a hex containing a 4 FP residual FP and survives the attack unpinned. It then spends another 2 MF to place the DC in an adjacent woods hex. According to the rule above, the squad would be attacked by the residual again but only after completing the placement of the DC. Does this mean the DC will attack in the AFPh regardless of the result of the second residual attack?
author: Lebenslicht
consensus_answer:
Thanks so much for the clarification! So, if the first attack vs. the squad entering the hex is "normal" FP and the second attack (for the 2MF placement) is residual, will a PIN (or better) result vs. the squad actually cancel the placement of the DC? Because my understanding of the second bullet point of A 8.22 is that the attack only happens AFTER the activity is completed.

Yes, anything that happens to the squad as a result of the placement MF expenditure (pinned, broken, etc.) will cancel the DC attack.

See rule A23.3 that covers DC placement where it states  -

"Should the Placing unit survive (unbroken and unpinned, even if newly berserk) all enemy Defensive First Fire, Subsequent First Fire, and FPF in the Placement Hex (including any resulting from the expenditure of MF in the Placement of that DC), the weapon is considered operably Placed. Thereafter, the Placing unit may move away or suffer adverse results with no effect to the DC. However, if the Placing unit is broken, pinned, or eliminated before or during Placement, the DC is not operably Placed, remains with the Placing unit (or in the Placing unit’s Location if the unit is eliminated), and may not attack—
although it is still usable for future Recovery/Placement attempts."

replies.body:
A 8.22, 2nd bullet point states: "Residual FP does not attack until any activity that a MF/MP expenditure allowed is completed (e.g., placing SMOKE grenades, SW Recovery, Searching, firing a Smoke Dispenser, etc.) [EXC: entering a vehicle; (un)hooking; D5.43]."

Assume a squad equipped with a DC enters a hex containing a 4 FP residual FP and survives the attack unpinned. It then spends another 2 MF to place the DC in an adjacent woods hex. According to the rule above, the squad would be attacked by the residual again but only after completing the placement of the DC. Does this mean the DC will attack in the AFPh regardless of the result of the second residual attack?
In this case the unit would not be attacked a second time. Per A8.22, "A unit can be attacked by Residual FP only once per Location [EXC: if, since that first Residual FP attack, the Residual FP has increased in strength or the unit is subject to more-negative-DRM/less-positive-DRM, it will be attacked again by that Residual FP upon further MF/MP expenditure]." The EXC does not apply in this case. Once the residual has attacked a unit it will not attack a second time unless one of the conditions in the EXC is met.

The common use case for the "additional expenditure" residual FP attack is when a unit enters a Location that does not have any Residual FP in it, is attacked for entering in a way that leaves a new residual FP counter then attempts an additional expenditure. In that case it *would* be attacked by the residual since it has never been attacked by the residual before. This often happens in DC placement, but again the residual does not attack twice. There are two defensive attacks, but the first is non-residual and only the second is residual FP.

Thanks, Ron. I'm glad to have played it correctly for the past 39 years. 😉 But I still think that A8.22 2nd bullet and A23.3 contradict each other. I would read the former this way: If you throw a smoke grenade, the residual FP will only attack you AFTER placement. So, regardless of the outcome, the smoke placement attempt will not be affected. However, if you place a DC, the residual can (as per A23.3) cancel the placement. I don't quite see the difference between placing SMOKE grenades (and the other examples given in A8.22) and placing a DC. Or is this an example of the rule mentioned in the Introduction: "Lastly, whenever a seeming contradiction appears between rule cases, the higher alpha-numeric rule case always takes precedence, barring mention of a specific exception (e.g., B1 is a higher numbered rule than A1)?"

Yes, the highest numbered rule (in this case A23.3) takes precedence.  

I don't really find it contradictory myself since the A8.22 is about Residual FP (which is a form of DFF when reading A23.3) in general, whereas A23 is specifically about DCs.  When applying General rules found earlier in chapter A to specific weapons/items that have their very own sections in the rulebook (e.g., smoke grenades, DC, FT, BAZ, PIAT, PFs, etc.) it is always important to check the specific rules for the specific weapon/item as they may contain specific instructions/limitations on how they are used.
Thanks, Ron. That makes sense!

title: Rout Question
question: Can a DM broken unit rout to the nearest building/woods hex even if it is out of his LOS?
author: Bombadil929
consensus_answer:
I have a different rout question. I'm just learning ASL so apologies if this is basic. 

The closest building/woods hex to a DM broken unit on the flank is actually forward, two hexes away, not closer to any enemy unit. However, routing to that hex would expose the unit to interdiction or low crawl and forcing it to surrender or be eliminated. The next closest rout target is back where the unit came from, three hexes away and not subject to interdiction, out of view of the enemy.
Is the routing unit forced to select the first hex and surrender?
Yes. Although you may have a sense of "forward" and "backward", the routing units and the rules do not.

Note that the distances to potential rout targets for priority are measured in MF not hexes [A10.51]. I have assumed the potential rout targets in your hypothetical still have the same priority by MF.

Thanks for the quick response. My careful reading of the rules got me to your answer, but it seemed counterintuitive (heh) so I wanted to check before I learned it wrong. And your assumption is correct; the priority holds using MF.

Your situation is why understanding the rout rules is so important. Knowing where is safe to rout from will only improve your game.

replies.body:
Can a DM broken unit rout to the nearest building/woods hex even if it is out of his LOS? 
Yes.

Does not always make reality sense, but them's the rules.

title: Seaborne Assualt
question:
The Americans are conducting a seaborne assault. The LC has 4 MPs. On the fourth MP the LC is beached. I assume that the ramp can remain up and the infantry units can wait until the next Movement Phase before they have to unload “asap”. Correct? 

(There are no vehicles onboard the LC)
author: Bombadil929
consensus_answer:
Could I choose to expend 2 MP (instead of the normal 1 MP) when entering a shallow ocean hex that is adjacent to a beach? 
Since you spent your last MP to enter you can't ESB with a LC. In other circumstances per G12.1 LC are vehicles, so they should be able to spend more MP than required per D2.18.

Or have I misunderstood, and you entered the hex adjacent to the beach on the third MP? In that case the LC can "beach for free" on that same third MP [G12.3; E5.23]. It can then unload on the fourth MP. A boat or LC must expend an "extra" MP if it wants to beach in its current hex and does not use the "beach for free" option when entering the hex.

replies.body:
The Americans are conducting a seaborne assault. The LC has 4 MPs. On the fourth MP the LC is beached. I assume that the ramp can remain up and the infantry units can wait until the next Movement Phase before they have to unload “asap”. Correct? 

(There are no vehicles onboard the LC)
The ramp remains up until the first Passenger unloads [G12.41]. The LC does not have the option to drop its ramp if no Passengers have unloaded. Vehicles aboard the LC will not affect this answer.

Note that the LC is not required to beach itself when it enters a hex adjacent to a shore [G12.3]. There may be reasons to consider not beaching the LC: it remains a Moving Target if not beached. But it will cost one MP to beach spent in the next MPh, and if in the meanwhile the LC is Stunned its CA may change, so there are tradeoffs.

title: Bunker Advantages?
question: Team - please give me some pointers on the advantage of placing a pillbox and a trench counter in the same hex. I am unsure of the tactical advantages. Thank you in advance for any comments on the subject.
author: Bombadil929
consensus_answer:
Team - please give me some pointers on the advantage of placing a pillbox and a trench counter in the same hex. I am unsure of the tactical advantages. Thank you in advance for any comments on the subject.
The only time I have done that is to allow a weapon, usually an HMG, 360 degree fire with the option to duck into the pillbox. Another reason could be protection for more units - 1 unit in a pillbox, 2 more units in the trench.

As an aside, because the pillbox is a separate Location, the stacking limits for a pillbox and its outside (here a trench) are independent. There could be up to three squad squad equivalents inside a large-enough pillbox and another three squad equivalents outside the pillbox, perhaps in a trench, with no overstacking.

These are certainly among the most likely reasons. A pillbox's CA is limited, and at some point the enemy will often try to go around. If the terrain is suitable then putting the trench in an adjacent hex might be acceptable, and if the terrain is not suitable (e.g. a solitary hill hex like like 2F7) then you might choose to put the pillbox and the trench in the same hex. In the other case units, especially crews, are vulnerable to CC in a pillbox, so a Gun crew in a pillbox might be safer with a friendly unit outside. As long as there are friendly units outside units in the pillbox can't be attacked. As mentioned before the presence of a trench outside does create cover for enemy units, but if the enemy can send in infantry for a 2:1 or similar CC attack against a crew, they may take the trade of outside units attacking next turn even if the terrain outside the pillbox is open ground.

That said my first preference would be to have the pillbox and the trench in separate hexes. But I will not say they are never in the same hex.

SMOKE is sort of ambiguous whether it is a good reason for separate hexes. On the one hand one of the two, trench or pillbox, is out of the SMOKE. But on the other hand if the units attacking can use the SMOKE to move ADJACENT to the pillbox, they can Advance in and there's no outside protection; the pillbox dies in most cases.

As for lucky rolls, in most cases attacks only affect one Location. To hit both inside and outside the Pillbox you'd have to use something like Area Target Type, Spraying Fire, Canister or OBA. OBA can affect two hexes just as easily as two Locations. For ATT a CH will randomly select a Location, so you'd have to be super-extra-special lucky to get both; otherwise the TEM applies to the effects DR for a Location not affected by CH. Spraying fire and Canister will always get TEM, and Canister can potentially affect two hexes too. I might worry for Spraying Fire if there is a really good, -2 or -3, enemy leader. To my thinking because the pillbox and outside are separate Locations, I would rank "lucky hits" fairly far down on my list of reasons to put a trench and a pillbox in separate hexes. It's something to think about, but it's not often going to change my mind.

title: Bunker question
question: The rules state that a pillbox in the same hex as a trench is a bunker.  It also states the a bunker is treated like pillbox in almost all respects. Do vehicles entering a bunker hex (assume there are no enemy units in hex) still treat the hex as a trench for bog? Can halftracks enter a bunker hex (pillbox with trench)?
author: Jgolch
consensus_answer:
While I have you on the line JR V ... 

A question I have that I can't find an immediate answer to that relates to the OPs question in a way ...

If a trench is in an unpaved road hex, does that still cause a Bog check to tracked vehicles/prevent halftrack entry?  Even if the unit in question is moving by road across a road hexside?

No reason to think the trench rules don't apply. As a realism argument, the trench is usually dug after the road. If the order were typically the reverse the rules would probably cover that. Likewise foxhole MF/MP costs would be added for a foxhole in a road [B27.43].

replies.body:
The rules state that a pillbox in the same hex as a trench is a bunker.  It also states the a bunker is treated like pillbox in almost all respects. Do vehicles entering a bunker hex (assume there are no enemy units in hex) still treat the hex as a trench for bog? Can halftracks enter a bunker hex (pillbox with trench)? 
Yes; no. The pillbox becomes a bunker, which allows infantry to move to and from the bunker/pillbox in new ways, but the other stuff in the hex does not change. If the hex is also, say, a brush hex or a woods hex, it remains a brush hex or woods hex, and if the hex is a trench hex, it remains a trench hex.

The rules state that a pillbox in the same hex as a trench is a bunker. 

For the benefits of not only your understanding of the rules, but also any newbie stumbling upon this thread ... That is NOT true.  The rules state that a pillbox in the same hex with a trench OR in a hex Accessible to a hex containing a trench is a bunker.  I will explain this momentarily.

 It also states the a bunker is treated like pillbox in almost all respects. 

Meaning all the rules of pillboxes found in B30 apply except as modified by B30.8.

 Do vehicles entering a bunker hex (assume there are no enemy units in hex) still treat the hex as a trench for bog? Can halftracks enter a bunker hex (pillbox with trench)? 

"Yes; No;" as explained by JR V, but that is IF and only IF the "bunker hex" contains a trench counter (as a hex can be a "bunker hex" WITHOUT the hex containing a trench counter).  And there is the rub in your question in that it illustrates a misunderstanding of what a bunker is and what a bunker can be in the context of the rules.

To understand the concept of what makes a "bunker" in ASL you need to understand the definitions of Location (i.e., a pillbox is a separate Location from the Location of the hex it occupies with a separate stacking limit that is in addition to the stacking limits within the hex Location), adjacent (vs ADJACENT) {which are entirely different animals}, and Accessible (all of these terms as defined in the ASL Index).

In nutshell layman's terms - A bunker represents that a single narrow slit line trench has been constructed from the back door of the pillbox to the adjacent hex Trench (and thus it also can apply to a same hex Trench).  The purpose of this narrow slit trench (that turns the pillbox into a bunker {but does not require placement of a counter in ASL}) is so that occupants of the pillbox can egress into the main trench line without unduly exposing themselves to fire (or vice versa ... occupants of the main trench line can reinforce the pillbox without unduly exposing themselves to fire). 

However, placing a Trench counter in the same hex as a pillbox, in nearly all cases, is a completely wasteful use of a Trench counter if you have the option to place the Trench counter in a hex adjacent to the pillbox hex wherein the the pillbox hex is accessible to the Trench counter hex.  

Now I have played a scenario (in PB HASL) that required me to put a Trench counter in the same hex as the pillbox (which really irked me), but in 99% of cases that is NOT the smart thing to do.  For one thing, putting a Trench marker in the pillbox hex provides a convenient source of cover for the Enemy infantry to camp in the pillbox hex under cover of being under a Trench counter to assault/DC the pillbox.  For another thing, it is a complete waste of the advantages of taking advantage of the benefits of a bunker by placing the Trench counter in an adjacent hex.

Now, in order for a pillbox to be considered in an adjacent hex Accessible to a Trench counter, the hexside between the adjacent hex with Trench counter must be a hexside that a unit in the adjacent hex Trench could advance across during the Aph (i.e., it cannot be a cliff hexside or a partial water obstacle hexside {such as found in an instance or two on the PB HASL map}).  But if that criteria is met (and it will be met in the majority of ASL mapboard circumstances), then what you have is a bunker where your units can advance/move between two adjacent hexes without having to first get up out of their Trench/pillbox and expose themselves to fire in (typically) OG ... they get to move as if moving Trench to Trench (including the TEM/? retention benefits from that).

Bottom line for newbies = you don't need to waste a Trench counter (by putting a Trench counter in the same hex as the pillbox) to create the benefits of a Bunker.

title: Flamethrower firing at one level above (or below).
question:
Hi, all. 

Rookie doubt: A flamethrower fires at a target located in the adjacent hex but one level above it. What modification, if any, does the FP of that flamethrower undergo?

Thanks in advance.
author: Pavlo
consensus_answer:
The rule is in A22.32. It can fire at a target one level higher at full FP and two levels higher at half FP. This in addition to the halving if fired at long range.

title: Rooftop height of a factory?
question:
So section B is confusing us ...

We have a unit that wants to advance to the rooftop of a factory in the RB "The Last Bid" scenario where the factory has a printed stairwell, so it is a "level 2.5 obstacle to LOS".

The Soviets have a unit on lvl 2 of a building.

The question is... does the rooftop person lose concealment because they do not have "height advantage" over the lvl 2 unit?  Some of us are arguing that even though the factory is a 2.5 level obstacle, the unit on the rooftop is magically treated as being on level 3.

Some of us are arguing that since the factory is a 2.5 level obstacle and "half levels" are mythical in ASL, the rooftop unit must be treated as being on level 2.

We're confused....
author: kbernatz
consensus_answer:
Half levels are not "mythical." They exist just like full levels. They are not considered when calculating blind hexes [A6.21], but otherwise they otherwise an elevation a unit can be at. If you are going to play with hillocks and/or embankment RRs (e.g. Hatten, Festung Budapest, desert), you will find yourself facing half-level terrain.

Normal two-story houses and multi-story buildings are one-and-a-half [B23.22] and two-and-a-half [B23.23] level obstacles respectively. If rooftops are not in play then the highest Location a unit can be in them is at level one or level two, despite there being another half-level of building obstacle above the unit. If rooftops are in play there is an additional Location at the full height of the building, i.e. a rooftop Location at level one-and-a-half or two-and-a-half.

Factories are exactly the same except that if rooftops are not in play, there is only a ground level Location. When rooftops are in play there is another Location at the obstacle height. This last is not fully stated in the aslrb. B23.88 alludes to what is meant by describing "quasi-Locations" at level one (and level two for a 2.5 level factory) where DFF can be targeted and RFP placed. But if you took B23.8 literally, "Rooftops are treated the same as another building floor level at the next higher half-level elevation," rooftops in a factory would be at level one-half. That is clearly absurd; the rooftop Location is at the obstacle height.

With regard to concealment, B23.82, "A unit can remain hidden or concealed on a rooftop only if there are no Good Order enemy ground units within 16 hexes of it that are at the same or higher level with a LOS to it." For a unit on a low factory (level one-and-a-half), it can remain HIP/concealed only if all Good Order enemy ground units with LOS and within sixteen hexes are at level one or lower.

Foxhole is a term you would probably only hear from the US Army. Other allied nations had terms like slit trench or fighting pit. In modern times it would be called an individual fighting position, however nobody on the NATO side of the world would set up individual positions these days, instead using a minimum of two soldiers per fighting position. A metre deep fighting position for two soldiers would be expected as a basic defence within a few hours of a defensive position being occupied. A shell scrape is probably going to be expected for a short halt of a few hours, and if the position is to be held longer then the shell scrapes will eventually be extended into sleeping bays off the fighting pit after it is fully dug. If the position is to be held for a few days then the pits get deeper so that the soldiers can stand instead of kneel and overhead cover is worked on. After a week you would expect shallow communication trenches between the fighting positions, but not yet the extensive trench works that would be part of a fortified position.

A long preamble but Commonwealth infantry in fighting pits would be best capable of enduring artillery or direct fire, and then repelling attack with their personal weapons.

title: Smoke grenades & residual FP
question:
8.22 says that a unit can only be attacked by residual FP once per location. It also states that an exception is when the residual FP there is increased, further MF/MP expenditure in that location can subject it to another attack. I get this exception. So in this case, attempting smoke grenade placement would cause another attack.

The other exception is when the unit is subject to more negative or less positive DRMs. Since 8.22 also says that smoke grenade attempts are considered a non-simultaneous expenditure of MF (e.g., in addition to the cost to move into the location), would an attempt to use those smoke grenades subject the unit to another residual FP attack there? As the grenades if placed would not be causing more negative DRM to the target unit (but adding to its defense), am I right that there wouldn't be another residual FP attack? Even if the placement attempt failed, that too wouldn't change the DRM picture, right?
author: PaulusBorgia
consensus_answer:
As Marti and Robin comment, but I'll add some clarification that I /think/ are correct....

If you started your MPh in the hex and another unit first entered your hex, drawing fire (and placing a residual fire marker), if you then attempted to place smoke grenades anywhere (expending 1 or 2 MFs) you would be subject to the residual fire attack because you were expending MFs in that location and had not yet been subject to it.

Furthermore, if that squad was moving and entered a new hex, was fired on and a residual fire marker was placed, and THEN they attempted a smoke grenade placement at 1 or 2 MFs, they would ALSO be subject to a residual fire attack (as they had not yet been attacked by that residual fire).

Conversely, if a residual fire marker was in a hex and a squad entered that hex (and was attacked by the residual fire marker), THEN attempted to place smoke grenades from that hex, they would NOT be subject to an additional residual fire attack as they had already been attacked once by the residual fire and none of the exceptions for a second attack by that residual fire apply.

Attempting smoke grenade placement would not trigger an additional residual power attack if there is no other specific change since the first RF attack. There is no increase of the RF in the Location and there is no change in the drm of the unit doing the smoke placement attempt.
If the unit placing the smoke grenade was not attacked by the RF yet - e.g. the RF was caused by an attack against it - it will be attacked by RF, though.

title: What does the bracketed [9] after the H# on C8.31 chart refer to?
question: See question in thread title (I am at a loss at the moment to figuring out/remembering what is up with the bracketed 9) -
author: Xenophobic_Luddite
consensus_answer:
It's called Ballistics  (which is a science of physics unto itself) 

It is all about ratios between length of barrel, strength of propellant charge, twist rate of rifling, muzzle velocity attained, weight of shell (heavier weight more affected by gravity), aerodynamics of shell (fat heavy HE shell versus light APCR tungsten core dart {which can actually, counterintuitively, reduce range due to instability of the dart versus wind/air resistance), etc., etc.

For example, an air rifle chambered in  .177 caliber pellet can fire that pellet at higher velocity and longer range than a similar air rifle chambered in .22 caliber.  However, due to the projectile's mass, a .22 caliber pellet releases much more kinetic energy upon its target on impact (albeit with a shorter effective range and less muzzle velocity than the .177 caliber pellet).  That is why it is considered inhumane to hunt rabbits or squirrels with a .177 caliber air rifle.  Instead you need to use .22 or .25 caliber air rifle to humanely take out a rabbit or squirrel (proper shot placement on target is also key).  A .177 caliber air rifle is only considered humane when used to take out rats and small birds.

When I find time later, I will post some more data on the Pak36 versus Pak38 versus Pak40 (from my hard copy encyclopedia that I referenced above) to further illustrate the ballistics involved.

title: Wrecks and TEM
question:
Confused by the wording in D9.3 - "... but cumulative with any SMOKE/Hindrance DRM applicable to the firer."

Firing through a hex containing a Wreck adds a +1 DRM. If that Wreck happened to be in an Orchard hex, would firing through it be a +2 DRM? Would Smoke then add another +1 DRM?
author: Fly by Night
consensus_answer:
On a related note (and figuring this fits the heading of this topic without creating a new thread) -

Burnt Out Wrecks

These are mostly (if not only) used in HASLs (in particular in the CGs).  The rules are clear that a Burnt Out Wreck is a LOS hindrance just like any other wreck.  

What I am curious about is if there is any official ruling regarding whether a Burnt Out Wreck is also Cover for infantry like any other (non-burning) wreck?

I say this because the rules seem to be silent on this.

IMO - A Burnt Out Wreck should be usable by infantry as cover just like any other (non-burning) wreck (and I have been playing this way even though the ASLRB and HASL SSRs appear to be silent on this).

This is WW2 when AFVs were made of steel (unlike Vietnam and later conflicts where some AFVs {notably the M113 series ... but also the M2/M3 Bradleys} were made of aluminum).  Yes, a blazing from RPG hit M113 would literally melt to the ground.  But WW2 AFVs made of steel did NOT melt ... they simply became charred.  Which means after they stopped burning and cooled down a bit they were essentially as much of a hunk of steel on the ground as any other AFV wreck (and thus should be usable by infantry for a +1 TEM for cover if no better cover is available in the hex).

I am wondering if the answer to my question lies in the fact that D10 (D10.3 in particular) applies to all "wrecks" (with exceptions for "burning wrecks"), and a Burnt Out Wreck is by definition a "wreck" that is NOT a "burning wreck" thus D10.3 is applicable to Burnt Out Wrecks?

Thoughts from the ASL gurus?

replies.body: Yes, wreck and SMOKE Hindrances are cumulative with other Hindrances in the same Location. Note that a burning wreck only has a +2 for the Smoke from the Blaze, however, and none from that wreck itself.

If the Smoke is not due to a wreck blaze it would be cumulative with the hindrances for the wreck and the orchard.

If the Smoke is not due to a wreck blaze it would be cumulative with the hindrances for the wreck and the orchard.

title: Do you have to declare a pre-registered hex?
question:
Mostly a hypothetical question, but consider a scenario where you have several potential pre-reg hexes for your OBA, some offensive and some defensive.  You don't really want your opponent to know where your pre-reg hex is because the ability to call down FFE immediately with a 1-4 accuracy can definitely catch people out in the open.

At some point, however, you want to drop a SR on that hex.  Are you able to roll for accuracy first without announcing that it is a pre-reg hex?  Assuming German or American and no hindrance, that means on a 1-2 it would be accurate regardless and on a 5-6 it would miss, regardless (though I suppose you'd have to announce that the extent of error was halved, so a 5-6 would still give away the pre-reg unless you rolled a 1 on the distance scatter).  On a 3-4, you'd obviously have to announce and reveal the pre-reg to show that the SR landed in the hex.

Basically, what is the general way that people play pre-reg hexes?  In the past, we've always just say "I'm placing an AR in hex XXXX, which is the pre-reg hex, so need a 1-4 for accuracy".  But there has almost never been a need for deception as the pre-reg has been in a scenario where one side is the clear attacker and one the clear defender.  We're currently starting The Last Bid and both sides will likely be defending and attacking, so I could see the desire to keep the opponent guessing as to the exact pre-reg hex location.

Nothing in the rules (including Artillery flow chart) seem to detail the announcement sequencing, which makes me think you could place the AR and, as long as you're not immediately converting to a FFE:1, just roll for accuracy.  Then if you roll a 3 or 4, you'd announce that it is accurate as that is the pre-reg hex.  On a 5-6, you'd roll for scatter and if you rolled a 2+ on distance, announce that the extent of error is halved as its the pre-reg hex.

Just curious what people thought and if the decision would be different in a friendly game versus a tournament setting?
author: kbernatz
consensus_answer: The pre-registered hex is secretly recorded [C1.73], so I play that it remains secret until I want to uses one of the benefits of C1.73ff.

replies.body: The pre-registered hex is secretly recorded [C1.73], so I play that it remains secret until I want to uses one of the benefits of C1.73ff.

Do you have to use it?  I.e. if you drop a SR in the pre-reg hex but don't really care if its accurate and roll a '3', could you voluntarily decline to declare the pre-reg and have it miss with full scatter?  Or would that be viewed as against the spirit of the rule and you'd have to declare it as the pre-reg hex and allow it to be accurate?

Not sure if there would ever be a time you wouldn't WANT to declare it ... just curious if people play it that the use of the pre-reg is optional in that way.
Per C1.732 a pre-registered hex is accurate on accuracy dr 1-4. You wouldn't be playing according to the rules if you let a dr 3-4 drift.

Likewise you can't let an enemy halfsquad pass through a minefield even though you'd be forgoing an entitled attack. Just because there's no referee doesn't mean you can choose when to apply the rules and when not.
Ok, that is how I would have played it.  Was just confused by the "remains secret" aspect.

One general rule for interpreting the ASLRB is to look for the word, "may," or similar phrasing. If the rule says, "may," the player has the option and sometimes may not. If not then it is usually a rule that must be played. I am sure this was not carefully studied during writing so there could be cases where this makes no sense, but as a first-pass for rules application it is probably a good heuristic.

title: FFE1 & FFE2
question: Is it legal to call in a Fire Mission (HE or Smoke) for FFE1 and then correct it for FFE2 so it strikes again up to 3 hexs away (using the same HE or Smoke of course)?
author: Fly by Night
consensus_answer:
Is it legal to call in a Fire Mission (HE or Smoke) for FFE1 and then correct it for FFE2 so it strikes again up to 3 hexs away (using the same HE or Smoke of course)?
In the same phase? No. In a later turn? Sure. The OBA flow chart is probably the best rules reference for this.

The procedure for FFE placement got changed very early in the ASL rules. In the original OBA the FFE:1 stayed on board for a turn before flipping to an FFE:2. Currently in a single phase you announce conversion of a SR or FFE:C, the FFE:1 is put on board, evaluated and flipped to an FFE:2. The FFE:1 as used currently is probably unnecessary, a legacy from when the rules were different.

title: Narrow streets?
question:
Can a Squad moving along a Narrow Street end it's Movement on a Narrow Street hex, or is it forced into one of the buildings along the road?
Example talks about Bypass Movement, but is that mandatory for Narrow Street Movement?
author: Fly by Night
consensus_answer:
Can a Squad moving along a Narrow Street end it's Movement on a Narrow Street hex, or is it forced into one of the buildings along the road?

This is a distinction without a difference. A unit moving in bypass is always in one of the two hexes (really Locations) of the hexside on which it is bypassing. Per A4.32, "Infantry may not voluntarily end its move using Bypass." The narrow street rules do not change this. Bypass does not create a separate Location, and Infantry may not end their MPh in Bypass.

title: Breach TEM?

author: Fly by Night
consensus_answer: Since neither "normal TEM" nor "full TEM" are defined as formal terms, I think we have to assume the rulebook is being chatty and not trying to define formal terms on-the-sly. title: Broken Squad under an FFE.
question: Does a Broken Squad in a Foxhole, not currently under DM, get placed under a DM if the FFE does not inflict a result?
author: Fly by Night
consensus_answer:
Does a Broken Squad in a Foxhole, not currently under DM, get placed under a DM if the FFE does not inflict a result?
Per A10.62, a DM is placed on "any already broken unit which is subsequently attacked by ... enough FP (taking the possibility of Cowering into account) to possibly inflict at least a NMC result on the target." With a TEM of +4 for the foxhole, the OBA would have to have at least four FP to get a NMC on a snakeeyes (as there is no cowering for OBA).

consensus_answer:
So B9.34 Indirect Fire infers that the TEM of a Wall or Hedge is reduced by one if using Indirect Fire, such as Mortars. 

Indirect fire is only OBA and Mortars. title: Concealment retention in Ambush vs ATMM check

A concealed unit advances into CC with an AFV at night (but illuminated) in LOS of another GO enemy unit.

Immediately prior to the resolution DR, the ATTACKER makes an ATMM check (which fails, but that is beside the point).

The ambushing ATTACKER succeeds in eliminating the AFV.

The Ambush rules state that the ambusher gets to retain concealment until it attacks in CC without eliminating a unit.

The Concealment Loss Table identifies an ATMM check as a concealment loss activity (and these kinds of concealment loss activities are NOT exceptions to concealment loss in the Night rules).

Does the ambushing attacker that successfully eliminates the AFV get to retain concealment due to Ambush rules?  or do they lose their concealment due to making an ATMM check within LOS of another GO enemy unit?

author: Xenophobic_Luddite
consensus_answer: Strictly following the rules, A12.141 is the later rule than A11.4, so by apparent rules conflict resolution the unit would lose concealment although it would not lose the other benefits of ambush, e.g. ambush withdrawal. That's my reading anyway.

title: Does a +1 Low Visibility count for Routing?
question: I have a Squad that needs to Rout.  The known enemy unit is adjacent and Broken as well. Would the +1 Low Visibility count towards the +6 needed to block LOS so I can rout or Low Craw in that direction?
author: Fly by Night
consensus_answer: Ah, I *knew* there was an exception. F11.6, "DLV is the term used to categorize Sun Blindness (11.61), Heat Haze (11.62-.621), and both Light and Moderate Dust (11.71-.72). A DLV Hindrance is treated exactly like a LV Hindrance (E3.1) unless stated otherwise. A DLV Hindrance does not apply (i.e., is not counted) when determining if LOS is blocked as per B.10." So if the LV Hindrance is a DLV hindrance, it does *not* apply toward blocking LOS.

As a side note (and something that may cause confusion to some people), I seem to remember there might have been a specific scenario out there in the weeds and mountain of published scenarios that had an SSR that allowed hidden DC heros at start.

Nagging feeling seems to make me think that is possible.

But an SSR on a single scenario does not an ASL Rule make.

For this particular question (Japanese player wanting to create a DC hero in the APh) my answer is somewhat simpler. I *believe* the only way to create a DC Hero is to do so with the procedure in G1.424 during the Japanese MPh, but I am clear (per G1.424 and also per the q&a I cited in my first reply) that regardless of whether a DC Hero can be created in the APh, it **can't detonate its DC in the CCPh**. This makes creation of a DC Hero in the APh pointless.

We have strayed into the question of whether a HIP T-H Hero can have a DC transferred to it by a mechanism other than by G1.424, e.g. from another unit during the RPh or at the start of the APh per A4.431. If done at the start of the APh, this runs into the same problem already mentioned, i.e. that the DC can't be detonated in the CCPh. So that leaves only one interesting case where the DC is transferred during the RPh and perhaps is used during the Japanese MPh. Here I have argued that loss of HIP during the transfer would be necessary, and that loss of HIP would result in the elimination of the T-H Hero/DC Hero because it couldn't immediately make its attack.

If the transfer takes place in the RPh, thereby revealing the TH-Hero (and transferring unit's) presence, isn't that a voluntary loss of HIP? So then he could charge in the movement MPh as required. One could just create a DC Hero at this point instead, but the advantage of using a 44-45 TH Hero is that its generation is automatic. Otherwise, why would 1.423 note that such a unit could carry a DC? How else could it get one?

Just remember that the rules committee (those that tend to rule on the Q&A, etc, and are considered the 'final word' on a ruleset that was written 30+ years ago) always focuses on COWTA.  So if you find yourself arguing inferred or implied teachings, chances are the counter argument is "If it isn't explicitly allowed, then it is not".  There is nothing in 1.424 that allows transferring of a DC other than the immediate transfer "in its own MPh" from a Japanese unit to the T-H hero they are attempting to create.

 1.424 DC HERO: A unit allowed to create a T-H Hero may, 
if possessing a DC, make such an attempt in its own MPh 
provided it is within eight MF of and has a LOS to any en-
emy unit/Gun and/or to any enemy-Controlled hex that con-
tains a Known Fortification counter; being within eight MF of 
and having a LOS to an enemy AFV is not required in this case. 
If the T-H Hero is created (the DC adds a -2 drm to this attempt; 1.421),
that DC is automatically Transferred to him and he is then termed a DC Hero. A 
DC Hero is treated the same as a T-H Hero except as stated otherwise. A DC 
Hero may not Place/Throw a DC in the normal manner, and may not make 
a CC attack.

If the transfer takes place in the RPh, thereby revealing the TH-Hero (and transferring unit's) presence, isn't that a voluntary loss of HIP? So then he could charge in the movement MPh as required. One could just create a DC Hero at this point instead, but the advantage of using a 44-45 TH Hero is that its generation is automatic. Otherwise, why would 1.423 note that such a unit could carry a DC? How else could it get one?
It is possible transfer is voluntary loss of HIP. However per G1.422 a HIP T-H Hero can lose HIP "voluntarily only at the times and in the circumstances in which a T-H Hero may be created during play." During the RPh is not one of the times when a T-H Hero can be created during play. If transfer of a SW is voluntary loss of HIP, then such transfer can't be done during the RPh by rule, and if it is involuntary it results in the immediate elimination of the T-H Hero. Pick your poison.

title: A7.72 - Upper Levels Encirclement
question:
I am seeking to clarify my understanding of this rule. Am I correct that if enemy units are in upper level building locations and a friendly unit is in the only ground level stairwell location, that the enemy units are Encircled?

7.72 UPPER LEVELS: Encirclement also applies to any non-heroic/non berserk unit in an upper level building Location that cannot trace a path
free of an unbroken, armed, unconcealed enemy unit/Blaze to ground level through (or past, if Scaling; B23.424) Locations it could legally traverse if so inclined. This type of Encirclement is broken the instant such a path can be traced.
author: Bombadil929
consensus_answer:
You made me read the rule again JR, cause I found it hard to believe. You are correct, but I wonder if the authors intended that effect. We’ll never know.
The designers were all-Seeing and all-Knowing. They foreSaw every possible DR, from raging two to the meek twelve. All possible drs, from winning one to weakest six, were Known to them.

Seriously, in comparison to using A7.211 & A7.212 (VBM sleaze freeze), this is is the weak sister of ASL sleaze. The units in the clock tower can still fire out to full long range for first fire. For SFF they are now restricted to the same hex, which is nearly the same as if the vehicle had parked adjacent. And for its trouble all the vehicle does is add a +1 DRM for DFF by the units in the tower, not even cancelling FFMO or ROF. VBM sleaze freeze is way more effective for taking out a high-perch fire position. And it can be done in buildings with more than one stairwell if there is only one vehicle handy.
