title: Street fighting
question: Do a Infantry unit that cc-reaction fire or CC attacks an AFV in bypass of a Wood get the Street fighting DRM?
author: Nslcole
consensus_answer: The street fighting DRM adds to the dangers of VBM sleaze freeze. The moving vehicle usually wants to avoid stopping in the hex, i.e. remain in Motion [D2.4]. This means it has to plan its expenditures carefully. The defender should watch to make sure that the moving vehicle has spent all its MPs or does not have enough MPs to enter a next hex. If it has not, then the vehicle is required to spend more MP, which may force the choice of stopping or exiting the hex. It can also enter a new bypass hexside but can only expend "extra" MP on entering a new hex, not in continuing on in bypass. Even if the vehicle has not muffed this, the defending unit can (assuming it passes its PAATC) attack at least twice using CC-RF with +2 for non-stopped and -1 for bypass "street fighting". For a squad that means a better than one-in-six chance of at least immobilizing the vehicle, assuming no other DRM apply. If the vehicle has some other vulnerability (e.g. an open-topped halftrack), the odds go up. And if the vehicle is forced to stop or does so voluntarily, the odds become fairly high that something bad will happen. This may still "neutralize" the defender because if it's using CC-RF, it's not shooting at other units, but at least the neutralization comes with a price.

consensus_answer:
So the Sleeze Freeze does not work on Broken units?

Sleaze Freeze usually refers to preventing units from firing out of the Location [A7.212]. A broken unit with an enemy unit in its Location (bypass or not, vehicle or not) is doubly-unable to fire out. It is limited by A7.212, *and* it is broken. "Sleaze Freeze" is not usually a reference to freezing movement, although if the enemy vehicle stops and the units end up in Melee after the CCPh, the enemy vehicle can also stop movement. Since a Melee won't form until after the RtPh, a broken unit will either rout away or be eliminated for failure to rout before a Melee forms.

title: Firing to reveal HIP AFVs and Guns
question:
Playing ASL24 "The Mad Minute", where several AFVs and Guns are likely HIP in the woods between board 12 and 16.
As I'm quite sure they will be hiding in the woods, I would like to reveal them with my AFVs before sending infantry and halftracks. I don't want to drive with my own AFVs into the woods, because I risk bog and other unpleasant surprises, so the best option is to shoot at several locations?

As they are no known units, can I only use ATT, or is it also allowed to fire with VTT or ITT, using case K for concealed target?
When would the HIP units be revealed? Case A of the A12.121 Concealment Loss Table states: "If it: ... is attacked resulting in at least a PTC". So the IFT result of my ATT attack on a HIP Gun must be at least a PTC to reveal it?
For vehicles I saw: "If it: ... is a vehicle hit by ordnance". So a HIP AFV is already revealed when the TH-attempt was successful?
author: phxhf
consensus_answer:
Note that if you are uncertain if you are shooting at hidden/concealed vehicles or guns - one trick is to not declare the Target Type.

C.9 UNDECLARED ORDNANCE TARGET TYPE: Any time ordnance capable of fire on more than one Target Type of the C3 To Hit Table makes a To Hit DR without first specifying the Target Type being used, the Target Type used for that To Hit DR is the topmost one listed on the To Hit Table that can legally be used vs a target in that hex by that firer (i.e., Vehicle, Infantry or Area in that order).

C2.21 choose the ammo type for you, if you don't specify: "In the absence of a declaration to the contrary, it is otherwise always assumed to be firing HE vs unarmored targets or AP vs armored targets, provided that ammunition type is available, is not Special Ammunition (i.e., has no Depletion #; 8.8), and is allowed on the applicable Target Type of the To Hit Table."When a unit fires a weapon, the firer knows--and deliberately chooses--which type of round he slides into the tube.

When there's no visible target in the hex (e.g., maybe HIP units, maybe not), it seems that the Infantry Target Type should be the default selection, as it's the first target type that can affect what the firer knows and sees to be in the hex: i.e., terrain only. Arguing for a quantum-physics transmutation of the bullet based on what it ends up hitting is foreign to the straightforward way that ASL works. If the firer is trying to hit a vehicle, he should have to specify VTT ahead of time; otherwise (assuming he has HE), he should get ITT.

C.9 is meant to handle cases where target type is obvious or the firer forgets to state it before he rolls; I doubt it was meant for the suggested tactic, which IMO would lessen this great gaming system. Please, MMP, consider patching this one.

C.9 UNDECLARED ORDNANCE TARGET TYPE: Any time ordnance capable of fire on more than one Target Type of the C3 To Hit Table makes a To Hit DR without first specifying the Target Type being used, the Target Type used for that To Hit DR is the topmost one listed on the To Hit Table that can legally be used vs a known target in that hex by that firer (i.e., Vehicle, Infantry or Area in that order, and assigns terrain as the target in the absence of other known targets).

Any target type is allowed. Case K will apply for all three. The primary reason for using ATT against "empty" hexes is to gain acquisition (which won't be gained for the other two target types unless a hit is made). In your case acquisition is not a primary goal.

When would the HIP units be revealed? Case A of the A12.121 Concealment Loss Table states: "If it: ... is attacked resulting in at least a PTC". So the IFT result of my ATT attack on a HIP Gun must be at least a PTC to reveal it?
For vehicles I saw: "If it: ... is a vehicle hit by ordnance". So a HIP AFV is already revealed when the TH-attempt was successful?

If you are considering the vehicles only, any hit will reveal it per case A. If vehicles are your primary concern then the vehicle target type is often more likely to hit at shorter ranges than the ATT. There are also A-T Guns HIP, so if you fire using the VTT you definitely won't hit one of those. With the ITT or ATT you have a chance of finding either, but less chance than the VTT for the M10.

Because the M10 is an OT vehicle, it is highly likely that your opponent has it CE (because otherwise it can't use turret-mounted weapons). That means firing MGs at it would reveal the M10 on a PTC or better, again per case A.

So depending on your weapon either cause for concealment (HIP) loss may happen.

A. Only if that non-ordnance attack is OBA.
Is a hit on any ordnance To Hit target type (VTT, ITT, ATT) enough to make an AFV with no vulnerable PRC lose its “?”?
A. Yes.

Because the M10s will almost certainly have vulnerable PRC, i.e. be CE, they will lose concealment on a PTC or better, but that determination will include their CE DRM.

title: Hindrances Possibly Affecting Mortar Shot into 2-Story Building
question:
The 81mm German mortar in CC3 wishes to fire upon the French stack that occupies the ground floor of the building in O4.  In this example LOS passes thru T3 and S4 (both Grain-Trench), and R3 (Grain only).  However, the upper level of building O4 is clearly above those Grain hindrances and, this being an Area Target Type shot, would also be affected if the mortar scores a hit. So...

Question 1:  Is the mortar's To Hit DR adjusted for the Hindrance of any of the Grain hexes, or not?
Question 2:  If Grain Hindrances apply even though Lvl 1 of the Building is clearly visible above them, do the Trenches in S4 & T3 negate two of those Hindrances so that the modifier is only +1 for R3 alone? 
Question 3:  If the mortar opted to shoot Smoke instead, and gained a hit, would that Smoke permeate all of O4, both inside the Building on Lvls 1 & 2, and outside the building as well?
author: A2SimGamer
consensus_answer:
Q1:  OK, so both any applicable Hindrances and location-specific TEM are determined separately for every Location within a given hex being targeted by Area Target Type.

Two things to note here. First the TEM does not apply as a TH DRM when using the Area Target Type [C3.331]. It instead affects the effects DR. A building Location with levels above it gets extra TEM when targeted by Indirect Fire like a MTR unless a CH [B23.32].

Q2:  At first we hadn't thought that Trenches could clear other terrain from the hexes where they were dug, but using VASL's LOS and Hindrance checker, we saw that it ignored Hindrances for Grain-Trench hexes, so questioned whether we'd missed a rule somewhere.  In the example VASL indicates that only the R3 Hindrance applies. 
How very curious indeed. vasl does skip over hindrances for grain hexes with trenches. It also skips over foxholes. But not pillboxes. That's a vasl bug.

replies.body:
The 81mm German mortar in CC3 wishes to fire upon the French stack that occupies the ground floor of the building in O4.  In this example LOS passes thru T3 and S4 (both Grain-Trench), and R3 (Grain only).  However, the upper level of building O4 is clearly above those Grain hindrances and, this being an Area Target Type shot, would also be affected if the mortar scores a hit. So...

Question 1:  Is the mortar's To Hit DR adjusted for the Hindrance of any of the Grain hexes, or not?

At a ground-level target, yes. The hindrance DRM applies to all same-level TH DRs. If there were another target at level one, that target would not have the hindrance DRM applied to the TH DR. Note that this means the attack might hit units on the first level (or rooftop, if in play) but not the ground level.

author: runrun
consensus_answer:
Not by the same vehicle. They can be "frozen" at the same time by different vehicles.
Not on the same hexside. Only one vehicle (/wreck) can occupy a hexside in bypass [D2.31]. A second vehicle could freeze the second Location using another hexside, but not using the hexside with the first vehicle.

replies.body:
The vehicle, as in Bypass, is always IN one or the other obstacle hex (B31.11: "A unit Bypassing along a Narrow Street hexside is always assumed to be on the road within its hex").

A unit is always in exactly one Location, and a vehicle can only freeze the Location it is in. The positioning of a counter in bypass on the hexside is ambiguous visually, especially if there is bypassable obstacle on each side but for rules purposes the vehicle is in only one of the two Locations. title: Wall Advantage and Fire Lanes
question:
The Russian unit wants to put a Fire Lane towards O10. What effect, if any, does it have that he does not have Wall Advantage?

author: norev
consensus_answer:
One way to 'zen' it is that if you are close enough to the wall that you /could/ have gotten wall advantage (i.e. are in the hex adjacent to the wall), it doesn't mean the enemy with wall advantage is directly adjacent the wall and your guys are 40 m away at the far edge of the hex (in this situation, one would like to think the wall would block LOS; e.g. to O10, because the unit isn't adjacent the wall and that is how non-adjacent walls work).  But instead, think of your guys are also up close to the wall, but are more pre-occupied with the guys that have wall advantage to be exceptionally concerned with using the wall to their advantage when firing at someone else (or, conversely, are close enough to the wall that the other people being fired at don't really gain any benefit from it unless they can get even closer; i.e. also claim wall advantage).

Remember that a unit can still get wall TEM even if it doesn't have wall advantage.  So they are still 'close' to the wall, relatively speaking.  So a German in O10 firing at the MMG would have to add +2 for the wall TEM (see B9.31).  So clearly the Soviets have some wall benefits...just not versus the German HS.

Yes, HIP in general is a fancy form of concealment [A12.3]. Use of radio is not a cause for concealment loss (as above), and it is not one of the actions that requires placement on board concealed [A12.32].

 An Observer who uses a radio (including any unsuccessful attempt to make or

that PFPh (and may not move in the following MPh) or DFPh and if not 
hidden/concealed is marked with a Prep or Final Fire counter, but does not

would not be visible over the open sights of most weapons. However, concealed units
≥ 16 hexes away are considered conducting themselves in such a cautious manner that 
better optics are not of particular value in “seeing” them—at least not automatically.

title: Mortar Fire -- Duds?
question:
Last night I scored a critical hit with an 81mm mortar having rolled snake eyes against an infantry target.  We figured we'd resolve the attack by rolling on the IFT with 2xFP, but then I rolled a DR = 12 (box cars) for the effect of the attack.  H'mmm... DR = 12 is always supposed to be some rando bad luck thing right?  So I looked up Duds.  The only references about Duds that I could find in either the Chapter C rules or in the Index all seemed to indicate that Duds are intended to apply to any type of ammo when one rolls an original 12, but apply to TK To Kill rolls (only).  Meanwhile I can find no rules reference defining this roll on the IFT as being considered a TK or a TK equivalent. 

Question:  Is an 12 original roll on the IFT for the effects of a mortar's hit to be scored as a Dud (i.e. no effect on the target)?
author: A2SimGamer
consensus_answer: Duds only happen on TK rolls (C7.35). Mortars never use a TK roll, so they never use that rule.

replies.body: no, resolved on the IFT as DR=12
Duds only happen on TK rolls (C7.35). Mortars never use a TK roll, so they never use that rule.

I'm not 100% sure whether a roll using C1.55 against a vehicle for an Area Target Type attack is a TK DR or not. If it is, then I would read it as being subject to Duds. But in most cases an original twelve using C1.55 will have no effect anyway, at least against an AFV, and so trying to pin down whether it is a Dud or not is wasted effort.

What is clear is that an attack vs a non-vehicle will never be a TK DR, and so a Dud result has no meaning in that case.

An ATT attack is an attack on the IFT, to which DRM can apply vs an armored target.
It is not a TK DR, su Dud is NA.

title: Fire lanes and burning wrecks
question: A burning wreck is in front of an MG that lays a fire lane through it. The fire lane is not effected by smoke, but is the fire lane effected by the +1 wreck hindrance? Rules seem to say no, but Perry Sez seems to say yes. Please respond with rules sections. Thank you.
author: igycrctl
consensus_answer:
B25.2: 25.2 SMOKE: Any Burning Wreck or terrain Blaze is automatically shroud-
ed by smoke up to four levels [EXC: none in Heavy Winds (25.63); two levels 
in a Mild Breeze (A24.4)] above the level of the Fire in that hex, so no actual 
smoke counters need be placed on those Fires. However, Wreck Blazes cause 
a +2 Hindrance DRM rather than the +3 Hindrance DRM of regular smoke. 
The SMOKE Hindrance DRM replaces the normal Wreck Hindrance DRM 
(D9.4) except in the case of an already established Fire Lane (A9.22), or in 
Heavy Winds (25.63), where only the Wreck Hindrance DRM would apply. (emphasis added)

I was thinking it stated that the Wreck Hindrance replaced except for an already established, but its the other way around.  So now I think 'already established' is just poor phrasing on their part...  Go with what Perry Sez :).

Also note that they can't claim the Wreck DRM if in the same Location as the Burning Wreck (D9.3) or if it didn't qualify as cover per D9.3, at least from my reading of this section.  This is also a TEM, not Hindrance ... so it is cumulative with Smoke.  But this is for same Location units.

D9.4 doesn't help, as it simply states that the Hindrance DRM doesn't apply while referencing B25.2, but doesn't include the exceptions in B25.2.  So seems like B25.2 controls and it just comes down to what is meant by 'already established'.

First, in the absence of Heavy Winds the Smoke will prevent FFMO for attacks by a Fire Lane into or beyond the wreck, so it isn't 100% correct to say the Fire Lane isn't affected.

I am assuming this is the q&a to which you refer:
A9.22 & B25.2
B25.2 states that the wreck hindrance applies to any already established firelane. Does it apply to any firelane, or only a firelane established before the wreck began to burn?
A. The wreck Hindrance applies normally (e.g., if it is not considered moving).
I suspect that the deficiency in B25.2 is in the sentence, the "SMOKE Hindrance DRM replaces the normal Wreck Hindrance DRM (D9.4) except in the case of an already established Fire Lane (A9.22)." The problem is with what  "an already established Fire Lane" in B25.2 is supposed to be contrasted with. I think it was meant to be contrasted with, "a Fire Lane that is currently being established, i.e. one that is announced as part of an attack," which is problematic because the Fire Lane does not attack as it is being established (and treating attacks by a newly-established Fire Lane against units in other Locations when using Impulse Movement as if an already established Fire Lane).

My guess is: when a unit is attacked in or beyond a burning wreck by an attack in the original Location that establishes a Fire Lane (i.e. not a secondary, Fire Lane attack due to Impulse Movement outside the original Location), that attack is affected by Smoke but not wreck; when a unit is attacked in or beyond a burning wreck by a Fire Lane, including attacks secondary to the original one due to the Fire Lane affecting units in other Locations when using Impulse Movement, the attack is affected by the wreck TEM but not the Smoke Hindrance.

It would not necessarily be bad to submit for a q&a to clear this up a bit. I would suggest that rather than trying to unwind what was meant by B25.2 and the q&a, you just present a list of cases and possible DRM, e.g.:

Non-Fire-Lane attack that also establishes a Fire Lane in same Location as Burning Wreck, non-heavy winds: TEM applies? Smoke hindrance applies?
Non-Fire-Lane attack that also establishes a Fire Lane in same Location as Burning Wreck, heavy winds: TEM applies? Smoke hindrance applies?
Secondary Fire Lane attack due Impulse Movement on attack that initiated a Fire Lane in same Location as Burning Wreck, non-heavy winds: TEM applies? Smoke hindrance applies?
Secondary Fire Lane attack due Impulse Movement on attack that initiated a Fire Lane in same Location as Burning Wreck, heavy winds: TEM applies? Smoke hindrance applies?
Non-Fire-Lane attack that also establishes a Fire Lane in Location beyond a Burning Wreck, non-heavy winds: TEM applies? Smoke hindrance applies?
...
Fire Lane attack in same Location as Burning Wreck, non-heavy winds: TEM applies? Smoke hindrance applies?
...
Fire Lane attack beyond a Burning Wreck, non-heavy winds: TEM applies? Smoke hindrance applies?

I regret there are a fair number of possible combinations, establishes Fire Lane vs Fire Lane, primary attack that establishes a Fire Lane  vs secondary Fire Lane attack due to Impulse Movement vs primary Fire Lane attack, heavy winds vs not-heavy-winds, but given how muddled the rule & the q&a seem to be, an explicit list would end all muddlity.

title: Prepared Fire Zone
question: I'm playing ASL 163 as the Finns. This is the first scenario in which I've experienced prepared fire zones. I have two factors (with the vineyard pfz showing on the scenario card). As I read the rules I can use one point to turn a woods hex into a vineyard and a second point to turn that vineyard into open group. Correct? Or can you only use one point per hex?
author: ozradio
consensus_answer:
In this scenario's case the SSR says only the AT Mines can be HIP, no other fortifications (trenches and pillbox).
As a technical point, Prepared Fire Zones are not "Fortifications" as defined in the Index, although in common parlance they are certainly fortification-like. But in game terms they are an independent thing. Any rule or SSR applying to "Fortifications" does not apply to PFZs. For that reason SSR2 does not apply, but then neither does A12.33 [Fortification HIP].

Thanks for the clarification!

replies.body: B36.22, "A brush, vineyard (including such converted per 36.21), orchard, cactus patch, olive grove, grain, palm tree, or kunai hex may be permanently converted into an Open Ground hex at a cost of one PFZ factor." So unless there is a SSR overriding this rule, you can spend two points on a woods hex to convert it to open ground.
See also the B36.22 EX.

Great, thanks! I wasn't sure since the icon on the scenario card featured the vineyard PFZ maybe I only had the option to place two vineyard PFZs. I didn't realize there were vineyards in Finland to begin with!
https://www.winemag.com/2021/11/19/finland-wine-guide/

as talking point, I think PFZ could also be HIP until used. Have to be by SSR, but the Japanese were particularly sneaky when it came to this, preparing fire zone traps that were not very obvious to the attacker. The first MG shots would put the attackers to the ground, seeking cover. A fortuitous fallen palm log is ideal.  Then the 2nd MG opens up right up that open flank..

Per Chapter B, footnote 21, "HIDDEN PFZ: PPZ may set up hidden as if a Fortitication only if specifically allowed to by SSR. Hidden PFZ may present difficult LOS challenges, and designers may want PFZ to become revealed whenever they affect LOS between unbroken units." 

If a hex is printed on map as dense jungle hex but is in fact an Open Ground hex, that should be pretty easy to notice even to the untrained eye. Where I think the FPZ rules fail is that they don't cover "keyhole" prepared fire zones well. I have read stories of the Japanese and also of the Germans in Reichswald trimming a "keyhole" at knee height through woods along which a specific MG could fire. In that case the basic terrain in the hex is not touched but that particular LOS behaves as a special one. If that is what you envision I think the B36 PFZ rules, even HIP, are too broad an axe to swing. I feel this situation would be better covered by a custom SSR that allows a MG to have LOS to a bore-sighted Location through woods(/brush/other stuff?) with the LOS treated as clear (causing concealment loss? including FFMO? these to be determined by the SSR) for any attack to the bore-sighted Location or along the path to it as long as the bore-sight is valid, and allow the establishment of a Fire Lane along said LOS. These could easily be kept HIP until the MG decided to fire down its "keyhole" LOS. To my mind something like that would work better for "keyhole" prepared fire zones, where it wasn't a gross mutilation of terrain (as with B36 PFZs, which you might see at Cape Torokina) but a calculated and precise tweak of the terrain for a very specific purpose. Bonsai!

title: AFV and the DM'd Squad
question: So my opponent tried to Overrun my DM'd Squad in the street.  He failed to get a result, mainly because his tank had no MG's. (Italian SMV).  My DM'd Squad can't Rout in the Rout Phase being held in place by the AFV, so its now the CC Phase.  How does a Withdraw work since his Italian AFV has no available MG's to apply the -2DRM too?  Would he apply it to a To Hit roll?
author: Fly by Night
consensus_answer:
There are many occasions when a broken unit will rout away from an enemy unit in its Location. One of the funniest things to watch is a berserk unit chasing a broken unit all over the board. Human waves can also lead to this, but if in the middle of the wave the broken unit may have nowhere to rout. 

For your case probably the best use for the AFV would not be for OVR but rather to form one half of a surrounding pair to eliminate for Failure to Rout. The tank moves to one side of the hex (it can remain in Motion), and another unit stands on the opposite side. The broken unit will either surrender or be eliminated. Leaders are good units to use for the other side as they often don't have much to do, although another AFV or a MMC will do. An OVR can lead to irritating results like HoB or Immob on the vehicle since it has no weapons to malf. With elimination for FTR there's not even a slight chance of a bad result.

title: PerrySez: mechanics of hopeless rout
question:
In certain cases it is obvious that a broken unit will be eliminated for Failure to Rout. In many of those you can just remove the broken unit from the map without tracing a path, rolling for wire, etc, but if it possesses a SW that it will drop the exact mechanics can have some importance. For the example I give in my question it matters because the Japanese unit above the wire could recover the MMG if it is dropped there. Per the answer to the q the broken unit will rout as far as it can then be eliminated, dropping its SW there. Again in this EX the MMG may be dropped under the wire or it may be eliminated when it is dropped in the creek, but it definitely won't be dropped above the wire. 

Side comment: this seems pretty "obvious" but I wanted to get it in print.

Rout, then elimination.

....Perry
MMP

A broken American squad possessing a MMG is on top of wire next to the creek in Suicide Creek. There is an unconcealed unbroken Japanese unit also on top of the wire in the same Location. The only rout option is under the wire (minimum one MF), into the Creek (three MF) and then into another hex that will be ≥ three MF, i.e. no matter what happens the American unit will be eliminated for Failure to Rout because it will end the RtPh ADJACENT to the Japanese unit on the wire. Does the American squad make its wire dr and end the RtPh and be eliminated either under the wire (wire dr=4-6, where the MMG will drop to the ground under the wire) or in the stream (wire dr=1-3, where the MMG will be eliminated)? Or is the American squad eliminated for Failure to Rout before it starts the rout without expending any MF (leaving the MMG on top of the wire) because of the impossibility of achieving a meaningful result?

He is asking about when using Area Target Type when the target is wading. When wading using Area Target Type the FP is halved for ATT and halved again for wading from the normal ordnance FP for the caliber, i.e. the nominal FP is ¼× the normal ordnance FP for the caliber. The CH is 2× the normal ordinance FP for the column. Hence the swing from ATT while wading goes from ¼× to 2× the normal ordnance FP for the caliber, a swing of eight times. There is some variability in the actual column used due to rounding on the IFT. The 50mm starts with the normal ordnance FP being six FP. This is halved once for ATT to three FP and then halved again to one-and-a-half FP. The CH is doubled to twelve, and the ratio between the two FPs is 8:1 before rounding. But of course the IFT only has a one FP column, so the one-and-a-half FP is rounded down to one FP, Both he and I ignored the effects of rounding due to the limited number of columns on the IFT. For the 60mm the values would be 2 FP Area Target Type against wading vs sixteen FP for the CH, and in this case there is no column rounding. The ratios between the nominal and actual FPs remains 8:1. 

In higher columns, i.e. normal ordnance FP of sixteen and twenty, the ratio between the actual FP value used is less than 8:1, again because of column rounding. For sixteen the ratio is 30:4 (= 7.5:1) and for twenty FP it is 36:5 (= 7.2:1). After that you start getting into heavy payload (C.7) and comparing nominal and actual FP isn't useful.

question:

"Assuming an otherwise clear LOS, even if a firing (or

Level 4 is two levels higher, so reduces the number of blin hexes by one. At 1-4 range, there would be 1 blind hex (unless a hill, there must at least be one blind hex).

The bolded part does not make any sense to me.
It seems to say that the blind hex is equal to the height of the obstacle. But this can't be the case.
(What does it even mean that a hex is equal to a height?)Barring additional elements, a n level obstacle has n blind hexes.
Why couldn't it be the case, as the rules say it?

The bold part means that the number of blind hexes behind the obstacle is equal to the height of the obstacle in full heights (discarding fractions of height like rooftops, slopes, hillock summits, etc). For example a unit in a level 3 hill looking behind a building of height 2.5 will have 2 blind hexes behind the building.

Thank you all for your answers.
My mistake was reading the sentence so that 'equal to the height...' referred to the hexes behind the obstacle (which doesn't really make any sense) when it actually refers to the number of the hexes (which makes perfect sense).

(But still, it is a bit oddly constructed sentence... isn't it... or... 🤔)
Yep, the equal means the number of hexes, not the size of the hexes or the height they represent. Lots of sentences could be better worded.

Calculating blind hexes is a multi-step process. The assumption is the higher unit is at at elevation > the obstacle.
1) start with the number of blind hexes = the number of levels the obstacle is above the lower unit (FRD). For example if the obstacle is a level 2.5 building and the lower unit is at level zero, your initial value is there are two blind hexes. If the obstacle is a level 2.5 building rising from level zero and the lower unit is at level one, your initial value is one blind hex.
2) add one blind hex for each five hexes of range (FRD) between the higher unit and the obstacle. For example if the obstacle is sixteen hexes range from the higher unit, add three blind hexes.
3) subtract one one blind hex for each full level > one of the higher unit over the obstacle height (FRD). For example if the obstacle is a level 2.5 building and the higher unit is at level three, by 1) above there are two blind hexes. If the higher unit is at level four, by 1) and 3) there is one blind hex.
4) For a non-hill-crest-line, including a cliff, the minimum number of blind hexes is one, regardless of the results of the above calculations
5) For a hill-crest-line obstacle, subtract one. The minimum number of blind hexes is zero.

First, every hex has a height. Generally 0. (Known as the Base Level.) A unit in that hex will generally be at that height (discounting building levels, gullies, etc.).

Obstacles also have a height. A few of them (hedges, rubble, etc) have a height equal to one-half level. Since you only worry about full-level heights, they can be ignored if you have any sort of greater elevation on them. Buildings often have a height with a half level (a typical two-hex building has two levels and an obstacle height of 1.5). Assuming you have a height greater than that of the top of the building, you ignore the half level. (But if you don't, that extra 0.5 blocks same-level LOS just like a wall or rubble would.)

And yes, the number of blind hexes is equal to the obstacle height (discounting those half levels). Note that you use the equivalent height. So, a unit in a valley (base height -1) is being viewed by someone at level 2, and there's a single-story building at normal ground level (0) in the way, the obstacle height is 2 (1 for being on higher ground, and 1 for the building itself), and there will be two blind hexes before worrying about distance or greater elevation advantages.

And you could rebase the map so that level zero is now level ten, level one is now level eleven and so on, and the answers for blind hexes should still be the same. I seldom think of levels as absolute numbers for calculations of blind hexes.

The "height equivalent" is the height of the obstacle as measured from the lowest unit in the case in question. Which isn't necessarily quite the same thing as what you said. Two units both at ground level 0, and a multi-story building in between in a valley would have a height equivalent of 1.

As for your examples. 'a' is correct assuming the lowest level unit you're checking is at ground level. If instead it's also on the level 1 hill, it'd be 1. title: Do WIRE and MINES affect friendlies?
question:
We play that any unit is affected by Wire - there are not secret routes through known only to the owner of the Wire.

For Mines the rules say " Whenever a unit enters/leaves a minefield hex, the owning player must announce a minefield attack vs the unit". It doesn't mention enemy unit. So do Mines attack friendlies just as they would enemies?

If they do affect friendlies that seems strange since the strength would have to be revealed to the opponent "to verify the IFT result".

If they do not affect friendlies is there a generic statement in the rules to the effect that "unit" always implies "enemy unit" unless stated otherwise? Have I missed something?

Cheers,
Neil
author: doktor avalanche
consensus_answer:
Mines attack anyone. Ask me about the time I moved a squad into a hex then realized it contained my own HIP mines. D'oh. You'd think they´d give out maps marking the places to avoid.

Wire is somewhat different. Per A12.33, "A unit entering/exiting a hidden Fortification (including Wire but not Panjis) pays no MF/MP to do so, provided that Fortification remains hidden including Infantry/Cavalry (only) crossing a roadblock hexside." This means you can *move* through HIP (only) Wire without paying extra MF. This does not give any other rights with regard to wire, so you can't Advance below Wire nor move below Wire while CX nor Dash nor avoid Wire immobilization DRs. And once they are on map, everyone pays. This makes placing wire in pillbox hexes troublesome if you might want to leave the pillbox.

title: LC Inherent MG use timing
question:
I'm going into details here but…

G 12.5 NON-CC ATTACKS FROM/BY LC: The Inherent weapon(s) of a LC may Prep Fire only if the LC is Fast Aground and Inherently crewed.

Why the "Fast" prerequisite? Being "Fast Aground" assumes the LC previously attempted to remove its Aground (and thus its Bogged) status in a previous MPh and didn't make it, basically. Why a LC couldn't use its MG when being "simply" Aground? 

And why the following:
G 12.211 FAST AGROUND: An otherwise-Mobile LC may attempt to remove its Aground (and thus its Bogged) status at the start of its MPh, provided it has not fired during its PFPh.

How could the LC have fired during the PFPh if it wasn't Fast Aground. This is confusing.
author: poifpoif
consensus_answer:
When aground but not fast aground the LC might try to unbeach [G12.3] itself. But this is not required, and units might unload (in hex) instead, going "over the side." Per D6.5, "Passenger/Riders may leave a vehicle that fired in the preceding PFPh and expended no MP in this MPh, although they could not leave the vehicle's Location during that MPh," so without G12.5 the LC could fire while the passengers unload. The rule prevents the LC from firing in the PFPh while the Passengers unload. The LC might even just sit there, for instance if unloading would result in much carnage on its contents and its fire support would help other units. I assume this is done for "reality reasons" (e.g. the crew was busy with the disembarkation) but I don't know for certain.

As to the apparently unnecessary phrase in G12.211 I have no idea, but it does not create a conflict so I'll just let it roll.

title: Personnel units in Shallow water
question:
How Personnel units should behave in Shallow water is rather unclear to me, particularly when exiting LC.

G12.4 (UN)LOADING deals with how/when should Infantry unload from LC. But what happens once they're in Shallow water? Are the units then considered to be Wading? If so, what does it mean in terms of Movement? Where can I find the rules governing the movement of Personnel units in Shallow water? Is it considered as an Hazardous movement? 
What about 5.532 SHALLOW WATER, do Personnel units exiting from a LC become Fording units? Hence having to spend all their MF to move a single hex?

From what I understand:
Personnel units (PU) never become Fording when exiting a LC. Even if the LC is destroyed, they’re still considered as Passengers (provided they’re still alive).
They spend either 1/2 or 1/4 of their allowed MF to exit a LC (depending on whether the LC is aground/immobilized).
PU can never voluntarily exit a LC until it is either immobilized/aground/beached. 
PU move from one Shallow water hex to the next paying 3MF. This is not considered as an Hazardous movement.
They’re to be considered as Wading units, but it’s irrelevant regarding movement (only for fire purposes).
I can’t find any situation where Passengers in LC would become Fording units.
author: poifpoif
consensus_answer: The question is perhaps better phrased, "what happens when they are out of the LC?" I suppose this depends on how the scenario defines the water hexes. In order to invoke E5.532 Shallow Water the hexes would have to be defined as "fordable" per E5.53. Most scenarios that use LC won't define water obstacle hexes as "fordable;" typically they will use OCEAN hexes per G13.1. Some scenarios might not have OCEAN hexes or even a mix of both, but "fordable" hexes would be river hexes or ponds. See the G13.12 EX. If in OCEAN hexes, units are wading per G13.42. As G13.42 says, "Wading—not Fording—rules apply in shallow-OCEAN." Also for both boats and LC, units can unload in a hex other than the one the boat/LC is in when the boat/LC is beached across a hexside.

title: Initial Setup Using Concealment -- Some OB-Designated and Some Not
question:
A12.12 Placement doesn't make sense to me because it seems to require that only the scenario defender's OB-designated concealment counters can be placed before the attacker sees the board.  If that were to be the case, then at the start of the game the attacker would know which of the defense's concealment markers cover real units and which are fakes.

Diagram provided shows a portion of initial setup for ASL-82 "For Honor Alone".  

The French setup first, and are provided with (10) scenario OB-designated concealment counters.  Therefore, our assumption is that before the German player ever sees the board, the French player places all 10 fake concealment counters on board as well as single non-OB-designated concealment counters on top of all counter piles that contain real units.  Is this correct?

Only after that placement of all French concealment counters does the German player see the board.  The diagram shows his setup in progress.  He wants to setup some of his own counters in concealment terrain (in this case grain and woods). Multiple choice question:  

1) Is he too allowed to place single concealment markers atop all his unit piles that start in concealment terrain before the defending French player sees the board again? Or...
2) If not, can he place concealment markers atop his unit piles that start in concealment terrain, but only after the French player has examined them? Or...  
3) As the scenario attacker, is he dis-allowed from placing any concealment markers unless those piles are out of the initial LOS of the French player's units?
author: A2SimGamer
consensus_answer:
Pretty much what JR V says.  Note that this is covered in A12.12.  After the side setting up first is done (and done out of sight of the opponent), they place their scenario-designed ?? but only in concealment terrain.  He can place these on existing units or make dummy stacks, as he sees fit.  E.g. if you have 12 scenario-designated ??, you could conceal 12 of your stacks or make 6 2-high dummy stacks or some combination of the two (almost always better to do a combination, as adding 6 2-high dummy stacks will quickly let your opponent know that you have exactly 6 2-high dummy stacks 🙂 ).

If your opponent does not also set up on the board, then you can /also/ place free ?? markers on any stacks that don't already have ?? (key being you never get to place a free ?? on top of a scenario-designated ??).

If your opponent sets up on board, he does so after your scenario-designated ??, then BOTH of you get to conceal units out of enemy LOS or >17 hexes from all enemies.  Note that you don't get to inspect the enemy stacks, ONLY THE TOPMOST UNIT (A2.9).  If he also has scenario-designated ??, he would do his setup and place those out of your view, then you both would check for free ??.

replies.body: Does the German player have any OB concealment markers? I expect not, but it would be different if he did.

The French setup first, and are provided with (10) scenario OB-designated concealment counters.  Therefore, our assumption is that before the German player ever sees the board, the French player places all 10 fake concealment counters on board as well as single non-OB-designated concealment counters on top of all counter piles that contain real units.  Is this correct?

No. OB-designated "?" can be placed on real units, so the most you can say when you see an OB-designated "?" is that it *might* be a dummy.

If the opposition player has units that he sets up on board, then yes, he will see the board with only the OB designated "?". If the opposition player has no on board setup, i.e. all units enter as reinforcements, often but not necessarily on the first turn, he can't see the board until both the OB designated and "free" "?" are put on board. 

The sequence is:
1) The first player to set up sets up his OB, including OB-designated "?". OB-designated "?" may be set up on real units and/or other OB-designated "?", making the lower "?" counters dummies. The player with second setup may not view the board at this time, and it is good manners to step away for a while while the first player sets up. Players who are familiar with each other may optionally engage in chit-chat, but the second player should not look at the board.
2) If the second player has on-board setup, he now views the board and sets up his OB, including any OB-designated "?". If he has no on-board setup. he may not view the board. As above the first player will often step away.
3a) If only one player sets up on board, that player now places "free" "?" counters on all stacks that do not contain an OB-designated "?". The opposing player still can't view the board.
3b) If both players set up on board, both can place "free" "?" counters.

For this scenario you perform 1, 2 then 3b, because both sides have on-board setup.
For a scenario where one side sets up on board and the second enters as turn one reinforcement you perform 1 then 3a.

For a scenario with both sides setting up on-board the player has to choose between using his OB-designated "?" to conceal real units that may not be able to gain "free" concealment (or that would gain "free" concealment but the player would prefer to hide anyway) and creating dummies.

I did not get into the technical details of where OB-designated "?" counters may set up, but as pointed out they must set up in concealment terrain. This means that even if the opposition is coming from offboard, any "?" counters in non-concealment terrain, often open ground (including behind walls and hedges) but also crags, graveyards, gullies, and shellholes, must be "free" "?" counters and so not dummies. Or perhaps about equally likely, they are dummies and your opponent has set up illegally. Whenever I think my opponent is likely to set up illegally (graveyards are probably the most likely for this), I will draw attention to the fact that OB-designated "?" must be set up in concealment terrain.

I think that you can even set up HIP a Gun in Open Ground.

True, but HIP is not OB-designated "?". HIP (for Guns only per A12.34) and "free" "?" counters at setup can be set up in non-concealment terrain.

Just for my own clarification now. That HIP gun comes on board (concealed) as soon as an Enemy unit has LOS to it, right?

And I think the Gun loses HIP immediately upon someone having LOS to it (being placed under a 5/8" ??), if I remember correctly ...  I know there was something wonky about setting up HIP in Open Ground.

A12.34, "An Emplaced Gun may also always use HIP if not in Concealment Terrain, provided it sets up out of the LOS of all enemy ground units—but must be placed onboard under a "?" as soon as a Good Order enemy ground unit has a LOS to it regardless of range, e.g., at the start of the first RPh."
Cool. Just wanted to make sure I didn't misunderstand a rule (again) ;-)

title: MTR used in Defensive Fire Ph and used as Intensive Fire
question:
Are the following true?
5/8" MTR are being considered as Guns, and may thusly Intensive Fire. 1/2" MTR can't.
1/2" MTR are SW but can't Subsequent First Fire, only MG can.

Q: Can a 5/8" MTR use Intensive Fire, even though its ROF has been previously exhausted?

Q: Is there any situation where a MTR FP wouldn't be halved on the IFT (CH excepted)?
author: poifpoif
consensus_answer:
Are the following true?
5/8" MTR are being considered as Guns, and may thusly Intensive Fire. 1/2" MTR can't.
1/2" MTR are SW but can't Subsequent First Fire, only MG can.

Q: Can a 5/8" MTR use Intensive Fire, even though its ROF has been previously exhausted?

Q: Is there any situation where a MTR FP wouldn't be halved on the IFT (CH excepted)?
1) Yes. One interesting case is that the MTR can Intensive Fire using SMOKE ammo. That also applies to non-MTRs, but with MTRs you can potentially get off a series of SMOKE with ROF, then throw an Intensive Fire SMOKE round down range for good measure.

2) There are technicalities where the weapon is called in real life a "mortar" but is not in ASL terms. So the British PIAT SW and the Petard on the Churchill AVRE are spigot mortars, and they use full FP. For a weapon marked as a MTR I can't think of any. When OBA represents the same weapon (e.g. 80+ OBA often represents 81mm mortars—not always because it might instead be a 25-lbr or a German 88), the OBA is at "full" FP, i.e. sixteen FP. But when used on board the MTR always uses Area Target Type, and so is always halved. Note it is the Target Type that halves the FP, not the weapon type.

As the title of the thread is about DFPh, a Mortar can only Intensive Fire during that phase if marked with a First Fire counter (i.e. First Fired during the Enemy's MPh and lost ROF), and only vs. ADJACENT hexes.
Which rules out most mortars which have a minimum range greater than 1.

The big take-away, which we had done wrong for a LONG time, is that 1/2" light MTRs only get to fire up to their ROF, then they are DONE done.  We kept thinking they could IF, which is /wrong/.  Only the big guys (5/8" Guns) can IF as you note...  Took us a long time to realize this!

title: MTR fire against Passengers in OT vehicle/LC (1)
question:
How to resolve a successful TH Mortar fire against Infantry units (passengers) being carried by a moving Armored but OT Landing Craft at sea (un-beached)? 
First, regarding G 12.63, although the counter is showing front and rear/side AF, as the LC is OT, should it be considered as fully armored or not fully armored for the Area Fire resolution?
Then, how should the MTR attack be resolved against the Infantry units being carried? Do G 12.672 Ordnance Hull Hit and 12.673 Ordnance Turret Hit apply when firing a MTR ordnance against a LC? Should the C 1.55 procedure be disregarded then?

This is quite confusing to me.
author: poifpoif
consensus_answer:
The difference between fully-armored and partially-armored is that a partially-armored vehicle or LC has a ★ for one or more of its aspects/facings [D1.22]. Any vehicle with numeric armor factors for all its aspects/facings is fully armored even if open-topped. 

As a side note, *all* partially- and fully-armored LC are open-topped.

On the LC Destruction Table (after G12.64) cross-reference the effects DR vs. the TK# on the HE (Area Target Type; OBA) column. For a fully-armored LC if it is ≤ the TK# on the IFT column, Passengers are attacked collaterally at half FP on a hull hit per G12.672. On a turret hit the crew is attacked but not the Passengers.

title: FFE2 and Smoke
question: I know another round of HE goes off on the FFE2, but if I opted for Smoke on FFE1, does another round of Smoke fall on the same hex's, basically refreshing the Smoke to +3 again, or is the Fire Mission over after the first round of Smoke has fallen on FFE1?
author: Fly by Night
consensus_answer:
Depends on when you called it...

Prep Fire for FF1, then +3 smokes are placed.  Assuming you don't correct, then during next Defensive Fire they'll drop ANOTHER +2 level of smoke (see A24.5).  This doesn't really matter too much as the max DRM is +3 (+4 if units are in the hex).

However, if you fire first in the DFPh, then the OBA places +2 Smoke...which is then removed at the start of your PFPh, only to be replaced by +3 Smoke.

If you correct Smoke OBA after firing during the PFPh, you can get some pretty impressive Smoke fields laid down... as you'll get 7 hexes of +3 Smoke and another 7 of +2 Smoke (though these latter will disappear at the start of your next PFPh).

-K

replies.body:
Depends on when you called it...

Prep Fire for FF1, then +3 smokes are placed.  Assuming you don't correct, then during next Defensive Fire they'll drop ANOTHER +2 level of smoke (see A24.5).  This doesn't really matter too much as the max DRM is +3 (+4 if units are in the hex).

However, if you fire first in the DFPh, then the OBA places +2 Smoke...which is then removed at the start of your PFPh, only to be replaced by +3 Smoke.

If you correct Smoke OBA after firing during the PFPh, you can get some pretty impressive Smoke fields laid down... as you'll get 7 hexes of +3 Smoke and another 7 of +2 Smoke (though these latter will disappear at the start of your next PFPh).

title: Capturing/Entering Abandoned vehicles
question:
The rules in A21.2 are pretty clear on capturing an abandoned vehicle. However, it does state that if infantry of both side in the location can both roll to capture the vehicle. 

The rules for entering an abandoned vehicle in D5.42 does not indicate if this is for only friendly MMC or both friendly and enemy MMC?

My read is that if you want to take two turns to capture the vehicle by moving to the vehicle location first turn and then occupy the vehicle in the second turn or take one turn by advancing into CC and capturing (Automatic capture if no enemy infantry in location) you choose. However, CC is the only method available if enemy in the location. 

Any clarification would be great. Thanks all.
author: rhunter1148
consensus_answer:
Per A21.2, "If there are no enemy Personnel in the Location with an Abandoned enemy AFV, it may be captured automatically by any Infantry unit in the same location at the end of a CCPh but Ambush is NA." The rule then continues on with "otherwise," i.e. the case where there are units from both sides. Note that the vehicle has to be *enemy* in order to be captured "automatically." A friendly vehicle not in a CC location would have to be re-manned per D5.42.

There is also this q&a: 
"A21.2 & D5.42 1). Friendly Infantry in the same Location as an Abanoned enemy vehicle are not in a CC Location if no other enemy units are present (because an Abandoned vehicle is not a Unit because it is incapable of movement (Index)). So said Friendly Infantry may not Capture the AFV using A21.2 mechanics because said Infantry is not in a CC Location. Yes?
A. No. Read the sentence right before that. An Abandoned enemy AFV may be automatically captured at the end of the CCPh, regardless of being in a “CC Location” or not.
2). May a Friendly AFV be Crewed this way?
A. No, unless actually in CC."

title: DRM when a 10-2 leader becomes a heroic leader
question:
1) If a 10-2 leader becomes a Hero can he use the leader DRM of -2 if he only directs fire from the location he is in, or must he use the heroic DRM of -1?

2) If he enters CC in a building, can he use the Heros stealty ability in Ambush and then the leader DRM of -2 in CC?
author: Nslcole
consensus_answer:
1) If a 10-2 leader becomes a Hero can he use the leader DRM of -2 if he only directs fire from the location he is in, or must he use the heroic DRM of -1?

2) If he enters CC in a building, can he use the Heros stealty ability in Ambush and then the leader DRM of -2 in CC?

1) a heroic leader may use either its leadership DRM or its heroic DRM in an attack. If it wants to use its leadership DRM it can't add its FP to the attack; conversely if it wants to use its heroic DRM it must add its FP (at normal range) to the attack.
2) Both the stealthy drm and any leadership drm would apply to ambush. The stealthy drm is not an application of the heroic drm, which does not apply to ambush. In CC the player can choose which DRM (heroic or leadership) to apply, except that a SMC attacking alone can't use the leadership DRM for itself but could use the heroic DRM.

OBA can be tough to wrap your head around at first, but it has a natural rhythm once you get the hang of it.  Hopefully you have the OBA flow chart available, it will answer most of your questions.

As to your specific question, the rule applies to the player that owns the OBA.  During that player’s prep or defensive fire phase, you will first roll to see if you maintain radio contact, then if you succeed you take the next appropriate action, such as moving a spotting round or blasting away with an FFE.

The official OBA flowchart was released in Action Pack #1. In the second edition ASLRB it was put on the back of the A/G National Capabilities Chart (printed on a yellowish-green background). There are various threads here on bgg and videos on youtube that claim to show you the process. I have not reviewed any of them, and I would expect that most are at least a little bit wrong but they probably get the broad points right.

All OBA actions and changes (other than attacking units that move into an FFE) happen during either the player's PFPh during the player's Player Turn or during the DFPh during the enemy Player Turn. When a player starts his OBA actions (in *his* PFPh/DFPh) if there is an FFE:2 on board he can cancel it or resolve it and convert it to a FFE:C as part of resolution. When a player starts his OBA actions and there is an FFE:C on board (which will be the next player turn after the resolution of the FFE:2), he must perform one of the actions in C1.34. If the player cannot perform one of the actions in C1.34, the mission is cancelled and the FFE:C counter removed.

Correction is done as part of the OBA actions. It is mandatory when, C1.335 "Disregarding SMOKE, if he currently has no LOS to the SR's or FFE's Blast Height nor to any non-Aerial Location in/adjacent-to the SR's hex that contains a Known (to him) enemy unit, he must Correct (1.4) or Cancel (as per 1.336-.337) that SR or FFE."

Second. From the rulebook:
1.22 MAINTAINING RADIO CONTACT: To maintain Radio Contact from a preceding turn, the player must roll lower than or equal to the radio contact value again in his next PFPh or DFPh (whichever comes first),…

How could the DFPh comes first? It is said the Radio Contact should be maintained from a turn to the next. PFPh necessarily comes before the DFPh. I don't get it. 
It is not any old PFPh or DFPh, it is *his* PFPh/DFPh, i.e. the player's. If the players starts OBA in *his* player turn, he will do so in *his* PFPh. When the next player turn starts, he does nothing for OBA in the *enemy* PFPh but can execute OBA actions, starting with rolling for radio contact, in *his* DFPh.

I also suggest reviewing the Advanced Sequence of Play (ASOP) regarding the exact order of actions during the PFPh/DFPh. OBA has to be done at a specific time in those phases. Players who play me will often hear me mumble, "SMOKE first then OBA," at the start of my PFPh/DFPh/AFPh (but no OBA in AFPh). After all SMOKE and after all OBA "ordinary" prep or defensive fire begins.

Thank you guys. I haven't struggled with such a rule point for a very long time tbh. It's a true nightmare. I found this very useful thread from Jay Richardson: 

However as he writes it down himself, all possible outcomes aren't covered unfortunately. But at least I have a better understanding of the overall "flow" of the OBA process.

One more thing: "…the Extent of Error is limited to a maximum of one hex for each multiple of three hexes (FRU) from the SR/FFE counter to the AR counter (inclusive of the latter only)…". 
So once you've determined the range of error (let's say an observer correct their SR 12 hexes away for instance; the error won't be more than 4 hexes away then), how do you practically determine the number of hexes the SR counter should be moved away eventually? How is a dr ranging from 1-6 supposed to be converted in a 1-4 result?

Note that is for Correcting a SR (/FFE, but they can only be Corrected three hexes).

If there is no SR/FFE on board for that OBA module, then you put down an AR (Artillery Request). Determine if you are on target (usually not). If so, swap AR for SR, done. If not, put the SR on the AR and roll for scatter.

If there is a SR on board, then you can Correct it, by putting a AR somewhere within 18 hexes of the SR. Check for error. If there is, put the SR on the AR and roll for scatter. normally But, the distance of scatter is limited by 1/3 distance Corrected. So, of you Correct 6 hexes, then if you roll a 1 for distance, it goes one hex in the direction rolled. Any other result will result in a two-hex error, as anything over 2 is treated as 2 (because that's your maximum).

In the case where a SR is corrected twelve hexes and the correction is not mandatory, you roll direction and distance if not accurate with a maximum extent of error of four hexes. On a distance dr of one, two or three the SR scatters one, two or three hexes respectively. On a distance dr of 4-6 the SR drifts the maximum, i.e. four hexes. If the correction is mandatory then there is no maximum error, i.e. the full distance dr is used.

Note that it is a very, very rare day that you would be correcting twelve hexes. The maximum error distance is only six hexes, and usually you want to bring the OBA in on the same target as before, or at least one close to it.

title: Pillbox, Trenches and Ambush in CC
question:
As per the rules: 
Whenever Infantry advance into CC in a woods/building Location or with/against a concealed unit(s) an Ambush can conceivably occur.

Are foxholes, pillboxes and/or trenches to be considered as building locations? Or maybe EXC that allow Ambush dr? Or there’s no Ambush to be rolled with such « fortifications »?
How is the +2 drm for « in Pillbox » status supposed to be applied then?
author: poifpoif
consensus_answer:
As per the rules: 
Whenever Infantry advance into CC in a woods/building Location or with/against a concealed unit(s) an Ambush can conceivably occur.

Are foxholes, pillboxes and/or trenches to be considered as building locations? Or maybe EXC that allow Ambush dr? Or there’s no Ambush to be rolled with such « fortifications »?
How is the +2 drm for « in Pillbox » status supposed to be applied then?

A11.4 "Whenever Infantry advance into CC (unless reinforcing a Melee) in a woods/building Location or with/against a concealed unit(s) an Ambush can conceivably occur."
Since pillboxes have limited CAs and LOS, it's almost trivial to enter a pillbox hex and remain concealed, even in open ground. But beyond that, pillboxes can be set up in grain,  orchards, etc., making it easy to advance in while concealed even if there are other units around to provide LOS to the pillbox hex. And pillboxes can set up in woods, which doesn't require a concealed unit at all.

Moreover, it could be the unit inside the pillbox that's the concealed one. Although B30.7 says attacks against a pillbox aren't affected by concealment, other effects of concealment still apply.

title: WA (Wall Advantage effects)
question:
There are 3 pages in the rulebook describing how to/when gain/loose Wall Advantage, but what does the WA do actually!? What's the benefit?
Does a unit need to get the WA in order to get the +2 TEM? Anything else I'd be missing?
author: poifpoif
consensus_answer:
Does a unit need to get the WA in order to get the +2 TEM? 

This is one of the more confusing aspects of Wall Advantage. The target does not necessarily need WA to use the wall TEM. In order to use the wall(/hedge/bocage) TEM it is sufficient that the *enemy* unit that is firing does *not* have Wall Advantage over the hexside. If the unit firing is not adjacent to the target, then it can't have WA over a hexside of the target hex and the target can use the hexside TEM. That's a simple case. When the firer is adjacent (and most likely ADJACENT) then by possessing WA it can deny the use of the hexside terrain to the target. Otherwise the target, whether because it possesses WA or because neither side has WA, can choose to use the hexside TEM.

Anything else I'd be missing?

There are lots of ifs, buts and gotchas with WA. This thread covers non-adjacent firers and also vehicles in hexes with positive TEM. PRC [EXC: motorcyclists (really?)] never get hexside TEM. Walls can only be at one level (ground or hilltop) and with hillside walls [B9.35, B9.62] only units on one side of the wall can use wall advantage. Hexside TEM can be reduced by sufficient elevation advantage [B9.33]; this can be very helpful in an urban setting where level two buildings have walls or hedges around them.

replies.body:
There are 3 pages in the rulebook describing how to/when gain/loose Wall Advantage, but what does the WA do actually!? What's the benefit?
Does a unit need to get the WA in order to get the +2 TEM? Anything else I'd be missing? 

Having Wall Advantage prevents adjacent enemies on the other side of the wall from getting the +2 TEM.
Got it. Thanks!

the main (and original) purpose of Wall Advantage was to differentiate between two adjacent units with a wall between them who actually was defending behind the wall.
So if an attacking unit moved adjacent to a defender behind the wall, the defender could claim wall advantage, gaining the wall TEM, and more importantly, denying the wall TEM to the attacking unit.

B9.322 then made WA much more difficult by making people choose WA over other TEM at the end of RPh when Defending. Probably not significant to new players, but a new learning of WA for older players, and with no sense or benefit I could see. Apparently allowing the defender minor shifts in-hex positions whilst the enemy moved was anathema to the rules lawyers.

title: Pillbox versus LATW
question:
Does the +7 TEM from the pillbox in KK5 apply to the TH number of the BAZ44? 

If so, how to get rid of that pillbox? Is CC the only way to get rid of units entrenched under such a pillbox counter?
author: poifpoif
consensus_answer:
From 30. PILLBOXES
30.2
…Fire from inside a pillbox into its own hex is limited to CC, or SMOKE grenade placement, or a Thrown DC (30.31), or to vertices of its CA, or to PBF vs units currently crossing the CA hexsides of its own hex.

30.6 SAME HEX: Same-level units inside and outside a pillbox in the same hex are ADJACENT…

How to understand "to vertices of its CA"? We're talking of units occupying the same hex here, no?
Can same-level infantry units outside a pillbox in the same hex point blank fire at enemy units inside the pillbox? If so, is the CA TEM to be applied?

Tracing LOS to(/from) the "vertex of its CA" would apply to an attack that traced LOS from the pillbox (i.e. the center dot of the hex) to a vertex of that same hex and by reciprocity vice-versa. The most obvious case for such an attack/LOS would be against a unit in bypass of an obstacle in that hex. If the pillbox is in a woods hex and an enemy unit bypassed that woods obstacle in front of the CA, the units in the pillbox could take a whack. Infantry can't remain in bypass, but a vehicle and (I believe) cavalry may, and as such may fire back at the pillbox through its CA [B30.1]. There may be a few other causes for such a LOS; underbelly attacks [D4.3] would be one example but that would not allow a return attack. Since Infantry can't remain in bypass of a hex I can think of no situations where an Infantry unit in a pillbox hex but outside the pillbox would trace LOS from the vertex of the hex, for making an attack anyway.

Why answering rules questions is hard, and why perhaps one should be a little bit cautious about thinking something is "obvious."

Starting with the COWTRA (Concentrate On What The Rules Allow) principle, you have to find a rule that allows doubling for fire at range one. This is fairly easily done, A7.21, quoted above. Even at this point you are wading in the weeds, as the sentence is a tough parse with lots of conditions. A unit in a pillbox is in a separate Location from the Location it is set up in, and you can only Advance from a Pillbox to its containing Location, not to an adjacent hex (unless a bunker). So looking at A7.21 the second half of the "while" clause, "adjacent to and either within one level or higher than its target," would seem to apply. If that were true it would seem that fire from the lower Location would be doubled to the Location containing the pillbox across a double crestline (because ADJACENT) but not INTO the pillbox itself (because not ADJACENT, no Advance is possible because it would require going through two Locations).

This would be odd already. But the other thing you have to worry about once you have found your COWTRA rule is that some other rule somehow changes it. And of course (sigh) that is true here. B30.2, "Units in an adjacent, ground-level Location within a pillbox's CA are treated as being ADJACENT to units in the pillbox (and vice versa) for purposes of Point Blank Fire, FPF, DM, rout, and for DC Placement vs the pillbox." By B30.2 units inside a pillbox and outside in the CA are ADJACENT even across a double crestline. They are ADJACENT in both directions for purposes of PBF even across a two-level cliff with a pillbox on the upper level. That means the first half of the "while" clause of A7.21 applies even when the second half may not. At this point I suspect that something is broken in the rules because a unit at a lower level firing up two levels across a cliff would seem not to get PBF against the non-pillbox Location (not ADJACENT, not adjacent and within one level or above), but would seem to get PBF against a pillbox in that same Location (ADJACENT for purposes of PBF by B30.2). 

That's how I read it as presently written. Of course I may have missed another, relevant rule. While I was not completely incorrect in stating that in most cases PBF applies, in fact in *all* cases applies because B30.2 makes the two Locations ADJACENT for purposes of PBF. And that is why answering rules questions is hard. And why it takes a long time to develop even a moderately good sense of what is "obvious."

title: #KIA and random selection
question:
7.301 #KIA: …  The number of units eliminated can exceed the number specified if Random Selection results in a tie for the last unit to be eliminated, but in no case are more units affected than are subject to the attack.

How could random selection results in a tie? I absolutely don't get it. I don't understand any if it.
author: poifpoif
consensus_answer:
I’ve always struggled with this bit. What does it mean?

See my just-completed example for the two different random selections after a Critical Hit. You can end up in a situation where different units are affected by different results. In my example, a 2KIA may not eliminate two units even though there are four present if only one of them is selected by Random Selection for the Critical Hit.

There are other ways that different units might be affected by different results. For example some units might be in a foxhole and some outside. Or some units may be holding flamethrowers. Or indirect Fire might hit a building and some units might be on upper levels and others on lower levels [B23.32]. I'm sure there are others. In each of these cases if there are multiple units but only one unit is affected by, say, a 2KIA, only that one unit is eliminated by that 2KIA. The other units are affected by their respective results (which may also be #KIAs, but may not be. 

So another quick example: 120mm OBA is firing on four units, three in a trench and one outside (with zero TEM). The effects DR is a three, a 2KIA for the unit outside the trench and a 3MC for units in the trench. The unit outside the trench is eliminated (but only one unit on a 2KIA) and the units in the trench take their 3MCs. No Random Selection is needed here.

A.9 describes Random Selection. The rule's example should illuminate you.

EX: A leader, crew, HS, and squad are stacked in that order from top to bottom in a hex which has just been attacked on the IFT yielding a K/1 result (7.302). The Random Selection dice are thrown and result in a white 3, a green 1, a red 2, and a black 3. As a result, the leader is wounded and the squad Reduced to a HS. The crew and both HS suffer a 1MC.

7.301 #KIA: …  The number of units eliminated can exceed the number specified if Random Selection results in a tie for the last unit to be eliminated, but in no case are more units affected than are subject to the attack.

How could random selection results in a tie? I absolutely don't get it. I don't understand any if it.
In ASL, random selection is defined in a certain way. Roll one die for each unit that can be affected, and all of the highest rolls are affected. So if 3 units are hit by a 1KIA, and the random selection rolls are 5,3,5, both units that rolled a 5 are eliminated.
This is why one fears the Yahtzee;-)

Extending the explanation slightly, the method for selecting when two units need to be picked (e.g. a 2KIA) is most commonly played with a house rule, a house rule that is so common that many players don't realize it is a house rule. The random selection rules say to use only the highest dr, but most players will use the next higher dr as well when necessary. So if four dice are rolled for four units, say 6, 4, 3 and 1, the KIA result will be applied against the "6" unit and the "4" unit. This "house rule" is so common that I have never seen anyone play differently. In fact the mechanics of random selection are not really well-defined in A.9 when two (or more) units need to be selected.

It is a logical application of the rule, where "unit" has a generic meaning.
Quite like if you say that a unit rolls a MC DR higher than its morale breaks: it also works when two units miss their MC, etc.
No one has ever asked a question about the RS rule in relation with the "house rule", because it is a logical application.
In fact the next paragraph of the rule, explaining how to deal with concealed counters, explicitly says to do exactly that: use the next highest number to keep selecting counters.

7.301 #KIA: … , but in no case are more units affected than are subject to the attack.

I’ve always struggled with this bit. What does it mean?

I think that means if only one unit is being fired at (eg a moving squad during defensive first fire) only that one unit can be affected by the fire attack, even if, say, a 2KIA result is rolled - even if there are other units in the location.

In fact the next paragraph of the rule, explaining how to deal with concealed counters, explicitly says to do exactly that: use the next highest number to keep selecting counters.
Only when a Dummy is selected. If there are no concealed units (or Dummies) that sentence is n/a.

For players who feel that using the next highest number to select is "obvious" when multiple units need to be selected, I won't argue because that's how it is generally played and that's how I play. I don't see that it is written in the rule, but if you say it is in there, hey that's ok by me.
I thought there was a Perry Sez on exactly this situation, but I can’t remember what he said.

There is this one:

"A.9 & A7.301 Four infantry units are in a Location that is effected by a 2KIA IFT result. The Random Selection DR is 6 , 6, 5, 3. How many are eliminated?
A. 2.
The Random Selection DR is 6, 5, 5, 3. How many are eliminated?
A. 3.
The Random Selection DR is 6, 6, 5, 5. How many are eliminated?
A. 2."

It doesn't say how the answer was arrived at, and I claim that you could not show this answer is correct from the rulebook. It does match how everyone I know (including myself) plays it, so you get no argument from this quarter.

Perhaps the more elucidating and illustrative question would be, what happens when there are multiple different results?

For instance an 81mm MTR is firing at four units in a fortified, single-level, stone building, +4 TEM. It rolls an original two (critical hit, area target type) on the TH DR, then an eight on the effects DR. What is the result?

First you need to roll a Random Selection to see who is affected by the Critical Hit. The Random Selection may pick one, two, three or four units. Next you apply the appropriate results to those selected and not selected for the Critical Hit. In this case the FP for a non-critical-hit is eight FP. Because the attack was on the Area Target Type, the TEM applies to the effects DR; the result is a Final effects DR of twelve on the eight FP column, no effect. For those units affected by the CH the attack will be on the thirty-two FP column with the TEM applied as a reverse DRM; the final result is a Final effects DR of four, a 2KIA. But only those units picked by the Random Selection for the Critical Hit would be so affected, and if only one were selected to receive the 2KIA, only that one unit would be eliminated.

If three or four units were picked for the Critical Hit then you would be back at the original question, what happens if there is not a tie for the highest dr? And again everyone plays that you use the second-highest Random Selection dr. Note that in this example there are *two* Random Selections, one for who is selected to receive the Critical Hit which can have from one to four units selected, and a second Random Selection for who is affected by the 2KIA. If the first Random Selection chooses only one or two units, there is no need to conduct the second Random Selection. That one unit or both those units are eliminated. If the first chooses three or four units, the second Random Selection needs to be made, and two, three, or four units may be eliminated.

In my example, a 2KIA may not eliminate two units even though there are four present if only one of them is selected by Random Selection for the Critical Hit.

There are other ways that different units might be affected by different results. For example some units might be in a foxhole and some outside. Or some units may be holding flamethrowers. Or indirect Fire might hit a building and some units might be on upper levels and others on lower levels [B23.32]. I'm sure there are others. In each of these cases if there are multiple units but only one unit is affected by, say, a 2KIA, only that one unit is eliminated by that 2KIA. The other units are affected by their respective results (which may also be #KIAs, but may not be. 

So another quick example: 120mm OBA is firing on four units, three in a trench and one outside (with zero TEM). The effects DR is a three, a 2KIA for the unit outside the trench and a 3MC for units in the trench. The unit outside the trench is eliminated (but only one unit on a 2KIA) and the units in the trench take their 3MCs. No Random Selection is needed here.

First you need to roll a Random Selection to see who is affected by the Critical Hit.

Something I didn’t know either.

C3.74 "Regardless of the number of targets in a Location struck by a CH, the special provisions of a CH apply only to the target(s) determined by Random Selection. Attacks on other units hit in that Location are resolved as if struck by a normal hit."

Another point to note is that Critical Hits do not affect terrain [C3.73]. That 6KIA you just scored with a Critical Hit vs a disrupted conscript halfsquad isn't necessarily going to bring the building down.

title: Multiple ROF and Sustained Fire
question:
From the digital rulebook:

9.2 MULTIPLE ROF:
…Once a MG has lost its Multiple ROF, it is marked with an appropriate Prep, First or Final Fire counter.

and 

9.3 SUSTAINED FIRE: A MG that attacks using Subsequent-First-Fire/ FPF (8.3/8.31), or during the DFPh while marked with a First Fire counter (8.4), is using Sustained Fire

1) In what situations would you mark a multiple ROF SW with a Final Fire counter straight away, if any? Or should a Final Fire counter always be placed necessarily after a First Fire counter?
2) Once a MG has lost its Multiple ROF, can it still use Sustained Fire?
author: poifpoif
consensus_answer:
From the digital rulebook:

9.2 MULTIPLE ROF:
…Once a MG has lost its Multiple ROF, it is marked with an appropriate Prep, First or Final Fire counter.

and 

9.3 SUSTAINED FIRE: A MG that attacks using Subsequent-First-Fire/ FPF (8.3/8.31), or during the DFPh while marked with a First Fire counter (8.4), is using Sustained Fire

1) In what situations would you mark a multiple ROF SW with a Final Fire counter straight away, if any? Or should a Final Fire counter always be placed necessarily after a First Fire counter?
2) Once a MG has lost its Multiple ROF, can it still use Sustained Fire? 

1) During the Defensive Fire Phase.
2) If marked with a First Fire counter. If fired during the Defensive Fire Phase, the MG will not get to use Sustained Fire.

Lesson - you get more opportunities to shoot during the movement phase, plus the ability to place Residual. Learning how to use firepower during the movement phase is one way to win at ASL.

title: Reducing an unbroken squad
question: I might have been playing this wrong for almost 2 years. Does a squad being reduced indeed keep their broken status!? So a full, unbroken squad, suffering reduction, would become an unbroken HS!?
author: poifpoif
consensus_answer:
I might have been playing this wrong for almost 2 years. Does a squad being reduced indeed keep their broken status!? So a full, unbroken squad, suffering reduction, would become an unbroken HS!?
For the most part true but it depends upon how the squad comes across its CR. On a K/# result [A7.302] an unbroken squad is reduced to an unbroken halfsquad that then has to take the corresponding #MC, but from its unbroken side with its unbroken ML. However if a squad rolls a casualty MC (an original twelve [A10.31]), it is CR and always broken, even if the final DR was not enough to break the squad. It's very rare to come across a situation where a unit, especially a MMC, could theoretically pass a MC on an original twelve. Such a situation can be found, but the resulting halfsquad is always broken anyway by A10.31.

In other cases, a CR in Close Combat leaves an unbroken halfsquad from a full squad. Booby traps [B28.9] leave an unbroken halfsquad. Crew Small Arms [A11.62] leave an unbroken halfsquad. PF abuse [C13.36] leaves an unbroken halfsquad. A Japanese or CPVA striped squad striping again leaves an unbroken halfsquad (this technically isn't CR I suppose). I'm probably missing some other, uncommon cases.

You surely know that game! 😄
Thanks
