title: BU Hellcats and options for fire
question:
Without getting into too many "boy we screwed up" background notes, we find ourselves in a situation where we have a BU Hellcat (OT Tank Destroyer) covering a potential movement path of a JPZ IV.  The JPZ IV isn't in LOS yet, but we're entering the German portion of the turn and there is some chance he moves up to engage the BU TD (there are other US AFVs in the area, as well as infantry with BAZ'45, so it isn't a cut and dry situation ...).

I'm posting to try to understand what our options are should the JPZ IV pull up into LOS of the TD.  My understanding is as follows:

1) The Germans will get a shot during their portion of the turn (either during MPH or their AFPh).  We cannot go CE, but could attempt to go in Motion or attempt to use smoke (either our smoke pot for a DR<= 3 (sP 5 -1 for BU, -1 for Hatten Special Rule) or a smoke grenade (dr=1).  I don't think we could do both, correct?  Only one or the other.

2) Assuming we don't go in Motion or get smoke /and/ the JPZ IV misses its AFPh shot at us, the turn ends and we get to the US player turn.  This is where I'm somewhat uncertain as to our options and how they play out.  We can't Prep Fire because we're BU, so during our MPh what exactly are our options?

- If we declare going CE and firing before starting the tank and leaving the hex, what happens?  Does this result in a Gun Duel option for the JPZ IV?  Would our lower die be doubled or would we just have to add +2 to our To Hit roll and not qualify for Acquisition?

- If we start up (1 MP), then the JPZ IV gets to shoot at us with no Moving/Motion vehicle DRM, correct?  As we haven't left the hex yet so we are not technically 'Moving'.  We could go CE or not, but if we expend the start MP then the JPZ IV is always going to get the first shot on us.  Or is this another "gun duel" opportunity (this time for us)?

Obviously if we managed to go into Motion the previous MPh, we could move out of the JPZ IV's LOS before he could get a shot on us during our MPh ... but chances are the JPZ IV would only expend 2 or 3 MPs in our LOS, so not a guarantee of being able to go into Motion.
author: kbernatz
consensus_answer:
1) The Germans will get a shot during their portion of the turn (either during MPH or their AFPh).  We cannot go CE, but could attempt to go in Motion or attempt to use smoke (either our smoke pot for a DR<= 3 (sP 5 -1 for BU, -1 for Hatten Special Rule) or a smoke grenade (dr=1).  I don't think we could do both, correct?  Only one or the other.

Can only do one. The smoke grenade would dissipate at the end of the enemy MPh. In that case the German would likely wait until the AFPh, assuming he has timed his MP expenditures correctly and come into LOS in the last two (or three) MP. If he hasn't the smoke grenades may force him either to take a premature shot or to spend more MP than expected in LOS. The smoke grenade is slightly higher odds but the sP has slightly better coverage. No clear winner.

2) Assuming we don't go in Motion or get smoke /and/ the JPZ IV misses its AFPh shot at us, the turn ends and we get to the US player turn.  This is where I'm somewhat uncertain as to our options and how they play out.  We can't Prep Fire because we're BU, so during our MPh what exactly are our options?

Correct, can't Prep.

- If we declare going CE and firing before starting the tank and leaving the hex, what happens?  Does this result in a Gun Duel option for the JPZ IV?  Would our lower die be doubled or would we just have to add +2 to our To Hit roll and not qualify for Acquisition?

Declaring a shot without expending MP *does* allow the rarely seen DEFENDER Gun Duel. The lower dr is not doubled for the attack because you are not non-stopped, and in any case the doubling does not apply to the Gun Duel calculation [C2.2401]. The attack would be liable to both case B & case C DRMs (case B *always* applies when any case C does except case C³), and because the M18 is not eligible for a Gyro, that means a minimum +4 TH DRM for the Gun Duel. Unless the JgdPz IV has done something really stupid (e.g. it has to change its CA), it wins the Gun Duel.

- If we start up (1 MP), then the JPZ IV gets to shoot at us with no Moving/Motion vehicle DRM, correct?  As we haven't left the hex yet so we are not technically 'Moving'.  We could go CE or not, but if we expend the start MP then the JPZ IV is always going to get the first shot on us.  Or is this another "gun duel" opportunity (this time for us)?

The Moving Target DRM (case J) does not apply. On the other had if the JgdPz IV has moved in close, point blank range (case L) no longer does.

This would be a Gun Duel opportunity for the ATTACKER this time but again the DRM are such that the DEFENDER wins. In both cases if the unit wanting to declare Gun Duel has to change CA, it can't declare a Gun Duel.

Obviously if we managed to go into Motion the previous MPh, we could move out of the JPZ IV's LOS before he could get a shot on us during our MPh ... but chances are the JPZ IV would only expend 2 or 3 MPs in our LOS, so not a guarantee of being able to go into Motion.
If the JgdPz IV has not moved to point blank range your best bet may to to go CE and attempt to throw smoke grenades. The sP is lower odds.

I assume you know that an AFV must use its entire MP allotment. If it stops and has not expended all its MP it is assumed to spend the rest of its MPh in Delay, which will increase the chances of a successful Motion dr. If your opponent is not careful he may make a mistake. If he does not, in the words of the great American armor leader, Captain Dezi Arnez, "Lieutenant Lucy, you got som' 'splainin' to do."

Reality arguments aren't helpful in playing against another opponent who probably is as good as telling reality stories as you.

As to the reality argument in this case, although the fire button could probably be pressed with everybody's head below the armor, the design and the doctrine of the US TDs meant that at least some of the crew (and in particular the commander) had spend a fair amount of time with their heads above the armor searching for targets, directing the movement of the vehicle to firing positions, watching for threats, etc. An "attack" is not just the second the fire button is pressed but includes all the time leading up to that instant, and being CE does not mean all the crew have their heads stuck out 100% of the time, but that the crew has parts exposed sufficiently long enough to be vulnerable to fire that could not penetrate the armor. In a vehicle with vision slits or vision blocks in a cupola or a rotatable periscope or multiple periscopes the crew can keep themselves protected from such fire (at a cost in situational awareness to be sure), but I believe the M18 only had a single (relatively narrow) gunsight for the gunner and periscopes for the driver and assistant driver. The commander would have no way of seeing what was going on except to stick his head out. Other crew members also probably spent a fair amount of time with their heads out looking for targets and threats outside the arcs of their vision devices too.
You can see in this historical footage (for the M10, but I believe the M18 would be about the same) the commander has his head above the armor with the field glasses (at t=52s and t=60s)

I don't believe the crew can fight an American TD without the commander's  head sticking up over the parapet. There's no vision device for him, none. If he doesn't stick his head up all that he can see is the steel insides of his box. Historically this was probably a deliberate choice, as the TDs were not intended for close-in fighting but for ambush against enemy tank attacks. But that's not how the fighting developed.

title: 15.2 A pinned leader becomes heroic
question:

author: Malcolm C
consensus_answer:

Since it is official (published in the ASL Annual), I would take it as an erratum.

title: berserkers that charge melee
question: how does it work if the only KEU for a berserk is locked in melee ? I 've played it like this : berserk enters the melee location - there is no any defensive fire form the melee location - in the AFph the bersekers fire TPBF/2 vs all enemy and friends - in the CCph the bersekers join the melee , not sure if they have to attack and defend alone or they may add their FP to friendly units ....  and they remain locked in melee and berserk until eliminate all or are eliminated. Am I right ?
author: adolfinger
consensus_answer:
how does it work if the only KEU for a berserk is locked in melee ? I 've played it like this : berserk enters the melee location - there is no any defensive fire form the melee location - in the AFph the bersekers fire TPBF/2 vs all enemy and friends - in the CCph the bersekers join the melee , not sure if they have to attack and defend alone or they may add their FP to friendly units ....  and they remain locked in melee and berserk until eliminate all or are eliminated. Am I right ?
Correct regarding the choice of target and lack of DFF/DF. Although the Berserk unit may attack in the AFPh it is not required to do so [A15.432]; if it does all Melee units would be attacked. Berserk units may not be part of a multi-location fire group [A7.54] but by their nature CC attacks are never multi-location, so that restriction does not affect Berserk units' attacks in the CCPh. Like other units, a Berserk unit might come out of Melee in other ways, e.g. if an outside attack or SAN eliminated the enemy unit holding it in Melee, or an outside attack eliminated it, or if the enemy unit was a vehicle, and it decided to drive away, or some other unit also in the CC/Melee eliminates the enemy. But most often you are right the Berserk unit will remain in Melee until the Melee ends "normally." It cannot attempt to withdraw while Berserk [A11.2].

replies.body: Looks good to me on all counts. On attacking/defending alone: I think the choice is yours for all units involved, the ones already in Melee and the Berserker unit.

title: Concealed units entering into a Melee
question:
I'm 99% certain I know the answer, but wanted to make sure I wasn't missing something...

We have a melee on-going between our US 8-1 leader and a 6-6-6 versus a 5-4-8 SS after we got a lucky ambush during the GE player turn and killed a second 5-4-8 that had advanced into the hex.  We can get a second concealed unit and another 6-6-6 into an adjacent hex during the MPh.

My understanding is the following:

If we advance the ?? unit into the melee, we will again roll for Ambush at a -3 for us (-2 for the ?? unit and -1 for the 8-1 leader already in the melee).  If we Ambush, we can conduct a 2:1 attack, with -1 for leadership and -1 for Ambush.  If we fail to kill the 5-4-8, our ?? is lost and he can attack one or both our squads.  If we successfully Ambush, then if we kill him we can withdraw to a different hex (if valid for withdraw per A11.41).  If we don't Ambush, then the CC is simultaneous, but if our ?? does NOT attack and he attacks it, he attacks with only 2.5 factors (though I'm not sure if this applies if he targets BOTH our ?? and non-concealed unit together.... I kind of think it doesn't).

I believe the same applies if we advance both the ?? unit and the additional 6-6-6 unit into the melee, except our attack would be a 3:1 (which can be an automatic kill if we declare HTH, given -1 for ambush and -1 for the leader).

So questions are: 

1) If a lone concealed unit advances into a melee, you roll again for Ambush with all DRMs (which, in theory, could result in the ?? side being ambushed with horrible rolls/bad other DRMs, e.g. vehicle, etc.).  I believe this is correct.

2) If a mixed stack of ?? and non-?? units advances into a melee, I /think/ the same applies.  I.e. 11.4 doesn't require anything more than "... or with/against a concealed unit(s)"... so as long as there is at least one ?? unit involved, ambush must be checked.  I believe this is correct.

3) If we Ambush, then we can withdraw after all CC rolls have been made IF there had not already been a Melee marked on the hex and this is whether the 5-4-8 is eliminated or not.  I /think/ this is correct per 11.41....but not 100% certain as I'm not sure if the phrase ", but only before Melee occurs" applies solely to the ??/advancing in units or the hex in total (i.e. the units advancing in aren't placed under the Melee marker immediately, but there IS a Melee in the hex).  My guess is that we can only withdraw if we eliminate the 5-4-8 (which would remove the Melee)...but even that I'm not 100% certain on, as its unclear if the Melee ends immediately or after the option to withdraw.

4) If the 5-4-8 is able to attack and targets our non-attacking ?? unit /and/ a 6-6-6, does he attack with 5 strength or 2.5 strength?  A11.19 uses the wording 'a' concealed unit, so I tend to think he attacks at full 5 strength if he targets both the ?? unit and one of the 6-6-6s.
author: kbernatz
consensus_answer:
Here is my attempt to answer your very abundant question (I would suggest that you asked more synthetic questions, so that one doesn't get lost in the maze of detailed descriptions):

You don't roll for Ambush in a Melee.
A concealed unit which advances into a Melee Location will only retain concealment if not in Open Ground (A12.14).
A concealed unit in a Melee is not held in Melee as long as it remains concealed - i.e. it doesn't attack (A12.14 again).
A11.19 explains how concealed units are dealt with during CC.
11.15 EXC can also help:
 [EXC: Any unit which retains its concealment (11.19) is not locked in Melee itself nor can it hold opposing units in Melee. It is free to fire in its next Fire Phase (into the Melee at TPBF; 7.212) or leave the Location in its next MPh/APh. Therefore, a concealed unit may wish to decline its CC attack opportunity in an effort to save its concealment. Upon losing its “?” such a unit in a Melee Location is immediately held in Melee]

consensus_answer:
And, by SSR there is Mud which will slow down the Shermans and make it slower for them to redeploy to other areas, and SSR 2 is a beauty - it might lead to unexpected casualties for the US, or even loss of a Sherman.

I think the Germans have a reasonable chance of winning this scenario.

Skulking (i.e. moving out of LOS during the MPh to avoid suffering Defensive Fire, and coming back during the APh) is one of the essential tactics of ASL.
Also, you won't need to bunch all the Germans in the VC buildings : having some approach the tanks and try for Panzerfausts is a threat that the Usaian cannot ignore.
Being also able to replace broken German by other ones held in reserve, with leaders in the rear to quickly rally the brokies, is also a way to win time.
A scenario has a lot to do with time management: seven turns can be short to the Usaians to reach their objective.

EDIT : you posted the full card now.
The tanks enter from the south on turn 2, which means that they won't be able to do a lot of harm before turn 3.
And a TH vs infantry in a building is not an automatic hit, far from that - the Shermans should better keep BU, to avoid Stun results, btw.
The VC are quite steep for the Usaians : a lot of buildings to control. The tanks will be able to pound some Germans, but they cannot be everywhere.
And the US infantry has low morale, and a puny ELR of 3.
So things seem more balanced than you will think.

If a Sherman finds a German in a stone building and drives up (but three or more hexes away), in the AFPh the DRM will be +4 Sherman moved, +3 stone building and +1 BU (probably). Hit on a TH DR of five with no chance of critical hit. That's not exactly a sure thing. With two acquisition it's a net +2 TH DRM, hit on a TH DR of six with no chance of critical hit. If you do that enough eventually something bad will happen but there's games when it doesn't happen before the scenario ends. And probably the German will move to another hex.

Some important points. Don't stack. Think about your rout routes and your leadership placement so you can catch the units that do get the short straw. Rather than worry about the tanks, concentrate on the American infantry; if you can break enough of them, it's the armor that is helpless.

It's important to remember the distinction between DRMs and To Hit Modifiers.  E.g. the +3 for Stone building and +1 for BU means a DR of 2 is modified to a 6.  6 is not less than half of 8, so can't be a critical in ASLSK.  Even with -2 Acquisition, the DR of 2 is still modified to a 4, which is still NOT LESS THAN half of 8. author: poifpoif
consensus_answer:
I've always played that the second attack from a Thrown DC (A23.6), which is against the thrower's Location, can affect friendly units, including the thrower itself.

So in theory the DC thrower should be protected by A7.4... strange?

title: Bombardment in Hatten
question: Does anyone know if the player purchasing the pre-scenario bombardment have to be able to see the 'pre-registered' hex associated with it? author: kbernatz
consensus_answer: Since the hex is recorded prior to setup [footnote e], there's nothing to have LOS to. For regular OBA the pre-registered hex need not be in LOS to be recorded. It only needs to be in LOS of the Observer to be used [C1.73]. There is no Observer in bombardment.

title: Concealed Infantry vs Bypassing AFV
question:
Infantry (Defender) is concealed in a jungle hex (for instance), while an AFV (Attacker) is bypassing the hex. How does it work?  

1. Should the Defending Infantry unit take a PAATC as soon as the AFV bypasses their hex? Or is the AFV considered as occupying neither of the adjacent hexes?
2. Can an AFV OVR a concealed unit? 
3. Can a bypassing AFV OVR a defending unit occupying any of the adjacent hexes?
4. Can the Defending Infantry unit CC Reaction Fire the bypassing AFV during its MPh? How does it work then? Is the CC then sequential and should the Infantry roll first? Does the defending Infantry stay in their hex afterwards, as they would in a  street fight? 
5. Is there any Ambush option available when a defending Infantry unit CC Reaction Fire a bypassing AFV during its MPh?
author: poifpoif
consensus_answer:
Infantry (Defender) is concealed in a jungle hex (for instance), while an AFV (Attacker) is bypassing the hex. How does it work?  

1. Should the Defending Infantry unit take a PAATC as soon as the AFV bypasses their hex? Or is the AFV considered as occupying neither of the adjacent hexes?
2. Can an AFV OVR a concealed unit?
3. Can a bypassing AFV OVR a defending unit occupying any of the adjacent hexes?
4. Can the Defending Infantry unit CC Reaction Fire the bypassing AFV during its MPh? How does it work then? Is the CC then sequential and should the Infantry roll first? Does the defending Infantry stay in their hex afterwards, as they would in a street fight?
5. Is there any Ambush option available when a defending Infantry unit CC Reaction Fire a bypassing AFV during its MPh?

1. Not necessary unless the defender wants to CC-RF. Per A12.42 a vehicle using bypass does not force a unit in the hex to PAATC to retain concealment. See below regarding what hex the vehicle occupies.
2. A vehicle may OVR a concealed unit in general. The timing for declaring the OVR differs if all defenders are concealed [D7.1].
3. A vehicle in bypass may not OVR any hex, including its own [D7.13].
4. Yes. 

It is important to understand that a unit bypassing is actually in one of the two hexes. When there is only one hex on a hexside that the vehicle (/infantry unit) could be bypassing (i.e. one hex on the hexside has building/woods and the other doesn't have either), it's obvious which hex the bypassing unit is in. If bypass on the hexside is ambiguous the player has to declare which hex the bypassing unit is in. This is important for things like range and in this case, for whether the vehicle can be attacked in bypass. If the vehicle is bypassing in the hex with defending infantry, they can potentially CC-RF. If the vehicle has a choice of which hex to bypass and is bypassing the other one, the defending unit may not attack [EXC: village streets, B31.132]. The infantry have to pass a PAATC, and if they do they attack on using CC. They get the "street-fighting ambush DRM" for bypass even though it isn't street fighting. When using CC against a vehicle in bypass infantry do not move to the hexside; they remain as they were. During the MPh the vehicle cannot return the CC attack. Only the CC-RF unit attacks.

5. Not during the MPh, but against a bypassing unit an infantry unit gets the "street-fighting ambush" DRM [A11.8].

One additional thing to note: if the vehicle ends its MPh in bypass the units in the hex automatically lose concealment [A12.42].

title: Multi level building
question: When a multi level building is attacked,are all the levels attacked at once by a fire group or only one specific level?
author: JTV656
consensus_answer:
Correct on Steeples, yes.

It is worth looking at A2.8 Locations: "A hex may contain separate subdivisions within itself (i.e., units may occupy the same hex but still be in separate Locations within that hex). The most common application of this is when additional vertical levels exist within the horizontal dimensions of a hex."

And A7.4 Target Determination: "Except during Defensive First Fire (8.1), all the Personnel-units/unarmored-vehicles/Vulnerable-PRC in the same Location are considered targets of fire that does not have to specify a particular target, with the outcome of such fire affecting all those enemy (or Melee) units in the target Location (except those to which the LOF is blocked, such as being entrenched behind a wall [B9.21], Area Target Type [C3.33], or non-Crest units in a Depression [B20.92])."

So the target of of a fire attack will be one Location in a hex (which could be the only Location in the hex...). DFF of course only affects the moving units in a Location. ATT generally hits all Locations in a hex, Spraying Fire can affect two adjacent Locations, OBA usually affects all Locations in a group of seven hexes... and the extra fun one is canister shot, which can affect three locations—usually a group of ground level ones, but can be three levels within one hex.

replies.body:
When a multi level building is attacked,are all the levels attacked at once by a fire group or only one specific level?
Only one specific level, though there are exceptions like Mortars and OBA.

Good question. I think a fire group and other direct fire can aim at a particular level. However, same question, what about indirect fire such as from a mortar? If you get a hit on the TH Table, how do you determine which level of the building got hit?

When a multi level building is attacked,are all the levels attacked at once by a fire group or only one specific level?

This depends. In most cases only one Location (level) is attacked. Spraying Fire [A9.5, A7.34] can be used to attack multiple Locations, including multiple levels of buildings. Ordnance firing using the Area Target Type [C3.33] also attacks all Locations in a hex. Locations must be in LOS unless the firing unit is a mortar [C3.33].
Thanks everyone!

In standard ASL I believe this occurs only with pillboxes, but some of the Historical Modules have cellars in buildings which are sometimes at a different Level and sometimes at ground Level. Attacks generally affect only the target Location regardless of whether there is another Location at that Level with exceptions for Area Target Type, Spraying Fire, and OBA.

Surprisingly the rule does not specify how much higher. There are a couple q&a:
B31.2 Does a Steeple Location increase the obstacle height of the building that it is a part of? If so by how much? (Presumably the height is increased only in the hex containing the Steeple.)
A. Yes. By one full level. (Correct.) {2}

A. One full level higher than the building below it. {2}
I assume the steeple is one level higher than the building, so a steeple in a two-level building would be at level three.
Sorry, I was misreading your statement as "at the same level," not as "at a specific level" as you wrote. You are correct they are an additional Location. They are not at the same level as any of the other building Locations. See below.

There is a q&a which specifies the height of the steeple Location:
B31.2 Let us say we have a multi-hex building with a steeple. The steeple is at level 2 and connects directly to the ground level of that same hex. What is the cost in MF to go from ground level to level 2 steeple location? Is there an intermediate location at level 1 where you can be shot at? If there is an enemy unit at level 1, is it still possible to move directly from ground level to level 2 as they connect directly or not? If there is an intermediate level and you get shot there, are you then placed back where you started or at the level 1 Location (or anywhere else for that matter)? If there is an enemy unit at level 1, am I encircled in the steeple location as it does not connect to the level 1 location?
A. If the steeple is in a Single Story House, it is at Level 1, with an inherent stairwell connecting it to Level 0. If the steeple is in a Two Story House, it is at Level 2, with an inherent stairwell connecting it to Level 1 and connecting Level 1 to Level 0. If the Steeple is in a Multi-Story Building, it is at Level 3, with an inherent stairwell connecting it to Level 2, Level 2 to Level 1, and Level 1 to Level 0.

Interesting... I was thinking Hatten (which is the CG we're playing now), which has the following:

2.4: "This church is a Single-Hex Two-Story House (B31.3) that also contains a Steeple Location (B31.2) in the hex - i.e., an additional, Level 2 Location."

Which I interpreted to mean there were /2/ Level 2 Locations... but reading B31.3, I see that isn't the case...
The "two stories" would be level 0 and level 1, so the steeple would be above them at level 2.
Yeah.. I realized that after re-reading B31.3 :).  When I first read it in Hatten, the 'an additional' Level 2 had my brain thinking "Oh, there are two Lvl 2 locations in that hex, then...".  D'oh!

title: advance vs (very) difficult terrain
question: can a non cx unit advance if it  would expend  more MF than normally  allowed in the  Mph ? i.e.  an MMC in crest status in a shallow stream woods want to advance in the wood hex opposite to the crest status side ;  5MF to leave crest status and go IN depression plus 4 MF to enter higher level wood hex .....
author: adolfinger
consensus_answer:
can a non cx unit advance if it  would expend  more MF than normally  allowed in the  Mph ? i.e.  an MMC in crest status in a shallow stream woods want to advance in the wood hex opposite to the crest status side ;  5MF to leave crest status and go IN depression plus 4 MF to enter higher level wood hex .....

A unit may spend more MF than its MF Allotment during the MPh by performing a Minimum Move [A4.134]. During the APh a unit can always move one Location without regard to the cost, except in the sense that if the cost is ≥ the lesser of four MF or the unit's remaining MF allotment after PP deductions, the Advance vs. Difficult Terrain must be used [A4.72]. There are some other restrictions e.g. the unit must retain at least one MF after deducting for portage.

replies.body:
Yes. If it can at least spend 1 MF it can move in terrain that costs more than what it has.
Here is the way I parse the rule, as it could seem ambiguous :
4.72 vs DIFFICULT TERRAIN: An advance into any hex whose MF cost (excluding SMOKE) is ≥ :
- four MF or
- all of a unit’s available non-Double Time MF allotment 
(whichever is less) may not be made if the unit is already CX [EXC: Climbing, B11.432; Deep Stream Entry, B20.43]; otherwise it may advance but becomes CX in the process. In no case may a unit advance if it retains no MF after deducting for portage costs.
The "≥" doesn't govern "four MF" only, but "all of a unit’s available non-Double Time MF allotment " too.
I added a ":" after the "≥" to make things clear.

title: BAZ/PSK vs. Infantry Behind Bocage
question:
A friend and I are preparing to play ASL A59 - Death at Carentan.  In this scenario both sides have LATW.  Given the following two rules, my question is whether these weapons can be used against Infantry behind the bocage.

1) C8.31 says that, "HEAT may only be fired... at Infantry/Cavalry behind a wall or in a building/rubble/pillbox."
2) B9.35 says that, "Bocage... is a special form of hedge grown on top of low earthen mounds to form a natural wall.  All rules pertaining to hedges are applicable to bocage except as modified below."
author: A2SimGamer
consensus_answer:

When this question was submitted to MMP they ruled that bocage does not allow HEAT to be triggered. Bounding Fire, on the other hand, *does* allow HEAT to be triggered by bocage, e.g. Beyond the Beachhead SSR 5. I have seen histories that say that bazooka ammunition expenditures in Normandy were way up, so I think as a historical matter Bounding Fire probably got the answer more right than MMP. I think the Americans were using BAZ as a RPG in the bocage, but by rule, MMP does not allow it.
If you *do* allow it, remember that all the Germans are toting inherent PFs as well carrying the odd PSK SW.

I'm seeing bocage treated as a wall in many 3rd party products as many hedgerows have old stone walls inside them from antiquity.

Which, IMO, is another reason to disallow BAZ vs bocage.
I do not doubt that BAZ were fired at bocage, but I do doubt its effectiveness.
But I am no expert.

But I am no expert.

One source I have found is Steven J. Zaloga, ST LÔ 1944: The Battle of the Hedgerows from Osprey

Both sides made extensive use of anti-tank rocket launchers as improvised artillery in the bocage fighting.

The M1A1 2.36in. “bazooka” rifle launcher was another popular weapon in the bocage fighting. These weapons were not widely distributed in the rifle companies, with only five per company. Once their value in bocage fighting became evident, many infantry divisions took the bazookas allotted to service units and headquarters units and transferred them to the rifle companies. Although intended primarily for anti-tank defense, their high explosive warhead was effective against dug-in defenses.

I have also seen another piece of data, I think from Osprey again, that said that Bazooka ammunition expenditure was much higher than expected in Normandy because the troops were using them against German positions. But I can't find that one.

This does not specify whether they were used against units that had pillbox-like positions, which is a possible explanation.

There is also this, from the army Greenbook on Normandy:

During their training period the men found that the light machine gun was not the best weapon to support infantry attacks in the hedgerows. They discovered that two 15-pound charges of TNT in burlap bags opened a gap in a hedgerow bank large enough for a tank. Learning that without demolition 50 percent of the hedgerow dikes could be breached by engineer tank dozers, the division attached dozers to the tank units. The men were reminded that the Germans particularly feared white phosphorus shells, which were highly effective against hedgerow positions. They were instructed to use the bazooka as more than a antitank weapon since its rocket head, when employed in high-angle fire and against a hard object, was almost as effective against personnel as the 60-mm. mortar shell.

https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USA/USA-E-Breakout/USA-E-Breakout-5.html

It isn't clear what "hard object" was intended as target, but I think it might mean hard ground. Not sure what else would be around.

And what is a high-angle fire? Firing a BAZ aiming to the sky like a MTR?
I think that the speed of the BAZ projectile means that it could go through soft obstacles like hedges, without exploding. But if some bocage had stone walls on their bases, maybe they pointed there? But with a low angle...?

Bocage in Normandy was not a soft target. It was not a hedge, although it might have a hedge or trees on top. If it were a hedge a tank would drive through with not many problems. It was a mound of dirt reinforced by roots of things growing on it. I don't know how many had stone walls in the core; I have never heard that mentioned before. Even assuming it detonated I believe a HEAT round would have trouble penetrating five or so feet of dirt. To give some idea of how substantial Bocage was in Normandy note that troops used "two 15-pound charges of TNT in burlap bags" to create a gap, not something that would be necessary for an ornamental Boxwood. As an example for scale this picture shows a breach in bocage cut by a Rhino. My understanding is that they could be higher or lower.

https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/ac/Holeinhedgerow.png

What I have read is that the fuse of a Bazooka expected to hit something "hard" before detonating. Bazookas had trouble if they hit sand-covered bunkers, for instance. They also had trouble if they hit even hard things obliquely; they tended not to detonate and skip off. I suspect that dry, compacted earth is probably hard enough to detonate a Bazooka round if struck straight-on, but I don't have evidence for that.

I don't think the idea was to fire the Bazooka at a really high angle because the backblast would flow off the ground and strike the firer. Perhaps at a 45° angle might be safe? And although the normal use of the Bazooka was to penetrate, I think the idea against infantry was as much to affect those on the near side of the explosion, not the far side, rather like a 60mm MTR shell exploding.

All this said, I can't anything better than hints that Bazookas were used against infantry in Normandy. There's lots of stories of bazookas used against tanks and some of bazookas against pillboxes (where again the idea seems to be to get the bazooka shot through the embrasure rather than have it penetrate the concrete). I can find very little evidence they were used against infantry. It's hard to tell if this is a case where there is no evidence because it was not done, or where there is no evidence because it was not news and so not reported. Firing a bazooka against the side of a Panther might win the Medal of Honor; firing against a German halfsquad probably won't.

Based on the evidence I can find I don't think MMP's position, that bazookas can't be used against bocage, is unreasonable. But I see enough that suggests it is possibly wrong.

title: Area Target Type vs Armored Assault
question:
I'm using the 1st Edition rules (don't know if that makes a difference or not). But this one has me stumped.
I'm moving some infantry with a tank using Armored Assault. After expending a MP, the AFV-Inf combo is fired on by HE using the Area Target Type. How do you figure the To Hit? The inf is moving FFNAM, but the tank obviously is also moving (+2, Case J and is a Large Target, Case P). As I understand it, the Area Target Type means that the fire is directed at the hex and not any particular units therein. But what TH DRMs do you use, those for the inf or those for the AFV? 

I'm just getting back into ASL after some years away (hence the 1st Ed rules). Admittedly, the Area Target Type has always confused me a little.
author: Don_Cossack
consensus_answer: As a follow-on, it is also possible that different units have different DRM for the effects DR too. Assume the tank is CE and has Riders, the targets are in a hex with a wall hexside and the attacking weapon is using indirect fire (i.e. a MTR). The wall TEM would not apply to the CE crew [B9.3] but the crew would receive the CE DRM for the collateral attack. Riders would receive neither for their collateral. The Infantry would receive TEM (either for the Armor Assault vehicle or the (reduced; B9.34) wall TEM). The vehicle would have a +1 DRM (TEM) on effects, the crew would have a +2 DRM (CE DRM) on collateral effects, the armored-assaulting Infantry a +1 DRM and the Riders +0 DRM on collateral effects. The effects may be different for different units. To get effects requires that the target be hit of course, and it is not necessarily the case that all are hit.

C6.51 works indeed.
Note, after the sentence about a target moving out of LOS, the further reference to 6.5 and the Acquisition loss conditions.
If the eliminated target's Location doesn't present any of the Acq. loss conditions (such as becoming ou of LOS or the Gun firing at another target, etc.), Acq. remains and can be used against another target.

First technically it is not a "vehicle target" acquired counter. It is a ½-inch acquired counter, and can be used for either VTT or ITT. It can also be switched to a ⅝-inch acquired counter as appropriate.

The reasons for removing the acquired counter are given in C6.5. Destroying a vehicle is not one of the reasons given for removal. In fact there could still be other vehicles and/or Infantry in that Location, and the acquired counter DRM might be used against them. But even if there aren't any other enemy units the acquired counter remains until the occurence of one of the reasons for removal given in C6.5.

title: AP Critical Hit Die Roll & Multiple Hits
question: If snake eyes are rolled for the To Hit, a Critical Hit occurs.  Should Multiple Hits occur per rule C3.8?  C3.8 says non Critical Hits only.  We are playing Scouts Out scenario in ASL Journal 1.  Lines 522-524 show a critical hit and multiple hits occurring together.  Any help appreciated.
author: Wild Admiral
consensus_answer:
e.g. his Panther rolled snake eyes on the To Hit roll vs the "Motion" TD... even with Motion, would have still been a hit, I believe...just not a critical

If the TH DRM mean that only a TH DR of two will hit, then after rolling a TH DR of two you roll a subsequent dr. On a dr of one, it's a Critical Hit. On a dr of two or higher it's a normal hit [C3.7]. This does not have a name.

If the TH DRM mean that even a TH DR of two is not ≤ the modified TH DR, a TH DR of two is an Improbable Hit [C3.6]. On a subsequent dr of one it's a Critical Hit, two or three is a normal hit and four or higher is a miss.

So it's always possible to get a Critical Hit on the Vehicle Target Type, but sometimes it requires a subsequent dr.

title: Motion status attempt question
question:
Hello,

My friend and I are continuing our study of asl journal 1, scouts out replay. On lines 460 and 461, our American AFV makes a motion status attempt in reaction is a moving German unit. Since the German used 2 movement factor to enter a building, we think the AFV should have to roll a two or less on one die to succeed. (D2.401) However, the replay says that the motion status attempt was automatic, could someone please explain why?

Also, from what we can tell a motion status attempt can only be made if the opposing unit had not been in the vehicle’s los earlier in that turn prior to moving. We think the German unit was in the AFV’s line of site earlier. 

In case it matters the American AFV is a M31A and the German unit is a concealed half squad carrying a PSK.

Thanks for the help.
author: plainscape
consensus_answer:
At one time it had been ruled that Motion Attempts could be made at the end of *the* MPh, i.e. the vehicle could sit still for the entire MPh but remember all movement made in its LOS and, after movement was completed, roll a Motion Attempt based on any movement in its LOS during that MPh. I'm guessing that the action that triggered the Motion Attempt was the movement of the Pz IIIN to 41Q3 (event 452). The AAR does not spell out the exact path, and with a carefully chosen path (up the hill in 41R2 expending all but three MF—LOS blocked by 41R3, move to Q3, stop) the Pz IIIN might not have caused an automatic Motion, but I'm guessing the move was not as well thought-out as that.

The rules were changed so that now you have to make Motion Attempts during the enemy MPh after any expenditure and based on that moving unit only. I will guess that the Motion Attempt was in accordance with the rules at the time but under the current rules regime it would not be allowed.

title: Intensive Fire
question:
In our latest game session on VASL we had some uncertainty about Intensive Fire.
As I've understood you can only use it after your ROF has been used up as a kind of final additional shot you get once per player turn with penalties.
In which Fire Phases can it be used then? 
As I think:
-Defensive Fire Phase: 
1)First Fire: possible after ROF has been used up. 
2)Subsequent and Final Protective Fire: not possible since this is an ordnance weapon (AT gun) which doesn't have IFE.
3)Final Fire: possible or not? I should say only if it didn't First Fire and only started to fire in the Final Fire segment? Is that correct? And only after ROF has been used up? I suppose it only gets a Final Fire counter after it First Fired? Not if it didn't?

-Advance Fire Phase: only possible if it was marked as an Opportunity Firer according to the rules.

-Prepare Fire Phase: not mentioned in the rules but I should say possible since it can do it in the Advance Fire Phase as an Opportunity Firer?
author: neo.colpaert
consensus_answer:
Intensive Fire is allowed during the enemy MPh with penalties but no range limitations. In contrast SFF & FPF have limitations on range, e.g. within normal range, not when there is a closer known enemy unit for SFF, and adjacent only for FPF. You are correct that SFF & FPF can't be used by Ordnance attacks, i.e. attacks involving a TH DR. 

During the Defensive Fire Phase per A8.4, "Any such units/weapons that are marked with a First Fire counter may also fire again (by flipping their First Fire marker over to the Final Fire side) ... only at units in an adjacent (or same) hex." During DFPh there *is* a range limitation to Intensive Fire, i.e. only against adjacent units. Also during the DFPh if a weapon is not marked with a First Fire counter, it can attack until it loses ROF at which point it is marked with a *Final* Fire counter [A3.4], i.e. a weapon can't make both normal attacks and Intensive Fire attacks in the DFPh.

As you note during the AFPh only if using Opportunity Fire. There is no range limit.

During Prep Fire it is allowed with penalties but without range limitations.

The way we think about it is (in layman's terms):

If you think you are going to want to IF as a defending unit, you /need/ to do it during the MPh because, chances are, you won't be able to during the DFPh.  This is because the target needs to be adjacent.  Also, note that lt mtrs cannot IF as they are SWs, not a Gun.

For the attacking side, you can IF at any point when you can fire with no penalties (in layman's terms)...ie Prep Fire or if marked Op Fire during the AFPh.

title: Journal 1 Scouts Out LOS & DRM Questions
question:
In ASL Journal #1 Scouts Out Replay Line 408 has the German 447 in Hex 41R7 use a Panzerfaust to fire at the stopped American AC in Hex 40Q1.  We think the shot is blocked by both the hill in 41R8 and the Hedge in 41R9.  Is this shot blocked?  Also, isn't a Panzerfaust limited to a 3 hex range?  

Line 408 also says the shot has a +6 modifier.  If the shot is not blocked, we calculate +2 Backblast, +1 Small Vehicle for +3 Total.  What are we missing?  Any help appreciated.  Picture below:
author: Wild Admiral
consensus_answer:
The PF has a maximum range that changes by scenario date, starting at one hex prior to June 1944, increasing to two hexes through the rest of 1944 and becoming three hexes in 1945 [C13.32]. Scouts Out takes place on 19 November, 1944, in the two-hex range phase.

It would surprise me if anyone took a PF shot at range five. I will speculate the attack is not against AC-E but against AC-C instead. That would be within range and LOS. The DRM would be +2 Case J moving target, +1 small, +1 height advantage, +2 case C³ Backblast weapon in ground level building for a total +6, matching the printed value. It would be a near useless shot as the basic TH# is ten made into a modified TH# of six by the range [C13.33]. With the +6 DRM no TH DR would be ≤ the modified TH# so only a snakeeyes followed by a dr 1-3 would be an improbable hit [C3.6].

ASL Journal #1 was published in the pre-SK era.  In those years, physical ASL maps were all mounted. 

Owing to variance in the cutting and mounting of  ASL mapsheets, close LOSs across board seams depended very much on the actual boards in use and could easily disagree re some same coordinate-to-coordinate squeaky-close LOS  traced using two different physical copies of same-numbered abutted boards.

A12.3 "Hidden Status is considered the equal of concealment except as otherwise specified."

The mention that it "can gain concealed status" hints that when revealed, it is not concealed.

So if they were concealed in HiP, they remain concealed... if not concealed in HiP, they remain not concealed.
There actually is no unit "concealed in HIP" : HIP is a form of concealment, and there is no concealed or unconcealed additional status of a HIP unit.

You have missed a key point. When firing SMOKE case K is *not* used unless there are on-board enemy units and none of them are Known to the firer [C6.2; "EXC: when firing SMOKE, Case K applies only if the target hex contains ≥ one non-hidden enemy ground unit but none of those units are Known to the firer/Spotter"]. So if you fired SMOKE at a hex without on-board enemy units, case K does not apply. If you fired SMOKE at a hex with on-board enemy units but none of them Known to the firing unit (under "?" and/or out of LOS), case K does apply to the SMOKE placement itself. So if a multi-story building has a HIP unit on the second level, an attempt to place SMOKE does not use the case K DRM. But if the unit on the second level is concealed but not HIP (and there are no unconcealed enemy units in the hex), case K *does* apply, both to whether the unit is hit for WP NMC purposes and also whether a SMOKE counter is placed in the hex.

In some circumstances there might be a mix of concealed and unconcealed units. with case K applying to whether individual units are hit (for WP NMC) but not to whether the SMOKE is placed. For instance if there is a multi-story building with a concealed unit on level one and an unconcealed unit on level two, if WP is fired at the hex case K applies to whether the WP affects the individual units for purposes of the NMC but as long as at least one of the enemy units is "hit", the SMOKE counter is placed.

author: plainscape
consensus_answer:
So there are 2 blind hexes and this shot was not valid.  This method  matches the result I got from the other resource above.  Thanks again.

I have thought a bit more about the formulae, and they are not wrong (once you understand that there are two formulae). But I find those two unintuitive and hard to understand from the rules, as I said. The problem starts with the expression of "2*obstacle height". Where does that "2" come from? The answer is that the formulae use absolute heights, e.g. a case where a unit at level two firing at a target at level zero over a level one obstacle has different parameters than a case with a unit at level three firing a target at level one over a level two obstacle, so you subtract the obstacle height out once to get into relative units.. This misses the commonality that if the observer is two levels above the target and the obstacle is one level above the target the number of blind hexes will be the same (for same range and type of obstacle) regardless of whether the target is at level -1, 0, 1, 2 .... It's the relative heights that matter. I find that a lot more satisfying and it's fairly close to what the rules say and it's actually quick to calculate using the steps I gave.

I have thought a bit more about the formulae, and they are not wrong (once you understand that there are two formulae). But I find those two unintuitive and hard to understand from the rules, as I said. The problem starts with the expression of "2*obstacle height". Where does that "2" come from? The answer is that the formulae use absolute heights, e.g. a case where a unit at level two firing at a target at level zero over a level one obstacle has different parameters than a case with a unit at level three firing a target at level one over a level two obstacle, so you subtract the obstacle height out once to get into relative units.. This misses the commonality that if the observer is two levels above the target and the obstacle is one level above the target the number of blind hexes will be the same (for same range and type of obstacle) regardless of whether the target is at level -1, 0, 1, 2 .... It's the relative heights that matter. I find that a lot more satisfying and it's fairly close to what the rules say and it's actually quick to calculate using the steps I gave.

My quick method:

Number of blind hexes at start is height of obstacle over height of lower unit (with fractions removed; the "floor" operator removes fractions, e.g. ⌊3.5⌋ = 3), ⌊height obstacle⌋ - ⌊height lower unit⌋
Add one for each five hexes from higher unit to obstacle, FRD = ⌊range from upper unit to obstacle/5⌋
Subtract one for each full level more than one full level the higher unit is above the obstacle = max(  ⌊height upper unit⌋ -  ⌊height obstacle⌋ - 1, 0 ). The "max" makes sure the difference is not < 0.
Subtract one if a non-cliff crest line.
Minimum zero if non-cliff crest line; one otherwise.

title: DRM question from asl journal 1
question:
Hello,

A friend and I are trying to learn asl using the scouts out replay from asl journal 1. We are on turn two. The Americans are trying to find hidden in place units by firing at 40L7. See image below, the AC is literally one hex away and this is during his movement phase. The magazine says we should get a +4 drm. But, we’re getting +6 because +2 for area fire (trying to shoot at a hidden in place unit) and +4 for case c (+2 for case b and +2 for turret type). What are we missing? 

Thank you!
author: plainscape
consensus_answer:
I believe you are referring to event 99,
AC-E in 40R4/6 to M8/6 Stop
BF MG at 40L7 - 4 FP, +1, 1,6, NE
BF MA ATT at 40L7, +4, 1,5, Miss

There seem to be some problems here. The moving vehicle is declared to be using Area Target Type ("ATT"). Per C3.33 "The Area Target Type cannot be used within the firer's own hex (i.e., at zero hex range), or as Bounding First (D3.3) or Motion Fire (D2.42)." So the whole attack is not allowed as declared. I will guess they were also applying case L, Point Blank Range, which does not apply to Area Target Type [C6.3]. The corrected attack should  probably be HE using the Infantry Target Type, +4 cases B & C, +2 Concealed, +1 TEM and -2 Point Blank Range for a net +5 DRM. With a DR of 1,5 that's still a miss but ROF. The MA can fire again if desired but only from hex M8.

Yep, that's an error.  When we do replays we record the way we actually played without rewinding for rules errors but they should be noted; this one was not, unfortunately.

Which leads us to the obvious conclusion, if you are going to make a mistake, at least make sure your mistake works in a way that *benefits* you.

Once players learn what they can move and fire in the AFPh (LMGs, FTs, DCs, LATW such as PF, BAZ, PSK, ATR, PIAT) and what they can't (listed in A4.41), the next step is to realize that if the weapon itself does not move, a moving unit may recover it in the MPh and fire it in AFPh. Often the weapon is an abandoned enemy weapon.

So they dropped it on their side of the road before moving out to glory and hutzpah, letting a follow-up unit move in and attempt to recover it, so they could provide covering fire with it (still halved for fire in the Advance Fire Phase, but better than not being able to fire).

title: Does the Intensive Fire DRM add to previous DRMs?
question:
Let's say a Gun is firing outside their CA using a Defensive First Fire; case A DRM does apply. He later fires again using an Intensive Fire, but doesn't need to change its CA anymore. He then only has to apply the Intensive Fire DRM? Or does the Intensive Fire DRM adds to the previous CA change DRM case A modifier?

Same question regarding an AFV using Bounding Fire during its MPh. Does the +2 TH DRM for Intensive Fire add to the initial Bounding Fire DRM? Or does the Bounding Fire modifier only applies once with the first fire attempt?
author: poifpoif
consensus_answer:
Let's say a Gun is firing outside their CA using a Defensive First Fire; case A DRM does apply. He later fires again using an Intensive Fire, but doesn't need to change its CA anymore. He then only has to apply the Intensive Fire DRM? Or does the Intensive Fire DRM adds to the previous CA change DRM case A modifier?

Same question regarding an AFV using Bounding Fire during its MPh. Does the +2 TH DRM for Intensive Fire add to the initial Bounding Fire DRM? Or does the Bounding Fire modifier only applies once with the first fire attempt? 

Answer to your first question is no - case A only applied to the first shot (C5.12). This is the same for both keeping ROF and using Intensive Fire.

Answer to your second question is yes - case F and case C are cumulative. Note that the AFV must spend a MP between shots (D3.3) allowing Defensive First Fire and case C for the AFV might change depending on the number of MP with LOS to the target (C5.3)

For example a turreted vehicle fires its MA and does not have ROF. It then fires its CMG, changing TCA as it does so. The CA change DRM applies to the CMG attack. If the vehicle now fires its MA as intensive fire, the TCA change DRM *would* apply in addition to the Intensive Fire DRM. This is probably not what you had in mind, but I throw it out for consideration.

Bounding (First) Fire DRM apply to all ordnance attacks made by the vehicle during its MPh, including ROF attacks and also Intensive Fire attacks. Per D3.3, "to use Bounding First Fire, any vehicular ordnance must use one of the Case C To Hit DRM (either Case C, C1, C2, or C4; see C5.3-.33, C5.35)."

Answer to your first question is no - case A only applied to the first shot (C5.12). This is the same for both keeping ROF and using Intensive Fire.

NT AFVs have better chances to hit with an Intensive Fire in their CA than First Firing outside of their CA.

title: Entering WP Location
question: do take precedence rule A 24.31 ( no NMC ) OR C 1.51 ( yes NMC ) ? Or there is something I've missed ? many thanks
author: adolfinger
consensus_answer:
What amazes me is how people like JR V, Robin, Bruce, etc. have somehow internalized all these rules that they can answer these questions with such nuanced accuracy without spending 45 hours combing through the rules to find all the possible exceptions (and the exceptions to the exceptions... and the exceptions to the exceptions to the ... well, you get it 🙂 ).
In this particular case it's helpful to understand how WP causes casualties. Although it produces unpleasant fumes, they are not so noxious that you will fall over gasping (unless in a very confined space). When a WP shell explodes, it spreads many small particles of phosphorus everywhere. If any of these come in contact with flesh, it causes a very painful burn, and the particles will continue to burn and are hard to extinguish. There's an episode of M*A*S*H where the doctors dig a piece of white phosphorus out of a wounded soldier. It looks very unpleasant. After the initial explosion the WP continues to generate smoke but it would be hard to become injured by it unless you rolled over a piece of it or picked it up or something. Hence when the WP counter is placed there's some chance of injury, but after that there isn't. Except in the case of OBA where there is assumed to be a continuous rain of shells. Note that this is actually pretty much the same as HE. When you are done your shooting, other units can move through that Location without effect (EXC: residual FP), and again an exception for an HE FFE.

One thing to thing consider about ASL the game vs. the simulation is that if you have an on-board gun and you fire at a target PFPh & DFPh turn after turn, you are more-or-less doing the same thing as OBA, but the two behave very differently in terms of stopping movement through the Location.

title: Depletion numbers showing two letters
question:
How to understand D6 *superscript* J4E on the back of a 57L Anti-Tank gun?

D is for APDS
"6" is the depletion number
"J" should be for the 10th month of the year (October)?
"4" is for 1944
But why the "E"???
author: poifpoif
consensus_answer:
Regarding Depletion Numbers. How to use them actually? The rule mentions the "original" TH DR? How to understand "Original"? The first one being rolled? The unmodified roll (no DRM involved)? Or am I just overthinking the matter?
Should the very first TH DR being rolled determine if the special ammo is available for the whole scenario (or not)?
Or should the Depletion Number be considered each time a new TH DR is being rolled? And the special ammo would be available until rolling higher than the Depletion Number?

Per the Index, "Original DR/dr: a DR/dr prior to any applicable modification by DRM/drm of any kind."

For Depletion Numbers, per C8.9 "the firer announces his intention to use Special Ammunition prior to a To Hit DR." If the TH DR is < the Depletion #, that attack uses the depletable ammo and the weapon has more of it. If the TH DR is == the Depletion #, that attack uses the depletable, but the weapon has run out. It can't attempt to use that particular type of ammunition. If the TH DR is > the Depletion # that weapon does not have that type of ammo and the attack is not considered to have happened (EXC: Low Ammo, Malfunction). Note that for a HIP weapon, announce the shot and make the TH DR *before* putting the weapon on board. If the weapon does not have the Ammunition it remains HIP, and it's kind of a bummer to spoil the HIP position if you don't have the ammo.

The weapon can call for the use of a depletable ammunition type until it rolls a TH DR greater than or equal to its depletion number. After that it can't use that depletable ammunition any more. The per-shot procedure is the same whether it is the first attack with that depletable ammunition or the tenth attack, assuming the ammunition did not deplete in the previous nine attacks.

title: LATW firing options
question:
Can't LATW ever fire more than once per turn? They can't obviously Subsequent First Fire (as they aren't MG) nor Intensive Fire (only ordnances seem to be allowed to). So my guess is they can only be fired once per turn.

Are they marked with a First Fire counter when used during an enemy MPh?
author: poifpoif
consensus_answer:
Can't LATW ever fire more than once per turn? They can't obviously Subsequent First Fire (as they aren't MG) nor Intensive Fire (only ordnances seem to be allowed to). So my guess is they can only be fired once per turn.

Are they marked with a First Fire counter when used during an enemy MPh?

Some LATW have ROF, for example the Japanese 20L ATR. Otherwise LATW can't fire more than once. As you say they can't use SFF/FPF because they are not MGs. But LATW, even ones with their own TH table (e.g. BAZ, PF) *are* ordnance. Per the Index, "Ordnance (any weapon which must score a hit on a To Hit Table before rolling again on the IFT or To Kill Table to resolve that hit)." Per C5.6, "Intensive Fire is available only to Guns (not SW)."

There is one additional time SW can fire more than once without ROF, FPF non-CC Reaction Fire [D7.221]. A SW that is subject to OVRs can fire as long as its owner passes the FPF MC.

Once they fire they can be marked with a First Fire counter. If the unit holding the weapon is a squad it can still fire its inherent FP (or another SW) as First Fire. Once the unit holding a SW is marked with Final Fire, all of its possessed weapons are also marked as Final Fire.

Certain LATW have ROF, in particular for ASLSK the Japanese 20L ATR that comes in ASLSK#4. But as you point out they can't use SFF/FPF as they are not MGs. LATW, even ones with their own TH table (BAZ, PF, etc.), *are* Ordnance (in general, but ATRs vs. infantry). Per the 2.0 definitions, "Ordnance: A Gun, SW (Mortar or LATW), or vehicle MA that must first secure a hit via the To Hit process prior to resolving an attack via the IFT (6.0) against Infantry or prior to the To Kill process against a vehicle (7.9)," and also 4.4, "LATWs are Ordnance SW." They can't use Intensive Fire because, per the 2.0 definitions, "Intensive Fire: After losing ROF a Gun or vehicle MA may make one final attack (3.2.4)," and "Gun: Any non-vehicular Weapon on a 5⁄8˝ counter." LATW are on ½-inch counters and so cannot use Intensive Fire.

Note that ATRs that aren't 20mm weapons (i.e. most ATRs) can't fire at infantry using TH/TK; they instead fire using their one FP directly on the IFT (4.4.4).

title: When do you mark a Gun Prep Fire?
question:
Ok, ok ... its not just "In the Prep Fire Phase" 🙂 .  The question is as follows:

We have a US Lt MTR that wants to fire WP (1945). It needs a 5 or less to secure a hit due to Hindrance, range, etc. and has a WP7 number, with a ROF of 3.  It rolls a '2' (colored die) + '5', meaning it had WP, but failed to secure a hit, but also kept ROF.  If no other unit wanted to fire SMOKE, this would be all fine and dandy, we would just keep firing the Lt MTR until it lost ROF and we would mark it with a Prep Fire counter then.

But we have other Guns that want to attempt to fire SMOKE.  Looking at the ROF rules in both A and C, we saw nothing that prevented us from swapping over to other Guns/Lt MTRs to fire SMOKE, then coming back to the first Lt MTR to fire HE.  We did believe that if we chose to have the Lt MTR /not/ fire HE, it would still be marked Prep Fire (as it had successfully attempted to fire WP), even though it did not lose ROF.  

Q) Is this correct?  That one can fire a weapon during a phase, NOT mark it as fired in that phase if it kept ROF, fire other units/weapons, and then come back to that first weapon to finish up its firing (or just to mark it as fully fired)?  Or must the unit/weapon be immediately marked Prep Fire after it has fired at least once, even if it has not exhausted its ROF at that point?

Rules we felt were involved:
A3.2 (Place a Prep Fire counter on those units which fire);

A9.2 (If that colored dr is ≤ the MG’s applicable ROF, the MG retains its Multiple ROF and may be fired again during that phase (A.15). ... Once a MG has lost its Multiple ROF, it is marked with an appropriate Prep, First or Final Fire counter.); and

C2.24 (However, a number encased in a square on the counter indicates a Multiple ROF equal to that number, thus conceivably allowing it (and certain ordnance SW such as light mortars and some ATR, as well as MG making TH DR) to fire many times during a Player Turn. If the Original colored dr of its TH (or IFE IFT) DR is ≤ its ROF, that weapon may fire again during that Player Turn unless otherwise prohibited. If the Original colored dr of the TH (or IFE IFT) DR is > the firing weapon’s ROF, it is marked with an appropriate fire counter (Prep, First Fire, etc.) and may fire no more in that Player Turn (EXC: Sustained/Intensive Fire if so allowed).)
author: kbernatz
consensus_answer:
Looking at the ROF rules in both A and C, we saw nothing that prevented us from swapping over to other Guns/Lt MTRs to fire SMOKE, then coming back to the first Lt MTR to fire HE.  We did believe that if we chose to have the Lt MTR /not/ fire HE, it would still be marked Prep Fire (as it had successfully attempted to fire WP), even though it did not lose ROF.

Both statements are correct. Units/weapons may fire in any order except where otherwise limited (e.g. SMOKE before other ammunition) including allowing other units/weapons to fire between its own attacks.

This is independent of ROF when that is applicable. For instance in the enemy MPh if an enemy unit spent two MF entering a Location, a DEFENDER could fire on it once then another DEFENDER could fire on the enemy unit once then the first DEFENDER could fire again (as ROF, SFF or FPF) then the second DEFENDER could fire again (as ROF, SFF or FPF). Or the first DEFENDER unit could fire twice then the second DEFENDER unit fire twice, or the first DEFENDER unit could fire once then the second DEFENDER unit could fire twice then the first DEFENDER unit could fire again.

Per A3.2 units that fire in the PFPh are marked with a Prep Fire counter. There are other places where you can also determine that units that fired in the PFPh cannot move or fire in the AFPh even if they kept ROF, but A3.2 is the simplest.

Likewise a firing unit can fire an underbelly shot before or after a regular attack when a vehicle is crossing a wall.

title: Pillbox ambush
question: Played a scenario yesterday with Pillboxes.  There is a +2DRM for Ambush if in a Pillbox, but the Pillbox wasn't in a forest, where Ambushes are stated to occur. Is a Pillbox therefore considered a building?
author: Fly by Night

B30.1, "Except for its two CA hexsides, the pillbox hex itself is not in the pillbox CA;" B30.2, "LOS from inside a pillbox may be traced only within its CA." There is no LOS.

A Pillbox is not considered a building, for ambush or any other purpose of which I am aware. Having a pillbox alone does not cause Ambush drs, just like being CX does not cause Ambush drs even though CX is also an Ambush drm.

Only woods, building, jungle, kunai, bamboo or a concealed unit will have the possibility of Ambush. Since pillboxes can't set up in buildings, to get the pillbox drm the pillbox either has to be in woods, jungle, bamboo, kunai or there has to be a concealed unit involved (just the same as with the CX drm). Even if terrain does not cause Ambush, it's not uncommon that there is a concealed unit involved, either in the pillbox, possibly still HIP from setup, or in the Advancing stack. 

Note that if the Pillbox will not be involved in the CC due to friendly (to the pillbox occupants) units outside the pillbox, the pillbox drm does not apply to any Ambush drm.

title: AFV Turret weapons fire bad memory
question:
Fellow ASL'ers

I have a bad memory ... please help ...

An AFV fires (DFF ) it's cmg at moving Infantry a few hexes away .. VCA/TCA identical 
Q1: does this lock the TCA for the MA firing later in the same DFF Ph ?
Q2: Vice-versa if MA fires first then cmg separate target ?
Q3: or same questions but is it Line of Fire along the Hexspine fixed for shots ?
Q4: or have I got different games/rules mixed up entirely ? very probable in this instance ..

I'm sure I saw something/vague memory some time ago about turreted weapons LoF locking along a hexspine for cmg/MA fire in any Fire Phase once one or other fires first. i.e., turret weapons
but .. I've searched the ASL rulebook and just cannot find the thing i'm looking for .. 
I take a lot medical tablets a day and it's messing with my memory ... 

thanks guys
author: Mixy_1963
consensus_answer:
As per previous answers, if there is a Known target (and there are no terrain restrictions), no. In your case the target might be Known or not. Firing at a target where there is no Known Enemy unit *does* lock the CA. This is because of some "sleaze" you can perform here. The TCA (VCA) change DRM for a particular shot does *not* "remember" and accumulate with previous TCA (VCA) changes [D3.51].

So for instance assume there is a unit that you really want to take a shot at (with CMG or MA) but currently you have to change TCA three hexspines to get the desired target in CA. You can change CA two hexspines and take a shot at a KEU using the weapon you don't want to use, then take a shot with a one hexspine change at the target you really want to attack. The CA change DRM for the second TCA change is only the cost of one hexspine, i.e. the previous two hexspine TCA change is "forgotten". But if the target of the first TCA change attack is not Known, the TCA is frozen. This reduces the opportunity for sleaze somewhat, even if it doesn't eliminate it.

As a follow-on, you can't use this trick using a mix of the VCA and the TCA. While a second TCA change makes the unit forget its first *TCA* change, a mix of VCA and TCA changes are cumulative. Only the most recent TCA and VCA change as above, but that is usually enough to make it not especially good to mix them.

title: My AFV can be Moving Target on my turn but need not be on Opponents?
question: Am I right that, despite player turns being simultaneous, an AFV that starts my turn Stopped, moves to new hexes, then stops is a Moving Target on my turn but when we flip to my Opponent's turn the AFV is no longer considered a Moving Target? I can't find anything in C.8 that contradicts this.
author: doktor avalanche
consensus_answer:
Having thought about this some more, I think the friendly player turn may comprise more "actual time" of the friendly player's forces than the enemy player turn. All of movement is stuffed into the friendly player turn along with most of the "serious" attacks (the PFPh). Although the player can also use the DFPh for "serious" attacks, skulking makes it definitely the second-best for such attacks. So if a Game Turn notionally represents two minutes of "real time", perhaps 90 seconds of that "real time" is spent in the friendly player turn and 30 seconds in the enemy player turn. As far as "game time" is concerned a friendly player turn is just as long as an enemy player turn, but they map to different amounts of "real time". The friendly player turn has all the friendly actions that are performed not in reaction to the enemy force's activities, and the enemy player turn has all the actions that are primarily in reaction to the enemy force's activities.

I don't mean the numbers or ratio given, 90 seconds:30 seconds, to be a scientific statement. The ratio may vary depending on circumstances. For instance if a scenario has two sides move onto the board in such a way that they don't gain LOS to each other the first Game Turn, the friendly player turn may represent 100% of the actual time and the enemy player turn 0%. What I am suggesting is that more of the "real time" for the friendly player may be spent in the friendly player turn, i.e. that each side's experience of "real time" is not 50:50 between the two player turns of a game turn.

It's not clear that the friendly player turn and the enemy player turn for a given game turn represent simultaneous time. The breakdown of "simultaneous" time into sequential, board-gameable actions in ASL is a abstract mapping that gives an illusion of real time to players while not necessarily  modeling it accurately in all aspects. A vehicle that moves during its MPh then stops behaves like a "real" vehicle that is moving forward using leaps and bounds, i.e. stopping every so often and acquiring battlefield awareness and performing stationary actions before bounding again. If the vehicle keeps on a Motion counter between turns, that models a "real" vehicle that is moving throughout the entire game turn. Since the vehicle that starts at the beginning of every MPh and stops at the end loses only two MP, it probably isn't an exact mapping of "real" time into "game board" time/phases, but it at least models somewhat that such units performing different modes of movement are not moving at the same speed and does indicate that at least somewhat a vehicle that moves in bounds moves slower than one that is moving continuously.

title: Bocage B9.53 - AA Gun CA change
question:
Review the attached image. Q: Russian MPh, Can the AA Gun first fire at the Russian AFV in L2, maintain ROF and then change CA and fire at the 2nd Russian AFV in H4 through the Bocage? Clarify specific aspects of the rule about a Non-Vehicle Gun changing CA when firing through Bocage.

The first attack is irrelevant. B9.53 "A non-vehicular Direct-Fire Gun may not both change CA and fire through a bocage hexside in the same fire phase (counting Defensive First Fire and Final Fire as one phase—A.15)." The Gun may not both change its CA and fire through the I4-J3 hexside, assuming hedges are Bocage. It could not make the attack if that were the only attack it wanted to make.
author: IR226_79ID
consensus_answer:
Why is the First Fire Irrelevant? Does the Rule prohibit the AA Gun from making the second shot even if it retained ROF? It could make the First Fire shot and if retained ROF, it still could change CA and fire at another target just not through the Bocage hexside, correct or no? It would seem to me, if a turret on a AFV can change CA and fire through the Bocage, how is that different from an AA Gun?

The Gun could change CA and fire at a target as long as it does not fire through a Bocage hexside, whether the attack is a first DFF attack, an attack after retaining ROF, a Sustained or Intensive Fire attack, or even an OVR Prevention attack. It could turn its CA from K2 to L3 and, say, fire on L3 or K4. I believe it could even turn its CA to H3 (an "unnecessary" extra hexspine) and fire to H2 as long as walls are not Bocage in the scenario. Note that the Gun could not change CA during the enemy MPh in response to movement in H4 because any change of CA during the enemy MPh would have to be part of an attack. The Gun would have to wait until the DFPh and use a "free" CA change to turn toward H4 (unless it found a reason to change CA to fire in that direction where it did not fire through a Bocage hexside).

You would have to speak to the rule designer to get an authoritative reason why this is so for Bocage. My made-up, how-would-this-work-in-a-ww-ii-movie explanation is that when firing through Bocage "changing CA" actually requires some physical translation of the gun, i.e. it is not pure rotation. A vehicle can perform this in-hex translation quickly enough in game terms to be allowed to both change CA and attack. A non-vehicular gun isn't quick enough. It would be like taking a 32-pound gun from a broadside gun port of HMS Victory and moving it to a bow chaser port. It can be done but it would take a while. But that is 100% guess and worth exactly what you paid for it. What ever the reason, the rule is clear. If the hexside is hedge, you can change CA and fire through it. When it is Bocage and you have a non-vehicular Gun, you can't.
