So Robin's post had me curious, so I did a search through the eASLRB for both 'known' and 'Known' and came up with the following (only for sections A - F):

1) 'Known' is used /extensively/ in these sections as one can guess, primarily as 'Known enemy' or 'Known armed enemy' with a few variations.

2) "Known mines", "Known Minefield", and "Known minefield" are used extensively in B28 and F.7.  Also uses the term "Normal" minefields when referencing B28 and in B28.  I suspect the capitalization of "Minefield" in "Known Minefield" is a typo, as the majority of the time the rules use "Known mine(field)" with a lowercase m.

3) There are no other uses of "Known" (capital K) than with regard to enemy units or minefields.

4) For 'known', B28.413 Rout uses "known minefield" 

5) 15.45 Berserk units Terrain Restrictions: "Known enemy" followed up by two occurrences of "known enemy" which appear to be obvious typos (should be "Known enemy").

6) 10.51 Rout Direction: "known minefield" twice

7) 7.212 Target Selection Limits: "known enemy unit".  Another one that appears like it should be "Known enemy unit".

So its just the two in B28.413 and A10.51 that could be interpreted either way (capital-K 'Known' or lowercase-k 'known').  It is unfortunate that the term "Known minefield" is explicitly defined but then these two locations use 'known minefield' because I could see either interpretation being supported by the rules.

If the intent is truly that a unit of the player who placed the minefield MUST rout into that minefield if required (i.e. they cannot avoid it), then A10.51 and B28.413 should be edited to recite 'Known minefield' as used through-out B28.

If the intent is that a unit of the player who placed the minefield KNOWS the hidden minefield exists and can avoid it even though it isn't on map as a Known minefield, then I would suggest amending A10.51 and B28.413 to recite:

 Otherwise, a routing unit may move toward an enemy unit. Assuming it can abide by the previous requirements, a routing unit must move to the nearest (in MF calculated at the start of its RtPh) building or woods hex (even if overstacked) unless that route is through/into a minefield known to that side (even if still hidden) or FFE, or is not traversable (e.g., through a Blaze, unbridged Water Obstacle, Cliff, etc.). As long as it reaches that hex during a single RtPh, it need not use the shortest route, but as long as it follows the shortest path in MF otherwise, it may enter a shellhole/entrenchment/pillbox to avoid Interdiction even if it can no longer reach that woods/building hex in a single RtPh. A routing unit can rout into/out of/within a minefield known to that side (even if still hidden) or FFE at its option, but is not forced to do so merely to reach the closest woods/building hex. 

and

 28.413 ROUT: A routing unit need not move through an A-P minefield hex known to that side (including if still hidden) and may opt to take a longer route to a building/woods hex instead. However, if a broken squad is Reduced to a broken HS by minefield attack, that HS may continue its rout in the same RtPh at its option. Should a routing unit also be subject to Interdiction, the Interdiction would be resolved after any minefield attack. 

Either option would clarify the rule one way or the other, IMO.

title: What is meant by Case K "Or Area Fire"?
question:
This came up in our last session when we had a lt mortar firing at a concealed target at 5 hex range.  We understood that the To Hit number is a 7 (Area, range 0-6) and the DRM would be +2 (Concealment).

What confused us was "when does the "(Or Area Fire; C.4)" come into play?  If a Gun was firing as Area Fire, wouldn't one just use the Area Fire row to determine the To Hit?  And if one was firing at a Concealed unit, wouldn't one just use the Case K - Concealed Target?

When would there be a situation where one would apply a +2 DRM for "Area Fire"?  We couldn't think of one, but figured there had to be occurrences ...
author: kbernatz
consensus_answer:
Some other, non-ordnance, uses of Area Fire off the top of my head: vs Dashing units, Snap Shots, Spraying Fire, and Motion Fire. Also, Advancing Fire and Subsequent First Fire/Final Fire are applications of Area Fire.

Well, advancing fire would, instead, be subject to Case B/C, right?  And LATW can't do Sub FF or Final Fire, right?  Not a 'Gun', so can't Intensive Fire and not a MG, so can't Sustain Fire.  I guess a MG using Sustained Fire going for an AFV kill would apply the Case K "or Area Fire" modifier, though.

(edit: Actually, in hindsight, think 'no', as that also isn't due to the TARGET'S status... they would, instead, apply Case F probably?)

Spraying Fire doesn't really apply as that is IFT only, right?  And Motion would be Case B/C or J, not K.

I thought Dash might be one, but just looked it up and it specifically states (in A4.63) that /non-ordnance/ uses Area Fire and that ordnance applies case J.  No mention of case K, so don't think Dash applies.

Same thought with Snap Shot, but that apparently is "Small Arms/MG Defensive First Fire attack" only (A8.15).

title: Some Night rule queries
question:
Just played a Night scenario and a couple of queries came up we weren't sure about.

1. If my unit is on the ground floor inside a 2-level building, and is firing into the adjacent hex at a target in the same building, do I get a +1 LV Hindrance for Night? It would appear yes by E1.7. Same question if firer and target are both on the top floor-- it would appear to be no LV Hindrance by E1.7. Is that correct? Seems a bit counter-intuitive given the "reality argument" in footnote 8 of chapter E.

2. I have three Cloaking counters and an unconcealed Squad in a hex. What do you know, the enemy Sniper is triggered in that hex. Do I lose all three Cloaking counters? Or do I do random selection between the 3 cloaking counters and the squad (i.e. 4 RS drs), and just reveal any cloaking counters chosen by RS? Or do count all 3 Cloaking counters as 1 concealed stack (as per A14.23) and roll RS between the squad and the "concealed stack" (i.e. 2 RS drs)?
author: angelgabriel
consensus_answer:
1. In the first case, no, the +1 LV is NA because the target is in terrain that is >= 1 full level higher than the firer.  In the second case, the +1 LV does apply because the target's terrain is NOT >= 1 level higher than the firer.

Note that the comparison is "firer's level" vs "target's terrain height" -- NOT "firer's terrain height" vs "target's terrain height".

2. Each Cloaking counter is a separate potential target, as is the squad.  So you do random selection between 4 targets.  A14.23 doesn't apply because the Cloaking counters are each a separate "stack".  E1.72 applies if a Cloaking counter is the affected target.

title: VOTG8 Hammer and Nail and cloaking
question:
In VOTG 8, the SSR says I as Russian (and the Germans) “may” setup cloaked. 

All MMC with MMG/HMG and SMC setup with them may setup using HIP. 

Do those HIP stacks with MMG/HMG have to setup under a HIP Cloak counter? What about my HIP guns and their crews, also under a HIP Cloak counter?

Can I choose *not* to setup infantry under a Cloak counter?

(E1.42 says Cloaked SW must be dm if possible. Presumably that means my .50 cal and  the German HMG/MMG have to be dm even though they are probably setting up (the Germans at least) in a static defensive position. That's why we may want to setup our MGs HIP but not Cloaked.)
author: angelgabriel
consensus_answer:
Do those HIP stacks with MMG/HMG have to setup under a HIP Cloak counter?

No such thing as a "HIP Cloaking counter".  What would be the point?  The advantage of a Cloaking counter, as opposed to regular concealment, is that it's easier to move at night (you don't pay the extra MF for moving through concealment terrain, and you have a guaranteed 6 MF, even if you're just a bunch of conscripts).  Also, dummies.  (You get a Cloaking counter for every squad-equivalent, but you don't have to put each squad under a separate counter.)

The emphasis in the SSR is not "may", it's "both may", because both sides are declared to be Scenario Attacker (very unusual for a Night scenario).  Also, the scenario gives free HIP to all of the HMG/MMG (and attending infantry) so if you don't want them to move you're better off just leaving them as HIP, not cloaked or concealed.  If you do want them to move then Cloaking is a far better option.

But yes, if you really don't want to HIP or Cloak your units, you don't have to.

title: Some TEM and foxhole questions
question:
Mostly theoretical, but some came up in our last session.

1) For a woods + wooden building hex, our understanding is that bypassing units = +1 TEM (woods), but non-bypass units get +3 (wooden building +2 and woods +1).  Or do they just get the +2 for the building?

2) If hit by OBA, would they have a net +1 TEM (+2 for building and -1 for air bursts)?

3) Can a foxhole be built in a woods+building hex? B27.1 prohibits placement in a building, but is a woods+building hex considered 'woods', 'building', or both?  Think both, correct (so NO foxhole placement).

4) Units can advance into/out of a foxhole during the Advance Phase, correct?  This seems clear per B27.44.  Also believe a unit in an adjacent hex could advance into the foxhole hex /and/ enter the foxhole, correct?

5) How does a foxhole in a shell hole hex work?  Presumably units would have to specify which they were in and could not be in both a foxhole /and/ a shellhole (or could they?).  Neither creates a separate 'location' in the hex, per se (other than B27.13).

If a unit had a foxhole+shellhole and was in the foxhole, could they expend 3 MFs (2 MFs??) to go from the foxhole into the shellhole, thereby avoiding the FFMO due to exiting the foxhole?  B27.4 is unclear to me.  If trying to enter the foxhole from outside, it seems you would pay the COT (1 or 2 MF?? or 0 or 1 MF if same hex?), survive DF, then pay another MF to enter the foxhole.  But the wording for exiting implies the same payment procedure; i.e. pay the 1 or 2 MF COT to enter the shellhole, THEN decrement the +1 MF for having left the foxhole.

27.4 The cost of entering a hex containing a foxhole is equal to the COT of the hex entered. However, Infantry moving beneath an existing foxhole counter or from beneath a foxhole counter must pay one additional MF separately after payment of the COT to enter the hex and after suffering any Defensive First Fire that MF expenditure may have enticed.  

Intuitively, I would have thought the payment cost on leaving would have been "1 MF to leave, suffer DF, then pay COT"...but seems like that is not correct.

6) Routing seems to work differently where you can combine the +1 MF with an adjacent hex COT, so it would seem like the routing cost (to an adjacent building, for instance) would be 3 MF (2 MF + 1 MF for leaving foxhole).

7) Actually, now I'm confused on the cost to leave a foxhole.  If I have a foxhole in an Open Ground hex, then it would cost me 2 MFs to enter the foxhole from an adjacent hex (COT =1 +1 MF for entry).  But B27.4 implies it would also cost me 2 MF to leave the foxhole and be placed above the foxhole ("must pay one additional MF separately /after payment of the COT to enter the hex/").  Looking at B.2, nothing overrules this interpretation, though it seems counter-intuitive (that one must pay a COT to enter a hex one is already located in).
author: kbernatz
consensus_answer:
1) For a woods + wooden building hex, our understanding is that bypassing units = +1 TEM (woods), but non-bypass units get +3 (wooden building +2 and woods +1).

Correct.  Note that B.1 doesn't have any LOS requirement, i.e., if the LOF to the centre dot hits the building without touching any woods artwork, the woods TEM is still cumulative with the building TEM.

2) If hit by OBA, would they have a net +1 TEM (+2 for building and -1 for air bursts)?

Yes.

3) Can a foxhole be built in a woods+building hex? B27.1 prohibits placement in a building, but is a woods+building hex considered 'woods', 'building', or both?  Think both, correct (so NO foxhole placement).

No foxhole.  The hex is both woods and building, so all restrictions applicable to either still apply.

4) Units can advance into/out of a foxhole during the Advance Phase, correct?  This seems clear per B27.44.  Also believe a unit in an adjacent hex could advance into the foxhole hex /and/ enter the foxhole, correct?

Yes (unless they are carrying so much gear that they have 0 MF available).  Yes.  (Note that the extra MF to exit/enter the foxhole may invoke A4.72.)

5) How does a foxhole in a shell hole hex work?  Presumably units would have to specify which they were in and could not be in both a foxhole /and/ a shellhole (or could they?).  Neither creates a separate 'location' in the hex, per se (other than B27.13).

You're either in the foxhole (and therefore foxhole TEM applies) or you're not in the foxhole (and therefore shellhole TEM applies).  They're not cumulative.

If a unit had a foxhole+shellhole and was in the foxhole, could they expend 3 MFs (2 MFs??) to go from the foxhole into the shellhole, thereby avoiding the FFMO due to exiting the foxhole?

Only in the RtPh.  In the MPh, exiting (or entering) the foxhole costs 1 MF that must be expended separately.  That's a flat cost; the other terrain in the hex is irrelevant.  You are still eligible for the shellhole TEM, per B2.4:

If it ... starts the phase therein, it is considered in a shellhole and not subject to FFMO penalties.

Exiting a foxhole never requires that you pay extra MF to enter the terrain of the hex you're already in.

6) Routing seems to work differently where you can combine the +1 MF with an adjacent hex COT, so it would seem like the routing cost (to an adjacent building, for instance) would be 3 MF (2 MF + 1 MF for leaving foxhole).

Yes.  B27.4.

7) Actually, now I'm confused on the cost to leave a foxhole.

I MF, flat cost.  No rules imply anything different.  You can combine that 1 MF with adjacent hex entry cost during the RtPh (only), but it's still only 1 MF to actually get out of the foxhole.

title: M3A1 Halftrack
question: The M3A1 half track has a significant amount of removable weapons. If the crew abandons the half track can it take all of the weapons with it?
author: drmark64
consensus_answer:
Vehicle Notes applicable to the M3A1 ht. Note I is probably the relevant one here

E. The inherent crew may fire only the .50-cal MA unless it is malfunctioned or disabled, in which case the crew may fire a secondary AAMG instead. Otherwise, only a Good Order Passenger may use a secondary AAMG (as signified on the counter by printing such FP in red). If such a Passenger is a lone SMC, it can fire only secondary AAMG; if ≥ two SMC or a MMC, all secondary AAMG can be fired. Assuming they are properly manned, the MA AAMG and any/all secondary AAMG may be fired together as a FG or at separate targets (as per D3.5 and within any applicable field of fire restrictions). Each red-FP AAMG fired by a Passenger counts as use of a SW for the purpose of also using that Passengers inherent FP. See U.S. Vehicle Note H.

H. Each AAMG malfunctions and is repaired or disabled independently of the others. If a vehicles MA AAMG malfunctions, mark it with a MA Malfunction counter to show that its non-MA AAMG FP is still usable. Whenever all of a vehicles non-MA AAMG malfunction, indicate this by using an AAMG Malfunction counter. If a vehicle has more than one non-MA AAMG and one of them malfunctions, mark the vehicle with a One AAMG Malfunction counter; thereafter, in each friendly fire phase in which that AAMG is not repaired, the remaining still-usable non-MA AAMG may fire in its own allowed direction or in the malfunctioned AAMGs direction at no extra penalty. [EX: An LVT4s port-side AAMG malfunctions. As long as that AAMG is not repaired, the starboard-side AAMG can be used in either AAMGs side-rear field of fire; i.e., its field of fire is then in any direction except through the VCA. See the diagram for U.S. Vehicle Note 51.] Since the ROF applies only to the MA (A9.2), the owner must announce before he fires that he is using the MA if he wishes to possibly retain a multiple ROF. An Armor/Passenger leader may direct the fire of more than one vehicular-mounted/Passenger-fired MG only if those MG are firing together as a FG.

I. The AAMG FP actually consists of two MG: one .50-cal HMG (MA; 4 FP) and one secondary .30-cal MMG (2 FP)—as signified by 4MA&2 on the counter. Each MG may be Removed as this given type (i.e., as a .50-cal. or MMG respectively). See also U.S. Vehicle Note E.
  	
Z. This vehicle starts each scenario carrying one BAZ of the latest model (signified by BAZ on the counter), which does apply to the vehicles PP capacity (D6.1) when it takes counter form. (Thus it must remain inherent if the vehicle currently has no unused PP capacity.) In a single Player Turn the inherent crew may fire either the vehicles normal armament or the BAZ (as per C13.8-.81). Otherwise, the BAZ may only be Removed (D6.631) by the crew or a Passenger (who can claim possession of it automatically), or Scrounged (D10.5). These principles also apply to the inherent SW in the German SPW 251/10.

title: Red Barricades Campaign 1 Initial Scenario Victory Conditions
question:
Per Chapter O 11.51, the Germans must Control >= 15 Stone Locations at scenario in order to win the initial scenario.

Question:  What establishes control of Stone Locations that happen to be within a multi-hex, multi-level building that includes cellar locations and upper level locations?

The German was the last to move through all six ground level hex locations of Building C18.  However the Germans have not entered any upper floor location, nor have they entered any cellar location, nor have they Mopped Up.  Meanwhile a Russian squad still resides in one the cellar hexes.  All six hexes of the building are within the German Perimeter Area determined after the game ended.

Does the German receive credit for 6, 12, 17, or 18 Stone Locations associated with this building at scenario's end?
author: A2SimGamer
consensus_answer:
Question:  What establishes control of Stone Locations that happen to be within a multi-hex, multi-level building that includes cellar locations and upper level locations?

Because No Quarter is in effect for all RB scenarios/CG, there is one and only one way of gaining Control of a Location: be the last occupant of the Location with an armed MMC.

You must walk up (and down, for cellars) all of those building Locations.

Building Control means absolutely nothing in RB, but even if it did, it wouldn't help, because gaining Control of a building does not confer Control of the Locations in that building.  (Nor would it give you Control of the hexes in that building, but that's OK, because Hex Control also means nothing in RB.)

If No Quarter was not in effect, then Mopping Up (A12.153) would be an option; and Mopping Up gives you Control of the entire building and all hexes and all Locations in that building (A26.11).

Bruce - qq on this - I believe during the Refit Phase, anything inside your perimeter BECOMES controlled, but your point is very important since I think victory is determined earlier in the refit process.

A belated thanks Bruce for the helpful reply.  Thunderstorm damage has had most of SE Michigan without internet for the better part of a week.  

Neither the Russian player nor the German player was aware of any relationship between No Quarter and Mopping Up because the index entry for No Quarter mentions only A20.3.  After reading your response, it seemed to me that the remaining question was whether scenario victory is supposed to be determined before or after the campaign game's Refit Phase. However, they start the next scenario controlling 17 of the 18 Stone Locations within Building C18 (all except the Cellar location that is controlled by the Isolated Russian squad) because the building ends up behind the German perimeter.

title: Chapter K Training Manual
question:
This is one of the best walkthroughs you can ever imagine for such a complex game as ASL.
It should be interesting if this could be expanded towards chapter D Vehicles (and how to use them) and even other rules like those from chaper E (night, air,...) and CHAPTER F Desert and G Pacific Theatre.
author: neo.colpaert
consensus_answer:
Agree ... but that manual was written mid to late 80s, and with all the instructional videos out these days, I think the need for the expanded training manual has gone with the "way of the carrier pigeon" (quoting the ASLRB).
Most videos don't even come close to what CHAP K portrays.
I hope to correct that.

One of the best worked out videos is according to me this one: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bbgVZsMGneU&t=197s
Should be very interesting for ASL-newbies (especially if from other countries where there is no strong ASL-"community")  if veteran players would make some more video series like this one.
And the strength of Chapter K is especially the way it gives you some kind of exercises which make you understand the system much better. That's why it would be very interesting they would develop it towards other chapters like D and E as well. What some ALS-regular and veteran players (from Anglo-American countries) sometimes forget is that newbie players like me from other non-English speaking countries (Belgium in my case) don't speak/understand English as their mother language. And as I always mentioned in other threads the ALS-rules are made in a more difficult "academic" language which demand a bigger effort to understand them. You need to have an EXTREME passion for this game (which I have!) to try to read and understand everything. They should wonder what they should do if these rules were made in - let's say - my mother language Dutch. It should be a pity that the most fantastic WWII tactical game ever made should only be reserved for English speaking people.

title: Concealed and Hidden units
question: Let's say I have a Concealed Infantry unit in a hex that also contains a Hidden Tank.  If I am fired on by another infantry unit (on the IFT), does that effect the tank in any way with regard to removing the Hidden status?  What if I'm attacked via HE Ordnance?
author: Randy Mauldin
consensus_answer:
Not sure the exact clause parsing, but I find it odd that they use "PTC" instead of just PTC if they weren't intending it to also encompass pseudo-PTCs; i.e. ones that have no chance of generating an effect, such as against BU CT AFVs. 

The use "PTC" in quotes in several places: A7.305, A7.8, A12.13, A12.141... all of these for real infantry effects, not any pseudo-PTC. I guess it was something from the first draft that stuck.

replies.body:
It's strange to have a hidden tank, but not impossible.
An AFV will lose concealment if hit on the TH table (adding Case K), note that ITT ignores amored vehicles (its the target type that matters, not the ammo).
If there is exposed PRC, it can also be hit with IFT fire. Both PRC and vehicle share concealed/HIP status, so if one loses it the other also loses it.

Hi, I believe if the squad looses its concealment the tank would also loose its hidden status. I think A12.2 shows this. Hope this is right and it helps you. If not could someone else clarify because that is how I have been playing it.

Well the SSR allows the tank to be hidden.  And the infantry is not a PRC, just a regular infantry unit.  So if the enemy fires a HE round at the concealed infantry, I need to see if it hit the tank, and if so, reveal it, or just put it under a "?" marker?

Generally true.  For the purposes of losing HIP (only) the vehicle is revealed if a PTC or better result is scored on the IFT (which is sufficient for an infantry unit to lose concealment), even though the PTC or NMC would normally not have any effect on an AFV.  (If the vehicle is unarmoured, or it is CE, then of course it is vulnerable in the usual way.)

As stated above, the vehicle will also lose HIP if actually hit by an ordnance attack (either Vehicle Target Type or Area Target Type).  The hit does not need to cause any damage to cause loss of HIP/Concealment.

This is, of course, all spelled out in the A12.121 Concealment Loss/Gain Table.  Read it, study it, learn it, love it.  You cannot play ASL correctly if you don't understand this table.

HIP is a special case of Concealment. According to the Concealment Loss/Gain Table, case A applies to both infantry and vehicles in Concealment Terrain. If the Concealed infantry unit is revealed by a PTC or better on the IFT then the tank also loses Concealment/HIP regardless of whether it has Vulnerable PRC or not. However, if the infantry unit is fired on by ordnance using the Infantry Target Type, the tank cannot be hit so cannot lose Concealment/HIP.

title: More Hill 621 Q&A
question:
I'm pretty sure we did this correctly, but wanted to get input to make sure.

Background: 4 Grogs playing Hill 621; 2 GE and 2 SOV.  Turn 5, SOV MPh, soviets are entering their big SUs and trucks/6-2-8s.  Germans have their 75L PAK and the 10-3 with an HMG on the lvl 3 hills, but not in optimal position (read: limited LOS).

So the Soviet player enters a Truck carrying a 6-2-8 and starts it along the road. Question 1: Trucks, without inherent crews, always use the 1/2 MP cost of the road (under 'Truck' Movement chart it lists '1 if buttoned up', but we figured that was for vehicles that use truck movement but have inherent crews).

Question 2: We forgot about concealment, but he would have had a choice about whether starting the truck + 6-2-8 passenger as concealed, correct?  The reason for NOT choosing this would be that it would give the HMG free LOS checks to determine loss of concealment before making a decision on firing.

The HMG fires at the Truck + 6-2-8 at range 26.  This puts it at 3.5 FP, or column 2 on the IFT.  The * vehicle number is '4'.  No TEM applies for this shot, so the German player rolls and gets an 8 (keeping ROF).  This is modified due to leadership to a '5', which means no effect on the vehicle.  Question 3: Correct that leadership affects * vehicle to kill determination?  Question 4: Since vehicle did not get eliminated, we apply the 5 IFT result from the 2 column against the 6-2-8 passenger as a specific collateral attack, correct?  It passes its MC.

Later, the HMG fires at this same truck at a range of 18 hexes across an adjacent wall (to the truck).  Question 5: The same procedure as above applies, but there is an additional +2 TEM to the IFT roll due to the wall, which affects both the * vehicle result and any resulting specific collateral attack versus the passenger.

Question 6: Later even still, the HMG fires at a second truck carrying a second 6-2-8 and rolls a 7, modified to a '4', which Immobilizes the truck AND gives a MC to the 6-2-8, which it failed. The 6-2-8, being broken, must remain in the Truck and cannot be unloaded even though the Immobilized Truck had additional MPs, correct?

Question 7: During the rout phase, the 6-2-8 can rout out of the truck (for 1 MP???) and, if desired, continue routing to other hexes (??).  This one we're not sure of.

Oh, and the HMG still kept its ROF :)
author: kbernatz
consensus_answer:
Q1 : that has nothing to do with inherent crews. Unarmed trucks have an inherent driver. BU is NA for an unarmored vehicle. So, say, a GAZ-MM truck spends 1/2 MP per road hexside.

Q2 : as soon as the truck moves into the LOS of the enemy l, it loses Concealment.

Q3 : Leadership applies to an attack on the IFT, which includes the * value vs unarmoured vehicles.
Note that A9.4 doesn't apply (i.e. considers infantry as concealed), as the 628 are Passengers, not Infantry.

Q4 : Yes

Q5 : Yes

Q6 : 1MC (4 on the 2 FP column). Unload NA (the 628 is broken, so it only can move during RtPh).

Q7 : it routs under the truck, no further.
D6.1 : ... Passengers may remain in their vehicle even while broken or may rout beneath a Stopped vehicle per 5.311
D5.311 :  ... If it breaks it must rout from the vehicle using normal Infantry rout procedures [EXC: it expends all its initial-RtPh MF to be placed beneath the vehicle].

title: LLTC at rallies
question:
Hello everyone.

A 9-1 lead stacked with three 838 squads has rolled a 12 and then a 5, with which it has been eliminated. The squads must roll for LLTC, or this is only for Morale Checks?. I had always applied it only in MCs but my opponent says that in rallies it also applies.

author: jesuspiebatlle
consensus_answer:
Please make sure to read the entire rule section... this is a HUGE issue in our group, as we read a section, see something that appears to answer our question and stop...only for the very next word to completely change our interpretation, lol.  Seriously, this has happened like 3 or 4 times to us in just the past couple sessions!

The full rule is A10.2:
10.2 LEADER LOSS MORALE CHECK (LLMC)/LEADER LOSS TASK CHECK (LLTC): Whenever a MC/TC is required, leaders must 
check before other units (with higher Morale Level leaders checking before lower Morale Level leaders). For each leader eliminated (whether by breaking when already broken, a mortal wound, or any other cause), after resolution of that attack (if any) all other friendly Personnel units with a currently lower Morale Level and in the same Location (or in the same moving stack, e.g., during Defensive First Fire) must take a LLMC [EXC: Riders (13.52, D15.55), Passengers (D6.651), Climbers (B11.42), and units at a different level (2.8), or in CC (11.141) neither take or cause LLMC/LLTC (as a result of their breaking or elimination). Passengers take/cause LLMC/LLTC only to fellow passengers of the same vehicle (D6.651)]. A LLMC is always based on the unit’s current Morale Level, even if that unit is broken or has a reduced or increased Morale Level. Any negative leadership modifier of the eliminated leader must be reversed to a positive DRM and added to each LLMC. A leader eliminated/broken during Defensive First Fire does not cause other units in the same Location to take a LLMC/LLTC unless they were moving with him as one combined stack.

Should an unbroken leader break, all unbroken friendly Personnel units with a lower Morale Level in the same Location (or moving stack during Defensive First Fire) must take a LLTC [EXC: if exempt from pinning]. This LLTC is handled in the same manner as a LLMC except that if the LLTC is failed, the unit is pinned instead of broken. 

But what you omitted in your original quote and which you appear to have overlooked is: "... or any other cause), after resolution of that attack (if any) ... ".

I.e. the second bold "(if any)" clearly opens this statement up to situations where there was no attack; e.g. a rally check.  This makes the second sentence in A10.2 much clearer: "For each leader eliminated (whether by breaking when already broken, a mortal wound, or any other cause), after resolution of that attack (if any)".

Could this be clearer in the rules?  Yes, IMO.  I could have been in a section that started differently than "Whenever a MC/TC is required" ... which implies the entirety of this rule ONLY refers to situations where a MC/TC is required, but that isn't the case.  The ASL rules are replete with situations like this, where an initial sentence implies that the rule is directing a narrow situation, but subsequent sentences are directed to broad interpretations (I had an exact same situation just a couple days ago, but don't remember which rule).  The moral of the story is: when reading the ASL rules, you need to (1) make sure you read the ENTIRE section and (2) read each sentence separately and make sure you understand the scope that /specific/ sentence is covering.  There are many times that the scope between two adjacent sentences will be different.

consensus_answer:
Could someone have a look at this question as well, please?

What exactly is your question?

Encirclement (by fire) occurs when attacks against a single unit/stack are made sequentially (subject to a couple of conditions).

When trying to encircle a unit, you have to make sure that the attacks are made in the correct order, and you can't interrupt the sequence by shooting at something else.  Nor can you interrupt the sequence by firing something (on its own) that can't cause encirclement, even if it's at the same target.  It's always a case of "I fire this, then I fire this (and sometimes you have to fire a third time), and now you're encircled".  [Note that it is, in unusual circumstances, possible to encircle a unit with a single attack (a large multi-hex FG that hits the target from several directions simultaneously).]

Using the illustration in A7.72 EX:

The 4-6-7 can be encircled if the Russian in U2 attacks first, then is attacked by either S5 firing alone (which would be case a) or by S4 firing and then T4 (second case c).  S4 & T4 can FG, or S5 can FG with either or both of S4 & T4, and all of these options would be encircling attacks.

What would not be an encircling attack is U2 firing first, then T4 firing alone, then S5 firing alone.  U2+T4 cannot encircle by themselves, and T4+S5 cannot encircle by themselves, so firing T4 on its own has interrupted the encircling sequence.

Smart play is to make the first attack the smallest possible attack, and then follow up with a larger encircling shot, as not only does that shot have a better chance of getting a result, the target's morale will be reduced to that attack.  In the EX, you would fire U2 first, and then encircle with S4+S5+T4 FG.  You could do it the other way around, and it would still be an encircling shot, but it would be less effective.

Suppose that there are additional Russian squads in U3 and U4.  In that case, you could FG all of them together, and that would be a case of encirclement with a single attack.

Could someone have a look at this question as well, please?

What exactly is your question?

Encirclement (by fire) occurs when attacks against a single unit/stack are made sequentially (subject to a couple of conditions).

When trying to encircle a unit, you have to make sure that the attacks are made in the correct order, and you can't interrupt the sequence by shooting at something else.  Nor can you interrupt the sequence by firing something (on its own) that can't cause encirclement, even if it's at the same target.  It's always a case of "I fire this, then I fire this (and sometimes you have to fire a third time), and now you're encircled".  [Note that it is, in unusual circumstances, possible to encircle a unit with a single attack (a large multi-hex FG that hits the target from several directions simultaneously).]

Using the illustration in A7.72 EX:

The 4-6-7 can be encircled if the Russian in U2 attacks first, then is attacked by either S5 firing alone (which would be case a) or by S4 firing and then T4 (second case c).  S4 & T4 can FG, or S5 can FG with either or both of S4 & T4, and all of these options would be encircling attacks.

What would not be an encircling attack is U2 firing first, then T4 firing alone, then S5 firing alone.  U2+T4 cannot encircle by themselves, and T4+S5 cannot encircle by themselves, so firing T4 on its own has interrupted the encircling sequence.

Smart play is to make the first attack the smallest possible attack, and then follow up with a larger encircling shot, as not only does that shot have a better chance of getting a result, the target's morale will be reduced to that attack.  In the EX, you would fire U2 first, and then encircle with S4+S5+T4 FG.  You could do it the other way around, and it would still be an encircling shot, but it would be less effective.

Suppose that there are additional Russian squads in U3 and U4.  In that case, you could FG all of them together, and that would be a case of encirclement with a single attack.

title: Bypass during routing
question:
Paragraph 10.5 p. A24 states: Broken units may not use Bypass (4.3).

But then in the example on p. A27 I read: It elects to rout to R3, expending 3 MF via rowhouse bypass at the S3/R3/S4 vertex.

Is this correct? According to the first mentioned rule this is not possible at all.
author: neo.colpaert
consensus_answer:
Infantry in a Rowhouse may move/rout/advance/
Withdraw-from-CC directly into another Rowhouse hex of the same
building only at the ground or Rooftop (23.8) level; if at the ground level they
must specify which side of the building they are “bypassing”. 

Moving at ground level from one Rowhouse to an adjacent Rowhouse is not Bypass movement in the sense that is used in A4.3.  It has some passing similarity with Bypass (mainly that the unit is vulnerable to fire at the Open Ground vertex between the two hexes), which is probably why the Rowhouse rule uses "bypass".

The Rowhouse rule quoted above specifically allows rout using "bypass" of that kind, which strictly speaking is not Bypass.

title: Infantry moving as a stack questions
question:
This came up in my last post where we got it wrong, so now I have a few more questions on how this interaction works when you have two units activated together, but are expending different MFs.

Let's consider the following:
A single hex has a British 4-5-8 and 4-4-7 squad, an unpossessed German MMG and a 1S foxhole.

1) Assuming neither squad is in the foxhole, based on prior forum discussion, if the two squads were activated together and the 4-5-8 wanted to lay smoke in an adjacent open hex, both it and the 4-4-7 would be considered to expend 2 MFs in their current hex, meaning neither could Assault move into the now-smoke filled hex.  Both could move into this hex, however, using their 3rd and 4th MFs.  I think I get this.

2) Now, let's assume that while the 4-5-8 is expending 2 MFs to lay smoke, the 4-4-7 wants to recover the German MMG in its hex (1 MF).  Neither unit is in the foxhole.  I presume this is allowed and occurs while the smoke is being laid by the 4-5-8, along with a "delay" MF.  So the two units are activated as a stack, the 4-5-8 is declared laying smoke and the 4-4-7 is declared as recovering the German MMG. Then both units have 2 MFs remaining.  Correct?

Now ... what happens if the German player wants to use DFF at the activated squads?  Can they fire after only 1 MF is expended because the 4-4-7 is recovering the MMG for 1 MF?  Does this answer change if the 4-4-7 states they are 'delaying' for 1 MF, then expending a MF to recover?  Or does all DFF get resolved after the stack expends the 2 MFs associated with the higher MF cost action (laying smoke in an adjacent hex)?  Would DFF affect only the 4-4-7 or both units if fired at the 1 MF portion of the move versus the 2 MF portion?

3) Now, let's consider the 4-4-7 is in foxhole and the 4-5-8 is outside of it.  They are still considered in the same location for activation, so while the 4-5-8 is laying smoke, the 4-4-7 could be leaving the foxhole (1 MF) and recovering the MMG (2nd MF).  Would DFF be granted against the 4-4-7 after either of these MF expenditures?  Would it affect only the 4-4-7 or both squads?

4) Now, let's consider the 4-4-7 in the foxhole and the 4-5-8 doesn't lay smoke, but attempts to recover the MMG (1 MF) while the 4-4-7 exits the foxhole (1 MF).  Seems like this is easy, as both are activated, both are expending 1 MF, so any DFF on them would affect both units.  But is this allowed? Or would the 4-4-7 have to 'delay' while the 4-5-8 recovers and the 4-5-8 have to 'delay' while the 4-4-7 exits the foxhole?

5) Along a similar vein, but instead of recovering the MMG, the 4-5-8 lays smoke in its own hex.  Don't think this changes anything as the +1 MF is only to enter its location and the 4-4-7 in the foxhole is already /in/ the smoke location (so no need to expend 2 MFs to leave the foxhole).  Correct?

6) Finally, what if the 4-5-8 outside the foxhole just wanted to 'delay' and move to an adjacent hex with the 4-4-7.  In this case, the first MF expenditure is the 4-4-7 leaving the foxhole and the 4-5-8 'delaying', then both units expending additional MFs to move beyond their current hex.  Seems allowed and easy.  DFF after the 1st MF would affect both the 4-4-7 and 4-5-8, correct?
author: kbernatz
consensus_answer:
Seems like everyone feels that if someone in a stack does something costing MFs, the entire stack pays that MF cost and can't do anything else during those lost MFs.

Not everybody, only the people reading the rule incorrectly.  🙂 A4.2 says exactly what you think it says.  The Q&A quoted by Daniel confirms this, although, being a Q&A for 1st ed. ASL, it's irrelevant, because it has already been incorporated into A4.2, i.e., that last sentence, which I'd bet a whole doughnut is not present in the 1st ed. rules (I'm too lazy to drag out my 1st ed. rules to check).

It is just a question of whether the 4-5-8 outside the foxhole would expend a 'delay' MF waiting for his buddy to climb out of the foxhole.

As I think I've said before, you need to be careful with your terminology.  "Delay" in ASL has a specific meaning, and infantry don't do that.  It's just a question of how many MF are expended by the units in the stack.

I think the main reason people are having difficulty with your question is that you're describing a hypothetical situation that will never, ever actually happen in a game.  Not only is there no good reason for those two squads to move as a stack, there are at least half-a-dozen very good reasons why they shouldn't.*  You should tweak your brother's nose and say "don't do that, you're being stupid", and the difficult questions magically go away ....

Concentrating on the purely theoretical nature of the question, though, you're fundamentally correct in your original interpretation.  The two squads are in the same Location and are therefore eligible to move as a stack, despite the colossal idiocy of doing so.  The squad not entering the foxhole is "burning" 2 MF unless they can do something else (like attempt a SMOKE grenade placement).

Note that if there is a Leader present, and you want to use the Leader's bonus 2 MF moving as a stack, being "in the same Location" is not sufficient!  Per A4.12, the units stacked with the Leader must share the same "Wire/entrenchment/Panji/paddy status".

* The fundamental reason for not moving as a stack when you don't have to, of course, is only the currently moving units are affected by First Fire.  The guy in the foxhole might get shot to pieces but his buddy not in the foxhole will be completely unharmed (or vice-versa).  Being attacked by Residual FP might suck, but it will always suck less than being attacked by the FP that placed the Residual!

replies.body: I'm going to let one of the heavy hitters answer your questions ... but I have one for you. Why are you insisting on moving the two units as a stack? I cannot think of any reason, tactically, that you would do such a thing since there is no leader involved. I have also never heard of an "infantry delay" as you mention ... vehicles delay movement points, but I have never heard of any infantry delaying.

Answering first part of your questions.
A stack always spends MF as a whole.
458 places smoke : all units spend 2 MF.
The 447 must enter the foxhole (1 MF) to try retrieve the MMG (1 MF).
Both squads spend that 3rd MF and the 4th MF for the recovery attempt.
Only 1 MF remains, as late Double Time.
Enemy DFF can occur vs the stack on each spent MF.

There is no "delay", as the whole stack expends the MF.

I'm an average (at best) ASL player and I'll chime in here by seconding @albcann question - "why are you insisting on moving the two units as a stack?".  Your opponent can only fire at units that have expended MF performing some action (moving, smoke, etc) during your movement.  If you decide to Assault Move a stack, they can fire at the stack.  However, if you move the squads individually, they have to decide when and if to fire.  

For example, if you Assault Move an entire stack of 3 squads into an adjacent hex, your opponent can Defensive First Fire against the ENTIRE stack (assuming they have LOS and can fire).  But, if you move each squad individually, your opponent has to decide when to fire or not and who to fire at - will he fire at squad 1 or wait to see if squad 2 moves and then what about squad 3?  Remember, once a unit ends its turn and the next move is started, you can't go back to perform an action on/with a previous unit.

My 2 cents for what it's worth.

These are theoretical (other than the first).  My brother wanted to move them as a stack because he was thinking the residual wouldn't benefit from the smoke (but he was thinking I had an MG to lay a fire lane, but I did not).  This is how it all started, lol.  Otherwise, we both agree with you that 99 times out of 100, one would just move them separately.  But that is the beauty of ASL, right ... every once in a blue moon, you'll actually _want_ to use that 1 out of of 100 :).

There are rare times when one would want to avoid a FL residual (which doesn't gain 'soft' DRMs) and move units as a stack, but otherwise I agree that this is definitely a rare occurance.

Regarding Robin's post, that makes the most sense, but how do you interpret the last sentence of A4.2?
Units moving as a stack expend MF simultaneously and need not spend MF for the same purpose, but must designate at the same time all actions for the same MF.

From the other BGG post, the answers seem to imply that the 'need not spend MF for the same purpose' and 'must designate at the same time all actions for the same MF' implied that you could have a stack of units doing both recovery (1 MF) and laying smoke in its own hex (1 MF) at the same time.  Or is this sentence taken to mean that some units can do an action and others don't (my calling this a 'delay' in quotes, because I appreciate there is no official infantry 'delay' rule).

I blame my brother for wanting to move them together, lol.

Seems like everyone feels that if someone in a stack does something costing MFs, the entire stack pays that MF cost and can't do anything else during those lost MFs.  I get this, I do ... but when I read A4.2, I really don't see where it says that.  Need not spend MFs for the same purpose and must designate at the same time all actions for the same MF.  Why does it say 'all actions' and 'not ... for the same purpose' if it isn't allowing stacks to expend MFs on different actions?  E.g. recovery + smoke laying or exiting foxhole + smoke laying?

This is particularly relevant to the foxhole + non-foxhole question (#6) that I posed because the two squads /are/ considered in the same location, so I don't agree with Marti that they aren't allowed to stack.  Units in a foxhole aren't in a separate location except for weapon recovery and TEM (per B27.13).  So for activation purposes they clearly ARE in the same location, so they clearly can stack, IMO.  It is just a question of whether the 4-5-8 outside the foxhole would expend a 'delay' MF waiting for his buddy to climb out of the foxhole.

FWIW, we'll play as you guys are espousing here: stacks (effectively) have to all do the same action and expend the MFs for that action /as a group/ even if some members of the stack can't or won't perform that action.  But I really don't think A4.2 says that...

Would be interested to hear Perry and/or Bruce's take on this.  If they agree, then I'd recommend the rules committee consider rewording that last sentence in A4.2 because (to paraphrase Princess Bride), I don't think it says what you think it says...

I found this: http://www.klasm.com/ASL/ErrataQA/QA/SR%20ASL_QA%20v22.pdf

A4.2 When a stack of units is moving together, can the different units in the stack perform different actions in their hex when simultaneously expending one MF (i.e., one unit attempts SMOKE placement, one unit recovers a SW, one unit places a DC on an ADJACENT target)?
A. Yes, but for each MF expenditure, he must designate all actions at the same time. [An97; Mw]

Damn ... I wrote essentially the exact same thing, but chickened out and deleted it thinking maybe I had missed something, Bruce (obviously) is right, you are concerned with a fringe case that will never happen. I have logged 500+ scenarios and 2500+ hours of (largely mediocre) play, and I have never moved a stack as you describe or seen it done against me. In your example with weapon recovery and smoke placement, you would have each of those units move separately to complete those tasks, not as a stack.

I fully agree that it should almost never happen!  *I* wouldn't have done it, but hey ... he did and we were puzzled on "what the heck do we do now?", lol.

I also understood his logic of /why/ he wanted to do it (even though he was wrong about me having a MG available to establish the FL).  His thought process was: if the 4-4-7 moves with the 4-5-8, it can assault move into the SMOKE and avoid the fire lane ignoring the SMOKE DRM. Now...we were wrong about the 4-4-7 being able to assault move (since it would have to also expend 2 MFs while the 4-5-8 laid smoke) /and/ he was wrong about me having a MG, but I understood the logic of why he wanted to do that crazy thing :).

We thought it was an interesting enough question to ask the gurus.  We certainly learned a few things from these two threads (not surprisingly, more stuff we were doing wrong, lol).

FYI, the example would be a 5 factor MMG at normal range firing at two squads and a leader assault moving into a smoke hex.

If the second squad moved in with the squad laying smoke and the leader, he'd be subject to a 4 +2 attack.

If the smoke laying squad moved first with the leader (assault moving into his just laid smoke), he would be subject to this 4 +2 attack, then the MG would establish a 2 factor FL.  The second squad would now be subject to a 2 +0 attack, which is worse than the 4 +2 (*).

Rare ... yes, but definitely one time when you WOULD want to move both squads together if you wanted to min/max the potential effects on them.

* I'm also not considering the case where the leader might be a -1, -2 or -3 leader, in which case moving the squads together allows that negative DRM to apply to /both/ squads versus only the first squad, as well as situations where you want both squads to not use assault movement and, instead, continue moving after crossing the smoke.

I also understood his logic of /why/ he wanted to do it

I sure don't.  Moving the units correctly (i.e., separately), if the smoke attempt fails, only the smoke-placing unit is in peril.  If the smoke attempt succeeds, both moving units will benefit from it.  Possible FL be damned, there's no good reason to move the units the way he wanted to move them.

If the smoke laying squad moved first with the leader (assault moving into his just laid smoke), he would be subject to this 4 +2 attack, then the MG would establish a 2 factor FL.  The second squad would now be subject to a 2 +0 attack, which is worse than the 4 +2 (*).

Rare ... yes, but definitely one time when you WOULD want to move both squads together if you wanted to min/max the potential effects on them.

No, because the 4+2 would be affecting multiple units.  That's multiple chances for units to pin or break (or trigger a Sniper attack).  It's only the one DR, but it has the potential for catastrophic cumulative failure.

The cumulative possibility that bad things won't happen to everyone is slightly less if you move the units separately, which of course is why you move the units separately.

It seems a "safe enough" decision when a 4+2 or similarly-low odds attack is all you're facing; it's a lot clearer if the initial attack is like, 12+2 or something similarly meaty.  Generally speaking, wherever possible, you want as few moving units facing that first attack as you can manage, because it's the first one that has the most potential to cause pain.  Even when it's a 4+2.

Or to put it another way ... don't move as a stack!  Even if you think you need to!  Especially if you think you need to!  (Unless, of course, you really need to.)

title: More questions from our latest session
question:
Not Hill 621 this time, but the scenario: Putut-en-Bessin 2 from Battle magazine's site.

One of our Hill 621 grogs is on vacation, so my brother and I figured we'd try this scenario as it seemed short and relatively easy for us to pick up.  It is actually quite a fun scenario so far, but we ran into a couple questions that I /think/ we figured out, but wanted to ask to make sure our logic was sound.

1) Squad laying smoke as part of multi-squad hex...can they move together?  E.g. we had a 4-5-8 and a 4-4-7 in the same hex.  My brother wanted to activate both together, have the 4-5-8 attempt to lay smoke in an adjacent hex, then move both squads forward together.  We felt this was definitely possible, but just a question of whether the 4-4-7 would be considered to have spent 2 MFs or not.  We felt that since they did not lay smoke, they would not be considered to have spent those MFs.  The reason was question 2, below.

2) If they can be activated together and move together, then if they are declared as using Assault Movement, are we correct in understanding that when the squad that laid the smoke moves into the clear hex+smoke, they lose their Assault movement benefits, but the 4-4-7 (who would have only spent 2 MFs at this point) would maintain the no FFNAM.  E.g. the 4-5-8 and 4-4-7 are activated together and are stated as using Assault Movement. The 4-5-8 attempts (successfully) to lay smoke in an adjacent clear hex (2 MFs), then both units move into that clear hex (4 MFs total for the 4-5-8, negating its Assault Move, but only 2 MFs for the 4-4-7).  Fire at the two units would be without FFMO (smoke) and only the 4-5-8 would have the additional -1 for FFNAM.  Correct?

3) This SSR gives the British E and 1st line squads a +1 to their smoke number.  We had one of the 1st line squads suffer ELR failure, dropping it from a 4-5-7 (smoke 2+1) to a 4-4-7 (smoke 0).  Would this one squad maintain the +1 smoke (so 0+1 = 1) or would it also lose that when it suffered ELR failure?  We kind of felt it made more sense that it would maintain the +1, but didn't really think the rules supported that.

-K
author: kbernatz
consensus_answer:
#1 - Yes, they can all move together, but the other squads all consume MFs when the first one uses smoke.

I assume you're pointing to A4.2, last sentence?
Units moving as a stack expend MF simultaneously and need not spend MF for the same purpose, but must designate at the same time all actions for the same MF.

E.g. when the 4-5-8 spends MFs 1 and 2 to lay smoke, the 4-4-7 would have to designate how they are expending those MFs.  I.e. either delaying in the hex or moving into the clear hex /before/ the smoke is actually placed.  So if they want to move with the 4-5-8, they would have to delay 2 MFs (as it laid smoke), THEN move into the hex with the 4-5-8 ...  Ok, we did this wrong.

 #2 - Declaring AM is a promise not to change location more than once, and not to use all your available MF. So, once declared you *can't* violate either condition, and you don't 'drop' AM. (Getting under Wire is about the only exception I know of offhand.)

Ahh, I think we missed the last sentence in 4.61 (or at least did not appreciate its full scope).
 Otherwise, once declared, Assault Movement cannot be voluntarily voided.
We were thinking that it applied to the movement of > 1 location only, but I see that it isn't that limiting ... not only does it prohibit you from moving >1 location, but it also prohibits you from expending all your MFs or going CX (exceptions being breaking, going berserk or wire).

Well, we got that wrong.  Don't think it changes much, as my brother could have had the 4-5-8 move first, then moved the 4-4-7 second (would have taken residual fire, but would have still benefited from the smoke DRM).  I think he might have been thinking I might establish a FL, which would have subjected the 4-4-7 to residual w/o the smoke DRM, but I don't think I had any MGs in the right locations to really make a good FL in this situation.  Seems like moving the two units separately was the way to go and we just made things more confusing by trying to move them together, lol.

replies.body: for number 3, what is the wording of the SSR? Having that will give you better results to your query.

#1 - Yes, they can all move together, but the other squads all consume MFs when the first one uses smoke.

#2 - Declaring AM is a promise not to change location more than once, and not to use all your available MF. So, once declared you *can't* violate either condition, and you don't 'drop' AM. (Getting under Wire is about the only exception I know of offhand.)

for number 3, what is the wording of the SSR? Having that will give you better results to your query.

"Canadian units (Elite and First only) have smoke emplacement factor increased by 1."

author: A2SimGamer

title: Fully-tracked woods bog checks
question:
A recent session on VASL which had us looking up what the bog roll was for driving a tank into a woods hex made me think I have played this wrong in the past - not the entering but the exiting. I thought you had to roll for a bog check when exiting as well as when entering (also VCA changes) but my playing partner said no. We didn't chase it up at the time as my tank was happily shooting off 75L rounds having made it's entry bog check.

Looking at the rules afterwards the second sentence under D8.2 BOG which says ‘A vehicle must make a bog check as dictated by the Terrain Chart for entering, or exiting or making any VCA changes in, certain terrain types termed bog hexes’, made me think I was right. I.e. it states the general rule and then directs you to look at the Terrain chart to tell you which are the 'bog' possible terrain types.
 
However the Terrain Chart seems to show that the only time/terrain that you ever have to do a bog check roll for exiting a hex (in a fully-tracked vehicle) is when leaving a stream. This seems an odd way to state the rule - i.e. state a general principle and then detail criteria that it never applies except in a very limited case. 

It also seems to be inconsistent with the 'trail-break' rules in B13.42. A tank that enters a woods hex creates a partial trail-break and then when exiting (without a further bog check apparently) creates a full trail-break across the hex based on which hex sides it entered and exited. However if it only creates a partial 'trail-break' (I am guessing as it reversed out) then although another tank can enter via the partial trail-break without a bog check, when it exits it has to take one, even though the vehicle that originally created the trail-break would not have had to do so.
author: domus_ludorum
consensus_answer:
Correct - exit of a woods hex does not normally entail a Bog Check. You do have to take one if you are in a woods-road hex and on the road and exiting not using the road.

Also, I don't think a partial TB ca be used by another vehicle - only a full TB,  IIRC.

title: OBA - Observer Questions
question:
If we have a 10-3 Leader with a radio stacked with some nice 8-3-8 squads, the following are correct:

(1) If the Leader uses his Leadership DRM (LDRM) to modify DFF by the squads during the enemy MPh, the Leader cannot do OBA/radio actions during the DFPh.

(2) If the Leader does CC Reaction, modifying the CC Reaction roll and CC rolls with his LDRM, likewise - he cannot do OBA/radio actions during the DFPh.

(3) If the Leader does CC Reaction (or directs the fire of the 8-3-8s), but does NOT use his LDRM to modify anything - he still cannot do OBA/radio actions.

(4) If he has in possession two radios (one 80mm, one 100mm), during (for example) a PFPh, he gains contact and places a 100mm SR. During the next DFPh, he converts that to an FFE:1/2. During the next PFPh, as his first 'radio OBA activity' he attempts to gain contact/btty access to the 80mm OBA, placing a AR->SR if successful.  The 100mm FFE:2 will stay where it is and is resolved to become an FFE:C.  This is because he is not voluntarily cancelling the FFE or voluntarily not rolling for contact - he is prohibited from doing so by the rules because he can only operate one radio at a time.  Or is this considered a 'choice', and hence voluntarily not rolling, so the 100mm FFE:2 would be immediately cancelled versus staying in its current hex to be resolved?
author: kbernatz
consensus_answer:
The first three are certainly right. He can fire (/perform CCRF), he can direct fire, or he can use the radio.

4) Note that failing to roll for contact for any reason is only a "voluntary" loss of contact if you do not currently have LOS to the Blast Height of the SR/FFE (see the end of C1.22). So, contact one battery, get a SR down. If your leader can see the blast height, then switching to the other radio next time is involuntary loss of contact. This also applies to, say, not contacting the battery in PFPh so you can move the leader+radio.

Keep in mind that voluntary rout is voluntary loss of contact, even if you could see the blast height (end of C1.6), and not being GO is an immediate loss of contact (though not specified in C1.61, presumably involuntary loss); pinning is fine, but breaking and Melee cause loss of contact.

So, contact one battery, get a SR down. If your leader can see the blast height, then switching to the other radio next time is involuntary loss of contact. title: OBA vs vehicles + Infantry in same hex
question:
I /think/ I know the answers, but just want confirmation...

Per C1.5, each HEX receives its own DR.  So this DR is used both versus the Infantry /and/ any vehicles in the hex, correct?

Example: An 80mm OBA hits a wooden building hex with a BU ht (in bypass) and two squads (in the building).  If the IFT DR result was a colored 3 and a white 2, the players would apply a hull hit against the ht with a IFT result of '3' (-1 for all af <= 4 and -1 for OT) and a '7' IFT result against the squads.  This would mean the ht is eliminated (with chance for crew survival) and the squads would take a 2MC.

Does the crew also take a 2MC due to being OT and subject to OBA??  I think /no/ ... the effect versus the vehicle is either kill or not.  Would this change if the crew was CE, though?

If the crew survives and bails out, are they subject to a separate IFT roll or same IFT roll?  I think they get hit by a separate IFT roll that only affects them, as they are becoming more vulnerable within the OBA hex.

 What if the hex was open ground, the ht was a fully armored AFV with no DRMs for OBA, and the original IFT roll was a '3' (1KIA)?  Would one use random selection to determine which of the AFV, squad 1, squad 2 suffers the KIA?  I think 'yes', right?
author: kbernatz
consensus_answer:
1. Use the same DR vs all Vulnerable targets in the hex (C3.33).

2. A BU OT ht Crew is not Vulnerable except per D5.311 (Air Bursts or elevation advantage). A CE OT ht Crew is Vulnerable and would be attacked with the same DR if its vehicle was not outright destroyed (D.8).

3. Only Riders Bail Out (by being forced to leave its AFV other then by the destruction of their AFV). When an AFV is destroyed, PRC roll for Survival. Surviving PRC are not subject to any Collateral Attack from the shot that destroyed their vehicle (D5.6). If units in a FFE change position and become more vulnerable, they are attacked by the FFE with a new resolution DR each time (C1.51).

4. Use RS among all units sharing the same result, with possible ties affecting more units (A7.301).

title: Clarifications/questions from our last session
question:
Playing Hill 621 and getting our feet wet with OBA.

I /think/ we did everything correctly, but wanted to run the following things past the powers_that_be and see if we screwed anything up.

Soviet turn 2, during DPh the GE leader manning the radio rolls for battery contact (succeeds), then draws a chit (black).  So they place an AR on a hex with lots of Soviets nearby, where they can see both the ground level of the hex and many of the Soviets.  A '1' is rolled for accuracy, so we replace the AR with an SR and that ends the DPh for the Leader+Radio.

Correct?

The Leader survives all Advancing Fire and during the German turn 3 Prep Fire Phase rolls to maintain battery contact (+1 due to Bttn MORs), succeeding.  They then declare that they are correcting the SR 1 hex and converting to FFE.  We place a red AR in the corrected hex and roll for accuracy (a 2, so accurate).  We immediately place a FFE:1 in the hex and resolve a 16 factor attack on all seven hexes (woods being at -1 DRM; grain and open at +0 DRM).  We roll a KIA on a grain hex, so make a Kindling roll needing >10 (EC = no DRM).  After resolving the FFE:1, we leave it as a FFE:1 and that ends the Leader+Radio's Prep Fire.

Correct?

During Soviet DPh during the German MPh, a sniper wounds the Leader with the radio.  Since only a light wound, this has no impact on battery access, etc.  Correct?

During the GE MPh, we have a ht w/ a loaded 75L AT Gun on a lvl3 hex.  The crew, previously broken and now rallied, is 4 MFs away.  We move the crew to the ht hex, where it is fired on at a net +1 (+1 for height advantage, +1 for the ht Hindrance, -1 for FFNAM).  It survives all the fire against it.  We then have the ht start its movement by attempting to lay smoke grenades (fails), which costs it 0 MPs.  It then expends 8 MPs to unhook (C10.12) the gun. This appears to be valid even though the crew used its entire 4 MFs to move to this hex, as nothing in C10.111 talks about the crew needing to expend MFs ... only that the towing vehicle expends 1/2 its MP allotment (8 MPs for the ht).  The ht/crew/gun all survive fire and the gun is now allowed to be placed unhooked at any CA in this hex.

Can it fire during the AFPH?  If 'yes', does it have any DRMs associated with it (given that it never moved to a new hex ... the ht and gun began the MPH stopped in that hex)?  I think the answer is "Yes, it can fire ... and 'only Case B, +2 DRM' to its fire".  Correct?

During the German MPh, a HMG manned by a squad needed to Dash across a Road to avoid the oncoming Soviet horde.  This cost 3 MFs (road + forest), which was the exact amount the squad has (4 PP HMG). If Smoke has been laid in the road hex, he could have still Dashed ... but would have had to declare CX at the start of the move.  Correct?
author: kbernatz
consensus_answer:
This is a place where the rules could use a rewrite, since its apparent that C10.1 expects you'll always have the crew for the gun inside the vehicle that's towing it. Note that all the references to 'crew' in C10.1 and subsections are Infantry (or Passenger) crew, not Inherent vehicle crew (well... maybe if you've got a Bren carrier towing something...). So, normally, the ht would go along, stop, and unload+unhook, with the Gun crew taking possession of the Gun, who would become TI (C10.12). As usual with loading/unloading procedures, the crew would be expending MF as part of the ht's MPh. 

So... without riding in the vehicle, most likely, the (future) Gun crew would have to start in the hex, the ht comes up, unhooks, the crew goes TI (forgoing its normal MPh) and gets possession of the Gun (and there needs to be a crew for the Gun to unhook). (See here)

And since the crew will be TI, no it can't fire in AFPh (since TI prohibits fire).

We missed the TI part, agree completely on that.  Not sure I agree with the argument for the crew moving.  One of the reasons is that C10.11 explicitly mentions movement wrt hooking up the Gun
10.11 HOOKING UP: A Stopped vehicle not in Bypass may hook up a 
Gun (if the vehicle’s T# ≤ the Gun’s M#) by spending half (FRU) of its 
MP/MF allotment [EXC: if the Gun’s M# is circled (e.g., M 6 ), the vehi-
cle must expend two-thirds (FRU) of its MP/MF allotment] in that Gun’s 
hex (in addition to any required MP/MF cost to enter the hex), provided a 
crew (as per 10.111) is on foot in that hex. This expenditure does not itself 
qualify that vehicle as a moving target, but does allow Defensive First Fire 
opportunities against it (that Gun shares its target status and is destroyed 
or missed depending on the fate of the vehicle). That Gun is then placed on 
top of that vehicle to indicate that it is in tow. Neither that Gun, its crew, nor 
that vehicle/its PRC can fire during that PFPh/MPh and all are TI for the 
rest of that Player Turn. That crew may also load into that towing vehicle 
at no extra MP/MF cost as it hooks up that Gun, but if it expends > half 
its MF allotment in pushing/entering that Gun’s hex, that Gun cannot then 
be hooked up by that unit in that MPh. A non-QSU Gun (10.23) must first 
be limbered (10.21) before it can be hooked up. See 10.31 for pushing and 
hooking up a Gun in the same MPh.  (emphasis added)

But C10.12 has absolutely no similar mention...
10.12 UNHOOKING: A Stopped vehicle not in Bypass may unhook a 
Gun only by spending half (FRU) of its MP/MF allotment [EXC: if the 
Gun’s M# is circled (e.g., M 6 ), the vehicle must expend two-thirds (FRU) 
of its MP/MF allotment] under the otherwise same conditions as were 
necessary for hooking up (10.11). That Gun’s crew may disembark from 
that vehicle at no extra MP/MF cost as part of that unhooking procedure, 
but that crew and Gun must remain TI in that hex [EXC: that vehicle may 
expend its remaining MP/MF]. After being unhooked, certain Guns must 
still be unlimbered (10.21) before they can be fired. Neither the crew nor 
the vehicle/PRC may fire during that PFPh/MPh prior to unhooking. A 
Gun’s CA may be changed simultaneously as it is (un)hooked.

This made us feel that the omission of that language was intentional and that a crew could move TO the vehicles hex and assist in unhooking the gun, provided the ht can expend the requisite MPs.

-K

Ahh... ok, so in our PFPh we convert the SR into an FFE:1 by placing the AR, rolling for accuracy, placing the SR (temporarily) in the hex and - if the conditions of 1.333 are met - then replace the SR with an FFE:1 and resolve the effects.  We then immediately flip it to its FFE:2 side and we'll resolve the FFE:2 during the Soviet DPh of the next turn (unless cancelled).

After resolving the FFE:2, I presume we flip to an FFE:C ... which will only effect people who advance into the hexes, as it will be removed at the start of our next PFPh.  Correct?
That would be correct.

a crew could move TO the vehicles hex and assist in unhooking the gun, provided the ht can expend the requisite MPs.

I agree.

It's important to remember that it's the crew (i.e., the infantry that have possession of the gun when hooking up, or will have possession of the gun when unhooking) that drives the procedure.  The vehicle expends MP as the crew expends MF to perform the task.  If it turns out that the vehicle has insufficient MP available, then the task can't be performed, but otherwise it's all about what that crew is doing.

Thanks all.  The crew/unhooking thing took us quite a bit of time trying to parse the rules ... so I do tend to agree with James that perhaps those sections could be made a bit clearer for situations where the crew is not also a passenger of the vehicle (either in our situation or one where the vehicle simple doesn't have the PP to tow the gun /and/ carry the crew, so the crew has to go in a separate vehicle)

title: Scrounging
question:
What is meant by this?
"Such arms cannot be given voluntarily by a manned AFV."
Scrounging is always in an empty vehicle/wreck, I thought?

And for what do you have to throw the dr? 
For small arms and SW's or only for SW's? 
And 1-3 means no scrounging on 4-6?

"To scrounge anything of value, a 1-3 dr (Δ) is necessary. The dr also doubles as the number of SW that may be scrounged (selected randomly) if more than one exists."
author: neo.colpaert
consensus_answer:
An AFV can’t voluntarily offload its MG/MA, unless allowed by the vehicle notes.

Scrounging is only successful on a dr of 1 to 3, roll 4 to 6 and the vehicle is not scrounged but still marked as scrounged. The scrounger receives 1-3 MG, depending on the dr.

replies.body:
An AFV can’t voluntarily offload its MG/MA, unless allowed by the vehicle notes.

Scrounging is only successful on a dr of 1 to 3, roll 4 to 6 and the vehicle is not scrounged but still marked as scrounged. The scrounger receives 1-3 MG, depending on the dr.
Right, 1-3 but limited by how many MGs the AFV actually has.

author: rhunter1148

The .50 cal has a ROF of 3, which is the best ROF level in ASL.
The German MG variants of the MG40 and MG42 have : LMG ROF 1 ; MMG ROF 2 ; HMG ROF 3.

Possibly somebody tried to argue during playtesting that as a MTR the normal vehicular DRM would not apply?

title: When do you get Gunshield DRM (or 'what is a manning crew')
question:
So we had this come up in our current game of Hill 621 as the GE crew was unloading from the HT to set up the 75L AT gun.

Two Soviet MMGs had long range (exactly 16 hexes) fire at the crew and while the crew had Height Advantage, we weren't sure if they could (instead) claim the +2 Gun Shield TEM?

They were unhooking the gun and not in position to fire the gun...so does that qualify them as 'manning crew' per the Gun Shield rule (C11.5)?  Ultimately, we ruled 'no' and a IFT roll of '5' against them broke them regardless of whether it would have been a +1 or +2 DRM, but we did want to ask to know for the future.

Questions were:
1) Is there a definition of 'manning crew' for the purpose of Guns?

2) Do crews/squads unhooking a gun gain the Gun Shield DRM?

3) Do crews/squads PUSHING a gun gain the Gun Shield DRM (even though this is treated as Hazardous movement, nothing in the Hazardous Movement rules talk about not gaining a Gunshield DRM if the fire came through that CA).
author: kbernatz
consensus_answer:
Two Soviet MMGs had long range (exactly 16 hexes) fire at the crew and while the crew had Height Advantage, we weren't sure if they could (instead) claim the +2 Gun Shield TEM?

Gunshield is a DRM, not a TEM.

They were unhooking the gun and not in position to fire the gun...so does that qualify them as 'manning crew' per the Gun Shield rule (C11.5)?

No, they are not "manning the gun" until they have finished unloading/unhooking.  While they are in the act of unloading/unhooking they are just moving.

11.5 GUNSHIELDS: ... Infantry moving to a Gun or pushing it while being attacked by Defensive First Fire is not entitled to any protective DRM from its gunshield ... 

The "to a Gun" phrase above is effectively redundant.

 1) Is there a definition of 'manning crew' for the purpose of Guns?

Not in the rules that I know of, but it's pretty clearly covered by common sense.  What is a manning crew?  It's a unit that possesses the gun.  A unit that doesn't possess the gun clearly isn't manning it.  (The EXC would be in the case of 2 SMC combining to operate the weapon per A21.13; only one of the SMC can possess the gun, but the two SMC together would be the "manning crew".)

2) Do crews/squads unhooking a gun gain the Gun Shield DRM?

No, as above.  A squad (or HS, or any number of SMC) in any case will never qualify for the gunshield DRM -- only crews qualify.

3) Do crews/squads PUSHING a gun gain the Gun Shield DRM (even though this is treated as Hazardous movement, nothing in the Hazardous Movement rules talk about not gaining a Gunshield DRM if the fire came through that CA).

No.  This is stated explicitly in C11.5, as above.

Not explicitly, but by implication it is a crew (as opposed to a squad or half squad) possessing the gun.

Not clear to me after re-reading a couple rules.  I await Klas on this one.

title: A Bridge too Far ASL game rule question
question:
In the A Bridge too far, CG1 game, there is a second night turn, 18N. If both the British & the German players select an attack chit then a dual assault develops.

Since there is nothing in the rules to cover this, I would assume both sides setup under the rules as attackers (cloaking etc) and there is no scenario defender.

Thoughts?
author: rhunter1148
consensus_answer: Why do you say "there is nothing in the rules to cover this"?  R9.62133 specifically tells you to look at CG24, which in turn specifically tells you that "the side(s) selecting the Attack chit in a night scenario is considered the Scenario Attacker (E1.4; ...)".  Note the plural; they've already taken into account the possibility of a Dual Attack.  The rule then goes on in some detail about how to treat this; you can ignore everything referring to the Scenario Defender, because there isn't one.

title: OBA question
question:
There are lots of resources out there which help with this (OBA) and I /think/ I mostly understand the rules ... but one thing confuses me that I can't seem to find an answer for.

Looking at C1.332 it has the exception that "if the requirements of 1.333 are not met at this time", with C1.333 basically talking about the need for a Known enemy unit to be in the blast area (paraphrased).

Does that mean that C1.332 is saying that when one corrects + converts a SR to a FFE:1 during the same phase, it only converts to the FFE:1 if (after correction) there is at least one Known enemy unit in or adjacent to the SR's hex (assuming LOS exists between observer and SR hex/Blast height)?

So correcting an SR with a pre-designation that it will become an FFE:1 carries some 'insurance' that if the correction sends it exclusively over friendly units or to a location where there are NO friendly or Known enemy units, it won't convert to FFE:1?  But if the correction places it over at least one Known enemy unit (even if friendlies are in the blast area), it will convert?

This seems to contradict some of the things I've read, that if you choose the "SR -to- FFE:1 conversion" it converts to a FFE:1 no matter where it lands (good or bad).
author: kbernatz
consensus_answer:
So correcting an SR with a pre-designation that it will become an FFE:1 carries some 'insurance' that if the correction sends it exclusively over friendly units or to a location where there are NO friendly or Known enemy units, it won't convert to FFE:1?
It depends - if you see the Base Level of where the SR lands, it will be converted - so the "insurance" does cover all cases...

1.333 If he currently has a LOS to the Base Level of the SR’s hex, or to its Blast Height and any non-Aerial Location in/adjacent-to the SR’s hex that contains a Known (to him) enemy unit, he may Convert that SR to a FFE:1 and leave it in that hex for resolution; or,

If either (or both) of the red or blue text is fulfilled, then the SR is converted to a FFE:1.
