title: Questions from our last session
question:
In no particular order:

(1) Can a MOR can go back and forth between spotted and non-spotted fire in same phase.  E.g. first shot during enemy MPh was with a spotter; kept ROF; later in same MPh, a unit moved into its LOS (but not the Spotters), can the MOR fire at it?  We ruled 'yes', that the Spotter rules say /may fire/ and not /must fire/; e.g. Spotters merely add to what the Mortar can fire at versus changing its possible targets to a different subset.

(2) Does a stunned vehicle lose its acquisition? We ruled 'yes', but since vehicle died shortly thereafter was a moot point.

(3) Does an OT vehicle lose its acquisition if it goes BU? We rules 'no', but - as above - vehicle died shortly thereafter so was moot to us

(4) If a unit has to rout (e.g. starts adj to enemy) and the nearest building is 6 MFs away, with an orchard adjacent THEN a road/open ground hex that is subject to interdiction by enemy units, can the routing unit stop in the orchard hex (only expending 1 MF) or must they move through the open ground (road) to reach the building?  Alternatively, can they declare a low crawl to the adjacent orchard hex even if their initial hex wasn't open ground and that orchard would not be subject to any interdiction? We ruled that the Low Crawl rules never state that one can only do this to avoid Interdiction or only in Open Ground hexes, so a Rout of 1 hex by using Low Crawl to the adjacent orchard was considered valid ... but we were not sure because it kind of goes against the spirit of "must use all MFs to get to the nearest building/woods" and "routing units are not in the control of the player".

(5) GE Player turn.  They move a CE ht up adjacent to a broken US unit and stops. The US unit goes DM (adjacent, Known armed enemy) and must Rout during the Rout Phase.  Can the ht interdict the Routing unit if it moves to a non-adjacent, Open Ground hex?  Or is the ht considered to still be a "Moving" vehicle, and hence subject to half FP, which prevents it from Interdicting?  We ruled that it could NOT interdict, but the only rules we found talked about the ht still being a moving /TARGET/ for the rest of the player turn, not that it was consider a moving vehicle, per se, for Interdiction purposes.  E.g. a moving vehicle becomes a +1 Hindrance after the AFPh; i.e. is no longer "moving", per se, but there is nothing in the Interdiction rules or (from what we could find) vehicle movement rules that clarify when a stopped vehicle is truly considered 'stopped'.  We think we are correct given that the "moving target" language does say entire Player Turn ... but wasn't sure if there was something more explicit that we missed...
author: kbernatz
consensus_answer:
(2), (3): Neither becoming stunned nor becoming BU is on the list of things that lead to loss of acquisition in C6.5.
(4): In theory, you can low crawl even if you wouldn't be subject to interdiction. But in your example, if a known enemy unit is ADJACENT your unit might have to surrender instead if there's no legal rout path without interdiction or using low crawl. A20.21
(5): If you spend a stop MP, your FP isn't halved for Motion Fire any more, D2.42. Being fired upon and firing yourself is treated differently.

(5): If you spend a stop MP, your FP isn't halved for Motion Fire any more, D2.42. Being fired upon and firing yourself is treated differently.

Can a MOR can go back and forth between spotted and non-spotted fire in same phase.

Please, MTR, not MOR. 🙂 Yes.

Does a stunned vehicle lose its acquisition?

Yes, but you have to dig a bit to find the reason: a stunned vehicle is not Good Order (per the Index) and you lose acquisition when you are no longer Good Order (C6.5).

Does an OT vehicle lose its acquisition if it goes BU?

No, because it's not one of the reasons listed in C6.5 that causes acquisition loss.  (Of course, unless the Gun is bow-mounted, it won't be able to fire until it goes CE again, which won't be until the next friendly APh at the earliest, and possibly not until the next friendly MPh.)

If a unit has to rout (e.g. starts adj to enemy) and the nearest building is 6 MFs away, with an orchard adjacent THEN a road/open ground hex that is subject to interdiction by enemy units, can the routing unit stop in the orchard hex (only expending 1 MF)

Only by declaring Low Crawl.  In the absence of Low Crawl, if you can reach your rout destination, then you must do so (EXC: the presence of entrenchments can be used to "slow down" the rout safely).

or must they move through the open ground (road) to reach the building?

The answer is "maybe".  While you must reach your declared rout destination if you don't Low Crawl, you don't have to take the shortest route.  If a safe route is available you can use it.

Alternatively, can they declare a low crawl to the adjacent orchard hex even if their initial hex wasn't open ground and that orchard would not be subject to any interdiction?

Low Crawl is always allowed unless routing a single hex still leaves you ADJACENT to an enemy unit that you must rout from.

"must use all MFs to get to the nearest building/woods"

???

"routing units are not in the control of the player".

Eh, kind of.  Sometimes there are no choices, and sometimes there are.

GE Player turn.  They move a CE ht up adjacent to a broken US unit and stops. The US unit goes DM (adjacent, Known armed enemy) and must Rout during the Rout Phase.  Can the ht interdict the Routing unit if it moves to a non-adjacent, Open Ground hex?

As long as there's a weapon available not subject to any positive DRM, sure.

Or is the ht considered to still be a "Moving" vehicle, and hence subject to half FP, which prevents it from Interdicting?

Only if it's actually in Motion (and you stated above that it is not).  Post the AFPh, "moved" status is no longer meaningful for any purpose.

(2) Use their full MPs to move towards the destination building/woods hex.

You're still parsing it wrong.  The routing unit is not required to use its "full" anything.  A routing unit has 6 MF available.  (3 MF if it's a wounded leader.)  Available is not the same as must expend, so if you don't phrase it that way, you're less likely to make a mistake.

Incidentally, in case anyone's wondering, there is no routing equivalent of "minimum move".  If 6 MF isn't enough to get you into the next hex, then too bad.  (E.G., hex 50P2 to P3 costs 8 MF.)

If they use Low Crawl, they still need to 'follow the shortest path in MF' per A10.51, correct?

The "shortest path" phrasing is only used to determine the destination, not the route.  You determine the destination before you determine the route.  A unit using Low Crawl does not need to move closer to the destination, it merely needs to not move away from it*.  It must otherwise abide by the usual routing rules (e.g., not move closer to a Known armed enemy unit, etc.).

(* A change by errata from the original rules.  Once upon a time, a Low Crawl was required to move closer to the destination.)

Ok.  I agree that they don't need to use their full 6 MFs; e.g. if the destination is only 2 hexes away with each hex only costing 2 MFs, then they would only spend 4 MFs, reach their destination and then stop.  Still confused a bit on how much control a player has on a routing unit, so let's see if an example won't help see if I've got this straight.

Example: Unit is broken and must rout.  There is a building 2 hexes away with grain hexes surrounding the building (or SMOKE, etc. ... some sort of hindrance to make those hexes non-Open Ground).

(2) The routing unit could NOT move one hex, then 'slide' sideways another grain hex (maybe to put the building between it and the 30 FP stack, etc.) and then end its Rout. If this assumption isn't true, then can someone explain what the "must attempt to reach it" language in A10.51 is interpreted to mean?

(3) The routing unit could not (???  or could ???) move one hex, then slide sideways additional hexes such that they are obeying all Rout movement rules (i.e. not moving towards a known enemy unit, not moving further away from the destination, etc.) until they use up all but 1.5 MFs, meaning they would have insufficient MFs to enter the destination building.  My best 'guess' would be that this should not be allowed because of the 'must attempt to reach it' language in A10.51; i.e. once they are adjacent to the destination building, if they have 2 MFs left they NEED to enter the building during that Rout Phase.

The routing unit has no other building/woods and must designate this building as its destination. Again, based on the A10.51 "must attempt to reach" language.

We interpret it as meaning that the Routing unit has to enter the destination Location during that Rout Phase if there is a path between it and the destination that is 6 MFs or less (exception being if the path is 6 MFs considering moving through Open Ground versus Shellholes, Entrenchments, etc.). There is a side remark, though, where I would believe that you might be wrong.

Sure, but since in my answer I said the Gun won't be able to fire, where exactly is my error?  Nor will MGs or FTs have acquisition counters in place, and my answer was obviously in that context.

I misread you. Sorry.
I don't understand the "unless the Gun is bow mounted" : do you mean that there is an exception for a BU OT AFV when it comes to a bow mounted Gun?

(1) The routing unit could declare a Low Crawl and only rout 1 hex, perhaps this hex is in a blind hex from the 30 FP attack, etc., provided it was not ending the Rout phase adjacent a Known enemy unit and following all other Rout rules.

Right.

(2) The routing unit could NOT move one hex, then 'slide' sideways another grain hex (maybe to put the building between it and the 30 FP stack, etc.) and then end its Rout.  This is because A10.51 has the 'must attempt to reach it' language.

Right.  You can't just arbitrarily stop your rout wherever you like.  You either Low Crawl or you go as far as you can towards your destination -- no half-way measures.

(3) The routing unit could not (???  or could ???) move one hex, then slide sideways additional hexes such that they are obeying all Rout movement rules (i.e. not moving towards a known enemy unit, not moving further away from the destination, etc.) until they use up all but 1.5 MFs, meaning they would have insufficient MFs to enter the destination building.

This is exactly the same situation as (2), and is illegal for exactly the same reasons.  You cannot just arbitrarily stop the rout wherever it's convenient.  You pick a destination and that's where you're going.

(4) If the building was 2 hexes away, but an enemy unit was adjacent to the routing unit's hex and the hex between the routing unit and the building, would this still be a valid destination building?  The unit couldn't go directly to the building (since that would mean moving from one adjacent hex to another of the same known enemy unit), but they might be able to reach the building via a convoluted path.  I think the answer would be: "Maybe ... in that one would have to calculate the path to reach it to see if there was another building/woods that could be reached by expending less MFs" ... correct?  Assuming, obviously, that the unit wouldn't have to move closer to a known enemy unit to reach the destination building, etc.

Right.

(5) Let's say the building was 3 hexes away from the routing unit and all the hexes adjacent the building were Open Ground. The routing unit has no other building/woods and must designate this building as its destination.  It could Low Crawl one hex or, if it didn't declare Low Crawl, wouldn't it have to move through the Open Ground and into the building (assuming the first hex entered cost 3 or less MFs)?  Again, based on the A10.51 "must attempt to reach" language.

Right.  In that situation "Surrender via RtPh" is a real possibility (assuming that the enemy unit forcing the rout is ADJACENT to the broken unit), unless it's been made NA due to No Quarter or other reasons.

Our confusion seems to all come down to this one phrase and what it means.  We interpret it as meaning that the Routing unit has to enter the destination Location during that Rout Phase if there is a path between it and the destination that is 6 MFs or less (exception being if the path is 6 MFs considering moving through Open Ground versus Shellholes, Entrenchments, etc.).

Right.  There's really nothing complicated about it.  Step 1 -- pick the destination (shortest route in MF).  Step 2 -- either Low Crawl, or go there (by whatever route is safest).

It can't voluntarily stop before entering the destination unless it declared Low Crawl, was pinned, or used up all its MPs moving to the location due to entering shellholes/entrenchments, etc.

Right.  (NB: Personnel expend MF.  Only vehicles expend MP.)

The question about "how much choice does the routing unit have" comes down to the interaction of "destination" and "route".  If you have several equally valid possible destinations, then generally you will choose the one most beneficial to you (i.e., you the player -- not necessarily particularly beneficial to the routing unit).  As an extreme example, if you're prepared to have the routing unit eliminated in exchange for giving up some valuable info, you can sometimes choose to enter a Location containing a concealed enemy unit (or a hex you're sure contains a HIP enemy unit) and thereby force that unit to give up its "?"/HIP status.

title: ASL concepts - Halftracks
question:
edit(1): replaced "HT" with 'ht' to be correct with ASLRB abbreviations
edit(2): updated per corrections below, in bold+italics 

Not really a 'how to use them' post (though I certainly welcome comments to that effect), but more a summary of how we understand Halftracks (hts) to make sure we are getting those rules correct (can't think about /how/ to use something if we don't actually understand the underlying rules on them first!).

The following will be predicated on the GE SPW 251/1 ht

In no particular order, what understand about hts are:
* armored  hts are AFVs because they are armored. If unarmored, they are NOT AFVs.

* As AFVs, they have smoke grenades (D13.35). If BU, the placement roll is a '1'; otherwise it is a '2'.

* A Passenger can remove the MG as they dismount (D6.631) if the vehicle notes allow it, or the crew can while abandoning, which is a MG of the same or less factors (so a LMG in the case of the SPW 251/1). This costs no additional MPs/MFs.  Scrounging of the MG from a non-burning Wreck can also be done, but is always a LMG (D10.52).

* hts can be part of a FG if using non-FT, non-IFE, non-ordnance (D6.64).  Hatten in Flames modifies this slightly, FWIW, to allow the GE IFE hts to also form FGs.

* CE Passengers in a ht can form a FG with other CE Passengers or Infantry/Cavalry (D6.64)

* CE Infantry Leaders may apply their Leadership DRM to a FG including the ht and Passengers, but cannot modify the hts fire if fired alone. This includes an OVR if the Passengers participate (D6.65). A Leader must have LOS to the target to direct fire and cannot aid other units in the hex if the ht has entered a new hex/hexside or is in Motion. This implies that if a FG is formed between units in a Motion ht and other Infantry in the same hex, no Leadership applies unless the other units also have the same or better Leader.

* A CE Armor Leader in a ht may apply their Leadership as above, but cannot modify the /Passenger/ fire if the Passengers fire alone.

* Up to 4 SMC can be carried at 0 PP (D6.1).

* BU Passengers are immune to small arms fire unless the target has height advantage greater than range to ht or if subject to TPBF in the same hex as the firer, regardless of elevation difference. Excessive height advantage can reduce the +2 CE DRM to less. Most likely scenarios are: Lvl 1 at adjacent ht = no fire (1 vs 1).  Lvl 2 at adjacent ht = fire at +2 DRM (2 vs 1). Lvl 1 at same hex ht = Fire at +2 DRM.  Lvl 2 at same hex ht = Fire at +1 DRM.

* ht Passengers are halved in FP for movement, but not just for being Mounted (D6.63).

* Non-vehicle MGs can attempt to kill a ht via a To Hit procedure and a '4' TK#.  It can be Stunned even if BU this way (A9.61). Vehicle MGs that are Main Armaments can also do this, but non-MA vehicle MGs may not (D3.54).  This *IS* modified by the Case D to kill per the example in C7.24.

* Armored Assault (D9.31) is a way to move infantry and vehicles simultaneously AND provide the +1 TEM of the vehicle to these infantry even though the ht was moving.  The ht does /not/ need to end in the same hex as the infantry, but can move no further than what those infantry /could/ have moved (assuming, presumably, CX and/or leadership).  The ht movement is done as if the infantry were accompanying it, even if they got broken, pinned, stopped moving, etc.

* hts are /tracked/ vehicles, along with Fully Tracked.  This is important for some ECs/terrain/weather conditions; e.g. Ground Snow affects "untracked" vehicles, which is not explicitly defined in the rules, but seems intuitively to mean: non-half tracked or non-fully tracked (exception being sledges).  But hts have their own MP costs versus Fully Tracked and cannot enter buildings, etc.

* Apparently throwing a DC from a moving ht is a 'nirvana-esque' ASL experience that is on everyone's bucket list...  We don't really know the 'hows' and 'whys' to perform this task, though...

* hts are excellent for VBM "Freeze" (VBF) if one does not care if the ht will have a high risk of dying - the concept of getting a Motion ht into someone's hex to prevent them from being able to fire outside their hex (A7.211 and A7.212).  This also breaks any FL originating from that hex. hts VBF all elevations in its hex even if BU, because they are either in their Location (ground level) or are subject to being attacked with TPBF (higher elevations).

* Passengers can embark for 1 MF and 1/4 MPs of the ht (4 for the SPW 251/1). Passengers can debark a Stopped ht for the same.  Passengers lose 1 MF for every 1/4 MPs (4 MPs for SPW 251/1) spent.

* hts, being AFVs, provide a +1 TEM versus FLs /if/ they were/are not moving/Motion (D9.3; D9.4).

* hts can tow guns if marked with a T#.

* hts are Known, armed enemy units, so can dictate enemy Rout paths even if BU.

* Broken units IN a ht are safe from needing to Rout (even if ADJACENT or same hex) or Failure to Rout

* hts can be used to provide a place for units to Rout under them per D6.1 (though if ADJACENT, those units would still have to continue routing is our interpretation).

* A CE ht can also interdict (A10.53), provided it is not in Motion or subject to any other DRM/halving (A10.532).

-----
I think that is pretty much everything re: hts.  Let us know if we missed anything or if there are key uses that hts are valuable for.

title: CC Reaction walkthrough/questions
question:
We had a couple situations last session where we felt CC Reaction came into play, but weren't 100% certain if we did things correct.  So let me describe the situation and how we resolved it and people can correct what we did wrong...

Hatten in Flames scenario 2: Bertoldo the Brave.  GE Turn 3 MPh.  A BU AAMG HT starts up and moves towards a building with some US squads at ground lvl with a MMG and a US squad on lvl 1 with a MMG.  There are two leaders at ground lvl (8-0 and a 9-1).  (situation due to the 8-0 and the MMG squad having to rout to this building and then rallying during the Rally phase of turn 3).

The MMGs had fired at other units earlier in the turn (both losing ROF), but the squad on the 1st lvl and a separate 6-6-6 and the 8-0 leader on the ground lvl had yet to fire).  As the HT moves towards their hex, /if/ the MMGs had not already fired (or if they had kept ROF and the HT was in their CA), they could have tried to fire at it as a To Hit roll, perhaps establishing a FL with the ground lvl MMG.  But since they had already fired, they could not affect the HT so it moved into their hex.

Had the HT entered their hex from a road with a building on one of the other sides, we could have declared a Street Fighting CC Reaction, but they entered from a non-road hex.  So we could not CC Reaction them in the adjacent hex, nor did we have any LATW to Non-CC Reaction or DFF them in the adjacent hex.  So the HT enters their hex and declares bypass and remains in Motion.  They do NOT declare an Overrun.

We then allowed the ground floor squad and 8-0 leader (both not marked with any First or Final Fire markers) to attempt CC Reaction.  The squad succeeded in its PAATC roll and the Leader does not need to make one.  We immediately resolved the CC attack against the HT, rolling a '7' and missing a result by one :(.

A second HT then did the same thing to another building hex manned by a HMG.  The HMG proceeded to roll an '11' on its TH roll, failing miserably to kill the HT as it moved up, but the squad was not marked DFF (only the HMG).  Since there were still two Panthers that had yet to move, the adjacent M18 held its fire and the HT entered the HMGs hex (with a 9-1 leader and a 5-4-6 squad).  They declared CC Reaction, which was allowed as the provision against doing so with SWs marked First Fire is only if attempting Street Fighting.  We resolved the CC and rolled another '7', but this time we felt it was an Immobilization on the HT given the -1 leadership DRM (5 CCV for squad +1 CCV for leader -2 drm for OT vehicle +2 drm for motion -1 drm for leadership).

The biggest questions we had were:
1) Reaction Fire is only vs vehicles in YOUR hex, unless you are doing Street Fighting, correct?  This is even with Non-CC Reaction Fire (i.e. LATW or a Gun).  If we had a bazooka, we could have just used regular DFF against the HT in an adjacent hex.

2) Is Reaction Fire even allowed against a BYPASSING vehicle?  Or is Reaction Fire only allowed vs Overrunning vehicles?

3) In both our situations, the squads are marked CC (as the vehicle did not die).  Come the CCPh, is there /another/ round of CC between the vehicle and the squad?

4) We were correct in that the vehicle does NOT get to CC back against the squads during CC Reaction, right?

5) If the vehicle and squads were to CC each other, would a BU HT with only a 4 AAMG be able to attack the squad in CC at all?  If it was CE, it would have 4 factors to attack with, correct?  If it was CE and in Motion, would it still have 4 or would it have 2 factors due to halving for Motion?
author: kbernatz
consensus_answer:
1: Yes. Note that Non-CC Reaction Fire can only be used vs an OVR (D7.2); otherwise it's normal First/Final Fire procedures.

2: A vehicle bypassing your hex is in your hex, even if its not in the obstacle portion of that hex. As above though, you can only use CC RF vs a non-overrunning vehicle (note that a vehicle can enter the obstacle, and still not OVR).

3: Yes

4: Correct, it needs to OVR or use Bounding First Fire.

5: Correct on all, see the middle of A11.62, it mentions FP being halved for Motion, pinned, etc.

We definitely took our time and tried to read through things as we played (we're still very much in 'learning mode'), so that is kind of cool that we came to the right conclusions...

title: Vehicles in buildings Question
question:
Please confirm that we understand this correctly and/or add anything we missed.

Vehicles can enter or set up in buildings provided they can legally enter them during their MPh; e.g. open top vehicles, HTs, etc. cannot.

Vehicles must be BU to enter a building, but may CE once in a building.

Entry of a building is 1/2 total MPs and a bog check.  Expending more than 1/2 MPs doesn't change the bog check requirements.

Change of the VCA in a building incurs a bog check and is double DRM if done while firing.

Change of a TCA in a building is a double DRM if done while firing.

Vehicles in a building are NOT Hulldown, but qualify for a TH DRM of the TEM of the building (+2 or +3 for wood/stone, respectively).

If entering a wooden building, some (all?) vehicles have a chance to fall into the cellar.

I want to say there is a chance that a building collapses/turns to rubble when a vehicle enters it, but I can't seem to find the rule ... so I may be remembering something from another game or a SSR or something.

----------------------
The big thing is that a tank in a building, for example, is exchanging a hull-down "miss me if you hit the hull" defensive feature for a "harder to land a shell on me" TEM DRM.  As long as they do not have to change their CA, their return fire is unaffected by being in the building and, as such, being in a building can certainly offer advantages to inferior tanks facing superior ones.

We are not sure which is better ... HD versus a +3 TEM.  Part of me thinks HD since that can simply erase a Hit whereas part of the TEM can be erased due to ACQ over multiple shots.  But if you're able to take out the other tank before they can get the multiple shots, then maybe the DRM is better...

-K
author: kbernatz
consensus_answer:
Vehicles in a building are NOT Hulldown, but qualify for a TH DRM of the TEM of the building (+2 or +3 for wood/stone, respectively).

A vehicle in any Location can claim the TEM or HD (if otherwise eligible); but you can't claim both.  However, that would only be even possible if the reason for HD is a successful HD Maneuver Attempt (D4.22); D4.21 specifies that if you can be HD from a wall/bocage hexside, you are -- i.e., if your vehicle is in a building behind a wall, you are HD (and the building provides no TEM).

If entering a wooden building, some (all?) vehicles have a chance to fall into the cellar.

All buildings (not just wooden) [EXC: Factories], and certainly can affect all vehicles able to actually drive into a non-Factory building.  And there's no wreck stacking limit in a cellar -- a famous story from many years ago described a particularly unlucky player sending an entire platoon of tanks into the same cellar in the same MPh. :)

As with almost all things, "it depends".  The TEM offers better protection against being hit outright given lower TH numbers (ex terrain), but at higher TH numbers, the hull down advantage prevails.  

Another consideration is your turret versus your hull armor.  King Tigers, for instance, are always hull down for all practical purposes, so you might as well take the TEM.  

Yet another thing to think about is your future plan with this vehicle.  Is it going to fight and die here, or relocate mid or late game?  If the latter, you can position it facing 'backwards', away from the enemy and the wall, so you can just drive out without crossing the wall into the enemy's line of fire.  In that situation, you'd pick HD so you don't have to sweat rear/side shots on your AFV.

So at long range, where TH# are going to be low, the TEM is favored...but at close range or high likelihood of +2 ACQ, the HD is better.  That makes sense.

title: Motion.
question:
Hi, I have some doubts about the motion concept (maybe because it´s difficult to translate this concepto, very similar to moving vehicle in spanish, my language).

An example. A vehicle has moved and ends with the remaining movement points in the last hex. In the defensive fire phase, a gun shoot him.

For the modifiers to apply, the vehicle is "in motion" or stopped.

Thanks in advance.
author: Ignaciocoyote
consensus_answer:
An example. A vehicle has moved and ends with the remaining movement points in the last hex. In the defensive fire phase, a gun shoot him.

For the modifiers to apply, the vehicle is "in motion" or stopped.

You can't end a vehicle's MPh with remaining Movement Points. You have to spend them all.

The modifiers for "Moving Vehicluar Target" apply if during the current Player Turn the target 
- has entered a new hex, or
- used VBM (D2.3), or 
- began its MPh in Motion (D2.4), or 
- is currently in Motion.

So, "has moved" is insufficient information to determine whether the +2 apply or not.
You are right. I have not explained well. I mean the vehicle expends the remaining movement points in the hex and with the last one stops.
Thanks.

title: Can Sniper Check DR result in Sniper Activation?
question: I'm not sure if Sniper Check DR are TC for the purposes of sniper activation determination. Playing The Guards Counterattack, and a successful Sniper Check DR of 6 would result in a decrease in the SAN, but would it result in another sniper activation dr first?
author: donquijones
consensus_answer:
I would say 'no'.  Per the definition of Task Check:
TC (Task Check): A10.1 [Bog: D8.22] [Booby Traps: B28.9] [Deploying: 
A1.31] [Immobilization: D5.5] [Infantry OVR: A4.15] [Kindling: B25.11] 
[LLTC: A10.2] [Over The Wall: TCG16] [Passengers on LC: G12.13] 
[PAATC: A11.6] [Prisoner attacking Guard: A20.55] [PTC: A7.305] [Set 
DC: A23.7] [Swimming: E6.1]

I would say 'no'.  Per the definition of Task Check:
TC (Task Check): A10.1 [Bog: D8.22] [Booby Traps: B28.9] [Deploying: 
A1.31] [Immobilization: D5.5] [Infantry OVR: A4.15] [Kindling: B25.11] 
[LLTC: A10.2] [Over The Wall: TCG16] [Passengers on LC: G12.13] 
[PAATC: A11.6] [Prisoner attacking Guard: A20.55] [PTC: A7.305] [Set 
DC: A23.7] [Swimming: E6.1]

I'm not sure if Sniper Check DR are TC for the purposes of sniper activation determination.

The clue is either in the name or the description of the action in the rules (or both).

PTC = Pin Task Check -- obviously, this is a Task Check.
Deployment Attempt -- doesn't have "TC" in the name, but examining the relevant rule (A1.31) you see that yes, this is a Task Check -- not that it matters for Sniper Activation, as it can only occur in the RPh.
etc.

So when you look up Sniper Check (A14.4) you see that "TC" is not part of the name of the action, and the rule itself doesn't describe the action as a Task Check.  (Typically, non-TC actions like this are simply described as "DR", i.e., "Sniper Check DR".)

Since a Sniper Check DR is not a TC, and nor is it one of the other types of DR that can trigger a Sniper (as listed in A14.1), therefore your question is answered.

Fun rules fact, easy to overlook in the rules: generally, a specific rule will spell out the effects of failing a TC (e.g., if you fail a PTC, you become Pinned).  However, occasionally, there is nothing specified in the particular rule.  Does this mean that there is no consequence for failure in such cases?  No, but you have to pay attention to A10.1:

A10.1 MORALE CHECK (MC)/TASK CHECK (TC): Every Personnel unit has a basic morale rating printed on its counter. This is the number which the player must roll ≤ with two dice in order to succeed in performing some task or avoid damage inflicted by enemy fire. When an attack result dictates that a unit must check morale, it is termed a MC. Failure of a MC (by rolling > the Morale Level after modification) results in the breaking/Reduction/elimination of the unit. If a unit checks morale in order to be allowed to perform some action it is termed a Task Check (TC). Failure of a TC results in the inability of that unit to perform that task during that phase and prohibits the unit from attempting any other action during that phase [EXC: FPF PAATC; D7.212]. See 11.6 for effects of failing a PAATC.

Thank you all for your answers. Bruce, thanks for the cogent and comprehensive explanation. Much appreciated.
Cheers,
Jon

title: FT unit -1 IFT modifier applies to whole stack?
question:
Hi, I'm just trying to get into ASL and I have a question that may turn out to be nonsense so apologies in advance :-)

The rules say that when firing at a unit carrying a flamethrower a -1 modifier is applied on the IFT result. But if there is a stack of units and one of them has a FT, does the -1 modifer apply to a roll against all the units in the stack?

Thanks!
author: Pants101
consensus_answer:
It can be (very) dangerous to stack other units with a unit thar has a FT (probably like in real life)....if one e.g., gets a K/# vs the other units, the FT-toting unit might get a KIA (due to the extra -1 DRM).
Even worse ... if the stack gets a 1KIA against it, the FT unit will cop a 2KIA all on his own, effectively making it a 2KIA for the whole stack (since without the FT the 1KIA would "only" be a random selection amongst all the units in the stack).

When a unit possesses a FT, that unit generally attracts a lot of enemy attention, including fire. As such, I try to avoid stacking with that unit.

title: Improbably vs Critical Hits
question:
Can someone confirm that we played this correctly.

Rules at question are: C3.6 and C3.7.

We had a FL established by a MMG in a wooden building in Bertero in Flames scenario (Hatten in Flames, Scen. 2). The German player drove up a BU Panther at about 4 hex range and fired during its movement phase (after stopping).  He rolled a '2'.

We judged the TH# to be 8 (Infantry 0-6 range).
We judged the DRMs to be: +4 (moving, slow-turret); +1 (BU); +2 (TEM); +1 (an orchard Hindrance), for a net DRM of +8.

This fell under Improbable Hits, 3.6.  Meaning a subsequent dr was needed to secure an actual hit (with dr=1 being critical and 2-3 = regular).  He rolled a dr=4, so we judged this to be a 'miss'.

BUT...3.7 has "A CH also occurs while using the Infantry Target Type whenever the Final TH DR is < half the Modified TH# (not our situation), or on an Original TH DR of 2 followed by a subsequent dr of 1 or <=half of the Modified TH#".

Noting that this sentence does NOT have any reference to 3.6 (but the previous sentence in 3.7 does).  This would mean that even though the Panther needed a '0' DR to Hit, there is some implication that a '2' DR followed by a 1-4 dr (<= half of 8) would score a critical hit.  There would be NO chance of a regular Hit...either one misses or critical hits.

This didn't seem to make sense to us, so we ruled that 3.6 took precedence ... but we weren't sure if we ruled this correctly.
author: kbernatz
consensus_answer:
Great.  That is what we thought ... that C3.7 only applies when C3.6 doesn't.  Note that the reference in 3.7 to 3.6 appears to be referring to the sentence that only talks about IFF HE/WP and Vehicle type CHs, which is why we were confused:

3.7 CRITICAL HITS (CH): A CH is a hit so well placed that it increases 
the chance of causing damage on the resulting IFT Effects or TK DR. 
Even if the target is HD (3.9), a CH occurs on an Original 2 DR during the 
resolution of a HE (or WP; see 3.76) FFE (1.53), or on an Original TH DR 
of 2 on the Area/Vehicle Target Type or on a LATW TH Table. [EXC: De-
liberate Immobilization (5.72). If only the lowest Final TH DR possible for 
that shot would achieve a hit, a CH occurs only on a subsequent dr of 1 
following that hit; a 2-6 results in a normal hull hit (or a normal turret hit 
vs a HD vehicle); if the lowest Final TH DR possible for that shot would 
be a miss, 3.6 applies.] A CH also occurs while using the Infantry Target 
Type whenever the Final TH DR is < half the Modified TH# (3.3), or on 
an Original TH DR of 2 followed by a subsequent dr of 1 or ≤ half of the 
Modified TH#. MG (including all 12.7mm [.50-cal] and aircraft MG, but 
not 15mm) TK attacks have no CH possibility, since this effect is factored 
into their Basic TK# and Range modifiers. The effects of a HE FFE CH 
are resolved using the same Original 2 DR that caused it.

IMO, if 3.6 is supposed to modify CHs versus Infantry (which certainly appears to be the intent given the wording in C3.6), the 'Exception" clause in 3.7 really should be moved to either the very end of this paragraph or immediately after the "A CH also occurs while ..." sentence.

This makes it clearer that the Exception applies to both of these sentences.  Right now, we had confusion whether the exception only applied to the HE FFE, 2 TH roll on vehicle/area, and LATW TH rolls only (as exceptions usually modify the immediate preceding rule).

title: SNIPER: Selecting target
question:
Hi,
What happen if a Sniper is activated, and when rolling dice to select target, this is out of the board?
author: edugon
consensus_answer:
What happen if a Sniper is activated, and when rolling dice to select target, this is out of the board?

A14.2 advises you to use the C1.31 procedure to determine what hex the Sniper initially moves to, and C1.321 tells you what to do when the counter moves offboard.  Unlike a SR, the Sniper counter will always end up moving to hit a target somewhere on board, so the temporary offboard map is only required very briefly.

Do I add +2 to hit DRM if firing at empty hexes, and where do I find it in the Rulebook.

Case K.

6.2 CASE K; CONCEALED TARGET: Ordnance firing at a hidden/concealed target [EXC: pillbox/cave occupant; B30.7 and G11.812] must add the +2 DRM of Case K to its TH DR vs that target [EXC: when firing SMOKE, Case K applies only if the target hex contains ≥ one non-hidden enemy ground unit but none of those units are Known to the firer/Spotter]. It would be strange if it were true.  Fortunately, it isn't.  (I assume by "higher chance" you mean "easier to hit".)  The suggestion above that you have to add Case K when firing at a bridge is incorrect; the bridge is neither concealed nor HIP.  (Remember that different targets can have different modifiers applicable.  If you fire at a concealed infantry unit on a bridge, you can miss the unit -- which does get the Case K DRM -- but hit the bridge, which doesn't.)

title: Revealing AT mines

When a AT tank mines attack a vehicle do you have to reveal how many AT mines are in the hex? 

1) if the attack fails

author: GuusI

B28.1: "The presence of a minefield is not revealed until a unit susceptible to that type of attack enters that minefield Location or an MMC discovers it by Searching. The minefield's strength is not revealed if the minefield attack results in no effect."

So, if the attack has no effect, you only reveal that there's a minefield. If it has an effect, you reveal the strength also.

author: GS in KS
consensus_answer:
You can end up losing battery access without actually getting a fire mission off. For instance, if you get a black chit (automatic here), and put an AR down, and there are enemy units in or adjacent to that hex, and none of them are Known to the Observer, you must draw an extra chit.

If that chit is red (and this extra chit isn't automatically black), you lose battery access. You remove the AR, and on a future turn, you must get radio contact and draw a new black chit to regain access and put down a new AR.

author: albcann
consensus_answer:
Fun fact: if a friendly unit advances into CC with an already-Encircled enemy unit, and the CC becomes a Melee, the friendly unit is also considered Encircled*, and will remain Encircled until they leave the Location (or fulfil one of the other conditions as described in A7.7).  Winning the Melee does not, by itself, cancel the Encirclement!

*Unless the friendly unit is otherwise immune to Encirclement effects, e.g., a hero.

The other thing to note about being Encircled is that your morale is only lowered for attacks.  For example, a broken encircled unit attempting to Rally has its normal morale.

8.12 MOVING WITHIN LOCATION: Any action that requires the expenditure of a MF/MP in a Location qualifies it as a target for Defensive First Fire even though it might not have entered that Location during that MPh. Ahem.  A Location is always ADJACENT to itself (as confirmed by MMP Q&A many years ago).

As to why this is an important distinction, if a Location was not ADJACENT to itself, there would be certain actions a unit could perform that could not take place in the Location, contrary to all common sense (e.g., using Daisy Chain A-T mines).

Generally speaking, if a particular action genuinely cannot take place in the same Location as the unit performing the action, this will be explicitly called out in the rules (e.g., making an Area Target Type attack).

title: Is an AFV, which ran out of fuel, immobile?
question:
Still playing scenario 232 (Chance d'une Affaire), where SSR3 requires a secret dr to define the number of MPhs where each german AFV may move (low fuel).

Now my only AFV left has run out of fuel. Do I have to mark it as "Immobilized"? I guess not, because the amount of fuel left is secret.

And what happens when this AFV gets recalled (D5.341)? Does the crew have to abandon it, because it is immobile, or not? Of course, the definition of "mobile/immobile" (e.g. D.7) does not include this SSR case.
author: phxhf
consensus_answer:
SSR3 of 232 concerning the fuel-dr: "...the resulting value is the number of Movement Phases in which that vehicle may enter a new hex."
My understanding is that I would still be able to change VCA, when out of fuel, because I don't enter a new hex. This is also different to a "real" immobile/bogged vehicle, which confused me here.

The entire point of an SSR is "this is a rule that is different to the normal rules".  Complaining that an SSR doesn't comply with the rules is kind of wasted effort.

In general, it's best to take the text of a rule (whether in the rules book itself or in an SSR) as literally as possible.  (This doesn't always work, which is why there are questions.)  The SSR doesn't say anything about marking the vehicle with any kind of counter when it's "out of fuel" -- so don't.  As you note, the SSR prohibits entry of a new hex -- so the vehicle can do any type of movement it likes when it's "out of fuel" so long as it doesn't enter a new hex.  It is (on the face of it) in no way treated as being Immobile -- it can for instance happily remain in Motion.

If the vehicle is Recalled but is unable to enter a new hex (a basic requirement for Recall!) then it only seems logical that the inherent crew must abandon it as per D5.341 even though the vehicle is neither Bogged nor Immobilized.  However, you can argue that is "stretching" the intent of the SSR.  Since the SSR fails to cover the point, you and your opponent would need to mutually agree on how to resolve the problem.

The core of your (perfectly reasonable) uncertainty here is that the SSR is attempting to be "clever" but has failed to address all of the possibilities.  A well-written SSR would tell you exactly what all the consequences of being "out of fuel" are (possibly the simplest approach being to state "as soon as the vehicle is no longer able to enter a new hex, it is treated as being Immobilized for the remainder of the game").

title: When to enter an Abandoned AFV?
question:
Playing scenario 232 "Chance d'une Affaire" from CdG I am not 100% sure at which phases I am allowed to reenter my abandoned AFV.

D5.42 says during my MPh, while expending all MF. But there is an EXC pointing to the CCPh and A21.2. Although CCPh and A21.2 only seem to deal with capturing enemy vehicles.

At the beginning of the game my vehicular crews are located in the same Location as their AFVs. Although it is my AFV, can it nevertheless be seen as capturing it during CC? Then I could automatically enter in the CCPh? This would be a big advantage, as I don't have to wait for my own MPh to enter and then wait for another MPh to move.
author: phxhf
consensus_answer:
I have posted this on a different forum, but the discussion is the same. 

This came up in at scenario we currently play (DTF 15 Storming Lommel) where the brits set up two abandoned AFVs in road locations with the crews in buildings. 
If the crews can move or advance out into the road, and recrew them in the CCPh, the AFV come into play almost a full turn earlier, and have a much better chance to avoid being shot up. 
The rules on the subject are somewhat contradictory, and I do not find that the above mentioned Q&A solves the issue. 

First of all the Q&A above has a couple of mistakes. 
1)An Abandoned vehicle is a Unit, as it is normally capable of movement. If it had not been a unit, it would not be possible to capture an Abandoned vehicle in CC at all, as A11.1 specifically states that "CC is a form of attack which can occur .... between opposing units ....".
2)A Friendly AFV may obviously not be crewed in this way, as it is not Abandoned, and the A) here is not absolute, as it has the exception "unless actually in CC".
(BTW, where is this Q&A to be found - I'm not able to locate it.... )

To recrew an Abandoned vehicle, an infantry unit have to start the MPh in the same location (D5.42), but rule A21.2 is cited as a specific exception. 
A21.2 states that an Abandoned enemy AFV may be captured automatically by any Infantry unit in the same location at the end of a CCPh, if there are no enemy Personnel in the Location. 
It also states that "Otherwise", i.e. if enemy Personnel are present, "an Abandoned AFV can be captured only by a CC attack capture attempt in a CC Location", and that both sides could attempt capture. 
Here A21.2 is a specific exception to A11.1, as the Abandoned AFV is clearly not opposing neither your own nor your opponents infantry unit, but is quite passive until actually recrewed.

Now there is another interesting Q&A to A7.4 and D5.4
Q: Is an abandoned vehicle still a unit? If it is a unit, is a previously friendly vehicle which was abandoned still a friendly unit, thus preventing another friendly unit to fire on it? If it is not a unit, may an abandoned vehicle be fired upon?
A. An Abandoned vehicle is a unit, but it is neither friendly nor enemy and can be attacked by either side.

This makes it quite plain; an Abandoned vehicle is a unit, but neither friendly nor enemy, which makes sense to me, as it is not capable of any kind of action or combat. 
In other words; You cannot hug it, nor will it fight back if attacked…. 😉

Still, things are not crystal clear, as A21.2 uses the expression "Abandoned enemy AFV". 
To me it seems the better solution to ignore "enemy" in this sentence, as it otherwise would contradict the above Q&A (7.4&D5.4).

Imagine the following: 
1) A German PzI is immobilized in a hex with an Abandoned French B1-bis and an Abandoned German PzIII. The crew fail their TC and exit the vehicle. Now, if they survive until the CCPh and there are no enemy infantry units in hex, per the Q&A in the above post, they could neither recrew their own vehicle nor the other German Panzer, but they could recrew the B1-bis with which they are totally unfamiliar.
2) A German PzIV is immobilized by enemy prep fire. Per the Q&A in the above post they could not recrew their own vehicle in the CCPh, unless an enemy infantry unit actually advances in for CC (and they make the capture DR), which in my view would make things harder, not easier /possible.
Both 1) and 2) are nonsensical IMO.

OH

title: What happens if I set up in an enemy minefield?
question:
We are playing the Primosole Bridge campaign, and during set up of a later scenario, my opponent pointed to a foxhole I had set up and noted that he had a minefield there. I could not find rules (the campaign rules are short, but also the full rules) as to what should happen if my set up area extends into enemy minfields - do they just disappear, do they attack me.?

Any pointers would be appreciated,
Thanks, Neil
author: doktor avalanche
consensus_answer:
After the CG scenario in which that hex became part of your Setup Area - those mines should have been placed onboard:

3.6073 HIDDEN FORTIFICATIONS: Each still-hidden Fortification within a Setup Area of the purchaser’s opponent is placed on-map. Each such minefield is marked by placing a Minefield counter to reveal its presence but not its strength/type. Each on-map Fortification (i.e., from previous CG scenarios) is controlled by the side (if any) Controlling its Location.

title: Second Crack At Caumont concealment SSR question
question:
Hi there,

I'd like some clarity on SSR 2. which states: "German units which set up in Concealment Terrain may begin the scenario concealed." 

At what point is the scenario deemed to 'begin' and therefore at what point do this additional level of concealment get applied? 

Many thanks!
author: Nickgoulden
consensus_answer:
A12.12 specifically mentions concealing ALL units before the opponent sees the setup.

Sure but that applies for the case when the opponent starts with no pieces on board!

The issue about this scenario is that the opponent does start with units on board.

There would be no need for a SSR if the general rule in A12.12 applied. In this case that specific provision of A12.12 does not apply because both sides start with units on board. 

So the questions that arises from the SSR is whether a defending stack, in concealment terrain, has a concealment marker placed on top of it before the opponent gets a shot at checking LOS or not. If the answer is yes, then the opponent never gets to see the top unit of that stack. If the answer is no, then the opponent does see the unit on top of the stack but before the first rally phase a concealment marker is anyway placed on top of the unit. 

My interpretation is that it is the first case. The opponent never gets to see what is in that stack.

This is A12.12:

The player setting up first in a scenario does so out of
vision of his opponent, and after setting up his regular units may place only
scenario OB-designated “?” at first—but only in Terrain listed in red in the
Terrain Chart/Desert Terrain Chart/PTO Terrain Chart. After his opponent
sets up in the same manner, each unconcealed unit (of both sides) which is
either out of the LOS of all unbroken enemy ground units within 16 hexes
of it, or at ≥ 17 hexes from all of them, may have a “?” not designated by the
OB placed on it [EXC: only one non-OB-designated “?” can be placed per
stack of units and not on top of any previously placed “?”]. Therefore, if one
side begins with no forces on board, the other side will be able to place “?”
on all of its non-Dummy units after placing those units (before the opponent
may look at the board).

replies.body: German units set up first, so SSR 2 applies then. The twelve ‘?’ counters can be used as Dummies.

author: GamerKirk
consensus_answer:
You have to roll for ALL hexes in a Bombardment, as the dice may result in shellholes, rubbling buildings, etc. So if there are HIP units you just roll for that hex and check for the effects on the terrain and on your HIP units. If they pin or break they are revealed. If they pass, they keep HIP. (C1.8-1.823)

Remember that dummy stacks have a morale of 7 (A12.14) and if they pass their Bombardment 2MC they keep existing as a dummy stack!

title: Deploying AFV smoke, Motion Attempt, Baz smoke
question:
Would someone please point out the rule(s) that clarify if there is any required order to AFV smoke tossed/fired during movement and motion attempts?

So, which is legal for an AFV:  1) Motion attempt then sM use, 2) sM use then motion attempt...both?

Additionally, is smoke for hand-held SW, say from a Bazooka, required to be shot before all non-smoke shots in a fire phase?
author: GamerKirk
consensus_answer:
So, which is legal for an AFV:  1) Motion attempt then sM use, 2) sM use then motion attempt...both? 

D2.401 A vehicle may attempt Motion status only once per enemy MPh and may not attempt it at all if already marked with a First Fire(or Final/Intensive Fire) counter.

D13.2 During the opponent's MPh, a smoke dispenser usage attempt can be made...as if it were intervening with Defensive First Fire.

The rules don't appear to clearly specify whether an AFV that makes a smoke dispenser attempt in DFF is marked with a First Fire counter or not, but I would interpret this as saying the AFV is marked, and therefore cannot subsequently make a motion attempt.

C8.5 Smoke may be placed by ordance/OBA only at the start of the owner's PFPh/DFPh.

C8.6 Unlike Smoke, WP may be fired by ordnance during (but prior to any friendly unit firing anything other than SMOKE) any friendly fire phase--not just the PFPh/DFPh...

So yes, it must be fired before all non-smoke shots, but remember that bazookas firing WP can also fire in DFF or the AFPh.

Can you clarify your last statement about Bazookas?  The way I understand it is that a Baz can only fire once, so if it fires WP in the Prep phase, it can't also fire a shot in the AFPh.  And you are saying that if any non-smoke fire is performed, Baz or otherwise, no other smoke, including Baz, can be fired that phase?

And the jury is still out on whether there is an proscribed order to sM, for example, and Motion attempt, or one precludes the other (not marked with DFF counter, or marked with counter...)?!?

Additionally, is smoke for hand-held SW, say from a Bazooka, required to be shot before all non-smoke shots in a fire phase?

title: Hillock Railroad in Hatten in Flames
question:
Although wading through the tiny font and the involved hillock rules in ASL isn't great fun, how to treat the railroad in Hatten in Flames is even more confusing.

With hillocks, the rules and examples talk about separate hillocks, usually overlays, and LOS over them from various positions.  To note, the rules often talk about the hillock you are adjacent to or on, then being able to see past another hillock to perhaps even another hillock or to a unit adjacent to that far hillock.

With lots of reading and consideration, it's perhaps possible to figure all of that out, but with the "hillock" railroad in Hatten, it's hard to know.

Specifically, is the RR and all of the connected hexes of it, ONE hillock for LOS purposes?  Or if the LOS *leaves* the hillock hexes then re-engages them it becomes the aforementioned second or third hillock that the rules tend to mention?  Treating the entering and leaving of the RR hexes as one long single hillock definitely allows LOS that treating it as separate hillocks divided any time the LOS leaves the RR hexes then recrosses them doesn't.

The overlays don't have this problem because they aren't a very long snakey linear terrain which an LOS can enter and leave and enter and leave, but rather more circular in nature, making it clear when *another* hillock has been reached for LOS purposes.
author: GamerKirk
consensus_answer:
It's a great question.  Hillock rules SUCK!  You are exactly right that when originally introduced, they were always on little overlays and the hillocks were "enclosed" on the overlay.  You were either ON the hillock or next to it.

The way I play it:
Each railroad hex should be envisioned as a 1-hex completely 'enclosed' hillock.  If you treat every hex as such, then you can start to count how many hillock hexes you're crossing.  If you're LOS crosses the number of hillock HEXES as described in the rules, then LOS is blocked when it gets to that number (isn't it 3 if you're next to a hillock and 4 if you're on top of one?).  

If you're IN the railroad hex, you are ON the hillock.  If you're next to the hillock hex, you're adjacent to the hillock.  Count accordingly.

Does that help?  
The Hatten situation is not unique.  Almost all of the HASLs now use these hillock rules for railroads or in ABTF for the bridge ramp.  So now knowing these rules is essential.  I used to skip them when they only applied to Africa.

Um, no, they can't.  Why would you think otherwise?  It's just like a unit in a foxhole behind a wall -- non-adjacent units have no LOS to the units in the foxhole (although they do have a LOS to the foxhole itself).  You can't fire at units you have no LOS to.  (Well, you can, but your attack cannot affect them directly.)

A MTR wouldn't help in this case, because a MTR will only affect units out of LOS if it can hit something that is in LOS.

You could indirectly affect the unit in certain circumstances.  Depending on what's firing at the building, you might place a flame or even rubble it.  Also WP being placed in your hex will always ruin your day.

In this bocage situation, if there was an enemy unit claiming wall advantage you could fire a MTR against this unit in LOS, and if you hit it, you would also hit the unit in the building which was out of LOS. If there were two units claiming wall advantge and one of them was concealed, you would have to hit the concealed unit to hit the out of LOS unit.

I recently played a game were my opponent used this bocage situation to his advantage. There was a building with bocage. In the building he kept a leader that rallied broken units and those rallied took wall advantage and kept the defensive position. If they were broken, they just lost wall advantage, were out of LOS and the leader rallied them.

title: Hero in Fire Group with Bazooka
question:
I've read through the seemingly less than clear rules and just cannot determine if a Hero, firing as a Fire Group, say with a squad, that is using a To Hit SW, such as a Bazooka, gets to use his -1 modifier.

15.23  Weapons Use:  A hero may use a non-MG SW as if he were a leader but applies a -1 DRM to its To Hit or IFT DR.  In addition, a hero uses a MG (at full FP) or other SW normally requiring two men to fire by adding +1 to its To Hit or IFT DR as appropriate (which is negated by the heroic DRM).  A hero forfeits his own inherent FP during any phase in which he uses a SW.  A hero may fire any Gun <= 82mm that normally requires a crew as if it were captured and being fired by an enemy crew (2111 & 21.12), but his heroic DRM does not apply.  If firing a Gun>82mm, it may fire only once per Game Turn and only during the MPh/DFPh.  A hero cannot change the CA of a NT weapon [EXC: if its M# (C2.27) is >= 9).  A hero is the only unit which may fire an AFV AAMG while a rider.

A15.24  Heroic DRM:  A hero/any FG (even if just another SMC) he is part of (providing the hero is firing at Normal Range of either his inherent FP or his weapon counter) may deduct one from its IFT/CC resolution DR.  This DRM is cumulative with that of any applicable leadership DRM/addiional heroes present in the same attack.  Unlike a leader, a hero's IFT DRM is not contigent on being in the same Lodation with all other members of the FG or in combination with another unit.  A hero is always considered stealthy, and may use his DRM for Clearance attempts.  A hero's participation does not exempt other members of a FG from Cowering.  The heroic DRM is NA for FT/DC attacks.
author: GamerKirk
consensus_answer:
Note that a Leader can direct the fire of a BAZ (or most other SW) in order to apply his modifier, but that's not "forming a FG" as such.

Any two SMC stacked together can combine to fire a BAZ; if one of them is a Hero he can apply his Heroic DRM.  (I guess if both are heroes you can apply the DRM twice.)  Only a Hero can fire a BAZ by himself, and suffers a +1 DRM for doing so (which is offset by his Heroic DRM).

C13.45 SMC USAGE: Any combination of two SMC may fire a BAZ at full effect. Leaders cannot modify their own fire although a Hero can, (A15.24) whether singly or in combination with another SMC. A BAZ can be used by one SMC only if that SMC is a Hero (A15.23).

title: Side/rear armor
question: So would someone help me with how to play hits to the side with an afv that has a blocked lower number? I read rule C3.9. But doesn't cover the other.
author: dabrawley
consensus_answer: Yes, turret hits are judged by the TCA. When you get a turret hit on a vehicle, use the D3.2 diagram, but base it off which way the turret is facing (see the end of D3.12). If you hit the turret's front, use the front AF (with the front armor's inferior/superior modification). If it hit the side of the turret, use the side AF (with the side armor's inferior/superior modification).

replies.body: tl;dr if it hits the turret (i.e. lower colored die), then the armor is considered to be one class higher (see C7.11). So if the number inside the square block is a 4 and you hit the turret, the turret AF is actually a 6.

D1.63:
1.63 SUPERIOR TURRET: A printed AF encased in a square indicates that the AFV’s turret/upper-superstructure AF for that Target Facing is > that hull AF. The Superior-Turret AF is calculated by increasing that printed AF to the next-higher AF value given in 1.6.
So it's treated the same as hitting the front even when attacking the sides. Superior turrets for the win. Thanks for the reply.
Which AFV is it ?

No, it doesn't mean that at all!  On most AFV even a "superior turret side armour" is still going to be less than the front AF.

There are a few AFV where the front and side armours are quite similar, and thus a superior turret side might be the equal of or even better than the front armour, but those are not common.

Let's look at the German PzIIIJ.  The AF values are given as 6 / 3 (boxed).  So the front AF is 6, regardless of whether the hull or the turret is hit.  The side AF is 3 if you hit the hull, 4 if you hit the turret.

Now look at the German PzIVJ.  The AF values are 8 (circled) / 3 (boxed).  The front hull AF is 8, the front turret AF is 6, the side hull AF is 3 and the side turret AF is 4.  Four different locations, four different AF values.

An outlier example is the German PSW 231(6 rad).  AF values are 0 / 1 -- the side armour is always superior to the front armour!

The term Original DR/dr refers to one before the addition of modifiers; Final DR/dr refers to a DR/dr after the addition of all modifiers.

In most cases, you're looking at the Final roll, but things like malfunction call out the Original roll.

title: M3 Medium gyro-stabilized bow gun
question:
Per American Vehicle Note 7, either both the MA and SA are gyro-stabilized or neither is. As best I read, according to case C [C5.3] a stabilized bow gun will use a +1 TH DRM instead of the usual NT +3 TH DRM for Bounding Fire. author: jrvjrv
consensus_answer:

I think it's fair enough.  The M3 medium tanks are, as best as I can remember, the only vehicles that can have a Stabilized non-turreted weapon.  So any rules to modify the behaviour of those guns when Stabilized would be best seen in the vehicle note, not in the core rules.  Then it becomes a question of how fine do you want to splice the hair, i.e., is writing a modified rule for a Stabilized non-turreted gun worth the effort instead of just using the "generic" Stabilized gun rules.  The actual likelihood of a Stabilized M3 appearing in a scenario are pretty slim.  I vaguely recall reading somewhere that the M3 crews hated their stabilizers and would deactivate them by preference because the random swinging of the gun breach inside the vehicle as it was moving could be lethal for the gunner.  That's assuming that they were even given any training in the period that the vehicles were in active service.  I can't imagine that the Russian crews had any such training, and I doubt that the British crews did either.

title: Optionally Off Map and Scenario Attacker/Defender Status
question:
Scenario J13 "The Gorge" has the Japanese set up fully on map with no need to capture terrain. The Americans can set up completely on map, off map, or a mix of off and on.

If the Americans decide to set up fully off map, do the Japanese get classified as the Scenario Defender (and the Americans the Scenario Attacker)? If so I suppose after the Americans have declared their decision to set up fully off map, the Japanese could then set up bore sighted locations?

Thanks!
author: MikeWhit
consensus_answer:
The OP asked a concrete question: "If the Americans decide to set up fully off map, do the Japanese get classified as the Scenario Defender (and the Americans the Scenario Attacker)?" The answer to that is: "Yes."
If he'd asked: "Does it make sense for the Americans to set up fully off map?", the answer would probably be different.
No... the answer to that initial question was 'no'.

The Japanese player sets up. As the Americans are not defined as entering from off-map (they have the option), the Japanese are not a Scenario Defender. Once Japanese set up is complete, the Americans set up. They may end up completely entering from off map, but that is not decided until that point. (There are occasional scenarios where the attacker needs to make a decision like this before defender set up, but this doesn't seem to be one of them, from what has been said.)

Your reading seems to be that "enters wholly from offboard" actually means "must enter wholly from offboard". But why do you think that's the case?
That's easy.

The Japanese player can set up as Scenario Defender only if the Americans entirely enter from off board. That means he has to ask, before he sets up, if the American is going to do this.

The American player's response will be a shrug, and 'I dunno, I need to see your setup first.'

At that point, you have a causality loop. The American determines his set up after the Japanese, but the Japanese is asking him to determine... well, the general direction of his set up, before the Japanese setup is done. The obvious way out of this is that the Japanese player does his set up first (as said in the scenario) without making any assumptions about the upcoming American setup.

I think it's clear that we are engaging in rules exegesis that has no bearing on actual play. 🙂
But honestly, to me, the rules seem 100% clear. Since I'm in the minority, English is not my first language and I'm relatively new to ASL, the probability is high that I'm the one who's wrong here. Does someone care to explain your interpretation of the rules?

To reiterate, the index states (enumeration added by me):
"The Scenario Defender is the side that
1) sets up wholly or partly on-board and 
2) does not have to capture terrain (on other than its setup board) in order to fulfill its Victory Conditions, 
3) while facing an opposing side that enters wholly from offboard."

Your reading seems to be that "enters wholly from offboard" actually means "must enter wholly from offboard". But why do you think that's the case?

In all the scenarios that have instructions like this, I don't think I have ever seen the side setting up second not placing anything onboard - even a lonely HS - just to make it clear the opponent can't use Bore Sighting, free pre-game LOS checks, free "?" placement....

title: SASL - Panic of Leaders
question:
Hi, in SASL can enemy leaders panic ?  I presume they do as they are a 'unit' under the rules.  However the rules specify the 'double DR' required to panic for Elite, Conscript units, etc but remain silent on Leaders.  Am I missing something ??
a puzzled 'Corona' beginner of SASL.
author: Husar7
consensus_answer: A1.11: SMC are elite [EXC: Partisans].  Leaders being SMC, they are elite units (except for Partisans).

replies.body: A1.11: SMC are elite [EXC: Partisans].  Leaders being SMC, they are elite units (except for Partisans).

Hi, in SASL can enemy leaders panic ?  I presume they do as they are a 'unit' under the rules.  However the rules specify the 'double DR' required to panic for Elite, Conscript units, etc but remain silent on Leaders.  Am I missing something ??

ENEMY Leaders can Panick whenever the Action DR is such as to cause Panicking of an Elite unit. This practically means that Leaders will panic less often than other infantry units in the same stack (unless they are elite too)

title: Putting Guns in buildings—The story of the Soviet 76.2 obr. 36
question:
There are two rules I frequently see missed by Soviet players. The first is that the T-34es up until the T-34/85 and the KV-1es are all RST AFVs. I frequently walk up to games and see T-34es zipping around CE like they were Israeli tank aces in '67 Sinai. Stop it! You must be BU to fire the main armament.

The second is placing the 76.2 obr. 39 Gun [Soviet Ordnance note 15] in a building. These are great light field guns, especially in the early war. But in ASL they are classed as ART ordnance. Per B23.423 a Gun may set up in a building if it is *small* (the Soviet 76.2 obr. 39—and the 76.2 obr. 36, the real topic of this post—is a normal-size Gun) or it must be an AT/INF Gun that is not large (as said before, it is classed as ART). So the 76.2 obr. 39 cannot set up in buildings.

The 76.2 obr. 39 is so common in Soviet service that it is nearly universal in scenarios on the Eastern Front. Not so the 76.2 obr. 36, most instances of which were captured by the Germans early in Barbarossa. The Germans saw that the obr. 36 was a potent anti-tank weapon (16TK in ASL terms), so they re-issued them to their own troops [German Ordnance Note 11] and gave some to Romania too [Axis Minor Ordnance Note 5]. In the change of ownership the Guns are reclassed as AT Guns in ASL terms, so now they may set up in buildings. I'll leave you to ponder how the same Gun can fit in buildings when used by one side but not by the other.

As a final note, I'll point out that the 76.2 obr. 39 is also used by the Romanians [Axis Minor Ordnance Note 12], but it remains classed as ART and so can't be put in a building.

JR

consensus_answer:

A9.22 FIRE LANE: Whenever the DEFENDER declares a Defensive First Fire attack with a Good Order SW MG that is manned by unpinned Infantry (even as ordnance or as part of a FG), he may also declare a Fire Lane with that MG if it is not already marked with a First/Final Fire counter and is firing within its Normal Range (but not using TPBF) and at a same-level (B.5) target.

(my emphasis)

Secondly, I don't understand your comment about "not leaving residual".  MG TK attempts absolutely leave residual.

A8.2 RESIDUAL FIREPOWER: When a unit is attacked by Defensive First Fire/Subsequent First Fire/FPF, the target Location in which the attack is resolved (even if in Bypass) is marked with a Residual FP counter equal to half (up to a maximum of 12 after adjustment as per 8.26; FRD) of the highest IFT FP column used for that attack. If the attack includes a To Kill DR vs a vehicle, Residual FP is created in the same manner [EXC: If AP (unless fired by a MG), ATR, APCR, or APDS was used, or if a Dud (C7.35) resulted, no Residual FP is created].

(my emphasis)

Light Mortars are SW, not ordnance.

As others have said, light mortars *are* ordnance and in fact can only be used as ordnance. A majority of SW types can or must be used as ordnance, i.e. attacking using a TH table. In addition to MTRs, BAZ, PSK, PF, PIAT, MOL-P, (37mm) SW INF and American RCL all use *only* a TH table, the first five using their own private TH table while the last two use the standard TH table. MGs and ATRs are able to fire as ordnance, and also may fire as non-ordnance. The SW that are not capable of being used as ordnance are FT, DC, Radio, ATMM and MOL.

Note that for MGs and ATRs you do not necessarily have a choice whether to shoot them as ordnance or not. You can't use a MG or ATR as ordnance vs. infantry, for instance.

edit: I missed something here: a 20L ATR *can* be used as ordnance vs infantry. So many EXCs, so little time.

I may have missed an odd case or two, but I hope I got them all.

JR

Before asking us to explain a rule to you, it's helpful if you have confirmed that you have actually read the rule and can identify what exactly you don't understand about what it is saying.

Otherwise you're just asking people to type out paragraphs from the rules.

The brief summary is that at the top of every column of the IFT is a number on a line identified as the "★ Vehicle line".  When you make an IFT attack against an unarmoured vehicle, you compare the Final DR (taking into account modifiers like TEM, Hindrances, etc.) to that number.  If it equals that number, the vehicle is immobilised.  If it's < the number, the vehicle is destroyed.  If it's <= half of that number, the vehicle is burning.

If the vehicle is eliminated (but not burning), any PRC are subject to Crew Survival DR.  If the vehicle is NOT eliminated, the Final DR on the IFT table is used to determine the results on the PRC: MC, PTC, or whatever.

If that makes you think that unarmoured vehicles taking fire are very, very vulnerable, then you are completely correct.  I've seen 1FP residual attacks in a road hex utterly wreck a column of unarmoured vehicles.  Even if the vehicles remain unharmed, the same might not be said for the PRC.  Don't send unarmoured vehicles into the teeth of combat unless you have no choice in the matter! title: Trucks
question:
1. What is used to represent a Truck Inherent Crew when Routs?
2. A MMC/SMC can "drive" an Abandoned Truck?
author: Gwynor
consensus_answer:
Check D5.1 Only armed vehicles are maned by inherent crews. AFV have elite morale crews and unarmored vechiles have first line morale crews. Both of them exit the vehicle as vehicle crews (with lower strength than gun crews).

Unarmed vehicles have an inherent driver that never has a counter representation.

So your truck would have an inherent crew if it is an armed crew. Unarmed trucks don't have crews.

To man abandoned vehicles that need crews, check A21.22. That applies only to armed vehicles. Unarmed vehicles do not have a crew and its inherent driver never leaves the vehicle, so they cannot be manned by other units except by capture, in this case a MMC provides a driver at no cost or it it is an SMC it is removed from play until an MMC can provide a driver or the SMC leaves the unaremd vehicle (A21.21).

title: Pillbox and Fire Group
question: I have this feeling that a pillbox is never allowed to participate in a fire group with a unit not in the pillbox. Is this correct or am I imagining this?
author: drmark64
consensus_answer:
I agree that this seems to be the intent of the rules, the text itself is not so clear. Sure, a unit in a bunker can't form a firegroup with an other unit in the same hex, since the bunker is treated as a pillbox, and the pillbox rules forbid this explicitly.

But: A unit in a bunker and a unit in a trench in an ADJACENT hex are ADJACENT, so, according to the rules, CAN form a firegroup. The pillbox rules only forbid same-hex FGs. I think. But I'm not sure.

Well.  You have a point.  However, unless that trench is within the pillbox's CA, there is no LOS between the two Locations (B30.2).  They're Accessible, but not ADJACENT, because ADJACENT requires a LOS.

So I'd say that IF the trench and the pillbox counter are in adjacent hexes and IF that trench is within the CA of the pillbox then yes, units in the trench and units in the pillbox can form a FG, under the rules as currently written.  However, in practice, I should think the chances of that setup actually occurring in a scenario would be quite small, because it would seriously compromise the defensive value of the pillbox.

Well.  You have a point.  However, unless that trench is within the pillbox's CA, there is no LOS between the two Locations (B30.2).  They're Accessible, but not ADJACENT, because ADJACENT requires a LOS.

So I'd say that IF the trench and the pillbox counter are in adjacent hexes and IF that trench is within the CA of the pillbox then yes, units in the trench and units in the pillbox can form a FG, under the rules as currently written.  However, in practice, I should think the chances of that setup actually occurring in a scenario would be quite small, because it would seriously compromise the defensive value of the pillbox.

It's really very simple, but okay....

StuG A moves from S18 to T19 by Starting (1), moving in bypass of T18 (1 OG x 2 VBM = 2), and then moving into T19 (1) and Stopping (1; total 5 MP)

StuG B moves from W20 to V18 by Starting in reverse (1), moving in bypass of V19 (1 OG x 2 VBM x 4 reverse movement = 8), and then moving into V18 (4), and ending in Reverse Motion after using all 13 MP....

The CAFPs while in VBM are at the vertex at the front corner of the counter in both cases, and are marked with orange dots. All LOS and LOF checks are drawn to those vertexes while in bypass of those hexsides. The CAs are as shown in the rule book at D2.321. There are four, instead of six possible covered arcs, with the front and rear VCA more restricted than normal (and the TCA will be too if it lines up with one of those), and the side CAs (and therefore the TCA if rotated to the left or right) being much expanded with the penalty that all fire without Acquisition applies Case A to the TH DR (D2.321), and Case A is increased by one if the TCA actually changed for that shot.

For more complicated maneuvering:

The StuG moves from T19 to W19:
It Starts (BU) in T19 (1), moves to U19/U20 (1 x 2 VBM / 2 narrow street = 1), moves to U19/V19 (1 [CA change] + [1 x 2 / 2 = 1] = 2), moves to V18/V19 (1 [CA change] + [1 x 2 VBM = 2] = 3), and moves into W19 (1), and Stops there (1; total MP = 9).

Next turn the StuG decides this is too exposed, and goes into reverse along the same course:

It Starts in Reverse in W19 (1), moves to V19/V18 (1 x 2 VBM x 4 reverse = 8; total 9), and ends in Reverse Motion as it doesn't have enough MP for its next maneuver....

The next turn, it moves to U19/V19 (1 [CA change] + [1 x 2 VBM / 2 narrow street x 4 reverse = 4] = 5), then to U19/U20 (1 [CA change] + [1 x 2 VBM / 2 narrow street x 4 reverse = 4] = 5), and ends in Reverse Motion as it still doesn't have enough to get to T19, which is why tanks rarely go very far in reverse...

StuG B moves from W20 to V18 by Starting in reverse (1), moving in bypass of V19 (1 OG x 2 VBM x 4 reverse movement = 8), and then moving into V18 (1) and Stopping (1; total 11 MP).

Just for the record, I believe the move into V18 would cost 4 MP, as the StuG is moving in reverse.

It Starts in Reverse in W19 (1), moves to V19/V18 (1 x 2 VBM x 4 reverse = 8; total 9, and 10 for the turn...), and ends in Reverse Motion as it doesn't have enough MP for its next maneuver....
Don't think there is a 10th MP for a VCA change, as that is part of the move along the next hexside, which the StuG lacks MP for.

title: AFV Rear MG
question: Sorry if this has already been addressed. Does R2 after the CMG factor mean that the rear MG has a firepower value of 2? I have heard people try to argue that the 2 represents 2 MGs with the same firepower of the front CMG.
author: Jgolch
consensus_answer: D1.82 COAXIAL MG (CMG): The CMG FP may be used only when firing through the TCA. The Normal Range of a CMG is 12 hexes. Use of a CMG against other than an acquired target causes loss of any pre-existing Acquisition (C6.5) by the MA. Some AFV have a turret Rear MG which is reflected by the superscript R# after the CMG FP. A turret Rear MG has a Normal Range of eight hexes, may not be used in OVR or the same phase in which the MA fires, and can fire only though its rear turret Target Facing or at a target in the same hex (see 3.5).

replies.body: It's the FP of the Rear MG. Some vehicle that have a Rear CMG (KV-8 e.g.) doesn't even have a "normal" CMG.

I have heard people try to argue that the 2 represents 2 MGs with the same firepower of the front CMG. 

Presumably those people have no idea what a tank looks like, but that's ok; that doesn't mean that they can't play the game.  What is absolutely essential to playing the game is a copy of the rulebook, where (they may be surprised to discover) the various factors on the counters and what they mean are described in some detail.  Do these people making these "arguments" not have a copy of the rules?
