Use of a CMG against other than an acquired target causes loss of any pre-existing Acquisition (C6.5) by the MA. Some AFV have a turret Rear MG which is reflected by the superscript R# after the CMG FP. A turret Rear MG has a Normal Range of eight hexes, may not be used in OVR or the same phase in which the MA fires, and can fire only though its rear turret Target Facing or at a target in the same hex (see 3.5).

It came up in a Starter Kit game (I usually play full ASL)against a guy who was a real jerk. He was so adamant about it that it made me question my own knowledge of the rules for a quick second.  Anyway, I argued back that the number 2 was the firepower and NOT 2X4 that he wanted. He wanted an 8 firepower shot instead of a 2.  This would have been a huge difference! He may have been trying to cheat me outright.  

I just posted this question to see what other players out there thought.  The great thing about this forum is the questions can be answered in less than an hour. 

Thanks for all the responses.

Looking up things in the rulebook is part of the game. Surely, something like the firepower of a RMG being x times the FP of the CMG would be clearly spelled out if that were the case. If you and your opponent can't find it, it most probably isn't true. 

I learn something new - or relearn something that I have forgotten - almost every time I play.

title: Leader and Commissar Rally
question:
When multiple leaders are broken in a location, and there is no unbroken leader, then I can Self-Rally all of them, one after another, until the first leader succeeds? Then he will rally the remaining units, right? Also those leaders which failed Self-Rallying?
Or do I have to select one leader, and if he fails rallying I would have no further options?

Another situation: What happens when I have a broken MMC and a broken leader, and this MMC could still do the single allowed Self-Rally for the ATTACKER. May I still try MMC Self-Rally (Field Promotion), when the leader failed rallying? Or is this option reserved for locations without a leader?

Which leads to the final question: I understand that a Commissar always has to Self-Rally first, no matter if there are any broken or unbroken leaders (A25.221) in that location. What happens when the Commissar fails rallying himself? Can another leader attempt to rally him now? Can another leader attempt to rally any other units in the Commissar's location?
author: phxhf
consensus_answer:
Only one attempt per unit, so if the leader attempted self-rally, then a later rallied leader cannot attempt to rally that leader again in the same RPh.

So you can attempt to rally leaders until one succeeds, once one succeeds, he can attempt to rally all the units in the stack that have no already attempted rally.

The free self-rally can be used for a unit that is stacked with a broken leader. We always do the free self-rally as our first rally attempt but I don't remember if that is a requirement.

If the Commissar fails self-rally, then he is done for the RPh, no other leader can attempt to rally him. "Each unit may attempt only one type of action in a RPh." (A3.1)

replies.body:
All leaders may attempt self-rally.
A rallied leader may help other leaders rally if they didn't attempt self-rally previously.
A broken leadsr which doesn't rally allows a MMC stacked with it to attempt the first self-rally of its RPh.
That is why it can be wise to attempt all leader self-rallies before determining which broken MMC may attempt the first MMC self-rally.

If the commissar fails self-rally, other leaders in its Location may attempt self-rally.
If they self-rally, they cannot attempt to rally the commissar.
The golden rule here is that a unit may not make more than one action per RPh, excepted rallying other units.

If the Commissar fails self-rally, then he is done for the RPh, no other leader can attempt to rally him. "Each unit may attempt only one type of action in a RPh." (A3.1)

We always do the free self-rally as our first rally attempt but I don't remember if that is a requirement.The requirement is the first MMC rally (A10.63 : ...  In addition, one MMC may attempt Field Promotion (18.11) as the first MMC Rally attempt of its own Player Turn.).
SMC may freely attempt self-rally before that first MMC (self-)rally.

The golden rule here is that a unit may not make more than one action per RPh, excepted rallying other units.

Technically, He's assisting Rallying.   No recovery, Deploy etc. As those are other ACTIONS.  Rally is ONE action.
Got it. Makes sense. Thanks!

One other thing to remember about Commissars is that they suppress the leadership of other leaders when they are stacked with them (assuming the Commissar is unbroken).  So if you have a Commissar, a 10-3, and a squad + MG stacked in a Location together, the 10-3 gets to stand around and pick his nose.  The Commissar outranks him, doesn't improve his morale (since he's already at the maximum) and prevents him from using his -3 DRM for any purpose.  So: don't stack Commissars with other leaders!

A25.221 only limits it to "morale activities":

A25.221:
"...An unpinned, unbroken Commissar increases the Morale Level of all other friendly Infantry/Cavalry units in the same Location by one [EXC: Commissars and units with Morale Level of 10], while prohibiting the application of another leaders DRM to morale activities...."

...so seemingly a 10-3 stacked with a Commissar can still used his -3 DRM to direct e.g., an IFT attack. Unless there is some other rule I am not remembering.

Though stacking with a Commissar is not without risk - in one game of Shklov's Labors Lost that I witnessed the Russian 10-0 was stacked with the Russian 10-3 and three squads manning MGs. Commissar went Berserk and automatically took the entire stack with him to charge the German 10-3-led MG stack. IIRC, it was a 36 FP, -5 attack. Not pretty.

...so seemingly a 10-3 stacked with a Commissar can still used his -3 DRM to direct e.g., an IFT attack.
Indeed, I thought the same when reading A25.221, but wasn't sure about it. There must be a reason that "to morale activities" is explicitely mentioned.

Another situation which is not 100% clear to me: There is one Good Order 7-0 leader and a broken 9-2 leader together with some broken squads.

Once the 7-0 leader rallies the 9-2, can the 9-2 immediately take over and rally the squads?

Once the 7-0 leader rallies the 9-2, can the 9-2 immediately take over and rally the squads?

If the 9-2 would have self-rallied, he could. I have played it that he could rally other units in your case, too, but A10.71 seems to disagree:
A10.71: "... Having rallied himself, the leader may then attempt to rally any remaining broken units in his Location during that RPh."
(emphasis mine)

A. Yes. [An95w; An96]
Great! I‘m happy it works like that! :)

Official Q&A:

Why are you using 1st ed. Q&A to answer 2nd ed. questions?

If the Q&A was considered "valid" then it will have been incorporated directly into the 2nd ed. rules.  If it wasn't considered "valid" it won't have been and is no longer helpful.

Please don't answer questions with outdated information.  If the Q&A was incorporated (I know of no reason why it wouldn't have been) then there must be some 2nd ed. text to make that clear.
Which means, according to official 2nd edition rules the 9-2 may not rally the remaining units if he didn‘t self-rally first?

Which means, according to official 2nd edition rules the 9-2 may not rally the remaining units if he didn‘t self-rally first?

I didn't say that.  I am NRBH so I can't quote you anything.  I'd be very surprised if the 2nd ed. rules text didn't give the same answer as the 1st ed. Q&A.

There were a very small number of important official 1st ed. Q&A that were left out of the 2nd ed. rules, quite inadvertently, and most of them have been reinserted into the rules via errata.  This one might need to be added to the list.

My point is: don't look for 2nd ed. answers in 1st ed. Q&A.  Some of those 1st ed. Q&A are simply no longer valid, quite deliberately.  The ones that are still valid should be in the text of the 2nd ed. rules (somewhere -- not always in the "most obvious" location).

title: Broken unit in melee?
question: How might a broken unit wind up in melee? The Rout Phase comes before the Close Combat Phase.  Wouldn't a broken unit just rout away from an enemy unit by way of Low Crawl/Interdiction? Or surrender if No Quarter hasn't been established? Or maybe be eliminated for failure to rout.
author: Jgolch
consensus_answer:
If truly in melee... the unit Must attempt to withdraw (-2) and of course is broken (-1).  Ouch.

The CC defensive penalty for being broken is -2, not -1.  Ouch even more.

Also remember that broken units in Melee get one chance to successfully withdraw.  If they fail they are eliminated automatically at the end of the CCPh (A11.16).

replies.body: Units in melee cannot rout away, so broken units remain in Melee and are required to Withdraw instead.

4.4 PORTAGE: A SW may not move by itself; it must be carried or placed on a vehicle by Infantry/Cavalry at some cost to the latter's MF allotment. The various SW portage costs are listed on each SW counter in the form "#PP". Portage cost is assessed per item carried, not distance traveled; even if a unit carries a SW during only one MF expenditure before dropping it, that unit may not recoup the portage cost used for that SW for use in the remainder of its MPh. Otherwise, an unbroken Infantry unit can pick up and drop items at any point in its move provided it has sufficient MF to do so (subject to 4.431 & 4.44). No item can be portaged more than once per phase except as allowed by combined Infantry and vehicle portage within a single phase.

Otherwise I guess recovery is not allowed (although I don't see that explicitely mentioned in the rules)?

A single unit is allowed to possess any number of items, no matter what the total portage cost of those items is.

Of course, if the unit wants to move/advance anywhere, then it needs to have > 0 MF currently available.

The rules quote indicates that the currently-moving unit needs to have sufficient MF available after deducting for all of the PP it has carried in that MPh.  In your case that would be 6 PP (1 LMG + 1 HMG) even though it's not carrying the two items at the same time.  It needs 1 MF available to attempt recovery of the HMG, so I don't think it can have expended any MF prior to the recovery attempt, since 1 MF is all it's got for the entire MPh if the recovery attempt succeeds.  [EXC: if the unit declares CX at the start of its MPh, it has 6 MF less 4 for PP in excess of capacity (capacity being only 2 because it is CX) -- so it can expend 1 MF to attempt recovery and stll have 1 MF available to spend before or after; noting that the recovery attempt will be penalised for being CX].  Of course if the recovery attempt fails the unit is not burdened by those PP and therefore has additional MF available.

Hope that makes sense ....
Ok. So Klas was right, that I have to sum up the PP of all carried SW during the MPh. Thanks for clarification!

E7.401 ... The aircraft repeats this procedure (henceforth referred to as a Strafing Run) in every hex traversed until it occupies the target hex of its initial target. question:
Question about the German SPW 251/16. This weapon system has two flamethrowers mounted to its sides, with a "split" field of fire. This thing is madly overpowered, being able to shoot both of its FTs in one fire phase with possible rate to boot.

The question is, if this vehicle can turn its CA for firing during the DFPh? I'd argue no, because it's not a Gun, hence the rules for pivoting do not apply. Otherwise this vehicle would be able to shoot twice at the same target each fire phase, pivoting like crazy, but taking no penalties because it's a flame thrower. 

How does this work? Thanks!
author: takai
consensus_answer:
Question about the German SPW 251/16. This weapon system has two flamethrowers mounted to its sides, with a "split" field of fire. This thing is madly overpowered, being able to shoot both of its FTs in one fire phase with possible rate to boot.

There is no ROF.  The boxed "2" (note that it's in red) is there to signify that there are two FT which each can make an attack.

The question is, if this vehicle can turn its CA for firing during the DFPh?

Absolutely, unless otherwise prevented (e.g., if the vehicle is Bogged).

Otherwise this vehicle would be able to shoot twice at the same target each fire phase, pivoting like crazy, but taking no penalties because it's a flame thrower.

Yes it can, but why do you believe that there are "no penalties"?  The CA change DRM will penalise the attack.

D3.6 "FT: Vehicular-mounted FT are often more powerful than the Infantry SW variety of A22 and may have more FP, range, and different X# as depicted on the counter, but otherwise work the same [EXC: Motion Fire; 2.42]. Case A To Hit DRM apply as IFT DRM unless using Bounding First Fire (C5.13)."

The Case A DRM apply because the rules specifically say that they apply.  The "Gun" definition doesn't come into it.

replies.body:
I'd played it that it can turn, but now I'm unsure if that's actually allowed by the rules. If only Guns can change their CA, a vehicle using the IFE of its weapon couldn't turn, either.

Definition of Gun: for firing purposes, any weapon on a 5/8" counter currently firing as ordnance; for non-firing purposes, any non-vehicular weapon on a 5/8" counter.

Otherwise this vehicle would be able to shoot twice at the same target each fire phase, pivoting like crazy, but taking no penalties because it's a flame thrower.

Yes it can, but why do you believe that there are "no penalties"?  The CA change DRM will penalise the attack.

D3.6 "FT: Vehicular-mounted FT are often more powerful than the Infantry SW variety of A22 and may have more FP, range, and different X# as depicted on the counter, but otherwise work the same [EXC: Motion Fire; 2.42]. Case A To Hit DRM apply as IFT DRM unless using Bounding First Fire (C5.13)."

The Case A DRM apply because the rules specifically say that they apply.  The "Gun" definition doesn't come into it.

If only Guns can change their CA, a vehicle using the IFE of its weapon couldn't turn, either.

Firstly, (ordnance-armed) vehicles are Guns.  (That includes vehicles whose MA is a MG.)

C2.1 "GUNS/SW: Any ordnance-capable weapon depicted on a ⅝" counter is termed a Gun ... The rules that follow are also applicable to vehicular-mounted Guns."

Secondly, IFE is explicitly covered:

D3.52 "Any BMG/CMG/IFE firing outside its current respective CA must add a DRM to its IFT DR equal to the pertinent To Hit DRM of Case A (Bow MG = NT, CMG = T or ST depending on Gun Type; 1.3)."

Thirdly, as explained above, the Gun definition is irrelevant.

Thanks for the answers, that's very helpful.

Applying the Case A modifier for changing CA makes a lot of sense, that really puts a dent in the attacking firepower, and makes the weapon less powerful.

I think the rules on Ordnance and Guns definitions are not clear. The index defines Ordnance as:

Any weapon which must score a hit on a To Hit Table before rolling again on the IFT or To Kill Table to resolve that hit.

That clashes with C2.1 which mentions "ordnance-capable" weapons. One wight well argue that since a FT is not ordnance, the vehicle carrying it is not ordnance-capable, hence not a Gun.

It's a minor point, but I wish the rulebook was less recursive and more concise here.

I think the rules on Ordnance and Guns definitions are not clear.

Seems extremely clear to me.  Does it (or can it) make a TH roll?  Is it on a 5/8" counter?  Yes to both, it's a Gun.

 The index defines Ordnance as:

Any weapon which must score a hit on a To Hit Table before rolling again on the IFT or To Kill Table to resolve that hit.

That clashes with C2.1

No it doesn't.  The ordnance definition defines ordnance.  C2.1 defines Guns.  Being "ordnance" is only part of the definition of being "a Gun".  A BAZ is ordnance, but it is not a Gun (unless it's mounted on a vehicle).  FT are never ordnance, because there is no circumstance in which a FT needs to make a TH DR.

One wight well argue that since a FT is not ordnance, the vehicle carrying it is not ordnance-capable, hence not a Gun.

One would be silly to argue otherwise (assuming no other ordnance-capable weapons), because it isn't a Gun.  Again, the definition makes that crystal clear.

I really don't know what your point is, or why you're obsessed with FT maybe or maybe not being Guns (they're not, and it doesn't matter for any purpose).

Also take note that, during Defensive Firt Fire, if a unit enters your hex in the MPh (e.g. a Berserk unit) the FT that can fire is the one that includes the hexside crossed by the moving unit in its CA.
During the DFPh, both FTs may fire in their own hex (although they cannot form a FG).
Yes, it's a pretty intimidating vehicle but, in practice, one very difficult to use. It draws a lot of fire and it must get so close to the enemy to attack that survival is not guaranteed.

title: Close Combat with AFV and Ambush
question:
We had a hard time figuring this one out, not sure if we played it correctly. 

A Russian 6-2-8 advances into a building hex with a King Tiger  and a concealed officer.

We roll for ambush, the Russians get ambushed.

The Tiger uses the Nahverteidigungswaffe, but rolls a 10, so no effect.

The German leader could now withdraw, but choses to stay, not attacking, keeping his concealment.

Since its sequential, the Russian squad now attacks the Tiger and misses.

Tiger is next, attacking with the CMG for a FP of 5, which is equal to the Russian CCV of 5, German rolls a 5, casualty reduction for the Russian squad.

The Russian Squad now attacks the officer, who is concealed for 1:1, misses.

Did we play that correct?
author: takai
consensus_answer:
Looking at the QRDC table, I would say he is not "alone", but the more detailed table in A11.4 states "...alone (A10.7)". 

So, flip over to A10.7 and...it is not a great help because it does not define "alone". However, the phrase "...influence another Personnel unit's performance" suggests to me that in this case he is "alone" because there are no other friendly Personnel with performance for him to influence.

Put it on the list for 3rd edition?

replies.body: The Russian squad can only attack once per CCPh.

We had a hard time figuring this one out, not sure if we played it correctly. ... Since its sequential

It's not sequential.  A11.32 "Whenever one side ambushes another, the ambushing side resolves all of its CC attacks in that Location first, until a Melee develops in the next Player Turn."

(Also, note that normally the sN can only be used to attack after the Tiger has itself been attacked; the Ambush negates that limitation.)

Tiger is next, attacking with the CMG for a FP of 5, which is equal to the Russian CCV of 5, German rolls a 5, casualty reduction for the Russian squad.

The squad is eliminated, because the Tiger has a -1 DRM for Ambush.

And, as noted, why did you think that the Russian squad was eligible for two attacks?  Personnel in CC can never make more than a single attack.

Now let's back it up a bit, too.

Did the Russian squad have to pass a PAATC before advancing in?

Hard luck for the Russians to get ambushed. Did you remember the +2 Vehicle & +1 BU Ambush drm? Was either infantry unit Stealthy or Lax?
I have to admit that I am not clear if the Leader's DRM can be added to the Ambush roll because I do not know if the lack of other infantry make him "alone" (I would side with "alone" because the AFV cannot use his DRM).

Now into the CC. It was a gutsy move having the leader stay, because he was going to risk the sN9 friendly fire.

Otherwise, I have nothing to add to what others have posted.

Hard luck for the Russians to get ambushed. Did you remember the +2 Vehicle & +1 BU Ambush drm? Was either infantry unit Stealthy or Lax?

Well, the concealed leader gives a -2 drm as well; a net +1 makes an Ambush win for the Germans less likely but by no means improbable.  I've lost count of the number of times when I've been ambushed with even much better odds in my favour.

I have to admit that I am not clear if the Leader's DRM can be added to the Ambush roll because I do not know if the lack of other infantry make him "alone" (I would side with "alone" because the AFV cannot use his DRM).

It's a good question, but there's no specific game definition of "alone" as used in the Ambush modifiers so one is forced to fall back on the standard English meaning, and in that case the presence of the vehicle means that the Leader is not "alone".  I would not grumble, however, if MMP were to rule according to your interpretation.

Looking at the QRDC table, I would say he is not "alone", but the more detailed table in A11.4 states "...alone (A10.7)". 

So, flip over to A10.7 and...it is not a great help because it does not define "alone". However, the phrase "...influence another Personnel unit's performance" suggests to me that in this case he is "alone" because there are no other friendly Personnel with performance for him to influence.

Put it on the list for 3rd edition?

Thanks for the great feedback.

I had another question about the leader: does he keep concealment? This is covered in A11.19:

A unit loses its concealment in the CCPh only if it makes/directs a CC attack [EXC: a successful Ambush; 11.4] or suffers Casualty Reduction.
Correct.

title: Human Wave Attacks
question:
As I've read elsewhere in the forums, the Human Wave rules are kind of dense. I am having a hard time figuring out what the purpose of some of the specifics are, although I'm sure there's a perfectly logical explanation for why they're written the way they are. Here's the way I interpret 25.23 to 25.233. 

1. Pick a target hex
2. Pick the HW participants (at least 3 hexes and an average of 2 per hex, plus the leader from one of the hexes). 

3. The HW participants move toward the target hex in impulse fashion as per the rules with each using movement cost of the unit that has to expend the most MF. 

4. Each HW unit can move into a forward/side hex headed toward the target hex but in the process will  move into another forward/side hex containing a (armed, non disrupted) KEU but no (armed) friendly unit. 

I know in this description I'm leaving out lots of little details such as no HW participant can be guarding prisoners. 

Also, I don't understand the point of the whole range aspect (25.2321). Does it just mean that no HW participant can move in a way that increases the number of hexes from the unit to the target hex? 

I also don't get the purpose of the direction counters. Just move toward the target hex would seem to be the logical thing to do. What have I missed (I'm sure it's something). 

What have I gotten wrong about all of this?
author: jchron
consensus_answer:
IMO, if there's one thing that players new to Human Waves miss when reading the rules is that necessity to select a single (alternate) hex grain that defines the direction that the HW will move in.  A lot of folks think that "direction" is being defined for multiple hex grains simultaneously.  There is only one hex grain used to define direction.  All movement in the HW is either (a) towards that single hex grain; (b) parallel to that hex grain; or (c) away from that hex grain (which is limited in that the placing of the range counter means that you can't keep moving away).

To put it another way, while a HW can operate as multiple units moving in parallel, it will tend to converge on a point, with very limited ability to diverge away from that point.  The reason why you select a hex grain and not a single target hex is to avoid the problem of multiple units all trying to squeeze in to the same target Location; the HW thus has restrictions in the way it operates but retains some flexibility.

As JR points out, the reason the current HW rules seem a little ... mechanical ... in their operation is because the original HW rules barely defined anything, meaning that the HW could mean whatever you wanted it to mean, leading to general confusion.  Hence the point of the updated rules was to try and make sure that everything was defined.  The original rules were so poor that most players probably never, ever bothered performing a HW with Russian troops (thus depriving themseles of a potentially valuable tool); when the Japanese were introduced the Banzai ability made a lot of people take another look at the rules and really notice their limitations -- or alternately kept on ignoring them and never did a Banzai charge either, which seriously limits the effectiveness of Japanese troops.

title: Truck Road 1/2 [BU:1]
question: On B. TERRAIN CHART it implies that a truck can be BU yet I thought that CE/BU for road movement rates was only applicable to AFVs? So a truck must be CE to get the 1/2 MP rate? Isn't a truck unarmored and automatically CE? I'm confused.
author: recruit2112
consensus_answer:
Without cracking open the tome, I will give this answer. The chart shows you Truck type movement rate (i.e. the conjoined white dots behind the MP on the counter), not the rate for something that is a truck. So, it is possible for some AFV to use the Truck rate.

Now to crack open the Tome: look at D1.15 and you will see the Russian BA-20 is an AFV that uses the Truck rate.

OK, so some armored cars are actually trucks because of a truck drive train. Interesting distinction that Greenwood put in there.

Truck and truck movement type are two different things. There are AFV that have a truck movement type (i.e. they use the truck column of the Terrain Chart) but they are not "trucks". They are AFV and go CE/BU like an AFV.
As you probably already now, check the movement type symbol behind the MP valus. If you have two "wheels" that vehicle expends MP as a truck, but it is its armored/unarmored status that counts for CE/BU purposes.

title: German SPW 251/2
question: I have a question about the SPW 251/2 (the Half-track carrying the German 81mm mortar).  The chapter H note says to treat it as a normal OT SP gun for To Hit purposes.  Does it still have to use area fire like a normal mortar, or can it use direct fire and use the infantry target type?
author: shoes03
consensus_answer:
That's ... a really perceptive question, actually.  There is no rule that I could find that says "a MTR mounted on a vehicle must obey all of the normal rules applicable to MTRs (C7.345, C9, etc.)".  Indeed German Vehicular Note 59 kind of implies the opposite.  I believe that the intent behind that note is "treat it as a normal vehicular weapon (that can only fire on the Area Target Type, has a minimum range, etc.)" but it is true that this is not what it actually says.

Certainly I've never played them any other way, nor have I ever heard of them being played any other way.  This is I think an example of the rules forgetting to spell out something because "everybody just knows".

The equivalent US vehicles (Notes 31-33) don't even get the blanket statement applicable to the German vehicles [EXC: The M4A1 gets a "treated as a normal NT AFV" comment].  Ditto for the MTR-armed Carriers (British Vehicle Notes 66-67).

So, um, yeah.  There ought to be some errata added somewhere (not sure where would be best -- probably C9, rather than add an errata item to multiple individual vehicles) -- but MMP have historically been very reticent to add errata for stuff that "everyone already knows already", so good luck with that ....

title: Rulebook ... Pocket Edition or Binder version
question:
Greetings all,

I am about to buy Beyond Valor and have the first 3 starter kits.

The Binder version of the Rulebook is Temporarily Not Available, But the Pocket Edition is.

From what I have read, the Pocket Edition does not have everything the Binder version has. What is NOT in the Pocket Edition? 

I am trying to decide if I should wait to buy the Binder Version when it becomes available?

Thanks!

Regards,

JB
author: gmdjeb
consensus_answer:
Well, this has been answered in many other threads.  A little time searching would answer your questions very comprehensively.

The Pocket edition does not have Chapters H, J or K.

The Pocket edition does not have 99.9% of the charts and tables required for play.

The Pocket edition does not have the binder's summary display of different counter types and what the various factors and markings represent.

However:

The Pocket edition does come with Chapter F, currently otherwise unavailable.

The Pocket edition does come with Chapter G, otherwise available only in Rising Sun (which is currently unavailable).

The Pocket edition does include all of the replacement pages for Chapters A-G from various products (which are mostly otherwise unavailable, although several of the replacement pages are available for download from the MMP site).  This includes the replacement pages provided in H-P (at the time of writing, no more recent replacement pages for these chapters have been released).

The Pocket edition does include a summary of all of the errata applicable for Chapters A-G.  This list covers up to ASL Journal #10 (more errata has subsequently been provided in #11 and #12).  Note that the errata is listed, it is not integrated into the text (so you still have to do your own manual markups).  Note also that no errata for anything other than these chapters is provided -- for the "complete" listing you need to hunt around the MMP website (it's not very well organised).

Therefore: the Pocket edition cannot in any reasonable sense be considered a replacement for the full ASL rules binder.  It is, however, an excellent supplement to the rules binder and is strongly recommended as such.

Welcome to the hobby!

Two things that might push you toward getting the pocket rulebook:

MMP's estimates on when things will come out are usually wrong by a factor of 2. Not to rag on MMP, by the way, this is a near-universal characteristic of human beings. But "some time this summer" actually means more like "probably in 2019".

Also, are you planning on playing more face-to-face, or through VASL? VASL has the most important charts either built in (IFT, TH/TK, concealment), or freely available through extensions (Terrain, OBA). So if you are playing through VASL only, then you don't need the charts.

Someone will correct me if I'm wrong, but I can't remember having to use a physical chart in a good long while, but almost all of my play is through VASL.

Two things that might push you toward waiting:

You will need to buy the full rulebook eventually to get Chapter H for the Russians and Germans. That's a sine qua non. As folks have said, you can get away with playing infantry-only for a while, but that will scratch your itch for only so long.

Getting F and G in the pocket rulebook probably isn't that big a deal, since for Desert or Pacific scenarios, you are going to need the counters for them, and the rules come along with those counters. Although if you play VASL only, then you already have the counters, so maybe F and G will do you some good on their own.

title: VBM and Level 1
question:
A T34 closed top is using VBM around a building (remains in motion) with a squad at Level 1 (second floor).  

From reading rules and FAQ this is my interpretation.

If the T34 is CE then the squad can use TPBF and therefore can only fire at the tank.

If the T34 is BU then the squad has no valid target and therefore can fire at more distant hexes.

Am I wrong on this?  Thanks.
author: nekengren
consensus_answer:
Yes, you have interpreted the rules (A7.212) correctly.

Note that this is a special case of the usual rule (more commonly known as "VBM freeze"). (I.E., the vehicle is at ground-level with vulnerable PRC and the enemy infantry is in a higher-level Location within the same hex.)

If the vehicle and the infantry were at the same level, the infantry is prevented from firing at a different Location even if the vehicle has no vulnerable PRC (the more usual example of "the freeze").

title: M3 75mm vs 76mm M1
question: New to ASL. From what I gather in the rules, the only thing that matters for the HE TK# is the caliber. Is that correct? That seems way off for almost all American AT guns as the 76mm M42 projectile had much less TNT than the 75mm M48 projectile due to its much higher velocity. Am I missing something?
author: heinz_guderian
consensus_answer:
Essentially they are saying the only thing that matters is the size of the HE round and that the ratio of propellent to explosive is always constant - and that is patently false. There are plenty of other HE rounds that would not conform to that blanket treatment. As a retired armor officer, I must say this is really befuddling...

Just wait until you examine the destructive power of a Goliath vs. the destructive power of an AVRE mortar round vs. the destructive power of a shell from the Stürmtiger -- and then compare the real-world weight of explosives used in each.

Also consider the amount of HE that you can throw at an (ordinary) building -- e.g., by repeatedly firing 75mm rounds into it -- and yet the chances of the building rubbling or catching fire are usually tiny.  (Also not forgetting that there is one and only one way of breaching a wall or hedge -- the afore-mentioned AVRE -- and yet there are a few ways of breaching bocage.)

You can use a DC to blow a hole in the exterior wall of a fortified building -- or the interior wall of a rowhouse -- but not to blow a hole in the exterior wall of an ordinary building.

There are plenty of weirdnesses in the ASL rules if you want to find them, and they're all there for the sake of "keeping the regular game moving".  Everything is abstracted.

There are lots of folks that claim that ASL is "very realistic".  Sadly, even though most of those folks are fans of the game, they're quite mistaken.  ASL is the ultimate embodiment of "design for effect" and any time some particular rule fills you with rage for being contrary to your understanding of How Things Work -- just remember, if you enjoy the game, just roll with it.  If you're not enjoying the game, there are many alternatives that may suit you better.

ASL is a realistic abstraction of a 1950-60's war movie

I deleted my ignored post to ask again to the nomenclature being discussed.

76M42 and 75M48? What are you referring to? Round or gun or other maybe? Thoughts fly in vacuums.

Gun. 76 is the diameter of the projectile in millimeters. 42 is the length of the barrel in centimeters. With just those specifications, I know alot about a gun. The larger the diameter, the heavier the shot. Mass = damage. The longer the barrel the greater the exit velocity of the round. Velocity = penetration and range. All guns transfer energy to a projectile. e=mv^2. I'm simplifying here, but the objective of an HE round is to inflict damage by packing explosive that detonates at the point of impact. The more explosive you have, the more damage you cause on soft targets. A spherical object is the most efficient container for volume/mass. That's why early cannons were ball shots. As we moved into the modern era, AP rounds became darts, often discarding most of the projectile after firing. We refer to these as subcaliber rounds. You maximize penetration by packing a ton of energy in a projectile across a tiny diameter. This results in massive concentrations of energy across a tiny surface area at the point of impact (tank armor). Modern AP rounds don't even need an explosive because the splay of the penetrated armor is usually sufficient to wipe out everything in the crew compartment. ASL unfortunately, doesn't do a particularly good job of modelling any of this despite hundreds of pages of rules.

James M. McHaffey
LTC, USA (Ret)

Interesting, does M equate to L here (ie. barrel length) and in what platforms were they each used? 

In the US nomenclature system, "M" stands for "Model" and the number is usually the iteration of that model of "thing", where "thing" is a different type of equipment.  If further specification is required then a "A#" would be added.  Hence, when looking at US halftracks, you get stuff like:

M2 -- a standard model of halftrack
M3 -- a new standard model of halftrack (i.e., a new chassis etc.)
M3A1 -- that same chassis but with changes to the standard body
M3A2 -- same chassis again but with new changes to the standard body

and so on.

Note that every different thing gets its own "M#", but that "M#" is only unique to that specific type of thing.  So there's an M4 Sherman and an M4 halftrack -- obviously very different items of equipment.  Or with an even finer combing, you have the M3 Light Tank and the M3 Medium Tank -- again, very different things.

How the nomenclature system was applied to different types of ammunition I don't specifically know, but I'm pretty sure it wouldn't have anything in particular to do with the gun that fired that ammunition.

title: Concealment moving in open
question:
should be an easy question but after reading the rules and all the FAQ I am still not sure......................

A concealed squad moves from a building to the open.  one hex.  neither hex is in LOS of the enemy.  The enemy is 3 hexes away behind some other buildings.

Do I keep concealment?
author: nekengren
consensus_answer:
So, to be clear:  A unit assault moving within LOS AND into open ground does lose concealment, right?  (Absent snow and winter camo rules, of course.)

Yes.  Remember, however, that "open ground" is relative to the observer; more specifically, it's only "open ground" if the unit could be affected by the -1 FFMO DRM if it was being fired upon.  A normal hindrance, for instance, between the observer and the target is sufficient to prevent the application of FFMO and therefore the unit would not be in "open ground" for purposes of concealment loss.

This is all spelled out in A10.531.

This applies even if the unit is only in open ground "momentarily". title: Flamethrowers and FFMO
question:
I couldn't find (though it might be somewhere in the forum) an answer to this stipulation/question concerning FFMO and FTs.

A22.2 DRM states that, in general, TEM does not apply to FT attacks.

FFMO is defined as being applied as a -1 DRM to an IFT attack during defensive fire unless combined with an *effective protective* TEM.

If a FT fires at a unit moving through a hex with no TEM, the -1 would apply.

If a FT fires at a unit moving through a hex with a TEM of +2, e.g. wooden building, would the FFMO -1 modifier be directly applied and the TEM ignored?  

Since, according to A22.2, TEM does *not* apply to FT attacks, it would not be considered "effective protective TEM" and therefore *not* affect the -1 FFMO modifier.

For Orchard, B14.3 states that is has no TEM, but is treated as non-open ground so subsequently negates FFMO.

Hmmm, special disturbing case for Orchard, or hint at precedent that TEM is 
*not* ignored and therefore does affect FT attacks, negating the FFMO -1 and adding the TEM of the terrain occupied, such as +2 for a wooden building?

What say ye?
author: GamerKirk
consensus_answer:
OK, to address your points, though you haven't gone completely point to point to show where any of my 1-4 steps is incorrect ;) ...

Rule 10.531 fails on two accounts, one is that it is circularly defined, being effectively wherever one could apply the -1 FFMO is considered open ground, and wherever there is open ground is where we apply the -1 FFMO, which is actually the crux of what we are trying to determine and so therefore of no help.  

Secondly, this rule applies to "rout determination, Dash, concealment gain/loss, and Interdiction", no mention of attacks on the IFT and certainly not helpful specifically for FT attacks.

I have two rulebooks, the "latest" being the pocketbook 2nd edition purchased less than one year ago with no errata indicated for Index item Open Ground which references A4.6 which states: 

"A further -1 First Fire DRM applies to units moving in the open (FFMO), but whenever such movement is combined with another effective protective TEM or LOS hindrance feature (such as SMOKE or an AFV/wreck) between the target and firer or in the target Location itself, the -1 FFMO DRM does not apply."

So, points 1-4 still hold, being rephrased as...

Against FT attacks a unit moving does not have access to a TEM modifier A22.2, a lack of "effective protective" TEM defines the movement to be in open ground as per A4.6, without such TEM, the open ground FFMO modifier is applied and there is no TEM as per the A22.2 aforementioned:

"DRM:  FT attacks vs. non-Armored units are resolved on the IFT but receive no DRM due to leadership/heroism or defender's TEM except for non-CA attacks on a pillbox (B30.113), LOS hindrances and the +1 DRM for CX usage apply to IFT attacks."

So I am becoming more convinced that players are applying TEM to FT attacks, as respondents hint that they are presently doing, to avoid applying the -1 FFMO, but then somehow at that point forward deciding not to apply it any more to the attack, effectively deciding on their own that the TEM *does* apply to prevent FFMO, but *doesn't* apply to enable the moving unit to benefit from the TEM due to the terrain. 

I have yet to see any answer be able to justify the use of the rules in this way and so suspect that I am correct in my reading, but it goes against current accepted play for some reason.

title: FFNAM and FFMO
question:
Question for the ASL-smart people: What drm apply here?  A squad IN a depression spent 2 MF (and no other MF) to gain Crest Status. They are now at level 0 and in LOS of an enemy unit who take a DFF shot. Do the -1 FFNAM and FFMO apply?  There is no other terrain in the gully hex. Are those 2MF considered spent in LOS so for example a MG could take 2 DFF shots if it kept ROF?

Thanks!
author: YankeeGrunt
consensus_answer: Barring other terrain in the hex, gullies are considered Open Ground (B19.3), with various LOS oddities. It sounds like you have LOS, so it is OG.

replies.body:

Both MF would count as movement within LOS for defensive fire. But if they are pinned by the first shot the FFNAM -1 would no longer apply as they are considered to be no longer moving.

Hope that helps.

Crest status would void the FFMO -1. 

Crest status would void the FFMO -1 as long as the unit qualifies for Crest TEM.

title: Foxholes
question:
In this particular scenario I’m trying to play, the SSR indicates that the Russians may set up in foxholes; however, there is not any mention in the OB or SSR about total allowed squad capacity. Im assuming that because the SSR indicates units may set up in foxholes, they don’t need to make Entrenching Attempts for these. author: sblois
consensus_answer: No. every infantry russian can set up in foxhole means that Squad and half squad would set up in 1 capacity Foxhole, SMC will get 1 capacity foxhole, and if you set up more than one squad you will get 2 or 3 capacity foxhole. It doesn't mean you get a number of foxhole equal to the number of squad equivalents. it just mean that if you set up infantry in suitable location, that infantry may set up in foxhole.

title: BPV Allotment Quwstion
question:
What is the typical total BPV allotment for each side In a DYO scenario using 1 board, 2 boards, 3 boards, etc.

By year, per opponent (Germany v Russia) (German v France, etc) Britain vs Italy/ Germany, USA v Germany

Just want to get an average sense before I start a DYO game.
author: Leeds
consensus_answer:
There is no "typical allotment".  The DYO system in ASL has never been subject to much analysis or criticism because the vast majority of players never make any use of it, preferring to play prepared scenarios instead.

It's a fairly straight-forward system to use, but it will generate some weird results (e.g., if you purchase assault engineers you will get a truly staggering number of DCs and FTs).  Some nationalities get heavily penalised in terms of numbers of leaders and basic SW while others might end up with more gear than they can easily carry.  It's difficult to get "balanced" forces as a consequence, and that's before you consider what the effects of different board combinations can be.

IMO the best way to make the DYO system "work" is for a third-party to adjudicate everything (i.e., determine the board layout, determine the VC, decide on any special rules, etc.).  That person allocates the points to each side who go off and buy their forces (within the conditions specified by the referee).  THEN the referee examines each side and makes adjustments to try and keep each side "reasonable".

It's a lot of trouble to go through and it still won't come close to guaranteeing that the game will be "balanced".  Most of the time, it's just not worth the effort.

title: Sniper activates.  What all happens?
question:
So my Russian Guards inflicted an NMC on a German LMG Squad, but activated the German Sniper with an IFT roll of 6, which then rolls a 1. It moves between a stack of Russian Guards in a Wooden Building on one side and a Russian 9-1 Leader with MMG squad in a Wooden Building on the other side. I understand all things being equal (both have the same TEM) I get to choose.
But, if I chose the Hex with the 9-1, is he eliminated as well as the MMG squad being broken, or is it one or the other.
Or, do I not get to choose and it goes be descending order, SMC is auto-eliminated, if no Leader, then a squad is broken?
author: Fly by Night
consensus_answer:
If you choose the hex with the 9-1 and the MMG-toting squad, you roll Random Selection to see who gets "hit" by the Sniper "1".

If the 9-1 is choosen he dies and the squad might need to take a LLMC.

If the squad is choosen he breaks and nothing happens to the 9-1.

If the Random Selection drs are the same for both, you get to choose which gets the "1". Vs the other you make another Sniper Attack dr (a 1 or 2 will attack the other unit, 3-6 no effect).

title: Sniper Activation Sequence
question:
So the Russians inflicted a 3MC on a German Leader and his LMG Squad in my first game of The Guards Counterattack.  The Leader rolls a 6, which is the Activation number, as does the German LMG Squad.  How is the Sequence resolved?

author: Fly by Night

See last sentence of A14.1:

The Sniper attack occurs after resolving all effects of the DR that activated it, but not before resolving (14.3) all (if any) Sniper attacks made prior to it.

So in your example, all of the MC (and resulting HOB) are rolled first, THEN you do the SAN check.

title: Set-up Clarification
question:
When a scenario card says eg "...set up within 2 hexes of..." does it include the location/s also. I always thought the wording should be "...on or within..." if the location/s themselves were included.

I recently played a scenario which specified the American set up as "...Set up within two hexes of the bridge." The bridge in question was two hex long (but could have been more in a different context). We played it as not setting up on the bridge but this in itself posed further queries with other SSR.

We made a decision not to set up on the bridge and we enjoyed playing the scenario but if the bridge can be included in set up it would result in a different game.
author: csonson
consensus_answer:
In every game I can recall (not just ASL), phrases like "within 2 hexes" mean "within a distance of 2 hexes".

So in the same hex = distance 0 = within 0 hexes; in an adjacent hex = distance 1 = within 1 hex; and distance 2 = within 2 hexes; etc.

In all these distances, the hex itself is certainly within N hexes of itself.

Agreed, and if you did set up on either bridge hex, you would still be setting up within two hexes of it.

title: Scenario card question
question: What do the numbers in the first box of the Turn Record Chart by get nationalities mean? For example, for "The Citadel" you see 'RUSSIAN Sets Up First ' and 'GERMAN Moves First '.  Thank you.
author: Pertinax
consensus_answer:
See A16.1 Integrity Base
The integrity Base is the number of MMC points a side can lose before it must check for Battlefield Integrity. The Integrity Base for each side is 10% (FRU) of the number printed to the left of the Turn 1 box on the Turn Record Chart. In DYO scenarios, players must sum the BPV of all MMC (not inherent crews) in their starting OB and divide by ten (FRU) to determine their Integrity Base.

Remeber the heights of the buildings:

- single story house: 1 level obstacle
- two story house: 1.5 level obstacle
- multi-story building: 2.5 level obstacle

A unit in Level 1 of a two story house is cannot see past other two story houses, as they are 1.5 level obstacle and block the LOS. A unit in a two story house rooftop is at level 1.5 and then it can see past other two stoy houses to another unit in a 1.5 level, for example another rooftop. 

So if you have a city of two story houses and no rooftops available, units on Level 1 of each house do not see each other if there are other houses blocking the LOS. If the units are in the rooftops they see each other.

With a half level gain you don't gain vision over blind hexes, which require full levels.

title: Negative T#
question: The SdKfZ 7 has a PP/T# of 19 PP/T -4. What the heck does a T# of negative 4 mean???
author: heinz_guderian
consensus_answer:
Some Guns have a negative M#.

From memory you need a towing vehicle with a T# equal to or less than the Gun's M# to tow it.

So really, T is for torque (in inverse proportion to the T#).

title: Counter Relationships (Full Squad->HS identiy)
question:
I'm starting ASL and am looking through the Beyond Valor counter sheets.

I'm trying to understand which HS a Squad is reduced to.

Is this conclusion correct?

German Squad, Class E, Identity A  is reduced to:  HS, Class E, Identity A?

And for Class/quality reduction:

German Full Squad, Class E, Identity A, goes down to Full Squad (remains full), 1st Line, Identity A?

But what about Deployment?

German Full Squad, Class E, Identity A, splits into HS, Class E; but I'm not seeing two HS, Class E, Identity A counters. So what counters are used when you deploy from a Full Squad to two HS?

So... Are the first two assumptions correct?  Can you answer the question (third item)

Thanks, John
author: jcoyle
consensus_answer:
The identity does not matter for quality reduction, deploying, etc. You can use any unit of the appropriate type. The identity is used for:
- indicating the locations of hidden units (it may matter sometimes)
- linking acquisition markers to the units that generated them (ordnance and AFVs)

And for making sure you have your collection whole when you start sorting it!

title: Pillbox and Combat
question:
I searched through the whole forum and I clarified some points myself.
There's just somethin more I would be sure of:

1. Units in a Pillbox can fire on enemies in the Pillbox hex only by DFF (SFF/FPF) at the moment they enter the PB hex through PB CA in the MPh, right? 

2. Units in a PB can never fire on units in the PB hex (excepted for the above situation), right?

3. Units in the PB hex can attack units in the PB only through CC in CCPh without previously advancing in the PB (it is not allowed till the PB contains enemy units), or by setting a DC. No fire attacks allowed from the PB hex against the PB, right?

4. Units in the PB can attack units in the PB hex only by CC in CCPh. Do they have to advance outside the PB in the PB hex, or can they remain in the PB and fight CC from inside?

5. Do concealed units in a PB in Open Ground qualify for Ambush roll if attacked? (applying -2 DRM for being concealed and +2 DRM for being in the PB).

6. If they Ambush the attacker, can they withdraw from the PB to an adjacent location outside the PB hex being the hex enemy occupied?

Thanks a lot
author: Qwirz
consensus_answer:
#4 No, they do not need to advance out of the pillbox to engage in CC.

B30.6 "CC is resolved in the normal manner between Infantry units in and outside of a pillbox [EXC: Hand-to-Hand CC is NA; no Melee results (20.1; A11.15)]"

replies.body:
#5 - if any units involved are Concealed, Ambush is a possibility.

Note, however, that CC vs concealed units in a Pillbox does halve the FP.

So if e.g., the units advancing in on the Pillbox are not Concealed (and the Pillbox is not in woods), it might be a good idea to drop Concealment of the units inside the Pillbox, just to avoid the possibility of Ambush.

6 is No.

If they Ambush and kill all he enemy in the PB hex, they could withdraw to the PB hex outside, but not to a different hex.

#1 and #2

B30.2 "Fire from inside a pillbox into its own hex is limited to CC, or SMOKE grenade placement, or a Thrown DC (30.31), or to vertices of its CA, or to PBF vs units currently crossing the CA hexsides of its own hex."

So, if a pillbox was placed in a woods hex and a squad was bypassing the woods using a hexside with a vertex in the pillbox's CA, the units in the pillbox could fire at that bypassing unit from my reading of the rules.

Also, looks like units in a pillbox can throw a DC (and smoke) into the PB hex.

#4 No, they do not need to advance out of the pillbox to engage in CC.

B30.6 "CC is resolved in the normal manner between Infantry units in and outside of a pillbox [EXC: Hand-to-Hand CC is NA; no Melee results (20.1; A11.15)]"

Thanks all!
6 is No.
.

author: phxhf
consensus_answer:
Last lines of D8.1
"After all passengers /riders/SW/Guns have been unloaded/unhooked an unarmed/unarmored vehicle is flipped over to its wreck side...."

title: How I (mis)interpret A11.2 Infiltration, or how I would like it to be. A useless-or-not analisys of that dark paragraph.
question:
Following my last thread.

So the TWO rolled by Infiltration rule looks like a real benefit ONLY if rolled by the ATTACKER and, being a roll low enough to harm (eliminate etc...) his enemies, it looks like a mean to advance one location more during CC. Was this the real intent of this rule?
I'm not completely convinced on this. Why Infiltration should advantage the ATTACKER more than the DEFENDER?
If this was the intent I think the rule would have been written using more likely the terms ATTACKER and DEFENDER in capital letter. It would have been much more clearer. The fact it is not so, makes me having some doubts. And going deeper into the words makes my doubts growing.
The matter is only about the DR of TWO, the 12 is easier because being implemented by the enemy units, can take less into account the "dice roll sequence".
I don't know Who wrote this rule in the depth of time, but I THINK it was made to give some more unpredictabilty to CC and a chance to survive for the poor hopeless units attacking with low odds.
The following analisys can be quite useless, having Klas already kindly answered to my questions and Alan pointed me to an interesting article, but you are welcome to spend two minutes in reading it.

A11.22 INFILTRATION
"The simultaneous nature of CC is momentarily suspended following an Original CC DR of 2/12."....
It makes no references to ATTACKER or DEFENDER, so if either make one of those rolls, CC is not simultaneous anymore, and, I THINK this means the 2 or 12 take the precedence on the "other" results: If the ATTACKER rolls a 12, the DEFENDER can withdraw before rolling his dice, if the ATTACKER rolls a 2, he can withdraw before the DEFENDER rolls his dice. In the majority of the CCs the ATTACKER would eliminate the DEFENDER with the 2, and, having he advanced in the now CC location most likely with favorable odds, why should he take/hope-in the benefit of Infiltration? To "jump off" the enemy unit? It could be, but the chances to roll 2 are too low to rely on this. It looks like the infiltration following the 2 DR has been tought for the DEFENDER, not for the ATTACKER, allowing he (the DEFENDER) to withdraw from desperate CCs.
..."Provided it has not been eliminated/captured/pinned, any Infantry/Cavalry unit which rolls an Original 2 CC DR may withdraw from CC/Melee immediately thereafter in the same CCPh without being attacked...."
This is the tricky part. IF the simultaneous nature has been suspended, as stated above, the unit which rolls 2 cannot have been "already" eliminated, so it looks like this line refers to the 11.3 sequential CC provisions. Otherwise there are some contraddictions: Note that the words "without being attacked" and "provided it has not been eliminated[...]" are in contrast if this rule takes into account only the ATTACKER DR rolled before the DEFENDER's: - if the ATTACKER eliminates the DEFENDER and the DEFENDER rolls 2, the DEFENDER "has been eliminated" but he can withdraw "without being attacked". But the DEFENDER was already been "attacked" rolling he after the ATTACKER. So why write this rule this way? You can answer that "without being attacked" refers only to the fact that if the ATTACKER rolls its 2 he can withdraw before the DEFENDER rolls its dice, but in this case it is not possible he(the ATTACKER) "has already been eliminated" since no dice are rolled by the DEFENDER yet. So again,  why write this rule this way? 
Further thoughts: assuming that to implement the 2 result the DEFENDER should have not been already eliminated, what is the real benefit in withdrawing, since in the most cases this low roll harms (eliminates etc...) the enemy leaving him in the location with no/less enemies?
The common interpretation makes this rule giving more the benefit of moving one location further in CCPh, more than allowing units to save themselves, as I noted above. But if this is the intent, why use the word "withdraw" instead of "move, advance or better INFILTRATE"?
Last note: A11.3 SEQUENTIAL CC begins with the words: "There are three OTHER (my capital) instances in which CC is not considered simultaneous"... Doesn't this should mean the preceding paragraph is about one OTHER instance of sequential CC?

Perhaps my english knowledge is confusing my understanding of the rule, perhaps not.
With only 40 games under my belt, I have most likely not experienced all the application of this rule. 
Feel free to point out all my misinterpretation. 
Be merciful.
Thanks for your time.
author: Qwirz
consensus_answer:
Just to point out that even though CC is normally simultaneous, the rules are clear that the ATTACKER does roll/resolve his attacks first - so, yes, the ATTACKER does have an advantage in that regards.

A11.12:
"...Barring sequential CC, each side in a Location must designate all of its attacks in that Location prior to the resolution of any of them (ATTACKER designating his first). The DEFENDER then designates all of his attacks, after which the ATTACKER resolves all of his previously declared attacks. The DEFENDER then resolves all of his attacks—even if those units have been eliminated, Reduced, or captured...."

title: A very important question about Infiltration and CC
question:
Hi all!
American CCPh. A 6/6/6 squad advanced in a foxhole with a lone German 8-1 leader.
No ambush location. USA: 6-1. It rolls 5/3. German leader eliminated(black to kill number is ten).
German:1-6. It rolls......1/1!!!! (black to kill number is two!)
Now.
The German leader is able to withdraw. And he would do it.
Is the American squad eliminated as well?
In the Infiltration pargraph it states a unit which rolls 2 can withdraw "even if it did not eliminate the enemy" (I'm going by heart, NRBH). Does this mean that a unit can both eliminate the enemy AND retreat?
Why in the first lines is stated that a unit can withdraw "if it was not eliminated/pinned/captured"? Does this refer only to sequential CC?
a) both units are eliminated being USA the attacker and so the eight was rolled before the two(though infiltration would not mean so much....)
b) German leader withdraws and no other result is implemented
c) German leader withdraws AND American squad is eliminated
Hope I was not too confusing.....
author: Qwirz
consensus_answer:
The German leader is dead, and the American squad is Casualty Reduced down to a HS.

A11.22:
"...Provided it has not already been eliminated/captured/pinned, any Infantry/Cavalry unit which rolls an Original 2 CC DR may withdraw from CC/Melee immediately thereafter in the same CCPh without being attacked, even if it did not eliminate the defenders (see also Field Promotions; 18.12)..."

The German leader had already been eliminated when he rolled the 2 - hence he can't Withdraw.

I'm sorry, but that's not true.

D6.1 "Any vehicle capable of transporting a Passenger has its carrying capacity printed on the counter in the form '#PP'.  For Passenger purposes, a squad equals 10 PP, a HS/Crew five PP, and <= 4 SMC equal 0 PP. Thus a vehicle with Transport Capacity can carry any combination of MMC/SW, provided the transport's PP capacity is not exceeded."

(My emphasis.)

Thus the rule is stating that (a) you can transport SW (as well as people); (b) the limit to the amount of SW that can be transported is based on the PP capacity of the vehicle; (c) therefore you have to be able to add up the PP of the SW to work out how much you can carry.  How do I know how many PP a SW is worth?  It's printed on the SW counter, which you learned very early in your ASL career way (long before you ever picked up a vehicle counter) back in A4.4.

All of what Klas says above is correct.

The limitation on the vehicle's movement is based on the number of hexes that the accompanying infantry could have moved (and nothing to do with how many they actually moved).

The question of "could have moved" takes into account everything affecting the infantry units' movement.  Did they declare CX at the start of the move?  Are they eligible to declare CX during their move (and would that get them 1 hex further if they did)?  Is there a path of 1MF hexes that the infantry could have legitimately taken?  Were they eligible for road bonus?  It includes negative things as well, e.g., if they were eligible for road bonus, but only if they moved up a hill along the road, then you have to factor that movement cost in too.

It's only the number of hexes (the range) that limits the AFV's movement.  The AFV expends MP in the normal manner and can do anything it likes so long as it does not exceed the range imposed by the infantry.  As Klas mentions, a moving vehicle must expend all of it's MP in some manner, even if they're mostly spent in Delay.

EX: An AFV and an infantry leader and squad start the MPh stacked together and declare Armored Assault.  The infantry do not declare Double-Time at the start of movement.  They are not in a road hex.  So: regardless of where they actually go, and regardless of how many MF they actually spend, the infantry have a potential of 7 MF available to them (6 for the leader and one for potential late CX.)  What you do is count the maximum number of hexes that the infantry could move, based on their current situation -- the direction they move is unimportant, you are only considering what is possible given the terrain they are in.  That might be 7 hexes, or it might be less.  Whatever the number is, that's the number of hexes that the vehicle is limited to.  That number of hexes is the only limitation on the vehicle; it can expend MP however it likes, performing whatever activities are legally available to it, so long as it does not travel more than the hex limit.

Note also that there is no requirement that the vehicle and infantry actually move stacked together.  Once the Armored Assault has been declared, the range limitation on the AFV is in effect.  (Obviously once they separate the infantry no longer get the TEM for the vehicle!)

No.  Why would it?  The only limitation on the vehicle's movement is the range limit imposed by the infantry's theoretical movement.

Now: in a hypothetical situation where the infantry and the vehicle are in a hex completely surrounded by enemy units: the infantry would be able to move a grand total of 0 hexes, therefore, if using Armored Assault, that would be the number of hexes that the vehicle can move.  That would make the AA completely pointless, right?  Well, probably -- but if the infantry is armed with a DC, they could use AA to provide some cover while they place the DC on one of the ADJACENT units.  Armored Assault is movement, and "movement" covers more than just entering new hexes.

That´s a neat idea!! Will keep that in mind!! :D
Is there a limit to the number of MMC that can Armored Assault with just one AFV?
No -- normal Location stacking limits apply.  (Of course, if you're overstacked, the penalties for that will negate the defensive benefits of the AA.)

The defensive benefit would still mitigate the negative DRM due to overstacking.
If I wanted to move four squads with a tank, I would have one ride the thing.
But stacking is a very bad idea most of the time - and armored assault usually makes sense when you are expecting enemy fire, so stacking (not speaking of overstacking) and armored assault are mutually exclusive...

title: Two questions about VBM...
question:
Hi All!!!
Two questions during my (first!) VASL game. Scenario 194 The Attempt to Relieve Piper.

1. If the StuH bypasses C2 through C2-B1and C2-D1 is it affected by the FFE2 Blast Area?

2. Per Victory Conditions the Germans must exit (20 VP) ON/BETWEEN 2Z10 and 2P10.
Can the StuH exit bypassing Z10 through Z10-AA10?
 

What is the right route it should move through?
For ex: 
a) from AA10, bypass through Z10-AA11....mah
b) from BB9, bypass AA9-AA10, Z9-AA10, Z10-AA10, Z10-AA11
c) other?
Thanks a lot
author: Qwirz
consensus_answer:
Thanks Brent!!!
Without looking at the rule book:
1. No

Is this because the vehicle actually bypasses C2 (that is NOT part of the blast area) and not B1 that IS part of the Blast Area?

2. I am going to guess that there is not enough counter-thickness-room to permit it to bypass Z10-AA10 (as per D2.3). There seems to be even less room for Z9-AA10. So, I am going with either a) (and I will need to read up on off-board composition of half-hexes) or c), which means you need to somehow overcome bog checks in Z10 (e.g. enter using all movement).

EDIT: I went and read A2.6 (off-board (half)hexes are mirror image) and B13.41-.42 (all MP or half-MP both require a Bog check). If Z10-AA10 is too narrow for bypass, then you also can't bypass the mirror image Z10-AA11. There seems to be no bog-free way of getting into Z10.

I didn't consider counter thickness. But being enough room, is it possible to exit in bypass on the far point of an exit area (being AA10 in this example NOT part of the exit area)?

I didn't consider counter thickness. But being enough room, is it possible to exit in bypass on the far point of an exit area (being AA10 in this example NOT part of the exit area)?

1. If the StuH bypasses C2 through C2-B1and C2-D1 is it affected by the FFE2 Blast Area?

VBM (like infantry bypass) is not some weird mystical location not physically present on the board.  When you are using bypass movement, the unit is still located in a particular hex.  So: is that hex in the blast area, or isn't it?

If there are two possible hexes that the bypassing unit might be located in, you have to state, in advance, which hex the unit is actually in.  There should never be a reason to wonder "just where is that unit?".

So the answer to your question is: since the vehicle is bypassing C2, and C2 is not in the blast area, therefore the vehicle does not enter the blast area.  (The vehicle cannot bypass C2/D1, I assume you mean C1/D1.)

2. Per Victory Conditions the Germans must exit (20 VP) ON/BETWEEN 2Z10 and 2P10.
Can the StuH exit bypassing Z10 through Z10-AA10?

Yes in theory because bypassing Z10 is IN Z10.

No because in reality the StuG has no bypass options on that side of that hex.

What is the right route it should move through?

Um ... move around the woods to Y8 (or bypass Z8 on the Y8/Z8 hexside) and drive off down the road.

Alternatively, drive INTO Z10 and hope you don't bog.

Remember that a bypassing unit is always in the hex of the obstacle that it is bypassing.
The impression that it is moving along a hexside shared by two hexes doesn't mean that it is moving into both hexes.

If the hex is not affected by an FFE, the bypassing unit isn't (even if the hexside that it is moving along belongs to a hex which is).
If the hex of the bypassed obstacle is among the hexes through which the vehicle can exit, exit is legit.

Got it!
Thanks all for your help!

title: CC Vs. Vehicle some clarification needed
question:
Hi all!
We just finished to play J1 Urban Guerrilla, a Great scenario, useful to learn some rules.
I'll describe here a situation and you please clarify if you will.

Hero and two Russian squads(6-2-8, 4-5-8). Advance in a CE motion HT hex (AAMG 3 FP). PAATC passed.
CCPh. A 6-2-8 and the Hero attack first: CCV 6, -1hero DRM, -2 OT, +2 motion. NE. HT attacks : 1.5FP to 4. NE. 4-5-8 attacks: CCV 5, +2 motion, -2OT. NE.
Since the vehicle is in Motion, no one is held in Melee. No markers.
On the ensuing German Turn, during PFPh, the HT, being subject to Target Limitation, fires TPBF on the Russian units in its hex. Halved for being in motion.
A PzVg fires in that hex on ITT. HT crew undergoes a Collateral Attack (though in Motion and not in Melee)
In DFPh Russian units, being subject to Target Limitation, fire TPBF on the HT crew (+2, -1hero DRM).
CCPh, they all repeat the above sequence.
Russian Turn PFPh, squads fire on the HT crew with TPBF and in DFPh HT fires TPBF on the squads.

After a couple of turns, a lot of heroes created and eliminated, the HT is Immobilized in CC and so the russians are marked Melee, although the HT is not actually held in Melee. Does this change something? (+2 Motion DRM apart)? Are the Collateral Attack still the same? Do we handled German fire from outside in the right way?
Please give me all the knowledge you can on the subject.
Thanks for your time.
author: Qwirz
consensus_answer:
Which is why I would not marked the Location in the described situation (because I don't think there is any rule calling for it [granted, I could be missing something]), because should the units remain in that Location until the next Russian APh, the 6-2-8 and the Hero should not be prohibited from advancing.

Well, certainly in the case of concealed units that is correct: A11.15 explicitly states that concealed units are not marked as being in Melee and are free to leave in their next MPh/APh.  If the concealment is lost (for any reason) then the units are immediately locked in Melee if it's already a "Melee Location" but are apparently not otherwise marked or affected.  There's no reference to placement of a CC marker in lieu of the Melee marker.

For units that are not concealed, however, the issue is, there really isn't a general rule about when to place a CC marker, just a handful of specific circumstances.  A15.432 refers to berserk units entering enemy Locations and requiring placement of the CC marker.  A25.233 refers to placement of the markers  during a Human Wave and A25.234 refers to the inability to advance when so marked.  D7.21 refers to the placement following a CC Reaction Fire attack.  (I don't think that the E7.22 placement of a CC marker for Aerial Combat is relevant here.)

D7.22 does add the interesting twist that placement of a CC marker also prevents Non-CC Reaction Fire (I'm sure I've played that wrong in the past!), which is certainly a good reason to not place one if it's not explicitly called for.  This is particularly relevant in Qwirz's example that started this thread.

So I guess I'm wrong in saying you should place one when not explicitly required to, and yet I still think it's a good idea to mark Locations where enemy units are co-habiting.  I guess that I would like a "this is a potential CC Location but this isn't a CC marker" marker!

title: SPW 251/10 - may a passenger half squad fire the ATR?
question:
A couple friends asked this question on Facebook: an SPW 251/10 has a 248 passenger that wants to fire the inherent ATR.  May it do so?  

The Vehicle note for the 251/10 points to US MAVN Z, which in turn says the *crew* may fire the inherent BAZ (ATR) in lieu of firing the MA, and passengers may remove the inherent SW.  However, the same note says a passenger "...can claim possession of it automatically" which muddies the waters.  I think that last bit just refers to an unloading passenger but it provides a narrow window of ambiguity for the hopeful 248.
author: jrtracy
consensus_answer:
6.1 last lines "LMG, PIAT, and Thrown DC are the only SW which can be fired by Passengers [EXC: Desperation attacks by SCW/RCL as per C13.8-81]."
C13.8 "Due to the attendant back last of these weapons, a PF/PFk, BAZ, PSK or RCL may not be fired from inside a vehicle, rubble, pillbox, cave, sewer or building without a Desperation (13.81) penalty".

Actually these rules refer to SW, so to weapons depicted on a 1/2" counter, so I don't think they apply to inherent weapons.
But this thread makes another question arise: Can Passengers fire vehicle inherent weapons????
Is the HT inherent crew able to fire all the inherent weapons, or HS passengers are needed to this???

replies.body:
By way of thinking aloud:

"... can claim possession ..." seems to imply that the 248 does not automatically have possession of the ATR just by being a passenger.

And maybe it cannot "claim possession" outside one of the normal times possession of a SW is obtained:  RPh or MPh (including when unloading).

But that is really by way of analogy with obtaining possession of a non-inherent SW - which might be a bit of a stretch.

Interested in others' views.

title: Burning wrecks and blazes
question:

title: When do you lose concealment?

The situation is as follows: a concealed unit of the ATTACKER is in LOS of only one DEFENDER's concealed unit (no other DEFENDER's unit has a LOS to that ATTACKER's unit), and the DEFENDER decides to not reveal that the unit is not a dummy when the ATTACKER makes a concealment lost action, in this case, the ATTACKER's is shooting at the DEFENDER's. I know that if the attack has no effect nobody loses concealment; if the DEFENDER's is pinned or revealed because the result is PTC or better, both units lose concealment. The question is: does the ATTACKER's unit lose concealment if the DEFENDER's unit gets broken as a result of the shooting, since then it is not a Good Order unit? consensus_answer:

The fact that the concealed unit was real (and presumably Good Order) at the time the attack was made is proven by the result of the attack being sufficient to strip the concealment (demonstrating that it was not a Dummy stack). Case C4 is for Motion fire when you are in motion during the enemy's player turn (as Klas indicates, marked with a 'Motion' counter); otherwise, case C4 applies in your OWN movement phase for 'Non-Stopped' firing.

title: A7.212 example a little clarification needed
question:
Hi all!
I'm about to learn once and for all (I hope!) Reaction Fire, sleaze freeze, VBM etc etc
But the last sentence of the ex is still a bit obscure:
"If the squad were in an upper-level Location and the halftrack were a BU CT AFV, then neither would be restricted by the other."
Why?
Isn't true the rule "Whenever a unit is eligible for TPBF vs Known enemy units, it can attack only those units".
Or the fact that infantry could not harm a BU CT AFV, does not limit infantry target selection?
In this case, does a CT AFV freezes infantry only if CE?
Thanks for your help!
author: Qwirz
consensus_answer:
I think the key is: if you are elligible to attack in TPBF, you cannot attack any other units except for those units. A7.211 reads that only PRC in CE CT AFVs (or OT AFVs no matter BU or CE) are elligible for TPBF, so those units in upper levels would not be forced to attack TPBF a BU CT AFV. And A7.212 reads that 
"A unit does not have the freedom to attack units in other Locations while its own Location is occupied by a Known enemy unit (even if disrupted) unless the only known enemy unit in its Location is an unarmed/unarmored vehicle."
So a BU CT AFV would prevent any unit in its location (but not in upper levels) from attacking outside their location.

So actually there are TWO instances:
One is that a unit in your location does not allow you to attack outside that your location whatever the units are.
The other is the TPBF limitation.
If this second instance only applies, units are not freezed; IF the first one applies they are.

Paolo, I know the Italian forum: Thanks to it I started playing ASL time ago!!!;)

You got right the two limitations.

Note that "freezing" is actually not a rulebook definition nor status. It is simply something the players call units that have this state of being "frozen" in place by an enemy unit, usually a vehicle in their Location. In reality there are several situations that could lead to this condition and each has its rule (and none is called "freezing").

There are two limitations that you can apply to an enemy unit: fire and movement. Fire limitations is covered by your OP. Note that there are many other limitations to fire (like during Subsequent First Fire, blocking LOS, etc). Movement is usually only restricted for units in Melee. They can only either fight in CC or either Withdraw from Melee. If a vehicle moves to an enemy unit's Location it is not blocking it from moving away. It is simply the Player Turn of the vehicle, not the other one. So they maybe could voluntarily break and rout away, for example.

Ok, there are instances were there could be a movement during the other Player Turn, but it's rare. For example, there could be a Melee between your Infantry unit and a Stopped enemy AFV, then a friendly AFV comes by and the enemy rolls a Motion attempt and becomes Motion instead of Stopped, so *puff* your Infantry unit is no longer held in Melee and it can move away! But these are strange situations that make players scratch their heads.

So stick to each real rule, if you use words like "freeze", know that it is only player lingo.

Reaction Fire is your reaction (during the MPh) to an enemy vehicle entering your Location.  It can be CC Reaction Fire or Non-CC Reaction Fire.

title: Melee and hex control
question:
Quite sure I read something sometimes ago.
If a game ends with a melee in a VC hex, the side who controls that hex is the last who solely occupy it, or the hex is "contested" in some manner?
Thanks
author: Qwirz
consensus_answer:
while we're on the topic, a related corollary is building control...

A26.11 A side gains Control of a building by occupying it with an armed Good Order Infantry MMC without the presence of an armed enemy ground unit in that same building...

in other words, you must completely eliminate all armed enemy ground units in a building to control it... if you have control of a building, and have at least one unit in it, and armed enemy ground units enter it, you still control it...

but, say, if you leave the building with your last unit, control reverts to the enemy, even if you just left the building and came right back in... you would have to eliminate all of those enemy units in the building to regain control... (ie can't reenter the building and jump into melee and regain control by eliminating the enemy in just that one hex)
