I just remembered one exception - vehicular control is less solid.  A vehicle controls a location as long as it occupies it but an enemy unit entering the location causes the it to revert to its prior state (uncontrolled or enemy controlled) as long as it shares the location with the vehicle:

A26.12 VEHICULAR CONTROL: An armed, non-bypassing vehicle temporarily gains Control of the Location it presently occupies if that Location is devoid of armed enemy units. Control immediately reverts to its prior status (either un-Controlled or enemy-Controlled) if the vehicle leaves the Location. A vehicle which Controls the only Location in a hex also Controls that hex.

Here we are with another question arised during the Primosole bridge campaign.

Questions like this should be specifically in the "Primosole Bridge" folder.  "Strategic Locations" are not a generic ASL topic, they are defined in each HASL.

Is it a Strategic German Location? Is it still a Brit Strategic Location? Is it none of the two?

The rules on p.Z48 are not defining what is and is not a Strategic Location, so I don't know why you are trying to use those rules to do so.

Strategic Locations are defined on p.Z42.
Each building/rubble/bridge/British Controlled Axis Entry Hex/Objective Hex/Pillbox/entrenchment and each Location occupied by a non-Abandoned Immobile vehicle with functioning MA, by an unhooked, non-malfunctioned Gun, and/or by a glider is a Strategic Location.

So, a functioning Gun is a Strategic Location so long as it is unhooked.  Crew is optional.

The table on p.Z48 addresses various things on the map and what might happen to them.  You go down the table and find the thing you're looking for, then apply what is said there.  Is an unpossessed Functioning Gun a "Personnel/Mobile-Vehicle"?  Nope.  Is it an "Abandoned (but otherwise Mobile) ... other than Functioning Gun"?  Nope.  Is it a "Crewed, Immobile Vehicle etc."?  Nope.  Is it a "Crewed, Immobile Vehicle with Functioning MA-or Functioning Gun"?  Hey, yeah, it is.  So there you go.

This then tells you that it becomes a Strategic Location.  Of course you already knew that, because you had already read the definition on p.Z42.

(The comma is used to separate distinct clauses in a sentence, or in this case, distinct adjectives all applicable to a single noun.  The hyphen here is used to separate two distinct phrases -- the first phrase is "Crewed, Immobile Vehicle with Functioning MA" and the second phrase is "or Functioning Gun".  It's not what I'd call ideal English grammar to do so, but the intent is clear enough.)

F12.42.....

When a sand dune overlay has been selected, an extra, Final dr of ≤ 1 must be made in order to place it. Not exactly ... "must not" is not accurate.  Rout or don't rout, you can't be eliminated for Failure to Rout.  However, you still have to abide by the regular rout rules otherwise, e.g., no routing towards Known enemy units; and a broken unit adjacent to a Known unbroken enemy unit must still rout away if possible.  The main differences are, all routs are always Low Crawls, and situations that would eliminate the broken unit (or force him to surrender) in a day scenario have no effect in a night scenario.

The practical upshot of this is that casualties (in terms of units eliminated or captured) in a night scenario will be fewer than in a day scenario ... but broken units in a night scenario will typically stay broken, as it's difficult to remove those pesky DM markers.

There's not really any such thing as a "typical" night scenario, but if there were, it would be a defending force approached by an unseen enemy until suddenly fighting breaks out in isolated clumps (each "clump" rarely in a position to provide much assistance to any other "clump") finishing with a sea of broken units all crying in the darkness.

Well, as I said above, it's my belief that the Night rules don't change the "core" routing rules: don't rout towards Known enemy units; if a broken unit is ADJACENT to a Known armed unbroken enemy unit, then it must rout, if possible.

If it isn't possible, then you don't.  There are no direct consequences for failure to rout at Night.

Now, this Q&A is saying that you don't have to rout, period.  I don't quite see how that answer is derived from the rules text, yet it isn't really contradicting anything in the rules text either.  Still, it's from 2002, and no errata yet to make it official.  I hate that.

How should you play it?  However you want to play it.  No-one can point a finger at you and say "you're doing it wrong".  Just make sure that you and your opponent are in agreement beforehand.

For the more general question of "how do I treat unofficial Q&A?", here's MY approach (many other players take a different tack):

1. Does the Q&A introduce anything "new", i.e., was the question "valid" to begin with.  By "valid" I mean, "is the answer to this question not already in the rules".

2. If the question is not "valid" by the above definition, and the answer is exactly what the rules say the answer should be, then the whole thing is a non-event.  Nothing to see here, move along.

3. If the question is not "valid" by the above definition, but the answer supplied contradicts the printed rules, then I ignore it, pending the issuing of actual official errata.  Yes, MMP sometimes gets things wrong.  It's not a common thing, but it happens.

4. If the question is "valid", then the answer, whatever it might be, is almost always something "new" -- or at least a clarification of something that wasn't especially clear to begin with.  As long as that answer does not, itself, contradict something else, then there's no reason not to accept it.  So I do, and I eagerly await the errata that will introduce this "new" thing into the printed rules.  Sadly, in the majority of cases, that can be a very long wait indeed.

5. Every now and again a perfectly "valid" question gets a non-answer.  That's frustrating to me beyond words.  I don't mean that there's no reply (although that's often the case, at least for me); I mean that the answer provided doesn't address the question that was asked.  The whole exercise becomes pointless, and we're no farther along than we were before.  (Still waiting for answers on those marsh questions, Perry.  Still waiting.)

6.  Again, every now and again, a "valid" question gets an answer that might be good for the question being specifically asked, but causes problems in other areas of the rules.  Let me stress that this is vanishingly rare, but when it does happen, there's not much to do except ask follow-up questions and see what shakes out.

7. All of the above works fine for me.  However, if my opponent is unfamiliar with the unofficial Q&A, he may have his own ideas, and with no printed text to show him, it can be difficult to "prove" him wrong.  I also don't carry around a collection of these unofficial Q&A, and besides all of that, I know I don't have anything remotely resembling a "complete" collection.  Floating around out there are hundreds, if not thousands, of these Q&A ... we hope that they don't disagree with each other, or with the rules, but they might (and sometimes do).  A great deal more effort is required on MMP's part to issue errata on a regular basis.  It won't stop the questions being asked, but it can do a great deal to make the answers more readily available.

title: Assault movement into Entrenchment
question:

There's no question that a bunch of 1st edition rules said "hex" when what was clearly meant was "Location".  That had nothing to do with the definition of "Location", which has always been crystal clear.  When I said "it's never been an issue" I was referring to ASL rules, day 1.

What the rules did not and still do not have is a defined simple way of distinguishing between where an individual unit might be within a Location at a given point of time.  The closest we get is being IN a gully (as defined in A.6) as opposed to being in Crest status.  I like to use the word "position" but that's just me, not a rules definition.  So a unit currently in the act of using infantry Bypass Movement is in a different "position" to a unit currently occupying the woods or building obstacle of that hex, but both units are in the same Location.  A unit in a foxhole is in a different "position" to a unit not in the foxhole, but both are in the same Location.  Etc.

[The one that trips a lot of newer players up is Wall Advantage.  So if I'm in a building hex but have claimed Wall Advantage I'm not in the building, right?  Wrong!  Wall Advantage does not change your Location, and it doesn't even change your "position".  What it changes is the TEM that you are eligible to claim (and in the case of bocage, it can change what you can see and be seen by).]

title: A7.9 cowering
question:
Ok...question time!!! I'm reading the comprehensive example on journal #6 and it is a good way to (re)read some paragraphs.
A7.9 last sentence: "if a FG cowers, Random Selection is used to determine the unit(s)....that becomes marked with a Prep or Final Fire counter."
Does this mean that in PFph a FG which fires and cowers is not marked Prep as a whole? Just the selected unit(s)......others can fire again?
Does this mean that in enemy MPh a FG which use SFF and cowers is not marked FINAL as a whole? etc...etc...

Help please!
author: Qwirz
consensus_answer:
Guessing this would apply to inherent SW e.g PF / Mol ….?

Yes.  (Although actually NA for MOL, since you can't make a MOL attack separately from your inherent FP.)

One of the ASL "tricks" quickly learnt by experienced players: cowering does not apply to any attack that must make a "To Hit" DR.  So if you have a squad armed with a BAZ, maybe you want to fire the BAZ before using the squad's inherent FP; if you do it the other way around, the squad may cower and you won't get to fire the BAZ at all.  (Obviously, this is only a general rule; the specific situation may dictate a different approach.)

SW MTRs throw in an extra twist.  By the principle above, a squad armed with a MTR may wish to fire the MTR first before using his inherent FP.  However, if gaining and keeping acquisition is important, he may want to do it the other way around -- or not even use his inherent FP at all; because acquisition is lost if the firing unit makes any other attack (including Interdiction!) (C6.5).

title: Concealment loss
question: so I’m trying to get a handle on the concealment gain/loss chart and I’m a little confused. Case A says “Non-Assault Movement”. So if my infantry uses Assault Movement it’s good to keep concealment. Case B though reads “moves/advances”. So does “Assault Movement” count as “moves”?  So does my Assault Moving infantry into Open Ground concealment or not. Seems like both cases apply here.
author: YankeeGrunt
consensus_answer:
Check the definition of Open Ground - it isn't just a hex without TEM or hindrance terrain - the LOS of enemy units _to_ that hex is also a factor (for retaining concealment while assault moving).

-N
Here is the rule :
A10.531 OPEN GROUND: For purposes of rout determination, Dash, concealment gain/loss, and Interdiction, an Open Ground hex is any hex in which the particular enemy unit(s) could apply, during a hypothetical Defensive First Fire opportunity (regardless of what attacks it actually made in previous phases), the -1 FFMO DRM.

replies.body:
Yes, if you advance into some kind of cover (behind a hedge, in to a grain field, etc.) you can retain your concealment.  If you advance into a location that is open ground to any known enemy unit, you lose concealment.  

(If the opposing unit that sees you do this is also concealed, he'll have 
to prove it's not fake to make you lose concealment.  Yes, it's a cunning way to do some recon if you suspect something is fake.)

There's an exception in the night rules, but I don't think you have to worry about that yet.
right continue reading the columns assault move in applicable terrain

so I’m trying to get a handle on the concealment gain/loss chart and I’m a little confused. Case A says “Non-Assault Movement”. So if my infantry uses Assault Movement it’s good to keep concealment.

As long as you're not doing your movement in Open Ground in LOS of an enemy unit.  You have to check all the cases.

Case B though reads “moves/advances”. So does “Assault Movement” count as “moves”?

Assault Movement is Movement.  It's right there in the name.

So does my Assault Moving infantry into Open Ground concealment or not. Seems like both cases apply here.

Multiple cases may always apply, but you only need one of them telling you to lose concealment for it to be lost.

If any one thing in the table tells you that you lose concealment, then you lose concealment, no matter what else is going on.  (Of course, this always assumes that there's a Good Order enemy unit with LOS!  The only way to lose concealment when no enemy unit has LOS is if you are not eligible for concealment at all -- e.g., if the Sniper breaks a squad way off in the middle of nowhere, you lose concealment because broken units cannot be concealed.)

What trips many players up is Case C "any other action".  This will usually trump any other conditions.  So it doesn't matter if your stealthy squad is Assault Moving in Dense Jungle covered by SMOKE, if he attempts to Place a DC he loses concealment, because Placing a DC is one of those "other actions".

- Does hex L6 have LOS to M5?  ...due to the building touching that vertex.
author: PzrLehr
consensus_answer:
Hello again-
 Please look at board Z (If you have it) from the starter kit #1. I know there's no 1st level rules in SK#1; my question is: 
- Does hex L6 have LOS to M5?  ...due to the building touching that vertex.
 

The answer is "no", because the building art is not touching the vertex, it is crossing the hexside L5/M6.  Only by a tiny amount, sure, but that's enough.

If the building art was drawn in such a way that it truly did only touch the vertex, then the LOS would not (could not) be blocked, because the obstacle art has to show on both sides of your LOS string (A6.1).

This does not make the board "crazy" or illustrate some weirdness in the ASL LOS rules (that are plenty of other examples for those sort of issues).  It's perfectly straight-forward.  The only thing that makes it stand out in any way is that you have to take a good close look to see what's going on.  That does not make it unique in ASL in any way.  (It's maybe a poor choice for a Starter Kit board, but the kids have to grow up and learn the facts of life at some point ....)

Why would you "suppose" anything?  Look up the relevant rule:

A8.2 RESIDUAL FIREPOWER: When a unit is attacked by Defensive First Fire/Subsequent First Fire/FPF, the target Location in which the attack is resolved (even if in Bypass) is marked with a Residual FP counter equal to half (up to a maximum of 12 after adjustment as per 8.26; FRD) of the highest IFT FP column used for that attack. If the attack includes a To Kill DR vs a vehicle, Residual FP is created in the same manner [EXC: If AP (unless fired by a MG), ATR, APCR, or APDS was used, or if a Dud (C7.35) resulted, no Residual FP is created]. Thereafter, any unit entering (or expending MF/MP in) that same Location in the same MPh is attacked on the IFT with the FP represented by that Residual FP counter, a new IFT DR, and any applicable FFMO/FFNAM DRM. A unit expending MF/MP to leave a Location is not subject to Residual FP attack in the Location it is leaving. All non-hexside TEM and SMOKE/FFE-Hindrance DRM of the target Location apply to a Residual FP attack (even vs Bypassing units).

Fire Lane Residual FP and regular Residual FP are similar, but not the same.  The major difference between them are the different modifiers that apply to the attacks.

title: Broken unit not under DM...
question:
Hey guy's-
 When a broken unit gets fired on, does it immediately go under DM before the IFT DR?  or after?
author: PzrLehr
consensus_answer:
It does matter. Place the DM marker after you have fully resolved the attack. You might blow the roll so badly that you have to partially or entirely remove the counter (EX: Casualty reduction; ELR Failure; HoB). So, instead of having to also remove the DM marker to get at the counter, just wait out the entire attack.

But, yeah, per the rules, it doesn't matter.

Defensive Fire is one of the things that's not quite right in either incarnation of the system, IMO.

In SL, as mentioned, after the enemy finished moving, you could temporarily "back up" his units to any hex traversed during their moves to fire upon them. In essence, this allowed you to see all the enemy's moves before deciding what shots to take, and even allowed you to fire at *every* unit that passed through a single hex, even if all those units ended in different destinations. At first blush, it seems to give the defender an unrealistic advantage, but it was meant to counter-balance the fact that the attacker already has an advantage of his own--he can (rather unrealistically) move all of his units in perfect coordination. The idea was that the attacker gets to make an unrealistically "perfect" move, so the defender gets to take an unrealistically "perfect" shot.

The major drawback of this approach is that it required players to remember the exact paths taken by all the moving units so the defender could conduct his Defensive Fire. The game equipped you with crosshairs "Tracking" counters you could place as a memory aid, but it was still a chore, particularly in larger scenarios.

In ASL, Defensive Fire is conducted immediately by temporarily halting units as they move. It's no longer necessary to remember the paths of all moving units, but this approach has issues of its own. First of all, it requires several new and quasi-fiddly rules that allow each defender to fire multiple times during the enemy Movement Phase under certain conditions (called First, Subsequent, and Final Fire) and to leave "Residual Firepower" in hexes attacked during Defensive Fire that will attack additional units moving through those hexes for the remainder of the Movement Phase. (Without these additions, it's just too easy to draw off and avoid enemy Defensive Fire.) Despite all these new rules, the ASL system makes it far too easy for the attacker to pull off intricately choreographed assaults. Three stacks spread across multiple hexes (several hundred meters) and all attacking the same enemy position can launch an intricate series of coordinated feints and maneuvers designed to draw off and/or reduce the effectiveness of enemy DF.

So, what is the difference between defensive fire in Squad leader and defensive fire in ASL?

So the main change as Chuck says is Defensive First Fire, which takes place during the opponent's Movement Phase, with immediate effect.

So typically units move, and the defenders may be tempted to have a shot. This is Defensive first fire, and defending units that don't cower may subsequently first fire again, at half FP and only at moving units hat are closer than any other target. So drawing a defender to shoot can free up opportunities for attacking units. I'll note here only moving units are targeted, not the whole stack in a hex.

If a unit conducts Subsequent First Fire, they are done, with the exception of a desperate First Fire against units moving ADJACENT to them. This attack is also a morale check on the defender (and it can happen that defenders suddenly go Berserk or Battle Harden, or suffer Fate).

After all movement, Defensive Fire is conducted as per Squad Leader, but can target whole stacks but only in their final positions (no winding back moves).

There are a few other features I have skimmed over, the most important being residual firepower (some FP left in target hexes to effect subsequent moving units) and Firelanes (which are when MGs lay a row of residual firepower).

The changes to Defensive Fire are probably the MAJOR change to ASL from SL, and make the game far more interactive for the defending player. They have to watch each move, and make tough decisions with each MP spent.

I'm not sure what point you're trying to make regarding AREA ratings--that just never interested me. FWIW, I've been playing ASL regularly since day one (I go all the way back to the original SL days). I've played against scores of opponents, over the years, including several of the "name" designers (and yes, Marc and Bruce, I recognize your names).

When I say ASL's Defensive Fire rules make it too easy for the attacker to launch intricately coordinated assaults, I'm critiquing the game's "realism" not its "playability." Imagine three platoons, spread out along 6 hexes or so assaulting a machine gun nest. In ASL, a skilled player will typically dispatch individual squads from those platoons in a series of methodical attempts to draw fire, move some squads in a fashion designed to protect others (only the closest enemy unit is subject to SFF), carefully dance around Residual Firepower, see how the movement of each squad goes before moving the next, and so on. The idea that the three platoon commanders, located some distance apart, could improvise and coordinate such a carefully sequenced plan is highly implausible. I'd argue that original SL's defensive fire mechanics led players to adopt more historically accurate tactics. That doesn't at all dampen my enthusiasm for the game

What could be interesting, would be to explain what is a better existing system exists for defensive fire in a sequential game turn, WW2 tactical game.

If it doesn't exist, then there are some logical conclusions :

- With all its limits, ASL is has the best existing game mechanics

- If someone wants to craft a better system, we are in a free world - but I have doubts that it would be able to win over many players

I think that nobody here denies that the DFF rules are not perfect.
But what is strange, is to have a negative opinion about them, while it is one of the major improvements over the SL system and that - as much as I know - no other comparable game has succesfully beaten ASL in that domain.

As for any game, and in general in tactics, the rule is to understand, adapt and overcome.
Most well designed scenarios take the game mechanics in account to make the situation challenging for the defender as well as the attacker.
So even if one considers that attacking is "easier", good scenarios have VCs which adapt to that "problem" and which overcome it.

That said, I have won plenty of games as a defender against competent players (organising a sneaky Japanese defense facing a seemingly overwhelming USMC assault was one of my last successes as a defender).

title: encirclement
question: So I was looking at the rules for encirclement. I want to know if i am understanding it right. So two squad would have to score a NMC at least to cause the encirclement rule to apply. Is this a correct interpretation?
author: dabrawley
consensus_answer:
As I read it, you just have to be “able” to inflict at least a result, NMC
Not actually achieve it..I.e you roll but miss, still encircled 

A7.72 also reads as , no free path downstairs, also encircled, no reference to fired at restrictions..?

replies.body: It isn't necessary to actually achieve a NMC. It is only necessary that both attacks be capable of getting a NMC result. e.g. if one of the units would be unable to attain a NMC if it cowers, it cannot result in encirclement, even if a non-cowering attack would have been able to do so. Therefore, you must take all factors into consideration to verify that the attack "could" achieve a NMC. The actual result may be only PTC or NE, but it could have gotten the NMC.

Not actually achieve it..I.e you roll but miss, still encircled 

A7.72 also reads as , no free path downstairs, also encircled, no reference to fired at restrictions..?

No need to score an NMC, just be able to. Example: a 4 +3 shot gets an NMC on a 2 or 3 roll, so that is good enough to encircle. a 4 +4 shot cannot get an NMC if the 2 cowers, so does not cause encirclement.
Thanks

e.g. if one of the units would be unable to attain a NMC if it cowers, it cannot result in encirclement, even if a non-cowering attack would have been able to do so.

Uh, no.  The firing unit/FG has to be theoretically capable of achieving a MC result.  The possibility of cowering only comes into it if the only way the firing unit could score a MC is by not cowering.

So: a 1 FP attack with a total DRM of +2 can only score a MC if the unit cannot cower.  If that's true, then the attack can count for Encirclement; if it's not true, it can't.

A 1 FP attack with a DRM of +1 can score a MC by rolling a "3", so it doesn't matter if the unit is subject to cowering or not; the theoretical MC is possible.  Therefore the attack can count for Encirclement.

A 1 FP attack with a DRM of +3 cannot score a MC no matter what, so cannot be counted for Encirclement purposes.

Under no circumstances does it matter what the actual DR is.  The only thing you need to consider is whether it's possible to inflict a MC result.

title: Human wave - no LOS
question:
If a Human Wave is declared from a group of friendly units against an enemy unit and then it is proved that there is no LOS to the target enemy unit, what happens? Is there a penalty or simply the HW is not declared and you can do other things with the involved units?

Related, can you make free LOS checks in order to declare a HW?
author: esparver73
consensus_answer:
The requirement is that at least one unit in the HW chain has a LOS to a target.  No LOS = no HW.  Nothing happens, false alarm, go about your business.

Any activity that requires a LOS before it can occur must implicitly involve a "free" LOS check.  The issue is whether the activity in question still occurs if the LOS check comes up bad.  Attacks on enemy units is an example of "yes, the activity still happens"; the rules for each particular activity will specify (or not).  Since nothing in A25.23 mentions any penalties for "attempting" an illegal HW, there are no penalties.

title: Crest Status Confusion
question: You can only gain Crest status in Depression hexes, and I don't think the dry river is a Depression, it is just -1 Level terrain.
consensus_answer:
^^^That's right, you can't go into a crest status position alone a river hexside. Basically,this river bed is best seen terms of hill crest line rules. 

Think of the river as a 'negative hill' and the boundary of the river is the crest line of a hill. The small amount of green indicates a crest line. 

The wall is considered as per rule B9.62 as a hillside wall at the higher level. Hence a unit in the dry river will never get wall advantage next to such a wall. 

As for the move into the Olive Orchard across the wall, if you have a leader providing a movement bonus to the infantry yielding 6MF for the stack, then you could assault move at 5MF and avoid the minimum move situation. But if a lone squad declared CX, it would have 6MF to start and could spend 5MF to enter the hex without minimum move, but of course precluding assault move.

Rule 6.4 says that the number of blind hexes created equals the height of the obstacle, so there are two blind hexes.

 Rule 6.41 doesn't apply as the range from Q6 to S7 is less than

Thus, I arrived at my conclusion that the MMG at Q6 cannot see the unit in U8.  Correct?
Correct, thanks to the magic of offsetting errors!
  
Devil's Hill is basically a clinic on LOS issues.  Ultimately it will be second nature to you but the combination of crest lines, cliff crest lines, buildings, and woods all add up to give you 90% of typical elevation-related LOS hassles in one scenario.  Good luck, and keep asking questions.

title: Smoke in Internal Building Hex
question:
If a MMC throw a smoke grenade in an Internal Building Hex of a multi-level building and there is no stairs in the Internal Building Hex.
Will Smoke spread to the higher-level Internal Building Hex？
author: zhaopengyu1985
consensus_answer:
If a MMC throw a smoke grenade in an Internal Building Hex of a multi-level building and there is no stairs in the Internal Building Hex. Will Smoke spread to the higher-level Internal Building Hex？

Yes.

Why?  Because no EXC is provided in A24.4 for Interior Building hexes.  The presence of absence of a Stairwell is irrelevant.  (SMOKE does not use the stairs.)

[Aside from Sniper attacks (A14.22) and Indirect Fire attacks (B23.32), "interior building hexes" -- as defined in the Index -- are not treated differently to other building hexes.]

Regarding cellars, you should be specific about what sort of cellars you're talking about.  Cellar rules are only found in certain HASL modules, and the cellar rules for one HASL are not necessarily identical to the cellar rules of a different HASL.  In any case, you don't need a Stairwell (printed or inherent) to "permit" Smoke (or flames) to rise to a higher elevation in any building hex, cellar or otherwise.

All of that may offend your personal sense of "realism".  On behalf of the rules, I apologise for that.  The rules don't apologise, because they don't care.  They just are.

There's realism and then there's realism.  It means different things to different people.  For example, I've heard the argument that the +1 LV "Mist" Hindrance for Heavy Falling Rain (applies at ranges of 6 or less) should not apply for attacks within a building, on the seemingly-reasonable assumption that inside the building, it isn't raining.  I would counter those arguments as follows:

1) How do you know what the condition of that building's roof is like?  It could be leaking like a sieve.

2) I can't speak for anywhere else, but in this part of the world, when it's raining heavily, it gets dark.  I don't think it's a common practice to turn on all the house lights in the middle of a battle, even assuming that the building is fitted with electricity in the first place (and that the power is working in this part of the battlefield, and that all of the light fittings are intact).  I have no problem with heavy rain making it harder to see things even when you're not actually getting wet.

You can run up similar arguments for SMOKE.  We see a little drawing of a house on a game board and immediately ccmplete the mental image with our own particular prejudices and ideas ... which sometimes is fine and sometimes is not.  Your two-hex building on board 4 can represent something "typical" in 1940 France and something completely different, yet equally "typical", in 1941 Soviet Union.  In game terms it's all the same, in reality ... well, who knows.  So arguing what "reality" the game should depict 100% of the time is, IMO, pretty silly.

Regardless ... it doesn't hurt to ask the question.  If it moves Perry to issue errata, fine.  I can deal with errata.  The original question, though, is what are the rules on this situation right now.

title: VBM and WHat Hex Is That Tank In?
question:
I have a vehicle moving along a village narrow road using VBM. We are trying to figure out if a broken unit can route to an adjacent hex, but whether it can or not depends upon what hex the vehicle is actually in.

I believe that normally bypass is dictated for a single hex at a time, as with infantry, but when a vehicle changes its VCA and enters a new hexside it is in the hex bounded by those two hexsides. 

Obviously, for purposes of Fire during the MPh, the CAFP is used, but for this purpose, determining direction of rout, it's about the hex it's bypassing, and that changes, maybe, from hexside to hexside.

Did I get it right?

Thanks in advance.

Also, a rules reference is always appreciated. I did a lot of research on this and found it to be a bit vague.

Doug
author: dcooley
consensus_answer:
I have a vehicle moving along a village narrow road using VBM. We are trying to figure out if a broken unit can route to an adjacent hex, but whether it can or not depends upon what hex the vehicle is actually in.

See C.5C.

C.5C The hex containing the target by definition must include the building/woods obstacle being bypassed, or the hex the target would remain in if affected by that fire (e.g., Snapshot [A8.15], Rowhouse “Bypass” [B23.71], Underbelly Hit [D4.3]) or the lower side of a cliff hexside being Climbed (B11.42).

So when you enter into Bypass alon a hexside you have to declare which hex you are actually in. But note also B31.11 for Bypass along a Narrow Street:
"...A unit Bypassing along a Narrow Street hexside is always assumed to be on the road within its hex—and, if that hexside is also a Crest Line hexside, in the lower of those two hexes...."

replies.body: at the moment of bypass you need to decide which hex the vehicle is in at each hexside. I do believe you can announce a switch to the other bypassed hex along the road after changing CA and moving to the new hexside; I know of no rule prohibiting this. But the owner of the vehicle can't decide what is convenient at the moment. BFP provided some CA bypass markers to indicate which hex is being bypassed as a mnemonic -- I forget which module.

title: Stun+1 counter means "stunned" or not?
question:
Just a clarification: When my AFV gets stunned (failed MC) it is marked with a "stun" counter. At the end of the turn it is flipped to the "+1" side and D5.34 states: "This indicates that the AFV is no longer Stunned". Ok, seems clear!

Then I read under C5.6: "Intensive Fire is available only to Guns (not SW), and can be used only if crew of the Gun is not pinned shocked, stunned [...]"!

So I guess with the "+1" counter my AFV is no longer stunned? But then I don't understand this restriction, because with a "stun" counter it cannot fire at all.
author: phxhf
consensus_answer:
The vehicle is "Stunned" when the red side of the counter is showing.

Once it's flipped, the vehicle has that marker permanently attached to it to affect subsequent activities ... but it is no longer considered "Stunned".

Yeah, the C5.6 wording is just being extra-explicit.  You never know when someone might come along and somehow squeeze out a weird interpretation that works in their head-space.

replies.body: Well, it can't fire when "shocked", either, so it seems they are just being thorough.

title: Multihex FG with Leader, ROF and Cowering
question:
I ran into an interesting situation today, which I was not completely sure about. I had a building with a FG on two different levels:

Level 1: 447 squad A.
Level 2: 447 squad B with 5-12 MMG (ROF 2) and a 8-1 Leader

An enemy unit moved for 2 MF into a hex in LOS and Normal Range and I First Fired all my units in this building as a FG. To my understanding the Leader DRM cannot be used in this FG over two Locations. But nevertheless I declared that my Leader directs the Fire of his squad and MMG.

The DR was 4 with cdr 2 (which means ROF for the MMG). It also means that my FG is Cowering. So the attack would be on the 8 FP column, instead on the 12 FP (shift left by one).

In my opinion the Leader-directed squad B does not cower, so I won't do Random Selection but mark squad A with a Final Fire counter. Squad B gets a First Fire counter and the MMG can still fire.

As the enemy expended 2 MF I fire the MMG again (alone). Now I think that I can apply the leader's -1 DRM to the shot, because he was directing this local group from the beginning. Correct?

At last I wondered whether I can also fire squad B's inherent FP as SFF after the second MMG attack, but I guess that would be illegal because of Mandatory FG (A7.55)? Squad B would have to attack together with the MMG. But then the MMG would have to use SFF (Sustained Fire) as well (A8.3)...?
author: phxhf
consensus_answer:
I ran into an interesting situation today, which I was not completely sure about. I had a building with a FG on two different levels:

Level 1: 447 squad A.
Level 2: 447 squad B with 5-12 MMG (ROF 2) and a 8-1 Leader

An enemy unit moved for 2 MF into a hex in LOS and Normal Range and I First Fired all my units in this building as a FG. To my understanding the Leader DRM cannot be used in this FG over two Locations. But nevertheless I declared that my Leader directs the Fire of his squad and MMG.

You are not eligible to make that declaration.  The Leader directs everything in the FG or nothing.  There is no in-between possibility.

The DR was 4 with cdr 2 (which means ROF for the MMG). It also means that my FG is Cowering. So the attack would be on the 8 FP column, instead on the 12 FP (shift left by one).

Yes, but ....

In my opinion the Leader-directed squad B does not cower, so I won't do Random Selection but mark squad A with a Final Fire counter. Squad B gets a First Fire counter and the MMG can still fire.

... incorrect on all counts.  The FG had no Leader direction, and all involved units are eligible to cower.

As the enemy expended 2 MF I fire the MMG again (alone). Now I think that I can apply the leader's -1 DRM to the shot, because he was directing this local group from the beginning. Correct?

No, as above.  Even if Squad B did not cower, and thus kept the ROF, the Leader was not involved with the initial FG and so cannot just insert himself into the action.  This remains true for the remainder of Defensive Fire (First and Final).

At last I wondered whether I can also fire squad B's inherent FP as SFF after the second MMG attack, but I guess that would be illegal because of Mandatory FG (A7.55)? Squad B would have to attack together with the MMG. But then the MMG would have to use SFF (Sustained Fire) as well (A8.3)...?

No, if the MMG still has ROF, SFF is n/a.  However, as soon as the manning unit uses SFF, it and all of its SW are marked with Final Fire (whether they are used in the attack or not), so the MG would not be eligible for any further ROF.

The issue of when Leaders do and do not participate in a FG is one of the more fundamental rules in ASL, so it's worth taking the time to read the rules and absorb them until they become second-nature.  Points to note:

1 - as I stated above, the Leader directs everything in the FG or he directs nothing.  There are no EXC to this!

2 - once a FG has formed, the Leader has to participate in the initial attack in order to participate in any subsequent attacks of that FG.  You are allowed to drop units from a FG after it has made any attack, but you are not allowed to add units to an existing FG (and that includes Leaders).

3 - "Leader directs fire" and "Leader applies his DRM to an attack" mean the same thing at all times.  The only EXC to that is firstly, a MMC using a FT can be directed by a Leader (to prevent cowering), even though the Leader's DRM cannot be used to modify the attack; and secondly, in CC/Melee attacks, a Leader's DRM can be declined if desired (although strictly speaking, Leaders don't "direct" CC attacks, they "participate" in them).

Well, that is what I was saying, and that's the peril of (a) answering without having the rules handy and (b) assuming years of experience is the same thing as knowing what you're talking about.  I strongly suspect that this is something I have regularly played incorrectly.  On re-reading A8.3 where it says "... if using a MG/IFE is treated as Sustained Fire and penalized accordingly" I withdraw my earlier comment.  Never be shy in questioning what another player assures you is true, unless he can cite the exact rule! :soblue:

To be clear, your original thought was correct: if the manning squad is using SFF, then any MG it fires must use Sustained Fire, even if the MG was not previously marked with a First Fire counter.

Of course if your multi-Location FG has a participating Leader in each Location, then the entire FG will be Leader-directed (using the worst Leadership DRM) and no unit in the FG would be subject to Cowering.
So in theory here I could apply a better DRM from a single MG/leader combination in a later attack, provided this MG keeps ROF? Or is it also forbidden, because the leader with the better DRM didn't direct the FG in the first attack...?

And when only one leader in the chain is missing, then all squads are in danger of Cowering, and I cannot do like in the previous sentence? I read the rules several times, but found nothing which explicitely demands that. For example, A7.351 only mentions the leadership DRM of the whole FG, but not the effect of leader direction for their own Location (to prevent Cowering).

Thanks for the correction!

So in theory here I could apply a better DRM from a single MG/leader combination in a later attack, provided this MG keeps ROF?

No!  A leader cannot participate in a FG that he did not ALWAYS participate in.

A7.53-.531 states this, very explicitly:

"Leader direction used during Defensive First Fire can be used again in Subsequent First Fire, FPF, or Final Fire, but again only for one firing unit/SW or FG -- and that unit/SW/FG can only include firers he directed during First Fire; if forming a new FG or using a different SW during that Player Turn, the leader cannot direct its fire (even during FPF)." (my emphasis)

There's no way to interpret that to mean "a leader can join an existing FG any time that it's convenient, or switch to a different FG whenever he wants".

For example, A7.351 only mentions the leadership DRM of the whole FG, but not the effect of leader direction for their own Location (to prevent Cowering).

Correct.  It doesn't say that.  Since it doesn't say it, why do you think that it's a rule?  This is the principle of COWTRA; the rules are not whatever you think might be reasonable, the rules are what is printed.  If it's not printed, it isn't a rule.

The rules for Cowering (A7.9) are equally explicit.  "... unless a leader directs that attack".  A7.53 tells you what you need to know about how a leader directs an attack, and when he can't direct an attack.  It's got nothing to do with him just hanging around in the Location; he has to be actively involved, from the first attack, and once he commits to being involved he can't change his mind and commit himself somewhere else.  If it's a multi-Location FG, he can only be involved when there is a leader in every firing Location.  If you don't meet that condition, he's not part of the FG and he can't join in later when it's convenient.

But I would have trusted you, when an experienced player who played this situation multiple times against similar experienced players, says this is not the case.

Always, always, always challenge rules interpretations until you understand them.  That's how any of us learn anything about the game.  There is no ASL grognard alive who doesn't regularly get some rule wrong every single time he plays.

That being said, you don't want to interrupt the flow of the game too much by constantly asking questions.  When you're very new to the game, obviously that's too be expected and is OK; once you've got a few games under your belt, try and save the rules questions until after the game is over, when you can read the rulebook at your leisure.  Maybe some rule was played wrong and it cost you the victory; don't sweat it, there are plenty more battles to be fought, when you'll know more than you did before.

No!  A leader cannot participate in a FG that he did not ALWAYS participate in.
...
There's no way to interpret that to mean "a leader can join an existing FG any time that it's convenient, or switch to a different FG whenever he wants".

If it's a multi-Location FG, he can only be involved when there is a leader in every firing Location.  If you don't meet that condition, he's not part of the FG and he can't join in later when it's convenient.
And neither may he decide to direct a local FG out of units which are part of this multi-Location FG. Yes, this makes everything clear.

title: Mortar Spotters and free LOS-checks
question:
There is one sentence in C9.3 (Spotters) which always seemed strange to me and which I don't really understand:
"A new Spotter may not be designated until the original Spotter is eliminated, broken or captured".

Does it mean, whenever I designate a Spotter, I have to use him for the whole scenario, as long as he remains in Good Order? When the Spotter moves away, doing other tasks, I cannot replace him?

And here is another question, which I ignored to answer precisely, since I switched to full ASL:

According to A12.14 I am allowed to do free LOS checks, to verify if a Concealed enemy unit is still eligible for its "?" counter. I read "LOS checks are free and require no attack or penalty" as that I can check multiple LOS, but I don't have to attack these units. Would it also allow me to check all kinds of impossible LOS from my units to the enemy's concealed units, before I finally find a valid one?

When the enemy does not want me to do these free LOS checks he would just voluntarily drop Concealment of the units in question? Is this how it is played?

As Klas says ... yes.  I.E., the unit stays as the designated Spotter until you become eligible to replace him.  However, just because he's the designated Spotter doesn't prevent him from doing other things.  He's not tied to the MTR's hip; if you need him to run off and fight somewhere else, he's allowed to do that.  It just means that the MTR would only be able to fire without the benefit of the Spotter, i.e., at enemy units that the MTR's manning Infantry can see for itself.

Also, you're never required to use Spotted fire if you don't need to.  Depending on the exact situation, a Spotter may be absolutely essential to get any use out of the MTR ... or it might merely an option available to the MTR.

Ok, thanks. Although I would have hoped I could declare a new Spotter whenever I want. ;)

Coming back to the free LOS-checks once again: Can I really try all possible LOS from all my units to a Concealed enemy? Or do I have to stop my checks when the first valid LOS removes Concealment?

Coming back to the free LOS-checks once again: Can I really try all possible LOS from all my units to a Concealed enemy? Or do I have to stop my checks when the first valid LOS removes Concealment?

I am NRBH, so I don't know exactly the text of the rule in question, but it's my habit to check in order of "closest in hexes, most likely" and then proceed to the more unlikely possibilities, stopping when a LOS is found.  It might be rulebook-legal to check every LOS but I think you would find that to be a tedious interruption to the game in most circumstances, and your opponent may well get shirty about it, especially if you've already found a good LOS.  Of course, if we're talking about concealment-stripping, as soon as you have found a good LOS the concealment is stripped, and you no longer have an excuse to conduct further free LOS checks.

Ultimately this boils down to a "style of play" thing and as long as you and your opponent are comfortable with the approach being used you should be OK.  A lot of stuff dealing with concealment simply relies on trust between the players to work at all (e.g., moving dummies onto a hidden minefield), its just something you work out as you get familiar with the game.
Ok. Indeed, the rule book doesn't specify the exact procedure, as far as I can see. It certainly makes sense to play it the way you described.

question:
Two questions while playing U35 "Semper Paratus":

1. The attacker in the Pillbox hex, outside the Pillbox location, was Concealed before the CCPh. He loses Concealment during his attack. Both sides survive. Does he immediately regain "?" at the end of the CCPh (provided no other unbroken enemy unit has LOS)?

2. A4.2 Mechanics of Movement states in the last sentence: "Units moving as a stack expend MF simultaneously and need not spend MF for the same purpose, but must designate at the same time all actions for the same MF". Now I wonder if three squads, capable of laying smoke, are allowed to try that at the same time, together. If yes, will there be three individual Smoke-dr? May they continue to move as a stack after this action?
author: phxhf
consensus_answer:
1. The attacker in the Pillbox hex, outside the Pillbox location, was Concealed before the CCPh. He loses Concealment during his attack. Both sides survive. Does he immediately regain "?" at the end of the CCPh (provided no other unbroken enemy unit has LOS)?

No, unless the enemy unit in the pillbox is not Good Order.  Just because the unit in the PB cannot fire at the unit doesn't mean that he can't see it.  B30.2: "the pillbox Location and the same-level Location outside the pillbox are ADJACENT".  (The definition of ADJACENT requires that there is a LOS.)

2. A4.2 Mechanics of Movement states in the last sentence: "Units moving as a stack expend MF simultaneously and need not spend MF for the same purpose, but must designate at the same time all actions for the same MF". Now I wonder if three squads, capable of laying smoke, are allowed to try that at the same time, together. If yes, will there be three individual Smoke-dr? May they continue to move as a stack after this action?

Yes.  Yes.  Per A24.1, each squad must pre-designate the hex they are attempting to place SMOKE in before making the dr, but they can wait to see the results of each attempt before making their own attempt.  So it is legal to say "these three squads moving as a stack will each attempt to place SMOKE in an adjacent hex" (so they all spend 2 MF simultaneously) and then you make the dr for each squad, only picking the hex for each attempt just before rolling the die.  A couple of points to note:

1 - All of the attempts, collectively, have to be pre-designated.  So if you say all three squads are making the attempt, then you must make three dr (even if the first one succeeds and you don't need any more).  (Of course you can put multiple SMOKE counters in a single hex; but you can't decide to have one or more of the units not bother to roll at all);

2 - this is pretty much the only way outside of a Human Wave for an infantry unit to expend MF "doing nothing"; you can pre-designate that 2 out of 3 squads make SMOKE attempts, but maybe the 3rd squad doesn't have a SMOKE exponent; if you want him moving as part of the stack, he still has to expend the MF even though he isn't actually doing anything.  If there was something else he could expend MF doing, though (e.g., attempting to recover a SW), he could do that.

A pillbox is Rally bonus terrain, but I'm not sure that makes it a "required" rout destination (in the same sense as woods/buildings).  I don't have my rules handy so can't give you a definitive answer there.  Of course there will be circumstances where a routing unit can choose the pillbox as a destination any way, so your question is still valid. The broken unit doesn't "know" about them, so if that's where it must go, then that's where it goes, and then it must face the consequences of that.  In the case of the PB, in the situation as you describe it, yes, the broken unit will only "discover" the enemy units when it enters the PB hex, or (if they're HIP/concealed) when it attempts to enter the PB Location.

Whoa.  Who says a PB is like a building?  The rules certainly don't say that.  There absolutely will not "always be an ambush".  The PB is a separate Location within the hex, so even if it's a woods hex, you're not automatically going to get an ambush.  You will get an ambush possibility in the usual way: advancing into CC where either or both sides are HIP/concealed.  No advance = no ambush.  If the PB is located in an open ground hex, then it will be unlikely that an enemy unit can advance into the hex without losing concealment (it can happen, though).  If the PB is in a woods Location, and the occupants advance OUT to engage a unit in CC, then that is an ambush situation (in the normal way; i.e., the PB is irrelevant); but note that nobody is required to advance in order to initiate CC between units inside the PB and outside in the same hex.

Generally, the occupants of a PB will want to avoid ambush opportunities if they can, because they are heavily penalised (+2 drm on the ambush dr, IIRC).  That penalty of course only applies when they are inside the PB at the time of the ambush dr, so advancing out is one way to avoid that.

title: question about routing in  desert  battles.
question: So you can not rout toward an enemy, or in open ground in front of any fire. What about Desert battles? There's not cover at all. So are squads just dead?
author: fortyfiverevolutions
consensus_answer:
In addition to the rule J.R. quoted, there is also the extremely important:

F.5 SURRENDER: In all scenarios set in North Africa (as defined in F11.2), Surrender may not be refused -- i.e., a surrendering unit may not be eliminated thereby invoking No Quarter (A20.3).

If you don't have F11.2 handy, North Africa is defined as: Egypt, Libya, Tunisia, Morocco and Algeria.

This is one of ASL's infamous "hidden rules".  It's not really hidden, of course, it's right there in plain sight, but a lot of players forget that it exists.  While almost all scenarios set in Egypt and Libya (and there are many) are desert scenarios (so the application of a Chapter F rule is hardly surprising) there are several scenarios set in Tunisia that do not "look like" desert scenarios and therefore it's easy to forget that this Chapter F rule can apply.

replies.body:
There is a lot of nuance to the rout rules and I suggest a careful read. 

For example, you can in fact route toward the enemy. Just not a "known" enemy unit - meaning an enemy unit in LOS of the routing unit. For example, if an enemy unit is out of sight (from the routing unit's perspective), you may rout towards it. As soon as it comes into view though, it is now "known" and you likely will have to pick a new route target.

Another example - you can in fact rout in the open and within firing range of enemy units. Your routing unit will undergo "interdiction" while routing normally, or it can "low crawl" a single space and avoid interdiction.

Even within those two examples there are nuances and there are other route rules as well. These rules really make the game and need to be fully understood.

So in the desert, you can route and suffer interdiction but possibly still survive, or low crawl. You don't suffer interdiction when routing through terrain that provides a defensive benefit so even some scrub or rough kind of terrain (I don't own any desert modules) may allow you to route.

No time to look up particular rules references, but here's the outline:

If you are broken, and cannot rout without going through Open Ground, you must surrender... if there's anyone to surrender to. If there isn't (no Enemy is ADJACENT or in your hex), you may rout. If you rout through OG in normal range of Enemy units, you are subject to Interdiction... unless you use Low Crawl.

Expect to see a fair amount of Low Crawling happen in desert scenarios.
No rule book handy, but I believe that units in a desert scenario can be eliminated for failing to route only if an enemy unit is within 6 hexes of it.

The Rout rules are also tweaked a bit for desert scenarios:

F.1C ROUTING: In any scenario, a broken unit forced to rout but unable to reach a woods/building hex in that RtPh may rout to any terrain hex consistent with A10.51 but is not required to rout to the nearest woods/building hex. In a non-night scenario which uses only Desert Board(s) that are not Broken/Steppe Terrain (13.1-.2), a unit can be eliminated for Failure to Rout (A10.5) only if the enemy unit(s) forcing it to rout is within six hexes of it.

Yes. As you can see from J.R. Post, desert Rout provisions are slightly different. This is stated in Chapter F. Lacking buildings and woods, you can choose any kind of NON-open terrain as your rout destination. Often they are far more than 6MF so in order to avoid interdiction you must seldom rely on Low Crawl.(as James suggested)
Note that DUST, one of the desert major features, can positively increase your chances to survive interdiction.

If you don't have F11.2 handy, North Africa is defined as: Egypt, Libya, Tunisia, Morocco and Algeria.

While almost all scenarios set in Egypt and Libya (and there are many) are desert scenarios (so the application of a Chapter F rule is hardly surprising) there are several scenarios set in Tunisia that do not "look like" desert scenarios and therefore it's easy to forget that this Chapter F rule can apply.

title: AFV MG as MA and Acquiring the own hex
question:
Some questions, which I noted down during my last session:

1. An AFV has AAMG as its MA, with a note "AAMG NA VCA":
a) The VCA includes the hexsides of the covered area(C3.2). Does that mean "NA VCA" covers all the rest, but excluding these hexsides?
b) A11.62 states that a CMG cannot be used in CC when it has a restricted CA. But what about a restricted CA of an AAMG? Can I use it in CC?
c) Are there any restrictions in CC for a remote controlled AAMG, when the crew is BU?

2. The AFV has an MG as MA and can use ROF with it. As far as I understand there is no IF for an MG MA, so I can do SFF and FPF with it, like with a SW MG?

3. A Squad is in a hex adjacent to an AFV, which has put an Acquired Target counter on it during DFPh. In the APh the Squad advances (after passing PAATC) into the AFV's hex.
a) Does the Acquired Target counter still move with the Squad, into the firer's hex?
b) Assuming both units survive CC unharmed, can the AFV fire into its own hex, using the Acquired Target? C5.5 makes me think that Case E and Case N must be used together.
c) When I fire into my own hex during PFPh with HE, then all units are affected? Also the firing AFV's crew, when they happen to be CE? (Probably not. That would be really strange.)
author: phxhf
consensus_answer:
Some questions, which I noted down during my last session:

1. An AFV has AAMG as its MA, with a note "AAMG NA VCA":
a) The VCA includes the hexsides of the covered area(C3.2). Does that mean "NA VCA" covers all the rest, but excluding these hexsides?

Yes.

b) A11.62 states that a CMG cannot be used in CC when it has a restricted CA. But what about a restricted CA of an AAMG? Can I use it in CC?

Yes, unless the specific vehicle note says something different.

c) Are there any restrictions in CC for a remote controlled AAMG, when the crew is BU?

Only whatever restrictions are noted in the specific vehicle note (if any).  Are you talking about German MAVN O?  It specifically says "treated as a normal AAMG" for any purpose other than the listed specific restrictions.  If there was meant to be an EXC for CC, it would say so.

2. The AFV has an MG as MA and can use ROF with it. As far as I understand there is no IF for an MG MA, so I can do SFF and FPF with it, like with a SW MG?

No.  A vehicular MG may use Sustained Fire as per the last sentence of A8.41 if it is the vehicle's MA (A9.3).  That is, if already marked with a First Fire counter, it may fire again during the DFPh using Sustained Fire, but only vs. adjacent/same-hex targets.

SFF/FPF are options only available to Infantry.

3. A Squad is in a hex adjacent to an AFV, which has put an Acquired Target counter on it during DFPh. In the APh the Squad advances (after passing PAATC) into the AFV's hex.
a) Does the Acquired Target counter still move with the Squad, into the firer's hex?

Yes, unless it's a 5/8" acquisition, or unless the acquired weapon is unable to fire at range 0.

b) Assuming both units survive CC unharmed, can the AFV fire into its own hex, using the Acquired Target? C5.5 makes me think that Case E and Case N must be used together.

Yes.  Yes (all DRM are cumulative except where specifically indicated otherwise).

c) When I fire into my own hex during PFPh with HE, then all units are affected? Also the firing AFV's crew, when they happen to be CE? (Probably not. That would be really strange.)

All enemy units, and all units in melee can be affected.  Remember that a vehicle is never held in melee (A11.7).  With a couple of specific EXC (e.g., Thrown DC) you can never affect yourself with your own attack.

A8.4 FINAL FIRE: That portion of Defensive Fire which occurs during the DFPh is called Final Fire.

(my emphasis)

It is unbelievably extremely important that you pay attention to the usage of terms in ASL.  What is Final Fire?  It is explicitly described as above.  It has nothing to do with any form of Defensive Fire that occurs during the enemy's MPh, which is called Defensive First Fire (A8.1), Subsequent First Fire (A8.3), or Final Protective Fire (A8.31). title: Trenches/Foxholes, Defensive Fire, and MF
question:
OK, trying to get this nailed down.

Trenches and Foxholes are separate locations for very specific actions within a hex location, I've got that figured out. 

What I'm not as sure on is moving in and out of these fortifications and how that affects Defensive Fire. 

Assuming a very basic case, clear LoS throughout, level ground, etc. I move an MMC during the MPh from an adjacent hex into a trench. It costs 1MF if I'm *not* going into the trench, and obviously there are DFF opportunities as a result, one per firing defender because the move only cost 1MF. FFMO/FFNAM would apply (or not) as usual. For our purposes, the trench is in OG and this is not an assault move. 

Now let's say the unit wants to enter the hex and move into the trench. 1MF for moving into the hex, 1MF for jumping into the trench. 

As I'm reading it, DFF can occur, applying FFMO/FFNAM, for the first MF expended in the hex, then again for the trench jumping into, but without the FFMO/FFNAM for the second MF. Let's leave rout out of it for now, the interdiction rules seem clear to me. I know! When Rout seems clearer than, oh, anything else, I must be very confused. 

The same applies when leaving the trench (again assuming level ground), you pay 1MF to emerge, take your lumps, then keep going. I'm pretty sure I'm getting this part right. 

This is a bit confusing to me because I've played Red Barricades scenarios with printed shellholes (same for polder in the SK Decision at Elst set), and those assume you go directly into the shellholes and get their benefit immediately if you play 2MF to enter the hex, but OG if you pay 1MF. Once you stop moving in that hex, you are considered to be in the shellhole because there isn't any way to track that.

Obviously, all of this applies to Foxholes as well, although you can't move foxhole to foxhole like you can with trenches.

We've played with trenches before, but as I'm learning, I need more learning. 

Thanks in advance!

Doug

consensus_answer:
OK, trying to get this nailed down.

Trenches and Foxholes are separate locations for very specific actions within a hex location, I've got that figured out.

Almost.  DO NOT describe them as "separate Locations", because "Location" has a very specific game meaning.  Better to say that they are separate positions within the hex.

Assuming a very basic case, clear LoS throughout, level ground, etc. I move an MMC during the MPh from an adjacent hex into a trench. It costs 1MF if I'm *not* going into the trench, and obviously there are DFF opportunities as a result, one per firing defender because the move only cost 1MF. FFMO/FFNAM would apply (or not) as usual. For our purposes, the trench is in OG and this is not an assault move. 

Now let's say the unit wants to enter the hex and move into the trench. 1MF for moving into the hex, 1MF for jumping into the trench. 

As I'm reading it, DFF can occur, applying FFMO/FFNAM, for the first MF expended in the hex, then again for the trench jumping into, but without the FFMO/FFNAM for the second MF. Let's leave rout out of it for now, the interdiction rules seem clear to me. I know! When Rout seems clearer than, oh, anything else, I must be very confused. 

Well, I think one source of your confusion is that you are treating the two different choices as if they were  two different types of movement.  They are not.

The unit expends 1 MF to enter the hex.  That is true regardless of the existence of the trench, and regardless of the unit's intentions.  That 1 MF expenditure can trigger Defensive First Fire in the usual manner, and FFMO/FFNAM can apply as usual.

THEN -- only then -- the moving unit, if able, may expend an additional MF to enter the trench.  Or, of course, he could expend additional MF to leave the hex, or make a smoke grenade attempt, or whatever.

Entering the hex and entering the trench are separate, distinct activities during the MPh.  Do not conflate them into a single action!

This is a bit confusing to me because I've played Red Barricades scenarios with printed shellholes (same for polder in the SK Decision at Elst set), and those assume you go directly into the shellholes and get their benefit immediately if you play 2MF to enter the hex, but OG if you pay 1MF. Once you stop moving in that hex, you are considered to be in the shellhole because there isn't any way to track that.

Correct.  Shellholes are not entrenchments and don't use the same rules.  A shellhole hex is a special type of terrain where, during the MPh, the TEM it offers differs depending how many MF you expended to enter the hex.  This is completely different to the way entrenchments work.

author: dcooley
consensus_answer:
If Defender is ALL HIP setup..........the Attacker setup is then onboard................Can the defender prevent Concealment gains for Attacker units in LOS during Setup????

To deny concealment (at setup or at any other time) there needs to be an unbroken unit with LOS (so even a dummy stack is sufficient).  The A12.121 Concealment Loss/Gain Table is one of the most important tables in the entire game.  Study it.

So if all enemy units are HIP then there are no unbroken enemy units on the map.  There is no way to prevent concealment gain in that situation, unless the enemy voluntarily forfeits HIP (which he can choose to do at any time).

However, the Setup A12.12 rule is not clear whether this can be done during the setup sequence.

Which part of the rule you quote is unclear?  It states exactly which units gain concealment!

title: Concealment at Setup
question:
Setup procedure is incorrect.

Russian sets up, using only provided concealment counters (and only in Concealment terrain).

Then German sets up, using only provided concealment counters  (and only in Concealment terrain).

Then Russian and German units out of LOS gain concealment, no matter what the terrain.

If one side has no units on-board, then they may place non-provided concealment counters on unit when they setup and before the opponent looks at the board.
consensus_answer:
Brian's summary is correct.

The important things to remember are that during setup, "?" counters provided in the scenario OB may only be placed in Concealment Terrain (the terrain types marked in red on the Terrain Chart); and, during setup, units that qualify for concealment gain, either because they are out of all enemy LOS (even if in open ground), or because they are in LOS but in Concealment Terrain at extreme range (typically > 16 hexes) do not have to make a Concealment dr.

Neither of the above rules apply once play of the scenario begins.

To check the nitty-gritty details, consult the Concealment Loss/Gain Chart (learn it, love it, make it your best friend) and the Advanced Sequence of Play (the scenario setup section).

Incidentally, I know it's a suggestion printed in the rules, but the give-the-enemy-lots-of-dummy-counters-when-playing-solo rule is not very effective if you're actually playing solo.  ASL is not really geared for solitaire play (not counting the actual Solitaire ASL expansion, which is a different kettle of fish altogether) and lots of enemy concealment is not going to do much to make the play interesting, although your plan is about as good as you can make it.  If you had a live opponent, he would be planning all sorts of things with his dummies that you can't reasonably replicate in solo play.  In general, you'll get a better solo game by picking scenarios that don't make use of lots of dummies.

4. According to D5.42 I enter my previously abandoned AFV with its crew, expending all their MF. May the AFV now fire in the AFPh of the same turn? Would it be Bounding Fire Case B (because the AFV didn't move into a new hex) or Case C?
author: phxhf
consensus_answer:
1. Yes, the wreck remains in VBM and will block other VBM in the hexside. Check D9.4 for hindrance requirements. Check D9.3 for TEM requirements. To understand the rules remember that a vehicle in VBM is inside the hex and in the same Location that the obstacle it is bypassing.

3. Yes

replies.body:
1. Yes, the wreck remains in VBM and will block other VBM in the hexside. Check D9.4 for hindrance requirements. Check D9.3 for TEM requirements. To understand the rules remember that a vehicle in VBM is inside the hex and in the same Location that the obstacle it is bypassing.

Elaborating a bit on Marti's answer to Q1:

(NRBH, so can't give you eaxct rules quotes, sorry.)

A vehicle/wreck is only a hindrance when the hex containing it is in same-level LOS of both the firer and the target.  Since by definition that hex must contain either woods or building, the odds are fairly high that the obstacle itself will block LOS, making any hindrance irrelevant.

However, certainly there will be situations where the LOS will pass through the hex but not through the obstacle.  In that case the core principle applies: both firer and target must have a same-level LOS to the vehicle/wreck, which in this case (since it's in VBM) has to be drawn to the applicable CAFP.

So if the LOS doesn't pass through the obstacle, and both firer and target have a LOS to the CAFP where the vehicle/wreck is located, it will create a hindrance -- even if it's in a hexside not being crossed by the LOS!  (That's because, as Marti says, the vehicle, even in VBM, is still IN the hex -- and vehicle/wreck hindrances behave as if they were Inherent -- i.e., they "fill" the hex, if all the other pre-requisites are met.)

For a wreck in Bypass, the LOS has to cross the hexside (not necessarily the CAFP) is bypassing in order for it to constitute a Hindrance.

Of course both firer and target still needs a LOS to it (i.e., the CAFP).
Klas is correct, of course.  The hexside requirement is stated in D9.4.  The hazards of providing answers without rules handy (and/or being an idiot) bite me once again.

For those like me who find it difficult to remember to check if a SAN is rolled, I now roll a red sniper die on all TH, IFT and MC rolls. After all 3 dice are rolled, look at the red sniper die first. If it is not a 1 or 2, forget it. If it is, see if the two main dice equals the other side's SAN. Good tip I got from somewhere. I used to hate ending a scenario and thinking I hardly ever remembered to think about SANs - a shame as snipers add real flavour and can be game changers.

Three SAN checks. You'd roll each Russian SAN as they happened (as the only result of that DR, the squad passing, is already resolved), and then the German SAN.

This is an extremely important point, overlooked by many players (including myself until it was explained to me by Scott Romanowski).

The SAN dr is made when the action that triggered it is fully resolved.  If the action that triggered the SAN was "an attack DR was made against a stack of units" then that action is "fully resolved" when all subsequent MC, PTC, LLMC, HOB DR, etc. etc. caused by that attack on that stack have been completed.

However, if the action that triggered the SAN was a single unit's MC/TC, then it is "fully resolved" as soon as that unit has made the MC/TC DR (unless there was a HOB result or similar).

EX: A German 4-6-7 squad fires at a stack of American units: a 9-1 leader and two 6-6-6 squads.  The SAN for both sides is "3".  The German IFT DR is a "3", resulting in a 1MC (after applying TEM, DRM etc.).  The American player notes that he has to make a SAN dr after the attack has been resolved.  He then makes the MC DR for his units: the leader checks first and rolls a "2".  HOB!  A HOB DR is immediately made and the result is Battle Hardening -- the 9-1 is immediately replaced with a 9-2.  The squads now have a better chance of passing their checks!  The first squad now checks and rolls a "3".  He passes, but he has triggered the German Sniper.  This check is made immediately as the action that triggered the Sniper -- the squad's individual MC -- has now been completed.  The German player rolls a "1" and as luck would have it, the Sniper moves to that hex and Random Selection results in the 9-2 leader being the target.  He is immediately eliminated.  The American player begins to cry.  Now the second squad must make his 1MC (now with no leadership) and rolls a "7", breaking the squad.  Now, because the leader died, both squads must make a 2MC (LLMC) and both fail, breaking the first squad and casualty reducing the second.  Now, finally, the American player gets to make his Sniper dr and rolls a "6".  No sniper for him, and he cries some more.

As with many things in ASL, getting the timing of the sequence of events correct can be critical.
Thanks, Bruce, been playing that wrong!

Bruce:

Awesome example of the interactive nature of ASL.

Cheers,

Mark

Thanks!

Technically, prisoners aren't "enemy units".  They aren't really units at all (they have no movement capability of their own, they only move as their guards move).  Prisoners are more like SW than they are like units.  Thus they can be (or more specifically, their guards can be) attacked by non-CC methods normally and the prisoners may be affected as a result.

Prisoners who have escaped, or have been released (abandoned) are units, of course, even though they may be unarmed, and thus will have the same immunity to friendly fire as other types of units.  It is important to remember the distinction: unarmed units are units, except when they are prisoners.

CC with prisoners is a different kettle of fish, though.  And it can get quite complicated if you're playing a scenario where unarmed units are representing "neutral" participants, like civilians.  The scenario SSR in such cases needs careful wording, because technically a true "neutral" unit is enemy of no-one and thus under normal ASL rules are immune to most forms of attack by anyone!

title: Leadership bonus
question: Very new ASL player with a quick question.  If a squad is in a hex with both a +1 and a -1 leader and is firing do they get the better -1 leaders bonus?  Thanks!
author: Bones67
consensus_answer:
An EXC to the above replies is when an unpinned, Good Order Commissar and a normal leader are together in a hex.  The Commissar pulls rank over any other leader and prevents the application of another leader's modifier (even if the Commissar isn't otherwise involved!), and if it's the RPh and there are broken units present, the Commissar (and no other leader) must attempt to rally them.  (I don't have the specific rules references to hand but it's all in A25, or you can see my article in ASL Journal #8.)

A25.222:
"A Commissar must attempt to rally broken units in its Location..."

There might an exception if said broken unit is itself a Commissar - I think they always have to Self-Rally.

This has some implications for Japanese leaders; since all Japanese leaders are Commissars,...
G1.41:
"A Japanese leader [EXC: Inherent armor leader] is equivalent to a Commissar for all rally and berserk purposes; i.e., he bestows all the same benefits and penalties given in A25.222-.223...."

So there are some subtle difference between a Russian Commissar and a Japanese leader:
A Japanese leader increases the Morale Level of all other non-berserk Japanese Infantry/Cavalry units, even if he is pinned, a Russian Commissar needs to be unpinned to do that.

Also, I think a Japanese leader can receive the leader DRM of another leader when performing any action, a Russian Commissar can't.

I think those are the two difference.

If the +1 is the only leader in the hex and you're trying to rally the squad, and it's not your self-rally attempt, then you would have to apply +1 to the MC

title: Slopes and Vineyard help needed
question:
Hi all!
KGP2.3 :"Being Up-Slope affects LOS only in that an Up-Slope location is treated as being 3/4 of a level higher than normal to LOS that begins or ends in that location and crosses an Up-Slope hexside of that location. Thus, barring other obstructions to LOS, an Up-Slope unit[...]can trace a LOS across an Up-Slope hexside of its hex to a lower elevation and/or over obstacles and hindrances whose topmost height is = one slope hexside does not change the elevation of that hex's Base Level."

Now. What about intervening vineyard hexes? What is their height? Are they lower than 3/4? (They are treated like Brush...)

In the situation above, the Bofor in the right up corner is Up-Slope. Assuming the Correct CA, does it have a clear LOS to the Foxhole in the lower left corner(it has an ATR atop)? Does its LOS passes OVER vineyard and walls?
Thanks
author: Qwirz
consensus_answer:
Is there a paragraph where I can find the height of brush/vineyard?

B12.2 "... it is only the presence of brush in a same-level hex between the same-level firing (or observing/spotting) and target hex that forms a LOS Hindrance ...."

Whenever any terrain type is described as having some LOS effect (whether it's a Hindrance or an Obstacle) that only affects same-level LOS then you can assume (barring some explicit statement to the contrary) that the terrain type is only a half-level high.

(In all cases "same-level" of course includes "continuous slope" (B.5).)

Fundamentally, the function of slope hexsides is to enable units in qualifying hexes to "see over" intervening half-level obstacles in contravention of the normal LOS rules that would otherwise apply.
