title: First Fired MG and not First Fired inherent FP
question:
A pretty common situation: A squad only fired its MG on an approaching enemy unit and loses ROF. When the enemy enters the next hex (further approaching this squad) I want to fire both, the MG and the inherent FP.

I am pretty sure that because this shot would be SFF for the MG, I also have to mark the squad with a Final Fire marker. Where I'm unsure: Is the squad's inherent FP now halved or not? I played it with half MG-FP and full squad-FP in the past.

On one hand the squad didn't fire before, but on the other hand it seems to be a SFF shot for the MG and the squad...
author: phxhf
consensus_answer:
.

Note that had it been the squad that was marked "First Fire", the MG's FP would have been halved, so it is different depending on which unit/weapon is marked "First Fire".

I disagree and the flowchart seems to do so as well.

Is there a rule specifically pointing this out?

Hey Jeff,

Klas has it right. 

Read the first and second sentence of A8.3 Subsequent First Fire, which reads in part, "A DEFENDING Infantry unit already marked with a First Fire counter may  Defensive First Fire again during that MPh as Area Fire by flipping its First Fire counter over to the Final Fire side... MG/IFE is treated as sustained fire and penalized accordingly."

I would say the Flowchart also supports this: Bottom right corner,4th bullet.

Hope this helps...

replies.body:
The MG and the Squad are marked First Fire seperately... unless you cower when firing one or the other or both, then both are marked Final Fire.

In your situation, the MG FP is halved for SFF and the squad FP is full strength.  SFF is Sustained Fire for the MG so remember all the things that go with that (lowered b/x# etc).

Intereseting that you say "a pretty common situation".  I find it a somewhat rare situation unless the MG placed a Firelane during its first shot.  In that case the Squad could only fire alone (at full FP).  However, if on that shot, the Squad Cowers, the Squad/MG is marked Final Fire (remember to use RS on a FG) and the Firelane is canceled.  

Rare?  Ok, an exageration.  But the 1 in 6 chance of Cowering usually makes me want to fire everything at once to get maximum effect on all my shots.  And when I do place a Firelane I rarely (unless a decisive PBF shot arises) fire the squad subsequently for fear of Cowering and losing the Firelane.

Of course there are always situations where splitting shots is the right call.  For me it seems those situations arise about 15% of the time, and well, 1/6... you get where I'm going with this...

:)

In the end I think you played it right in the past.

I "think" the Squad alone could even fire at enemies unrestricted by the SFF range requirement.

I hope someone chimes in to confirm or correct me.

title: Sewer Movement
question:
Is it correct that a unit in a manhole location can enter the sewers and move to the next sewer location in a single MPh? The first sentence of B8.41 makes me think so.

I'm currently playing The Czerniakow Bridgehead, which has the regular Russian/Polish army and the Polish Partisans. Only the latter may enter the sewers. Then I read in A25.241: "Partisans that are moving as a combined stack together with non-Partisan units may endow the regular units with whatever SSR-endowed movement advantage they have".
Like sewer movement?

Why are there only four Sewer counters (Beyond Valor and Yanks combined)? I could need a lot more.

The Sewer Emergence Chart defines three states of a sewer-unit, which I determine at the end of their MPh. But there is no way to remember that state with a counter? How are you doing it? Turn the sewer-counter by 45 degrees when discovered, or something like that?
author: phxhf
consensus_answer:
Is it correct that a unit in a manhole location can enter the sewers and move to the next sewer location in a single MPh? The first sentence of B8.41 makes me think so.

Yes, but that is the only movement option for the unit in that MPh.  You can't combine regular movement (of any sort, for any purpose) with sewer movement.

I'm currently playing The Czerniakow Bridgehead, which has the regular Russian/Polish army and the Polish Partisans. Only the latter may enter the sewers. Then I read in A25.241: "Partisans that are moving as a combined stack together with non-Partisan units may endow the regular units with whatever SSR-endowed movement advantage they have".
Like sewer movement?

It seems a reasonable argument.  I'd be happier about it if the term "Partisan" was actually used anywhere on the scenario card.  As it is the argument could be made that the Home Army units are just Russians who use counters that have the same values as Partisan counters, but are not actually Partisans (and thus don't use any Partisan rules).  If you (and your opponent) accept that the Home Army units are Partisans, then A25.241 should certainly apply.

Why are there only four Sewer counters (Beyond Valor and Yanks combined)? I could need a lot more.

You're free to make your own.  The fact is that Sewer Movement is not a rule that gets a lot of use in most non-CG scenarios, and there's only limited space on the counter sheets.  Compromises have to be made.

The Sewer Emergence Chart defines three states of a sewer-unit, which I determine at the end of their MPh. But there is no way to remember that state with a counter? How are you doing it? Turn the sewer-counter by 45 degrees when discovered, or something like that?

Whatever works for you.  You could drop a different counter on top of the Sewer Marker to signify the status -- e.g., the DM counters with a red back (OBA chits), or whatever else is handy and won't be confused for something else.  In ASL, while sometimes you may not have the exact counter you want, you can be sure that you will never be lacking for spare counters for any particular purpose. :)

title: Routing adjacent to a known enemy unit
question:
I have a unit that wishes to rout out of hex K19 on the Red Barricades board. There are enemy units in hexes J18 and L19, meaning that the unit is surrounded. However, there is a black bar between J18 and K19, so J18 is out of LOS of K19 and thus not a known enemy unit at the start of the rout phase. J19 is the only possible rout direction, but once entering that hex, the broken unit is in the LOS and ADJACENT to the enemy unit in J18. Is the broken unit allowed to rout from K19 to J19?

Argument for allowing it: the enemy unit does not become known until after the routing unit enters J19, so the initial move from K19 to J19 is not considered routing ADJACENT to a known enemy unit

Argument against allowing it: the timing of when the enemy unit becomes known not mentioned in the rules, so once the routing unit enters J19, it is in a hex ADJACENT to a known enemy unit, and since it is not leaving J18, the rout is not allowed

Obviously, if routing into J19 is allowed, the routing unit must continue to rout because it cannot end the rout phase ADJACENT to J18.

title: Advance and Concealment
question:
Does an Advance is considered "Non-Assault-Movement" ?

Do I loose a concealment marker if I do advance in the APh ?
author: LarsHolgerRoth
consensus_answer:
To a concealment terrain, no. To open ground yes.

Not quite.  The issue is "open ground vs. not open ground", NOT "open ground vs. concealment terrain".  Never confuse "concealment terrain" with "not open ground", they are different concepts.  (So different that there is even one type of concealment terrain that is also treated as open ground!  Anyone care to guess what it is?)

If your advancing unit is in open ground vs. any good order enemy unit within 16 hexes with a LOS to it, then it will lose concealment (Case B on the Concealment Loss/Gain Table). [EXC: Winter Camouflage (E3.712) can negate this.]

Remember hindrances cancel open ground consideration.

Terrain hindrances, yes.  LV Hindrances, no.

title: In gully visibility from outside adjacent hex
question:
Hi Folks,

The current scenario that I'm playing features gullys.

The way I am playing them, is that a same level adjacent hex, cannot see units that are actually in an adjacent gully. They have to wait for the units to crest or exit to some other ground level hex.

Does this sound right? It kind of feels right given that the hexes are 40 mtrs across but alas, the gully rules don't seem to provide many examples of this.

Also, what would be the effect on adjacent enemy broken units? I have been DM'ing them to route them away, even though the gully unit is out of view?

Regards
RobP
author: FlashPan
consensus_answer:
The current scenario that I'm playing features gullys.

The way I am playing them, is that a same level adjacent hex, cannot see units that are actually in an adjacent gully. They have to wait for the units to crest or exit to some other ground level hex.

Does this sound right?

Uh, no.  The best way to play LOS into gullies is the way the rules describe in A6.3.

The general rule is, to see INTO a gully, the observing unit must have a height advantage >= the range in hexes.  So a unit one level higher at a range of one hex (i.e., in an adjacent hex) can see INTO the gully.  If you are 2 hexes away, the height difference must be at least two levels, and so on.

There are many exceptions to this general rule.  E.G., units in adjacent gully hexes do not have LOS to each other if their respective gully hexes do not share a common gully hexside (i.e., they do not "connect"). (A6.8, first EX)  However, units can see INTO depression hexes without necessarily having the height requirement described above, if they are looking along a depression (A6.3 EX).

Okay, let's start with 'same level'.

You have two hexes, one is open ground with a gully running through it and the other is open ground adjacent to it. There are no crest lines.

Both hexes are Level 0. However, units IN the gully are in a Level -1 Depression (B19.2). Units in Crest status are at Level 0. Units in either hex can see each other. Note that this is a common application of A6.3. You're one hex away, and you have a one-level advantage over the contents of the gully. If you're two hexes away, you can't see IN the gully unless you're at Level 1 or higher.

No, it doesn't cover it under gullies, but it does in the LOS rules (A6.3)
"A unit in a ground level hex always has LOS INTO an adjacent level -1 depression hex..."

A routing unit can not rout adjacent to an enemy unit if it knows it's there, nor can it move closer to a known enemy unit, so if your routing is doing any of these things then you have a problem. A unit that starts in a gully and adjacent to an enemy unit is visible and must rout away.
Also IIRC, Gullies are considered Open Ground for rout purposes.

Half FP is a MTR's "full FP".

It's not complex.  You use the ordnance calibre to determine the base FP column on the IFT.

e.g., 81mm = 16 FP.

When you fire a MTR, you must use Area Target Type.  When using ATT, the actual FP column used is half of the base FP.

So, 81mm MTR = 8 FP.

That's all you need to know.  MTRs make up for the "lack" of FP in many ways.  They typically have a high ROF, which means you get to make those TH/IFT DR many times.  That dramatically improves the odds of getting a useful result.  Even if your target is in a stone building, 8+3 is not a terrible attack.  (As noted above, a CH result doubles the base FP, i.e., 30 FP on the IFT for an 81mm MTR.)

Although sometimes being restricted to the ATT is a detriment, most of the time it actually gives you a better chance to hit, especially at long ranges.  And if your target is concealed, using the ATT is the only way to gain acquisition.  If you're lucky enough to have a MTR that fires SMOKE, the combination of that and high ROF means you have the chance of blanketing your enemy -- very useful if you're trying to cross open terrain to get to them!

Even the puny Belgian 46mm MTR has the potential to be very destructive.  I'm always a little disappointed if my side in a scenario has no MTRs.

Also good to keep in mind with Mortars is Air Bursts. Often your opponent doesn't even want to get into those woods if you have a Mortar there keeping watch. Can sometimes be more useful than the actual effects the Mortar does during the scenario.

title: CC Reaction Fire
question:
Hi all!
This is one of the rules I still can't grasp.
Reading and re-reading rules and Backblast #2 wonderful article "Dance with the Tiger", I still have doubts.
D7.2 last lines "Reaction Fire vs an OVRing vehicle is resolved immediately after the resolution of that OVR"
Pag. 29 Backblast #2, CC Reaction Fire paragraph "If an infantry or cavalry unit is unbroken, unpinned, armed, not in melee, and in a moving vehicle's location, it may attempt to attack the vehicle using the CC rules. This is true whether the vehicle is overrunning the location or not."
Now, playing 137.Italian Brothers the following occurred.

L3 is about to OVR the 8-1 and three 4-3-7 in N9. 
Being not able to harm the BU AFV with fire, can the Infantry units attack the vehicle when it enters the hex, BEFORE the OVR resolution????
Are there other means of defence?
Any help is much appreciated.
Thanks!!!

EDIT: Sorry for the poor focus of the picture.
author: Qwirz
consensus_answer:
It means you may conduct Defensive Fire that is not CC RF on the MP expenditure announced for the OVR. So if the unit being OVR has an LATW, it may use it.

A Gun has a special rule for OVR prevention, enabling it to fire one more time on the onrushing tank before the OVR is resolved. Note that this always counts as an intensive fire shot, regardless of wether the Gun has fired before. So it can easily break during the attempt. If a kill is scored, the OVR will still take place, but FP is halved.

5.64 OVR PREVENTION: Regardless of the number of shots a non-vehicular Gun has already taken during a Player Turn (including Intensive Fire), it is entitled to the possibility of one more Intensive Fire shot at a target in its own hex if it is about to be OVR [EXC: OVR Prevention cannot be used by a Gun with a "No IF" listing on the back of its counter; 5.63]. Immediately after the OVR MP expenditure (D7.1) is announced (but before the OVR is resolved) the Gun makes its To Hit DR vs the vehicle making the OVR, but not until its CA covers the hexside entered by the OVR vehicle. If a Gun has already fired from woods/building/rubble, it is not allowed to change its CA (5.11) and is not eligible for OVR Prevention vs an AFV entering its hex from outside the Gun's CA. A Gun which has already Intensive Fired during that MPh suffers only one set of Intensive Fire penalties (i.e., the Intensive Fire DRM and B# reductions of the two Intensive Fire shots are not cumulative). The Original To Hit DR of the firing Gun also acts as a NMC vs its own manning Infantry. If the manning Infantry is pinned or broken as a result of that NMC, the To Hit attempt is voided (except for any Gun Malfunction or Low Ammo (D3.71) it may have caused) and the OVR vehicle resolves its OVR. If the NMC is passed by rolling < the manning Infantry's Morale Level, the To Hit DR is resolved vs the OVR vehicle and may possibly lessen the OVR attack (D7.11). Regardless of the outcome of the To Hit DR, the Gun is marked with a "No Fire" counter to indicate that it may not fire again during that Player Turn—even if it is about to be OVR again.

title: Guns - Case B Adv Fire Phase
question:
Hi folks,

I have always found this one to be a little confusing. On the surface it seems to penalize stationary vehicles over moving ones, which doesn't seem to make much sense.

I'm guessing the designers are relying on the fact that a moving vehicle will have other penalties applied to it? Or am I misinterpreting its use?

author: FlashPan
consensus_answer:
Thanks Folks,

That does clear things up. Having now read the Case C penalties in the rules (5.3) and on the quick reference card I'm not sure how I ever missed this!

Disrupted units "may not use Low Crawl" (A19.12 14th line)
If in Open Ground they rout normally.

If it's in Open Ground in normal range of a Known Enemy Unit, a disrupted unit will rout normally, unless it is currently adjacent to a KEU, in which case it will Surrender (assuming No Quarter has not been declared).

Any unit which routs and comes ADJACENT to a previously-unknown enemy unit must rout away from it. If it cannot, either because there's nowhere left to go, or because it's out of MF, is eliminated for Failure to Rout. (Beginning of A10.5)

title: Can a PF be fired at Infantry in a building?
question:
I ask because it's a HEAT round, so should be able to, but I can't find it's IFE equivalent value to perform the shot. Bazookas and others with counters have that value on the counter, but alas, the PF lacks these.

Thanks
RobP
author: FlashPan
consensus_answer:
Hello RobP.

Panzerfausts indeed may be fired at such a target. For this purpose they have an IFT equivalent of 16. Note that the IFT has a "PF" at the top of the 16 column as a reminder.

Also, as per  Rule C13.31, due to the fact that a Panzerfaust is a one shot weapon, it must use random selection when determining its final target (Though a target manning a gun/SW may be predesignated).

And finally, remember a Panzerfaust does NOT leave Residual Firepower in a hex.

Hope this helps!

Rob

author: Currie_p1
consensus_answer:
So, I don't get the FPF cos it's not another unit moving adjacent? Makes sense, thanks

No, you don't get FPF because the berserker only expends 2 MF to enter the Location, which means the occupants of the Location only get at most 2 opportunities to fire at him (A8.3).

Remember that once the berserker is in the enemy unit's Location, that enemy unit loses the ability to make any attacks at anyone not in the same Location (A7.212).

Finally remember that berserkers must move first in the MPh before any non-berserker unit (A15.43 and the ASOP).

Further clarification: FPF is a type of attack that can only occur during the MPh, and never during the DFPh (A8.31).

title: SAN target determination with multiple LOCATIONS
question:
My nemesis Bill (!) and I are playing Pavlov's House and I activated his Sniper.  He rolled for the target hex but since there were no eligible targets, we triggered 14.21 "ALTERNATE TARGET: 14.21 Should greater than or equal to 2 such hexes be equidistant, the Location with the lowest TEM is the target." and moved the Sniper to the closest hex that contained enemy units. I had Russians on the Ground floor (fortified stone building TEM +4) and 1st floor (stone building +3 TEM). 

Here is our question - 14.21 specifically uses the term 'hexes' not 'Locations' being  equidistant to select the 'Location' with the lowest TEM.  There was only 1 eligible HEX for the Sniper to hit but it had 2 Locations.  We weren't sure if the sniper attacked the +3 Location or we triggered 14.2 that says "if that new target hex Contains greater 1 Location occupied by an eligible enemy unit, the Sniper player selects which of those Locations to attack".  So, we let the Sniper select the Location.

Did we play this correctly??
author: tobiwonknobi
consensus_answer:
There's a lot of confusion here which would go away if you pay attention to what exactly it is that you're doing each step of the way.

A14.21 is all about selecting the target HEX.  The first sentence of A14.21 makes this clear.  Everything in A14.21 is about determining which HEX you're moving the Sniper to.  First choice: nearest hex with eligible targets.  If there's still more than one choice, you choose the hex that has the lowest TEM.  If you still have more than one choice, then the player decides which hex the Sniper is moved to.

Congratulations!  You now know which hex the Sniper is attacking.  Now you actually move back to A14.2 to determine WHO in that hex is actually being attacked.  This is where we see the rule "If that new target hex Contains > one Location occupied by an eligible (14.22) enemy unit(s), the Sniper player selects which of those Locations to attack."  The Location with the lowest TEM is completely irrelevant to this choice.  The Sniper player can choose the Location with the highest TEM, if he wants to!

In other words:

1 - Select the target hex per the criteria specified in A14.21.

2 - Having selected the hex, if you have a choice of multiple Locations, the Sniper player chooses which Location to attack.  That's all it is -- a simple choice!

3 - Having at last decided which Location is being attacked, you then select the actual target of the attack, if there is more than one eligible target.  Usually this will be by Random Selection (but A14.21 lists the EXC that enables the Sniper player to bypass RS and just pick a particular target).

In the entirety of the above procedure, the only time "lowest TEM" comes into the picture is in step 1, and even then, only when there is more than one possible hex to attack.

title: Advanced squad leader starter set 2. Rallying in close combat/melee
question:
I have a broken SMC in a combat situation.
Cannot find the rule about weather or not he can rally during the "Rally Phase" at the beginning of the next turn, whilst still in combat. 

What is the definition of "Eligible" that would define what units can be rallied.
author: jerryhaworth
consensus_answer:
Broken units can certainly appear in CC situations.  An important consideration is whether a Melee exists or not.

As stated above, broken units must attempt to Withdraw from a Melee in the CCPh (and cannot move in the RtPh).  If it is not a Melee, then they have no options in the CCPh at all -- they must sit and take whatever is coming to them -- but will usually rout in the preceding RtPh.  There are EXC, typically if the enemy units are concealed and the broken unit is not under DM, they can move up to the broken unit and advance in (with a very good chance of scoring an Ambush).

None of the above tells us much about what a broken unit in CC's options during the RPh are, though.  There are a couple of clues:

A10.6 tells us that a Good Order leader can attempt to rally broken units in his Location.  If there's a Melee going on, the leader will not be Good Order, unless he is not involved in the Melee somehow -- e.g., if he is concealed.

Fairly definitively, A11.15 tells us that "Units locked in Melee may not Interdict routing units nor conduct any other activity other than CC or Withdrawal from Melee."

So, if the broken unit is actually held in Melee, no form of (deliberate) rally attempt can be made -- the broken unit is forbidden from such activity (and any leader present would also be similarly forbidden if he is also locked in Melee).

What if the broken unit is not in Melee, though?  For example, if the only enemy unit in the Location is a non-stopped vehicle, then there is no Melee.  "Other activities" (such as rally attempts) then seem to be allowed.

There is an (unofficial) Q&A from MMP that says:

A10.6 & A11.15
Can a broken unit be rallied while in CC or melee?
A. Only via HOB.

That's pretty definitive, but the "CC" portion is not (as above) actually supported by existing rules text (unless there's some other buried rule that I've missed, which is always possible).  As such, it constitutes errata-in-waiting.  It would be up to the players to decide whether to accept it in their game.  Personally I don't really see a problem with it, but if my opponent didn't want to accept it, it would be hypocritical of me to argue against him, given my prior public statements concerning unofficial Q&A. :D

For one thing, broken units in melee are compelled to attempt to withdraw in the CC phase (or the rout phase if you aren't yet locked in melee, but I may be wrong about that one). You can't stay in the same hex as an enemy unit if you're broken.

If it is not a Melee, then they have no options in the CCPh at all -- they must sit and take whatever is coming to them -- but will usually rout in the preceding RtPh.  There are EXC, typically if the enemy units are concealed and the broken unit is not under DM, they can move up to the broken unit and advance in (with a very good chance of scoring an Ambush).

None of the above tells us much about what a broken unit in CC's options during the RPh are, though.  There are a couple of clues:

A10.6 tells us that a Good Order leader can attempt to rally broken units in his Location.  If there's a Melee going on, the leader will not be Good Order, unless he is not involved in the Melee somehow -- e.g., if he is concealed.

Fairly definitively, A11.15 tells us that "Units locked in Melee may not Interdict routing units nor conduct any other activity other than CC or Withdrawal from Melee."

So, if the broken unit is actually held in Melee, no form of (deliberate) rally attempt can be made -- the broken unit is forbidden from such activity (and any leader present would also be similarly forbidden if he is also locked in Melee).

What if the broken unit is not in Melee, though?  For example, if the only enemy unit in the Location is a non-stopped vehicle, then there is no Melee.  "Other activities" (such as rally attempts) then seem to be allowed.

There is an (unofficial) Q&A from MMP that says:

A10.6 & A11.15
Can a broken unit be rallied while in CC or melee?
A. Only via HOB.

That's pretty definitive, but the "CC" portion is not (as above) actually supported by existing rules text (unless there's some other buried rule that I've missed, which is always possible).  As such, it constitutes errata-in-waiting.  It would be up to the players to decide whether to accept it in their game.  Personally I don't really see a problem with it, but if my opponent didn't want to accept it, it would be hypocritical of me to argue against him, given my prior public statements concerning unofficial Q&A. :D

title: Very noobie question regards ROF and firing an LMG (ASLSK 1)
question:
Still trying to get my head round some of the rules

I have a German (3-8)LMG that is with an German infantry counter (4-6-7).
In the Prep fire phase I roll a (colored) 1 and  a White 3. According to the rule 1.2.4 as the colored dice is equal to the ROF (1) that LMG may fire again.

1) How do I do this?, is a separate dice rolled for that LMG on its own factor (3)after the initial combined FP, or is the factor added again into the initial FP attack

2) Is this re roll done in a separate phase
author: jerryhaworth
consensus_answer:
I have a German (3-8)LMG that is with an German infantry counter (4-6-7).

You make a new, separate attack in the PFPh with the LMG.  

If the original attack was directed by a leader, he could direct the LMG again.  The 467 can't attack again.  The LMG could FG with an adjacent unit that had not fired yet (although then it could not be directed by the leader that we are pretending is there also).

This is the EXACT question I had since I do not believe the rule books (ASLSK and ASL) are clear on this.  I looked under A9.2, C2.24 in the full rule book and pg. 4 sec. 1.2.4 in the Starter Kit and neither explained this well.  

Thank you for the clarification Perry!

1. Yes you roll again as you stated with only the MG's FP (which will allow for the MG to possibly retain ROF yet again, or malfunction).
2. Well yes and no. No per 1.2.4., but yes is suggested in section 2.0 Definitions. If there is possibility to shoot again with limitations and penalties, then more shooting is allowed. If you mark the MG with a Prep Fire counter, then it is done. However, if it is marked with a First Fire counter, it is possible for it to fire again with Subsequent First fire and Final Protective Fire. If the MG was marked only with a First Fire marker, then it could still fire in the Defensive Fire Phase but with limitation of only at target that is adjacent. 

Hope that helps.
Note also that you can fire other units/weapons in the PFPh, before shooting that LMG (that had ROF) again.

title: Bypass example from A4.34
question:
I was casually reading the entirety of chapter A, cover-to-cover, you know how it goes. I had a question with the example they give for bypass LOS in A4.34.

The paragraph says "if it declares D4-E4, D4-E5....the firer can trace it's LOF to the D4-E4-E5, D4-D5-E5, or the D4-C5-D5 vertices."

How is the last vertex a legal choice for the firer? The actual rule says a firing unit "has the option to make its one allowed LOS check per attack to either hex vertex along a hex side traversed by a unit moving in bypass (thus a choice of two vertices for on hex side bypassed, three vertices for two hex sides bypassed, etc.)"

So the three vertices are D4-D3-E4, D4-E4-E5, and D4-D5-E5, correct? Of course, LOS is blocked for the first. But D4-C5-D5 isn't allowed, yes?

Thanks in advance for the clarification!
author: Kris2476
consensus_answer:
I was casually reading the entirety of chapter A, cover-to-cover, you know how it goes. I had a question with the example they give for bypass LOS in A4.34.
Thanks in advance for the clarification!

I don't think the example is stating that D4/C5/D5 is a valid location for a shot against a simple bypass move around the back of the building. It's simply stating that a potential firer in C7 can trace a LOS to that vertex. 

The vertex does become a valid target if the mover chooses to perform a continued bypass to move along > 2 hexsides. 

The point of that sentence is more to show that the wall TEM is active for all of those vertices. If they had left D4/C5/D5 out of the discussion, then questions would have arisen, since the wall ends right at that point.

title: Skulking question, with apologies
question:
I hate to bring this old thing up but Ive been away from ASL for almost 15 years and am wondering what the current thinking is in the industry. Recently I got the notion to revisit this old favorite of mine and picked up the various Starter Kits, New RuleBook and Beyond Valor.(I sold off my entire collection years ago, unwisely it appears)

Skulking was a 'no-no' in our group back in the day. Absolutely legal but unethical and frowned upon. Ive been reading around the net and see that opinions still vary however. 

One that bothers me a bit is the notion that scenario designers assume Skulking and to eliminate it (through rule change or simply a gentleman's agreement) may unbalance scenarios.

Is this true? Has it therefore always been an accepted tactic, even among the developers? Did I and my buddies have it all wrong back then?
author: rgrove0172
consensus_answer:
Good answer but it's not realistic to consider ASL covering 2 minute gaps of time per turn. It's highly variable.... consider turns in Red Barricades... cheers :) 
Note the Rulebook Section A3, first sentence, "Each game turn represents 2 minutes of actual time..." 

This is a pretty clear statement of design intent. ASL was designed to represent a quick clash between two small forces, usually a mere slice of the action. 

Over the years designers have really stretched this original concept, especially in big CGs. Many players really enjoy large CGs and I'm fine with that because it keeps the game active.  

But I also like Bruce's concept of "cinematic time" since ASL is a really great dramatization of WWII action. And two minutes of cinematic time can represent almost anything. :)

We know what it says in the hallowed book. Regardless, I don't think even early on that the designers ever met this intent.

But the development of RB threw that baby out with the bathwater in an obvious way and it became a big discussion with Kibler during our playtests. Finally he stated that the scenario action was to represent the most intense fighting of the day -- as if to justify that these turns really are only two minutes long. 

Does anyone really think action in Stalingrad only lasted 12-18 minutes and after that, nothing? It should be clear to everyone that ASL is much too bloody for it to only portray two minutes of real time each turn and always has been, except on 'mad minute' occasions, regardless of design intent, which is mostly a residual 'appendix' from the old Squad Leader. 

In general, most wargames are too bloody to represent what actually occurred in real time situations, but gamers aren't interested in the hours of lulls to bring up reinforcements, get commands from HQ about objectives, truces to pick up the wounded and dead, etc... they just want to go directly into the battle parts.

replies.body:
Out of the dozens of folks I have played(which includes monthly games at MMP playtest), I have never played anyone that didn't use skulking.  

It has never seemed to me to be as disruptively powerful as I have heard it described.

Did I and my buddies have it all wrong back then?

Correct.  Small groups often get concepts wrong.

Of course, you can play any way you want.

Any experienced serious player will use skulking.  It's not all powerful and comes with the disadvantage of not being able to shoot in the DFire phase.  Scenarios are all designed with it in mind.  

If anything disallowing it will unbalance the scenario and give a disadvantage to the defender.

Thanks guys for the quick reply. A vast majority of my play will be solitaire but Id still like to get it right. I can absolutely see how Skulking decreases the defender's exposure to fire and I concur that in a round about way it could be seen to represent the defender 'hunkering down' in cover etc. It has always just seemed so awkward when represented on the table. Something Ill have to get used to I guess. 

Thanks again!

Played ASL back when it came out and then have been playing again over the last few years - we use skulking as it's allowed by the rules and it's therefore obviously taken into account when scenarios are designed/balanced. There are a LOT of discrepancies in ASL if you want to start looking.  And every one of them can be argued to death from both sides.

Skulking's negative connotation was most likely applied by someone who experienced it and was upset they didn't think of it first.  :)

One thing I dislike, but can be overcome by scenario design... board edge creep.  (Discuss at your leisure.)

As Gordon pointed out there could be a "heads down" counter that would accomplish something similar... but it would actually be worse.  "Skulking" requires a safe place to go.  Therefore the opposition can maneuver into position and remove those safe places, defeating "skulking" in that case.  If the "heads down" counter was introduced, then a squad in a single location stone building could "skulk" to their hearts content... and that would really seem strange.

I would argue that defensive fire and skulking are no more / less realistic.

During you turn, you mostly have to make a choice of moving or firing.  It is the burden of the attacker to balance the moving / firing / advancing of the attacking units. The defender can return fire or shoot at the moving units.

The defender gets his own turn to reorganize / retreat and perhaps fire away.  A lot of attackers consider the defenders turn just another free prep fire phase.   If the defender can't hunker down/skulk/hide etc when the attacker is NOT moving then they will easily be pushed aside (taking away all of those tough decisions of moving vs firing that the attacker is supposed to be presented with).   

If you want take advantage of the DFF as the attacker then you have to put the defender in a position that he has to react.

title: Scrounging
question:
May please someone explain me the meaning of this D10.5 sentence?
...I think is just a problem of language....

"The dr also doubles as the number of SW that may be scrounged (...)if more than one exists."

Thanks
author: Qwirz
consensus_answer:
It means that the dr number is also the number of SWs that may be scrounged.

For example, if your dr is 1 and there are more than one scroungeable SWs in the wreck, you may only choose to scrounge 1 of those SWs.

"the dr also doubles as the number..." is equivalent to "the dr also represents the number of SWs..."

"the dr also doubles as the number..." is equivalent to "the dr also represents the number of SWs..."
Thanks a lot! An English use of "doubles" I didn't know....

title: HIP foxholes and ? units clarification needed
question:
Hi all!
I'm playing Le Manoir. German Foxholes are set up Hidden.
According to rules when an enemy unit is in LOS (regardless of range) I have to reveal them.
What about units inside (HIP as well)? Do I place them too under a "?" Counter beneath the foxhole?
Or do I reveal them per HIP units rule?
What about units in foxholes NOT in concealment terrain? Should I reveal them with no "?" Counter since FHoles are not concealment terrain?
Thanks
author: Qwirz
consensus_answer:
Yes, but 12.33 says "Fortifications set up in non-Concealment terrain are treated as if set up in Concealment terrain [exc: They also lose their HIP status due to enemy LOS regardless of range].
And here start my doubts........

Right.  Units are not Fortifications.  The rule permits the foxholes to be HIP.  The guys in the foxholes are not HIP, unless you have an SSR explicitly permitting this!

The only Fortification that grants "free" HIP status to the units within it is a pillbox (B30.7, last sentence).

If a unit is granted HIP by SSR, then generally it must be set up in Concealment Terrain.  There are EXC, but they are not important right now.  Fortifications may be set up HIP regardless of the terrain, but usually they will lose that HIP status very easily, as per A12.33 and the Concealment Loss/Gain Chart.

If a scenario granted you the ability to HIP a unit in Concealment Terrain, and you placed a foxhole in that same hex, then the foxhole will be revealed as per A12.33, but the unit will only be revealed via the normal rules for Concealment Loss.

Does that make it clearer?

And yes, the fact that the foxhole will lose HIP much more easily than the unit inside it means that the sudden appearance of a seemingly- empty foxhole may make your opponent suspicious.  Use that to your advantage.  The possibility of a hidden unit may make your opponent nervous about moving close to it.  Alternately, he might waste a lot of time trying to deal with it.  But is your HIP unit actually there?  If you can send your opponent on a wild goose chase, or make him scared of shadows, then you chances of winning the scenario are improved.

title: Wounded Leader MF bonus while carried
question:
Hi all!
Perhaps just a question of English comprehension.
Do the last lines of 17.2 mean that a carried wounded leader still applies his 2 MF bonus to the squad carrying him (actually allowing the MMC to move with 5MF), or they are separated from that and just mean that the bonus applies as usual to the MMCs he is stacked with? author: Qwirz

+2 MF yes, but the leader doesn't add his +1 IPC. So the stack ends up having 4 MF total, or 5 MF if running.

title: OVR question
question:
Hello,

Quick couple of questions about an OVR opportunity from a recent game.

Germans have an SPW 251/1 halftrack. MA is a 3 FP AAMG

Halftrack moves adjacent to a Russian 6-2-8.
Russian defensive first fires, 12/+2, inflicts a 1 MC.
Halftrack rolls a 7, plus one is a final DR of 8. So, pin?
Pin result for a half track does not force BU, instead must apply case D to future TH rolls. Is this correct?

Half track advances into the hex with the 6-2-8, declaring an OVR
**note, I'm not sure this is tactically sound, but it was fun to do**
6-2-8 can declare Final Fire BEFORE the OVR attack is resolved, is this correct?

I am really at a loss for words with the CC reaction fire vs. non-CC reaction fire rules. I think the 6-2-8 can elect CC reaction fire based off the example with street fighting for D7.21.
-Can the 6-2-8 declare either? Maybe someone can clarify when I can/should use CC vs. non-CC reaction fire.

Anyways, 6-2-8 declares CC reaction fire. They pass their PAATC
CCV is 6 (5, plus an 8-0 leader stacked with the squad)
Modifiers are +2 because the halftrack is in motion. I assume the +1 for small target doesn't matter, since it doesn't usually matter for non-TH...
6-2-8 rolls a 4, so the halftrack is immobilized. 
Half track now determines its FP. By my count it's 3FP (AAMG) tripled (for TPBF), halved (for Bounding Fire), halved again (immobilized), so a 2.25. Add to that the "base" of 2 FP, for a net 4 FP attack. Or is this FP halved because of the earlier "pin" result? What should the final FP be?

Thank you very much in advance for the help!
author: Kris2476
consensus_answer:
Non-CC reaction fire is firing on IFT, using LATW, or a gun.

CC-Reaction fire is attacking the vehicle with the CC table while the vehicle is spending MP.

All the non-CC options are available before and after an OVR is resolved. 

 CC-RF is available after the OVR is resolved (or when no OVR declared or streetfighting).

You will usually chose non-CC reaction fire if you can kill the vehicle with IFT (unarmored) or have a better weapon to shoot at the vehicle (AT Gun or Panzerschreck).  CC-reaction fire is what you try to do when you want to destroy a tank with an mmc that has no better tools to use.  High morale usually helps make the decision since low morale means you are likely to get pinned for failing the PAATC.

Thanks for your response!

So, it was illegal for me to have used CC-reaction fire before the OVR? And, the 6-2-8 could ONLY have used non-CC RF before the OVR attack was resolved?

I'm assuming, legality aside, I would have been better off as the Russians using non-CC RF. I assume my FP would be modified by TPBF, possible halved for Final Fire, and a +2 for the CE TEM?

There is no PAATC for non-CC RF, I'm guessing. So, in "real" terms, non-CC reaction fire is just shooting at an AFV while it's close to you (i.e., useless against a tank). CC RF is running out to the AFV and.... sticking grenades to it?

Assuming the halftrack was not destroyed (you're right, I missed the -2 CCV modifier for OT vehicles), was my OVR FP calculation correct? 

Thanks again for your explanation :)

title: Amphibians in Shallow Ocean hexes
question:
OK here goes:

Amphibians in Shallow Ocean hexes ver 1.1

A Shallow Ocean hex is at -1 Level, is not a Land hex and is not a Water Obstacle to an amphibian because an amphibian is not a boat or LC [G13.4 EXC]. In a Shallow Ocean hex, an amphibian is a Waterproofed vehicle [G13.42], uses Land MPs [G13.422], is Wading and treated as being in a shallow stream [B20.46, G13.42], checks for Bog when moving to a higher elevation [B20.46], receives an extra Target-Based +2 TH DRM by all ordnance TH attempts [G13.422], is no longer a Very Small Target [D16.3], is no longer Hull Down [D16.3], becomes a Hindrance [D16.3], may leave a Wreck [D16.3], and may carry Riders [D16.3]. An amphibian is treated as being in a shallow stream and does not Drift in the APh [B21.121 N/A; D16.22 N/A].
author: nisada
consensus_answer:
Detail amendment: while Shallow Ocean hexes are at Level -1, they are treated as being at Level 0 for LOS/movement purposes if Beach Slope is Slight (G13.21) or Moderate (G13.22) -- in both cases when the LOS/movement is crossing the Beach-Hinterland hexsides, and in the case of Moderate slope, the hexside is thusly treated as a Deir hex (F4).  (Whew.)

The correct rules reference for Waterproofed vehicles is G13.4221.

The vehicle may become a Hindrance per the conditions of D9.4 -- your summary makes it sound like it will automatically become a Hindrance; and D16.3 is not really the correct reference for that.  Nor is D16.3 the correct reference for the Wreck and Riders comments.  Better to use "D16.5-.7 NA" instead.

The second "shallow stream" comment is redundant.

Otherwise all seems correct.  You might care to add that CC is NA (G13.495) and Passengers may be (un)loaded directly to/from an adjacent pier (G13.731).

Bruce -

title: Confusion with A7.212 Target Selection Limits
question:
The rule text seems clear. When I have a known enemy unit, or an armed or armored vehicle, in my location I cannot attack anything outside of it.

But the example below confuses me.

1. When the squad is in the upper location, then it is in a different location. But still unable to fire outside? Why? The rule only mentions its own location. TBPF is also strange, while the PRC can only use PBF.

2. Why on earth can the HT suddenly start firing outside when becoming CE? They should be even more vulnerable to fire from the squad than in its current BU state. Or does it mean that they could theoretically always fire outside, but being BU they cannot fire at all?

Is this just a special case for OT HT, which can exchange fire through their open top against a unit with elevation advantage, which isn't mentioned in the actual rule?
author: phxhf
consensus_answer:
When the HT is CE? And they can use TPBF when it is BU? (Still confused.)

The HT, like any other OT vehicle, must be CE in order to fire any weapons other than bow-mounted MG/FT (D5.3).

Passengers of the HT must normally be CE in order to fire (D6.62) but as that rule notes Reciprocity (A6.5)applies, so any enemy unit that can attack the Passengers even when they're BU (A7.211) can be attacked by those Passengers.

Except that the A7.212 EX states that BU Passengers can't attack back, which seems at first to be a contradiction; but Reciprocity is specifically discussing high-to-low shots (and the reverse), and D6.61 explicitly states that BU Passengers can attack back when their CE DRM has been reduced to < its normal value due to elevation advantage.

So the summary is, if the HT and the enemy unit are in the same Location, the enemy unit can attack the HT's Passengers with TPBF even if the latter are BU; but in that case the BU Passengers may not attack back.  (The BU HT itself can't attack anything anywhere [EXC: OVR].)  If the enemy unit is in the same hex, but in a different, higher Location, the enemy unit still qualifies for TPBF vs. the HT, the CE DRM is reduced by 1 for every full level of elevation difference, the HT is treated as an unarmoured vehicle if the CE DRM is so reduced, but the BU Passengers may attack back (but not with TPBF) at that enemy unit.

For the HT/PRC to qualify for TPBF, they must be CE (and the target must be in the same Location -- since HT are not known for their ability to climb stairwells) [EXC: if the HT is at ground-level and the target is in a Cellar Location (e.g., RB, FB, etc.) then the HT might be able to get TPBF vs. the unit in the different Location -- but I don't have any of those rules handy and there might be a Cellar rule that prevents that.]

OK?

replies.body:
1. A7.212 Target Selection Limits:... Whenever a unit is eligible for TPBF vs Known enemy units, it can attack only those units. Target selection is not limited just when enemy units are in the same location.

PBF vs. TPBF is explained in the footnotes at the end of chapter A. Basically it is dropping grenades vs. throwing them upstairs.

2. See D6.61

1. When the squad is in the upper location, then it is in a different location. But still unable to fire outside? Why? The rule only mentions its own location. TBPF is also strange, while the PRC can only use PBF.

The exposed PRC are subject to TPBF because of A7.211: "Any PRC not BU in a CT AFV which are in an enemy-occupied hex are subject to TPBF attacks from enemy units in that Location or any higher Location in that hex ...".

Because the units are able to use TPBF, they are subject to A7.212: "Whenever a unit is eligible for TPBF vs Known enemy units, it can attack only those units."

2. Why on earth can the HT suddenly start firing outside when becoming CE?

Because they are not eligible for TPBF, they are not restricted, as above.

They should be even more vulnerable to fire from the squad than in its current BU state.

Indeed they are.  They are very vulnerable, as per D6.61 ("... the +2 CE DRM applies but is reduced by one for each full level elevation advantage > the range (to a minimum CE DRM of 0) ..." and then D5.311 applies ("If an OT AFV's crew would receive a CE DRM reduced by Elevation Effects/Air-Bursts to < its normal CE DRM, that AFV is instead treated as unarmored and the attack vs it -- but not vs its PRC -- is resolved (with no Air Burst TEM) either as per A7.308 (for non-ordnance/Indirect-Fire-HE) or on the proper TK Table using the pertinent Unarmored Vehicle TK#."). title: MG Ordnance, COT, OVR, Rev. Movement and Unloading
question:
A couple of new questions (sorry). ;)

1. I fire my MG as Ordnance on the VTT. As far as I understand it can keep ROF while doing so. Assuming I still have ROF after that VTT shot, may I switch to normal Small Arms fire for the next shot? And switch again?

2. The Terrain Chart shows "COT" for tracked vehicles into Shellhole hexes. When I move (CE) into a Road / Open Ground hex with Shellholes, is the COT 0.5 or 1 MP?

3. Can I attack unmounted horses? In OVR? In CC?

4. Do I still have the option for a BFF or BF attack after an OVR? As I understand there is no fire marker on the unit after OVR, so the answer is probably yes?

5a. D2.21 states that Reverse Movement quadruples the entry costs for an AFV. How about the MP for changing VCA in a VBM vertex? Is it quadrupled too?

5b. Vehicle is in VBM movement on a hexside. When I stop and then start Reverse Movement in VBM, my new CAFP is immediately the Rear CAFP? I don't have to drive the hexside, which I currently straddle, backwards first?

6. A 16 MP halftrack is unloading an infantry unit for 4 MP, whereby the infantry expends 1 MF. How much Defensive Fire do they have to endure? First four shots for 4 MP, then one shot for 1 MF? And will both units (halftrack and infantry unit) be attacked together, as their movement is more or less connected? Or first the halftrack and then the infantry?

7. I'm still wondering that infantry fire on moving targets is not penalized in any way. Or did I miss a rule?
author: phxhf
consensus_answer:
1. I fire my MG as Ordnance on the VTT. As far as I understand it can keep ROF while doing so. Assuming I still have ROF after that VTT shot, may I switch to normal Small Arms fire for the next shot? And switch again?

Yes.  There's no rule explicitly stating it, it is more the absence of any rule prohibiting it.

2. The Terrain Chart shows "COT" for tracked vehicles into Shellhole hexes. When I move (CE) into a Road / Open Ground hex with Shellholes, is the COT 0.5 or 1 MP?

0.5.  The "COT" designation on the chart essentially means "pay whatever you would pay if this terrain feature was not present".

3. Can I attack unmounted horses? In OVR? In CC?

Well.  An interesting question.  Horse counters, by themselves are one of those great ASL mysteries.  The Index, under Unit, states: "Any game piece or counter with its own MF/MP allotment and normally capable of movement without being portaged, pushed, or towed.  Cavalry [but not horses], ... are all different types of units."  This makes sense: a horse counter, by itself, is incapable of movement.

Then we get to A13.7 HORSES: "Horses are units, but are never considered enemy units."

Uh ... what?  Which rule do you believe?  There's also A13.34 MF ALLOTMENT: "A Horse counter's basic MF allotment is 12 MF."  If a Horse is not a unit, then by definition it has no MF allotment at all; it would be Cavalry that has a basic MF allotment of 12 MF ("Cavalry" defined as per A13.1).  It's a bit confusing.

So let's consider the two possibilities.

(i) Horse counters ARE NOT units.

A7.1: "Fire attacks are the main process by which a unit attacks enemy units."  So does this mean that if you're not a unit, you can't be "attacked"?  Generally that's true -- other things like various terrain types and unpossessed SW can be affected as the result of certain types of attacks, but those attacks are not targeting those things specifically.  We have the first sentence of A13.511 "Horses, whether mounted or not, are attacked using the  Vehicle Line of the IFT in addition to, and at the same time as, fire against any Cavalry unit(s) riding them." (My emphasis.)  Uh, what?  If the horse counters aren't mounted, what "Cavalry unit(s) riding them" are being attacked as a pre-requisite?  The sentence doesn't make much objective sense.  It's my guess that the sentence is trying to indicate that yes, you can shoot at an unmounted horse, but that's not actually what it's saying.  A7.308 actually says something very similar, but uses "Personnel target in the same Location" instead of "Cavalry", which is a better way of expressing the idea.  In that case you always have the "I am testing to see if there is a HIP unit in that hex" excuse to fall back on; of course such a shot would be Area Fire.

(ii) Horse counters ARE units.

Does that help?  Actually no, since by A13.7 they are very explicitly not the enemy.  So the A7.1 comment applies again.  Of course forms of attack that don't distinguish between friendly and enemy units (e.g., OBA) would certainly affect them.  We also have the same A13.511 dilemma as above.  But otherwise, in general, non-enemy units are not affected by fire, with specific EXC (A7.4).

All of the above, which interpretation you want to follow, applies equally to OVR as to other fire attacks.

As for CC, the answer is pretty clearly "no".  Horses have no CC value (not even a "(1)") and are not vehicles, so are not attacked with CCV.  A13.7 tells us that Horse counters are "captured in the same manner as a SW via Recovery".  But further on you get "A unit leading a Horse counter may eliminate that counter as if it were a SW."

After all that, note of course that the only reason you might have to want to eliminate a Horse counter is to prevent an enemy unit from using it.  They are not otherwise any sort of impediment or worth any VP.

4. Do I still have the option for a BFF or BF attack after an OVR? As I understand there is no fire marker on the unit after OVR, so the answer is probably yes?

Good lord, no.  D3.3 BOUNDING FIRST FIRE: "... Any vehicle that fires during its MPh is using Bounding First Fire and is marked with a Bounding Fire counter ..." and D7.1 "An OVR is a form of Bounding First Fire ...".

5a. D2.21 states that Reverse Movement quadruples the entry costs for an AFV. How about the MP for changing VCA in a VBM vertex? Is it quadrupled too?

No.  VCA change is a separate MP expenditure to the hex/hexside entry cost (D2.11, D2.33).

5b. Vehicle is in VBM movement on a hexside. When I stop and then start Reverse Movement in VBM, my new CAFP is immediately the Rear CAFP? I don't have to drive the hexside, which I currently straddle, backwards first?

I never thought of it that way before, but yes, in a way.  See the second EX on p.D6 -- having traversed (but not exited) the hexide in one direction, you don't need to (indeed, cannot) traverse it again, no matter which direction you choose to move in.  However, your CAFP does not change -- that's determined by the VCA while you're using VBM (D2.32).  Switching to Reverse Movement does not change your VCA, and hence does not change the CAFP.

6. A 16 MP halftrack is unloading an infantry unit for 4 MP, whereby the infantry expends 1 MF. How much Defensive Fire do they have to endure? First four shots for 4 MP, then one shot for 1 MF? And will both units (halftrack and infantry unit) be attacked together, as their movement is more or less connected? Or first the halftrack and then the infantry?

The vehicle is expending 4 MP, and hence can be shot at a total of 4 times (by any 1 firer).  The infantry has expended only 1 MF, and thus can be fired at only once.  The MP and MF are expended simultaneously.  If the attack can affect both targets, then yes they will both be affected (to a maximum of 1 time).  Of course if the attack is using the VTT it cannot affect the infantry, and similarly if it's using the ITT it cannot affect the vehicle.  Note that D5.43 explicitly defines the target status of the infantry.  In essence, as soon as PRC declares the exit from the vehicle, that exit is automatically successful (although the now-infantry unit might not survive the process!).  The reverse is not true -- an infantry unit trying to become PRC must first survive all attacks "unpinned and in Good Order".

7. I'm still wondering that infantry fire on moving targets is not penalized in any way. Or did I miss a rule?

I don't understand the question.  Why would stationary firers be penalised?  Bullets and fragments from exploding grenades move a heck of a lot faster than men, even men riding in a truck.  Enough bullets and grenade fragments in a given space are difficult to dodge -- the best defence is to lie as flat as possible, behind cover -- not normally compatible with the idea of "moving".  Sometimes you get away with it -- and sometimes you don't.  If you roll a high number on your IFT attack, does it represent that your men are bad shots, or that the enemy unit was doing a fantastic duck-and-cover routine?  You decide!  If you rolled a low number -- then clearly they weren't dodging well enough.

The first rule to note is in D2.22 RESTRICTIONS: "Any hex entered with Reverse Movement must be one of the two hexes which formed the rear vehicular Target Facing of the vehicle prior to that move, and the only hexside that can be Bypassed by that Reverse Move is the hexside joining those two hexes.  Once backed into that new hex, it may change its VCA (barring other restrictions) within that new hex at the normal cost."

The wording of that rule only works when the vehicle is not already using VBM, hence doesn't really address your question.  So let's dig a little deeper:

D2.33 VCA CHANGES: "VCA changes by a vehicle using VBM are limited to the two hexsides of the VCA at the CAFP ..." (my emphasis).

That appears to be outright prohibiting using Reverse Movement with VBM around an obstacle, as the first thing you must do in order to VBM around an obstacle is to change your VCA at the vertex of the hexside you want to move along (D2.33 again: "... or pay one MP for a VCA change to continue Bypass along a connecting hexside ...").

I don't see anything else addressing the issue.  I would conclude that using "Reverse Movement VBM around an obstacle" is simply NA.  The key point (the rule that specifically prevents it) is that phrase in D2.33 restricting VCA changes to the CAFP.

Note that it is allowed to expend a Start MP to enter Reverse Movement, expend a MP to change CA, and then move into the (new) hex now directly in the rear of the vehicle.  See the EX on the bottom right of p.D6: Assume the Tiger is already using VBM along the J1-K2 hexside.  It's rear hex is currently K1.  If it starts in Reverse, and then changes VCA to point along the J2-K2 hexside, its new rear hex would be J1, and it could then reverse into that hex.  This is explicitly permitted in D2.33: "A VBM vehicle making a VCA change cannot voluntarily end its MPh in that position; it must move to the next CAFP or reverse into a new hex in its rear." No definitions, as such, just references to applicable rules.

Generally speaking, Infantry Movement (A4) just uses the terms "moving", "movement", "moved", etc.  Routing (A10.5) predominantly uses the terms "rout", "routing", etc., although the occasional use of "move" occurs -- but usually in combination with "rout" (e.g., "A routing unit may never move ADJACENT to a Known enemy unit ...".

Before you get too hung up on the "peculiarities" of it -- consider that a single hex represents approximately 1600 square meters of territory.  Where, exactly, is the tank in that vast expanse of ground?  Where, exactly, are the infantry?  The answer in both cases is "everywhere and anywhere".  When, exactly, in the 2 minutes of time represented by a game turn, did the infantry actually assault the tank?  The answer, similarly, is "some point in time and every point in time".

The game system is designed from the ground up to make precise answers to such questions impossible.  How many rounds of ammunition does that StuG enter battle with?  You don't know, and the answer (depending on the vagaries of the dice) might be none!  Alternatively it might be "as many as it needs, with plenty to spare".  You don't know.  ASL gives the impression of being obsessive about lots of precise details -- but the reality is that it's the living embodiment of the concept of "design for effect".  The game system is telling a story, and you play the game hoping that the story will be interesting and exciting (and usually, it is, because ASL tells a very good story indeed).  If you start picking away at the details, you will inevitably just enjoy the story less.  Why would you want to do that?

Instead of complaining about how the game seems to allow the StuG to perform impossible feats, why not instead speculate on why it would be possible?  Why wouldn't the squad pick a "safe place" to sit and be immune to the StuG's gun?  Well, just maybe, they think that there is no "safe place".  Maybe they believe (for some reason known only to them) that they would be horribly exposed to other enemy units.  Maybe the StuG is positioned in such a way that they cannot hope to physically assault it without exposing themselves to its fire.  Maybe they really are that stupid (or, at least, inexperienced).  There are a million "maybes".  Pick one or pick none, but just play on and enjoy the story as it unfolds before your eyes.

author: phxhf
consensus_answer:
Which attack options has a cavalry unit (besides Charge)? A13.4 only mentions it uses half FP, like the Mounted Fire for PRC. But reading D6 didn't help here.

As far as I understand, a PRC can fire in the same phases as an AFV? Or even together with an AFV.

Can Cavalry attack in the PFPh, MPh (Bounding Fire?), AFPh?

Cavalry may fire like any other unit as Mounted Fire (halved) - this is in Prep Fire, Defensive Fire, or First Fire vs moving units and so on.  It can also fire in the Advanced Fire Phase though it will be halved again in that case.  

The only way it can fire during its own Movement Phase is with a Charge (A13.6).  It does so as Triple Point Blank Fire (TPBF) with no halving for being mounted; however, it has to survive all defensive fire first.  Read the paragraph carefully as there are extra MF expenditures, a Gallop requirement, and so on.  Good luck!

+2 for the wall: B9.3 "Fire traced through a wall/hedge hexside or hexspine may be subject to a TEM for that wall/hedge if the target is in the Location formed by that hexside/hexspine."  (My emphasis.)

I don't know that there is any option to decline a better TEM that is available to you (WA being an EXC as it is the mechanism to determine whether the wall TEM is available/applicable).  In the specific case of a wall hexspine, the only reason I can think of to decline it would be to negate a HEAT attack (if the American possessed a BAZ, for instance) -- but I don't believe that there is any choice involved, the Wall TEM is available so it applies.

Both B9.31 and C8.31 specify that a HEAT attack requires that the target be "receiving Wall TEM".  "Receiving" is unfortunately a bit of a wishy-washy term in this specific case, since it seems to imply a choice on the part of the target, but I don't believe that it really comes down to "choice" when WA is not an issue -- the Wall TEM exists whether the target wants it or not.

1b.  If you lay a Fire Lane, it's 4FP - one left of the column normally used by that MG (A9.22); if you did not lay a Fire Lane, you'd leave 1FP (7FP halved to 3.5FP, using the 2FP column, then halved for Residual).

title: Allowed LOS Checks?
question:
I'm not sure if I understand when it is legal to check LOS. Some rules are driven by LOS and seem to require lots of LOS checks, while at the same time, particularly when firing, it seems one should not be allowed to check LOS without risk (e.g. you may waste a shot if it turns out LOS does not exist).

It is my understanding that during a scenario one cannot first check LOS and then decide whether to fire or not. You must declare the attack, then check LOS, and if there is no LOS, the attack still takes place but has no effect. This implies you should not be allowed to check LOS whenever you want and that whether two locations have LOS to each other is a bit of a guessing game until you actually take an action.

However, there are other things that require LOS checks. For example, route paths and interdiction. When routing can either player check LOS whenever they want, or does the non-routing player declare things like "I think this unit can see your routing unit, let me do a LOS check?"

Similarly, concealment/loss gain. As units move or take actions, can you be constantly checking LOS, or does a player have to say "I think this unit can see that unit, let me check if it has LOS to remove your concealment?"

Thanks!
author: MikeWhit
consensus_answer:
The Index is your friend.  Look up the various rules covered in "LOS Checks".  Most rules explicitly label "free" LOS checks (e.g., in A12.14, the last sentence in the second column of p.A35; C6.51); at other times, the free LOS is implied (and necessary) to make the rule work (e.g., Case J1 and J2 Limited Aim -- those are mandatory DRM if they apply, but some times you'll need to check LOS to various hexes to see if they do actually apply).  In the case of hidden fortifications (A12.33) the LOS checks are not only free and mandatory, but since it might be revealing information to just string the LOS in front of your opponent, such LOS checks are done secretly.  The same is true of, say, a concealed Gun changing CA -- if it's done in LOS of an enemy unit the concealment loss is automatic, but you might need to string the LOS to see if that's the case.

Generally speaking, the context of a rule (or action) that might invoke concealment loss will guide you as to whether the LOS check is "free" or not.  Take note of the "honor system House Rule" discussed in A12.16 and apply the same principles -- which is basically "Trust but Verify".

replies.body: LOS to strip concealment is a free one...it's buried in there somewhere. That's why it is sometimes better to voluntarily drop "?" so your opponent has to commit to the shot to check LOS.

No.  Using a DC is "any other action" (Note C) on the Concealment Loss/Gain Table.

The only way you can place a DC and not lose "?" is if no Good Order enemy unit has a LOS to the unit.  (E.G., you're placing the DC onto a stack of broken units, or a Berserk unit, or a Melee, and no other enemy units can see you do it.)

If you are not already intimately familiar with the Concealment Loss/Gain Table, you should take the time to study it.  It is one of the most important charts in the game.

Generally speaking, you should assume that anything you might want to do will cause you to lose your "?" -- unless the chart (or the rules) specifically says otherwise.

author: GamerKirk
consensus_answer:
Rocket OBA is not a type of fire mission. 
Fire missions are [C1.7]: HE concentration, SMOKE concentration, Harassing fire, IR, Barrage, SMOKE barrage and Creeping barrage.

Rocket OBA uses HE concentration fire mission.

Rockets never saw much use in Red Barricades. Nobody would buy them. 

The AHGC found itself with a warehouse chock full of them. The company considered heavily discounting the RG, and flogging it at a Black Friday sale. That is until a bright spark in the accounting department suggested that they charge extra for a pre-reg hex.

While a few punters fell for the ruse, most rockets continued to collect dust. 

The rest, they say, is late '90s history.
HIP observer with field phone dropping rockets on self.... thats The Barrikady!

As a technical matter, it is hard to see how rocket artillery could realistically benefit from pre-registration. For Cannon artillery the preregistration process involves firing at a specific point until one starts getting hits (or near misses) and then recording the resulting settings on the gun. In theory one can simply use those settings again in a future fire mission. If, however, the gun relocates, the process must start over.

I don't believe rocket artillery had the capability to do any of this. I don't think there was a way to 'preserve'  the settings on the equipment. By its nature it was an area effect weapon, so even if you fired a test rocket there was no assurance the rest of the salvo would land in the same spot.

The advantage of preregistration is that after the gun is registered you can fire OTHER missions and return to the registered target if required. Rocket artillery would not do this. The entire point of rockets is to drop a large quantity of explosive on the target in a minimum amount of time. Often by surprise. Firing test rockets would've worked against this. 

A quick look at both the common Russian and German launchers does not reveal anything that appears to be the kind of sighting equipment needed. Apparently the German weapon couldn't even fire single rockets - it was all or nothing. As a further consideration, one of the drawbacks of rocket artillery was the huge signature which made it vulnerable to counter battery fire. Typically they would shoot and scoot. Again, this precludes preregistration. 

While apparently ASL allows this by the rules, I think it is an error, historically, and should be disallowed.

What is the point of firing as bounding fire if you can't gain acquisition? (Gyrostabilizer excepted).  It even looks like you lose acquisition if you fire as bounding fire.

Note that you are asking about Bounding (First) Fire (i.e., BFF; i.e., firing during your MPh).  Bounding Fire takes place after the MPh (i.e., in the AFPh).

The point of firing at anything is to make something bad happen to it, right?

If you are successful with BFF, your target may end up destroyed, broken or maybe even just pinned.  That maybe allows your other units to move safely whereas before they may have been at risk.  Or maybe those other guys weren't moving at all, but your opponent was planning to shoot at them in his DFPh.

A common situation is that your opponent is waiting for a particularly juicy target to come along.  You don't want him shooting at those juicy targets if at all possible.  BFF gives you the opportunity of eliminating or at least interfering with his waiting game.  Maybe the threat of your BFF will cause him to shoot at you instead; if so that sacrifice may ensure the survival of more important units.  It's all about trade-offs.  Essentially, you're exchanging the possibility of gaining acquisition in the hope that you'll achieve the result you want now.
With a min TH: +4 mod for moving and possibly +1 for BU, Bounding First Fire is usually not going to be a high probability shot though.

Firing at infantry   HELL NO

Firing at a Large Target SHERMAN TANK?  Yes....take the shot.
especially if you go PB...
Easy peasy

With a min TH: +4 mod for moving and possibly +1 for BU, Bounding First Fire is usually not going to be a high probability shot though. 
NUT UP and go CE!!

With a min TH: +4 mod for moving and possibly +1 for BU, Bounding First Fire is usually not going to be a high probability shot though. 

True enough.  There are ways to ease that pain, though (most obviously: get up-close and personal for that point-blank DRM).

As I said above, it's all about trade-offs.  Every action you take involves some risk, and "probably going to miss" is obviously right up there as a risk.  You're not (or should not be) considering the risks of any individual unit though -- the only risk worth considering is the combined risk of all of your forces.  "What happens to my troops if I don't take that risk?"  You're not always going to get the same answer for every situation.  There are plenty of possible scenarios where attempting BFF shots would be an incredibly stupid thing to do.

One of the many things that makes ASL great as a game is that so often you have options.  Often, those options have relatively even risk/pay-off calculations.  It helps keep the game fresh.

[Something that annoys me personally are games (any games, not just ASL) where your opponent does something that by all reasonable expectations should not work, and he's dopey for even making the attempt -- but then it does work, and all of your carefully-crafted plans have just been flushed.  Grr!  That being said, any game that doesn't restrict you to "well there's only one thing I can do" is probably better than games that do.]

With a min TH: +4 mod for moving and possibly +1 for BU, Bounding First Fire is usually not going to be a high probability shot though. 
NUT UP and go CE!!

That's the spirit of the true ASL player.

Anyway, the main reason for firing ordnance during the AFPh is to "mark" a target, rather than to harm it.

If a tank that has moved at least 1 hex pays a MP to Stop, at which time it fires, does it gain acquisition? I realize if it moves it loses one. 

Related:the only way an AFV which has moved can fire is via bounding (first) fire, correct? 
The only way a vehicle can fire in the advance fire phase is if it was marked with a bounding fire marker during the prep fire phase, correct? 

Also it seems as if you cannot, by rule, fire on the area target type/smoke as bounding fire.

D3.32 Final Fire:...However, if the vehicle did not exhaust its Multiple ROF during its MPh, and did not fire any other weapons (including PRC) during its MPh, it may fire that Multiple ROF weapon (only) again once (C5.3) during its AFPh using the Case C To Hit DRM for ordnance, or halved FP for MG/IFE.

Vehicles cannot use opportunity fire. [D3.3]

Gyrostabilized guns can get acquisition using Bounding first fire. [D11.12]

Area target type cannot be used as a bounding fire. [C3.33]

What is the point of firing as bounding fire if you can't gain acquisition? (Gyrostabilizer excepted).  It even looks like you lose acquisition if you fire as bounding fire.

Firing during your Movement Phase is not as uncommon as you think. Drive a Stuart behind that Panther and the odds are not so bad. +4 for the Bounding Fire, -1 for Large Target, and another -2 for Point Blank would be a 9 to hit the Panther in its rear. With two more Stuarts lurking nearby, you can do the Dance of Death - the Panther spins against one threat and another threat comes flying in.

And sometimes you just want to do a drive by. Shoot, then get out of LOS.

Sometimes you want to get up there and hose the guy down with your machine guns. Since you can't split your fire between different phases, you may as well take a long-odds MA shot as well, as long as the odds of hitting are better than the odds of malfing the weapon or getting your best leader sniped.

If a tank that has moved at least 1 hex pays a MP to Stop, at which time it fires, does it gain acquisition? I realize if it moves it loses one.

It's critical for your rules understanding that you are aware of the differences between Bounding (First) Fire (which only takes place during the MPh) and Bounding Fire (which only takes place during the AFPh).  When the rules refer to BFF, they are not talking about Bounding Fire, and vice-versa!

You cannot gain acquisition during BFF [EXC: Gyrostabilizer].

Related:the only way an AFV which has moved can fire is via bounding (first) fire, correct?

Not correct.  You can fire in the AFPh (and may gain acquisition by doing so, if otherwise permitted).

The only way a vehicle can fire in the advance fire phase is if it was marked with a bounding fire marker during the prep fire phase, correct?

Completely incorrect.  It sounds like you might be thinking of Opportunity Fire; vehicles cannot use Opportunity Fire.

In their own player turn, vehicles may either fire as Prep Fire (PFPh, marked with a Prep Fire counter), Bounding (First) Fire (MPh, marked with a Bounding Fire counter), or Bounding Fire (AFPh, marked with a Bounding Fire counter).  An individual vehicle can fire in only one of those three Phases [EXC: A vehicle that fires as BFF and maintains ROF and fires no other weapons during the MPh is not marked with a Bounding Fire counter and therefore may fire in the AFPh.]

Also it seems as if you cannot, by rule, fire on the area target type/smoke as bounding fire.

You can't use the ATT with BFF.  You certainly can with Bounding Fire (i.e., the AFPh), but you cannot fire SMOKE in that Phase.  Note that to use the ATT at all you must be firing either HE or SMOKE.

(Sorry, NRBH, otherwise I'd provide you with the exact rules references for the above.)

You can get Rate of Fire in the MPh, but not in the AFPh. In some cases, that offsets the disadvantage of not getting an acquire marker.

Also, if you want to end your MPh in a spot where there is not LOS to an enemy, you can shoot at an enemy on the way there without losing anything.

title: Rowhouse-Rubble Movement
question:
So, one hex of a rowhouse has been rubbled.

By B23.71, the black bar between the rubbled hex and the adjacent rowhouse hex is still there.

But how does movement between those two hexes work? B23.71 just says three MF to bypass the black bar from one rowhouse hex to another. It doesn't say anything about three MF plus one for going into rubble.

In fact, it only specifies "Infantry in a Rowhouse may move/rout/advance/Withdraw-from-CC directly into another Rowhouse hex...", but doesn't say anything about a former rowhouse hexes with the black bar still in place.
author: Rindis
consensus_answer:
So, one hex of a rowhouse has been rubbled.

By B23.71, the black bar between the rubbled hex and the adjacent rowhouse hex is still there.

But how does movement between those two hexes work? B23.71 just says three MF to bypass the black bar from one rowhouse hex to another. It doesn't say anything about three MF plus one for going into rubble.

In fact, it only specifies "Infantry in a Rowhouse may move/rout/advance/Withdraw-from-CC directly into another Rowhouse hex...", but doesn't say anything about a former rowhouse hexes with the black bar still in place.

No, it doesn't say anything like that, but it doesn't have to.  What it does say is that you can move around the black bar using "bypass" movement (note that it's in quotes; it's not "real" bypass in the normal sense of the rules).  It specifies that this "bypass" costs 1 MF, expended in the hex that the unit is leaving.  The MF cost to then enter a rubble location is 3 (B24.4).  So total MF cost is 4.
