title: CC random selection and leader creation
question:
As the ATTACKER in a simultaneous CC, my unit gets a Casualty Reduction result against two enemy MMCs. I roll RS to see which are affected.

The DEFENDER then rolls a natural 2, decides not to withdraw, and a leader is created. The presence of the leader doesn't change the result of my original DR, so the result of my attack is still a CR.

The question is, do I reroll the Random Selection to take account of the fact there are now 3 defending units?
author: angelgabriel
consensus_answer:
IIRC, the Field Promotion rules say you re-calculated as if the leader was present all the time.
Yes, at least my eASLRB says the following:

Unless one or both sides Withdraw due to Infiltration (11.22), both attacks are re-figured using both of the originally-rolled Original DRs and the new leader's FP/Leadership just as if he had been there all along.

Yes, that's a good point. The correct rule is A18.12 here. So that last bit would mean that the original RS would be tossed out, and a new RS for three units be made.

Notice that there is a recalculation ONLY if one or more sides don't take advantage of withdrawal. Which covers the case mentioned by Russell, the defender, if they do stick around, -- well it looks like they need to reroll the RS.

A11.22 infiltration indicates that results are momentarily suspended, but does not indicate such are re-rolled. Hence, the leader won't be part of yet another RS.

title: long range fire during AFPh
question:
Is the FP halved TWICE?

thx 
Bill
author: severn8212
consensus_answer:
Is the FP halved TWICE?

Or even more, depending on the circumstances.

Any application of Area Fire (i.e., halved FP) is cumulative with any other application of Area Fire.

So: if your unit is a Passenger on a truck, is pinned, is firing in the AFPh, at long range, and the truck is in Motion, and the target is concealed, your FP is divided by 64!

A funny little fact about Assault Fire: it can only apply when the target is within normal range, but aside from that, if you qualify, then your minimum FP will be 2, no matter how many times you are halved.  The reason is that after all halving is applied, the result (which will be a number > 0, even if it's only a tiny fraction) is FRU (to at least 1) and then you add 1.  So: minimum of 2 FP -- even if your unit is a Passenger on a truck, is pinned, is firing in the AFPh, and the truck is in Motion, and the target is concealed -- but NOT at long range.

title: Riddle me this Batman
question:
I'm still confused as to the rule that units in CREST status get fired upon in the OPEN when their MF is added to the terrain going into...

You can argue realism...but this is really dumb imo...

Units exiting a BUILDING are much more restricted in their egress from the structure as it moves to the next terrain.   To apply this to CREST status units is dumb.  ESPECIALLY since units IN the depression do not suffer the same penalty when crossing (and expending MORE MF)the exact same hexside.

To me, this rule is OBVIOUSLY broken.

Just curious if anyone else has a similar opinion...

Yes, its a game and yes its in the RB...but so many other things are incorrect and nonsensical.
author: ASLChampion
consensus_answer:
what you have to understand is that units in CREST status are in a very specific position close to that side of the hex that is higher than the level IN the hex. 

if they move out of the hex on the other side, they first go down INTO the hex to then go up the other side to exit it which results in much more movement within the same hex, while units IN the hex already start down there so it takes them less movement.

also, while thus changing position, those units in CREST status do so in the view of the enemy, while units IN the hex are generally out of sight.

compared to a building, the units are expected to start their movement in the middle of the hex so again there is no extra movement from the side of the hex to the middle of the hex.

title: Tank trying to overrun and go HD on slope at the same time.
question:
This cropped up during a game yesterday - an AFV on a level 1 hill moved into the slope hex of the hill and wanted to try to go hull down but was also attempting to overrun an infantry squad (already broken) in the same hex.

How does this work through - is it possible? Does the AFV spend the HD manoeuvre MF's before the overrun or after? Does it get HD (if successful) against defensive fire it takes in the hex?

Thanks.
author: domus_ludorum
consensus_answer:
I was wondering if I was missing something, and thought that these would be discrete, separate expenditures, until I had a closer look:

There are four things happening as the AFV enters the hex:

* It's expending MP to enter the Location.

* It's expending MP to perform an OVR.

Per D7.1, these are a combined expenditure, unless all of the enemy units in the hex are unknown (A12.41) (which was obviously not the case here, since the enemy unit was broken).

* It's expending 2 additional MP to perform a HD Maneuver attempt.

D4.22 makes it clear that these are spent as additional MP when entering the Location.  So it's actually combined with the above.

* Finally it's expending a MP to stop (if able) (required by the HD Maneuver attempt).  This is definitely a discrete, separate expenditure, but doesn't answer the question of the timing of the other events.

Since all Defensive First Fire must await the outcome of the HD attempt, and the resolution of the OVR must await the outcome of any DFF attacks, and the MP for the HD attempt and the OVR are simultaneous with the entry of the hex, then it seems to me that the rules are crystal clear: roll for the HD attempt, resolve any DFF attacks, resolve the OVR (which as noted, will still happen even if the vehicle has been eliminated; D7.11).  Then, finally, assuming the vehicle has not already been immobilised, it expends a MP to stop.  If it still has MP available, it must then expend them either in Delay or further movement. and ends its MPh.

I don't see any need for a Q to MMP.  The situation is a little convoluted, but it doesn't throw up any questions that the rules can't already answer.

Note that if the enemy unit was unknown, the sequence would be different.  The entry of the Location and the HD attempt are still a combined expenditure, and are still resolved first (because of the no-DFF-until-HD-attempt-completed rule).  Then the enemy unit must either drop its concealment voluntarily or take a PAATC (unless exempt) (because that's done instantly per A12.41; I guess that means it must happen before any DFF).  Then the vehicle must expend the Stop MP (D4.22 says it's immediate), and only then (after any DFF provoked by the Stop MP) does it decide whether it will declare an OVR or not (and if so, that is then a separate MP expenditure, which of course may provoke further DFF).

replies.body:
It's an interesting question and I can certainly think of good reasons for doing so.

The question in my mind is the timing.  Since OVR is a form of Bounding First Fire, and you declare the MP expenditure for the OVR as you enter the hex, could you then also add in the extra 2 MPs for the HD attempt?  Which would get resolved first?

So I look at the ASOP and I think I find the answer.  "During the Mph" your AFV MAY declare OVR attack;  MAY Attempt HD Maneuver.  (it lists it in that order too)

So after resolving your OVR, I think you can then do your HD Attempt.  However, you have to add in the extra 2 MP for the HD attempt before entering the enemy's hex.  e.g.  AFV with 20 MPs would expend 4 MPs for the OVR +2 MP for the HD attempt, for a total of 6 as it moves into that hex.  Then, resolve the OVR, resolve the HD attempt and then must stop per D4.22..regardless of the outcome of the HD Maneuver Attempt, the vehicle must then immediately end its MPh by expending a Stop MP if still Mobile.

The MPs are spent simultaneously and before any DFF against the AFV.

realistically, it seems weird to do both at the same time;
with overrun you are driving into a position to eliminate the target effectively
with hd you are maneuvring to put your vehicle in a specific spot to reduce incoming fire
as such performing both maneuvers at the same time seems counterintuitive, you would have to be really lucky that its the same position that allows you to do both together, ovr is more likely to require intensive driving while hd needs careful driving.

i feel you should make a choice either ovr or the hd maneuver but not both.

Nevertheless, it is perfectly true that one of the weaknesses of the vehicle simulation aspects of ASL is that it does not portray vehicle speed at all well (especially when performing proportional calculations, like an OVR).  Without a complete overhaul of the ASL vehicle system, which I doubt very many players would be in favour of, I don't see that this will ever change.

For example: the slowest AFV in the game is the FT-17, with 5 MP (and it can't even get the 1/2 MP rate on roads).  This means that an FT-17 performing an OVR must expend a minimum of 1 MP to enter the hex plus an additional 2 MP (5/4 FRU), for a total of 3 MP.  Any units able to attack the FT-17 as it is doing this maneuver could attack up to 3 times.

The fastest tracked AFV in the game is (I believe) the M18 GMC, with 24 MP.  It has no problem using the road rate when CE -- and since it's open-topped, that will be most of the time.  So the least expensive (in terms of MP) OVR attack that it could make would be 1/2 to enter the hex via a road, plus an additional 24/4 = 6 MP, or a total of 6.5 MP.  Any units able to attack the M18 as it is doing this could attack up to 6 times.

So, if we say expending MP is a measure of the passing of time, then the M18 is actually penalised for being nearly 5 times faster than the FT-17, since the OVR takes twice as long!

More simply, we can see that pure speed is also not taken into account when firing at a moving vehicle: an FT-17 crossing 5 open ground hexes will expend 1 MP per hex and can be fired at 5 times.  The M18 zooming across the same terrain also expends 1 MP per hex to do so and can similarly be fired at 5 times!

If you're looking for "absolute realism", then this cannot be considered as anything other than a failure in ASL.  Just as well, then, that ASL is not sold as a simulation, but rather as a game.  ASL does, in fact, simulate many aspects of WW2 warfare tolerably well.  We forgive it for its weaknesses because its strengths are unmatched by any other game that I am aware of. title: Pre registered hex
question:
Hi all, 

Just like to to check something..:)

I´m turn 2 of Campaign 1 of Valor of the Guards. As the Germans I´ve bought a module of 80 mm OBA and a pre planned hex. 
In my defensive fire phase, I get to place a FFE straight away, provided I have radio contact, a black chit and LOS. This I have. 
I roll for placement, and get a 6. That´s bad. The shot drifts of, 3 hexes awayy. No Russians hit.

Ok. so Far so good. I grumbl and wait for better turns.. 

Then it´s turn 3. FFE1 is on the board In the Prep fire phase I try again..  Now here´s where my question starts.. I did the following, and would like to know if I did it correctly.. 

I went thought the following flow chart questions (on the LFT RAT Pocket charts, edition 2) 

- Do you wish to cancel SR? NO
- Does observer has LOS to blast height? Yes 
- Do you wish to correct the SR? Yes
- Place ST within 18 hexes. I did. Back to the pre planned hex. 
- Does observer have LOS to location in hex? Yes
- Are there any enemy units and all unknown? Yes 
- Draw Chit. I did. Black
- Place SR a roll for accuracy. Which I do. I roll a 1. Fire lands on the spot. I can blast away those pesky Russians.   

So my questions are: 
- I don´t seem to have any advantage anymore of the pre planned hex. Or do I? Could I have simply started again like I did before, and place it on the pre planned hex and roll for accuracy? Is a pre planned hex just an advantage in your first shot? (besides getting an extra black chit)?
- Note that I used the word "SR". In the flow chart I couldn´t find a flow which starts with "FFE 1 on board". I used the flow chart for SR because it had the pictogram  "SR" but also "FFE1" in the top left corner..

Man, arty is a bit of a hassle in ASL.. :wow:

Thanks,
Peter
author: pveenstra
consensus_answer:
In the flow chart I couldn´t find a flow which starts with "FFE 1 on board".

That's because you will never start with an FFE:1 on board.  Once an FFE:1 has been resolved, it immediately flips to an FFE:2.  The FFE:1 counter is, in effect, only a temporary place-holder.

Man, arty is a bit of a hassle in ASL.. :wow:

Yes, which is why the flow-chart was designed.  (Historically, there were several different iterations created by various people, until MMP finally first published the original official chart in Action Pack #1.)

Once you've run through it a few times the process is actually pretty straight-forward, most of the time.  It only gets complex when you run into the special cases.

Most people cut through all of the red tape by just drawing two red cards in a row. :p

title: Guards and interdiction
question:
Hello everybody,

I have a question (or two) about guards.
We had a broken guard with prisoners in our last game.

*When guard undergoes interdiction so do the prisoners?
*When guard is eliminated by interdiction what about the prisoners? Eliminated too?

Rules states that routing unit can be interdicted, but are the prisoners routing unit?

Thanks in advance...
author: Anatoly45100
consensus_answer:
Prisoners do not Rout, they just accompany their Guard (A20.53). So they do not roll interdiction as they are not routing.

If the broken guard is eliminated by interdiction, A20.5 applies: either another unit is the Guard or the Prisoners are freed.

title: Ordnance Area Fire on Woods with no LOS to ground level?

Situation is that a Sherman sees some Woods (in a wood hex) over a grain field in season and also over a couple of hedges blocking his LOS to the ground level of the woods. The example in C 3.331 shows that a unit out of LOS IN a gully can be affected by Area Fire despite being out of LOS. What differs from my example is that the firer actually sees the ground level location so the problem is not really there in the example.

In your example, neither MTRs nor direct fire Guns can fire Area at the Woods. LOS to a Location in the hex must exist for any fire to occur.

In the case of a building, the difference is direct fire vs indirect fire. Direct fire goes straight to the target, so nothing/less hits the out of LOS targets. Indirect fire comes down onto the target, which will hit all targets no matter the LOS.

title: Throwing Smoke from Bypass on board 3
question: In playing Gavin's Take on Board 3, a US elite infantry unit is bypassing the woods in J2 (on the hex side next to the hill).  Can it place smoke in K3 while bypassing the woods?  Or does the woods depiction in the middle of the hex block the ability to throw the smoke into the adjacent location (K3)?
author: Dave-Dennis
consensus_answer:
In playing Gavin's Take on Board 3, a US elite infantry unit is bypassing the woods in J2 (on the hex side next to the hill).  Can it place smoke in K3 while bypassing the woods?  Or does the woods depiction in the middle of the hex block the ability to throw the smoke into the adjacent location (K3)?

The answers you've received about the LOS requirement are correct (assuming that the statement about SMOKE placement requiring ADJACENT is correct; I'm NRBH, so cannot confirm; see below).  However, when posing questions like this, it helps considerably for you to be precise with the details.  There are two hexsides "next to the hill" in hex J2, and the answer to your question is different depending on which hexside(s) you're talking about.

If you're bypassing only the I2/J2 hexside, then the answers already posted are correct; at no point does the squad have LOS to K3, and thus cannot attempt to place SMOKE in that hex.

If you're bypassing only the I3/J2 hexside, OR if you're bypassing both hexsides, then the squad does have a LOS to K3, from the I3-J2-J3 vertex.  Thus, it is ADJACENT and can attempt to place the SMOKE.

Now, all of that being said: do you actually require ADJACENT Locations?  Certainly not always, as you can place SMOKE from an upper Level building Location (or across a Cliff hexside) to an adjacent (but not ADJACENT) Location.  It depends on the exact wording of the rules.
If it turns out the rule does NOT require ADJACENT, then the whole question of LOS becomes moot.

In order to be ADJACENT there must be a LOS.

So if in your case there is no LOS between MMC and target Location, they cannot place SMOKE.

Check out B23.32 INDIRECT FIRE in the rule book.

title: Smoke and Residual Fire Power
question:
Does smoke have any effect on residual fire power in a hex.

For example 8FP would normally leave 4FP of residual fire power  in an open hex. If the hex contains a ½” smoke counter would its +2 DRM shift the residual FP 2 columns to the left to the 1 column?
author: turpid
consensus_answer:
Does smoke have any effect on residual fire power in a hex.

For example 8FP would normally leave 4FP of residual fire power  in an open hex. If the hex contains a ½” smoke counter would its +2 DRM shift the residual FP 2 columns to the left to the 1 column?  

No, It does not - when it is in the hex. However the +2 will apply to the attack.

Additionally, if you fire through smoke hindrance in hex A and leave Residual FP in hex B, the residual FP is reduced accordingly.

A side note: Firelane Residual FP is not effected by smoke (or other "soft" hindrance - see the index for a definition), note however that the shot that places the Firelane is effected.

author: oivind22

So, if you retain ROF in your MPh, you move in a different HEX and you end your MPh, your AFV is not marked wit Bounding Fire counter

If and only if you fired no other weapons that also retained ROF.  (I.E., if you fired any MGs, you are marked with a Bounding Fire counter regardless of whether your MA retained ROF.)

but you have to remember that in yout AFPh you can't use any not-MA MG, right?

Um, no.  If, in the AFPh, you are not marked with a Bounding Fire counter, you are eligible to fire any usable weapons.  (If you are marked with a Bounding Fire counter then you cannot fire any weapons.)

Right.

title: What changed from 1st Edition?
question: The question is exactly what it says on the tin. I might be getting my hands on a 1st Edition rulebook and would like to know if I will have any problems playing an opponent with a later edition. In other words, are there significant innovations I have missed?
author: Michael Hopcroft
consensus_answer:
IIRC, the only thing that really changed is the Human Wave rules. 

Technically they changed in the errata pages originally included in Doomed Battalions -- but that didn't predate the 2nd ed. rules by very much.

The 2nd ed. rules attempted (and almost succeeded) to include every official Q&A that had been published up until that point.  (A couple were missed by accident, and have been added to 2nd ed. via errata; one or two were deliberately omitted because it was decided to overturn them.)

In addition, an unknown (but quite large) number of additional changes were made because of unofficial Q&A (that had not previously been published widely, if at all), as well as some improvement in the rules language here and there.

The most "obvious" changes were moving the Collateral Attacks rule from Chapter A (where it confused new players) to Chapter D (where it makes more sense); improved Wall Advantage/Bocage rules; and the additions of Chapters E and K (and dropping of Chapter N).  Some sections got new/better Examples.  The IIFT was added as an official option, and the OBA and OVR flowcharts were added.  There were several new/improved charts and tables added to the rules dividers.

To answer the original question: the game still played fundamentally the same, but there are some detail differences here and there.  Every now and again you might trip up on something specific but mostly you'd never notice.  That being said: there is no reason to go out and spend money on a used copy of 1st edition.  That money would be better invested in a copy of the 2nd ed. rules (the Pocket version, at the very least).

title: MGs and FF, SFF, FPF
question:
I am not sure if I understand the rules for machine guns (MGs) and first fire (FF), subsequent first fire (SFF) and final protective fire (FPF).

I believe a MG that is NOT marked FF can continue to fire at moving targets with full fire power (FP) until it fails a rate of fire (ROF) roll, even if its manning squad is marked FF. As soon as it fails the ROF roll, it too is marked FF. True?

I believe a MG MUST fire with the squad that mans it if the squad chooses to SFF or FPF. It would fire at half FP and would be considered sustained fire. True?

I believe a MG CANNOT fire alone for SFF or FPF. It only takes part in SFF or FPF if the squad that mans it is firing. True?

Any other subtleties I might be missing?

Thanks!
author: MikeWhit
consensus_answer:
Full squad with MG fire MG only in the first fire phase at a target that is two hexes away.
MG is marked with FF, but not the squad.

Q1.Can the squad FF at a target more than two hexes away?

Yes. To count as SFF the unit/weapon (either SW or inherent FP) has to be already marked with a first-fire counter [A8.3]. Unless the MG cowered the inherent FP would still be unmarked. The counters that come with Beyond Valor aren't sophisticated enough to make this distinction. Players often put the MG to the side and mark it alone to indicate the current state. Later modules come with "SW first fire" & "Inherent first fire" counters. Later versions of Armies of Oblivion have them. Despite not having a perfect system for marking a squad and MG firing separately, the squad may use its inherent FP (or a second MG, or a second ordnance SW) as first fire at any range otherwise allowed.

Q2.If the squad did not FF, I assume that in the SFF, it can on,y fire at adjacent target as the MG is marked with
An FF counter?

Once a unit/weapon is marked with a first fire counter and using SFF, the unit/weapon can fire at any target in normal range and no farther than any Known enemy unit [A8.3]. That might be adjacent, but in your example (as far as you have stated) the target for SFF would have to be at range less-than-or-equal-to two hexes.

Comment: I am not 100% sure what you mean by, "in the SFF." I assumed you meant, "as SFF," i.e. during the enemy MPh. It is possible you are asking about the DFPh instead. If so there is still no restriction on the use of the inherent FP of the squad as long as it is not marked. If it is marked with first fire, it can only fire at ADJACENT targets [A8.4].

I believe a MG CANNOT fire alone for SFF or FPF. It only takes part in SFF or FPF if the squad that mans it is firing. True?

Um, not really.  A squad can use SFF to fire a MG only if that's what it wants.  However, since both the MG and the squad will be marked with a Final Fire counter regardless, there's not often a good reason to not fire the squad as well.  Typically the only time it would happen is if the target is beyond the squad's inherent FP range, but still within the MG's normal range -- a Russian 4-4-7 firing a MMG at 9 hexes, for instance.  (It may also happen if there's odd combinations of FP and adding the squad's Inherent FP won't push it to a new FP column on the IFT.)

When it comes to FPF, a squad MUST use any MG available to it IF POSSIBLE.  (It may not be possible if the MG's CA is restricted.)  So if a squad is carrying two LMG and gets into a FPF situation, both MGs will be fired and the squad cannot use its inherent FP.

Since you were asking about subtleties: a common thing that seems to trip people up a lot is the situation with a HS or crew manning a MG.  In FF, the HS/crew may use either its inherent or the MG FP (not both).  In SFF, the HS/crew can make the same choice again.  A lot of people seem to believe that if they fire the MG in FF, they must use the MG again in SFF.  That is not the case.  (Again, in a FPF situation, the HS/crew MUST fire the MG if possible.)

A8.2: Residual Firepower: When a unit is attacked by Defensive First Fire/Subsequent First Fire/FPF, the target Location in which the attack is resolved (even if in Bypass) is marked with a Residual FP counter 

A6.11: Should the LOS check for an attack reveal a block LOS, the units which were to have made the attack are still considered to have fired for all purposes (they thought they saw something); that fire would not generate DM status nor affect units in the obstacle that block the LOS

Attack is not resolved, so no residual FP.

title: A couple of more questions about AFV's firing
question:
Question 1: Let's say you fire other weapons than the MA as bounding fire. The rules say that the only way the AFV can fire from another hex after this, is if it's the MA maintaining ROF. Can the MA maintain ROF by choosing not to fire from the same hex, or does it have to fire it's first shot in the same hex as the rest of the weapons, and thus risk losing ROF?

Question 2: If an AFV fires only it's MA in the PFPh and maintains ROF, can it fire again in the AFPh, like it could if it uses bounding fire and maintains ROF?
author: oivind22
consensus_answer:
Anyway, during real play you don't usually have so many options, you usually just stand and shoot or move, stop and blast away.

The OP's questions have been answered, but I just wanted to follow-up on this comment: vehicles are all about giving you options.  If "standing and shooting" and "moving, stopping and shooting" are the only things your AFVs are doing, you're getting about 10% (maybe) of their game value.

Obviously it varies depending on nationality and timeframe, and the particular scenario VC may dictate particular actions -- but in general "shooting at things" is probably one of the lesser functions of an AFV.

Always try to keep in mind everything a vehicle might do for you in a given Player Turn.

title: Using MA and MG on vehicles
question: I'm trying to get into AFVs, but there is one thing which is not clear to me. The rules say vehicle armamaments except MA with ROF can only fire once. How do you keep track of this? Does this mean that if non-MA armaments fire, the AFV is marked with the appropriate fire phase marker? That is, there is no (further) ROF if you fire other armaments than the MA? How else would you rememember that the non-MA armaments have fired. I assume that if you fire only the MA, and it maintains ROF, all armaments can be fired later.
author: oivind22
consensus_answer:
Note this little rule as well which is buried in the CA rules:

C3.51 MAINTAINING COVERED ARC: ...Once any vehicular weapon fires, its other weapons may fire in that phase only from that same hex [EXC: OVR; and MA retaining a Multiple ROF may fire again from another hex if the previous shot(s) were Bounding First Fire].

So in answer to Q1, the MA must fire with the the other weapons in the same hex before moving to another hex if it wishes to fire from another hex, assuming it can maintain ROF.

Q2. A weapon is marked with a Prep Fire marker once it stops firing in the PFPh regardless of whether it maintained ROF. As it states in rule A3.5 "The ATTACKER's units which did not fire in the PFPh or attempt to perform a task requiring TI status may fire at half FP..."

So if you fire in the PFPh you can't fire in the  AFPh even if you maintained ROF.

Thanks, I didn't know that you can't fire in the AFPh if you fired and maintained ROF in the PFPh, but I see now that this goes for infantry with SW MG's too. I guess all units should be marked with an appropriate fire phase marker at the end of a phase, if they fired, and even if they maintained ROF, so that you can remember that it fired in a previous phase. I seem to remember now that there's a rule saying that a unit can only fire in one phase (but MPh and DFPh is considered the same phase for this purpose). So I guess a MA firing alone as bounding fire, maintaining ROF and then firing again (only once) in the AFPh, is the sole exception to this rule.

replies.body:
I believe there are counters someplace that you can use to track MG vs MA fire.  If the Non-MA MG fires it does not exhaust the ROF of the MA.  If the MA fires it does not use the MGs ability to fire later as long as the MGs have not fired yet.

Sometimes you just have to keep a side note if it gets too complicated to keep track in your head.

Craig

Most of the time you'll fire all the MGs and the MA on an AFV before moving to the next. But I believe the only requirement is to fire them all in the same phase. So you can fire the MA on 10 tanks and then cycle back and fire all the MGs if you like in any order that you like. 

There are counters that came with Bounding Fire's "Crucible of Steel" that indicate the weapons fired, such as MA only, MA plus BMG, MA plus CMG etc. The standard ASL counters don't do this and you have to remember or otherwise mark the AFVs as seems best. 

You can see them in this image:
There were counters for this that came with the AFV cards from way back when as well.

It's true that if you fire only MMG armaments in one fire phase, you are marked for fire, and you cannot fire them in a later fire phase (e.g. AFPh)-- excepting defensive first fire and defensive final fire being treated as the same phase for such fire. 

Yes you are correct if the ROF is maintained, but, if you chose not to use ROF in the prep fire phase, you still mark is as completely fired for all armaments with a prep fire marker.

Don't get too hung up on the "procedure of placing status markers" in ASL.  There is some memory required as you go deeper into the game.  Most people have little ways of placing markers to indicate certain things.  But the rules are the rules, the markers are not.

I would say that you might want some markers initially, but I think you will find that once you are more familiar and more experienced with the use of AFVs, you will be able to remember most of that just because of the amount of attention you are paying to what you are doing.

title: Fortified building
question: In a multi-hex fortified building may an opponent enter an unoccupied building hex starting outside the building?
author: The Old Man
consensus_answer:
I also found this odd one:

B23.922 If a Good Order squad in a Fortified Building declares Wall Advantage, may an enemy unit then advance into that Building Location?
A. Yes, if the squad is still marked with a Wall Advantage counter. [An95w; An96; Mw]

Has that been incorporated into 2nd ed. text?  It seems a bit counter-intuitive to me (in the sense that, just because a unit declares WA doesn't mean that it is not in the Location any more).  It's as official as official can be, though.  Stupid old fart brain.
Yes, I agree that Q&A seems odd. Whenever I see a 1st Edition Q&A that has no "trace" of it in the 2nd Edition I usually thing one of three things:

1. It was overlooked when 2nd edition was compiled.
2. It was deemed not to apply anymore.
3. It was considered that the rules text already supported what it says.

Of course, guessing which option is correct isn't easy, and this one of the problems with the old 1st edition Q&A. :)

In this case, though, I am leaning towards 1 or 2, since I can't see much (any ?) support for it in the currect rules.

This sentence from B9.32 suggests that the second explanation may apply.

B9.32 Wall Advanatage (WA): ...A unit claiming WA is still considered occupying any obstacle/terrain as it would if not claiming WA for all purposes (e.g., Concealment Terrain, firing backblast weapon from building) [EXC: 9.31].

title: Hazardous movement for manhandling a gun: when does it stop?
question:
Manhandling a gun is a hazardous movement. Hazardous movement applies a -2 DRM to fire on the manhandling unit. At which moment does the DRM ceases to apply?

The A4.62 rules say that the manhandling unit receives a -2 DRM to any fire attack regardless of fire phase until it is pinned. 

Also, the C11.3 EX makes clear that a unit firing during the DFPh on a gun that has been manhandled during the previous MPh still applies the -2 DRM as Case O.

ASL SK EP#1 rules go further to say "[...] any fire attack directed at it that player turn regardless of fire phase [...]". Note that it is said explicitly that the -2 applies during the whole player turn.

Now, searching on the Internet I've found some GS threads that settle on the contrary, that the -2 applies only during the manhandling unit's own MPh and no further. That is based on a 2003 Q&A from Perry that says that the -2 DRM for manhandling applies only during its MPh, no further.

The Index adds no information to the description of Hazardous Movement, and there are no changes on these particular rules from the 1st Ed rules.

Now, what is your take on this? When does the Hazardous Movement penalty ceases to apply to units that have Manhandled a Gun?
author: esparver73
consensus_answer:
Solid and interesting reasoning, but why ignore A4.62, which clearly delineates that pushing a gun results in hazardous movement (HM), hence application of the -2 DRM, regardless of fire phase? That much seems very clear. A4.62 does not stipulate that any of the listed activities are exempt in other fire phases...other than whence pinned. Now, pin status is removed at the end of the player turn, giving us a hint that HM DRM goes away only at the end of the player turn, not the end of a unit's MPh.

I agree that the HM DRM applies regardless of phase, but only while a unit is so engaged. Perhaps it is worth posting the entire Q&A in order to provide more context.

A4.62, A23.7, B8.3, B21.41, B23.41, B24.7 & C10.3
Q. Do all Clearance attempts receive the Hazardous Movement penalty until the Clearance DR is made?
A. The appropriate Clearance attempts do.

Q. Does Pushing a Gun (C10.3), Setting a DC, or Crew exiting a Cellar (B23.41) receive the Hazardous Movement penalty only
during the applicable MPh?
A. Yes.

Q. Does the Hazardous Movement penalty apply to Sewer Movement and Fording as long as the unit is in that terrain?
A. Yes.

Is it your suggestion that E.2 be invoked, so that C10.3 supersedes A4.62?

No. Unless a unit is actually "engaged" in a dangerous activity that warrants the application of the HM DRM, the DRM is NA. 

Pushing a Gun, Setting a DC, and exiting a destroyed vehicle are special cases. The latter can occur during any phase in which the vehicle is destroyed (including falling into a cellar), hence the stipulation in A4.62 that the HM DRM can any apply "regardless of fire phase." (Note the wording. The rule does not specify that the HM DRM applies in any/all fire phases, only that it applies "to any attacks against units so engaged [in HM] regardless of fire phase.")

I also agree, for example, that a unit that Sets a DC is only subject to the HM DRM during its MPh.

23.7 SET DEMOLITION: A DC which is neither Placed nor Thrown is considered a Set DC and has special advantages and requirements. A Set DC is one which has been Set prior to play by SSR, or which was Set and declared during play by an Infantry unit which spent all of its MF (using Hazardous Movement) to Set the DC in its Location during its MPh and made a dr ≤ its US# (subject to leadership drm by any leader assisting the unit to Set the DC) without being pinned or broken.

The problem seems to be unclear language in reference to the sequence of play; the rulebook indicates 'engagement' in activity, also, 'having just pushed.'

Agreed. Some rule sections such as C10.3 could use a clarification. Others, already make it quite clear that the HM DRM only applies during a specific time period. Take, for instance, paratroops, which are only subject to this DRM during DFF, i.e. when they are considered to be Aerial targets.

9.3 DEFENSIVE FIRST FIRE: After the Drift of all parachutes has been resolved, the DEFENDER may use Defensive First Fire and Subsequent First Fire vs them—even if they have drifted offboard (9.41). Aerial paratroops are subject to Hazardous Movement DRM, and can claim neither Height Advantage, TEM, concealment (9.11), nor any Hindrance other than LV/SMOKE (E.6). Hazardous Movement DRM even apply to an attack (only) on an Aerial SW in an attempt to destroy/malfunction it (A9.74) although such attacks will usually be caused by mistaken identity due to Random Selection.

Putting a labor status marker could indicated ongoing 'engagement' until it is pinned by fire. There is nothing in the rulebook exempting that interpretation because the rulebook does not define 'engagement' -- at least not anywhere I have found so far. Not that I have gone over it with a fine-tooth comb, but nothing in my ASOP (not sure which version it is other than 'rev') explains when the HM DRM goes away.

Which brings us back to the Q&A above, and which helps delineate when HM ends wrt A23.7, B23.41*, and C10.3.

*FWIW, my version of B23.41 includes this info.

23.41 CELLARS:...If the AFV rolls an Original 6 on the colored dr of the Bog Check DR, the AFV has fallen through the floor to the cellar and is removed. Should the AFV crew survive, it is automatically placed at ground level subject to Hazardous Movement for any subsequent fire during that phase (D5.6).

replies.body:
Typically a formally answered Q&A is considered a solid ruling.  Is there a reason you're not satisfied by that? 

If it was only a "Perry Sez" (i.e. an informal reply in a forum like this or ConSimWorld) then I would agree the answer is unclear.

-N

A4.62 actually doesn't say that. It says that the hazardous movement modifier applies regardless of fire phase.

The C11.3 EX is suspect, but I've been told that examples should be considered rules.

The Q&A you mention seems like a logical application of A4.62.

A4.62 actually doesn't say that. It says that the hazardous movement modifier applies regardless of fire phase.

The C11.3 EX is suspect, but I've been told that examples should be considered rules.

The Q&A you mention seems like a logical application of A4.62.
In my rather vague memory with NRBH, Haz Move has generally applied throughout the entire player turn.  I'm thinking that there was some rule (possibly back to SL) where Haz Move as it applied to Crew Survival would still be in effect in the AFPh (assuming the surviving crew was from a defender's vehicle and thus had a reason to be targeted then).

Rulebooks not available ATM to double check this, unfortunately.

Edited to reflect that it was a pretty piss-poor answer!

Ordinarily (and ideally) the rule invoking Hazardous Movement also specifies for how long it is in effect once invoked.

The "regardless of fire phase" quote from the general rule simply means that (unlike, e.g., FFMO) the DRM can apply in any fire phase where the unit might be attacked.  Or to put it another way, it doesn't have to be the MPh.

I am NRBH, but having just looked it up recently, I know that the HazMove penalty for Crew Survival applies only during the phase that the vehicle was eliminated in.  Once you move on to the next phase in the turn, the crew is no longer subject to that penalty.  So any claim that "Hazardous Movement always applies for the entire turn" is not correct.

I am pretty sure that some HazMove activities -- e.g., mine clearance -- do last until the end of the CCPh (when the actual dice for mine clearance are rolled) -- so pretty much the entire turn in that particular case.

If the Manhandling rules don't specifically set a time limit, then I'd agree that they are vague in that respect, but I have no reason to disbelieve the Q&A that says it only applies during the MPh.

In the absence of anything else, I would argue that in general the HazMove penalty would only last for the specific phase that activity occurs in -- but each specific rule should make it clear.

Good catch on the ambiguous rule here...

A4.62 has a specific list of hazardous activities that require the -2 DRM regardless of fire phase as long as 'so engaged.' The rule also points out that hazardous movement does indeed apply to PRC survival. 

The C11.3 rule is supportive of A4.62 in the case of a gun pushed that 'has just been pushed out of it's emplaced hex' -- whatever 'has just been pushed' means in terms of turns or phases, is not clear. We can assume it means sometime during that player turn (not the entire turn)...maybe.

The problem is the use of the word 'engaged' in A4.62. 'Engaged' is not found in the Index. Looking up labor status, C10.3 (in the case of gun pushing), does not illuminate any information about the duration of engagement, especially now that it may be marked with a labor status -- does that status indicate that it is still 'engaged?' 

At this point, I think we must turn to the definition of 'movement' in ASLRB V2. Per A4 and A4.2 and undoubtedly other places (i'm not looking into all instances, the ASOP, etc.), movement ends at the end of a unit's movement phase. 

I think we are to glean that, as an exception, hazardous movement drm does apply to the end of the player turn for the activities listed in A4.62 (i.e. beyond the MPh to the very end of the player turn). However, the rule A4.62 probably should read 'engaged for the rest of the player turn' or some such....

edit -- typos

Typically a formally answered Q&A is considered a solid ruling.  Is there a reason you're not satisfied by that? 

If it was only a "Perry Sez" (i.e. an informal reply in a forum like this or ConSimWorld) then I would agree the answer is unclear.

-N

Nadir, I would be satisfied by the 2003 Q&A but it is both in direct contradiction of the 2000 C11.3 EX and the 2011 ASL SK EP#1 rule, which is explicit in saying that hazardous movement penalty for manhandling lasts for the whole player turn.

It seems that the penalty for other actions is quite clear that either applies only for that phase or for the whole turn, but in this case it's not explicit so it could be either.

A Q&A says one thing and two versions of the rules say the contrary.

A4.62 actually doesn't say that. It says that the hazardous movement modifier applies regardless of fire phase.

The rule seem to be in need of clarification. I have been basing my play on an assumption that the gun-push hazard DRM ends when the player turn ends.

A close read of C10.3 suggests that the application of the Haz Mov DRM is even more circumscribed than for CS. If, as the text in parenthesis below suggests, Pushing a Gun is equivalent to making a Manhandling DR, the Haz Mov DRM only applies when the Gun is actually being Pushed, i.e. during the MPh of the unit(s) Pushing the Gun, or its MPh. 

C10.3 PUSHING: ...Pushing a Gun (i.e., making a Manhandling DR) is Hazardous Movement, prevents Assault Movement, and cannot be attempted while carrying PP, or moving beneath a Wire/Panji counter, or attempting a Minimum Move. ...If the Final Manhandling DR is > the M#, neither the Gun nor any pushing unit(s) can be moved farther during that MPh but the pushing unit(s) receives a -1 Labor counter for use in its next attempt. If the Final Manhandling DR equals the M#, the Gun and pushing unit(s) can enter that hex but cannot be moved any farther during that MPh. If the Final Manhandling DR is < the M#, the Gun can enter that hex and either attempt to be pushed another hex or can be hooked up (see 10.31), provided all the Infantry which has engaged in pushing during that Player Turn have sufficient MF left to expend in that hex. In all three cases, the Gun and its pushing Infantry become TI for the rest of that Player Turn when their pushing/hooking up has ended...

I think that the Haz Mov DRM is applied differently depending on the activity. If a unit remains vulnerable in a real-world sense, such as when engaged in Climbing or Fording, the Haz Mov DRM continues to apply, and not necessarily just for that Player Turn. However, once a unit has completed a "hazardous" task, it is no longer subject to the Haz Mov DRM. 

Pushing a Gun is not a "process" in the sense that a Clearance Attempt is. While a Clearance Attempt requires until the CCPh to complete, Manhandling a Gun is accomplished (or not) solely during the Pushing unit's MPh.

This line of reasoning also makes sense when one considers that a unit engaged in Haz Mov immediately ceases to be subject to the Haz Mov DRM the moment it pins.

A4.62, A23.7, B8.3, B21.41, B23.41, B24.7 & C10.3
Q. Do all Clearance attempts receive the Hazardous Movement penalty until the Clearance DR is made?
A. The appropriate Clearance attempts do.

No. Unless a unit is actually "engaged" in a dangerous activity that warrants the application of the HM DRM, the DRM is NA. 

Pushing a Gun, Setting a DC, and exiting a destroyed vehicle are special cases. The latter can occur during any phase in which the vehicle is destroyed (including falling into a cellar), hence the stipulation in A4.62 that the HM DRM can any apply "regardless of fire phase." (Note the wording. The rule does not specify that the HM DRM applies in any/all fire phases, only that it applies "to any attacks against units so engaged [in HM] regardless of fire phase.")

I also agree, for example, that a unit that Sets a DC is only subject to the HM DRM during its MPh.

23.7 SET DEMOLITION: A DC which is neither Placed nor Thrown is considered a Set DC and has special advantages and requirements. A Set DC is one which has been Set prior to play by SSR, or which was Set and declared during play by an Infantry unit which spent all of its MF (using Hazardous Movement) to Set the DC in its Location during its MPh and made a dr ≤ its US# (subject to leadership drm by any leader assisting the unit to Set the DC) without being pinned or broken.

Section A4.8 certainly appears to put a damper on any suggestion that the HM DRM only applies while a unit is actually Pushing a Gun during the MPh.

However, a TI counter is used in other cases simply to prevent a unit from engaging in other activities (e.g. firing (even a Starshell), advancing, etc.). For example, a dozer is not Infantry, but it nevertheless earns a TI counter when clearing fortifications (G15.21).

But let's get back to A4.62. The rule states that neither FFNAM nor FFMO apply when the HM DRM applies.

A4.62: ...Neither FFMO nor FFNAM apply to shots affected by Hazardous Movement;... 

But what happens when a Gun is Pushed and hooked up during the same MPh?

C10.31: A Gun can be pushed and then hooked up during the same MPh, but only if its pushing Infantry can still attempt to push that Gun another hex in that MPh (i.e., can attempt another Manhandling DR), and only if the vehicle has not yet exceeded the specified MP/MF expenditure for hooking up (10.11). No Manhandling DR is actually required for hooking up or unhooking.

C10.11 HOOKING UP: A Stopped vehicle not in Bypass may hook up a Gun (if the vehicle's T# ≤ the Gun's M#) by spending half (FRU) of its MP/MF allotment [EXC: if the Gun's M# is circled (e.g., M6), the vehicle must expend two-thirds (FRU) of its MP/MF allotment] in that Gun's hex (in addition to any required MP/MF cost to enter the hex), provided a crew (as per 10.111) is on foot in that hex. This expenditure does not itself qualify that vehicle as a moving target, but does allow Defensive First Fire opportunities against it (that Gun shares its target status and is destroyed or missed depending on the fate of the vehicle). That Gun is then placed on top of that vehicle to indicate that it is in tow. Neither that Gun, its crew, nor that vehicle/its PRC can fire during that PFPh/MPh and all are TI for the rest of that Player Turn. That crew may also load into that towing vehicle at no extra MP/MF cost as it hooks up that Gun, but if it expends > half its MF allotment in pushing/entering that Gun's hex, that Gun cannot then be hooked up by that unit in that MPh. A non-QSU Gun (10.23) must first be limbered (10.21) before it can be hooked up. See 10.31 for pushing and hooking up a Gun in the same MPh.

C10.111: A crew must be in Good Order and unpinned in order to (un)hook/(un)limber/push a Gun it possesses. See D5.43 for attack effects while (un)hooking. A HS (even if inherent in a squad) equals a crew for such purposes, but it takes five SMC to equal a crew for such purposes.

D5.43 FFNAM: An Inherent crew Abandoning its vehicle as per 5.41 (as well as any other Personnel unit exiting/entering a vehicle) is considered Infantry and subject to FFNAM (until pinned) vs all attacks declared against it due to either its embarking/debarking MF expenditure or the vehicle's simultaneous MP/MF expenditure (6.4; 6.5). If also attempting to (un)hook a Gun while doing so, it succeeds in (un)hooking it only if it survives all such attacks unpinned and in Good Order. Likewise, Infantry attempting to enter a vehicle succeed only if they survive all such attacks unpinned and in Good Order.

Per A4.62, the FFNAM and HM DRM cannot apply concurrently. Therefore, I contend that the HM DRM applies while the unit is Pushing the Gun (i.e. when it makes its Manhandling DR), and that FFNAM applies during the hooking-up/loading process. If I am correct, then why would the HM DRM be "reinstated" following the hook-up/loading process?

EX: A BU halftrack is in a road hex ADJACENT to an Infantry crew (also on a road hex) with a ATG. During the MPh, the Infantry crew passes its Manhandling DR and Pushes the Gun into the same hex as the ht. The Infantry crew is subject to the HM DRM while Pushing. The opposing side declines to fire on this MF expenditure. 

The Infantry crew then declares its intention to hook up the Gun and enter the ht. At this point, the Infantry crew is subject to FFNAM per D5.43. The opposing side declines to fire. 

Once inside the ht, the Infantry crew becomes a BU Passenger, and is therefore largely immune to Small Arms fire [EXC: TPBF; HA; etc.]. But let's assume that the PRC of the ht were CE instead. Would the HM DRM continue to apply for the remainder of the turn? And if so, would only the Infantry crew be subject to this DRM, despite the fact that all PRC (and the AFV) are TI for the remainder of the turn?

IOW, I do not think that being TI, in and of itself, warrants continued vulnerability to the HM DRM. Rather, it is the continuation of a hazardous process that warrants this penalty.

How many?  Hundreds, if not thousands.  That's always been true.  It didn't used to matter that much, when TAHGC still existed, because you got semi-regular updates in issues of the General and in the Annual (which, most of the time, actually was published annually).

Now we only get updates if they are phrased as actual errata, and a relatively small number of them at that, and published at very irregular intervals.  In terms of changes to the rules I think that works well enough.  In terms of helping players to interpret the rules ... not so much.

There are two huge problems with the unofficial Q&A system as it currently stands: firstly, it's pretty much impossible to stay across all of it, and many players have no idea how to access any of it.  It totally relies on "word of mouth" to propagate.

Secondly, it's not always reliable.  Sometimes the same question gets two different answers, depending on when it was asked.  Very occasionally the answers are simply wrong, because something was missed at the time it was answered, or Perry simply changed his mind on a particular point.  The Q&A don't get as much back-and-forth scrutiny as the errata does.  Personally I always check every "unofficial" answer I see to determine if it matches my understanding of the rules (and heaven knows I can get things wrong! -- so that doesn't necessarily "prove" anything ...).

There's no "easy solution" for this.  Currently ... you just do the best you can with whatever information you have.  Ultimately it comes down to what the two players can agree on between them (or in the case of a tournament, the organiser acts as final arbiter, so at least the game stays consistent across all the participants).

IOW, I do not think that being TI, in and of itself, warrants continued vulnerability to the HM DRM. Rather, it is the continuation of a hazardous process that warrants this penalty.
Good analysis, Chris.  However, I don't quite agree with these conclusions, at least for pushing a Gun.  

To me, any act that results in TI status implies an ongoing effort; that's why the unit is tied up for the rest of the turn.  And thus, if the act is one that's vulnerable to Hazardous Movement, I would expect the HM to continue as long as the TI does.  NRBH to be sure, but I think we've established that Setting a DC and CS (which I think we all agree at this point do not have long-term HM involvement) also don't result in placement of TI.

To me this also ties in well with what I think the Labor status is supposed to be emulating, but I realize that part is a disputable reality argument.

As for the argument about pushing and then loading a gun, I agree you've found an apparent contradiction there with "under HM for the rest of the player turn".  But it would not be surprising if this rarely-performed combination of activities results in some rule inconsistencies that the designers never considered; I'd say those would be better dealt with by MMP making some actual rule changes, as opposed to just trying to figure out how to keep both existing rules whole by threading a fine needle.

title: Sff question regarding PTO
question:
The Japanese squad enters a HIP American squad. American squad first fires on Japanese squad at tpb fire per G.4 reducing them to a half squad and breaking them. Can the American squad subsequent first fire outside it's own hex with a now broken enemy unit in their own hex? And would the Japanese squad be eliminated for failure to rout?

Thx
author: whodat09
consensus_answer:
The Japanese squad enters a HIP American squad. American squad first fires on Japanese squad at tpb fire per G.4 reducing them to a half squad and breaking them. Can the American squad subsequent first fire outside it's own hex with a now broken enemy unit in their own hex? And would the Japanese squad be eliminated for failure to rout?

Thx

The restriction is found in  A7.212. The American squad cannot fire outside of it's own hex. 

The Japanese squad is allowed to rout out of the hex during the rout phase barring any other considerations resulting in failure to rout. See A10.51.

Indeed.
And if the Japanese spent 2MF to enter the American's Location (which is orobable) it can be fired upon as SFF (and FPF if it spent 3+ MF).

title: Khamsin LOS
question:
Hey gents, 
Thinking I will finally play Khamsin and wondering about how the Germans break platoon movement. Do they need to roll for light dust after each impulse? For each los check as well?
Thanks!!
Paul
author: Pjs4131
consensus_answer:
Hey gents, 
Thinking I will finally play Khamsin and wondering about how the Germans break platoon movement. Do they need to roll for light dust after each impulse? For each los check as well?
Thanks!!
Paul

Hi Paul - see F11.6:

11.6 DESERT LOW VISIBILITY (DLV): DLV is the term used to categorize Sun Blindness (11.61), Heat Haze (11.62-.621), and both Light and Moderate Dust (11.71-.72). A DLV Hindrance is treated exactly like a LV Hindrance (E3.1) unless stated otherwise. A DLV Hindrance does not apply (i.e., is not counted) when determining if LOS is blocked as per B.10.

You don't have to sweat the Light Dust roll when figuring out when you can break platoon movement.  Have fun!

title: Concealment placement during setup
question: Just when I think I have it, I don't.  In Commando Schenke the Russians set up first out of sight of Germans and have OB designated ? counter to put on.  Now the German sets up (I assuming out of sight of opponent) on board.  Does he get to place ? counters on his units in concealment terrain that are out of LOS before Russian player gets to look at the board?
author: The Old Man
consensus_answer:
I thought units under ? counters are not considered, "known enemy units" and therefore do not prevent ? counter gain.

You are correct that they are not "known enemy units".  However, "known" is not a requirement for preventing concealment gain.

It's worth spending a little time studying the Concealment Gain/Loss Table.  It will tell you many things that the text of the rules barely mention (or sometimes don't even mention at all).

The core rule to remember is that "unbroken unit" is sufficient to DENY GAIN, but "Good Order" is required to CAUSE LOSS.  Thus dummies can stop you from becoming concealed, but your opponent has to reveal a real unit to make you lose concealment that you already have.

The other important thing to remember is to note the difference between "Concealment Terrain" and all other types of terrain.  Just because a hex has positive TEM does not make it "Concealment Terrain" (e.g., graveyards).  Only the terrain types listed in red on the Terrain Chart are Concealment Terrain.

Note also the different effects of long range (> 16 hexes).  Your infantry can become concealed at long ranges even if someone has LOS to them.  They can also move without losing concealment if the only LOS to them is long-range.

Emplaced Guns (and their crews) have their own special rules about concealment loss, of course.  Vehicles, in general, don't keep concealment very easily, and are not that good at getting it either.  It is often not even worth the effort of rolling to see if a vehicle gets concealed when it's out of LOS -- if it's not in Concealment Terrain, it will lose the concealment as soon as an enemy unit has LOS to it (at any range).  Also remember that (with a very few unusual exceptions) PRC keep or lose concealment per their vehicle.

Finally, probably the number one concealment rule most frequently played incorrectly: if you are provided with "?" counters in your OB, these counters can ONLY be placed in Concealment Terrain -- regardless of whether they are being used to conceal a real unit, or being used to create a dummy stack.  Again, just having positive TEM, or being completely out of enemy LOS is not good enough: it MUST be Concealment Terrain.  Remember that this rule ONLY APPLIES to "?" counters supplied in the OB.

title: Regarding the CA rules
question:
Before formulating a question to MMP regarding the following rules problem I wanted to hear your opinions.

Rule C3.2 defines the Covered Arc (CA). In the rules text it is obvious that the hex of the vehicle (or gun) is not included in the CA. This is also consistent with legacy rules from the Squad Leader system (SL 29.4) and ASLSK#2 and ASLSK#3 rules.

There is however an example text under the illustration in C3.2 that is ambiguous (should it be regarded as an exception rather than an example?). Added to this there is a Q/A in J1 that clearly states that a gun's own hex IS included in the CA.

Note that several other rules will depend on how CA is defined. Here are a few:
A11.62
C5.51
D3.1, 3.11 and 3.12
D1.81 (with errata in J7) and 1.82
author: Mattias
consensus_answer:
The C3.2 example is not ambiguous; it's clear the Gun's own hex includes the CA. The example also clarifies that during the Movement Phase, a vehicle enters the CA only through the two relevant hexsides. 

There is nothing in the rules stating that the text of an example is not part of the alphanumeric rule  -- as far as I am aware. Cite me a rule number that states that! :) I would concur that it's not good form for an important rule interpretation to be found in an example; but it all fairness, the example is embedded into the structure of C3.2. 

It's the incorrect assumption that such text is not part of the rules that leads to what appears to be a rules problem. 

A11.62 is not relevant to defining CA because E.2 applies to the definition of the CA being formed by the higher alpha-numeric rule C3.2 and there is no specific exception to C3.2 in A11.62.

C5.52 supports the example in C3.2 by referring to C3.2 as the fundamental rule for CA.

D3.1 referes to C3.2 as defining CA.

D1.81 and 1.82 refer to special conditions of covered arc known as VCA and TCA, which are still defined under the auspices of C3.2; that is, no exceptions to C3.2 are stipulated or overwritten by these rules.

Lets say you have a Sherman in Melee w/a German 4-6-8.  Rules say the 468 is held in Melee but a mobile vehicle is never "held" in melee.  Does that mean the Sherman can TPBF the 468 in Prep or Defensive Fire while the 468 needs to wait for CC??

The two rules sections that apply to your questions are:

1. From A11.15: "11.15 MELEE:...Infantry are also held in Melee by enemy Cavalry, cyclists, and non-Abandoned, Stopped, "unbroken" (12.1) vehicles."

2. From A11.7: "11.7 VEHICLE WITHDRAWAL FROM CC: A vehicle is never held in Melee and, if Mobile, may move out of a CC Location normally in its MPh. An Immobile vehicle or a vehicle which opts to stay in a Location where it started its turn with Known armed enemy units may only fire at enemy units in that Location (7.212) and must use To Hit Case E for any ordnance attacks. Even though a vehicle cannot be held in Melee, a non-Abandoned, "unbroken" (12.1) vehicle holds all Known enemy Infantry occupying the same Location after a CCPh in Melee as long as it remains in the Location (unless in-Motion/Non-Stopped."

So, if the Sherman is:

a. non-Abandoned
b. "unbroken" (12.1)
c. and NOT in-Motion/Non-Stopped

it will hold the 468 in Melee.

If any of either a, b, or c apply, then the 468 is not held in Melee, but rather is marked with a CC counter.

In either case for the 468, Melee or CC, the Sherman is free to fire TPBF at the 468.

The 468 would be free to fire back at the Sherman if it is only marked with a CC counter. If in Melee, the 468 is limited to attacking the Sherman in the CCPh, unless for some reason the Sherman goes into Motion, in which case it is no longer held in Melee.

Bill

title: Rally in openground
question:
Good evening,

*Can broken unit make rally in openground? 
*Can broken unit make rally in openground and LOS and Normal range of known enemy unit?

Thanks in advance :)
author: Anatoly45100
consensus_answer:
Is a broken unit in a building that previously lost DM put back under DM when a flame in it's hex becomes a blaze?
I think so yes, since only DM units can rout, IIRC.

ASOP, Step 6.11B
"...Place DM counter on each non-DM unit/stack that must rout (A10.62)."
We went with the section in B25.4 that says that units which are unable to voluntarily break (which would include already broken units)may move during their rout phase into an accessible location just as if withdrawing from melee. 

Although it seemed odd to have a broken unit move at all without going back under DM. The ASOP you quoted certainly overrides when combined with A10.4 which says that broken units cannot move in any way except to rout or to withdraw from CC. 

So the broken unit must "leave" the blaze location but he can only leave by routing per A10.4 and the ASOP says that units that must rout go back under DM. Problem solved :) Though a bit convoluted.

title: First Rising Sun game, a few questions.
question:
My gaming associate and I played our first game of Rising Sun the other day and had a few questions. 

1. Paths. So this seems like an easy one but the scenario stated that all roads were to be treated as paths. The only real difference between roads and paths is line of sight, yes? For example you could shoot down a road but due to the winding nature of a path that doesn't apply. And is it possible to move into a path hex but remain in the woods/jungle along the path and not lose TEM?

2. Berserk units. We had a Japanese squad go berserk under FPF from the Marines. So the Japanese unit gains additional MF, can move into the occupied hex in the Mph, then TPBF and engage in H2H? 

3. And finally, mortar placement in the PTO. We were playing Cibik's Ridge, and had a hell of a time trying to figure out where to place our mortars. Since dense jungle prohibits mortar fire, even on paths, and the jungle blocks line of sight, how do you work around the mortar's minimum firing range? My Japanese light mortars had some success in pinning Marines but they were fired from practically point blank in the open. My opponent couldn't figure out where to place his Marine mortars so they practically went to waste.
author: The Old Man
consensus_answer:
My gaming associate and I played our first game of Rising Sun the other day and had a few questions. 

1. Paths. So this seems like an easy one but the scenario stated that all roads were to be treated as paths. The only real difference between roads and paths is line of sight, yes? For example you could shoot down a road but due to the winding nature of a path that doesn't apply.
You still thread LOS as normal.  If the art allows the shot, the LOS is good, even though the LOS is along a Path.  Use of Path movement rate incurs no FFMO risk, though, because the zero-TEM Path portion is not Open Ground.  G.1.

EDIT:  No, the Path art in Dense Jungle is in fact Jungle terrain (and TEM) as per application of B13.6.  As Dense Jungle is Inherent terrain, I suppose you may not trace LOS through it's Path art any more than you could trace LOS along an Open-Ground land hexside.  (Re Light Jungle, I think you could trace LOS down a Path, though.)

2nd EDIT:  It occurred to me later that there can be no LOS down a Path at all.  B13.6 says Path art is Woods (usually).  A Woods is an LOS obstacle.  So, no down-Path LOS, and I was twice wrong today.  Sorry for leading any reader down a bad Path, earlier.

And is it possible to move into a path hex but remain in the woods/jungle along the path and not lose TEM?
Versus D1F, if not moving at the Path rate, then the non-Path TEM would apply.

2. Berserk units. We had a Japanese squad go berserk under FPF from the Marines. So the Japanese unit gains additional MF, can move into the occupied hex in the Mph, then TPBF and engage in H2H?
Correct.

3. And finally, mortar placement in the PTO. We were playing Cibik's Ridge, and had a hell of a time trying to figure out where to place our mortars. Since dense jungle prohibits mortar fire, even on paths, and the jungle blocks line of sight, how do you work around the mortar's minimum firing range? My Japanese light mortars had some success in pinning Marines but they were fired from practically point blank in the open. My opponent couldn't figure out where to place his Marine mortars so they practically went to waste. 

Looks like a tough problem.  Note that use of C9.31 Spotted Fire would effectively shave one hex off MTR Minimum Range.  The penalty is offset a bit by the SSR-granted Bore Sighting for eligible US weapons.  HTH.

title: Leaving a hex in VBM crosses a wall/hedge?
question:
THE BOTTOM LINE: If a vehicle is in VBM and enters a new hex, does it go through the vertex and always cross a wall/hedge that goes to the vertex?

Example: on board 3, a vehicle is bypassing the building in hex T4. The bypass is parallel to the T3/T4 hexside, but the vehicle is in hex T4.

The vehicle moves into hex U4. The T4/U4 hexside is clear. However, the T3/U4 hexside has a wall.

Does the vehicle incur the movement costs for crossing the wall? Even though the hexes it moved through do not share a wall terrain feature?

I've always assumed the vehicle will pay the wall costs. But I don't see anything in the rulebook saying that is the case. There are lots of words in the rulebook that describe the effect when going into a hex in bypass, but not a lot about leaving the hex.

A rules reference would be appreciated.

Thanks.
author: GS in KS
consensus_answer:
Remember that a unit in bypass is not really on the hexside, it's inside the hex being bypassed, though it is not inside the obstacle (building or woods). So having a wall on a vertex is not enough to pay its cost. It must be on the hexhexside being crossed.

Edit:evil typo

title: Residual Fire and Snipers
question:

We did not see anything indicating it did not and played it as such, but wanted to check.
author: keethrax
consensus_answer:
Short answer is yes.

Snipers activate in PFPh, MPh, DFPh and AFPh on TH, MC, TC, non-OBA IFT or entrenching DRs. (A14.1)

title: Casualty reduction and CVP
question:
Greetings my brothers in arms,

We are playing Revenge at Kastelli recently. Greek player has to achieved 20 victory points by eliminating enemy units (CVP). I have two questions.

*What happens, when Greek player causes casualty reduction to enemy squad? Can he counts "eliminated" HS to his CVP? I think he can.

*What happens, when this casualty reduction is caused by "Fate" (DR12 on rally). Can Greeks counts "eliminated" HS to their CVP?

Thanks in advance
author: Anatoly45100
consensus_answer:
The Greek player gets CVP for both instances. See below:

26.221 A player receives CVP equal to the VP value for all enemy units/equipment that are eliminated. Units/equipment that leave the map­ board are considered eliminated for purposes of CVP [EXC: ifunder Re­ call, Guards escorting prisoners (2053), Paratroops/Gliders landing off­ board, or if satisfying Victory Conditions or a SSR by such exit]. CVP are not awarded for units/equipment which are merely broken. wounded, disrupted, malfunctioned. shocked or Immobile, nor for a disabled MA.

title: Continuous Bypass
question:
Hi,

Got a bit puzzled by the bypass rule for infantry and hoping you could help out. Could the 7-4-7 in 3AA6 bypass both woods hexes (3AA7-3AA8) and reach 3AA9 using 3 MF? Would seem logical but can't find any support in the RB. What say you?

Thanks! /M
author: aluco
consensus_answer:
Yes it can. There are two contiguous hexsides in AA7 and AA8 each, which is normal 1MF bypass. (If for example the unit would start movement from BB6 and bypass AA7 and AA8 to AA9, it would have to pay 2MFs for AA7, because that bypass would exceed the two contiguous hexsides rule.)

A4.31...Bypass may consist of one or two contiguous unblocked hexsides of the building or woods hex being traversed. Bypass may exceed two contiguous unblocked hexsides per hex, but in so doing the Bypass cost for that hex is doubled.

title: Forcing rout
question:
I'll rephrase the questions in my previous thread, since I'm a little bit wiser now:

1. Does an adjacent, broken, known enemy unit force a broken unit to rout?

2. Does a pinned, known enemy unit which has one of your broken units in open ground within it's LOS and normal range force it to rout?

Regarding the first question, the rules seem to me to say no, but there's a Q&A from rule 10.5 about what happens when to broken units are adjacent to each other, and whether or not the defender has to rout after the attacker routs away first. If broken units don't force routs, this shouldn't even be a question.

Regarding the second question, the rules in 10.5 (routing) and 10.62 (DM) refer to 10.532 (interdictor) when they mention normal range. Also, the starter kit rules state clearly that it is units which could interdict your broken unit which force it to rout, and a pinned unit (or a unit with any other halving or positive DRM) can't interdict.

I think the answer is 'no' to both questions, but the rules seem a bit vague on the second question. It should be stated clearly in 10.5 and 10.62 that units must be able to interdict to force non-adjacent units to rout, or to give them DM. This is not stated clearly in the flowchart on routing I found on the Texas-ASL site either. A possible 'interdictor' is more than an unbroken enemy unit which has your unit in LOS and normal range. If the answer is 'yes' to the second question, then the flowchart is very clear.
author: oivind22
consensus_answer:
checking the rules A10.5;
"a broken unit cannot remain in an open ground hex within LOS and normal range of a known non-melee enemy unit, nor may it END its routphase adjacent to a known enemy unit that is both unbroken and armed"

so, for open ground purposes a "known enemy unit" is sufficient to force it to rout (so even broken units and pinned units can force it to rout).
while for "adjacent" purposes, it must be a known,unbroken armed unit that would cause failure to rout" (ending the rout phase adjacent to a broken or unarmed unit does not cause failure to rout)
broken units of both sides can remain adjacent to each other as long as they are both not in open ground.

to be able to inderdict, a unit must be able to fire with at least 1FP into the routing unit's open ground hex at normal range ( with either inherent FP or any sw) and may not be affected by any form of area fire, regardless whether the unit has already exhausted all of its firing options for the turn.
given that a pinned unit halves its fire, it cannot interdict.

the reference to 10.532 is only to indicate how "normal range" is determined/defined, so while a pinned unit cannot interdict, it still has a normal range.

the rules often differentiate many situations as such; the possible threat of being fired upon is sufficient to affect enemy units (instill fear) in some way, while only actual fire will cause casualty losses. so a pinned unit can threaten broken units but doesnt cause actual losses

I agree with your interpretation. It's the starter kit rules which confuse me, since they say:

'During the RtPh a broken unit not in Melee may not end a RtPh adjacent to or in the same location as an unbroken Known Enemy Unit and may not remain in the same Open Ground location in the normal range and LOS of a Known Good Order enemy unit that would be able to interdict it if it were routing in that hex.'

But I guess that this could mean 'able to interdict unless prevented because of having halved FP or positive DRM'. After all, the rule says 'Good Order enemy unit', which should include pinned units, etc. I don't think there is supposed to be different interpretations of rules in starter kits and full ASL, it's just that full ASL has more rules.

I guess this means the Texas-ASL flowchart is correct, which is nice to know, since it gives a good summary in case I forget something again.

Not sure about this. What about this? If a pinned unit is the interdictor, then Open Ground is not invoked per 10.531. That rule is very specific how Open Ground is defined in this case. Even if the pinned unit is in normal range (by itself or with a SW), as far as the routing unit is concerned, it's not in open ground because the pinned unit cannot interdict.

I don't have time to check if the comprehensive routing example covers this situation.

title: Desperation morale and routing
question:
1. Does a broken unit become DM and forced to rout if it is in open ground within LOS and normal range of a broken, known enemy unit?

2. Does a broken unit become DM and forced to rout if it is adjacent to a broken, known enemy unit?

The rules seem to indicate this, so does the routing flowchart I found on Texas-ASL. But starter kit rules says that only unbroken enemy units force routs.

Edit: I think I have found the answer. First, both the flowchart and the rules seem to indicate that broken adjacent unit force broken units to get DM, but that only unbroken units force them to rout. Second, I guess 'within normal range' excludes broken units, since they don't have range, am I right?

To sum it up: Broken enemy units give DM to adjacent units and you can't rout towards them, but they never force routs. Correct?
author: oivind22
consensus_answer:
Here is a Tips From The Trenches, from ASL Journal 7, page 44.

A 1 FP attack with +1 DRM inflicts DM on a broken unit and is potentially eligible to inflict encirclement. Both rules (A10.62 and A7.7) require “enough FP (taking the possibility of Cowering into account) to possibly inflict at least a NMC.” On such an attack, an Original 3 DR could inflict a NMC. In contrast, a 2 FP attack with a +3 DRM could qualify only if the attacking unit were exempt from Cowering (e.g., Fanatic, Elite British, leader directed, etc.) since an Original 2 DR would Cower.

title: Fire Group and Cower
question:
Hi everybody,

Does the last sentence of A7.9,

“If a FG cowers, Random Selection is used to determine the unit(s) (and its SW) that becomes marked with a Prep or Final Fire marker.”

mean that the other units are not marked, and are free to fire again?

For example, Squad A with a ROF 1 LMG and Squad B fires during Prep Fire; rolls 1,1 and cowers. Squad B is Randomly Selected.

What is marked with Prep Fire?

Thanks,
John
author: Suulthanaur
consensus_answer:
Hi everybody,

For example, Squad A with a ROF 1 LMG and Squad B fires during Prep Fire; rolls 1,1 and cowers. Squad B is Randomly Selected.

What is marked with Prep Fire?

Thanks,
John

The correct answer during Prep Fire (PFPh) has been mentioned above and applies similarly to Defensive Fire (DFPh).

However, the multifarious affect of random selection and cowering is more pronounced during Defensive First Fire (MPh):

'A' is marked with a first fire counter (but not the LMG as yet since it may retain ROF). 

'B' is marked with Final Fire and if it also possessed an LMG, then that weapon  would also be marked with Final Fire. 

Residual firepower in the target hex would be reduced for the cowering (and likely even more if a conscript/green unit B was the cowered) and would not include the firepower of the LMG belonging to 'A' (unless ROF were forfeited).

After that, there are different ramifications for SFF, FPF, TBPF, etc. for each unit depending on marked fire status -- as the ATTACKER  continues his MPh.

title: Hidden unit attacks AFV in open ground
question:
Hi folks,

Let's say my hidden squad with an ATR advances into CC with an AFV in open ground after passing his PAATC. Is he eligible for an ambush? He loses concealment for advancing into open ground, but does that happen before or after the ambush opportunity?

Let's assume both the squad and the AFV survived CC. Now the squad is trapped in melee and can't use his ATR at any point during the turn unless the AFV chooses to leave the hex. The AFV is not trapped in melee, but must fire all its weapons at the squad, unless it wants to leave the hex and risk being shot in the rear by the ATR. Is this correct?

If the AFV fires its MGs using TPBF and eliminates the squad, can it then fire its MA outside the hex?

Thanks for your help!

              --David H.
author: hull00
consensus_answer:
Before he advances anywhere, your HIP unit is placed on board, concealed.  He then advances into an open ground hex in the LOS of an enemy unit (the tank!) which causes him to lose concealment (unless some other condition permits him to keep concealment, e.g., winter camouflage).  So with no concealment on either side, there is no possibility of ambush.

If the AFV is Stopped, then yes, the squad is held in Melee, and cannot use his ATR.  Note that the Melee condition is removed as soon as the vehicle is non-Stopped (not "leaves the hex").  However, with an ATR, the squad would probably be better off waiting until the AFV has left the hex before taking the shot (because of the Case E penalty).

You have the vehicle's choices essentially correct: it is not held in Melee, but cannot fire at any target outside of its own hex so long as the enemy unit is still there.  If it eliminates the squad with MG fire, then yes, the MA could fire at a different target.
