title: Questions about Air Support
question:
Hi folks,

I recently started a RB CG as the Russians and I've been reviewing the E7 Air Support rules, as I expect to be attacked by Stukas at some point during the campaign. After reading through the rules, I have (only) a few questions:

(1) Aerial LOS and strafing attacks

Let's say a Stuka lines up a strafing attack on a multi-hex factory. The first target hex is an external factory hex and the second hex is an internal factory hex. Both have units at ground level. Clearly, it can attack the first hex, but can it attack the second hex, which is in the blind zone created by the first hex? What about if the factory is roofless? What about if the second factory hex is also external, but behind the first factory hex in the direction of the attack? What if the factory is instead a multi-level building?

(2) Sighting TC vs. a dug-in tank

Is a dug-in tank considered a vehicular target for purposes of a sighting TC? Typically, armored cupolas are represented by smaller turret counters, so I was wondering if that might change the answer.

(3) Near miss vs. AFV

According to E7.421, a near-miss vs. an AFV results in the Basic TK# being halved, although cases A and B (C7.21-7.22) still apply. My question is: do cases A and B apply before or after the TK# is halved? According to C7.23, for a CH, the TK# is doubled before modifiers, so I was wondering if the near-miss case should be treated similarly. Unfortunately, the rule is unclear to me as written.

(4) Recall

As far as I can tell, the only way a Stuka gets recalled is on an original sighting TC of 12. Otherwise, once they enter, I'm stuck dealing with them until the end of the scenario unless I can shoot them down with AA fire (of which I have very little). Is that correct?

Thanks for your help getting me prepared for this challenging task!

              --David H.
author: hull00
consensus_answer:
(1) If the factory hex is roofed, then the Stuka has no LOS to the interior hex.  If the factory hex is roofless, then there is a LOS.

A building hex, factory or not, always creates a blind hex to an aircraft (roofless factory hexes being the EXC).  The only way I can think of for an aircraft to see two building hexes in a row would be if the first building hex has a small, offset depiction (or some other gap) that misses the hex centre dot.

(2) Dug-in tanks and armored cupolas use similar rules but are not identical.  The precise differences are described in Chapter D.  I'm going by memory, but a dug-in tank is still a tank, i.e., a vehicle (obviously, a non-moving one).

(3) You say it yourself -- the Basic TK# is halved.  You then apply modifiers normally to get to the Final TK#.

(4) NRBH, but that sounds about right.

title: Penalty for carrying MMG/HMG?
question:
Edit: This thread was based on a misunderstanding. I now know that a russian MMG is 5PP, not 2.

There's no penalty for an MMC carrying an MMG/HMG, right? Well, the HMG is 3PP (IIRC), so with a CX-counter they will lose MF. But MMG is never a problem, I think. You can rout with it, dash with it, etc., with no penalty, right? I'm asking because I know a Maxim MMG is a 140 lbs beast. I'm trying to picture someone dashing with it. :) Or dashing with an even heavier HMG.
author: oivind22
consensus_answer:
Here are the most useful rules paragraphs.

A4.4 PORTAGE: A SW may not move by itself; it must be carried or placed on a vehicle by Infantry/Cavalry at some cost to the latter's MF allotment. The various SW portage costs are listed on each SW counter in the form "#PP". Portage cost is assessed per item carried, not distance traveled; even if a unit carries a SW during only one MF expenditure before dropping it, that unit may not recoup the portage cost used for that SW for use in the remainder of its MPh. Otherwise, an unbroken Infantry unit can pick up and drop items at any point in its move provided it has sufficient MF to do so (subject to 4.431 & 4.44). No item can be portaged more than once per phase except as allowed by combined Infantry and vehicle portage within a single phase.

A4.42 INHERENT PORTAGE CAPACITY (IPC): A MMC has an IPC of three PP, and a SMC has an IPC of one PP.5 An Infantry unit loses one MF for each PP carried in excess of its IPC. A SMC may never portage more than two PP although one SMC can add its IPC to that of any one Good Order Infantry unit to increase the IPC of the latter, provided the two units start the phase together and move together as a stack. Otherwise, Infantry units may not combine their IPC. A broken unit may not portage anything in excess of its IPC (see 10.4) even if accompanied by a leader.

A4.52 PORTAGE EFFECTS: CX Infantry have an IPC one < normal. Each PP carried in excess of this reduced IPC is deducted directly from their increased MF allotment.

  	
EX: A squad carrying four PP has > a squad's IPC. However, if that squad Double Times, its MF allotment is increased to four (4 MF + 2 MF  - 2 MF [2 PP > CX IPC] = 4).

Here are the most useful rules paragraphs.

A4.4 PORTAGE: A SW may not move by itself; it must be carried or placed on a vehicle by Infantry/Cavalry at some cost to the latter's MF allotment. The various SW portage costs are listed on each SW counter in the form "#PP". Portage cost is assessed per item carried, not distance traveled; even if a unit carries a SW during only one MF expenditure before dropping it, that unit may not recoup the portage cost used for that SW for use in the remainder of its MPh. Otherwise, an unbroken Infantry unit can pick up and drop items at any point in its move provided it has sufficient MF to do so (subject to 4.431 & 4.44). No item can be portaged more than once per phase except as allowed by combined Infantry and vehicle portage within a single phase.

A4.42 INHERENT PORTAGE CAPACITY (IPC): A MMC has an IPC of three PP, and a SMC has an IPC of one PP.5 An Infantry unit loses one MF for each PP carried in excess of its IPC. A SMC may never portage more than two PP although one SMC can add its IPC to that of any one Good Order Infantry unit to increase the IPC of the latter, provided the two units start the phase together and move together as a stack. Otherwise, Infantry units may not combine their IPC. A broken unit may not portage anything in excess of its IPC (see 10.4) even if accompanied by a leader.

title: Casualty reduction vs broken squad
question:
1. When a squad suffers casualty reduction it must still take the morale check, right? It says 'other squads' in the rules, but then it also says 'any just-reduced HS'.

2. If the squad which suffers casualty reduction was already broken, then fails the morale check, is it then casualty reduced again, i.e. eliminated?
author: oivind22
consensus_answer:
1. When a squad suffers casualty reduction it must still take the morale check, right? It says 'other squads' in the rules, but then it also says 'any just-reduced HS'.

2. If the squad which suffers casualty reduction was already broken, then fails the morale check, is it then casualty reduced again, i.e. eliminated?

Correct.

Situation 1 - unbroken squad suffers a k/2.  It is immediately reduced to an unbroken half-squad, and that half-squad takes a 2MC.  If that half-squad breaks, it remains on-board under a DM counter.

Situation 2 - broken squad suffers a k/2.  It is immediately reduced to a broken half-squad, and that half-squad takes a 2MC.  If that half-squad breaks, it is removed from the map (breaking twice = eliminated).

Hope that helps!

title: rout in building
question: can a broken unit on the first floor of a building shared with unbroken enemies in same location (got there via humanwave) rout away to the ground floor without being taken prisoner?  does the CC token prevent rout?
author: usmint99
consensus_answer: Yes, as long as it is not under a Melee counter, a broken unit in the same hex as an enemy unit can rout away. See the line in the middle of A10.51 to the effect that a broken unit may never move ADJACENT to an enemy unit unless in doing so it is leaving that unit's location.

title: Having trouble with C.4 and Case K
question:
C.4 is the paragraph about ORDNANCE AREA FIRE.  It says OAF "never halves the FP effects of any hit.  Instead any shot affected by provision of Area Fire caused by the target's status uses Case K..."

OK, so I understand it's saying you use K only if the Area Fire is caused by something like the target being concealed, but when the hit is resolved you don't half it.

Now take a mortar which always uses Area Fire.  So am I right that if you're shooting at, let's say, infantry in a building or out in the open you don't use Case K, but you still half the FP on the IFT?  Now if that unit is under a Concealment counter you'd use Case K and half the FP on the IFT?
author: The Old Man
consensus_answer:
Correct. The key is Area Target Type is different from Area Fire.

Any fire using Area Target Type, which mortars must do, will have its FP halved. Firing against a Concealed unit forces Area Fire, which in this case applies Case K.

title: Subsequent first fire and SW that kept ROF
question:
I have been playing this game for three years, but after a game today I am wondering if I have been playing it wrong.

I have a 4-6-7 squad with a 3-8 LMG, and I first fire with LMG and inherent FP at a moving unit. The LMG keeps ROF, the squad is marked with a First Fire counter.

(a) If the LMG now fires alone at another moving unit, without the squad's inherent firepower, is that First Fire (because it kept ROF) or Subsequent First Fire (because the owning Squad is marked with a First Fire counter, and so the LMG cannot fire an moving units further away than the nearest Known enemy unit, and also means the LMG and squad will be marked Final Fire after this shot)?

(b) If, instead, the LMG and squad fire together at another moving unit during the same MPh, this is Subsequent First Fire for the squad. Assuming, say, range 2 hexes, what is the firepower of this shot? Is it 3+4/2=5 or (3+4)/2=3.5. In this case, can I get ROF again if I roll 1 on the coloured die?

replies.body:
Hi Russ!

If you decide to keep the ROF you mark the squad First Fire and you can fire the SW ONLY ALONE as First Fire again as long as it retains ROF. Of course always on further MFs expenditures.
If you don't want to keep ROF, you mark BOTH the squad and the SW as First Fire and subsequent fires are SFF/FPF.
When you shoot as SFF/FPF you MUST fire the SW you used in First Fire(IIRC) and you fire as Area Fire (FP/2...3.5 in your ex).
In SFF/FPF SWs can't retain ROF.

So here is the situation...

LMG -> No status (retained ROF)

1. Fire just the LMG.  You fire on the 2FP (1FP at long range) column.  If you retain ROF, there is no change.  If you roll doubles both the squad and LMG are marked Final Fire.
2. Fire just the squad.  You fire on the 2FP (1FP at long range) column.  Regardless of the outcome the entire stack, including the LMG, is marked Final Fire.
3. Fire both the squad and LMG.  You fire on the 4FP column (2FP at long range) and regardless of outcome both the squad and LMG are marked Final Fire.

title: AFV Overrun order of resolution -- Terrain Effects vs. First Fire
question:
An AFV enters a multi-story wood building to overrun an SS squad. The AFV makes a bog check and rolls a 1 on the colored die, converting the wood building to rubble, and automatically eliminating the squad.

Question: does the squad get a First Fire opportunity (to fire a PF) before it is eliminated?

(1) Overrun flowchart -- Terrain Effects box appears before the Defensive Fire box, indicating that the Bog Check and Rubble effects should be resolved first.
(2) Overrun flowchart -- AFV overrun is still resolved even if Defensive Fire destroys the tank, implying that a unit destroyed in a previous step can still take actions in a subsequent step. Should this also apply to (1)?
(3) Advanced Sequence of Play -- Defensive Fire can take place during actions including Bog Checks

The evidence above does not provide a clear answer to this question. Is there an unambiguous answer to this question somewhere in the rules?

- then OVR

title: Case B & C gives me a headache
question:
I can't get a handle on how or why the Firer-based hit determination DRM Case B & C works. 

CASE B; FIRE IN AFPh: All ordinance which did not enter their current hex during that Player Turn (Only during the MPH?) and are not using OP fire are subject to Case B.

So if you didn't move during the MPH there's a penalty?  Why?

CASE C; BOUNDING FIRER: A vehicle which HAS (Emphasis mine) entered a new hex during its MPH but does not fire until its AFPh is using Bounding Fire and always uses Case C DRM (i.e. it must add the +2 DRM of Case B to the...(Is this an example or an addition?) applicable Gun Type DRM of Case C) as Bounding Fire Fire for shot it takes.

Can you see why I find all this confusing?  One thing it seems to say is B is one case, but if you're C you're also B even though the conditions of having moved is different.

Can anyone make sense of this for me?
author: The Old Man
consensus_answer:
If they haven't moved that turn and they have an op fire token on them neither B nor C apply.

D3.3 Vehicles cannot opportunity fire. they can bounding fire.

Yes it is confusing, and annoying, but in the end it makes sense.

Case B. If your vehicle has not moved or fired that turn, but all of a sudden you want to fire in the AFPh, that is +2 TH. Why is there a penalty? Because other moving friendly units may have forced the enemy to expose themselves, but you don't have as much time to fire if you had prep fire. 

Case C. hope this helps.

title: Off boared artillery advanced squad leader
question: It seems to me that it is better to call down OBA during the Def Phase VS the Prep phase. If done in the Prep phase, enemy has a chance to move during their own movement phase. If called down during Def Phase, the FFE1 is resolved during the enemy prep phase and no chance of movement. Correct?
author: ostwind
consensus_answer:
Prep Fire Phase OBA is best time to use SMOKE to significantly hinder the enemy fire for two fire phases and moderately so for another two (second ATTACKER game turn). This allows attacking troops to close with a dangerous enemy position. Not only that, the FFE can be cancelled in the next ATTACKER fire phase to make ready for a new FFE draw, with the possibility to land elsewhere one phase sooner. 

Often anything less than 120mm isn't going to much affect enemy in buildings or entrenchments as much as the attacker would like with a standard FFE, so better is use of SMOKE.

Def Fire Phase OBA is not as effective for laying a SMOKE. To get decent smoke, such an FFE is better to land in the Prep Fire Phase. 

So, as you say, DFPh is a better time to torch FFE to disrupt an enemy concentration for a back to back pounding in DF and Prep. Could be a good time to bring down Rocket FFE for maximum pounding (hoping it won't drift on top of your own stacks!)

Harassing Fire is mentioned above. Harassing Fire OBA is good to lay down in Prep, in order to block enemy attacker movement -- on their turn -- through and within the zone of effect, as they try to come to grips with the defender. This won't work as well if used in the Prep fire phase, although there will be an FFE C lurking around anyway if Harassing Fire is brought down then. However, if the Attacker has good cover on the way in, Harassing fire can be a waste of black card.

Hovering SR is a good tactic as suggested. esp with a bad ammo card hand and/or scarce ammo; once the atty comes down, could be tough to get that next black cbit draw.

I'm sure there are more ideas. Unmentioned are the best times to lay down barrages. I would think Prep to lay down a nice smokescreen.

So much depends on the circumstances.  There are a few reasons why it makes sense to call down OBA FFE:1 during the Prep Fire Phase.  Here are a few:

-- "Recon By Fire."  You just never know if there are any HIP units that you can possibly uncover if they break under OBA.  If you are worried about that flank full of concealment terrain that you are going to move over open ground in front of, it might make sense.  If you positively need every MMC to move on a particular turn, at least you get some sort of base of fire.  

-- "The Grey Blanket."  If you want even more hindrances out there to cover your move, using OBA to bring down some SMOKE may be the way to do it (when available).  Of course, you may not always want it on top of your movement path (eats up MP/MF that way), but using it to screen moves by calling it down in front of those enemy potential DFFers is a desired method at times.

-- "The White Blanket."  Think about combining some marvelous firepower effects with obscuration by firing OBA WP (when available). 

-- "A Bigger Bloom."  Harassing Fire is usually somehting you want to go down as an FFE:1 on the enemy turn to cause maneuver dilemmas for him.  But there are times when you can use the hindrances of the increased FFE area productively to hinder your enemy's Defensive fire opportunities.  Don't count it out!

Broadly. You usually want to hit a position with an FFE:1 and FFE:2 before the targeted units have an opportunity to move, so make the AR in your PFPh, hope for an accurate SR, then flip to FFE:1 at the end of the next DFPh and hit them again in your PFPh.

Two problems, though: the enemy may advance from a location receiving OBA, and accuracy / los to SR my cause difficulties. As of course can the contact roll.

-- "A Bigger Bloom."  Harassing Fire is usually somehting you want to go down as an FFE:1 on the enemy turn to cause maneuver dilemmas for him.  But there are times when you can use the hindrances of the increased FFE area productively to hinder your enemy's Defensive fire opportunities.

    

Harassing fire does not create a LOS hindrance.

A good tactic is to make the SR hover over enemy positions without converting it into a FFE. 
It can scare him enough to shift positions.

As OBA is a two sequence system most of the time (place SR on one game turn,call down fire on the next one) I would relativise the importance of the phase when you place the SR or FFE.

A good tactic is to make the SR hover over enemy positions without converting it into a FFE. 
It can scare him enough to shift positions.

Especially in a campaign game where you may be able to keep the OBA mission if you don't convert to FFE. :)

Thank you for all the answers. I thought I was reading the rules wrong. The Double pounding was my concern and the lack of the enemy being able to move away or at least move some.
Bob

title: Spotting Round LOS
question: Hey, Can an observer see a SR if it lands in a water obstacle (river)?
author: Pjs4131
consensus_answer:
Hey, Can an observer see a SR if it lands in a water obstacle (river)?
I was practicing with Landing Craft and Beach Landings recently and, as far as I could work out, SR and the rest of the OBA process works pretty much the same in water as it does on land. 

Which is a bit of a logic fail since a Spotting Round falling a couple hundred meters out in the ocean is hardly going to put up any visible smoke or blast. 

One other inconsistency regarding OBA in water rules is that OBA against boats and assault craft in rivers per chapter E hits for half FP while OBA against Landing Craft in the ocean per chapter G hits for full FP.

One other inconsistency regarding OBA in water rules is that OBA against boats and assault craft in rivers per chapter E hits for half FP while OBA against Landing Craft in the ocean per chapter G hits for full FP. 

Which one was written later?

title: Cloaking loss at night

Our question is whether a cloaked group moving into an illuminated hex loses cloaking even though the enemy has no LOS into the hex.

title: Reinforcement set up
question: Do reinforcements brought in off board during rally phase need to be set up exactly where they are entering in from for the movement phase to come or can you choose whichever hex to enter from during movement phase (but within restrictions of the scenario rules of course)?
author: usmint99
consensus_answer:
All good ASLers read the ASOP every day as part of breakfast, otherwise we forget what we're supposed to do next, "hmmm...is it pants on one leg at a time or am I supposed to just jump right in with both legs. And is it underwear before pants...and what about this damned pair of socks...or is it DTO/PTO and I can go with sandals?"

replies.body:
Without reading the actual verbiage, we've always played that they need to be positioned during the RPh. Set up is set up.

EDIT: you are allowed to spend MF/MP points off board during the MPh so long as, as you note, you enter in the allowable entry hexes.

Do reinforcements brought in off board during rally phase need to be set up exactly where they are entering in from for the movement phase to come or can you choose whichever hex to enter from during movement phase (but within restrictions of the scenario rules of course)?

title: Is Wreck/Vehicle Hindrance cumulative with other terrain Hindrances?
question:
Sorry if this is a stupid question, but I've tried reading the rules and it's just not making sense to me at the moment.

I have a Vehicle in an Orchard hex.  I'm trying to fire past it right down the hex spine to another hex.  Is the total TEM from this hex +1 or +2?

Thanks for any help.
author: wsmithjr
consensus_answer:
Sorry if this is a stupid question, but I've tried reading the rules and it's just not making sense to me at the moment.

I have a Vehicle in an Orchard hex.  I'm trying to fire past it right down the hex spine to another hex.  Is the total TEM from this hex +1 or +2?

Depends. Refer D9.4.

Yes, it depends, Not just on D9.4 but also on D9.3. 

D9.3 is often overlooked; basically it says that a vehicle that moved this turn does not create a hindrance until after the AFPh. 

Tactically it means you can't move vehicles and use them to create on-the-fly hindrance for other moving units or create hindrance for your opponents DFPh shots.

title: Human Wave example in Rule Book: Understanding Range
question:
I have a question on the Human Wave example in the rule book (page A53, my version ©2014). I’m having trouble understanding Range. 

The example says that the “units that entered N1 and O2 are marked with a Range counter since they increased the range to the HW alternate Hex Grain…” It looks to me that after they move they stayed the same range from the HW alternate Hex Grain of P1-P2-PO3-O4 – the unit in P1 moving to O2 is one hex away and staying one hex away from the HW alternate Hex Grain of P1-P2-PO3-O4, and the unit in O1 moving to N1 is two hexes away and remaining 2 hexes away. To my eyes, the unit in R2 moving to Q5 is in the same Range from the HW alternate Hex Grain as the unit in P1, but it doesn’t get marked. 

Any help grasping Range?
author: kaufmad
consensus_answer:
In the example given the Alternate Hex Grain selected is P1-P2-O3-O4.

The unit that starts out in P1 is 0(zero) hexes off the Alternate Hex Grain since it is sitting in P1 which partly makes up the Hex Grain. When he moves to O2 he increased his range from the Hex Grain to 1. So he is marked with a Range Counter.

Similarly the unit starting in O1 began the human wave 1 hex off the Alternate hex grain since O1 is one hex away from P1. When he moved to N1 he increased his range to 2 so he is marked with Range Counter. 

Your confusion seems to be from imagining that the Alternate Hex Grain is made up partly of the hexspines between hexes. But it's not. It is a series of four full hexes in this example.

Can I offer an academic, non-player opinion, (I haven’t yet learned and played this one.), based on my reading of the rules?

According to 8.1, a unit can be fired on more than once by a weapon with a multiple ROF, or by a different unit when it spends additional mfs in the same Location–but not twice by the same non-multiple-ROF weapon.

Residual fire can only attack a unit once in a location, unless, as we have agreed, the strength of the RFP is increased or the unit enters a less-protective environment, in which  case the unit can be attacked again. (A8.22)

So, yes, this unit would only be attacked once by the RFP (Although I think it’s irrelevant, I note that the new (small-l) location that is the location of the RFP attack is a more protective environment.), but it would be coming from the same weapon that fired on it in the first place, meaning it would be attacked twice by that same weapon.

title: Defensive First Fire into Melee
question:
I looked about for a similar question but didn't turn one up. Apologies if this is a repeat.

I had the situation below tonight. It's the German MPh and the 4-6-7 in P5 (Stone Bldg) is moved into the Melee in Q6 (Stone Bldg). Is it correct that the US units and SW in U6 can Defensive First Fire at the 4-6-7 (which is expending MP) upon entering Q6, and that Fire only affects the moving 4-6-7?

Thanks for any and all help here!
author: zaccardi
consensus_answer:
Hi Steve,

If memory serves me correctly (it's been years since I've played), the only way you could move that unit into the Melee hex during the MPh is if all enemy units in the hex are concealed. (A4.14: "Infantry may not move into the same Location containing an unconcealed enemy unit during the MPh...")

If that's the case then yes, you can fire at the unit as DFF; the fire attack would only affect the moving unit (A8.1: "Defensive First Fire attacks affect only the moving unit/stack regardless of other units that occupy the same or intervening hexes at the instant of the attack.")

(EDIT:  I'm wrong!  If the German squad attempted to move into the Melee hex containing Concealed enemies, an enemy unit would be forced to drop concealment and the German squad would be forced to go back into the hex it was in before moving into the Melee (A12.15))

replies.body: You can't use the MPh to enter an enemy-occupied hex unless you're doing something like overrunning a SMC or you're Berserk.  You have to wait for the Advance phase.

title: Weighing in...
question:
I only just realised that everything other than vehicles/wrecks (EX: passenger, SW and Guns) are "weightless" in this game. The FlaK 18 is Wikipedia'd at 7.4 tonnes! And a PaK40, 1.4 t. Those likely ignore ammo. You've got figure that a squad is roughly 10 x 75 kg = 0.75 t. Granted, the B6.42 is calculated in jumps of 5 t over 10 t limit, but you have to figure it'll push things over for some vehicles, especially with overstacking/wrecks.

Also, the Index and B6.42's entry list neither "Weight" nor "WGT", which is only defined in the key on page H11.

Now, having typed that, I have never, ever had to make a B6.42 DR. 

Nev-er, ev-er. 

Well...maybe once...maybe.
author: WBRP
consensus_answer:
Size and weight of support weapons, ordnance, and vehicles is factored throughout the rules. The PP ranking for s/w accounts for the weight as well as other factors in moving and prepping the weapon to fire. For ordnance, the QSU feature and Manhandling also have reflect to some degree the weight. 

Finally (to be complete :)), the ground pressure rules are directly related to the weight of the vehicle. Also the movement number with its color or the target size reflect some aspects of weight.

I suspect the OP is regarding the fact that the bridge and ice collapsing rules ignore the weight of personnel, ammo and guns and only factor in vehicle weights.

title: Advance vs. Difficult Terrain
question:
Hi, I don't know if this topic has been discussed already, but I find this rule might bring to absurd situations.
Consider this example: a squad moves in Open Ground for four hexes during its MPh. Then on its APh it advances in a bamboo hex one level higher.
The squad becomes CX.
Now, assume the squand were already at the bottom of the hill, adjacent to the bamboo hex one level higher, at the start of its MPh. It may claim Minimum Move and reach that hex, becoming CX and Pinned in the process. Thus, no Advance available.
Comparing the two examples, I have in the first case a squad that moves 4 hexes plus one "difficult" hex (combining MPh and APh) and becomes "only" CX.
In the second case the same unit can move in its whole turn only the same "difficult" hex, and becomes CX and also Pinned!
Don't you think, too, there's something wrong with that?
Don't you think rule A4.72 should be rewritten someway?
Thanks for you thoughts!!

I don't really find this to be absurd at all. In both examples, once you climbed up the hill through the bamboo you were so exhausted you were essentially done for the turn. The fact that, in one example, you had an easy walk on the flat before the exhausting bamboo does not change the fact that the uphill bamboo is totally exhausting and ends your movement. 

In both cases you end your turn CX. In both cases you can't move further after going uphill into the bamboo. 

That being said, it's far the best to not get too bound up in making reality based arguments against the workings of your boardgames. It will never end and it will impact your enjoyment. It's all just a very rough abstraction designed to support challenging and fun game play.

title: Offboard AA against Gliders
question:
I'm playing through scenario 93 (Tavronitis Bridge) right now. One of the SSRs is that the British get 2 free AA shots against the incoming German gliders. I'm a bit confused with the AA-against-gliders rules, and want to make sure I'm doing things right.

First, I use the * column on the IFT. So, if the SSR says I get a "4 FP attack", would that mean I use the *4/30mm/2FP column? Or the *5/37mm/4FP column?

Next, the rules seem to indicate that I compare my result with the * number on the glider counter. But... the German glider has a * number of 1? I'm not entirely sure how I could possibly hit it? Or do I use the IFT result (e.g. KIA, K/, etc.)?

I'm confused. Thanks in advance for any guidance!
author: qpzil
consensus_answer:
IIRC, gliders are attacked using the *-row on the IFT, exactly as if they were unarmored trucks.

The number in the star in the glider counter is a positive DRM to this attack. 

So, in your scenario, you have two 4FP attacks. The number in the *-row of the IFT is 5, and since you have a +1DRM (due to the number in the star in the counter), gliders are damaged on a 4 and destroyed on a 3. Also, 4 and 5 force evasive action.

Hope this helps. Enjoy the scenario, it's really fun!

author: Angelsenior
consensus_answer:
-can a concealed leader apply his leader movement bonus to unconcealed units moving with him, or is he forced to loose his concealment to apply it?

Regarding the concealed leader, the question is whether the leader and unconcealed units are conducting a non-AM in the los of an unbroken enemy ground unit within 16 hexes. If so, concealment is lost. If not, then concealment is maintained.

Regarding your second question, see A8.312. The unit must fire, but it could be first fire or subsequent first fire.

title: Dare-death Squads: exception
question:
Hi, a have a question on Dare-Deah Squads.
I cannot fully grasp the Exception on G18.6 which states: "it cannot thusly goes berserk if......any marsh/swamp/cliff/unbridged-water-obstacle would prevent it from reaching that enemy unit's hex during that MPh...".
But if that is true, than that enemy unit is not within 8 MF of the Dare-death squad, that is the prerequisite for becoming berserk...
I tend to think that Exception is simply repeating something that's already been stated... can anyone tell me what I am missing?
Thanks!
author: federicost
consensus_answer:
"to have a professional tech writer review the rulebook"

Don't pin your hopes on a "tech writer". The ones I have met, they are paid based on volume, not accuracy. 

And before I get beat about the head and shoulders, I am sure there are some out there that have to met accuracy standards, but I have never met one. 

Also note, that I am apposed to someone trying to simplify the ASL rulebook.

McK

Well, since this would be an independent contractor situation, the metric of quality would be whatever MMP chose to use. The writing in the ASL rulebook can be improved for clarity without being simplified.  E.g., B23.22 -- it currently reads in part, "a multi-hex building which contains no stairwell symbol is considered a 1-1/2 level obstacle to LOS despite also having another vertical level in each hex besides the ground level in the form of a level 1 capacity." This could be re-written as "a multi-hex building which contains no stairwell symbol has ground level and level 1 locations in each hex of the building and is a 1-1/2 level obstacle to LOS."  The latter is 29 words versus 37 words, still completely accurate, and is clearer without any sacrifice of complexity in the rule, IMHO.

title: Encirclement
question:
If a good order infantry unit is on a second floor of a building that contains a stairwell and a good order enemy infantry unit is on the ground floor of the stairwell, are the unit on the second floor encircled, or is it required for them to be on the first floor?
I know the rules state something about having a clear path to the ground floor of the building.
author: grahamj
consensus_answer:
Yes they're encircled

7.72 UPPER LEVELS: Encirclement also applies to any non-heroic/non-berserk unit in an upper level building Location that cannot trace a path free of an unbroken, armed, unconcealed enemy unit/Blaze to ground level through Locations it could legally traverse if so inclined. This type of Encirclement is broken the instant such a path can be traced.

This type of Encirclement is broken the instant such a path can be traced.

An interesting edge case is that of a single-stairwell multiple hex building in which the stairwell hex is rubbled. I may be wrong but my reading of the rules is that pre-rubbling, if all ground level hexes of the building are occupied by KEUs a unit is encircled but if the stairwell is rubbled it is no longer encircled, despite having no means to exit :)

If the upper level unit has scaling ability (typically commandos) then it it not subject to upper level encirclement.
It depends.

You still need a path free of "unbroken, armed, unconcealed enemy unit/Blaze to ground level" - so if the enemy has such units in e.g., all ground level Locations of the building, even scaling-capabale units will be Encircled.

The second floor unit is encircled, as it cannot trace a path free of (unbroken, unconcealed, armed) enemy units to ground level. The unit at second level has to be able to move to the ground floor location, which is blocked by the KEU present at ground level.

Using 4-6 squads to do this is a Victory for the guy in the Upper level.

title: SPW 251/21
question: This halftrack (Veh. Note 66.1) has a puzzling note. Three TK DR are made on the MG column (TK 4) as opposed to the 20L table I would expect to use (TK 6). Why is this the case?
author: drmark64
consensus_answer:
This halftrack (Veh. Note 66.1) has a puzzling note. Three TK DR are made on the MG column (TK 4) as opposed to the 20L table I would expect to use (TK 6). Why is this the case?

Mark,

A proper answer to this question probably requires input from an armorer, but from the ultimate source, Wikipedia:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MG_151_cannon

Production of the MG 151 in its original 15 mm calibre format began in 1940. After combat evaluation of the 15 mm cartridge as the main armament of earlyMesserschmitt Bf 109F-2 fighters, the cannon was redesigned as the 20 mm MG 151/20 in 1941 to fire a 20 mm cartridge. Combat experience showed that a more powerful explosive shell was preferable to a higher projectile velocity. The MG 151/20 cartridge was created by expanding the neck of the cartridge to hold the larger explosive shell used in the MG FF cannon, and shortening the length of the cartridge case holding the longer 20 mm shell to match the overall length of the original 15 mm cartridge. These measures simplified conversion of the 15 mm to the 20 mm MG 151/20 simply by changing the barrel and making other small modifications. A disadvantage of the simplified conversion was reduction of projectile muzzle velocity from 850 metres per second (2,800 ft/s) for the 15 mm shell to 700 metres per second (2,300 ft/s) for the larger and heavier 20 mm shell. With an AP projectile the new 20mm cartridge could only penetrate around 10-12mm of armor at 300m and at 60 degrees, compared to 18mm penetration for its 15mm predecessor in the same conditions, but this was not seen as a significant limitation. The 20 mm version thus became the standard inboard cannon for the Bf 109F-4 series onwards. The 20 mm MG 151/20 offered more predictable trajectory, longer range and higher impact velocity than the 580 metres per second (1,900 ft/s) cartridge of the earlier MG FF cannon. The MG FF was retained for flexible, wing and upward firing Schräge Musik mounts to the end of the war.

Still, it would seem that even with a reduced penetration capability, maybe a TK=5 would be more appropriate as this is the 15mm/12.7 TK column.

Bill

title: Qs: ASLSK 2 ASL by 8 steps arcticle
question:
Hello guys!
I'm on a way from ASLSK to ASL with "Eight Steps to ASL" article and questions arised after several readings some special situation.

Q1: A7.7 If there are several MMC in a location under Encirclement counter, could they move to an adjucent hex and move back (one by one) to remove encirclement status, OR they must do it as stack (all together)? What does mean under "momentarily" here?

Q2: A9.223 It was written two time by me and didn't understand still.  CAN a MG crew cancel LOF (in any moment of current phase of turn) to make SFF/FPF for example, or MUST cancel LOF in the case of TPBF/CC-reaction Fire? OR these two cases don't exclude each other, but complement?
author: longbearder
consensus_answer:
1) As long as Encirclement exists, it applies to all units, including ones that just entered the Location. The only way the status goes away is for everyone to leave. So for your example, they would have to move as a stack. The fact that the hex was empty for the time of one hex(/Location) of movement is "momentarily".

2) I'm not sure on the first half (voluntarily cancelling the FL to SFF/FF), but I think so. The second part will obligate the manning infantry to cancel the FL so they can fire. (I don't have the time to look up a few related things right now. :P)

title: Walls, hedges, wall advantage--my head hurts
question:
I'm a SL player from the early 80s who got ASLSK#1 last year and futzed around with it a little.  I decided to go whole hog and a buddy and I have jumped into ASL feet first.  I'm a dedicated rules reader and have also watched a number of instructional videos from Russ, idjester and Joe Steadman.  But I'm struggling with B9.  I have trouble telling when a shot is blocked or simply a TEM and I really don't understand wall advantage.  

Can anyone point me to what they think is the best training--written or video--that might clear this up for me?
author: The Old Man
consensus_answer:
Note that when a positive inhex TEM is applicable, WA can be chosen or not (thus forfeiting the in hex TEM or not):
B9.31 The wall/hedge TEM is not cumulative with positive TEM of other terrain in that hex, although it is cumulative with LOS Hindrances and SMOKE. A target unit claiming WA (9.32) does not receive in-hex TEM [EXC: Runway (7.3); Air Bursts (9.34)], but receives wall/hedge TEM if applicable [EXC: it may elect instead to receive appropriate TEM for Emplacement or for a friendly AFV with which it shares WA (D9.3)].

But if in OG, WA is mandatory :
B9.323 MANDATORY WA: A unit unable to claim in-hex TEM of at least +1 must claim WA as soon as possible (even if having in-hex Hindrance), and cannot voluntarily forfeit it. Neither Emplacement, Gun-shield, Height Advantage, nor a friendly AFV with WA are considered to provide an in-hex TEM for this purpose. A "Wall Advan" counter is not necessary in this case, unless there is an enemy unit sharing one or more of the unit's wall/hedge hexsides.

No tutorials, but a couple of notes:

For TEM/blocking, Walls/Hedges are generally like other terrain. If you're in a hex with woods, you get TEM from the woods. If you're behind a hex with woods, the woods blocks LOS. If you're in a hex bordered by a wall/hedge, you get TEM from it (...if LOS crosses the appropriate hexside). If you're in a hex behind one bordered by a wall/hedge, it blocks LOS.

That last does operate differently, in that wall/hedges are considered half-level obstacles to LOS, so if you are above the level of the wall/hedge it no longer interferes with LOS (though it can still grant TEM).

Wall Advantage gets complicated, but the question it answers is simple: When enemy units are on opposite sides of the same wall/hedge, who has the TEM? Generally, this only comes up when enemy units are adjacent, and WA is generally assumed when that is not true.

title: Rules: How much of it is there?
question:
I understand the answer probably depends on how stuff is defined, but anyway...
How many pages of rules are there for this game? If you have all of it?

/A curious non-ASL:er
author: Tommy_la
consensus_answer:
I understand the answer probably depends on how stuff is defined, but anyway...
How many pages of rules are there for this game? If you have all of it?

/A curious non-ASL:er
Here is a quick rundown of the page counts for the chapters of the rule book. I don't have some of the chapters handy for the moment but will return and update this reply as soon as possible. All in all there are about 1000 pages.

Index, 34 pages
Chapter A, Basic Rules, 62 pages
Chapter B, Terrain, 44 pages
Chapter C, Ordnace, 26 pages
Chapter D, Vehicles, 26 pages
Chapter E, Miscellaneous, 28 pages
Chapter F, North Africa, 18 pages
Chapter G, Pacific, 50 pages
Chapter H, Vehicle and ordnance notes, about 200 pages
Chapter I, Campaign game - never published
Chapter J, Deluxe ASL, 2 pages
Chapter K, Training manual, 44 pages
Chapter L, Online ASL - never published
Chapter M, ASL Analysis - never published
Chapter N, Armory, over 150 pages
Chapter O, Red Barricades, 24 pages
Chapter P, Kampfgruppe Peiper, 24 pages
Chapter Q, Pegasus Bridge, 18 pages
Chapter R, A Bridge too Far, 22 pages
Chapter S, Solitaire, 34 pages
Chapter T, Tarawa, 22 pages
Chapter V, Valor of the Guards, 36 pages
Chapter Z, Other Campaigns, 86 pages
Chapter FB, Festung Budapest, 54 pages
Chapter dividers are 2-6 pages for each chapter

A few comments regarding each chapter:

Index: The index actually contains some definitions and rules that are important, but you don't need to memorise it.

Chapter A, Basic Rules: As with most of the core chapters you don't need to read all of chapter A to play ASL. Some rules are only applicable to specific scenarios (cavalry will not be in every scenario for example). A few rules are optional.

Chapter B, Terrain: This chapter should probably be treated as a glossary - you only need to know the rules for the terrain that is on the maps of the scenario you are playing.

Chapter C, Ordnace: Again you only need to read what is relevant (off board artillery is not in every scenario for example).

Chapter D, Vehicles: Only applicable for scenarios with vehicles in them. 

Chapter E, Miscellaneous: This chapter is labelled as optional. It has rules for rare situations (like scenarios with aircraft or night scenarios).

Chapter F, North Africa: Only applicable for scenarios set in North Africa (the desert).

Chapter G, Pacific: Only applicable for scenarios set in the Pacific theatre.

Chapter H, Vehicle and ordnance notes: Conatins some rules pertaining to specific vehicles and guns, but mostly historical notes. Should be used as a reference and only consulted to determine specific rules for equipment used in the scenario at hand.

Chapter I, Campaign game - never published

Chapter J, Deluxe ASL: This chapter was actually 4 pages in the first edition if memory serves. It actually has one rule that is implemented in some of the campaign games (hth close combat).

Chapter K, Training manual: This was the first attempt at a simple way to learn ASL. This chapter is mostly superceded by the Starter Kits, but can be a fun read nevertheless.

Chapter L, Online ASL - never published

Chapter M, ASL Analysis - never published: A few old Generals had a series of articles which apparently were intended to be developed into this chapter, but that never happened.

Chapter N, Armory: This is just a list of all counters from all modules. This chapter is only published as a pdf.

Chapter O, Red Barricades: A campaign game (a BRILLIANT campaign game). The rules are only relevant to the campaign and the associated scenarios.

Chapter P, Kampfgruppe Peiper: Similar to chapter O.

Chapter Q, Pegasus Bridge: Similar to chapter O.

Chapter R, A Bridge too Far: Similar to chapter O.

Chapter S, Solitaire: Solitaire ASL is almost a completely separate game. 

Chapter T, Tarawa: Similar to chapter O.

Chapter V, Valor of the Guards: Similar to chapter O.

Chapter Z, Other Campaigns: This chapter collects the rules for a number of smaller campaign games that don't have their own chapters.

Chapter FB, Festung Budapest: Similar to chapter O.

All in all, even if the game has 1000 pages of rules, I think you would be able to play some basic scenarios after only reading 20 to 30 pages. If you want to add ordnance you would probably need to read a further 20 and perhaps another 20 for the vehicle rules. This means that only about 5-10% of all the rules are important to know in order to play vast amounts of scenarios. The remaining 90% of rules can be treated as something you look up when you need it for a specific scenario.

(Edit: added the missing page counts)

title: The ★ Vehicle Line
question:
You are shooting a MMG at a Truck, perform a RTC (Rules Task Check), dig around in the MG rules and all A9.6 says is "...otherwise it is resolved on the ★ Vehicle line...". You look up "★", "Vehicle line" and "Star Vehicle line" in the Index and find nothing. If you continue to Search the Index, you will find "Unarmored" is (somewhat) synonymous with ★, but there is no reverse citation.

The ★ Vehicle Line is the row of horizontal numbers on the IFT (or IIFT) underneath the FP row (confusingly displayed as DR/FP, where DR refers to the column of Dice Roll (DR) results and FP refers to the horizontal row of numbers). This ★ Vehicle Line can be read in a somewhat similar fashion to the Close Combat Table, with a Burning Wreck for a DR less than half this number, elimination for a DR less than this number and immobilization for a DR equal to this number. There is also a maximum number of vehicles that can be eliminated on the ★ Vehicle Line; a RTC can be performed for the (odd) situation of more than one vehicle unit in the hex. 

Rules citing the ★ Vehicle Line include A7.308, A7.309, A9.6, A9.61, A13.511 (Cavalry), D6.7 and E7.511; D15.5 (Motorcycles) - ★ Vehicle Line NA.

I was fortunate enough to persuade MMP to include "Pivot" in the 2nd Edition ASLRB; I'll lobby for "★ Vehicle Line" should there be another edition.

title: Dismounting Cavalry
question:
What exactly are the penalties for dismounting cavalry riders (I'm sure FFNAM applies) that dismounted at the start of their MPh in an OG hex? Are the dismounting cavalry riders governed like unloading from a vehicle (D6.5)? Does any First Fire effect the now unmounted horse counter as well?
Thanks in advance! :)
author: Tyrone_Slothrop
consensus_answer:
Cavalry spends MF instead of MP, so dismounting cavalry units just spend the required 1 MF to dismount and go on.

It's not allowed to use Assault Movement when dismounting (or riding), so FFNAM will apply.

If there's D1F against a unit that has just dismounted, fire will affect both the (now) Infantry and the unmounted horses at the same time, as usual when firing on the IFT. See A13.511 for the details on the attacked horses. Basically, they are treated like unarmored vehicles.

title: SW Recovery & Concealment Loss
question: It doesn't say in the rules, or on the Concealment Loss/Gain table, but does a unit attempting SW recovery lose its concealment? Thanks again!
author: Tyrone_Slothrop
consensus_answer:
Yes

See "C" in the Loss/Gain Chart  - since recovery is "Any other action" and it not one of the excepted ones, it loses conceal if less than or equal to 16 hexes in LOS of a GOOD ORDER enemy unit.

C If it engages in any other action [EXC: using a radio/field phone; Spotting; taking a PAATC (and Leader DRM applied to such a PAATC) not caused by a vehicle entering its Location; SW/Gun repair attempts]; e.g., attempts to entrench, kindle a Fire, Deploy, Recombine, make a Sniper/PF/MOL/ATMM Check, rally a broken unit, apply Leader DRM [EXC: PAATC; Armour Leader],use Clearance, place SMOKE grenades/DC, etc.

author: Tyrone_Slothrop
consensus_answer:
I think you got it.

A10.531 Open Ground: For purposes of rout determination, Dash, concealment gain/loss, and Interdiction, an Open Ground hex is any hex in which any Interdictor could apply, during a hypothetical Defensive First Fire opportunity (regardless of what attacks it actually made in previous phases), the -1 FFMO DRM.

A6.7 LOS Hindrance:... All same-level Direct Fire and spotting attempts traced through (not just into or out of ) an effective LOS Hindrance hex are modified by a +1 DRM to either the IFT or To Hit DR, or the Artillery Initial Accuracy dr. The presence of such a Hindrance always negates Interdiction and FFMO.

E3.1 Low Visibility (LV):...A LV Hindrance [EXC: Fog] is treated exactly like a LOS Hindrance except that a LV Hindrance DRM is cumulative with other Hindrances regardless of range and does not by itself negate the FFMO DRM or Interdiction, or affect the placement of (or attack by) Residual FP (A8.26), or prevent concealment loss [EXC: Winter Camouflage].

title: Opportunity Fire (and beginners encouragment!)
question:
Hi all!
I know quite well SK rules, so Now I'm sistematically going through the full RB.

Anyway. I read about Opp Fire and the rule is clear but I'm trying to figure out its TACTICAL use.
I haven't read concealment yet but one of the use of Opp Fire should be waiting to fire on units which go unconcealed during MPh/DFPh.....I suppose!

You Vets would help me for sure....

author: Qwirz
consensus_answer:
Some tactics:
1. You already mentioned this, but if the opponent is concealed, use Opp Fire, then in MPh send a half-squad out to strip concealment (either by "bumping" into the concealed stack, or if the opponent shoots at it). Full FP in AFPh!

2. Opp Fire, then in the MPh move your 9-2 leader into that Opp Fire stack. He can give his -2 bonus during the AFPh.

3. Bazookas, panzerfausts and the like have to take a +2 backblast avoidance penalty if firing from within a building. But if you Opp Fire, you don't have to take that penalty! (rules C5.34 & C13.8)

replies.body: In my experience opportunity fire is not used very often, but you are correct in that it may be useful against defenders who become unconcealed (or unhidden) after prep fire.

Some tactics:
1. You already mentioned this, but if the opponent is concealed, use Opp Fire, then in MPh send a half-squad out to strip concealment (either by "bumping" into the concealed stack, or if the opponent shoots at it). Full FP in AFPh!

2. Opp Fire, then in the MPh move your 9-2 leader into that Opp Fire stack. He can give his -2 bonus during the AFPh.

3. Bazookas, panzerfausts and the like have to take a +2 backblast avoidance penalty if firing from within a building. But if you Opp Fire, you don't have to take that penalty! (rules C5.34 & C13.8)
The smoke mechanics may also make some units more vulnerable in the Advancing Fire Phase - check out the ASOP.

Also, firing without the CX penalty.

In all cases, you face the trade-off: Waiting to have more FP (in any of the ways above described), against firing after your opponent. Hence, it is a good strategy if you are in a safe position, AND your target is not a menace for your other moving units.

Finally, note that vehicles cannot Opp Fire.

title: About Slopes...
question:
Hi everybody,
I'm focusing on Slopes rules, since I own several historical modules involving these.
Even if I'm not a very experienced ASL player, so maybe I'd just better shut up, I must say that I'm a bit puzzled about these rules.
First of all, if the main reason for their introduction is to counteract the "plateau effect", I don't think the goal is reached.
After all, I think the Alpine Hill Option provided by standard rules may reveal much more effective.

Also, look at this example taken from "Slopes in ASL" article by Chas Smith:

Well, this seems to me a very unrealistic situation.
We see that L2 is higher than M2 (3/4 of level higher), but at the same time, it is lower than L1 (say 3/4 of level lower). Intuitively, I would think that L1 is 1,5 levels higher than M2, but it's not: it's at the same level.

I know that Slopes rules state that the base level of the hex is not changed by the presence of a slope hexside, but still this example makes me wonder about the sense of the whole operation. It seems to me that these rules only complicate further the game without adding anything realistic...

What do you think? Am I missing something?
author: federicost
consensus_answer:
You are correct in a purely logical sense. L2 can't be both lower than L1 and higher than M2 if L1 and M2 are level with each other. 

But this is only true if you conceptualize all the hexes as perfectly flat hex shaped segments of separate terrain. In reality the terrain would be undulating, ridged and irregular and, in a general sense, these areas could have this kind of a relation to each other. 

My advice is to not analysis ASL too much. It's a great game that's surprisingly fun and rewarding to play and has a great community. But if you start picking at the rules and attempting to apply a lot of logical analysis you will just drive yourself nuts. 

Don't question the inconsistencies... just play and SHUT UP!! :D

I think the best example of how slopes can be wisely used is in Crucible of Steel. 

You have maps that represent the great flat Russian Steppes. There are vast fields of grain. But the designer does not the fields of grain to serve as huge areas of unmitigated hindrance. 

It would be ahistorical and too defensively powerful to add a great number of hills. So a few slopes can be used to represent the undulations in the ground that would allow defenders to see over things like grain fields and hedges. 

This is how I believe slopes should be used in ASL: with subtlety to create specific LOS effects in a map. But they should not be used in large quantities to try to create more detail in what is already hilly terrain.

title: Hand-to-Hand CC
question:
Even after some years of ASL playing, I still find myself incredibly lacking of basics....
I still don't understand WHEN HtH can be used: I know it's mandatory if Japanese, I know it can be permitted by SSR.
But what about rule J2.31? is this rule ALWAYS effective or is it only when playing De Luxe ASL?
For example: berserk units, when attacking in CC, must declare HtH or not?

author: federicost
consensus_answer:
J2.31 is only in play in Deluxe / by SSR.

Otherwise, just in the PTO (in certain circumstances, such as Dare Death, IJA or Gurkha) or by SSR or Campaign SR (most of the Ost Front CGs, such as VotG and Festung Budapest, have h-t-h in play as standard).

So, in non-PTO, non-CG, non deluxe scenarios h-t-h generally isn't an option.

title: SW/Cowering
question:
The rules say any MMC that cowers has a Final Fire marker immediately placed over the light mortar/crew. My question is: Does that Mortar actually fire, or no? Thanks,
~Rob
author: Tyrone_Slothrop
consensus_answer:
Just to step back here ... doesn't the rule state that a Final Fire marker is placed on a LIGHT mortar?  And then, what is the definition of a LIGHT mortar?
See C9.2:
"...Any mortar ≤ 60mm is a light mortar and is treated as a SW because it is on a ½" counter...."

The Cowering rule (A7.9) says:
"...In addition, any unit that cowers (as well as all of its SW/Guns regardless of whether it was using its inherent FP) is automatically marked with a Final or Prep Fire counter as appropriate...."

It doesn't really say the red part today, but it probably should to be complete.

replies.body:
Rob,

Just to clarify. Per A7.9 ordnance attacks never suffer Cowering:

"7.9 COWERING: IFT attacks are adversely affected by any IFT resolution DR that results in Original "Doubles" unless a leader directs that attack. The penalty for rolling Doubles without leadership direction is that the attack is resolved on the next lower column of the IFT. An attack on the lowest column which cowers is reduced to no effect at all, although a malfunction result can still occur. In addition, any unit that cowers (as well as all of its SW regardless of whether it was using its inherent FP) is automatically marked with a Final or Prep Fire counter as appropriate. Cowering affects all fire except that from a SMC, berserk or Fanatic unit, Fire Lane, IFE, Canister, Aircraft, British Elite and First Line units, Finns, Sniper, ordnance, OBA, or any form of vehicular fire."

"Ordnance (any weapon which must score a hit on a To Hit Table before rolling again on the IFT or To Kill Table to resolve that hit)"

So, if the crew was firing the mortar (an ordnance attack) neither the original To Hit (TH) DR, nor assuming a hit was achieved, the ensuing IFT DR is subjected to Cowering. So, if that was the case, the crew and the mortar it just fired would both only be marked with a First Fire counter.

If the mortar had been fired by a squad, then only the mortar (SW) would have been marked with a First Fire counter and the squad would still have been free to use its Inherent FP. The only downside with this ordering for a squad firing second is that any Acquisition that would have been just achieved would be lost as soon as the squad follows up with an Inherent FP attack.

If the case is that the MMC fired its Inherent FP first and did Cower, then the MMC and the Mortar (SW) are both marked with a Final Fire counter and the unit is done firing unless it qualifies for Final Protective Fire.

Which is why, when planning your attacks, one should usually consider firing any SW ordnance attacks prior to using any Inherent FP or firing a SW using the SW's FP.
And if the cowering was while firing something that can cower, like inherent firepower or an MG, then yes, the unit is marked Final Fire and the fire is still solved, albeit at a reduced firepower.

title: Beginners question about LOS and blind hexes
question:
I have difficulties parsing the rules for LOS and blind hexes (english is not my first language). So did I get this right?
1) To see behind an obstacle the firer has to be one level higher than the obstacle (i.e. a wood hex on level 0 is a level 1 obstacle and you have to be on level 2 to see past it).
2) Even if the firer is higher, there are blind hexes behind the obstacle that are not in LOS.
3) Normally, there is one blind hex behind an obstacle.
4) There is an additional blind hex for every full five hexes the firer is away from the obstacle.
5) There is an additional blind hex for every level that the obstacle is higher than necessary to be an obstacle. (i.e. a level 2 obstacle has two blind hexes behind it, if those hexes are level 0)
6) There is one less blind hex for every level the firer is higher than he has to be to look over the obstacle, to a minimum of 1. (i.e. if you are 7 hexes away from a wood on level 0, and you are on level 2, behind the wood are two blind hexes. If you climb to level 3, there is only one blind hex)
7) This all is somehow different for hill crest line.
author: WuWei
consensus_answer:
1) To see behind an obstacle the firer has to be one level higher than the obstacle (i.e. a wood hex on level 0 is a level 1 obstacle and you have to be on level 2 to see past it).
You just have to be higher - not necessarily a full level higher. A 1/2-level higher will do. So e.g., being on level 1.5 is enough see past a level 1 woods.

A6.4:
"...unit is at an elevation > the height equivalent of any intervening full level obstacle..."

2) Even if the firer is higher, there are blind hexes behind the obstacle that are not in LOS.
Correct.

3) Normally, there is one blind hex behind an obstacle.
Behind an obstacle that is 1 level high, that is correct.

4) There is an additional blind hex for every full five hexes the firer is away from the obstacle.
Correct. 5-9 - 1 extra Blind hex, 10-14, 2 extra, etc.

5) There is an additional blind hex for every level that the obstacle is higher than necessary to be an obstacle. (i.e. a level 2 obstacle has two blind hexes behind it, if those hexes are level 0)
Correct, though I would not call it an "extra" Blind hex - more like a normal (per A6.4) Blind hex.

6) There is one less blind hex for every level the firer is higher than he has to be to look over the obstacle, to a minimum of 1. (i.e. if you are 7 hexes away from a wood on level 0, and you are on level 2, behind the wood are two blind hexes. If you climb to level 3, there is only one blind hex)
Pretty much.

7) This all is somehow different for hill crest line.

5) There is an additional blind hex for every level that the obstacle is higher than necessary to be an obstacle. (i.e. a level 2 obstacle has two blind hexes behind it, if those hexes are level 0)
Correct, though I would not call it an "extra" Blind hex - more like a normal (per A6.4) Blind hex.

6) There is one less blind hex for every level the firer is higher than he has to be to look over the obstacle, to a minimum of 1. (i.e. if you are 7 hexes away from a wood on level 0, and you are on level 2, behind the wood are two blind hexes. If you climb to level 3, there is only one blind hex)
Pretty much.

7) This all is somehow different for hill crest line.
Yes, there are some differences.
Thank you!

1) To see behind an obstacle the firer has to be one level higher than the obstacle (i.e. a wood hex on level 0 is a level 1 obstacle and you have to be on level 2 to see past it).
You just have to be higher - not necessarily a full level higher. A 1/2-level higher will do. So e.g., being on level 1.5 is enough see past a level 1 woods.

A6.4:
"...unit is at an elevation > the height equivalent of any intervening full level obstacle..."

2) Even if the firer is higher, there are blind hexes behind the obstacle that are not in LOS.
Correct.

3) Normally, there is one blind hex behind an obstacle.
Behind an obstacle that is 1 level high, that is correct.

4) There is an additional blind hex for every full five hexes the firer is away from the obstacle.
Correct. 5-9 - 1 extra Blind hex, 10-14, 2 extra, etc.

5) There is an additional blind hex for every level that the obstacle is higher than necessary to be an obstacle. (i.e. a level 2 obstacle has two blind hexes behind it, if those hexes are level 0)
Correct, though I would not call it an "extra" Blind hex - more like a normal (per A6.4) Blind hex.

6) There is one less blind hex for every level the firer is higher than he has to be to look over the obstacle, to a minimum of 1. (i.e. if you are 7 hexes away from a wood on level 0, and you are on level 2, behind the wood are two blind hexes. If you climb to level 3, there is only one blind hex)
Pretty much.

7) This all is somehow different for hill crest line.
Yes, there are some differences.

title: Final fire thru bocage
question: Hello All.  Say I have a German squad with a MMG in a level 2 bldg , that has a FF counter on it.  The Americans have a concealed half squad 6 hexes away that moves using assault movement into a open hex that is a level 2 hill and behind a bocage hexside, they then claim wall advantage.   The Germans have a LOS to this hex which is 5 hexes away. I want to shoot at the American squad using SFF. Is the fire halved for SFF and then halved again for concealment(for being behind Bocage ) and then with a DRM of +2 for Bocage  ? Am new to ASL and just starting out.  Hope this question has not been asked before.  Have I played this right? Thanking all who reply.
author: tm505pir
consensus_answer:
Hello All.  Say I have a German squad with a MMG in a level 2 bldg , that has a FF counter on it.  The Americans have a concealed half squad 6 hexes away that moves using assault movement into a open hex that is a level 2 hill and behind a bocage hexside, they then claim wall advantage.   The Germans have a LOS to this hex which is 5 hexes away. I want to shoot at the American squad using SFF. Is the fire halved for SFF and then halved again for concealment(for being behind Bocage ) and then with a DRM of +2 for Bocage  ? Am new to ASL and just starting out.  Hope this question has not been asked before.  Have I played this right? Thanking all who reply. 

Tommy - the bocage grants a +2 DRM as you note, but it does not automatically grant concealment status.  **IF** the unit was already concealed when it moved behind the bocage (and was otherwise out of LOS for its entire move) THEN it does in fact retain concealment (even if it used non-assault movement).  If it wasn't, it won't gain concealment until the CCPh and then only if it remains where all LOS to it is through a bocage hex side.

In answer to your question, yes, your unit will be halved for SFF* and halved again **IF** the target started concealed and never lost concealment during its move. Further, no, the -1 FFMO would not apply to the shot since it's being traced through a hex side that gives a positive DRM.  If it weren't assault moving, however, it would be subject to FFNAM (combined with the bocage TEM).

Bocage is a little twitchy, but it's a fun terrain in which to fight.

-N

*RE: SFF - be sure there aren't other KEUs closer than the target.  If there are, they can't fire at the unit behind the bocage anyway - always restricted to the nearest/equidistant target with SFF.

title: Long range fire
question:
I have a question on Long range fire.  Are single man counters say a 
1-4-9 capable of long range fire ? I think not,  are they considered a unit ?.  If so how would you conduct the fire. Thanks to all who reply.
author: tm505pir
consensus_answer:
A Hero may use Long Range fire (0.5 FP from 5-8 hexes) but by A15.24 his Heroic -1 DRM only applies if "...the hero is firing at Normal Range of either his inherent FP or his weapon counter".  You can give him an ATR and presto, he provides the -1 out to twelve hexes.

JR

replies.body: Not really, not by himself, because half of 1 is .5 and not enough to generate a FP. However, if he were stacked with another unit which was halved as well, you could cobble those together for a point of fire. EX: a 1-4-9 hero stacked with a German 5-4-8 firing at a target five hexes distant would generate a 3 FP attack ((1/2) + (5/2)), which would resolve on the 2 column (meaning the hero didn't really help get you up to the 4 column, but you'll still get the Heroic -1 DRM). Of course if you're playing IIFT then you'd get the 3 neg one which is virtually the same shot anyway.

A Hero may use Long Range fire (0.5 FP from 5-8 hexes) but by A15.24 his Heroic -1 DRM only applies if "...the hero is firing at Normal Range of either his inherent FP or his weapon counter".  You can give him an ATR and presto, he provides the -1 out to twelve hexes.

JR
Which brings up my main disappointment with the IIFT: no 0.5 FP column.

title: Residual Fire power
question:
Hello All.  Am new to ASL and have a question on Residual fire power.  Say I move a squad into a clear hex with a smoke counter in it (2 MF), this squad then takes DFF with a total of 8 FP. After the attack I then place a 1 FP residual FP marker in the hex. (half of 8 =4, minus the 2 TEM for smoke leaves me with 1 FP) Did I do this correctly ?
The squad then comes under SFF as it spent 2 MF in the hex, The FP of the unit is then halved so I use the 4 column on the IFT.  What becomes of the 1 residual FP counter is it now removed as 4 FP halved is 2 then minus 2 for TEM leaves 0.
Does the original 1 Residual FP counter stay in the hex or is it removed totally with now no residual FP counter in the hex or can residual FP never fall below 1 ?
Thanks to all who reply.
author: tm505pir
consensus_answer:
Hello All.  Am new to ASL and have a question on Residual fire power.  Say I move a squad into a clear hex with a smoke counter in it (2 MF), this squad then takes DFF with a total of 8 FP. After the attack I then place a 1 FP residual FP marker in the hex. (half of 8 =4, minus the 2 TEM for smoke leaves me with 1 FP) Did I do this correctly ?
The squad then comes under SFF as it spent 2 MF in the hex, The FP of the unit is then halved so I use the 4 column on the IFT.  What becomes of the 1 residual FP counter is it now removed as 4 FP halved is 2 then minus 2 for TEM leaves 0.
Does the original 1 Residual FP counter stay in the hex or is it removed totally with now no residual FP counter in the hex or can residual FP never fall below 1 ?
Thanks to all who reply. 

No rulebook handy, but here goes.

1) The first attack will leave 4 residual - target hex SMOKE does not affect residual. Firing through SMOKE will behave as you described.
PS Target hex SMOKE will affect residual attacks.

2) The 1FP residual remains until replaced by a higher residual marker.

replies.body:
Hello All.  Am new to ASL and have a question on Residual fire power.  Say I move a squad into a clear hex with a smoke counter in it (2 MF), this squad then takes DFF with a total of 8 FP. After the attack I then place a 1 FP residual FP marker in the hex. (half of 8 =4, minus the 2 TEM for smoke leaves me with 1 FP) Did I do this correctly ?
The squad then comes under SFF as it spent 2 MF in the hex, The FP of the unit is then halved so I use the 4 column on the IFT.  What becomes of the 1 residual FP counter is it now removed as 4 FP halved is 2 then minus 2 for TEM leaves 0.
Does the original 1 Residual FP counter stay in the hex or is it removed totally with now no residual FP counter in the hex or can residual FP never fall below 1 ?
Thanks to all who reply. 

No rulebook handy, but here goes.

1) The first attack will leave 4 residual - target hex SMOKE does not affect residual. Firing through SMOKE will behave as you described.
PS Target hex SMOKE will affect residual attacks.

2) The 1FP residual remains until replaced by a higher residual marker.

The residual will be 4 from the original attack. (8FP/2) TEM only effect the residual FP if it exists outside the hex in question.  Subsequent residual attacks use the TEM in the hex.  So in your case, other units moving into the hex will be attacked at 4FP + 2 for the smoke - FFNAM/FFMO if applicable.

Residual is removed at the end of movement, the the original 4 will remain there until the end of movement or if it is replace by a higher residual.

Residual can be reduced to less than 0 in which there is no residual left.

The general idea is that Residual FP is reduced for modifiers that wouldn't obviously apply to an attack in that Location. The Resid counter doesn't show where the fire came from, so smoke between the firer and target (or in the firer's hex) reduces the residual instead of applying a DRM to it. Smoke (and terrain!) DRM in the target hex are applied to the residual attack, but does not affect the FP.

..So in your case, other units moving into the hex will be attacked at 4FP + 2 for the smoke - FFNAM/FFMO if applicable...
Note though, that FFMO will not apply in this case, due to the SMOKE.
Thanks to all who replied.  4 FP residual FP in hex which is removed at the end of the movement phase,

title: ASL question on Bore sighting
question:
Have a question on Bore sighting.  Say I have a good order Infantry squad with a MMG in a level two building.  I have a LOS to a level 2 hill which is several hexes large, can I Bore sight the MMG to one of the level 2 hexes ?, or am I only allowed to Bore sight from/to a building at level 0.
Thanks to all who reply.
author: tm505pir
consensus_answer:
Robin & Luke are right.

The answer to your question though ..

C6.4 talks about boresighting LOCATION

Location (in the index) defined as: 
"a hex as well as any of the following sub-divisions of that hex: sewer, upper or lower building or bridge level, pillbox, cave"

Note also that under C6.41
"Bore Sighting may be used only by a Scenario Defender (see Index)"
Scenario Defender defined as: 
"The Scenario Defender is the side that sets up wholly or partly on-board and does not have to capture terrain (on other than its setup board) in order to fulfill its Victory Conditions, while facing an opposing side that enters wholly from offboard."

ie.. if the both sides start onboard, no one gets to boresight.

Regards, 
Jack

title: Portage Points and Passengers
question:
OK, So I've read through the various bits of the rules, and it seems like this is one of those moments where the apparently exhaustive ASL manual doesn't actually specify something quite simple and important.

Do support weapons count against a transport's PP? IE if a halftrack can carry 15 PP, does an LMG of 1PP count against that 15?

title: Are PTO paths different from ETO paths?
question:
I have a question.
At the end of B13.6, I read: "...a path has no other effect on a hex (i.e., inside the woods contour the path is woods; outside the contour it is not).".
Instead G.1 says: "No road exist (all brush-roads and woods-roads are Paths, with no Open Ground in the brush-/woods-road portion of those hexes;".
Does that mean that in ETO paths SOMETIMES are treated as Open Ground (e.g. when LOS crosses only path depiction), while in PTO paths are NEVER Open Ground?
author: federicost
consensus_answer:
I have a question.
At the end of B13.6, I read: "...a path has no other effect on a hex (i.e., inside the woods contour the path is woods; outside the contour it is not).".
Instead G.1 says: "No road exist (all brush-roads and woods-roads are Paths, with no Open Ground in the brush-/woods-road portion of those hexes;".
Does that mean that in ETO paths SOMETIMES are treated as Open Ground (e.g. when LOS crosses only path depiction), while in PTO paths are NEVER Open Ground?

No. It means that in PTO, when LOS only goes through a road depiction in brush/woods, that portion of the LOS is not Open Ground. That road depiction is also not a road, but is instead a path.

Path depictions are always paths, and are identical in PTO and ETO.

A SW is removed  when dropped in a march, stream, water, blaze (burning vehicle) or rubbled building location.

title: Vehicles and Wall Advantage
question:
We were playing a Hedgerow Hell (Deluxe) scenario today and had a situation where a German SPG was on a road hex with bocage on either side of it with occupying US infantry. On our reading of the rules as the SPG occupied it's hex before the US infantry moved adjacent it got to claim WA against both of them despite the fact the walls (bocage) were on opposite sides of it's hex.

This felt a little wrong but appears to be what the rules dictate. Were we right?
author: domus_ludorum
consensus_answer:
Gordon, Deluxe WA is by hexside, so the StuG should only be able to claim versus one Ami squad - the newcomer can claim its own hexside.

Stated with confidence, but wrong.  See my next post below:

9.321 A unit always has WA over all possible (as per 9.32) wall/hedge hexsides of its hex; if it forfeits/is-denied WA over one of those wall/hedge hexsides it cannot claim WA over any other hexsides [EXC: in Deluxe ASL, WA is claimed/retained/lost per hexside—not hex]. Adjacent units opposing sides can never both claim WA over a shared wall/hedge at the same time; thus one of them claiming WA over the shared hexside prevents the other from claiming WA over any hexsides at all [EXC: Deluxe ASL]

title: Routing non-DM units
question:
A situation came up in a current game of mine, where my opponent says I couldn't rout a unit without DM markers. Rule A10.5 says you may rout units which are DMd, but it does not mention units without DM markers. I was under the impression that all broken units may rout normally in the rtph. Have I missed a rule somewhere? 

Thanks.
author: bpmasher
consensus_answer:
See:

Rule A10.5 Routing: "A broken unit may rout if currently under DM."

Rule A10.6 Desperation Morale: "[EXC: A unit may opt to retain its DM status provided it is not in a woods/building/pillbox/trench so as to guarantee its ability to rout again in the next RtPh. If overstacked in a woods/building, it may also opt to retain its DM status]."

So only units under DM may rout.

I had a situation in which I had a broken unit in a woods hex under DM which failed to rally so it lost it's DM marker and was unable to rout in the subsequent rout phase unless fired on or an enemy unit moved adjacent thus putting it back under DM. It was likely that this unit would surrender so I took the risky measure of firing at it with my own men with a low FP shot - just enough to get  it back under DM and hopefully not CRing it. Well, it worked and the unit went under DM and I could rout it out of the woods in the next RtPh. :D

You cannot target your own units unless specifically allowed. See A7.4.

replies.body:
