title: Clarification of smoke usage while in bypass movement
question:
The setup is: Gavin Take, American side, units (leader, 2 7-4-7s) entering 3I1.

After expending 2 MF for I1 and 1 MF to bypass the woods in J1, the units expend 1MF and use bypass to move through J2 along the I2-J2 and I3-J3 hexsides. Expecting fire from the town to the right, one squad expends 2MF to throw smoke grenades in J3, an adjacent hex (A24.1). The other squad also expends 2MF and wants to throw smoke grenades into K3, also an adjacent hex to J2. The line in 4.3 (inserted it seems into 2nd edition, not in 1st ed, perhaps from the Q&A in General 22i6) reads: "Use of Bypass movement does not prevent placement of a DC (23.3) or SMOKE grenade (24.1)."  It seems likely that tossing the smoke into J3 is legal.

Is throwing smoke into K3 also legal for the bypassing units in this context? (i.e., is K3 an adjacent hex if the unit is in bypass along the hexsides mentioned above?).

Thanks in advance for your analysis.
author: resinaus
consensus_answer:
The setup is: Gavin Take, American side, units (leader, 2 7-4-7s) entering 3I1.

After expending 2 MF for I1 and 1 MF to bypass the woods in J1, the units expend 1MF and use bypass to move through J2 along the I2-J2 and I3-J3 hexsides.

So, 3 MF to get to that point, one each in I1, J1 & J2 (Bypass, all the way).

Expecting fire from the town to the right, one squad expends 2MF to throw smoke grenades in J3, an adjacent hex (A24.1). The other squad also expends 2MF and wants to throw smoke grenades into K3, also an adjacent hex to J2. The line in 4.3 (inserted it seems into 2nd edition, not in 1st ed, perhaps from the Q&A in General 22i6) reads: "Use of Bypass movement does not prevent placement of a DC (23.3) or SMOKE grenade (24.1)."  It seems likely that tossing the smoke into J3 is legal.

Agreed.

Is throwing smoke into K3 also legal for the bypassing units in this context? (i.e., is K3 an adjacent hex if the unit is in bypass along the hexsides mentioned above?).

There is LOS to K3 from the J2/J3/I3 vertex only.  They would be subject to D1F, there, for the MF spent to reach that vertex, before their MF declaration, at that vertex, for Smoke Grenade attempts.

Assuming that leaves them all okay, K3 is ADJACENT to that vertex, so, Yes, the Smoke Grenade attempt may be made, if otherwise allowable.

Note that the 2 MF cost of the attempt must be declared/spent before either is resolved, and will put the stack at 5 MF expended.  (The attempts resolve before any D1F vs the placement attempt MFs.)  So, they may make the grenade attempt only if they have 2 MF left after the 5 are expended, meaning, early or late Double Time will be required if/in-case the attempt into J3 succeeds because, from that particular vertex, they'll need 2 MF to get anywhere else, if they do get smoke into J3.

Thanks in advance for your analysis.

title: Deep streams and movement phase
question:
I'm not sure I have got this but just wanted to be sure.

If I am adjacent to a deep stream hex which costs 4MF to enter fully (from a non-stream hex) and I have a squad with 4MF (no leader) I have at least 3 options during the MPh:

1) The squad can move into the stream hex and declare crest status on my side of the stream without actually descending fully into the 'water' at a cost of 3MF (1 less that the COT B20.91). Presumably becoming CX per B20.43?

2) The squad can drop into the water at a cost of 4MF and stop - becoming CX in the process (B20.43). It could advance out on the other side in the APh so long as it requires less than 4MF (eg into open ground for 2MF).

3) The squad can declare CX before moving, drop into the water for 4MF then claim crest status on the other side of the stream for another 2MF (after which it can advance out of the stream hex in the APh - costs 1MF + COT B20.91).

Option 3 begs the question whether if the squad was with a leader that the units could move straight out in one MPh without declaring CX in advance, but they would get the CX anyway. 

Presumably a squad already marked CX from a previous turn cannot enter another deep stream hex?
author: CletePurcel
consensus_answer:
Option 3 begs the question whether if the squad was with a leader that the units could move straight out in one MPh without declaring CX in advance, but they would get the CX anyway. 

Yes, they could do that also possible without leader by declaring double time in advance.

Presumably a squad already marked CX from a previous turn cannot enter another deep stream hex?

It can enter. CX prohibits advance against difficult terrain, but not minimum move or entering a deep stream.

20.43 Deep: If a stream is deep, Infantry/Cavalry enter at a cost of four MF and become CX (A4.72 would apply to an advance entry) - regardless of whether the move is through a stream hexside or not, or whether the unit was previously CX or not.

title: Mortar v Pillbox
question:
OK so a mortar is probably not the best choice of weapon to take on a pillbox but if that's what is to hand then.....

My question relates to whether mortar fire against a pillbox is ever considered to originate within the pillboxes covered arc or whether it is always regarded as non-CA. This would have implications for CH's on mtr v pillboxes.

C9.1 states that mortars are 'treated as Indirect Fire weapons for fire resolution purposes' and  'the IFT effects of....hits are resolved using Indirect Fire principles and modifiers'.

C3.71 relating to critical hits vs non-armoured targets indicates that the TEM is reversed when scoring a CH but has an EXC of 'pillbox NCA (B30.113)'.

B30.113 states that the NCA TEM of a pillbox applies to FT/Ordnance attacks from outside the CA or where attacks 'are made by Indirect fire.....CH are resolved normally [EXC: the NCA TEM is considered to be zero for CH resolution]'.

1. Does all of this mean that mortar fire is always considered NCA v a pillbox and therefore always uses the NCA modifier?

2. If a mtr scores a CH vs a pillbox, that it gets it's FP doubled (normally halved as it's area-firing) but does not get a reversed TEM for the pillbox NCA.

3. Connected but slightly different - is a pillbox in a jungle hex subject to the the -1 Airburst TEM?
author: domus_ludorum
consensus_answer:
1. Yes.
2. Yes.
3. No. B30.3 Pillbox TEM is not cumulative with any other +/- TEM [EXC: mud/deep-snow TEM, for certain HE attacks; see E3.62 and E3.731], but is cumulative with Hindrances and SMOKE.

replies.body:
1. Yes.
2. Yes.
3. No. B30.3 Pillbox TEM is not cumulative with any other +/- TEM [EXC: mud/deep-snow TEM, for certain HE attacks; see E3.62 and E3.731], but is cumulative with Hindrances and SMOKE.

title: Smoke on the Water
question: Can you place ordnance smoke on a bridge over a water obstacle?
author: drmark64
consensus_answer:
Can you place ordnance smoke on a bridge over a water obstacle?

If using the Area Target Type, No.  The game treats Ordnance SMOKE differently from Infantry SMOKE grenades.

C8.52 says to place Ordnance SMOKE at ground level.  In the case of a bridge over Water, that would be in Water, a place SMOKE may not be placed (A24.1).

There is this Q&A:
A24.8 & C8.52 C8.52 states that when using the Area Target Type, SMOKE ammunition is placed at ground level of the target hex hit. If placing SMOKE in a Gully hex with Area Target Type (Crest status is Level 0, IN the Depression is Level -1), is the SMOKE counter placed IN the Depression, to be at Level -1, with a two level Hindrance measured from -1? Or is the SMOKE counter placed at Crest status, to be at Level 0, with Hindrance measured from 0?
A. IN; from -1. 

Separately, HoB has ruled Ordnance SMOKE =may= be placed on a bridge in at least one of their game products.  Treat that as a special rule, if applicable.

Otherwise, the answer is No.

replies.body:
C8.52 SMOKE ammunition is always placed at ground level in any target hex which is hit on the Area Target Type, except Interior Building hexes, even if the only visible part of that hex is the upper level of a building.

title: Berserk questions
question:
A few rules queries came up in our PTO game tonight, surrounding some Japanese units that went berserk.

A moving Japanese stack with a 10-1 leader, a crew, and a squad moved into a hex where there was already a Japanese squad which had completed its movement earlier in the MPh. Residual fire made the leader roll HOB and he went berserk. 

1. Did the non-moving squad have to make a NTC to see if it went berserk? (We thought yes: A15.41, and applied the leadership DRM to the NTC, but did not give the non-moving squad the +1 Morale bonus for being in the same stack as a moving leader.) 

2. It seemed to be impossible to mark the Japanese crew as Berserk in VASL-- is that right?

3. The moving Berserk units charged with the MF remaining from their new 8 MF allowance. But we thought the non-moving Berserk unit could not move as it had finished its MPh. Is that right?

4. The moving Berserk units moved into the same hex as my American 6-6-7, and survived TPBF, and I survived the AFPh. Could I voluntary break in the RtPh, and rout the usual 6MF away through non-open ground?

5. I didn't voluntary break, and the hex with the berserkers and my squad were joined by another Japanese squad Advancing in. Was it correct to roll for Ambush?
author: angelgabriel
consensus_answer:
A few rules queries came up in our PTO game tonight, surrounding some Japanese units that went berserk.

A moving Japanese stack with a 10-1 leader, a crew, and a squad moved into a hex where there was already a Japanese squad which had completed its movement earlier in the MPh. Residual fire made the leader roll HOB and he went berserk. 

1. Did the non-moving squad have to make a NTC to see if it went berserk? (We thought yes: A15.41, and applied the leadership DRM to the NTC, but did not give the non-moving squad the +1 Morale bonus for being in the same stack as a moving leader.) 

No NTC was required because all (except those Immune to HoB) go Berserk automatically (G1.41, penultimate, points to A25.223).

2. It seemed to be impossible to mark the Japanese crew as Berserk in VASL-- is that right?

Yes, because a Crew is not susceptible to HoB.  A15.1, 3rd.

3. The moving Berserk units charged with the MF remaining from their new 8 MF allowance. But we thought the non-moving Berserk unit could not move as it had finished its MPh. Is that right?

Yes.

4. The moving Berserk units moved into the same hex as my American 6-6-7, and survived TPBF, and I survived the AFPh. Could I voluntary break in the RtPh, and rout the usual 6MF away through non-open ground?

Yes, because the 6-6-7 is in CC but not yet Melee, it may voluntarily break so as to rout away.  A10.41 & A10.5.  NB:  If you are going to voluntarily break, you must declare it at the beginning of the RtPh.  A10.41, 1st.

5. I didn't voluntary break, and the hex with the berserkers and my squad were joined by another Japanese squad Advancing in. Was it correct to roll for Ambush?

If otherwise applicable, Yes.  Note that the IJA player will suffer a pair of  adverse Ambush +1 drms owing to the presence of Lax Berserkers in his force.  Table A11.4, and Berserk are always Lax in CC (A15.432, last).

replies.body:
off the cuff, I think only the moving units would be effected, and the crew is exempt from Heat of Battle.

so I think just the leader and moving squad go berserk. Berserk units that break suffer casualty reduction, so there is no routing option. 

I think Ambush would apply, because the other squad advanced in.

title: unarmed truck question
question:
How do I resolve an IFT attack of 4 FP factors on an unarmed and unarmored truck, if the final DR is 6, NMC?

The 'star' vehicle number for this column is 5.

I am guessing that the truck takes the NMC, and if it fails it is abandoned with no crew counter.

Thanks,

John
author: Suulthanaur
consensus_answer:
A7.308 vs UNARMORED VEHICLES: All non-ordnance Direct Fire attacks vs unarmored vehicles/horse counters are resolved on the  Vehicle line of the IFT using the same IFT DR (after any applicable modification) for any Personnel target in the same Location. Unless using Defensive First Fire, non-ordnance attacks vs unarmored vehicles/horses affect all occupants of the Target Location including Infantry and other vehicles/horses which are present in the same Location [EXC: a vehicle in Bypass and out of the firer's LOS cannot be affected, nor can more vehicle/horse counters be affected by a DR than the highest KIA# of that column as randomly determined (e.g., a 6, 8 or 12 FP attack vs the  Vehicle Line could affect no more than three vehicles; a 2 or 4 FP attack could affect only two vehicles; a 1 FP attack could affect only one vehicle)]. If that Final DR is < the Kill Number listed for the IFT FP column used, the vehicle is eliminated [EXC: Unlikely Kill; 7.309]; if it equals the Kill Number, the vehicle is immobilized [EXC: if HD the vehicle is unaffected by an Immobilization result]; if the Final DR is ≤ half of the Kill Number, the vehicle is eliminated as a burning wreck and all of its PRC are eliminated. Otherwise, the PRC of an eliminated vehicle must check for survival (D5.6). The surviving PRC of an eliminated vehicle are not subject to further effects from that attack. However, the Vulnerable PRC of a vehicle that has not been eliminated may still be subject to a Collateral Attack (D.8).

So if the final DR is higher than the star number, there is no effect.

title: Missing Rules for CH extension Panther Line
question:
Hi everyone,
I just bought ASL Comp Panther Line from Critical Hit.
I noticed that Slope Hexsides rule are required (Rules O2, P3). I really don't have any idea of what these rules are and where to find them. Anybody can help me?
Thanks, really!!!!
author: federicost
consensus_answer:
3.1 A slope hexside5 represents an undulation in the terrain substantial enough to give an Up-Slope (3.2) unit a LOS advantage. On the PB map a slope hexside is represented by brown hash-marks along that hexside (EX: PBK5-L5). The entire hexside (inclusive of vertices) marked by a slope, but not the slope artwork itself, is considered part of that slope hexside.

  	
3.2 UP-SLOPE/DOWN-SLOPE: A Location whose hex contains one slope hexside is either Up-Slope or Down-Slope to LOS drawn across that hexside to or from that hex. If the slope lines are in the Location's hex, the Location is defined as being Down-Slope across that hexside; if the lines are in an adjacent hex along the hexside common to both hexes, the Location is Up-Slope across that hexside. A Location can be both Up- and Down-Slope across two different slope hexsides.

  	
3.3 LOS: Slopes are neither obstacles nor Hindrances.6 Being Up-Slope affects LOS only in that an Up-Slope Location is treated as being ¾ of a level higher than normal to LOS that begins or ends in that Location and crosses an Up-Slope hexside of that Location. Thus, barring other obstructions to LOS, an Up-Slope unit - even if not in a hill Crest-line hex - can trace a LOS across an Up-Slope hexside of its hex to a lower elevation (i.e., across a hill Crest Line) and/or over (B.4) obstacles and Hindrances whose topmost obstacle/Hindrance height is < the Up-Slope elevation of the viewing unit [EXC: entrenched LOS restrictions would still apply as per B9.21, as would wall/hedge TEM as per B9.31. Otherwise, being Up-Slope or Down-Slope itself has no effect on LOS (e.g., slopes are ignored if the LOS goes through their hex or along their hexside, and also when calculating an A6.41-.43 increase or decrease in the number of Blind Hexes caused by an intervening obstacle). Being Up-Slope itself can neither grant HA nor allow an Up-Slope unit to make a HD attempt. The presence of one slope hexside does not change the elevation of that hex's Base Level.

3.31 FIRE LANE: For the purposes of Fire Lane LOS/LOF drawn across one slope hexside, assume that the term "same-level" means "same-Base-Level". See also 3.42 and its example.

  	
3.4 COVER: A slope can, in certain instances, provide a +TEM (3.41) or a +DRM (3.42).

  	
3.41 DIRECT-FIRE TEM: Ground-level Infantry in a hex containing three (or two non-contiguous) Down-Slope hexsides may claim a +1 slope DRM vs Direct Fire [EXC: FT], provided the attack originates from a non-adjacent firer whose elevation advantage (if any) over that of the target is < the range of the attack and the attacker's LOS crosses one of the target hex's Down-Slope hexsides. (A.5 applies to a FG attack.) Slope TEM is Cumulative with no other +TEM [EXC: Mud/Deep-Snow TEM]). Being Up-Slope itself provides no TEM, does not negate the FFMO/FFNAM DRM, and does not affect Wall Advantage rules.

  	
EX: See the 3.3 illustration, and assume the following attcks are Small Arms, Squad E can claim slope TEM if fired on by squad A or D, but not if fired on by squad B (whose LOS does not cross a Down-Slope hexside of DD13). Likewise, squad C could fire on adjacent squad E with no slope TEM and could claim the -1 FFM0 if otherwise applicable as could squad B. If squad E is fired on by squads C and D as a FG, squad E can claim slope TEM (A.5).

  	
3.42 FIRE-LANE DRM: Infantry being attacked by a Fire Lane receives a +1 Fire Lane slope DRM if the firer is Up-Slope from, ¾ of a level higher than, and not adjacent to, that target [EXC: if the Infantry is attacked by a Fire Lane Snap Shot (A9.221), the DRM applies only if these three conditions apply to each of the two hexes that form the Snap Shot hexside, as determined by the firer's separate LOS to each of them]. An Up-Slope attacker's Fire Lane cannot affect a target that lies at a different Base Level (see 3.3) from that of the attacker.

  	
EX: See the 3.3 illustration, and assume tha squads A and D each have it MG. If squad D places a Fire Lane counter in hex CC12, all moving Infantry in DD14, DD13, CC133, and CC12 (or EE14, DD13, DD12, and CC12; A9.221) can be attacked by that Fire Lane with no slope DRM (since squad D is not Up-Slope from any of those Locations), although Infantry moving in DD13 would get the slope TEM (3.41). If squad A places a Fire Lane counter in EE15, all moving Infantry in CC13 (or DD12) can be attacked by that Fire Lane with no slope DRM (since those hexes are adjacent to the firer) but moving Infantry in DD14 and EE15 would receive the slope DRM, while moving Infantry in DD13 would receive both the slope DRM and slope TEM (3.41). Moving Infantry in EE14 (assuming there is a LOS) would not receive the Slope DRM because CC12 is not Up-Slope to FF14, nor (for the same reason) would the slope DRM apply to lnfantry attacked by a Fire Lane Snap Shot at hexside DD14-EE14.

  	
3.5 ENTRY: A unit crossing if slope hexside that it is Down-Slope from is moving Up-Slope. A unit crossing a slope hexside that it is Up-Slope from is moving Down-Slope.

  	
3.51 MF COST/BOsNUS: Infantry/Cavalry (or a Wagon) must expend ½ MF + COT in order to move Up-Slope. Infantry on skis would receive a ½-MF bonus for each Down-Slope hexside they cross (cumulative with any bonus received for moving to a lower elevation). Crossing a slope hexside while moving on a road does not negate the B3.4 MF road bonus.

  	
EX: See the 3.3 illustration. Squad D must pay 2 ½ MF to enter hex EE14 (2  + ½ [moving Up-Slope] = 2 ½); if it were also crossing a Crest Line up to Level 2 the cost would be 4 ½ MF (2  x 2 [ascending across a Crest Line] + ½ [moving Up-Slope] = 4 ½). Squad C could expend 1 MF to enter DD14, since there is no additional cost to move Down-Slope. If, however, if had Rained (E3.54) or there were Ground Snow (E3.723), squad C would expend 2 MF to enter DD14 (3.54).

  	
3.52 MP COST: A unit that expends MP must pay one MP + COT in order to move Up-Slope.

  	
3.53 CREST-LINE SLOPE: No vehicle (or charging cavalry) may cross a combination Crest-line-slope hexside (EX:B16-B17) 7.

  	
3.54 RAIN/SNOW: When crossing a slope hexside, E3.54 (or E3.723), if otherwise in effect, applies just as if the moving unit is changing elevation (in addition to any application of that rule due to crossing a Crest line).

title: Guns and Crew Concealment
question:
So figure I trade some 1/2 inch concealment counters for 5/8 inch concealment counters.  I know that if you conceal a AFV you record the TCA on a piece of paper. My question is when you conceal a gun can you record that a crew is in that same hex.

title: Desert rout already covered in general rules?

I'm playing my first desert scenario and have a question on desert routs.

F.1C states that

In any scenario, a broken unit forced to rout but unable to reach a woods/building hex in that RtPh may rout to any terrain hex consistent with A10.51 but is not required to rout to the nearest woods/building hex. [...]

The rule is longer but the rest does not affect my question.

If no non-ignorable building/woods Location can be reached during that RtPh, a broken unit may rout to any terrain hex consistent with the above restrictions and need not rout toward the nearest woods/building Location.

They look pretty similar, don't they?

My question is, is rule F.1C really necessary? Isn't its content already covered in A10.51?

title: Skis and Concealment
question: Ground snow is in effect. An SMC with winter camouflage assault moves into open ground (1MF) and puts his skis on (2MF). Does he lose concealment?
author: drmark64
consensus_answer:
Ground snow is in effect. An SMC with winter camouflage assault moves into open ground (1MF) and puts his skis on (2MF). Does he lose concealment?

I believe so. Donning skis is similar to Recovering a SW in LOS of a GO enemy unit (within 16 hexes). In contrast, dropping a SW is not a ? Loss activity. Nor is removing skis, because neither action requires a MF expenditure. 

So in your example, you could declare Assault Movement, enter the hex, remove skis, and retain concealment, but not the other way around. (Even the uber Finns cannot retain concealment when donning skis in this situation, despite expending only 1 MF to do so.)

title: Boresighting

title: Deep Snow
question: A squad is inside a trench in deep snow. A T-34 with a 76L gun scores a critical hit against the squad. The TEM is reversed for the critical hit and firepower is doubled. So the attack firepower is 24 (IFT). What is the DRM?
author: drmark64
consensus_answer:
Looks like -3, as senseless as it seems. Unfortunately, E3.731 outranks B27.3 & B27.5. Instead of the +1 TEM, they should have gone with a one-IFT-column-shift-left, which is effectively a +1 TEM. Note that Sand halves HE IFT except for CH, which is doubled normally (F7.4). 

I think so little playtesting was done on Deep Snow that this just slipped through the cracks. Ask yourself how many times you've used E3.7, let alone E3.73; I think I've played more games using E1!

[Edit = MORE READING] B16 MARSH halves the HP, but doesn't give it normal doubling for CH. Given the 'muffling effect' wording of B16, I find it odd that neither Deep Streams (B20.43) nor Water Obstacles (B21) have an effect on HE FP until you get to E5.5, although there does not seem to be CH vs boats. Things get even weirder when we switch to LCs (G12.63) wherein indirect fire is resolved normally vs LCs in water. Note that Wading in Shallow Ocean is treated as per Deep Stream but does get halving of HE except for CH, so in that respect it behaves as Sand.

It's like no two rules are allowed to share a coherent treatment of blast muffling!

I'm sorry my eyes were muffled reading that :D

A22.4 VULNERABILITY: Any Personnel unit possessing a FT must deduct one (per FT possessed) from the IFT resolution DR of any attack (including ordnance hits) against it.

E3.731 HE ATTACKS: All HE (not HE Equivalency; C8.31) attacks in Open Ground (see 3.65) must add a +1 TEM (cumulative with all other applicable TEM/Hindrance DRM) due to the cushioning effects of Deep Snow [EXC: Mines, Air Bursts, Specific Collateral Attacks, Direct Fire ordnance vs a vehicle (and its PRC)/pillbox (and its occupants)]. The Residual FP of such an attack is reduced by one IFT column (A8.26). FFMO still applies normally.

title: Gyrostabilizers in a Gun Duel
question:
I have a buttoned up tank with gyrostabilizers. I stop. An enemy tank declares defensive fire at me. I call for a gun duel. What are my modifiers?

I count +1 BU and +2 Bounding First Fire. I think that is correct, but my opponent questions this.
author: drmark64
consensus_answer:
Caution - Uninformed opinion (NRBH) - isn't there some sort of halving of the Gun Duel DRM for gyros?

Not necessarily, but could be.

American Vehicle Note R: This AFV had a very fast and accurate turret traverse, and also a better-than-normal ROF for a MA of its caliber. Therefore, this AFV is allowed the possibility of Multiple Hits (C3.8) even though its MA is > 40mm. Moreover, in a Gun Duel (C2.2401) its total Firer-based TH DRM are halved (FRD) prior to adding any Acquisition DRM. title: Heterodox routing - what do you think?
question:
A recent thread on the facebook ASL list has made me question whether my understanding of the rout rules is at odds with orthodox interpretation.  In an effort to better isolate to what extent I may or may not be failing to grok the system, I have created several scenarios below.  Each scenario involves one broken squad attempting to rout.  

Do you agree with my interpretations or not?  Please indicate what you think happens, and why.  

Scenario 1 - "Crawling Cover"

Until today, I would have said the broken unit has two choices:
1) declare the woods in 33H7 its rout target and rout F5, G6, H6, H7, taking interdiction in F5, G6, and H6, or 
2) low crawl into low crawl to F5 without suffering interdiction.

After re-reading A10.5 today, I wonder though whether this sentence --
"A broken unit may end its RtPh in an Open Ground hex in the LOS and Normal Range of a Known enemy unit without Interdiction only if it has used Low Crawl (10.52) to increase the distance between itself and the nearest Known enemy unit during that RtPh" means that the broken unit either takes interdiction even if it chooses option 2) above or is not even allowed to choose option 2.  Thoughts?

Scenario 2 - "Shellholes or Potholes?"

SSR: 33E6, F6 and G6 contain shellholes.

I believe the broken unit in this case has essentially four options (although option 1 below seems pointless in light of option 2):

1) Rout directly to 33H7 via E6, F6, G6, paying the open ground 1MF cost in each, and suffer interdiction 3 times.  
2) Same as above, but pay the shellhole 2MF cost for one of E6, F6 or G6, and suffer interdiction twice.
3) Pay the 2 MF cost in each of E6, F6, and G6 and end the RtPh in G6, suffering no interdiction.   
4) Low crawl to E6 and suffer no interdiction.  

Scenario 3 - "Back to the Future"

SSR: Grain is in season.  No quarter is not in effect.  

I'm fairly certain of the rules here, although it does make it seem as if the routers are able to see into the future.  

I believe the broken unit is required to surrender to the unit in 33U3.  

Why?  I believe R6 is the only valid rout target, and the only path to that target will subject the unit to interdiction crossing the S hexrow.  The only way to avoid that is low crawl, but since it is adjacent to a KEU it will surrender instead.  

Scenario 4 - "Grain is out of season!"

SSR: Grain is out of season.  

Until today my understanding was that the broken unit had a bunch of options here.  

1) Don't ignore 33Y1 and rout there via Y4, X3, X2, X1, and take a bunch of interdiction along the way. 
2) Ignore 33Y1, and rout to X0 instead, again via Y4, X3, X2, X1, and again taking a bunch of interdiction.  
3) Low crawl to Y5, Z5, or AA5, taking no interdiction. 

Per the facebook thread mentioned at the beginning of this post, option 3 does not appear to be one that is accepted by most players (including at least one ASLOK three-peater), but I can't figure out why.  Give me some quotes if you can figure this one out.  

My reasoning is that a unit only has to rout towards the nearest building/woods if it is able to reach that building/woods in that RtPh.  If the unit low crawls it obviously cannot reach a non-adjacent but otherwise nearest building/woods in that RtPh, and therefore is merely bound by the first strictures of A10.51 -- i.e. can't rout towards a KEU, nor adjacent to a KEU (unless leaving their hex).  

The alternative reading seems to be that a unit using low crawl may only do so into the first of hex of a hypothetical shortest (in MF) rout path towards the nearest building/woods.  I don't understand this reading though, since it seems to turn the "to" in "a routing unit must move to the nearest (in MF) building or woods hex (even if overstacked)" into a "towards".  

Scenario 5 - "4 MF Down the Lane"

SSR: Grain is in season.  No quarter is not in effect.

43Z8 is only 4 MF away "as the crow flies", but that 4MF path is not a legal rout path for the broken unit.  

My interpretation is that the routers can go pretty much anywhere they like in the Z4 or AA8 grain fields.  Alternately they could even low crawl to Z4 or AA8 (although why would they want to when they could rout further free from interdiction?) 

I'm frankly uncertain whether they could rout down the road starting in AA7 (towards DD3)... on the one hand they have legal rout options that do not require interdiction or low crawl, so they should not surrender via RtPh method... however, does that mean that a unit is obligated to exercise a legal rout path that doesn't involve low crawl/interdiction even if another otherwise legal rout path exists that involves low crawl/interdiction when they start the RtPh adjacent to a KEU?  My guess is that the rout down the road is not legal in this case, but it seems like a gray area.  

Scenario 6 - "A Similar Scenario"

SSR: Grain is in season.

This time the broken unit is 5MF down the lane from a woods hex, but that path would not be a legal rout (since it would require going adjacent to the KEU in 43Y6).  I think the routers in this case could go pretty much anywhere north-east of a line running W2-AA4-AA7-W9, taking any applicable interdiction if they leave the grain fields e.g. crossing the road in AA5.  

Scenario 7 - "Routs Yours is Mined"

SSR: Grain is in season.

The building in 16O4 is obviously the closest woods/building for the broken unit (3 MF direct route). Obviously one option is to rout N4-O4, and eat a minefield attack.  However, routers are not required to rout through known minefields.  There is a 6 MF route to 16O4 (via L4, L3, M3, N3) that gets them there without going through a minefield.  The question is, may the routing unit instead rout to the woods in M2 for 5 MF (L4, L3, M3, M2)?  I am agnostic on this question.  If I had to rule, I'd actually say that if the unit chooses not to rout through the minefield it is obligated to choose the then shorter route to the woods in M2.  

Wow.  My thanks if you made it through all that, and even more thanks if you've got some opinions (or even better, citations).  Oh, and if you Schwerpunkt guys ever need some scenario names, call me!  :whistle:
author: funnymarx

Where does the imperative to rout towards a woods/building come from if you are not reaching that woods/building in one RtPh?

See last sentence of A10.52:
"...All other Rout provisions apply unchanged to Low Crawl, e.g., rout must still be towards the nearest woods/building Location within 6 MF."

The interesting thing here is my initial reading of 10.51 does not say this.  To me it doesn't say that a rout must be "towards" the nearest woods/building, but rather "to"!  

[...]Assuming it can abide by the previous requirements, a routing unit must move to the nearest (in MF calculated at the start of its RtPh) building or woods hex (even if overstacked) unless that route is through/into a known minefield or FFE, or is not traversable (e.g., through a Blaze, unbridged Water Obstacle, Cliff, etc.). As long as it reaches that hex during a single RtPh, it need not use the shortest route, but as long as it follows the shortest path in MF otherwise, it may enter a shellhole/entrenchment/pillbox to avoid Interdiction even if it can no longer reach that woods/building hex in a single RtPh. A routing unit can rout into/out of/within a known minefield or FFE at its option, but is not forced to do so merely to reach the closest woods/building hex. At the start of its RtPh, a routing unit must designate its destination and must attempt to reach it during that RtPh [EXC: if using Low Crawl]. 

I had assumed that the underlined "EXC" above meant that units using low crawl did not have to "designate its designation and must attempt to reach it during that RtPh".  Evidently the consensus interpretation though, is that the EXC only applies to "reach it during that RtPh" i.e. the decision to use low crawl is made AFTER a unit has designated a destination.  

My understanding of the rout rules in light of this thread is that units must:

1) find the woods/building hex(es) which has the shortest route (in MF) that doesn't involve moving closer/adjacent to a KEU (in other words not "as the crow flies" closest in MF)

2) if multiple hexes are determined in step 1, choose and designate one of them

3) if the route determined is greater than 6 MF in length, then rout wherever you like as long as you don't get closer/adjacent to a KEU, otherwise

4) do one of the following:
     4a) low crawl into the first hex of the route determined in step 1 and 2 and stop.
     4b) rout along the route determined in steps 1 and 2 and reach the target hex
     4c) if the MF cost to reach the target is less than 6 MF, route along a different route that costs up to 6 MF and still allows you to reach the target hex

Does this sound correct?  

My previous interpretation of these rules gave the router somewhat more leeway in their direction than what appears to be the consensus interpretation.

title: Loading passengers
question:
Hi guys.
I need your help to understand the example on D6.4 (1st edition rules) referring to loading passengers.
The text reads: "a squad carrying five PP has only two MF and must expend them both to enter that Open Ground hex and load onto the vehicle unless it is accompanied by a SMC (A4,12, A4.42) carrying no PP of its own, thereby leaving the vehicle with one-fourth of its MP remaining for that MPh.".

Now, doesn't a stack like that own four MF (two for the squad plus leader bonus)? That means it retains two MF after loading, therefore leaving the vehicle with half of its MP, not one.fourth....
What am I missing?

Thanks for your help!
author: federicost
consensus_answer:
Look at 6.4, last sentence. A leader cannot apply his MF bonus to units that load/unload during the same MPh, but he can add his IPC. 

So in the second case the stack IPC is 4, the SW PP is 5 and the stack MF capability is thus 3. One to move, one to load and only one MF is left. So the vehicle has 1/4 of its MP left.

author: phil d

...The exception is if you have a Forward Location containing an armed, Known, non-Disrupted enemy unit; in that case, you *must* enter that location whether it increases the Range or not, unless it is already occupied by a friendly armed unit (A25.233).
I am not sure that you can do that. A25.233 specifies that the Location must be "Enterable" and I am not sure it is "Enterable" if you would be moving away from the Hex Grain while marked with a Range-counter.

I know that there was an issue with this in the article in Journal 9 (?). I still have the email-conversation about it - I will look it up later.

Re-reading the rule, I believe Klas is right:

From A25.233:  "If a Forward Location enterable (my emphasis) by a HW Unit is devoid of armed, friendly units and contains an armed, Known, non-Disrupted enemy unit, the HW Unit must move to that Location, or to another enterable Location that contains either a Known enemy unit or a pillbox occupied by such a unit."

The Range paragraph (A25.2321) defines what hexes a HW unit may 'enter' so I think that flows through to A25.233.  I was fixated on the whole 'higher numbered rule' thing, but this is consistent within the context of the Human Wave segment.  Sorry to lead you astray, Phil!

JR

Phil, there aren't many silly questions when it comes to Human Waves (HW) - it's a lot to grasp the first time through.  The Soviet squads going into N1 and O2 are moving away from the HW Alternate Hex Grain (AHG) as defined in the example.  Both N1 and O2 are moving 'away' from P2, part of the HW AHG.  This just means they can't then go to M2 (offmap) and N2 respectively, and must veer back in to N2 for the N1 squad, and O3 for the O2 squad.  

It's a lot more clear when the HW runs along the hex grain, where you can move 'away' one hexrow and just continue down that row.  With an AHG Wave, you must zag back every time you zig out.  The exception is if you have a Forward Location containing an armed, Known, non-Disrupted enemy unit; in that case, you *must* enter that location whether it increases the Range or not, unless it is already occupied by a friendly armed unit (A25.233).  

JR

title: Unhooking and DF
question: A unit fires on a halftrack and gun in the act of unhooking.  The MG getts rate, but the gun crew pins.  Is the gun unhooked?  Does the PIN negate the hazardous movement?
author: Turdsocket
consensus_answer:
A unit fires on a halftrack and gun in the act of unhooking.  The MG getts rate, but the gun crew pins. Is the gun unhooked?
No - see D5.43 and its example.

Does the PIN negate the hazardous movement?
Attempting to (un)hook a Gun is not an activity subject to Hazardous Movement.

author: Lamskiy

The Index is your friend :

Good Order (a Personnel unit or vehicular inherent crew which is neither broken, berserk, captured, stunned, shocked, or held in Melee; or a SW which is fully manned by a Good Order Personnel unit, and is not malfunctioned, or restricted by an Ammunition Shortage)

C6.5 ... title: Shellhole Creation
question:
(Playing 'Eye of the Tiger' with the Prinz Eugen shelling the coastline).

A shellhole is created in a brush hex. I can't find the rule that says the brush no longer exists. Does it exist?
author: drmark64
consensus_answer:
I noticed that the PTO rules were specific in saying that the original terrain is removed.

Yes there is rule G8.72 which says:
"Shellholes can occur IN Drained/In-Season (only) paddy hexes, in which case the terrain characteristics IN those hexes will change accordingly (the banks in those hexes would be unaffected)"

With the example:
"Shellholes IN an In-Season paddy allow Infantry to enter both that hex’s interior and the shellholes simultaneously, at a cost of two MF plus any cost to cross a bank. In addition, the grain in that paddy hex is considered non-existent for all purposes."

So it looks like whoever wrote this rule assumed that Shellholes removes the terrain in the hex.

However, rule C1.823 indicates that the terrain is not removed, since it talks about Shellholes and Flame creation in the same hex during a Bombardement (and a Flame can only be placed if there is still some burnable terrain in the hex).

title: Newbie question on infiltration
question:
Gents would I be right in thinking that if the attacker had a roll of 2 in close combat
They can attack the defender and then withdraw and if the defender rolled 
A 12 the attacker would attack then could withdraw but if the attacker rolled a twelve would the defender be able to withdraw I don't think it can but I wanted to make sure, 
many thanks in advance.
author: phil d
consensus_answer:
Gents would I be right in thinking that if the attacker had a roll of 2 in close combat
They can attack the defender and then withdraw and if the defender rolled 
A 12 the attacker would attack then could withdraw but if the attacker rolled a twelve would the defender be able to withdraw I don't think it can but I wanted to make sure, 
many thanks in advance.

Phil, 2s and 12s temporarily suspend the simultaneity of CC - if the Attacker rolls a 2, the effects are applied and he may immediately withdraw.  If he doesn't withdraw, surviving Defenders (if any) may attack.  If the Attacker rolls a 12, the Defender may withdraw, but must forgo making a CC roll of his own.  If the Attacker rolls something other than a 2 or a 12 and the Defender then rolls a 12, the Attacker may withdraw, and finally, if the Defender rolls a 2, he may withdraw.  We always have the Attacker roll first for this reason - it's the possibility of snakes and boxcars that might scramble the results.

Here's the rule, just for completeness:

11.22 INFILTRATION: The simultaneous nature of CC is momentarily suspended following an Original CC DR of 2/12. Provided it has not already been eliminated/captured/pinned, any Infantry/Cavalry unit which rolls an Original 2 CC DR may withdraw from CC/Melee immediately thereafter in the same CCPh without being attacked, even if it did not eliminate the defenders (see also Field Promotions; 18.12). Any Infantry/Cavalry unit(s) attacked by an Original 12 CC DR may likewise withdraw from CC immediately thereafter, assuming it has not been eliminated by that 12 CC DR. If the option to withdraw is taken, it must be done immediately; the unit cannot wait to make its own attack (if it has not yet done so) or see the outcome of other attacks before leaving. See also Ambush Withdrawal (11.41).

title: ASL Rulebook -  Edition Changes
question: Have been playing ASL on the Starter Kit level and was wondering if I wanted to expand it to include the rules on Snipers and Heat of Battle, would these be covered correctly in the 1st edition rulebook, which now can be purchased at  give-away prices, or were there many changes to these rules in the 2nd edition?
author: Joel Marconi
consensus_answer:
That's why the Starter Kit route is recommended: less severe Personal Morale Check. :surprise:

Hold on now, the ASLSK path is definitely NOT recommended by everyone. 

Everyone should be made aware that thousands of players learned how to play this game before the advent of the starter kit. 

The starter kit came out in 2004. ASL came out in 1985. Count em. That's 20 years of people playing without the streamlining starter kits. 

In fact, it was only the success of ASL without starter kits that led to the idea of funding starter kits, as an overall trend in the hobby to streamline board games in general (in response to ever-increasing sophistication of computerized games the kids are more drawn to these days) 

The starter kit streamlines ASL play and is not ASL because critical aspects of game play are ignored to make it easier and faster to play. 

It's true that the ASLRB is more of an elephant but it's a more satisfying meal at the end of the day :) In other words, you wind up with higher morale and learn how to play the game properly. 

 what about voluntary breaking of squads, realistic or just a game mechanic?

They had to fix that voluntary breaking because some players used it to vol  break Japanese way back in the forest, rout them forward, then rally them along the trail because of the commisar effect (no DM). I had published the tactic in a replay in my fanzine and I got a bunch of grognards upset; as a result, MacNamara changed the rule so that vol break had to be in LOS of a known enemy unit. 

So that was unrealistic! 

But voluntary break under the LOS/fire of enemy is not. The old movie 'The Longest Day' demonstrates a voluntary break situation by the French attackers of that fortified building with an AA Gun on the roof. Until a Sherman tank arrives to save the day. 

So if the main gun has an issue, I suspect the loader, gunner, and tank commander will be very distracted.

Your suspicions duly noted. Since it's unlikely either of us served the armed forces in a tank, neither of us know.

With the gunner and TC being on the coax and AA MG, if they are focused on MG repair (so not finding targets, telling the driver where to drive, and calling out targets to the bow gunner), the machine gun fire will suffer greatly and will not be effective.  That's my story and I am sticking with it... :D

Well you make it sound impossible for a tank to operate even when all of its systems are functioning nominally. I don't think tankers were trained to panic when something went wrong and act like keystone cops :) 

Also these comments fail to address the real issue in the game, which is inconsistency in how the repair rules operate different with to tank MA, resulting in the non-sensical and slightly ridiculous tactic of avoid repair entirely.

Well that is where I landed and then thought, I didn't make a huge investment on some "game" so I came up with a new narrative...

The tank is engaged in intense combat with the enemy.  Something goes wrong with the main gun, maybe the ready rack is depleted, maybe it is jammed, maybe something broke, whatever.  So the tank crew can do one of 2 things.  Keep fighting with the tanks other weapons (tracks, machine guns) and forget the main gun for the moment or focus on repairing the main gun.  Sure, another tank may show up and if it does, they can try to repair the main gun or they can flee.  I think messing with the main gun would require a lot of the crews attention so for the immediate short term, the tank commander decided to fish for now and help the infantry locked in combat and cut bait later and figure out what is wrong with the gun after the combat dies down a bit.

But you all are probably right...:yuk:

I understand what you are getting at here :) The fact is, though, in the game, each tank can fire it's machine guns at will even when the MA is working. Only the gunner is going to be trying to fix the main gun, the driver and co-driver will still be manning the MGs in the front as usual. Maybe the commander would be trying to help if he's not CE firing the AAMG. 

Any way I slice it, the repair roll covers the narrative -- a roll of 1 clears the jam, 2-5 still working on it (or too busy as you say) and a roll of 6 breaks it ----

another question to consider -- which would also fix this malarkey -- why is there mandatory recall if the MA is broken? [edit -- disabled]

'Oh yeah I'm gonna stay on the battlefield by NOT trying to repair my MA because if I REALLY break it for sure by trying to fix it, I have to return to HQ' :laugh:

ASL is supercool but some of these notions they have carried forward from the old days.... heh

If that rule were eliminated, problem solved. Then, just like every other broken weapon in the game, the treadheads would try to fix their gun's MA every chance they got. Cheers, thanks for the discussion!

I will have you know that I have much experience in armored warfare.  I played a lot of  back in the day. Does that count? :D

To boil it down, fixing the tank main gun strikes me as very much an internal (to the tank) task, fighting and driving the tank is very much external task, I don't see how a tank crew can effectively do both at the same time.  Sure they have their individual duties but only one guy has a complete view of what is going on and only then if he pops his head out and looks around at great risk. They need their crew mates to help them know what to do and when. title: Rout with No Quarter penalties in effect
question:
Hi everybody. I need advice from ASL experts.
Referring to the Comprehensive Rout Example (page A28 in ASL rules 2nd edition):

The text reads (first paragraph, second sentence): "The broken squad in L8 would rout in L7 and suffer interdiction there and any survivors would be unable to rout further without moving closer to the KEU's in K6 and Q8: unable to rout away from the ADJACENT unbroken KEU in L8, the broken unit would be eliminated for Failure to Rout."

Now, there's something I don't get here.
First: what does KEU in Q8 have anything to do, since it's never in the LOS of the broken unit? I think the broken unit in L8 could rout in L7 suffering Interdiction and, if survives, could then enter M7 building...
Second: the broken unit could also try to rout in K8, since it's not getting closer to any enemy unit in LOS...

Am I missing something?
Thank you for any counseling!
author: federicost
consensus_answer:
First up I has to rout towards woods or building and the first non-ignoreable woods/building is M7 ( since that building will bring it farther away from all KEUs (in J9, L8 and M9) [10.51].)
Thus the prohibition of routing to K8.
Now whether the LOS from L7 to Q8 is clear is something I am not sure about from the picture but given the example I would expect it to have been checked.
Remember you are above thehedges in L7 so can see over them. You might clip the M8 woods but are unlikely.

Now if you are adjacent to a KEU and unable to rout away without using low crawl or suffering interdiction, you will surrender.
The Rout to L7 can be interdicted.
( squad in M9 as well as the AFV MG in L8 can Interdict the rout to either K8 or L7 because the +1 Height Advantage TEM does not apply when the LOS crosses the Crest Line traversed by the moving unit [B10.31])
Thus he will surrender to the adjacent unit.

I attatch the full paragraph:

The broken squad in L8 must rout since it is in the same hex as an unbroken KEU and not in Melee. It must rout towards building M7 since that building will bring it farther away from all KEUs (in J9, L8 and M9) [10.51]. The first hex it enters while routing cannot be L9 or M8 since that would be moving ADJACENT to the unbroken KEU in M9. It cannot enter K9 from L8 since that would be moving closer to the KEU in J9. Therefore, the first hex it routs through must be K8 or L7. It cannot Low Crawl when leaving an enemy-occupied Location [10.52] and the squad in M9 as well as the AFV MG in L8 can Interdict the rout to either K8 or L7 because the +1 Height Advantage TEM does not apply when the LOS crosses the Crest Line traversed by the moving unit [B10.31]. Therefore, the broken unit cannot rout without being subject to Interdiction and since No Quarter is not in effect, it Surrenders [20.21], and the squad in M9 accepts the Surrender.

title: Hooking a gun vs loading passengers
question:
In D6.4 we can read that:

6.4 LOADING: A vehicle must be stopped to embark Passengers/Riders. It may move in the same MPh after they load, but it may not move in that MPh prior to their loading (including the expenditure of a MP to bring a Motion vehicle to a stop) [EXC: Infantry hooking up a Gun, C10.11]. 

If we check C10.11,

10.11 HOOKING UP: A Stopped vehicle not in Bypass may hook up a Gun (if the vehicle's T# ≤ the Gun's M#) by spending half (FRU) of its MP/MF allotment [EXC: if the Gun's M# is circled (e.g. M(6), the vehicle must expend two-thirds (FRU) of its MP/MF allotment] in that Gun's hex (in addition to any required MP/MF cost to enter the hex), provided a crew (as per 10.111) is on foot in that hex. This expenditure does not itself qualify that vehicle as a moving target, but does allow Defensive First Fire opportunities against it (that Gun shares its target status and is destroyed or missed depending on the fate of the vehicle). That Gun is then placed on top of that vehicle to indicate that it is in tow. Neither that Gun, its crew, nor that vehicle/its PRC can fire during that PFPh/MPh and all are TI for the rest of that Player Turn. That crew may also load into that towing vehicle at no extra MP/MF cost as it hooks up that Gun, but if it expends > half its MF allotment in pushing/entering that Gun's hex, that Gun cannot then be hooked up by that unit in that MPh. A non-QSU Gun (10.23) must first be limbered (10.21) before it can be hooked up. See 10.31 for pushing and hooking up a Gun in the same MPh.

And 10.31,

10.31 A Gun can be pushed and then hooked up during the same MPh, but only if its pushing Infantry can still attempt to push that Gun another hex in that MPh (i.e., can attempt another Manhandling DR), and only if the vehicle has not yet exceeded the specified MP/MF expenditure for hooking up (10.11). No Manhandling DR is actually required for hooking up or unhooking.

As I read it, it means that a vehicle that starts its turn in Motion is forbidden to load passengers, but it can hook a gun and load its crew.

Isn't that strange?
author: esparver73
consensus_answer:
The sequencing is an obvious artifice:  move then hook up for Guns; load up then move for infantry.

Neither is "correct".  Both are an attempt to roughly model fluid events in a structured turn.

There are good reasons for the differences (in terms of game mechanics) because of the differences in the way Guns and infantry move without vehicles:  if a vehicle could only hook up before moving, in practical terms the vehicle would usually need to drive to the Gun's location the turn before [EXC:  Guns manhandled into the vehicles hex].

That consideration does not apply to infantry:  they are highly mobile on foot, so getting vehicle and putative passengers into the same location before the vehicle moves is much easier (EX: after the vehicle's previous turn's movement is finished the infantry could use its MPh and APh to reach the vehicle's location).

I think that is enough to justify the different mechanics for loading (and the hooking up of Guns comes up rarely enough that the scope for confusion is limited).

title: Journal 10 Errata:  Rule B10.1 (Terrain on hexes with Crestlines):  Example of it's impact
question:
We were having a discussion of the Journal 10 errata re: rule B10.1 in another forum (http://www.boardgamegeek.com/thread/962369/crest-line-los) and I decided to go look at some boards to see the impact.

I got no further than board 2.

Comments?  Other observations?
author: fubar awol
consensus_answer:
Is there really anything new here from when the late Ian Daglish wrote his article about vehicles in woods for VFTT #45?

http://www.vftt.co.uk/vfttpdf/vftt45.pdf

Finally, a few unrelated points which have certainly confused me in the past. When a crest line runs through a woods hex, all woods in the hex are considered to be at the higher level. In other words, treat the entire woods depiction as if it were sitting on the higher side of the crest line. This is true also for other terrain types: e.g., grain, brush, building, but not for Inherent Terrain which in effect follows the contour of the crest line (see B10.1 for Examples). In other words, all of the woods depiction in a hex always rises to the same height, but the height of Inherent Terrain depends on the crest line.

Also remember that any unit bypassing the woods in a hex is assumed to be moving through the higher level of the hex, and expend MF/MP accordingly, even if no crest line appears to be crossed. You can bypass the woods in the hex, but if you enter the hex you must do so at the highest level. 

Look at the B10.31 Example on page B13. If there were woods in the center of hex BB1, either German unit could bypass them, but the 4-6-7 would have to pay the doubled MF to ascend the crest line (though it would still be subject to FFMO/FFNAM as HA would not apply). Odd though it might sound, the 4-6-7 would still be visible over any half-hex obstacle such as a wall or hedge, but would not qualify for HA. 

Philippe Leonard’s “Look at Bypass” in Annual ‘93a addresses this and other issues.

Remember though, that this LOS is only clear if the players agree to "use" the new footnote (3A) to B10.1.

B10.1 (with J10 errata in red):
"...Other terrain (e.g., grain, brush, woods, building) is at the higher level throughout the entire depiction of the terrain in question for LOS purposes (but the actual Crest Line is always used for movement purposes), even if it appears to be rising from the lower level portion of the hill hex [EXC: Newer boards may depict visible Crest Lines beneath this other terrain (EX: 61F8), in which case the actual Crest Line is used to determine LOS as is the case with Inherent Terrain]3A...."

Finally, a few unrelated points which have certainly confused me in the past. When a crest line runs through a woods hex, all woods in the hex are considered to be at the higher level. In other words, treat the entire woods depiction as if it were sitting on the higher side of the crest line. This is true also for other terrain types: e.g., grain, brush, building, but not for Inherent Terrain which in effect follows the contour of the crest line (see B10.1 for Examples). In other words, all of the woods depiction in a hex always rises to the same height, but the height of Inherent Terrain depends on the crest line.

Also remember that any unit bypassing the woods in a hex is assumed to be moving through the higher level of the hex, and expend MF/MP accordingly, even if no crest line appears to be crossed. You can bypass the woods in the hex, but if you enter the hex you must do so at the highest level. 

Look at the B10.31 Example on page B13. If there were woods in the center of hex BB1, either German unit could bypass them, but the 4-6-7 would have to pay the doubled MF to ascend the crest line (though it would still be subject to FFMO/FFNAM as HA would not apply). Odd though it might sound, the 4-6-7 would still be visible over any half-hex obstacle such as a wall or hedge, but would not qualify for HA.

title: Wall Advantage question
question:
I originally learnt ASL under the 1st Edition rules and after a break of some 15 years am back playing it again now under 2nd Edition rules. The wording (possibly the rules themselves) appear to have changed for 'Wall Advantage' and my oponent and I were left struggling over the follwing (fairly basic) case yesterday.

An SSR was in effect that all hedges were stone walls. There were also more squads on the board but these were all that were relevant.

The British squad highlighted in green, fired at the German squad during the  Prep fire phase and the german squad used the +3 TEM for the building. This had no effect on the German squad.

In the movement phase the British squad highlighted in red, successfully threw smoke into F5 and then assault moved into it. The German squad then First Fired at the now adjacent British squad - does the British squad get to claim immediate WA against that defensive fire?

The example in the 2nd edition rulebook (and which I notice is still the same as the one in the 1st edition rulebook, despite the extensive wording changes) suggests not as the British squad has entered the adjacent hex during that move - however as the German squad used the +3 TEM of the building in the British Prep fire phase has it relinquished the ability to claim WA for subsequent actions that turn.

Thanks in advance.
author: domus_ludorum
consensus_answer:
The German unit could not claim the wall TEM during the British MPh - it would have had to have been marked with a WA counter from the preceding German APh (or a prior point in the game).
The Germans in F4 could also have claim WA during the British Player Turn Rally Phase.

Also, if the British unit in G5 (which took WA when it entered G5) later moved away in its MPh, the Germans in F4 can claim WA again (regardless of whether it has claimed the building TEM earlier this turn), per B9.322: "Claiming WA is voluntary [EXC: 9.323], and can be done by a unit at five times:... ...whenever all enemy units lose/forfeit WA over shared wall/hedge hexsides..."

replies.body: The British squad can immediately claim wall advantage. (Also note there were errata pages on this topic published in Action Pack 4, make sure you get those).

question:

- a unit can always see "downhill" as long as each hex depicts a "one level lower" Hill.

title: Vehicle Bounding Firre
question:
Quick question on vehicle bounding.

A vehicle starts its turn under a motion counter, and wants to move one hex forward, and take the best bounding first fire shot it can.  

So it moves one hex, and then delays for 4MP to get the best shot.  In order for it not to be moving during the shot, does it have to spend a movement point to stop?  If so, does it matter when it spends the MP to stop?  ie. if it does the delay first, then the stop, it is still a moving target if fired on during the delay.  

Thanks
author: Number_41
consensus_answer:
Quick question on vehicle bounding.

A vehicle starts its turn under a motion counter, and wants to move one hex forward, and take the best bounding first fire shot it can.  

So it moves one hex, and then delays for 4MP to get the best shot.  In order for it not to be moving during the shot, does it have to spend a movement point to stop?  If so, does it matter when it spends the MP to stop?  ie. if it does the delay first, then the stop, it is still a moving target if fired on during the delay.  

Thanks  

You're basically right, except that you can't actually spend delay while in motion. You can, however, always pay "extra" to enter a hex, so in this case (and many others) it's a distinction without a difference.

So whether you over-spend to enter and then stop or you stop and then delay, it's going to work out the same. And, yes, you will need to stop before bounding firing to get the best odds.

I assume you're just coming into LOS of the target? That's the only reason the MPs spent would matter at all.

S

The vehicle would be a moving target all the turn, because it is under a motion counter at the start of its MPh. Once you are a moving target (because either you moved at least one hex, or you started in motion), you are for the entire turn.

Another small point - you can only spend Delay MPs if you are Stopped.  However, you can simply 'overspend' as Spencer points out when you enter the hex.  Ideally, enter expending three MPs, spend the fourth to Stop, then fire.

JR
Remember that to get (or suffer from) the point blank modifier, you need to be stopped as does your target.
...and , before you both start flinging dice, reread the Gun Duel section to see if it is applicable.
... and IF you spent 4MPs as delay, you have to spend them one-at-a-time.
...but what Martin said still applies for PB TH DRM.

title: Quick Dash question
question:
I declare a dash, and bravely send a squad out into the street.  A concealed enemy squad drops concealment to fire it's MMG, declaring a fire lane.  The dash would 1/2 the shot, but the rules say: 

"All non-ordnance Defensive First Fire vs a Dashing unit in the road Location is considered Area Fire except for Fire Lanes and pre-existing Residual FP, but FFMO/FFNAM DRM apply normally."

If I'm reading this correctly, despite the dash being declared, this is a 4 down 2 shot for the MMG?
author: madDdog67
consensus_answer:
A9.22 ...he must place First Fire counter on the MG and, after resolving that First Fire attack in the normal manner, must also place a Fire Lane Residual FP counter..

You resolve the first fire attack normally as area fire, after that you place the fire lane. Fire lane would have to be already there when the dashing unit enters the road, for that bolded bit to be applicable.

replies.body: I have always understood this to be existing fire lanes.

A9.22 ...he must place First Fire counter on the MG and, after resolving that First Fire attack in the normal manner, must also place a Fire Lane Residual FP counter..

You resolve the first fire attack normally as area fire, after that you place the fire lane. Fire lane would have to be already there when the dashing unit enters the road, for that bolded bit to be applicable.

I'm pretty new to this, so for what it's worth, here is my take.  

They way it's worded implies to me it is talking about not halving the FP from fire-lane markers.  Residual FP and (marked) fire-lane FP is already halved, and the rules are saying don't halve those again.  So if a fire-lane already exists and you dash through it, the FP is as marked on the fire-lane counter and not halved.  

However, you declare a fire-lane in conjunction with a first fire attack.  The rules (9.22) are pretty clear on this - first you complete your DFF, then you place the fire-lane.  So if this is the first unit the defendiner is firing on and he wants to lay down a fire-lane, he must declare DFF at the dashing unit and that he will put down a firelane as well.  As this attack is DFF, it would be halved as Area Fire against a Dashing target (assuming all dashing requirements are met).  

Since fire-lanes are a special form of residual firepower, they will attack a unit entering the location, not leaving.  So if it's just the on unit dashing and the MMG opens up on it, it will get it's DFF attack at 1/2 FP (for dashing).  The defender can lay down a fire-lane, but that will not affect the dashing unit taking the DFF.  Any other units dashing across the fire-lane later will be affected by the fire-lane, but will not have to take any DFF (barring ROF).  

In all these cases though the FFNAM and FFMO both apply, so there's a chance it will get ugly regardless.

Successfully Withdrawing unit(s) enter(s) Accessible Location(s) (A11.21-.22); resolve, vs Withdrawing unit/stack (only), each FFE (C1.51-.53 (C1.71-.72; C1.9; E12.5; G14.65-.661})/minefield (B28.41-.412) attack as it occurs, and cheek for Column Disbandment (E11.533)/trip flare activation (E1.95)/Panji MC (G9.41). First, declare first/next sequential attack, or, ATTACKER first, all simultaneous attacks

Then, declare if HtH 

Then, reveal all units making/directing a CC attack

8.21B
1) Declare the first sequential attack
2) Declare if the first sequential attack is HtH

8.24B Resolve the first sequential attack. Repeat 8.21B for the next sequential attack.

title: Gun Size + Range Effect on Armor Penetration
question: It seems from reading the AP TO KILL TABLES, that smaller size weapons have greater armor penetration at smaller distances. e.g. at range 0-1, 25mm and under guns receive a +2 TK modifier, while a 65mm and over, receive only a +1 at the same distance.  Am I reading/interpreting this correctly?
author: Rammstein69
consensus_answer:
It seems from reading the AP TO KILL TABLES, that smaller size weapons have greater armor penetration at smaller distances. e.g. at range 0-1, 25mm and under guns receive a +2 TK modifier, while a 65mm and over, receive only a +1 at the same distance.  Am I reading/interpreting this correctly?

Yes, Richard, you're reading it correctly.  At very short ranges, the lightest weapons get a bigger boost.  By the same token, at longer ranges, the penetration of lighter weapons falls off at a faster rate.  

JR

The rule answers your question,

"Half-level LOS obstacle..."   It doesn't negate the Hedge/wall simply because the non-rubble hex occupants along the H/W may still gain the benefit of the H/W...  

I don't know of any obstacle that is SEEN through.

the point I was making is that the TEM is the part of the wall that is not negated

Yes, but that's not the issue. According to the Q&A posted here the TEM part is not negated but the LOS part is negated.  Which is contrary to the rule which states: 

“B24.3 Ground level rubble is a Half-Level LOS obstacle through the entire hex (including hexsides but without negating any hedge/wall).

So, according to the Q&A, when the RB says "without negating any hedge/wall" what it really means is "without negeating the TEM of hedge/wall" because according to the Perry Says Q&A the LOS part* is negated.  .  

*The "LOS Part" being that you CAN see along the length of a wall when adjacent, but you CANNOT see along the length of a rubble hexside when adjacent.  Therefore rubble negates the Wall/Hedge hexside-length LOS.

Looks to me that what the rule (B24.2) is saying is that even though the rubble does not negate the wall/hedge it is still inherent terrain along such a hexside.

There is nothing (as far as I know) that says a LOS along a wall/hedge hexside cannot be blocked/hindered by other terrain in the hexes of that hexside - e.g., an Orchard would hinder such a LOS (a graveyard would not, since those rules specifically say that the graveyard does not effect wall/hedge hexsides).

title: Concealment and Melee
question:
A concealed attacker and an unconcealed defender are about to start their first CCPh together. The attacker decides not to attack in CC. The defender attacks in CC and has no effect.

Normally no melee results. However the attacker wishes to drop concealment after the defender resolves his CC attack to force a melee to result. Is the attacker allowed to do this?
author: drmark64
consensus_answer:
I'd say yes.

A12.14 says you can drop concealment at any time (with the noted exception above).

A11.15 and 11.19 describes how concealment in melee is handled.

During the CCPh the concealed unit may choose not to attack. I would place a CC marker there. It is one sided though. The concealed unit is under the restrictions of the CC marker, i.e. it cannot fire outside the location. The unconcealed unit is under no such restriction. When one side or the other leaves the location the CC marker and TPBF restrictions go away.
Note though that it is not the CC counter that limits its fire opportunities.

Personally I wouldn't place a CC counter (since the rules don't call for it I think), but I see no harm in doing so either.
I'd place a CC counter only to remind me that the stack is not locked in Melee...

Hi Martin,

It was about a year ago… my recollection is that the unit had to rout away from the Adjacent enemy unit. The first hex of the rout "toward" the closest building/woods hex took the routing unit down over a crest line and completely out of LOS of all enemy units. No interdiction. Not even a LOS to the hex.

I wanted to simply Low Crawl away from that unit over the crest line and out of LOS. No interdiction.

So reading the rule you indicate above (A20.21), I always read that rule to mean that a broken unit had to surrender if the only way it could avoid interdiction was to use low crawl. I read this as interdiction forcing Low Crawl.

Thus, "or only able to rout while being subject to Interdiction or resorting to Low Crawl" did not seem at all to apply to my unit, because it simply wanted to low crawl the one hex out of LOS of all enemy units.

It wasn't forced to low crawl, as the hex it desired to rout to was totally out of enemy LOS and therefore not subject to interdiction.

What Gary brought into the picture was this idea (new to me and my rules) that the unit could not low crawl... because if the unit for some reason actually tried to rout it's full rout phase movement allowance, it would at some hypothetical future hex (the 3rd potential hex in this instance) become subject to interdiction.

So I was like "what idiot would rout the unit three hexes and get it interdicted… when the unit can simply rout one hex (using low crawl) and be safe and happy.

I still dont know where the clarification or errata or whatever exists that says that routing unit is somehow ineligible for low crawl???

He used low crawl because I wanted to rout the one hex out of enemy LOS.

The clarification that was presented to me was simply that "if at any future point in the unit's rout it would be subject to interdiction, then it must surrender."

Not sure if that is true or not. I assume it is because it came from Gary. Dont know where he heard it. But it is an interesting application of the rule. Different from how I would literally read the low crawl rule.

title: Rules Question: Advance Phase - can you advance into a hex that costs more MF than you have?

Can you advance into a hex that costs more MF than you have?

Hmmm... 4.72 seems to bracket the question and therefore allow it.

Am I missing something?
author: fubar awol
consensus_answer:
Hi Klaus - the Q&A reference from ancient times is probably the reason I've played interpretation (2) all these years.  However, I don't think your statement "doesn't limit it in any other way" is correct.

The statement is also intended to apply to "otherwise it may advance but becomes CX in the process".  in other words: the unit is "limited" by the statement in that it becomes CX if spending 4 or more or all.
I don't see the "becoming CX" as a limitation - it is a consequence of making the advance.

So I'll stick with my original statement: if you focus on what the rules allow - they do not allow you to advance if you have insufficient MF to enter the hex (per a strict reading).
I disagree - in fact rule A4.7 ADVANCE places no requirement on having any MF available at all. And then A4.72 only requires you to have a least 1 MF left after deducting for PP.

I think the Q&A was asked because the wording of A4.72 in the 1st Edition was diffent that it is now.

title: aquiring markers
question:
I find the aquiring markers provided with this game really annoying and suprisingly unevolved for a game that prides itself on intelligence.

Advanced Tobruk exhibits the same problem (though they are call Burst on Target in that series...)

There seems to be a plethora of different counters marked with letters that are meant to correspond with the letters on AFV or gun counters to show who has aquired who.

But there are never enough counters.or there are guns and AFVs with the same letters.

Lock n Load gets round this by providing PAIRS of markers, each sharing a letter or number. One is marked Aquiring and is placed on the shooting counter and the other is marked either - 1 or -2 to indicate hit modifiers and is placed on the target.

why didn't ASL do this?

look I'm making a pig's dinner of this. Someone please provide me with a rational system for plotting who has aquired who.

Sorry, early morning.
author: nickp
consensus_answer:
Someone please provide me with a rational system for plotting who has aquired who.
Hmmm... I've never had any problems using Acquisition counters.

Let's look at "Paw of the Tiger" as an example:

The Russians have 18 T-34s, 6 each of three different models, with IDs from "A" to "F". You obviously can't use a single color for all 18 Russian tanks, so instead each T-34 model gets its own color.

Once the Acq counters come into play, most players can remember which color goes with which T-34 model. If necessary, you can also jot down the assignments on a piece of paper (blue = T-34 M41, etc.), but I've never had to do this.

The Germans have two Tigers, two Pz IIIs, and an AT Gun, so they have a couple of options. They can carefully select their five units so that each one has a different ID, allowing them to use a single color of Acq counter. Or, like the Russians, they can assign a different color to each of the three types: Tiger, Pz III, AT Gun.

If you are just a starting out in ASL and only have Beyond Valor, then you might not have enough different colors of Acq counters to handle a scenario with a lot of different units. But many of the add-on modules include additional Acq counters, so as you expand your ASL system you should eventually have plenty of different colors to use.

Lock n Load gets round this by providing PAIRS of markers, each sharing a letter or number. One is marked Aquiring and is placed on the shooting counter and the other is marked either - 1 or -2 to indicate hit modifiers and is placed on the target.

why didn't ASL do this?
For ASL, this sounds like overkill that would just clutter up the map with unnecessary counters. ASL's single Acq counter system seems to work fine for most players.

title: Is a Dummy Stack revealed in the Advance Phase?
question:
Greetings all,

I hope it's okay to post rules questions and confirmations here. I record rules questions as I play and check them out later. Most questions I can find the answer but I really would like to confirm my understanding with this august body.

Please confirm that a dummy stack is NOT revealed when an enemy unit advances in during the Advance Phase.

If the dummy stack does not get revealed it would be revealed during any ensuing close combat; however, it'd be a neat trick to have the dummy stack achieve ambush and withdraw, thus retaining its dummy stack status.

How's my understanding?

Thanks very much.
author: BigAl737
consensus_answer:
Please confirm that a dummy stack is NOT revealed when an enemy unit advances in during the Advance Phase.
Correct.  Not revealed at that time.

If the dummy stack does not get revealed it would be revealed during any ensuing close combat; however, it'd be a neat trick to have the dummy stack achieve ambush and withdraw, thus retaining its dummy stack status.

How's my understanding?
Dummy stacks are eliminated at the very start of the CCPh.

See A11.19 and ASOP step 8.11B.

title: MPh and DM
question:
Hello ! 
I got a noob question about DM and MPh in ASLSK : a broken squad adjacent to an ennemy keeps his DM counter after RPh ; what does it means in MPh ? Does the unit flee with the DM 6MF at this point, or does it wait til RtPh ? Does it move (without Double Time because of the broken status) with 4MF in MPh, then flee again with 6MF in the RtPh ?
Thanks !
author: eldouco
consensus_answer:
No Heat of Battle in ASLSK, just a Leader promotion dr on a natural 2 in CC. 
In my case, the Axis broken unit tried to avoid a large Allied encircling movement and unfortunatly (very good DR on the Allied mortar shot) had to flee close to the Allied wing units : the Axis squad would otherwise have been able to rout away to a fresh leader with the 6MF and so couldn't have failed to rout. 
Allied player didn't resist to fire with his 3-stacked 447 with PBF... (I know : STACK IS BAD... most of times !). More, Allied player has to go very fast forward to get the scenario VC (6 turns only, 3 boards in column to cross through with many MF obstacles), and firing at the vulnerable Axis unit hampering his advance in the DFPh was the fastest way to go. 

The difficulty for the Axis player in this scenario is to measure the right moment  when to fire at the numerous Allied attackers to maximise the damages that will delay them, and when to retreat in an almost good order to regroup and reorganize the defenses in better further positions. 
Here, i think Axis unit fired once in excess and didn't have time to retreat wisely. Fatal excess of zeal, perhaps...  Nevertheless, the brave and bloody unit caused certain damages before. Maybe its sacrifice will not have been vain. Hope...

According to A2.51 (about 2/3 down the paragraph):
