In looking closer at the rules, I'm positive that Assault Movement is NA: a Straying unit must use all of its MF/MP, which is not possible when using Assault Movement ("Otherwise, the unit continues to move in that direction until it runs out of MF/MP"). Dashing will often be NA for the same reason, so the "etc." probably also includes it.

Stairs: specifically forbidden; a Straying unit becomes TI if it must otherwise traverse a stairwell.

Trench or foxhole: no restriction listed, so I would say yes, but it could not end its move there if it would have MF remaining.

Road bonus: I would say no due to the "etc." clause, because other means of increasing MF/MP are specifically excluded.

VBM: Yes, because the rules state that a Straying vehicle could bypass an obstacle that would otherwise require a Bog DR. And, if vehicle bypass is allowed, then I would think that infantry bypass would also be allowed.

Move under wire: There is no restriction to moving under Wire listed, so I would say yes. If a Straying unit on Wire has MF remaining, but not enough to move beneath the Wire, I don't think that it becomes TI, because the situations that cause a Straying unit to become TI seem to be specifically listed.

Use skis: I would say yes, because I can't imagine that a unit on skis would remove them when they Stray and start walking instead, but this is really just a guess. One could equally argue the the "etc." clause would exclude ski use as a form of specialized movement.

I think we are 100% definitely left without any answer.
The rules are certainly not very precise here, but one can work out the intent in many of the possible situations that could arise. The "etc." clause seems to exclude the specialized movement modes, while terrain restrictions are mostly spelled out.

This basically shows why many players believe that Chapter E – or at least parts of it – would benefit from a thorough rewrite if a 3rd edition rulebook is ever published.

I would read the pillbox rules more carefully.

They say very explicitly that the pillbox location and the pillbox hex are ADJACENT (so there is definitely have a LOS between the units in the pillbox and those outside the pillbox in the pillbox hex).

What is restricted in the pillbox rules is that the pillbox occupants cannot fire into the pillbox hex except with thrown DC, CC, or smoke grenades.

The LOS however, does exist, for all other purposes, such as:

* Broken units in the pillbox hex must rout away from the pillbox occupants. (Beware the pillbox with wire on it, lest you often surely die)

* Concealment is lost when units use non-assault movement into a pillbox hex, even if they do so through the NCA. No sneaking up on the pillbox and into the pillbox hex from behind anymore. (One will lose concealment upon non-assault moving into an enemy occupied pillbox hex.)

Pillboxes get much tougher when this rule is played correctly.

Randy

The part about firing from a Pillbox:

30.2 A pillbox is not an obstacle or Hindrance to LOS. However, LOS from inside a pillbox may be traced only within its CA [EXC: the pillbox Location and the same-level Location outside the pillbox are ADJACENT; 30.6]. Units in an adjacent, ground-level Location within a pillbox's CA are treated as being ADJACENT to units in the pillbox (and vice versa) for purposes of Point Blank Fire, FPF, DM, rout, and for DC Placement vs the pillbox. Fire from inside a pillbox into its own hex is limited to CC, or SMOKE grenade placement, or a Thrown DC (30.31), or to vertices of its CA, or to PBF vs units currently crossing the CA hexsides of its own hex. Mortar fire and fire vs an Aerial target are NA from inside a pillbox.

title: Entering a Fortified Building
question:
Other than a Breach with a DC. How else does one gain entry to a Fortified Building?

 What if the enemy is concealed? Does he have to prove there is an actual unit to prevent me from entering?

author: thegamer
consensus_answer:
Entering a multi hex building is what makes this confusing. So if the building in question is a 5 hex sized building and I had two MMC's in only two of those hexes, the enemy can just walk right in on any of the other three hexes of my Fortified Building? So a Breach is not needed in this case?

In ASL the status of "fortified building" is per building Location, which is every Level in an hex. To have upper levels fortified you have to fortify its lower levels first.

But to make things easier, imagine a multi hex building with no upper levels. It has five hexes, all of them fortified. If you have a squad equivalent in two of those five hexes, the enemy won't be able to move or advance into them. But they can surely enter the empty hexes, even if fortified.

The effect is that your occupied fortified hexes are secure both from outside the building and from inside the building proper.

title: Rout and shell holes..?
question:
Hi,

Can a DM MMC in a shell-hole rout into an adjacent building hex?  I know a shell-hole is not open-ground for rout activation purposes but, darn it, I have several broken units cracked-up in craters all over the VOTG's map and I can't get to them (safely)!

Best regards,

J
author: Jonathan Ward
consensus_answer:
IIRC, unless a) ADJACENT to a KEU, or b) DM at the start of the RtPh, broken units may only rout if they are c) in Open Ground, and in the LOS and normal range of an enemy unit/its-SW/Gun.

Unless I am missing something, a broken unit that begins its RtPh in a shellhole may only rout if one or more of the above conditions are met.

A10.5 ROUTING: During the RtPh a broken unit not in Melee may not remain in the same Open Ground hex in the Normal Range (10.532) and LOS of a Known non-Melee enemy unit/its-SW/Gun... [EXC: Night; E1.54]. ...A broken unit may rout if currently under DM.

A10.531 OPEN GROUND: For purposes of rout determination, Dash, concealment gain/loss, and Interdiction, an Open Ground hex is any hex in which any Interdictor could apply, during a hypothetical Defensive First Fire opportunity (regardless of what attacks it actually made in previous phases), the -1 FFMO DRM.

B2.4 If  expends two MF in entering the  hex, or starts the phase therein, it is considered in a shellhole and not subject to FFMO penalties.

replies.body: I don't know about "rout activation", but you MUST rout if in Open Ground and you MAY rout if under DM. Buildings and Woods hexes are what stop routing, and you still have some leeway there (ie. if you don't want to stop in the same building you started the rout in).

Read 10.51 Direction.

DM units in shell-holes are still eligible to rout,they pay either two MF per hex (diving in n out of the shell-holes) to gain the +1 TEM to avoid interdiction.
or 1MF (running along the top edges of the shell-holes) but risk interdiction. 
shell-holes count as non open ground hexes for rout,but only building/woods hexes terminate the rout.

although adjacent (and seperate) buildings/woods still allow continuous rout THRU those building/woods hexes to 6 MF.

Unless I am missing something, a broken unit that begins its RtPh in a shellhole may only rout if one or more of the above conditions are met.

A10.5 ROUTING: During the RtPh a broken unit not in Melee may not remain in the same Open Ground hex in the Normal Range (10.532) and LOS of a Known non-Melee enemy unit/its-SW/Gun... [EXC: Night; E1.54]. ...A broken unit may rout if currently under DM.

A10.531 OPEN GROUND: For purposes of rout determination, Dash, concealment gain/loss, and Interdiction, an Open Ground hex is any hex in which any Interdictor could apply, during a hypothetical Defensive First Fire opportunity (regardless of what attacks it actually made in previous phases), the -1 FFMO DRM.

B2.4 If  expends two MF in entering the  hex, or starts the phase therein, it is considered in a shellhole and not subject to FFMO penalties.
Open ground, adjacent, area fire/area target type. Three of the most misunderstood ASL concepts

A10.531 is one of the least understood aspects of the ASL infantry game both for routing questions like this and also for concealment gain and loss. 

A unit is not in OPEN GROUND unless there exists an enemy unit that could claim the -1 FFMO DRM during a hypothetical DFF opportunity. 

OPEN GROUND per A10.531 is not the same as Open Ground per B1 which is simply a hex devoid of other terrain features. 

I've often seen players pull concealment off a unit that is advancing or assault moving in an Open Ground hex in the LOS of the enemy when they are not in an OPEN GROUND hex per the A10.531 definition and should not lose the concealment at all. 

Agree. A10.531 would definately benefit from some re-write/clarifications. E.g., removing the reference to "Interdictor".

But these terms are deeply grandfathered into ASL and I doubt that any of this will ever be clarified no matter how much confusion is caused.

title: Errata and the 2nd edition rulebook
question:
MY understanding from the MMP website is that there is a lot of errata for the 2nd edition rulebook. I have not read anywhere that MMP plans to amend individual pages or issue a whole new rulebook. The errata is substantial and players making changes to the rulebook will surely make it quite messy and hard to read. 

As MMP keep reprinting there rulebook, why is there no talk of a 3rd edition or updated pages at least, isn't the latter point one of the benefits of having a ring-bound folder?

Anyone from MMP care to comment? I for one would pay for a new version of the rulebook if it was updated to get rid of the errors.
author: Biosphere
consensus_answer:

Anyone from MMP care to comment? I for one would pay for a new version of the rulebook if it was updated to get rid of the errors.

Hi - I am not from MMP.

My guess is that the work going into the electronic rulebook will be dual-use:  Once that work is complete, MMP will have the electronic wherewithal to incorporate all errata the next time they do a reprint of the RB.   I seriously doubt that they will issue replacement pages for a couple of reasons:

:d6-1: The number of replacement pages is large enough* that the labor cost involved in "culling" and packaging them for separate sale would drive the cost of providing replacement pages to a level that would rival that of simply sending out a complete replacement.

:d6-2: By incorporating all the errata, the start and end of each page will “shift” - e.g. If you add or delete 50 words to page 1 then page 2 will start with a different word.   In some cases the current “sticky errata” have dealt with this by using a smaller font size... or by reducing the space between paragraphs.   Most people would not want a new, revised rulebook with such “imperfections” - therefore MMP would have to make two versions of the new pages:  those that were formated for inclusion in a new RB, and those that were formatted to be replacement pages.   IMHO – not going to happen. 

:d6-3:My bet is that the art will be sharpened and improved and we will all want new pages anyway.

There are many ASL players (like you!) who would replace their current rulebook with an updated version.  Others, who have already incorporated the errata themselves might not. Most have done it using manual cut-and-paste using the comprehensive "sticky errata" that you can find on the Texas ASL club's website, others have done it electronically and then reprinted the pages themselves.

*Useless ASL Trivia:

I can't tell you how many errata items there have been - that number is not germane to ths discussion anyway.  However, I can provide the following statistics based on my own work producing an errata-free rulebook for my own use:

Number of page faces impacted by errata:  92 (this includes replacement pages already issued in Action pack #4 and Armies of Oblivion).  

The number of 2-sided pieces of paper that would need to be issued: 64. This is signficantly less becuase many of the corrections occur on back-to-back pages.

This includes all errata for Chapters A-E, J and H through ASL Journal #9.

title: Smoke on the water.
question: I really thought you couldn't put smoke into a stream. In Journal 10 the beginners article had smoke being thrown by infantry into and Effluent hex. I looked and couldn't find a reason why not. Have I misunderstood this all these years?
author: drmark64
consensus_answer:
I really thought you couldn't put smoke into a stream. In Journal 10 the beginners article had smoke being thrown by infantry into and Effluent hex. I looked and couldn't find a reason why not. Have I misunderstood this all these years?

Yes. You can place (and fire) SMOKE into a stream hex.

A24.1...A squad may not place SMOKE in Water Obstacles [EXC: Bridges (not foot bridges)], sewer, or marsh hexes (and neither may ordnance). 

B21.1 A Water Obstacle is a body of water large enough to stop the normal movement of men and vehicles, which cannot enter without special assistance. Any non-stream hex whose center dot is emplaced in a blue background is a Water Obstacle hex. 

8.52 SMOKE ammunition is always placed at ground level in any target hex which is hit on the Area Target Type, except Interior Building hexes, even if the only visible part of that hex is the upper level of a building. A Gun cannot place SMOKE in its own hex, although some AFV may place smoke in their own hex without their Gun (D13).

Emphasis added. I would assume that this means that SMOKE fired into a Woods-Stream hex would be placed IN the stream and hence only rise to Level 1, rather than Level 2 (EXC: WP would rise to Level 3).

B21.1 ... Any non-stream hex whose center dot is emplaced in a blue background is a Water Obstacle hex.

All mapboard-depicted ponds in a scenario that has a flooded stream are also one level higher than normal, as per 21.21. See 16.6 for a flooded stream's effect on marsh.

title: Do the 3 Starter Kits add up to the complete 3 Ring Binder contents?
question: And does the 2nd ed binder still contain the graphic images inside the covers, like the AH version?  That would be the only reason to get the empty binder.
author: Gronak
consensus_answer:
Do the 3 Starter Kits add up to the complete 3 Ring Binder contents? 

No - not by a long shot.  The Rules for ASLSK are an excellent complete game - and could be played and enjoyed alone as a complete game forever.  IMHO - they compare favorable to any other tactical WWII game system in existence.

The difference in the two systems is scope.  Full ASL is MASSIVE.  

ASLSK is not simpler than Full ASL (neither are difficult); but rather, it's just (a whole lot) smaller.

Full ASL:  A Humvee with a warehouse full of gear and attachments.

ASLSK:  A Smart Car.

You need to know how to drive to do either, and the details of that are the same.  However, the Humvee (+ gear) gives you a lot more options.

Basically, SK#1 presents a simplified version of chapter A, SK#2 is a simplified chapter C, and SK#3 is a simplified chapter D, and all three have rules on terrain, obviously, but there are far more terrain types in full ASL. 
 
This is a nit - but I'd call it a streamlined version of Chapters A, C and D.  Nothing is changed or dumb-down.   Instead, extra detail is left out.  

Examples of detail left out: 

Chapter A: concealment, bypass movement, dash movement, Machine Gun Fire Lanes, prisoners;  
Chapter B: Building levels, exotic terrain; 
Chapter C: Off-board Artillery, towing Guns
Chapter D: crew survival, platoon movement, bypass movement.

Chapter E is essentially a collection of special rules that are only used in certain scenarios when the are specifically called for, and never when they are not.  Example: Night, Weather, Air Support, Paratroop and Glider Drops, River Crossing (Boats).  Its contents are completely absent from ASLSK.

Other Chapters that are included in subsequent modules (not in the ASL rulebook) add rules for other nationalities and new terrain types (Desert, Jungle, the Japanese etc.).

What this means is that if you graduate to full ASL - you add to what you already know, rather than having to re-learn basics.  The scope expands (massively) in two ways:

:d6-1:  The theaters of war and types of scenario situations you can model,

:d6-2:  Your options during play: rules are added that let you do stuff that you could do (or that could happen, or that exist) in real life, but for which ASLSK does not have the "software" to model.

As far as I know there is only one difference between full ASL and SKASL and it is an obscure minor thing that is easy to learn "the new way" if you move up to the big game.

Not sure if your 'new way' is in reference to this but, in my experience, ASLSK matches tend to be far more bloodier due to the fact that the SK limitations brought on by the streamlining tend to favor an attitude of 'might as well go ahead and attack' since certain defensive maneuvers such as Dash make it easier to simply open fire on moving units. When we moved from SK to the RB, I noticed that there was a lot more consideration to holding fire if the odds weren't good enough and so forth.

One other point I'd like to point out is that the SKs feel more like you're just playing a game (a fine game, mind you) and that the RB adds a richer story-like experience to individual matches. Watching the creation of a Hero, for example, offers an evocative and deeper experience and it's the kind of thing you find yourself talking about long after. 'Remember that time...?'

So, for me, it isn't just the addition of rules, it's the fact it brings to the table an essentially new (and surprising, at times) play experience that the SKs simply can't match.

ASL Starter Kits contain everything you need to start playing ASL. Each kit adds new dimensions to the game while maximizing playability and fun. They are designed as stand-alone games that can be enjoyed either in sequence or on their own. 

Expansion Packs broaden the Starter Kit experience.

The core ASL modules contain the map boards, complete orders of battle for all the major combatants, additional notes and game scenarios. Historical modules add the flavor of a historical map sheet and campaign game to the mix.

Action Packs add additional scenarios and even more map boards. The ASL Journal and Out of the Attic contain articles, tactical tips, scenario replays and still more scenarios.

title: Canal question
question:
Hello,

This is probably a very easy one, but I cannot find the rule for it.
In a canal hex, which is deep, can I move on the shore. Meaning I am in the hex but not INTO the canal ?

Thanks !

No. Your answer is in B.1. Effectively, the entire hex is canal. There is no "shore."

S
consensus_answer:
Yeah, this is one of the big differences between Canals and Streams: No Crest Status. But even with Streams, you can't "bypass" the stream and walk along in Crest Status--at least that's not how I've understood it.

Yep, that's right. You can get into crest status, but no bypass. The number of terrain types that are bypassable is really quite limited (woods, buildings & most of their PTO cousins).

title: can I use ASL rules w/ original SL materials
question:
I have the original SL through GI:Anvil of Victory.  Can I use the counters & maps with the ASL rulebook?

What size are the hexes on the current MMP printed boards - same as SL? I'd like all boardgames to be on 1" hexes...

There were some giant-hex boards for use with 1/285 miniatures. Are they still in production?  Do they have a particular name, for me to search for references to them?
author: Gronak
consensus_answer:
The SK don't give many counters.  I kind of like to do points based encounters more than scenarios.
Full ASL has a lot of support for DYO (Design Your Own) scenarios: point values for the various units, rules for generating leaders and support weapons based upon the number and quality of troops that you purchase, and rarity factors for guns and vehicles (so a given gun/vehicle may not be available for purchase in a DYO scenario, depending upon how rare/common it was). But I don't hear about many players who actually play DYO scenarios regularly.

The Starter Kits don't really support DYO scenarios: they include the point values and rarity factors for the various units, but none of the required rules, charts, and tables are included.

I'm a miniatures guy.  What I'd really like is really large hexes so I can use the current generation of 20mm miniatures made for Flames of War.
The Deluxe maps were designed for 1/285 scale miniatures, although that idea never caught on. Most players just use the regular counters on the Deluxe boards.

The Deluxe modules have been out of print for a long time, but Deluxe isn't dead: there's often at least one new Deluxe scenario in each issue of the ASL Journal, and some third party publishers also release Deluxe scenarios on occasion.

MMP has considered reprinting the Deluxe boards (along with some new ones), but it will be a long time before this happens... if it ever happens.

Deluxe Pack?
http://www.boardgamegeek.com/thread/662300/deluxe-pack

Some players just enlarge the standard maps to get larger hexes, but if overdone it can really mess up the scale of the artwork (stone walls that are wider than a King Tiger, for example). Modest enlargements seem to work OK:

Click through to the picture's page to read the details on how these larger boards were made.

Are the MMP maps the same size hexes as the AH maps?
Yes, they are fully compatible with each other.

How about rolling a die each turn for LOS when it goes thru building hex(es)?  It represents the squad maneuvering a little within their own hex (& the target also) to see past the building.  The LOS can change from turn to turn because the enemy might shift away, successfully getting out of sight.
ASL players tend to frown on house rules like this, so while it's an interesting idea, don't expect anyone else to be willing to use it in a game.

You can always draw up your own maps to get buildings sized the way that you want; there's even a software program specifically created to make it easy to create ASL maps:

http://www.hexdraw.com/

But it's not free, and in the demo version that I tried out it seemed that the terrain library only supported standard size hexes (and not the much larger Deluxe hexes).

title: Hand to Hand CC?
question:
Hi,

I've just purchased VotG's and I'm presently working my way through the SSR'S before playing.  VotG10 mentions Hand-to-Hand CC with the reference J2.31.  I can't find any description or reference in the V or O chapters concerning H-to-H CC.  I can neither find anything to enlighten me in the RB.  I guess it's in another chapter.  Can anyone out there in the ether tell me what the heck H-to-H CC is and how it's used?

Much appreciated as ever..!

J

PS apologies if it's in an obvious place in the RB or V Chapter (I'm getting old).
author: Jonathan Ward
consensus_answer:
Folks .. note there's also
* Dare Death Squads (G18.62)
* Gurkhas (A25.43)

Rgds Jack

replies.body:
It is in Chapter J - the rule quoted.

J2.31
2.31 HAND-TO-HAND CC: Hand-to-Hand CC can be declared only by the ATTACKER and only if his involved unit(s) has not been Ambushed (A11.4) this turn, but once declared affects all units of both sides as long as that Melee exists in that Location. When Hand-to-Hand CC is declared in a Location, all Infantry/Cavalry in that Location must be physically stacked together, but attack/defend normally. Any vehicle/PRC in the same Location can attack/defend in the same CC but uses the black Kill Numbers rather than the red ones. Hand-to-Hand CC uses the red Kill Numbers on the CCT. A berserk ATTACKER must [EXC: if Ambushed] declare Hand-to-Hand CC vs an Infantry/Cavalry defender. Hand-to-Hand CC cannot be declared by or vs vehicles/pillbox-occupants.

Hand to Hand Close Combat basically adds a -2 to all CC dice rolls, making it a much bloodier affair. Originally, the rules appeared in Deluxe ASL, which is why they appear in Chapter J. 
The attacker gets to declare whether he's attacking with HtH, and you use the red numbers on your CC chart. There may be more details to it, but I don't have my rulebook handy.

title: Moving in stacks and failing to throw infantry smoke
question:
OK, we all know the rule "never move in stacks" and it would seem doubly applicable when in a position where smoke would be needed, but bear with me. A situation came up recently that had the potential to cause a question and so I'm asking it here.

First off we'll start with the basic case: one leader + one squad. By upping the MF to 6, it should be possible to smoke and still assault move, so that seems a decent reason to consider it. Or maybe you want to throw smoke (2 MF) into open ground move into it (2 more MF) and then keep moving, also possibly useful. Now that we have our motivation, the stack attempts to throw smoke but fails with a dr of 6.

Question 1: Is the squad done moving, or is the entire stack done moving? The rules seem to indicate the former but I'm not positive.

Question 2: Assuming just the unit is done moving, and not the entire stack, has the leader expended 2 MF?

OK. Now for the next version. Leader (Optional) + 2 (or more) squads. Squad #1 throws smoke and fails but *not* with a 6 (the 6 case is pretty much covered above.)

Question 3: If squad #2 wants to throw smoke is this MF 3 and 4 or still 1 and 2?

Thanks everyone.
author: keethrax
consensus_answer:
I am not sure you can do this, I believe you have to pre-declare stack MF expenditure ("my stack moves to zB3 for 2MF", or "my stack attempts to drop smoke in zB3 for 2MF").
But the members of a stack can do different activities with a given MF expenditure: "Units moving as a stack expend MF simultaneously and need not spend MF for the same purpose, but must designate at the same time all actions for the same MF." (A4.2)

So while you can make three attempts in a single ADJACENT hex, I don't believe you can attempt into 3 separate ADJACENT hexes - as long as you are spending it as stacked.
"Units attempting to place SMOKE grenades must specify the hex they wish to place them in before rolling the placement dr, but are otherwise free to observe the placement attempts of previous moving units before designating their own placement attempts." (A24.1)

The rule clearly states that the target is designated before the placing unit rolls its placement dr, but it does not require that a target be designated before any other unit in the stack makes a placement dr, nor does it require that a target be designated at the time that the MF expenditure is announced. Indeed, the last part of this rule, about observing other placement attempts, only makes sense for units moving as a stack... as units moving individually, or making smoke placement attempts on different MF expenditures of a stack, would of course know the results of any previous placement attempts before they have to designate their target.

I can't find any Perry Sez or errata that changes or contradicts these two rules, so I believe my answer was correct.

replies.body:
Question 1: Is the squad done moving, or is the entire stack done moving? The rules seem to indicate the former but I'm not positive.
Only the squad is done moving. A24.1 specifically says "unit" and not "stack".

Question 2: Assuming just the unit is done moving, and not the entire stack, has the leader expended 2 MF?
Yes.

Units moving as a stack always expend MF simultaneously. So, if one unit in a stack declares that it will spend 2 MF on a smoke placement attempt, every unit in that stack expends 2 MF (even if they don't actually do anything with those MF). The only way to avoid this is to split the stack before the smoke placement attempt.

OK. Now for the next version. Leader (Optional) + 2 (or more) squads. Squad #1 throws smoke and fails but *not* with a 6 (the 6 case is pretty much covered above.)

Question 3: If squad #2 wants to throw smoke is this MF 3 and 4 or still 1 and 2?
It depends. If a unit in a stack expends MF for a smoke placement attempt, the other eligible units in the stack could also make their own smoke placement attempts using the same MF expenditure. So a stack with three squads could, with an expenditure of just 2 MF, attempt to place smoke into three ADJACENT hexes... or make three attempts to place smoke in a single ADJACENT hex, etc.

You could, of course, do it the other way: the stack spends 2 MF for one squad to make a smoke placement attempt, and then spends 2 more MF for a second squad to make another smoke placement attempt, but I can't imagine why you would ever want to waste MF in that manner.

All of those fall in line with my interpretation as well. But there was just enough fuzziness that it was worth checking up on.

title: motion tank firing on moving tank
question:
I'm trying to get to grips with the armour rules and finding my brain is turning to cardboard left out in the rain.

It is the Russian movement turn, one of their T34's moves into the sights of a Tiger which is under a motion counter. I can see how BFF applies to a firing tank in it's movement phase but this is the movement phase of the Russians. Motion DRM apply to the target but what applies to the attacker?

thanks
author: Biosphere
consensus_answer:
Pup, the rules in this case are ok. There is just a problem of interpretation. 
I disagree. This section of the rules is a disaster and desperately needs to be revised.

 C5.35 states that for Motion/Non-Stopped vehicles case C4 applies, along with cases C, or C1, or C2 "as applicable".
The key is "as applicable". If you then read C5.31 and C5.32 it says that C1 and C2 apply to vehicles firing during their MPh. So, "not applicable" to a D1F from a Motion vehicle. 
You are saying that cases C1 and C2 are not "applicable" because they state that they apply to vehicles firing during their MPh. But in C5.3 it also states that vehicular ordnance firing during it's MPh uses the Case C DRM. It's the exact same statement that is made for cases C1 and C2.

If you exclude C1 and C2 because of the statement about it's MPh then you have to exclude C also. This would make section C5.35 absolutely meaningless. 

But the fact is that C5.35 says that you apply C4 to a Motion Firer and then apply C, C1 or C2 as applicable and even defines what "as applicable" means in parentheses as "depending on MP expended..."

 So, you see, no contradictions, no changes, no nothing. It's there in the rules. You can show it to your opponents. 
What I see in the Rules is that C, C1 or C2 apply to a Motion firer as applicable depending on the MP expended by the target just prior to the shot. That's what the rule book says in a muddled and confused fashion. 

But a poorly thought out and arbitary Q&A has been issued from on high so the loyal team of ASL oldtimers rally around the flag and try to pretend that nonsense makes perfect ASL sense.

C1 and C2 apply specifically to Bounding Firers only.

Angry much?  :)

I am going to agree with ASLNoob - the rules for C4 are written poorly. C4 is written well for Bounding Fire, but not for defensive Motion firers. Cases C, C1, and C2 all apply specifically to Bounding Firers, not defensive Motion firers. I could argue both sides of this, but I believe the intention is for case C to apply to the defensive Motion firer, but not C1 nor C2.

Case C = Case B plus [Stabilized Gun: +1][T/ST:+2][NT: +3]

consensus_answer:
There is no ambush when it is strictly Infantry vs an AFV by itself. 

Wondering about this. Isn't it the case that infantry advancing into CC with an AFV in woods/buildings gets to roll for ambush? This will not imply a change in the sequence of CC rolls (given that it is always sequential vs vehicles), but will net it a -1/+1 drms in CC. 

The rule for street fighting (A11.8) suggests so, by stating that the Street Fighting ambush drm vs vehicles is not cumulative with normal ambush, thus implying that the later is possible.

replies.body: One minor point. The freeze is effective even if he is not "in" your location provided you have a TPBF attack opportunity.  See A7.212. Of course this will generally be when you are in the same location but could occur when you are in level 1 and he is at ground level in the ame hex. Then funkiness happens with him having to be CE or OT and reduced modifiers etc.

A couple of minor points that I think apply too:

3) I agree - this is straight defensive fire.  And if the tank spent more than one MP to enter bypass (very likely) and the MMG keeps rate of fire, it can potentially try TH more than once.

4) Tripled, but also halved, for AFPh. And the tank will also have to pay a Case A DRM if he forgot to change his TCA to cover the hex when he moved in - I've seen this one missed many times - with (I think) a further +1 for shooting to the side in bypass even if he did change in the MPh.

J

5) Moving to the CCPh. My understanding is that CC is mandatory as always since the AFV is in my hex.
CC is not mandatory - you could elect to not attack the bypassing vehicle if you for a reason do not want to.

Thanks for the reply Klas. Do you mean that the entire CC is optional. Or do you mean that CC will still take place but I can elect to not attack him in CC while he will still attack me, for instance if I attempt to withdraw during CC?
Firstly you cannot attempt to Withdraw from CC - only from Melee. If you choose not to attack the vehicle, it can still attack you.

The usual situation when you might not want to make a CC attack is if you are concealed and want to keep your concealment. The enemy's FP will be halved and if he doens't Casualty Reduce you, you will keep concealment.

One other situation (which is probably not so common) is if it is not important if your unit (or the enemy) lives or dies, but what is important is that your opponent doesn't get an Infiltration result - i.e., you don't want to chance rolling a 6,6 - allowing the enemy to Withdraw (e.g., into a VC area, etc.).

Could you please point me to the section of the Rulebook that covers this point. I went round and round looking for it. 
There is this from A11.15: "...Therefore, a concealed unit may wish to decline its CC attack opportunity in an effort to save its concealment..."

But (IMO) since there is nothing in the CC rules that specifically states that making CC attacks are mandatory - they aren't.

Awesome! Thanks. That makes perfect sense. So basically the CC will take place but one or both sides could decline to attack. 

By the same token as you described above the AFV might decline to attack if it was absolutely critical that his opponent does not get an Infiltration result and be able to withdraw out of the hex.
Yes, or e.g., if the AFV has a B11 MA CMG and doesn't want to risk malfing it.

Even in the unlikely event that both sides decline to attack during CC I would assume that the infantry unit is still marked in Melee at the end of the CC. 
Yes, I'm pretty sure that is the case.

to the original poster:

1) many VBM sleezers like to bring supporting infantry adjacent to your "frozen" unit, hoping to break you in Advancing Fire. If they fail, they will often advance infantry into the location, hoping to take you out in CC. However, this is risky on their part (if you know the rules).

As Infantry has Advanced into your building location, there is now a realistic opportunity for Ambush. The Vehicle brings +2 vehicle and +1 BU (most of the time), so the attacker has a net +3. This should often allow you to gain the ambush - which allows you to either withdraw from the location immediately (before CC) or to through a round of CC (you attack first, sequentially) and THEN withdraw. 2) If you really do NOT feel like being "frozen" and have no heavy SW, you can always decide to escape from the position by declaring Voluntary Break at the start of your Rout Phase and use 6 MF to get out of Dodge (and hopefully to a much safer place).

title: Loading and Unloading Riders
question:
Can someone explain or point me to an explanation of loading and unloading riders from AFVs?  D6.4 and 6.5 are, umm, confusing.  I've read this sentence a dozen times: "The vehicle retains 1/4 of its MP allotment for use in the MPh for each MF remaining to the infantry that board it." Parsing that sentence grammatically leads to absurd results.

Many thanks.
author: txaal
consensus_answer:
Can someone explain or point me to an explanation of loading and unloading riders from AFVs?  D6.4 and 6.5 are, umm, confusing.  I've read this sentence a dozen times: "The vehicle retains 1/4 of its MP allotment for use in the MPh for each MF remaining to the infantry that board it." Parsing that sentence grammatically leads to absurd results.

Many thanks.

Divide the vehicle movement by 4. Every infantry movement factor counts as that much vehicle movement and vice versa. So, a German half track moves 3, stops for 4 (1 inf MF), unloads (2 inf MF) and has 8 MP left (3 and 4 inf MF). Does that make things any clearer?

replies.body:
Infantry havew 4 mf when they are passengers at any point of their move.
If you spend 2mf to reach the vehicle and 1 mf to load then the vehicle has only 1/4 of it's MPs left to move.

Likewise if they spend 1mf to load, the vehicle has 3/4 of it's mps left to move.

It matters not that the inf are stacked with a leader or go cx, they only have 4 mf even if green conscripts carrying excess PP.(although then they could only spend 1 mf to load).

I've read this sentence a dozen times: "The vehicle retains 1/4 of its MP allotment for use in the MPh for each MF remaining to the infantry that board it." Parsing that sentence grammatically leads to absurd results.

Many thanks.

Divide the vehicle movement by 4. Every infantry movement factor counts as that much vehicle movement and vice versa. So, a German half track moves 3, stops for 4 (1 inf MF), unloads (2 inf MF) and has 8 MP left (3 and 4 inf MF). Does that make things any clearer?

Edit:  others have beaten me to the punch and explained this better, but this is what I had intended to post.

The movement allowances of the infantry and the vehicle are spent proportionally.

Infantry has 4 MFs.  So for every 1/4 (FRU) of the vehicles MP allotment that is spent riding along, 1 MF is used.

The act of loading or unloading itself costs 1 MF for the infantry and 1/4 of the vehicle's MP allotment.

EX:  The vehicle has a MP allotment of 16.  The infantry starts on board as a passenger or rider.  The vehicle moves 7 MPs then 1 MP to stop for a total of 8 MPs (ie two x 1/4 of its MP allotment).  The infantry has used 2 of its 4 MFs riding along.

It then costs 1 MF for the infantry (and another 1/4 of the vehicle's MP allotment) to unload.

So now the infantry has used 3 MFs and the vehicle has used 12 MPs.

The key is proportionality.  1/4 of the vehicle's MPs = 1 of the infantry's 4 MFs.

Another EX:  if the vehicle only had a MP allotment of 14, and spend 8 MPs moving and stopping would have used > 1/2 of its MP allotment.  So, rounding up to the nearest quarter, 3 of the infantry's 4 MFs have been spent on board, and the fourth 4 MF is spent unloading.  The act of unloading would cost the vehicle 3.5 MPs (1/4 of its MP allotment).

So in that example the inf has used all 4 MFs and the vehicle 11.5 MPs to the point where the inf is on the ground in the vehicle's location.
Ok, thanks guys. This is where I was headed until I read the example at the end of 6.4 where the HS takes all of its MF to load and the vehicle still has 1/4 of its MF remaining.

I've found that (within a given MPh at least) it helps to think about MF and MP as expressions of time as well as distance - and that even though MP and MF means different sorts of distance, they take place in the same amount of time.

That way, that rule is basically saying - if it takes the infantry a quarter of their turn to get on the tank, the tank has to stay still for a quarter of its turn as well.

This has the added benefit of allowing us to intuit speed according to number of MP within a class of vehicle, and even across vehicle classes using road movement as a standard. In other words, higher MP = faster vehicle (on roads).

I've actually found the movement rules, once you take that time aspect into account, are quite intuitive... most of the time.

title: Double Time two turns in a row?
question:
Situation:

A FRIENDLY MMC uses Double Time movement and therefore becomes CX.

In the ENEMY's turn the CX MMC breaks due to Prep or Advancing Fire and therefore loses the CX status upon becoming broken.

The broken unit then rallies in the subsequent FRIENDLY RPh.

Question:

Can this MMC use Double Time movement in the MPh, effectively using Double Time in two consecutive turns?

I'm thinking it can because the unit is not under CX when it starts its MPh. My interpretation of the rules is that being under CX precludes the consecutive use of DT not the fact that you had used DT in a previous turn, otherwise why would you be required to remove a CX counter upon breaking?

NRBH so I can't cite specific rules/quotes to back up my argument but my opponent reads the Double Time/CX rules as saying that you can't DT two turns in a row and I tend to disagree.

Thank you for your attention...
author: sapper_D
consensus_answer:
You are right.  Once broke they lose CX.  If they rally they are eligible for Double Time.

Here is something that you can do with SS.  Take a stack of 3 SS squads and a -1 or -2 leader.  Double time them, run forward as far as you can to a position that will allow you to rout 'forward', voluntarily break them, rout them 'forward', They have a broken morale of 9 so with rally terrain and -1 leader they rally  on a 7 or 8 with a -2 leader.  Declare Double Time again and repeat.  Finding the spot that allows a rout 'forward' is the tricky part.

I think you can only voluntarily break if you have LOS to a Known enemy unit, so finding the spot that allows this is very tricky. Commissars also help when doing this trick.

title: AFV Overrun, OBA and Air SUpport
question:
I have now clocked up 30+ games of ASL that are mainly infantry-only, and while I'm not particularly good at the game, I'm starting to get the basics of handling infantry. Now I want more.

I've never played a game longer than about 5 hours, and I keep hearing about how great the game becomes when you have slightly larger OBs and more time to play around with, so I've scheduled a game of AP44 The Burial Mound from AP5: East Front.

But I've used OBA once (and didn't understand it) and I've never used Air support. I'm also really, really hazy on Vehicular OVR, and can't shake the feeling I'm missing something. Gamesquad seems to have no place for 'tutorial' threads,it's all rules questions, so I figured I'd try here.

1) AFV Overrun

My basic question is: just, seriously, what the hell? I keep reading in various places (like in Out of the Attic 2) about how infantry in CC are really dangerous to AFVs, but the last OVR I did with a few 4FP squads versus an overrunning TKS were completely without result and the TKS just got to stay in my hex. And that was with average squads but a lame tank - I hesitate to think what this would be like with a better tank.

What am I missing? Infantry just don't seem all that scary to tanks at all, especially tanks in motion. Why is everyone so scared of them? It seemed like the CCV of the infantry was down in the 2-3 range, and in my understanding of the rule you can't combine firepower factors in CC reaction fire?

Also, what's the deal with CC Reaction Fire being allowed outside the hex? and is it always TBPF if it's inside the hex? and if so, why would you ever fire CC Reaction fire at something outside your hex?

As you can see, I'm completely bewildered by this rule, and I must say the OVR flowchart only makes things LESS clear. Can anyone provide a link to a good tutorial for specifically AFV OVR, or give me (and other Noobs) a clean, simple rundown of a best-case-for-infantry description of one, that would really help. My google-fu is weak today and I can't find one.

2) OBA

This is another one where the flowchart makes things HARDER> As far as I can see, it goes - check for contact, check for access, AR->SR->FFE1->FFE2, over several turns. Is that about right? I know there's something about two red chit pulls but I don't understand the flow of OBA and it seems needlessly complex. Again, can anyone direct me to/provide me with a clean, easy to follow step-by-step tutorial of a best-case-for-firer process, without all the extraneous bolt-on chrome like aerial observers, off-board observers etc.?

3) Air Support

I haven't even read the rules for this one yet, nor ever got even close to playing with them, but on turn four of this scenario the Germans get two Stukas on Turn 4, and the Russkies have two AA trucks. As such I imagine I as the Russians will want to ensure good AA truck placement, which entails understanding anti-aircraft fire.

All I'm really after here is a tutorial on air support, as I've not read the rules and have NRBH, it would be inappropriate for me to ask you to do my work for me.

So please, O ASL gurus, help a noob out? I'd really like to get into the 'meatier' side of ASL and I'm a little tired of being scared of the more complex modular rules, and equally tired of all the buildup only to find they don't work as expected because someone fails a vital roll on turn 1, so I don't get to see how the rule actually works in play.

A tank (say a 50L PzIII) and ONE 4fp infantry squad unmarked by a fire counter(say a French 1st line) on a terrainless, level plane with NO OTHER UNITS. No other defensive fire fouling things up, nothing other than the barest bones required for an overrun. I want to see the very basic building blocks in action to understand why this is scary for tanks, and why CC is a good move for infantry.

In terms of OBA, I mean - one observer, one target, no terrain - just to give me a sense of the process uncomplicated by "real world" obstacles and impediments.

The ASL rulebook is singularly terrible at these 'bare-bones' systematic, procedural examples, because it's all about the exceptions. But I feel like you have to learnt he rule before you worry about the exceptions.
author: Boots01
consensus_answer:
1) AFV Overrun
My basic question is: just, seriously, what the hell? I keep reading in various places (like in Out of the Attic 2) about how infantry in CC are really dangerous to AFVsWell, it depends what infantry and what time of the war.
OVR is not used a lot in ASL, and when PF and other SCW weapons are around, its use becomes very rare.
What is a much more common tactic is Vehicle Bypass Movement freeze.
Why is everyone so scared of them? It seemed like the CCV of the infantry was down in the 2-3 range, and in my understanding of the rule you can't combine firepower factors in CC reaction fire?
All depends on what risks you want to take to lose a tank - and a PzI or PzVI are about as vulnerable vs CC, as armor and Gun calibre don't enter the maths...
Not everyone is scared by tanks.

Also, what's the deal with CC Reaction Fire being allowed outside the hex?I presume you are alluding to streetfighting.
Not very frequently used, not very efficient, but it can temper the tank's endeavour to drive within urban environement without infantry cover...
Street fighting is much more efficient during CCPh.

2) OBA

This is another one where the flowchart makes things HARDER
It doesn't.
It helps not have to delve into the rule when you want to convert, move, etc. your SR/FFE.
Now, in most "normal" situations, the flowchart is not needed - and players managed to play the OBA rules years before the flowchart existed.
However, the graphical display and the actual reading of the chart does enlighten one's understanding of some subtle mechanics of the OBA system

3) Air Support
I'm a little tired of being scared of the more complex modular rules, and equally tired of all the buildup only to find they don't work as expected because someone fails a vital roll on turn 1, so I don't get to see how the rule actually works in play.
I understand and I can be tired of some overcomplicated rules (Seaborne assault and panjis come to mind).
Air Support is rather simple.
First of all, it occurs quite rarely.
Second, you don't have a lot of AA defense resources most of the time.
Third, the most usefull AA is light AA : if your guns are in AA mode, you simply fire at the plane, using the IFE, the plane's DRM (in the black star) and remember that range is counted double (1hex = 2 hex).
Swinging the gun will add some CA DRM.
Fourth, as the aircraft can attack at any moment during MPh, about any unit, the placement of your AA resources never will be ideal.
At last, the Sighting TC is quite easy to compute : roll the dice, look up the DRMs : 8 or less, OK. 12 original : recall, 12 final : mistaken attack...

The ASL rulebook is singularly terrible at these 'bare-bones' systematic, procedural examples, because it's all about the exceptions. But I feel like you have to learnt he rule before you worry about the exceptions.The word that "you play 10% of the rules 90%" proves quite true.
When you are accustomed to the bulk of the rules, you will mostly look into the rulebook when special occurences happen - which are covered by the "exceptions".

Now, to get a grasp of the rules, a good way to go is to play along the Starter Kit rules : they are a simplified set of rules, which mostly don't conflict with the full thing.

I hope I helped a little...

title: Non-CC reaction fire when AFV is not overrunning question
question:
All,
I assume an AFV can enter an enemy hex without overruning that unit. If the enemy unit is infantry and is not marked by FF, Final Fire, or CC counters can it forgo the any reaction fire and instead fire TPBF on the exposed crew of the AFV? If you could point me to the rule number too that would be a big help.
Thanks All!
author: Coaltar
consensus_answer:
If he's CE and you're not marked you can CCRF or DFF on the CE crew.

D7.22 NON-CC REACTION FIRE is the rule reference

there's a reference in Chapter A that points you to this rule as well:

A8.312 TPBF: An armed, unbroken Infantry DEFENDER not in Melee must immediately attack any Infantry/Cavalry MMC unit that enters its Location during the MPh whether it uses Defensive First Fire, Subsequent First Fire, or FPF [EXC: A SMC with a MG/IFE already marked with a First Fire counter may not use Subsequent First Fire or FPF because it cannot use Sustained Fire; 9.3]. See also OVR; D7.2. All such FPF and any Defensive/Subsequent First Fire must be combined into one Mandatory FG (7.55)

title: Have tanks LOS over hedges/walls?
question:
Hi,

Crucial shot and not sure whether tanks (JgPz V) has LOS over a non-adjacent hedge between itself and the target.  I can see how infantry would lose LOS but not sure about a 'big tank'!

Any help much appreciated,

J
author: Jonathan Ward
consensus_answer:
Yes, LOS is blocked for everything on the same level as the wall/hedge.

Note that a tank adjacent to a wall or hedge cannot fire its BMG though the hexsides with the wall or hedge. These are not 'short' (2'-3') walls, but 'tall' ones (4'-5')!
A BMG could fire through the hexside if it is a hedge - not wall/bocage though.

Per D4.223 firing a non-MA is only NA if the vehicle is Hull Down, and a hedge does not bestow HD status.

title: Concealed unit entrenching
question:

does a concealed MMC in the act of entrenching (i.e., it has a labor -1 counter) lose its concealed status when a moving enemy unit moves into its LOS?

thanx and cheers
-Lamskiy-
author: Lamskiy
consensus_answer:
Case C on the Concealment Loss/Gain table: 

An infantry unit in either concealment or non-concealment terrain that is in LOS range 16 or less will lose concealment for attempting "any other actions; e.g. attempts to entrench."

As the OP pointed out, its not the TI marker that would make him lose concealment but the attempt to entrench (die roll) during that phase. 

If your unit is out of LOS, attempts entrenchment and gets a TI marker, he does not lose concealment.

If you unit is in LOS and attempts entrenchment, it gets a TI marker and loses concealement.

title: Q: Tank shoots another tank; how does this work?
question:
I've got the latest version of BV and the Big Orange Rulebook sitting right in front of me with the play aids for armor spread out over the floor. I still can't figure out what happens when a tank shoots another tank. Heres what I (think) I understand so far.

1. In the German Mph, a Tiger drives into the LOS of a T-34.

2. The Russian player states that they are firing at the Tiger with their T-34 along with what kind of ammunition they are using.

3. The Russian player rolls for ammunition availability and/or depletion if applicable.

4. The Russian player uses string to confirm that the T-34 does indeed have LOS to the Tiger.

5. The Firer-Based Hit Determination DRM's (as listed on Table C5) are calculated and then added to the Target-Based Hit Determination DRM's (as listed on table C6). The result is the final To-Hit DRM.

6. The Russian player consults the To Hit Table (C3). They find the appropriate column for the range, and row for Target Type (Vehicle). How do you know when to use the red numbers? They add the final To-Hit DRM to the number taken from the To-Hit Table and attempt to roll under this number on 2 Dice. What happens if the DR is exactly equal to the target number?

7. Assuming the result is a hit, the Russian player then compares the colored and uncolored die to determine the location of the hit.

8. After determining the hit location, the AF listed on the Tiger counter is inserted into one of many mathematical equations dependent on the combination of symbols on the counter.

9. The result of this equation is AF of the particular location that the T-34 has just hit.

10. The Russian player consults the appropriate To-Kill table for the type of ammunition they used.

11. The AF of the particular location hit by the T-34 is subtracted from number taken from the To-Kill Table. This is the To-Kill number.

12. The Russian player then tries to roll under this number. What happens if their roll equals the To-Kill number exactly?

Thats as far as I've been able to get. I'm guessing that a successful roll on step 12 leads to something on the AFV Destruction Table (C7.7) but I can't read the table at all. The combined usage of algebra, abbreviations, color codes, various symbols, superscripts and footnotes absolutely boggles my mind. Can someone set me straight on what I'm supposed to be doing here?
author: Unterschutze
consensus_answer:
Here's some detailed notes, but yes, you've got the essentials.

1. In the German Mph, a Tiger drives into the LOS of a T-34.
Okay...

2. The Russian player states that they are firing at the Tiger with their T-34 along with what kind of ammunition they are using.
Technically, he also specifies if he is using Vehicular, Infantry or Area Target Type. Since it is a vehicular target, VTT and AP ammo are assumed if it is not otherwise stated. ITT will not do anything here (though it could be used to fire on Riders or a CE crew), and ATT is mostly meant for concealed targets, but can be useful if the Gun is not able to penetrate the target's armor (immobilization and shock).

The only special ammo available to a T-34 will be APCR (noted by an 'A' and numbers on the back of the counter).

3. The Russian player rolls for ammunition availability and/or depletion if applicable.
Yes. But this is the To Hit DR. If he uses APCR and rolls under his depletion number (should be the same for all T-34s, but the depletion number will vary by year), then it is a normal To Hit roll (though using the APCR To Kill table if it hits). If it is equal to the depletion number, then proceed with APCR, but that T-34 has no more available for the rest of the scenario. If the roll is equal to the B#/X#, then the Gun malfunctions. Otherwise, there was no APCR for that tank, which cannot try for APCR for the rest of the scenario, and the To Hit DR is repeated, using normal AP this time.

4. The Russian player uses string to confirm that the T-34 does indeed have LOS to the Tiger.
Yes. In many cases, this will be obvious and can be skipped, just as in infantry fire.

5. The Firer-Based Hit Determination DRM's (as listed on Table C5) are calculated and then added to the Target-Based Hit Determination DRM's (as listed on table C6). The result is the final To-Hit DRM.
Yes. In this case, the Tiger is moving, so Case J will apply, and J1/J2 may apply because of lack of MP spent in LOS of the T-34. Case L cannot apply because of the Motion target. A Tiger I is a large -1 target (Case P). Cases Q or R (TEM & Hindrance) could apply.

Assuming the T-34 is not in Motion, the likely Firer-based mods are Case A (if it needed to turn the turret, or even body to make the shot), Case F (it had already fired and exhausted ROF, getting a First Fire marker for the MA), and Case L (Buttoned Up).

6. The Russian player consults the To Hit Table (C3). They find the appropriate column for the range, and row for Target Type (Vehicle). How do you know when to use the red numbers? They add the final To-Hit DRM to the number taken from the To-Hit Table and attempt to roll under this number on 2 Dice. What happens if the DR is exactly equal to the target number?
Note that you usually calculate the TH# and DRM before declaring the shot (possibly guessing on the Hindrances and the like), so you have an idea if it's worth taking.

7. Assuming the result is a hit, the Russian player then compares the colored and uncolored die to determine the location of the hit.
Yes.

8. After determining the hit location, the AF listed on the Tiger counter is inserted into one of many mathematical equations dependent on the combination of symbols on the counter.

9. The result of this equation is AF of the particular location that the T-34 has just hit.
Not really an equation. If it was a hull hit, use the number for front or side armor as appropriate. Rear armor is one point less than side.

A turret hit modifies the AF up if the appropriate AF is in a square, AF is modified down if it is in a circle. If neither, it is the same as the hull.

The possible AFs are given in D1.6. Adjust up and down the list of 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 11, 14, 18, 26 as needed above.

10. The Russian player consults the appropriate To-Kill table for the type of ammunition they used.
Right. Adjust for range, if needed.

11. The AF of the particular location hit by the T-34 is subtracted from number taken from the To-Kill Table. This is the To-Kill number.
The Final TK number (C7.11).

12. The Russian player then tries to roll under this number. What happens if their roll equals the To-Kill number exactly?
See the AFV Destruction Table (C7.7). Generally, in this case, a hull hit will Immobilize the target (C7.5), and a turret hit will Shock it (C7.4).

replies.body:
Looks good to me, but are more answers.

They add the final To-Hit DRM to the number taken from the To-Hit Table and attempt to roll under this number on 2 Dice. What happens if the DR is exactly equal to the target number?

The combined usage of algebra, abbreviations, color codes, various symbols, superscripts and footnotes absolutely boggles my mind. Can someone set me straight on what I'm supposed to be doing here?

Here's some detailed notes, but yes, you've got the essentials.

1. In the German Mph, a Tiger drives into the LOS of a T-34.
Okay...

2. The Russian player states that they are firing at the Tiger with their T-34 along with what kind of ammunition they are using.
Technically, he also specifies if he is using Vehicular, Infantry or Area Target Type. Since it is a vehicular target, VTT and AP ammo are assumed if it is not otherwise stated. ITT will not do anything here (though it could be used to fire on Riders or a CE crew), and ATT is mostly meant for concealed targets, but can be useful if the Gun is not able to penetrate the target's armor (immobilization and shock).

The only special ammo available to a T-34 will be APCR (noted by an 'A' and numbers on the back of the counter).

3. The Russian player rolls for ammunition availability and/or depletion if applicable.
Yes. But this is the To Hit DR. If he uses APCR and rolls under his depletion number (should be the same for all T-34s, but the depletion number will vary by year), then it is a normal To Hit roll (though using the APCR To Kill table if it hits). If it is equal to the depletion number, then proceed with APCR, but that T-34 has no more available for the rest of the scenario. If the roll is equal to the B#/X#, then the Gun malfunctions. Otherwise, there was no APCR for that tank, which cannot try for APCR for the rest of the scenario, and the To Hit DR is repeated, using normal AP this time.

4. The Russian player uses string to confirm that the T-34 does indeed have LOS to the Tiger.
Yes. In many cases, this will be obvious and can be skipped, just as in infantry fire.

5. The Firer-Based Hit Determination DRM's (as listed on Table C5) are calculated and then added to the Target-Based Hit Determination DRM's (as listed on table C6). The result is the final To-Hit DRM.
Yes. In this case, the Tiger is moving, so Case J will apply, and J1/J2 may apply because of lack of MP spent in LOS of the T-34. Case L cannot apply because of the Motion target. A Tiger I is a large -1 target (Case P). Cases Q or R (TEM & Hindrance) could apply.

Assuming the T-34 is not in Motion, the likely Firer-based mods are Case A (if it needed to turn the turret, or even body to make the shot), Case F (it had already fired and exhausted ROF, getting a First Fire marker for the MA), and Case L (Buttoned Up).

6. The Russian player consults the To Hit Table (C3). They find the appropriate column for the range, and row for Target Type (Vehicle). How do you know when to use the red numbers? They add the final To-Hit DRM to the number taken from the To-Hit Table and attempt to roll under this number on 2 Dice. What happens if the DR is exactly equal to the target number?
Note that you usually calculate the TH# and DRM before declaring the shot (possibly guessing on the Hindrances and the like), so you have an idea if it's worth taking.

7. Assuming the result is a hit, the Russian player then compares the colored and uncolored die to determine the location of the hit.
Yes.

8. After determining the hit location, the AF listed on the Tiger counter is inserted into one of many mathematical equations dependent on the combination of symbols on the counter.

9. The result of this equation is AF of the particular location that the T-34 has just hit.
Not really an equation. If it was a hull hit, use the number for front or side armor as appropriate. Rear armor is one point less than side.

A turret hit modifies the AF up if the appropriate AF is in a square, AF is modified down if it is in a circle. If neither, it is the same as the hull.

The possible AFs are given in D1.6. Adjust up and down the list of 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 11, 14, 18, 26 as needed above.

10. The Russian player consults the appropriate To-Kill table for the type of ammunition they used.
Right. Adjust for range, if needed.

11. The AF of the particular location hit by the T-34 is subtracted from number taken from the To-Kill Table. This is the To-Kill number.
The Final TK number (C7.11).

12. The Russian player then tries to roll under this number. What happens if their roll equals the To-Kill number exactly?
See the AFV Destruction Table (C7.7). Generally, in this case, a hull hit will Immobilize the target (C7.5), and a turret hit will Shock it (C7.4).

title: LOS Definitive grid sheet cross reference?
question:
I've been getting back into ASL lately and have been studying LOS as it was  confusing on some aspects (blind hexes, bocage and blind hexes, certain hillsides, etc). Russ Gifford's PowerPoint on the subject has been excellent. I've installed Vassal too mainly to check LOS but it craps out on some boards and is not always reliable:robot:.
I was wondering if anyone has tried to make like an Excel grid (similar to the original SL example) to cross reference LOS on single boards? 
For example:
"Oh board __ hex A1, let me see if I can see to C2" looks on left column for A1 and skims across grid to C2, a big "X" "nope it's not clear to it." 
Does this make sense? It could work mostly easily for single boards to clear up looking down from hills and blind hexes.
Anyone ever attempt something like this?
Thanks,
author: Diabolik771
consensus_answer:
IMHO this type of thing while informative, violates the spirit of the game.  

"Spirit of the Game" is a very loose term, at Best.

Knowing how to figure out the geometric analysis of LOS in Giffords article, violates the "Spirit of the Game".

Given enough time and exp. most LOS checks become second nature.  

Personally, a matrix of LOS is unnecessary.  If your opponent doesn't mind you using the matrix, then just take FrEE LOS checks, it's the same thing.  So, discuss it before hand.

Me, I'd let you make free checks since it might be your first game back. 
After that, no.  Live and die by the lay of the land

Of course, if you have no life, you could just string los's all day long and burn them into your memory.  Probably, against the "Spirit" and unethical, but not enforceable.  This is akin to people studying the rules, ypu either know them (rules/LOS) or you don't.  No one complains about the rules guru.  Why should there be complaints about LOS freaks? 

During a game, I would consider looking at "the Grid" as taking a shot and having to roll even if a blind hex.
It would be most tiresome to compile "the Grid" but I'm sure but there are many a OCD player who may have actually taken the string to every........single........hex.......on .......every.....board. :zombie:

title: Error in CC example illustration?
question:
All,
I was lookiing over the CC example and it shows a conceled 447 in a road hex. This isn't possible to be conceled in an open ground hex in normal range and LOS of a good order enemy is it?
Thanks
author: Coaltar
consensus_answer:
Generally, you'll need an Assault Engineer to lay the smoke and another unit to go into it. If you can have two spare to move forwards with one moving closer to the enemy first to restrict his SFF ability. 

I like to use a half squad to go into the smoke adjacent to the enemy and then, if he first fires, dash a full squad across the road through a no adjacent hex into the building beside the enemy to take adamant age of the better cover. The defender is then left with a quandary, fire on the dashing infantry and be unable to strip concealment from the concealed unit, making an ambush more likely or leave a full squad next to him in cover  Often it will force an outnumbered defender to retreat rather than risk the CC. 

Of course, this does require numerical superiority but as the attacker, you should be able to achieve this.

ASL is all about forcing your opponent to make hard choices.

That's a good tip.

title: Guard firepower in CC
question:
All,
If a full squad is guarding a full squad prisoner is the guarding units firepower halved in CC? Does it get full firepower during prep, and dFire phases? A20.52 kinda makes it sound like on guards that are smaller in unit size are penalized.
Thanks!
author: Coaltar
consensus_answer:
Thanks Martin.
So if the guard loses the CC since there are other enemy that advanced in to attack in CC, does the guarding unit become rearmed if the guard is eliminated? Technically they are not withdrawing "Escape" but there are no other units of the guards side left in the Melee location. A20.55 seems to imply that the prisoners must escape in order to be rearmed (e.g. withdraw or eliminate the guards, which they didn't in this case since they didn't pass thier guard NTC to allow them to attach the guard.)
Thanks

replies.body:
20.52 GUARD FP: A Guard whose US# is < the total US# of its prisoners may not attack any unit other than its prisoners except in CC and may not use a SW, Interdict, or Kindle. A Guard's FP is halved for attack (but not defense) purposes when attacking non-prisoners in CC .

He gets full FP in fire phases and defends with full FP but attacks with halved FP in CC. Doesn't matter how many prisoners he's guarding for the CC but if he's guarding too many he can't attack other than in CC.

Thanks Martin.
So if the guard loses the CC since there are other enemy that advanced in to attack in CC, does the guarding unit become rearmed if the guard is eliminated? Technically they are not withdrawing "Escape" but there are no other units of the guards side left in the Melee location. A20.55 seems to imply that the prisoners must escape in order to be rearmed (e.g. withdraw or eliminate the guards, which they didn't in this case since they didn't pass thier guard NTC to allow them to attach the guard.)
Thanks
Without looking it up, I believe an unarmed unit is rearmed if its guard is eliminated by any means. There are provisions, but that is the basics.
This is correct. If the guard is eliminated then an equivalent size of prisoners are rearmed. It atters not how the guard dies.

title: Rout question from a blaze to an upper level encirclement predicament
question:
All,
If a squad enters a building that has a flame marker in it in the movement phase and the flame turns to blaze in the Adv Fire phase it must rout out or be eliminated. When it entered the blaze it was adjacent to an enemy unit. The only legal rout is upstairs in the same building. Does the squad surrender instead since it will be routing to a location that will be an upper level building encirclement? Assume the building is only occupies one hex. In effect the squad is routing to a location that it could never escape from due to the blaze in the ground floor.
Thanks for your help in advance.
author: Coaltar
consensus_answer:
Martin, I think there are two questions here: if a unit can choose or not to rout, and if a unit in a blaze can choose it or not.

For the second one, just expand your own quote another sentence:

A10.5 Broken units must rout away (ATTACKER first—one unit at a time [EXC: Voluntary Rout; 10.711]) during that RtPh or be eliminated for Failure to Rout [EXC: Surrender; 20.21]. Otherwise, a broken unit must rout only if in a Blaze (B25.4).

For the first question, yes, it seems that I read it wrong: a unit could refuse routing and be outright eliminated (or surrender if the conditions apply). But I've never seen anyone refuse a rout and prefer being eliminated. Maybe in some weird ASL situations it could be the better choice, of course.

The rules I cited for surrender only say that surrender is forced if certain conditions apply.

So, my take:

1. When in a Blaze, a unit MUST rout.
2. If the only possible rout (in any case) is trough Interdiction or Low Crawl and ADJACENT to Known, Good Order, armed enemy Infantry/Cavalry, the unit MUST surrender.
3. If not in a Blaze, a unit has the option to refuse rout and either surrender or be eliminated if no enemy can capture the unit.

title: CC vs Melee question for bogged tank
question:
Hey all I got a question about CC vs Melee. I have a squad that was in melee with both an enemy tank and and squad. The tank is bogged with no accessible MG (its and AA mg and the crew is not CE). My squad eliminated the enemy squad. Is my squad now from from Melee?
Thanks
author: Coaltar
consensus_answer:
Hey all I got a question about CC vs Melee. I have a squad that was in melee with both an enemy tank and and squad. The tank is bogged with no accessible MG (its and AA mg and the crew is not CE). My squad eliminated the enemy squad. Is my squad now from from Melee?
Thanks

If I understand you correctly you are asking about the distinction between Close Combat (CC) and Melee. In this case the squad is held in Melee by the enemy immobile tank. The tank is not held in melee. If the tank spends a start movement point and successfully unbogs, the melee marker is immediately removed.

title: Best way to learn ASL's OBA
question:
What's the best way to learn the mechanics and rules associated with ASL's OBA rules?  I hoped that ASL Starter kit 2 would explain it in a way I could grasp, but it couldn't really do the job.  I've read through the rules several times and have got a bit of an idea how it works, but it still seems kind of clunky to me.  Any help would be appreciated.
Thanks,
turks1966
author: turks1966
consensus_answer:
OBA rules to read are little hard to conceptualize :soblue:and the rulebook locations can be little difficult (For example the ASLRB index doesn't include the information found on ASL Rulebook 2nd dividers)

Basically alot of #$%! events happen for a typical OBA attack (Different for NOBA Chapter G14.6 Rising Sun rules & Rocket Artillery C 1.9) :
1. Contact attempt (C1.2)
2. Battery access  (C1.21)
3. Contact access + Battery access then place AR counter
4. LOS check to AR counter placement (C1.3)
5. Accuracy roll for SR (C1.3)
6. LOS check for SR (1.3) 
   * Note placing SR ends actions for observer/battery OBA actions      
     (C1.322 End of actions) 
7. Correct -or- convert SR into FFE:1/2 (C1.33)

To start with you need to have someone (1 of the following in your forces OOB for the scenario) to call in the OBA:
* Observer + Radio (C1.2)
* Observer + Field Phone (1.23)
* Off Board Observer (C1.63)
* OP Tank/Observation Post Tank (C1.2,C1.6, H1.45-1.465)

Then you have the different types of Fire Missions:

* HE concentration           C1.72 Player decision
* Smoke concentration        C1.72 Player decision
* WP/White Phosphorus        OBA Nationality chart either- SMOKE in OBA
* Harassing Fire             C1.72 Player deicsion
* Pre-Registered Fire        C1.73 SSR or DYO
* Bombardment                C1.8  SSR or DYO
* IR/Illuminating Rounds     E1.93 OBA Nationality chart
 

So you have type of observer, then type of fire mission and THEN 'conditions' of artillery like:

Plentiful ammo (C1.21 + add black chit to draw pile)
US Plentiful ammo (A25.33) US always plentiful ammo unless SSR otherwise

http://www.vftt.co.uk/vfttpdfs.asp

title: Adjacent buildings, different levels LOS?

author: thegamer
consensus_answer:
What rule covers this in the main rule book.

B23.25 (with the Journal 5 errata in red):

23.25 ADJACENT BUILDING HEXES: A unit in a building is ADJACENT to an adjacent building level of the same building only if both are either on the same level [EXC: Rowhouse; 23.71], or are vertically connected by a stairwell (printed or inherent). Otherwise, no LOS exists between adjacent units in the same building, nor does a LOS exist between non-adjacent units in the same building, unless a LOS clear of the building depiction can be traced through intervening hex(es)—such as from 1M5 to N3 (see 23.1 illustration). LOS to a unit in a building Location [EXC: rooftop Location] can exist only if drawn to an ADJACENT unit or (for LOS between different hexes) if the LOS as it enters the hex does not cross a hexside within the building depiction (e.g., in contrast to 1X3/X4).

title: Night Scenario Defender Question
question: E1.2 states that the scenario defender receive dummy counters equivalent to the OOB.  I am reading this right in that if, say, I have 10 full squads, I get 10 "?" dummy counters?  I think so, but want to make sure.
author: cscottk
consensus_answer:
The actual wording is ...receiving Dummy counters equal to the number of squad-equivalents in his OB...

The key is is "squad-equivalents".  10 full squads means 10 Dummy counters.  8 squads and 2 half-squads would be only 9 Dummies.  No Dummies are received for AFV or Guns.  A12.2 allows for replacing any number of 1/2" Dummies with 5/8" Dummies, however.

author: patch_bunny
consensus_answer:
A squad is IN a gully/stream/wadi location, and wishes to place smoke grenades in an ADJACENT higher level location.

A24.1 reads, "Placement in an ADJACENT hex of higher elevation is only allowed across a single crest line or building level stairwell..."  Does that mean they can't?
If it's a single crest line, yes, they can try.  After getting SMOKE, they can, on a subsequent dr of 1..3, place the SMOKE at the higher level (up and over).  If the subsequent dr is 4..6, their SMOKE usually ends up in their own hex (rolls back downhill to them).

A24.1,  for the subsequent dr rule.  B10.11, 1st, for the definition of a Crest line.

title: Rooftop Concealment Question
question:
Question: A 5/8” mortar is on a rooftop location. There are unbroken enemy units with a LOS to the rooftop location at a lower elevation within 16 hexes to the mortar. Can the mortar can concealment? 

Situation: The situation arose during a playing of Festung Budapest CG II between two teams of players. The Axis team has 82mm mortars on rooftop locations of several buildings (L29, L33, N31 I believe). After loosing both their HIP status and concealment (as per A12.34), the axis team automatically grew concealment at the end of their player turns for all revealed mortars. The Russian team believes this is incorrect and the mortars should not be able to grow concealment. 

Axis argument: The Axis teams justification for the automatic gaining of concealment is:
	B23.82 CONCEALMENT: … A unit can remain hidden or concealed on a rooftop if there are no Good Order enemy ground units within 16 hexes of it 	that are at the same or higher level with a LOS of it; these same restrictions 	apply to gaining “?” on a rooftop [EXC: the enemy units need only be unbroken 	(as opposed to Good Order) to prohibit such gain]. 

The Axis player interprets this to mean that so long as there are no unbroken enemy units at ≥ level to the mortar, concealment gain is automatic.

Russian argument: The Russian team’s argument that the Axis mortar cannot automatically gain concealment on the rooftop is based on the following rules. 

B23.82 CONCEALMENT: A Rooftop Location is Concealment Terrain only for setup purposes. 

A12.121 CONCEALMENT LOSS/GAIN TABLE: The specific situation that allows “?” gain (or cause “?” loss) are given in the Concealment Table. … The Concealment Table always takes precedence over the body of the rules (e.g., an uncommon cause of “?” loss might be mentioned in the Concealment Table even though it is omitted from the rules for the sake of brevity). 

The Concealment Loss/Gain Table list “NA” for all Gun gain instances when in LOS of Unbroken enemy ground units. (C2.1 & 9.2 defines the mortars as Guns). 

The Russian player interprets the rules to read that unbroken enemy units with a LOS do prevent “?” growth per the A12.121 since a Gun cannot grow “?” in the LOS of an enemy unit. 

Follow-up Question: In the same situation, could a unit on the rooftop (with or without a SW, including a SW mortar) gain concealment?

Thanks in advance :)
