consensus_answer:
First, the Concealment table ALWAYS takes precedence.

B23.82 CONCEALMENT: … A unit can remain hidden or concealed on a rooftop if there are no Good Order enemy ground units within 16 hexes of it that are at the same or higher level with a LOS of it; these same restrictions apply to gaining “?” on a rooftop [EXC: the enemy units need only be unbroken (as opposed to Good Order) to prohibit such gain]. 

O.5 ROOFTOPS (B23.82 & B23.83): A Rooftop Location is Concealment Terrain only for setup purposes. Once the first RPh has been completed B23.82 comes into effect. A Rooftop Location is not considered a building Location for rout and Victory Condition purposes. A Gun may never be Emplaced (C11.2) on a Rooftop.

The roof is Concealment Terrain for Set-up purposes, which is what it means.  For set-up, it's like Woods when you set up.  (duh!)

In RB, since roofs are in play, you can set up Concealed on the Roof.  And so can anyone else.  Then, when you look at the ASOP, when the game starts that RPh, you lose concealment as per the Table.

And that's what Rule B23.82 is talking about.

And as the game progresses, if you are still the only unit on a roof and no one is higher, you gain/loss your concealment as per the table (as if you were in woods).  If you're on the roof, and no enemy has a LOS to you, you'll gain concealment, just like Woods. (their is no automatic gain, just like in Woods if you are in LOS).

As another example, if an HIP Spotter is on a Roof, and no one is higher, then he stays HIP.

Actually, pretty simple and very clear.  Not sure why some are not understanding the rule.  Granted, I've played the CG for Red Barricades over 10 times.

consensus_answer:

Apologize for the above picture quality but I wanted to make 100% sure I understand this correctly.

SL11 Defiance on Hill 30:
6 American stacks under "?" concealment counters - I could use my mortar (assuming it's not broken :cry:) to make area attacks on the concealed American units?

Sure you can. Provided the shot is otherwise legal. Maybe this will help:

[12.06] Area Target Type vs. Area Fire
These are easy terms to confuse, but they are separate concepts and actually refer to different things.

Area Target Type is an Ordnance TH procedure. MTRs always fire with ATT, and any weapon attempting to lay SMOKE must also use the ATT. Otherwise, use of ATT (as opposed to Vehicle Target Type or Infantry Target Type) is optional. Use of ATT consumes all of a unit's available ROF [EXC: MTR fire], and, if a hit is secured, the normal FP of the attack is halved. The advantages of ATT are that it's often easier to obtain a hit, at the penalty of reduced attack effectiveness. ATT is also the only way to gain acquisition against a concealed target.

Area Fire refers to any circumstance that causes your normal FP to be halved, e.g., firing at a concealed unit, firing in the AFPh, firing at long range are all examples of Area Fire. Ordnance is affected by Area Fire differently; it must add +2 to the TH DR, but if it hits, it attacks at normal strength *for the chosen Target Type*. Note that this means that *if* you are using the Area Target Type vs. a concealed target, you will have a +2 TH DRM *and* attack at half strength.

"Sleeze" is usually something gamey that seemingly contradicts historical behavior. True sleeze is completely legal, and will not get you banned at any regular tournament. Some people might be unhappy with you, but anyone who pouts too much over VBM-freeze or skulking is probably not worth playing with much (there are plenty of fish in this sea).

Using ATT to gain acquisition on a hex with no currently Known targets is perfectly fine. First off, 'concealed' is just that. Your forces are pretty sure there's someone there, they just aren't quite sure of where in that 40-yard hex they are, or what they are, and sometimes, there's just shadows there (Dummies). If there's nothing there, then either you figure that there may be HIP units there, or someone may want to move into/through the area, both of which are reasonable suppositions. In all cases, you're chancing weapon malfunction or a Sniper in return for being better prepared.

Another valid tactic when you have OBA is to drop WP onto an area. This will do two things for you. title: Sniper help
question:
I'm trying to get a grasp on the sniper rules. So let's say my opponent has rolled my SAN. Next the sniper attack is rolled, which turns up either 1 or 2. The rules ask me to roll for location like a spotting round. My DR is rolled, and colored die gives me direction, and the white die tells me how many hexes in that direction to locate my sniper. 

At this point I'm confused a bit about Location of my target(s). What determines what the sniper selects as a target? Is there a range in hexes that he can fire? And I assume he follows LOS rules? 

Thanks!
author: trox
consensus_answer:
Basically the sniper attacks any units (with certain exceptions) in the target hex you rolled for. If there are no enemy units in the target hex the sniper will target the nearest (in hexes) enemy unit, ie move the sniper counter to the closest hex with enemy unit/s in it. If there are more then one enemy unit in the target hex use random selection to determine which unit/s is/are affected (there could be more than one depending on the random selection dr)

See A14.21 which explains how to select an alternate target hex if the initial one is free of enemy units.

Hope that helps a bit...

replies.body: He hits a randomly selected unit in the target hex that you got in the previous step. No LOS with snipers.

There is no range/LOS with snipers. 
If there is no target in the determined hex
it attacks/is placed in the closest hex that it can attack.

If there are more than one target in a hex, a random selection die roll
is made.

If it lands in an empty hex, it then goes to the closest stack from there. If equidistant then the one with lowest TEM, if still tied, you can choose which stack to attack. Then, if in that stack there are more than one enemy unit make a random selection and in case of a tie you can choose which one to attack and make a new sniper roll for the other tied unit.

title: Residual Fire and Broken firers question.
question:

Having a 'forget the obvious moment'.  I have a German unit thats laid two Residual Fire counters during the enemy's movement turn.  It's just failed a Final Protective Fire roll versus an adjacent enemy unit and is now Broken.  Do I remove the Residual Fire counters for that German unit, being that they're broken now. author: Jonathan Ward
consensus_answer:
A good rule of thumb to keep in mind, is that once placed the FP of the residual never reduces for any reason. Not even concealment protect from the residual.

title: Platoon movement and LOS (a matter of errata)
question: I had a rules dispute the other day. Is there any LOS requirement for platoon movement? I can't find any. This was the situation. Three radio-less tanks move onto the board at the same time. The one in the middle has a tree in the way and bypasses to one side, blocking LOS to one of the other tanks. This is ok?
author: elcomadreja2
consensus_answer: Not 100% sure, but I think maybe not. D14.21 says that each AFV must be adjacent to another AFV in the same platoon and have LOS to that AFV at the end of each impulse. D14.22 says that gaps are allowed only if one of the platoon is destroyed, immobilized, etc. So that might mean that a platoon entering from offboard in the terrain described would have to do so in column (sequentially through the same hex or bypass hexside) instead of abreast.

replies.body: Not 100% sure, but I think maybe not. D14.21 says that each AFV must be adjacent to another AFV in the same platoon and have LOS to that AFV at the end of each impulse. The vehicles need to have LOS to one of the others not all of them so if one vehicle is in front of the obstacle and one in it and the last on the other side, they are still in a platoon despite lack of Los between vehicles 1 and 3.

author: madmat
consensus_answer:
Hi Matt - first off, great to see you here and let me know if/when you're free for another face-to-face session - I promise it'll help! :D  See my comments in italics within your quote.

Allowed AFV ranged fire/attacks?

Fire during (PFPh)
    Check!

Bounding Fire (during AFPh after movement into hex hex during MPh)
    As alluded to in Eddy's post, two types: (1) what you're describing, and (2) what Eddy mentions - firing during the AFV's movement phase.  The unique aspect of #2 compared to most other shots with main armament, is that AFV firing with Bounding *first* fire will NOT gain acquisition.  The only exception is a gyro-stabilizer-equipped vehicle (if you have one of these it will be noted in the scenario SSR).

Fire during (AFPh if didn't fire during PFPh & NO Bounding fire)
     Firing during the AFPh would still count as Bounding Fire (i.e. +2 TH DRM 

Fire during (Defensive Fire Phase)
     Which also includes firing during the enemy's Movement Phase (aka "First Fire").

Intensive Fire
     Check! There are restrictions on when this can be done, however.

Attempt Deliberate Immobilization
      Check!  Note the limitations on range, caliber required in order to be effective, and acquisition.  Can be very effective, however. 

Form Fire Group (per A7.5)
     Off the top of my head, the only AFV that can form fire groups with other units are Half-tracks, and it's a special exception just for them.  They may form fire-groups with other half-tracks or other Infantry (including leadership modifiers if in the same hex with Infantry and the leader is either with the Infantry or with the Passengers).  Of course, any AFV may fire-group its own weapons (e.g. bow machine-gun plus Co-Ax machine-gun).

Gun Duel (Defender using C2.2401)
     Check, but a Gun Duel is often declared by the *attacker* after a Defender declares a shot.  They are only successful (i.e. attacker gets to shoot first - using Bounding First Fire) if the DRM paid by the Defender exceed those of the Attacker or if they're equal then the one with the lower *final* TH DR wins.  When you consider that covered-arc change costs are doubled if the shooter is firing from a building or woods, you can begin to see where this can work out in the attacker's favor, especially if he's equipped with gyro-stabilizers, which cut down on his DRM for this calculation only.

title: PzKpfw II (Fl)
question:
OK, the PzKpfw II (Fl) has a special ability to place smoke at exactly 3 hexes inside the VCA. If you change VCA to use do this, then you used the same Case A penalties as if you were using a smoke mortar. There is a lot missing here from the rule, I am wondering if anybody has any thoughts on this.

For example is line of sight necessary to the hex where the smoke is placed?

If the PzKpfw II (Fl) is hull down, can it use this ability (i.e. similar to using other hull based weapons)?
author: drmark64
consensus_answer:
The chapter H note says :

The smoke discharger, if successfully fired, allows the placing of a smoke counter at three (only) hex range within the tank's VCA. Any VCA change pertinent to using the sD is treated as per D13.32.

The VCA change penalty is the only concession to the sM rule.
Otherwise, it is a sD.

That means :
- range blocked at 3 hexes ("only")
- within VCA (and not TCA)
- LOS not needed (hey, it can fire over a building, woods or any obstacle... or even through one!):arrrh:
- no +2 moving/motion penalty
- no Hindrance penalty
- it can fire from a building or deep jungle (:D)

I understand that some people can feel their sense of reality deeply contradicted by those facts, but that is how the rule is displayed.

One could not argue that the vehicle note was written before the sM rules were, as it directly refers to them.
Rules' lawyering supplemental argument : chapter H comes after chapter D, so it supersedes the latter unless otherwise stated.

So, until there is an erratum about that vehicle note - and, frankly, I do think that something should be done about it, as my "feeling of reality" is ruffled to - I will play along the present rules.
ASL is to WW2 what D&D is to Middle Ages : I don't mind having a super duper smoke puffing dragon around.;)

title: how far can a squad move?
question:
Let's see ....one hex = 40 meters, one game turn = 2 minutes.

A squad can conceivably move

Its Player Turn
Mph - 9 hexes (CX, Lder, Road bonus). - gets routed from defensive fire
RtPh - 6 hexes rout

Enemy Player turn
 - Our poor squadie gets fired at, DM'ed again
 - Enemy moves adjacent
RtPh - 6 hexes rout

Total = 21 hexes = 840 Meters
That makes it average 7 Meters/sec ...not near enough to sprint speeds but still faster than my normal walking speed at the games shop!!

hmmmm ...anyone else can add to that and see if we have potential olympic champions in our ASL Squads?
author: Lamskiy
consensus_answer:
While the rules officially define a turn as being two minutes in duration, this definition can be fudged quite a bit by various parts of the game system. Here's how Squad Leader designer John Hill explained it in his Designer's Notes to the original game:

The given time span of "two minutes" is actually not a hard and fast rule. With the given movement of 4MP per unit, we have a squad covering only 160 meters in two minutes. In reality, even carrying the usual assortment of equipment, you could go farther, if all you did was move. But, if you consider all the possibilities: rally, move, fire, counterfire, fire again, and close combat, then maybe each turn is really four minutes long. So, there is a possible internal contradiction. Then, throw in the whole problem of, "How long would it take for the actual platoon leaders to decide to do this?" and you begin to see how really "fudged" two minutes are.
With regards to the original question, issue #36 of View from The Trenches ran an interesting article by Wayne Hadady entitled "The Physics of ASL" which stated the following:

Case B alone would only apply for firing in the APh without entering a new hex (and without using Opportunity Fire). Watch out that it can be +3 for woods/building/rubble.

Case C always adds Case B. So maybe they could just simply add it into Case C modifiers... but it's the way it is.

title: Q: Infantry Defensive Fire/combat against moving vehicles with no AT weapons?
question:
Hi all,

I have to admit that normally I have been avoiding scenarios with vehicles in, but now that I have started using them I wish I had started earlier :)

In my last move in S125 (solo) I had a russian tank move on a road past a building containing German infantry. This is an early war scenario from 1941.

Would I be correct in saying that there isn't anything realistically that the German squad with an LMG could do given the tank was not CE? So in this case I just left the infantry in concealment without doing anything. 

Would I also be correct in saying that the only way the infantry could have realistcially attacked the tank is in the CC phase had the tank finished it's move adjacent to the infantry (it didn't as I think that would have been suicidal :)  )

Thanks
RobP
http://AncientArmies.co.uk
author: FlashPan
consensus_answer:
You can also streetfight (A11.8) an adjacent AFV in a road hex as it moves past you if there is a building on the other side of the road.

Generally you have to take a PAATC
If you pass it you can generally take out a tank on fours or less..

Five = close combat value of a squad
+2 = motion vehicle
-1 = street fighting bonus   

Generally this isn't worthwhile as the chances of success are low and you will get either pinned or marked first fire. 

Stack with a 8-1 leader (who adds one to your CCV and gives a -1 Dice roll mod and who doesn't need to take a PAATC) or against open topped vehicles (-2 DRM) or 1944-45 Germans with anti-tank magnetic mines (50% chance of a a -3 DRM) and it starts getting worth thinking about...

replies.body:
First you have to distinguish between armored and non-armored vehicles.

Non-armored vehicles are easy: they're attacked on the IFT table using the "star" row. Ditto for non-armored facings of partial-armored vehicles. They can also be attacked in CC.

With armored vehicles you must either attack them on the VTT (using the To Hit - To Kill procedure) or attack them in CC.

Infantry inherent firepower cannot attack using the To Hit procedure. Any MG (LMG, MMG, HMG) can. Just attack the AFV like any other gun would (applying roll modifiers) and for the To Kill use the MG column. There are some modifiers for distance, caliber, etc.

Usually only early war AFV can be destroyed using a MG as the TK# is low.

And also remember that CC can be used as a form of D1F, this is called Reaction Fire and can be used if the vehicle enters your Location. If it goes through a road between buildings you can also use Reaction Fire in an adjacent hex, this is called Street Fighting. And of course you can advance into the AFV Location during your turn and try your chances on CC there.

title: Is the squad inherent firepower includes the LMG of that squad?
question: I remembered I read somewhere in the rulebook that it includes the LMG but I found it's weird that the German LMG has FP of 3 while the German squad has FP of 4 only. Anyone confirms if I'm correct?
author: Ultracheng
consensus_answer:
I rather would refer to the preliminary paragraph of chapter A9 :
[A LMG counter represents a weapon additional to the inherent complement of such weapons present in a squad and accounted for by that squad's FP. The inherent LMG of a squad counter is not subject to any of the following rules, nor can it ever be turned into a LMG counter.]

The Inherent FP of a squad never includes an LMG in counter form.

Spraying Fire is not only linked to the presence of a "ghost" LMG:

A7.34 SQUAD SPRAYING FIRE: Spraying Fire is limited to those squads with an inherent LMG, multiple SMG, and/or superior tactical training. 

Counter MGs can use spraying fire.
But a squad with spraying fire only can fire at about the range of an SMG.
The example in the rule shows a 628 Russian squad, which typically represents the "SMG only" squads that were part of SMG companies.

title: Lend-Lease vehicles and chapter H notes
question:
This is a bit hypothetical question because I'm actually looking at a Starter Kit scenario which comes with it's own Vehicle notes booklet, but it still got me thinking what should I do if it were a full ASL scenario?

So if a scenario gives the Russian player some Lend-Lease vehicles, what chapter H notes should I study?

For example, Russian gets some Sherman III(a) tanks:
Should I only read the Russian note 50. Sherman III (page H28E, 2nd edition RB) and then I'm all set, or should I also review the British note 13. Sherman III(a) (page H55).

The British note gives the tank many peculiar capabilities, like Gyros, optional AAMGs, and a capability for Multiple Hits. Yet the Russian note has none of those.

So does a Lend-Lease vehicle have those capabilities or not (I could accept both ways, a Russian version might be stripped out of such extras. I don't know, I'm not a historian. :P)
author: Hipsu
consensus_answer:
After some further research, I think I'm going to have to disagree with you guys. I'm pretty sure you're supposed to refer to both the Russian and the British notes. 

First of, BV (even 3rd edition) doesn't even come with Lend-Lease vehicles (Russian note numbers 48-58). In page H28F, under Lend-Lease Vehicles it says the following:
"For DYO purposes use British counters to represent the following vehicles in the Soviet service. All pertinent Vehicle Notes apply normally."
(underline by me)

Interestingly Starter Kit 3 comes with 6 Russian colored Sherman IIIs (unique in the system?) and its Vehicle Note is a mix of both nationalities. Its fluff text is of the Russian note, but it has a special note of using Black TH numbers after 1943, which is lifted straight from the British notes. It doesn't mention Gyros or Multiple hits, but those concepts are not in Starter Kits so that's easily explained. They still have the white ROF indicating Multiple Hits, and a big G in the back for the Gyros, even in Russian colors.

A7.353 In both of the above cases, Subsequent First Fire (8.3), FPF (8.31), and Final Fire (8.4) vs adjacent units retain halved inherent FP for those attacks (regardless of how they were used during First Fire)—although use of full SW/Gun capability during such attacks can negate inherent FP in the normal manner. See the 8.41 EX.

AND

A8.3 SUBSEQUENT FIRST FIRE:
...Whenever a unit uses Subsequent First Fire, it must use all MG/IFE in its possession (up to the unit's normal operation capabilities; 7.35-.353) as Subsequent First Fire or forfeit their use for the remainder of that Player Turn (barring FPF); a squad may not split its usable inherent FP from that of its MG/IFE during Subsequent First Fire unless it opts to not use the remaining FP/SW at all. ...

I have several questions here:

1. Does the A8.3 mean:
A squad with a MG are all under the First Fire counter. If the squad take SFF alone, the SFF chance of the MG surely will be forfeited. But if the player claim to use MG SFF only, will the squad also be considered as SFF, so they will under Final Fire counter too after the MG SFF?

2. Another assumption:
MG First Fired but the squad did not. Can the squad use the MG to SFF only (then turn the counter to Final Fire), but hold its own FP and remain clear of  First/Final fire counter?

3.What does 7.353 imply to? I can't imagine such condition this rule can apply.

And also another question related here since it happened during my last game.

If a squad fires MG only as DFF in MPh and cowered. Will both the squad and the MG be under Final Fire counter, or just the MG?

Thank you for the help.

:laugh:
author: Xavier_Zhang
consensus_answer:
1. Does the A8.3 mean:
A squad with a MG are all under the First Fire counter. If the squad take SFF alone, the SFF chance of the MG surely will be forfeited. But if the player claim to use MG SFF only, will the squad also be considered as SFF, so they will under Final Fire counter too after the MG SFF?

Yes. In SFF, inherent firepower and MGs are bound together. The reason to forfeit MG usually is because of fear of potential breakdown.

So in this situation, if we want to maximize the MG and squad FP, we can:
1. Attacker spends MF
2. First Fire MG
3. Attacker spends another MF
4. First Fire Squad
5. Attacker spends another MF or if Attack is adjacent, wait until Defensive Fire Phase.
6. SFF both Squad and MG.

2. Another assumption:
MG First Fired but the squad did not. Can the squad use the MG to SFF only (then turn the counter to Final Fire), but hold its own FP and remain clear of  First/Final fire counter?

No.

3.What does 7.353 imply to? I can't imagine such condition this rule can apply.

It actually refers to 8.3.
7.351 and 7.352 says the inherent FP can be used only once and can add to MG, even if the MG retains ROF. This case applies to Prep Fire.
7.353 says that inherent FP can be used again in the same Movement/Defensive Fire Phase in forms of SFF, FPF and FP to adjacent target. All of these use 1/2 inherent FP.

And also another question related here since it happened during my last game.

If a squad fires MG only as DFF in MPh and cowered. Will both the squad and the MG be under Final Fire counter, or just the MG?

Both of under Final Fire counter.

Print this excellent First Fire with MGs Flow Chart play aid. It will help explain all to you.

1. Does the A8.3 mean:
A squad with a MG are all under the First Fire counter. If the squad take SFF alone, the SFF chance of the MG surely will be forfeited. But if the player claim to use MG SFF only, will the squad also be considered as SFF, so they will under Final Fire counter too after the MG SFF?

Yes. In SFF, inherent firepower and MGs are bound together. The reason to forfeit MG usually is because of fear of potential breakdown.

So in this situation, if we want to maximize the MG and squad FP, we can:
1. Attacker spends MF
2. First Fire MG
3. Attacker spends another MF
4. First Fire Squad
5. Attacker spends another MF or if Attack is adjacent, wait until Defensive Fire Phase.
6. SFF both Squad and MG.

2. Another assumption:
MG First Fired but the squad did not. Can the squad use the MG to SFF only (then turn the counter to Final Fire), but hold its own FP and remain clear of  First/Final fire counter?

No.

3.What does 7.353 imply to? I can't imagine such condition this rule can apply.

It actually refers to 8.3.
7.351 and 7.352 says the inherent FP can be used only once and can add to MG, even if the MG retains ROF. This case applies to Prep Fire.
7.353 says that inherent FP can be used again in the same Movement/Defensive Fire Phase in forms of SFF, FPF and FP to adjacent target. All of these use 1/2 inherent FP.

Both of under Final Fire counter.

D1.22 PARTIALLY ARMORED: An AFV that has armor protection along only its front and side Target Facings is recognizable by the presence of a * symbol along the right-hand margin beneath its Side/Rear AF. title: What's the meaning of "hook up" here?
question:
9.72 SW/GUN REPAIR:
....
Only a crew (not a Temporary Crew) can attempt to repair a Gun, and not while hooked up.

"Hook up" here means held in Melee or refer to sth. else?

Thank you.
author: Xavier_Zhang
consensus_answer:
The Index is your friend :

	
Hooking Up Guns: C10.11 [CMD DR: S16.35] [Towing on Narrow Street: B31.124]

C10.11 HOOKING UP: A Stopped vehicle not in Bypass may hook up a Gun (if the vehicle's T# ≤ the Gun's M#) by spending half (FRU) of its MP/MF allotment [EXC: if the Gun's M# is circled (e.g. M(6), the vehicle must expend two-thirds (FRU) of its MP/MF allotment] in that Gun's hex (in addition to any required MP/MF cost to enter the hex), provided a crew (as per 10.111) is on foot in that hex. This expenditure does not itself qualify that vehicle as a moving target, but does allow Defensive First Fire opportunities against it (that Gun shares its target status and is destroyed or missed depending on the fate of the vehicle). That Gun is then placed on top of that vehicle to indicate that it is in tow. Neither that Gun, its crew, nor that vehicle/its PRC can fire during that PFPh/MPh and all are TI for the rest of that Player Turn. That crew may also load into that towing vehicle at no extra MP/MF cost as it hooks up that Gun, but if it expends > half its MF allotment in pushing/entering that Gun's hex, that Gun cannot then be hooked up by that unit in that MPh. A non-QSU Gun (10.23) must first be limbered (10.21) before it can be hooked up. See 10.31 for pushing and hooking up a Gun in the same MPh.

title: indoor use of FT
question:
Under heavy winds, FT can't use long range fire (unless downwind).

Fire spreading rules are different within buildings (no drm because wind doesn't interfere).

It would be logical for FT to be able to fire at long range indoors, even under heavy winds ; it needs a LOS of course, which means that it would only be possible in a (non-roofless) factory.  

Your opinion please ?
author: Merrimac
consensus_answer:
Check B25.63 Wind Force

"No Wind" is always in effect in non-rooftop Locations of an Interior Building Hex. This is in the same section it's talking about wind effects on FT.

Note that Interior Building Hexes are only those that which are surrounded by building hexsides; it is presumed that there are broken windows/open doors that mean the "exterior" building hexes are still affected by the wind. You'd need a big Factory to take advantage of the exception.

Cheers,
Merric

title: When does a berserk unit lose it's berserk status?
question:
I just finished a solo attempt at scenario T3 Ranger Stronghold. The US win if they have any unbroken units within a certain area at the end of the game.

On the very last (US) turn a berserk US unit charged the nearest enemy (these were just outside the victory condition area). This was the last US unit available to claim victory as the others were all broken in the previous DFPh. So by being forced to charge outside the victory condition area US victory was not certain.

The charged units were already broken. I assumed that the berserker should attack them in the AFPh with TPBF (halved for AFPh). They survived this and then routed away in the following rout phase leaving the berserk unit out of LOS of any other units.

So during the last APh of the game can this unit advance back into the area needed for victory? I.e. when does it lose berserk status? I believe berserk units cannot advance. So if the berserk unit loses the berserk status after the rout phase then that is OK and it can advance into the zone required for a US victory (otherwise the Germans win - talk about a knife edge ending).

I have from the rules:
15.46 RETURN TO NORMAL: A berserk unit loses its berserk status and returns to Good Order whenever it (or the group it attacks with) eliminates all (but at least one) Known enemy units in its Location with either TPBF (halved) or FT during the AFPh or CC, or if at the end of a charge there is no Known enemy unit in its LOS (15.431).

Strictly speaking the unit was not out of LOS of enemies at the 'end of the charge' and had not eliminated any units. The units moved away during the rout phase and were not interdicted.

I assume that 'end of the charge' can mean any subsequent phase in which case the US unit returned to normal at the end of the rout phase and then could advance (and claim victory) in the very last phase of the game.

It would charge the last known location in LOS that an enemy unit occupied before leaving LOS.

title: Fired on while in CC v AFV
question:
Hi,

I have two German infantry Units atop a T34 tank (immobilised) attempting to destroy it in CC (now melee).  A couple of Russian units now have LOS (three hexes away) to the melee - can they fire on the tank with IFE and help their compatriots?  If so do the Germans get any TEM for the immobilised tank?  I have checked the rules but struggled to find a definate answer.

Help as always much appreciated,

J
author: Jonathan Ward
consensus_answer:
A11.15 [...] The Melee units may be attacked by non-Melee units during a fire phase (or even the ATTACKER's MPh in some cases) but all friendly and enemy units in the Location must be attacked. [...]

D9.3 WRECK/AFV TEM: All Infantry in the same Location with a wreck/friendly-AFV/abandoned-enemy-AFV are entitled to a +1 TEM [...]

So yes, you can fire on the Melee Location and probably will affect only the enemy infantry. The Germans won't get TEM because the AFV is not friendly and not abandoned.

title: recombining
question:
If two halfsquads are together, it is allowed to recombine them, but you get a squad of the lower quality type. 

What exactly constitutes "lower quality" ?

5-4-8s. Seems  illogical.

c) both criteria above must be fulfilled : avoid all such oddities, but this would disallow recombining an Italian 1-3-6 with a 1-3-7 to get a 3-4-6, still odd. (in fact, this recombining is one of the most logical)

author: Merrimac
consensus_answer:
A1.32 RECOMBINE: Any two Good Order HS of the same nationality with an identical Strength Factor may automatically Recombine as their sole action in that RPH into a squad of the same type and Class at the start of any RPh in which they occupy the same Location and terrain(see 2.8) with a friendly Good Order leader [EXC:Finns, Guards, Carrier HS and unarmed HS do not need leader presence to Recombine]. The sole activity of that leader during the RPh is to permit the Recombination of any eligible HS in his Location.

author: BigAl737
consensus_answer:
In FTF games, yes, you just have to remember; usually this will not be a problem for experienced players.

Easiest way is to orient the first fire counter and the MG so they are at a different angle to the squad.

What happens then if said "pocket" is adjacent to your perimeter ?

title: Casualty Reduction in CC?
question:
Hi,

Just a few questions that arose last night mid-battle:

When a unit suffers casualty reduction due to CC DR equal to To Kill number, is the unit also Broken as well?

Can a tank fire it's MG's as First Fire during the enemies MPh, then later during the same MPh fire it's MA at a different moving target.  OR, is a First Fire counter placed on the tank after the MG's have fired and the MA cannot fire later (unless Intensive Fire) even though it did not fire earlier...er...if that makes any sense?

On emplaced Guns, is it better tactically to hose them down with machine gun fire in an attempt to kill the Crew rather than attempt OVR with tanks or blast at them with tank MA's...which is what I attempted and wrecked a lot of my tanks accordingly with zero success!

Your input and advice is, as always, much appreciated

Best regards (and Merry Christmas, must remember it's xmas and get my head out of the damn ASL RB occasionally!)

Jonathan
author: Jonathan Ward
consensus_answer:
Hi Jonathan,

Dealing with your questions in turn:

1) No, a unit which suffers CR in CC is not broken as well
2) Yes, a tank can fire its MGs at one target and then fire its MA later in the MPh or even in the DFPh if you wish.
3) It depends. An emplaced gun crew will get the +2 TEM either way. A good way way to take out the crew is to appraoch from outside their CA and then advance into CC. This way the +2 TEM doesn't matter and as long as you are a full squad, you should get a nice 2:1 in CC. This also stops the crew self rallying back which can happen if you break them with fire.

Hope this helps.

Merry Christmas.

Paul

title: A way to enter minefield covered buildings?
question:
Playing Red Barricades we have had a discussion regarding a way to enter buildings covered by minefields.

The issue is about rule B24.74, the last part:

Good Order Infantry may enter a Known minefield hex free of minefield attack by placing a partial TB, provided they expend their entire MF allotment to do so, become TI, and attempt to clear the minefield at the end of their CCPh. Unless the minefield is cleared, these units may exit the minefield free if minefield attack only by the hexside through which they entered. No other units may use the partial TB. The partial TB counter is removed if they are eliminated or exit the hex.

We agree that if the minefield is in an Open Ground hex, if a squad enters it using this rule it can only exit the hex using the same hexside or they will be attacked by the minefield.

But if the minefield is in a non-interior building hex that belongs to a multi-hex building, if a squad enters this hex using rule B24.74, what happens?

A. Player A says that this squad is inside the building and thus after the Clearance DR, whether they succeed or fail, they are free to move to other parts of the building using building hexisdes, without being attacked by the minefield.

B. Player B says that until they succeed to clear the minefield they are in the minefield part of the hex and they can only move back using the partial TB or they will be attacked by the mines.

Question 1: Who is right?

If Player A is right, then using this method is a quite effective way of moving in the Red Barricades map through the minefield covered hexes, isn't it?

Question 2: If a unit that enters a minefield using rule B24.74 is subsequently broken in that Location before rolling for Clearance, can they exit the minefield without being attacked using their Partial TB or they lose their Partial TB when they are broken?

Thanks.
author: esparver73
consensus_answer:
I'd say the rule is clear enough  -  those units may exit the minefield free of attack by either successfully clearing the minefield, or by using their partial trail break counter to return to where they came from.

Ok in a non-building situation.

If they exit to another building hex without clearing the minefield, they'd get attacked by it.

Bute the minefield rules say:

28.412 A unit is considred to be in the minefield hex which attacks it when the attack is resolved.

28.41 Whenever a unit enters/leaves a minefield hex, the owning player must announce a minefield attack vs the unit (as per A12.11) on the IFT

B28.44 MINEFIELDS IN BUILDING/TRENCH HEXES: Minefields are allowed in non-Interior Building Hexes but do not attack units entering/exiting those hexes through a building hexside unless using Bypass Movement.

These rules are higher numbered than B24.74 so they take precedence. The unit attacked is inside the hex as there is no separate Location for the minefield. The attack only takes place as a unit enters or leaves the hex. A building hexside is an exception that allows units to move avoiding the minefield attack.

This is the point discussed. Do these rules create an exception for B24.74?

The only slight ambiguity is the use of the term hex instead of Location (a common problem in ASL rules). As written, they could go up to the 1st level (suffering an attack when they leave the minefield), and the trail break (only usable by them) would remain on the map until they leave the hex.

I don't think there is much ambiguity in the ASLRB between hexes and Locations. If a unit inside an Open Ground Location enters a Pillbox there, they enter a different Location but they are not attacked by the minefield because they don't leave the hex, only the Location.

title: HS & SW usage
question:
A7.352 states that a HS that uses a SW loses its inherent FP until CC or the end of the Player Turn. But where does it say that a HS that uses its inherent FP loses the subsequent use of its possessed SW? or is this just assumed by reciprocity of A7.352?

Also, the wording of A7.353 confuses me..is it just saying that if a HS uses a SW in D1F it can still use it's inherent firepower in SFF, FPF or FF?

I raise this issue as I had a situation where a HS with an ATR D1F at an enemy MMC with it's inherent FP. Then later in the MPh I went to fire the ATR at an AFV but was told I couldn't do this because the HS had all ready fired its inherent, but I can't find a rule that explicitly prohibits the use of a SW after a HS fires its inherent FP. So the citing of any rule that states this would be most helpful for me.

Thank you...
author: sapper_D
consensus_answer:
This is definitely one of the trickier parts of the ASL rules to learn.

A7.352 states that a HS that uses a SW loses its inherent FP until CC or the end of the Player Turn. But where does it say that a HS that uses its inherent FP loses the subsequent use of its possessed SW?
There is no rule that says that, because a HS using its inherent FP does not necessarily prohibit the subsequent use of its SW during defensive fire.

What A7.352 is actually saying is that when a HS fires, it must choose to fire either its inherent FP or a SW; it cannot fire both.

Also, the wording of A7.353 confuses me..is it just saying that if a HS uses a SW in D1F it can still use it's inherent firepower in SFF, FPF or FF?
Yes.

Here's an example of how this all works:

A HS with MMG will D1F at a moving enemy unit. It chooses to use its inherent FP in this attack. After resolving the attack both the HS and the MMG are marked with a First Fire counter. (The MMG cannot make a D1F attack of its own, from A7.352.)

The enemy unit now expends another MF, so the HS declares a SFF attack. Once again it must choose to use either its inherent FP (x 1/2) or the MMG (FP x 1/2 + Sustained Fire). Regardless of the choice made, both the HS and the MMG are marked with a Final Fire counter after resolving the attack.

Note especially that the use of the HS's inherent FP in the D1F attack does not prevent the subsequent use of the MMG in other SFF/FPF/FF attacks. And, had the HS used the MMG in the D1F attack, that would not prevent the use of its inherent FP in other SFF/FPF/FF attacks.

The enemy unit now moves adjacent to the HS, so the HS declares a FPF attack. The MMG must be used in a FPF attack, so the HS's inherent FP cannot be used (unless the MMG malfunctioned in a previous attack).

I raise this issue as I had a situation where a HS with an ATR D1F at an enemy MMC with it's inherent FP. Then later in the MPh I went to fire the ATR at an AFV but was told I couldn't do this because the HS had all ready fired its inherent, but I can't find a rule that explicitly prohibits the use of a SW after a HS fires its inherent FP.
When your HS makes its D1F attack, both it and its ATR would be marked with a First Fire counter, because A7.352 states that a HS cannot fire both its inherent FP and a SW. This then prevents the ATR from firing for the remainder of the MPh, because only Small Arms/MG/IFE can use SFF or FPF, and only Guns can use Intensive Fire.

But if you had fired the ATR in a D1F attack, you could still use the HS's inherent FP for subsequent SFF/FPF/FF attacks.

title: Rules summary for Partially Armored vehicles
question:
To make my life easier when playing with partially armored vehicles, I'm summarizing some rules concerning them

From what I've gathered from the rulebook and G&A, partially armored vehicles handles the following situations like this:

TH/TK C7.11
If hit in the * facing, treat as unarmored.

Small Arms and MGs QA
If the fire originates from the * side (even if only the turret is unarmored), the vehicle is treated as unarmored. TH process is not necessary for MGs.

Pin result A7.82
If the fire originated from the * side, treat as OT vehicle (meaning, the PRC just pins, but they keep their CE/BU status).

Driving into Residual FP D5.31
If the side is armored (usually) then the vehicle is treated as armored. Otherwise as unarmored (SdKfz 10/5).

Fire lane D5.311
Depends where the fire is coming from.

DC C7.346, QA
If placed through the * side, make an IFT (rather than a To Kill) DR vs the vehicle as if it were unarmored. DC position DR needs to be made.

Minefield QA
Unarmored only if the hull AF is 0, or if both its sides and rear are unarmored (SdKfz 10/5 again).

Close Combat A11.61, QA
Just the -2 DRM against it, even if it's also OT (not -3).

Sniper A14.22, 14.3
Treat as unarmored.

What about Aerial AF?
Depends on where the fire is coming from.

Behind a wall B9.36
If the fire originates from the * side:
- Small arms: The vehicle itself gets +2 DRM from the wall (cannot be hull down), but the PRC gets no protection.
- Ordnance: The vehicle is HD. If hit in the * turret, treat as unarmored.

Infantry and TPBF
This question is still unresolved and is currently discussed in GameSquad.

title: Question about gliders and vehicles - need Yanks?
question:
I am about to start some of the scenarios in FKaC and many of them use gliders so I read the glider rules last night.

There are two references to "US Vehicle note 51 (LVT4)" if you transport vehicles on a glider. Is this info in Yanks?
author: CletePurcel
consensus_answer:
I am about to start some of the scenarios in FKaC and many of them use gliders so I read the glider rules last night.

There are two references to "US Vehicle note 51 (LVT4)" if you transport vehicles on a glider. Is this info in Yanks?

Mark, here are the relevant bits from US Vehicle note 51:

51. LVT4: 

(snipsnipsnip - this is a looong vehicle note!)

PP CAPACITY: The LVT4 may transport any combination of the following items, with the total indicated PP applying to the LVT’s PP Capacity (D6.1):
  	
  Item	                       PP Cost
• Vehicle of ≤ 2 tons	         15
• Vehicle of > 2 but ≤ 4 tons	 30
• Non-MTR Gun with M# of ≥ 10	 10
• Gun with M# of 6-9	         20
• MTR of 76-107mm	          0
• Ammunition	             4 or 8 (1,3)
• Inherent vehicle crew	          0
• All other Personnel/SW     normal (2,3)

(1):	As per C10.13 (i.e., 4 PP for a Gun of ≤ 99mm, or 8 PP for one ≥ 100mm). This applicable PP cost is also used for a dm 76-82mm MTR, as well as for a 107mm mortar
(2):	As per their normal Passenger/Rider PP cost.
(3):	EXC: the PP cost of units/SW/ammo are reduced to zero if they are Passengers of a vehicle that is itself a Passenger.

VEHICLE: Unloading a Passenger vehicle consists of driving it off the LVT4 into the LVT’s Location at a cost of one MP for starting, plus one-fourth of the Passenger vehicle’s MP allotment, plus COT. There is no MP cost for entering the LVT’s Location (D2.14), but Overstacking will apply. Loading is the reverse of this procedure; i.e., the vehicle first enters the LVT’s Location if necessary (paying one extra MP; D2.14), and then expends one-fourth of its MP allotment plus one MP for COT to load onto it, plus one MP to stop. Otherwise, the normal principles of D6.4-.5 for (un)loading Passengers apply, including the “simultaneous expenditure” of each 25%-segment of movement allotment by both the Passenger vehicle and the LVT4 during the turn of (un)loading. An allowed vehicle can (un)load while towing a Gun (unless using Reverse movement; C10.1) by paying the extra MP for towing. A Passenger vehicle or Gun may not change its CA relative to that of its LVT. Since the LVT4’s ramp is at its rear, a vehicle’s VCA must coincide with the LVT’s VCA (or “rear” VCA) so that the vehicle is properly aligned for forward or reverse entry/exit onto/from the LVT. Overstacking does not occur due to a vehicle’s being a Passenger on an LVT4. A vehicle that is also a Passenger cannot claim or retain Motion status independently of the LVT4.

GUN: (Un)loading an unhooked Gun from/onto an LVT4 follows the same procedure as (un)hooking it from/to a towing vehicle (C10.11 & .2). A Gun may be (un)hooked from/to an allowable vehicle while both are Passengers on the LVT (any resulting TI status does not apply to the LVT).

SURVIVAL: If an LVT4 is destroyed (but does not burn) while on land, all unarmored vehicles and Guns aboard it are also destroyed; all vehicular PRC roll for survival using the LVT’s CS#. If an AFV is aboard such a destroyed LVT4, repeat the original attack, using its Original DR but now vs the AFV and adding an extra +2 TH (or IFT for non-ordnance) DRM as well as all other DRM applicable to that AFV. If the AFV survives it is bogged but may freely unload in a subsequent friendly MPh if it first passes a Bog Removal DR. The AFV’s PRC automatically survive the LVT’s destruction, but if the AFV does not survive they must roll for survival using the AFV’s CS#; if they survive they are placed on foot in the hex in the normal manner.

Hope this helps - enjoy!

JR

author: Jonathan Ward
consensus_answer:
From the Banzai!! 5.3 issue:

Tactical Analysis: Dreil Team by Matt Shostak

The British can only cross the stream at 4 points. These are the
two bridges and the two endpoints of the stream, which are
considered deep water by SSR (not flooded like the rest of the
stream is). Moreover, moving into the deep water is slow and
risky for the British. It costs 4 MF to enter such a hex, and the
unit automatically becomes CX (B20.43). This makes it difficult
to advance from W10 to V10 in the same turn that they entered
the water. The trick is to declare CX movement before moving,
enter the stream, and use whatever movement points are left to go
into crest status on the other side. Then the unit can advance out
in the same turn.

title: Searching in open ground
question:
A unit starts its MPh in open ground adjacent to some enemy concealed stacks. It spends only 1 MF to Search and achieves to remove concealment from those enemy stacks. The enemy stacks roll for search casualties with success. Now,

1. The searcher has spent 1MF and its MPh has ended. Now it is TI. Can it be fired as D1F only once (1MF spent), or more times?

2. If D1F fired, does FFMO apply?

3. If D1F fired, does FFNAM apply?

Rules ref welcome. Thanks.
author: esparver73
consensus_answer:
1. The searcher has spent 1MF and its MPh has ended. Now it is TI. Can it be fired as D1F only once (1MF spent), or more times?
You only spent 1 MF, so each defender with LOS may only fire once. A4.8 says nothing about TI status increasing your vulnerability to Defensive First Fire, so the normal rules will apply.

2. If D1F fired, does FFMO apply?
Yes, of course. You expended MF in a Open Ground hex.

3. If D1F fired, does FFNAM apply?
Yes. Assault Movement is NA if you intend to search (A12.152).

title: Another SFF question
question:
Hi again,

If a squad armed with an LMG fires only the squad's inherent FP at a moving target, then wants to SFF at another target, does the LMG fire full FP, or area fire?

Thanks again,

Chris
author: fatgreta
consensus_answer:
LMG fires at full fire power (squad at half fp)and then both squad and LMG are marked as Final Fired.

I don't think that's correct.

If the squad is marked with 1F and fires only the MG then both squad and MG are marked with 1F and then they can fire again as SFF.

But if the squad is marked with 1F and fires both its IFP and the MG, then it's SFF, the MG suffers Sustained Fire and its FP is halved. So both the IFP and the MG would be halved.

8.3 SUBSEQUENT FIRST FIRE: A DEFENDING Infantry unit/(its MG/IFE-weapon) already marked with a First Fire counter may Defensive First Fire again during that MPh as Area Fire by flipping its First Fire counter over to the Final Fire side. Such fire can leave Residual FP but if using a MG/IFE is treated as Sustained Fire and penalized accordingly.

Use for DFF is not prohibited. A MOL attack has to be made by a unit which has neither fired its inherent nor fired a SW, and if the unit is a squad it must use its inherent also at that same time [A22.611]. The unit must be capable of firing a SW it has not yet fired as First Fire, and if a squad it must be capable of firing its inherent as First Fire too.

Parsing the relevant sentences in A22.611:
Using a MOL in a PBF/TPBF attack entitles the firer to add four FP to that attack, even if it occurs as part of a Final Fire or TPBF attack. The MOL 4 FP bonus is always added after any modification of FP; i.e., it is not subject to modification.
These say a MOL always adds 4 FP--no more, no less.

A MOL Check dr can be made in neither Subsequent First Fire nor FPF, nor in both Defensive First Fire and later in Final Fire whether MOL were actually used in First Fire or not. {I presume this applies per unit, not per Location or per player turn.}
This says no MOL use in SFF/FPF. And a unit can't use a MOL in both DFF and Final Fire.

A MOL Check dr counts as use of a SW, ...
Self explanatory: a MOL Check doesn't need to succeed in order for it to count as use of a SW.

A squad which makes a MOL Check dr may not fire any other SW and must add its inherent FP to the attack.
A squad that fires a MOL has to combine the MOL's 4-FP with its Inherent FP. So a squad firing a MOL fully exhausts its fire capabilities (A7.351): 1 SW + Inherent FP.

Further assumptions:
--When a squad uses a MOL, the MOL has to be added to its full Inherent FP. (It can't be added to Inherent FP that is halved as Area Fire because the squad is marked with a First Fire counter.) [a statement refuted by the Perry Sez posted by JRV in the next post]
--A HS that fires anything in DFF cannot try for a MOL in Final Fire. [the correctness of this assumption is pending]

Conclusions:
--A MOL check cannot be made by a unit marked with a First Fire counter. 
--A MOL check cannot be made by a unit that possesses a Gun/SW that is marked by a First Fire counter (this also disqualifies any unit that has used--or has attempted to use--an Inherent SW).
--If a squad fires anything in DFF, it can't use a MOL in Final Fire.
--If a HS fires anything, it can no longer use a MOL.

I think part of the problem is that players forget it's JUST A GAME and not a reflection or a replay of real life. When one gets overly worked up about nuances of what the rules say then maybe it's time to step away from the GAME a bit and do something else less stress causing for them.

For me, an issue with ASL is this: 

(a) When I read the rules, I try to spot and understand the underlying principles that govern similar mechanics. In this instance, it's the usage of SW during Defensive First Fire, Subsequent First Fire, Final Protective Fire, and Final Fire. I can see certain principles, and would like it if those principles applied uniformly throughout those phases and across different types of SW. 

(b) Unfortunately the ASLRB can use awkward phrasing in places, and long sentences packed with qualifying phrases and exceptions and digressions, and isn't always precise in its terminology, or in expressing what I think are intended to be parallel thoughts.

(c) Faced with these realities, I'm often forced to choose: do I put greater weight on (a) and interpret a curious or ambiguous statement according to those principles, or do I put greater reliance on the precise phrasing of the rulebook and downplay (a)?

There're adherents to both schools, but the latter approach appears preferred.

Where does this matter? Take this current thread and A22.611, and this sentence:
A squad which makes a MOL Check dr may not fire any other SW and must add its inherent FP to the attack.

When I read this sentence, I have several questions:
(1) What time window is this sentence addressing: is it a statement meant to constrain the entire player turn, or only the current phase of fire (e.g., just Defensive First Fire, or just Final Fire)?
(2) Is this the ASLRB loosely restating A7.351, or is the rulebook establishing a new absolute constraint?
(3) What about HSs: why is there no parallel statement about what they can do?
(4) A22.611 talks often about a squad adding the MOL FP to it's Inherent FP: but it never tells us if it's talking about the squad's "full" Inherent FP, or if Inherent FP fired as Area Fire can also qualify.

If I put greater weight on (a), I'll answer these questions one way; if I put greater emphasis on the exact local wording, I'll answer these questions a different way.

The advantage of (a) is that it makes the game easier to learn. The disadvantage of the other approach is that it requires the identifying and remembering of many nuances.

If I understand correctly both ways of solving rules problems:

(a) leads to interpreting the rules after the whims of the interpreter (his fuzzy idea of what was in the unknowable mind of the designer). Thus that subjective method leads to multiple, often contradictory, applications of the rules.

(b) is a more technical approach and leads to one correct interpretation - I call it reading the RAW (rules as written) in contrast with RASITBW (rules as supposedly intended to be written). It has saved ASL from numerous divisions between "schools of interpretation" and MMP has played an excellent role as a custodian of a common set of rules.

Of course, ASL rules are complex and they may need clarifications - one can find loopholes to close - and struggling with rules questions is part of the hobby.
But, considering the volume of the rulebook, the problems - not speaking of the need of errata - are astonishlingy few.

My philosophy regarding rules interpretation is that one should be able to present a short, synthetic question, with a yes or no answer.
Perhaps a series of short questions allows to get around the issues of the problem.

This also is what MMP require for rules questions sent to them.
The Q&A/Perry Sez document is a good example of that way of doing.

Dumping large paragraphs of rules and considerations most often is the pre-synthesis stage of rules interpretation, that should be followed by a TL;DR sort of summary.

(a) leads to interpreting the rules after the whims of the interpreter (his fuzzy idea of what was in the unknowable mind of the designer). Thus that subjective method leads to multiple, often contradictory, applications of the rules.Rather than whims, I see it as making intentional, logical deductions of guiding principles. And  what's "in the unknowable mind of a designer" is immaterial: any guiding ideas have to be derived from the rules before us.

As an example, I see as a general principle that:
--A squad can use 2 SW to full effect, or its Inherent FP and 1 SW to full effect. After doing so, it's ability to fire suffers.
--A HS can use 1 SW to full effect, or its Inherent FP to full effect. After doing so, it's ability to fire suffers.
That's a principle embedded in my ASL understanding.

So when I read rule A22.611 on MOLs, and there's an ambiguity or a gap or a curious phrasing, I interpret the fuzziness in light of that understanding.

Take this sentence again: A squad which makes a MOL Check dr may not fire any other SW and must add its inherent FP to the attack.
I do the math: 1 SW at full effect + (full) Inherent FP = maximum squad firing ability at full effect.
This influences how I wrestle with a question that isn't answered in A22.611: can a MOL can be added to the Inherent FP of a squad if the squad has already fired its Inherent FP?
--If the answer is no, then it makes sense that a squad that uses a MOL can use no other SW during that turn.
--If the answer is yes, then I tend to think the prohibition on using a different SW applies only to the current sub-phase (DFF or DFPh). E.g., a squad using 1 SW to full effect and its Inherent FP to half effect, has "the space" to have used a different SW to full effect.

The literal approach, contrarily, takes the orange sentence in isolation and makes it a blanket fiat--no matter how that interpretation might jar with how other SW work. But if I try to take the orange sentence as absolute, not only can't the squad use any other SW in any other sub-phase this turn, but it also must use a MOL with its full Inherent FP.

What about an aircraft attack? Is it somehow based on where the attack is coming from? I could imagine it with MGs, but Bombs gets trickier. Besides both C7.12 (Aerial AF) and E7.41/7.421 (Aircraft MGs and Bombs) instructs to ignore the actual hit location and just use the Aerial AF...

author: Hipsu
consensus_answer:
This is my reading of it, too [as per the quote, Eddy's, not Brian's], with one addition for Stukas. This is the sequence I read it in:

AFV in INDEX = D1.2 = partially armored is still an AFV

E7.42 = mentions that C7.21 & C7.22 are always used

C7.21 = for air attack, it applies if an armored aspect is hit, but does not cancel out the actual Target Facing/Aspect (C3.9) hit and does not always make it a de facto hit against the rear aspect

C7.22 = only applies if the hit is "vs an armored Target Facing/Aspect (C3.9)"

C3.9 = TH DR determines Aspect (i.e. hull vs turret) hit through the Target Facing (D3.2)

D3.2 = E7.402 attacks comes in through a hexside, so you use the normal hexside procedure. A Stuka uses E7.403 so its attack originates from "within the target hex" and uses the colored dr of the TH DR to determine the Target Facing.

AF is only pertinent to TK resolution, so it seems that the first step is to determine if an aerial attack hit the unarmored or armored part of a partially armored vehicle. I don't see how this can be decided without the conventional facing/aspect practice. Once a hit is determined to have been secured, then the resolution can proceed dependent upon which category is proper: Star Vehicle for unarmored or the proper Aerial AF, no? C7.12 AERIAL AF: The Aerial AF is listed on the C7.11 AF Table and is used instead of the normal AF if an AFV is hit by an aircraft attack, an optimally positioned DC (7.346), or in its Underbelly (D4.3). Such an attack uses the Aerial AF listed beneath the AFV's worst AF (either hull or turret -- regardless of the "location" of the hit) -- even if attacked through the vehicle's front Target Facing.

If the Final To Hit DR yields a hit, but is not ≤ half of the Basic TH#, the result is a Near Miss and is resolved vs the Aerial AF but with only half of the bomb's Basic TK# and half FP for any Specific Collateral Attack...

Looks to me there are no sides, only the Aerial AF.

Per the Index, a Partially Armored Vehicle is "treated as an armored target unless specifically attacked through a non-armored Target Facing inclusive of Elevation Advantage that reduces its CE DRM to +1."
Since a direct bomb hit is "resolved vs the Aerial AF of the AFV" (E7.241) and all AFs are determined by location/aspect of the TH DR, it seems that the target aspect is determined in the conventional manner: facing and colored die vs white die. Obviously, one would not think the left side of a vehicle could take a direct hit from an aircraft coming at it from the right side, etc. so I don't see an inherent difficulty in determining the hit location. I might be looking at this too simplistically, and expect to learn something here.

3.9 LOCATION OF VEHICULAR HITS: It is often necessary to know the location of a hit vs a vehicular target in order to determine the correct AF (or in the case of a HD target, whether a hit has been scored at all). title: To Hit DRM for Motion Defensive First Fire vs Non-stopped
question:
The Chart
Case C4 for Motion firer, directs to use the "applicable C/C1/C2" case.
Case C lists BF (not BFF). No mention of MP is listed.
Case C1 lists BFF with Restricted LOS (2.5-3MP in LOS)
Case C2 lists BFF with Limited LOS (< = 2MP in LOS)

Observations:

2. For BFF with > 3 MP in LOS, Case C is used as the MP in LOS is neither Restricted nor Limited.

consensus_answer:
No, Defensive First Fire will not use the C1 or C2 modifier. Per the rules, they only apply to a vehicle First Firing during its own MPh. (C5.31 and C5.32)

Instead, cases J1 and J2 might apply. (C6.11 and C6.12)
What about C (C5.3)?

replies.body:
No, Defensive First Fire will not use the C1 or C2 modifier. Per the rules, they only apply to a vehicle First Firing during its own MPh. (C5.31 and C5.32). Edit: Case C will still apply, because C4 says it must use the Case C, or C1, or C2 DRM as applicable.

No, Defensive First Fire will not use the C1 or C2 modifier. Per the rules, they only apply to a vehicle First Firing during its own MPh. (C5.31 and C5.32)

Instead, cases J1 and J2 might apply. (C6.11 and C6.12)
What about C (C5.3)?

The cases that apply for DFF vs. a non stopped attacker are J, J1, J2, as they take in account the MP spent by the target.

C4 would be used by the defender if it is in Motion (during DFF, DFPh) or non stopped (during its MPh (BFF) or AFPh (BF)).
During DFF* C1 and C2 are not applicable (C4 clearly says that those special BF(F) modifiers apply "as applicable", which is not the case during DFF). 

Case C is the usual case for BF - that is, during AFPh, when the MP spent don't count.
C1 and C2 simply add to that basic BF DRM as, during the AFV's MPh, if it fires, the time the firer has seen the target must be taken into account.
It is, in some aspects, the reverse of the J, J1 and J2 DRMs, where the Defender during DFF must take in account the time its target has been in its sights.

Hope that helped.

title: Hexsides and hindrance, hexsides and mines
question:
1. If a LOF goes along a wall which happens to be a hindrance hexisde, can a target unit claim both thE wall TEM (if able to) and the hexside hindrance?

2. A unit Advances into a ground level building Location from outside the building. The Defender reveals A-P mines in the Open Ground part of the hex and solves them. Some Attackers survive. The Defender reveals then that the building is Fortified and occuppied to expell the Attackers. Is this correct or were the MF expended outside and the mines should not have attacked? If correct, do the expelled units suffer a second mine attack?

Thanks.
author: esparver73
consensus_answer:
B.6 INHERENT TERRAIN: Certain terrain depictions (orchard, crag, graveyard, shellholes, etc.) and counter contents of a hex (SMOKE, Bridge, rubble, AFV, wreck) [EXC: Bypass AFV/Wreck (D9.4)] identify the entire hex (inclusive of hexsides) as having the characteristics of that terrain type. It is not necessary that a LOS actually cross such a symbol to be affected—mere entrance of the hex (even if only to trace a LOS to or through a vertex of such a hex) or a LOS exactly along one of its hexsides (A6.1) suffices. A LOS traced exactly along such a hexside is considered to have passed through only one such hex—not two—even if that hexside is shared by another LOS Hindrance hex. If the Hindrance DRM of two such hexes differ, the larger of the two Hindrance DRM is used.

	

B9.3 TEM: The TEM of a wall is +2; the TEM of a hedge is +1. Fire traced through a wall/hedge hexside or hexspine may be subject to a TEM for that wall/hedge if the target is in the Location formed by that hexside/hexspine. If the LOS crosses the wall/hedge hexside through a road depiction (such as 6W9-X9) the wall/hedge TEM can only apply if the target is a non-moving unit. PRC [EXC: Motorcyclists] never receive a TEM for a wall/hedge. The wall/hedge TEM is NA for DC attacks [EXC: if thrown across a wall/hedge hexside, the TEM applies to both the target and thrower’s Locations; A23.6].

	

B9.31 The wall/hedge TEM is not cumulative with positive TEM of other terrain in that hex, although it is cumulative with LOS Hindrances and SMOKE. A target unit claiming WA (9.32) does not receive in-hex TEM [EXC: Runway (7.3); Air Bursts (9.34)], but receives wall/hedge TEM if applicable [EXC: it may elect instead to receive appropriate TEM for Emplacement or for a friendly AFV with which it shares WA (D9.3)]. A target unit not claiming WA receives only in-hex TEM, but may instead use wall/hedge TEM vs enemy units which do not have WA over the hexside. In any case the wall/hedge TEM applies on as per 9.3. In order for a wall to justify firing HEAT at Infantry/Cavalry (C3.81), those units must be claiming-WA/receiving-Wall-TEM. The amount of Residual FP left by an attack that crosses a wall/hedge hexside is reduced by that hexside TEM (A8.26) if hexside TEM could have been claimed against at least one firing unit—even if the moving unit is not claiming hexside TEM. See 9.36 and D4 for wall-TEM/HD-status for vehicles.

title: Snap Shot and SFF query
question:
Situation: A unit moves from one building hex directly into another building hex using 2 MF.

Can an enemy unit make a Snap Shot on the first MF and then a SFF shot on the second MF at the unit now in the building or can it only take the one Snap Shot?
author: sapper_D
consensus_answer: One. Read the last sentence of A8.15.

replies.body: One. Read the last sentence of A8.15.

That's the sentence that is confusing it for me...clearly it is saying that you can only make one Snap Snap as the unit crosses the hexside but is it ruling out the possibility of any other fire - I'm not sure on that one...

That's the sentence that is confusing it for me...clearly it is saying that you can only make one Snap Snap as the unit crosses the hexside but is it ruling out the possibility of any other fire - I'm not sure on that one...

What A8.15's last sentence is saying is that Snap Shots can follow other fire from other units.  

Weird as it seems, one unit can fire at the moving unit in its destination hex and then a second unit can make a Snap Shot against the unit on the hexside "before" the destination hex.*  

The one shot limit is just that each firing unit is limited to one Snap Shot per hexside per target unit.

However, I believe your original question is can a single unit make a Snap Shot and then a Subsequent First Fire shot in the destination hex.  The answer to that question is yes, I believe, assuming all of the other conditions for SFF are met.

*EDIT:  Actually, I see no reason you can't First Fire in the target hex and then SFF a Snap Shot, either.  Boy, that's goofy.  (And I don't know why you'd do it).

S
Yep. Only one Snap Shot per unit, even if they spend more than one MF, but it can be combined with other Defensive Firs as usual.

title: Bypass vertex woes
question:
1st question:

First of all, I just learned you can't bypass CC5 when moving from DD5 to BB4. Even though there is plenty of room. Did you guys know that? Rulez:

4.3 BYPASS: A hexside... ...covered by a Water Obstacle (24L9-M9), may not be Bypassed (B26.44) on either side of the hexside.

However, what about moving from BB3 to CC5, bypassing BB4? The whole hexside is not covered by water, only that one vertex. Seems like the intention is that it's not allowed though, but man, that's restrictive.

---------------------------------

2nd question:

I don't even know why I'm even asking this but that's not allowed right, bypassing S6 from that angle for only 1 MF? Even though it would make soooo much sense... Imagine an enemy unit in S5. To avoid him I'd first have to move to S7 and then bypass S6 and T5, but it seems like such an unnecessary detour...
author: Hipsu
consensus_answer:
I disagree with you on the BB4 point.  The hexside is not covered, so bypass is allowed.  Imagine if that pond was a hedge...you could still BP that hexside in BB4 and not pay for the hedge, so why would that vertex of pond impede you?

If it were a hedge, you'd have to cross it and spend 1 extra MF. See the A4.3 example where it crosses the wall when leaving bypass. For exactly that reason I interpreted that the intention propably is that the water is there and is uncrossable thus no bypass allowed.

On the other hand if it were a hedge then it wouldn't affect the first example of bypassing CC5...

The A4.3 example isn't relevant, because in bypass you're always IN one of the two hexes.  If you enter the one with the wall, you pay for it.  If you enter the other, you don't.

So if our pond is a a hedge, there is no +1 to bypass BB4, but there would be to bypass CC4 (assuming you can bypass grain, which you can't).

S

TK rolls don't count.

title: Sunken road (hex 41W7)
question: What does it cost for infantry to move from W7 to V6? Is it an abrupt elevation change (first up, then down)?
author: Hipsu
consensus_answer:
I'm going to have to disagree with the consensus.

COT is the cost to enter the hex, not leave it.

B4.41 Infantry/Cavalry entering a Sunken Road hex through a non-road hexside do so at a cost of two MF. There is no cost for leaving a Sunken Road hex other than the normal penalties (10.4) for moving to higher elevation.

When moving to V6, you are not moving to a higher elevation, so the cost would be 2 MF.  While moving from W7 to V7 would be 4MF (2MF doubled).

Check out the B10.5 Abrupt Elevation Change examples I listed above that are also "same level."

12Y4/Y5 is gully to gully with no connecting hexside, so up-down.**

15BB8/AA9 is level 2 hill to level 2 hill with a level 1 "slice" along the hexside, so down-up.

Like 41W7/V6 these both start and end at the same level, but still meet the definition of AEC because the unit "enters two or more levels while crossing one non-cliff hexside."  Net elevation change doesn't matter, only the gross number of levels changed, be they all up, all down or up/down or down/up.   (Think of it as absolute value rather than net value if that helps you)

Another gotcha on this...  If you were playing this with snow, you'd have to pay twice on that hexside because you've changed elevation twice.  There are a couple spots in AP23 Agony at Arnautovo where movement gets really ugly on account of this*.

title: Can enemy vehicles occupy the same hex?
question: Can enemy vehicles occupy the same hex?
author: bluetiger80
consensus_answer:
Vehicle can always enter an enemy occupied location no problem (no matter if its infantry or enemy vehicle). Each side have their own stacking limits, so two opposing vehicles do not exceed the limit.

You can enter normally, or declare an Overrun, it's up to you. You can even Overrun the CE crew of the enemy vehicle.

BUT, to answer your question, a vehicle cannot stay in the same location with an enemy vehicle UNLESS it could theoretically cause a Shock/Elim on an original TK/IFT DR of 5. (D2.6)

Check the Overrun Flowchart and the box in lower right "Staying in the Location".

Don't you just love these unnecessary complications? ;)

After studying the basic rules so much one starts to get a feel of some general trend lines of the game mechanics (even if I'm still relatively new to this game). It feels like this should be ATTACKER's action only. The ATTACKER makes the first CC rolls anyways so in that regard it also sounds strange if the DEFENDER can initiate it.

It matters in a situation where player A already has fighters in the area and player B arrives later with Stukas with bombs. If player A cannot start a dogfight during player B's CCPh then the Stukas can always make bombing runs before a dogfight is possible. So it may also be a deliberate decision to let the DEFENDER start a dogfight and intercept those bombers before they get to their target (oh no, a reality argument).

ASOP is dead silent on this issue.

So, how would you play it? I haven't sent anything to Perry yet fearing this will go straight to bottom of his priority list.

(We are going to play scenario 132 - Hill 253.5 which has infantry, tanks, mines, OBA and planes for both sides. Basically everything but the kitchen sink. This will be fun.)
author: Hipsu
consensus_answer:
Here's how my mind works. I'll paste the whole rule here divided in steps. I don't have answers, only speculation.

Step 1, initiate Dogfights. E7.22:
Only an undamaged FB can voluntarily enter Aerial Combat. To enter Aerial Combat, a player places his FB on top of one or more enemy aircraft during the CCPh and covers them with a CC marker. He may place several of his FB on one enemy aircraft, one FB on several enemy aircraft, or place several of his FB on several enemy aircraft in one or more groups. Each group (or stack) of aircraft beneath a CC/Melee counter is termed a Dogfight.

Comment: I underlined what I think let's both players do this. But, let's give 3 FBs to both sides. Player A wants to form three 1 on 1 Dogfights. Player B wants to gang up 3 to 1 and leave the other 2 planes alone for now. Which player's decision takes precedence? You can't please both because of the definition of a Dogfight (a stack of aircraft under a CC counter).

I think this could be the main problem of this whole mess. If only the ATTACKER could form the Dogfights then it would be neat and simple.

Step 2, resolve the Dogfights (E7.22 continues)
In each CCPh, the ATTACKER's aircraft in each Dogfight attacks one enemy plane in that Dogfight in sequential CC. All ATTACKER planes resolve their attacks (including any additional attacks allowed by retained ROF; 7.222) before any surviving DEFENDER plane can return fire. The DEFENDER'S plane cannot attack back if eliminated.

Also E7.221 DOGFIGHT RESOLUTION:
Aircraft in each Dogfight must predesignate their initial targets (ATTACKER first); i.e., a plane may not await the outcome of earlier attacks in its Dogfight to determine which opposing plane in that Dogfight to attack. A plane can attack only one opposing plane at a time -- regardless of the number of enemy planes in that Dogfight.

Comment: I underlined what I think reinforces that this whole process takes two steps. In step 1 Dogfights are formed, in step 2 each Dogfight is resolved separately, Attacker first.

(Step 3, which handles the outcomes of these Dogfights, would come next but is irrelevant to this discussion)
As written, the phrase "a player" combined with "the CCph" instead of "his CCph" is clear. Either player. The rules, including earlier in E7.2, consistently use "a player" and "his" to mean ATTACKER. 

Allowing both players makes sense game-wise as it allows defending FBs a chance to intercept enemy bombers before they can drop their load. (Not an argument this is correct, just a possible reason why the rule might be intended this way). Unfortunately that leaves the glaring hole of possible conflicting assignments with nothing I can see in the rules to help.

It's possible this is a mistake in the rules and it's supposed to be "his CCph". That would fix the assignment problem.

Either way there is a flaw in the rules:
If E7.22 is correct as written then there was an oversight in not specifying whether ATTACKER or DEFENDER assigns first. DEFENDERs do get a chance to intercept new planes before they can make ground attacks.

If E7.22 should say "his CCph" instead of "the CCph" then the written rule is incorrect but there is no need for further clarification. DEFENDERS do not get a chance to intercept new planes before they can make ground attacks.

In the absence of a clear statement of error I prefer to assume the written rule is correct and that a side-effect (possible assignment conflicts) was overlooked do to its rarity.

Until an official clarification I would play ATTACKER declares first because it is their turn, and they are resolving first so seem to have initiative as it were. No rule basis for that. If argued I would dice for it.

Hill 253.3 was the only scenario I have ever played where a dogfight occured.
