title: The bolter rules assistance thread (help needed)
question:
I am teaching myself how to play ASL and have a few (hundred) questions + a few things that I would like to make sure that I am doing right. I am just going to post them here and hope people can help. 

Situation 1: A 4-6-7 HMG opens fire on a 4-4-7 in the movement phase (defensive first fire) and rolls a two on the coloured die, under its ROF. The target is out of LOS when it is checked (in 1M7 firing at 1O4). 
Question 1: how/where is the first fire counter placed? 
Question 2: what fire options exist for this squad if a new target appears?

Situation 2: Three 6-2-8 and a 10-2 leader is hit with a 1/KIA result (yes, I know stacking is bad). The random selection rolls are 5,5,4,5 (the four is a 6-2-8). This mean that two squads and the leader are eliminated right?

Situation 3: A 6-2-8 rocks thorough a street hex with a 1 firepower fire lane running through it. The die roll is snake eyes. 2 -1 for non assault more, -1 for no cover equals a final total of 0. You just use the equal or less than zero column of the IFT which give you a 1KIA right?
author: bolter
consensus_answer:
Situation 1: A 4-6-7 HMG opens fire on a 4-4-7 in the movement phase (defensive first fire) and rolls a two on the coloured die, under its ROF. The target is out of LOS when it is checked (in 1M7 firing at 1O4). 
Question 1: how/where is the first fire counter placed? 
Question 2: what fire options exist for this squad if a new target appears?1) If you added the Inherent FP to your shot (as your example seems to indicate), the squad is marked by a First Fire counter, and the HMG is not marked (however, if firing from a building or woods, you will have to place a CA marker as the HMG's further fire will be limited to that CA).

2) Either it fires the HMG alone (hoping to keep ROF) or it chooses to use Subsequent First Fire.
In that latter case, it may opt not to fire the HMG (to avoid sustained fire penalties), but the HMG will still be marked with a Final Fire counter as the squad.
Remember, too, that Subsequent First Fire may only be fired at a target that is closer or at the same range as the nearest enemy unit...

Situation 2: Three 6-2-8 and a 10-2 leader is hit with a 1/KIA result (yes, I know stacking is bad). The random selection rolls are 5,5,4,5 (the four is a 6-2-8). This mean that two squads and the leader are eliminated right?Yes. And the remaining 628 is broken and will have to pass a LLMC (with a +2 DRM penalty, due to the leadership or the lost leader).

Situation 3: A 6-2-8 rocks thorough a street hex with a 1 firepower fire lane running through it. The die roll is snake eyes. 2 -1 for non assault more, -1 for no cover equals a final total of 0. You just use the equal or less than zero column of the IFT which give you a 1KIA right? Right.
And the Firelane hits at the same power even if your 628 was dashing across the street.
Note, too, that cowering does not apply to a Fire Lane.

I hope the two last situations did not occur in the same scenario : that would be bad luck... But in ASL such nasty things do happen.

title: Subsequent first fire with an adjacent broken MMC?
question:
Does a broken enemy squad adjacent to a friendly squad that has First Fired prevent it from SFFing at non-adjacent enemy squads?

The situation: imagine two US squads coming from opposite sides toward a German squad with a LMG. The first squad comes adjacent to the Germans and gets lit up and the breaks. The LMG loses RoF and a First Fire counter is placed on the German squad. The other US MMC comes in from the opposite side...can the Germans shoot while it is still 2 hexes away?
thanks
author: hemepositive
consensus_answer:
No...See A8.3 subsequent first fire is limited to the closest armed, known enemy unit - nothing said about being broken. I think you meant "yes" here ... it is an armed KEU, so does prevent SFF at units farther away but in normal range.

title: Ohhh!!!  Finding that elusive rule is a pain in the &^$#&
question:
Was having a session with my son (as he is the only opponent i can find in Malaysia) ....and we were having an argument about concealment. The situation was : a stack under "?" counter is not in concealment terrain; in fact they were on open terrain. His ANZAC infantry came within LOS and < 16 hexes. Does the stack lose their concealment?

We spent a better part of the next half hour poring through ASLRB to no avail. The rules did not specify such a situation and i was with the opinion that "?" is not lost as the rules did not specify. His argument was that since they are not in concealment terrain, it should be lost.

Finally found the answer in Q&A compilation....and i was right. The point is ....such a pain just to clarify one situation :cry:
author: Lamskiy
consensus_answer:
I empathize.  When I first started ASL I thought the rules were laid out great, but the more I play, the more I find little things that are organized poorly, or simply missing from the revelant part of the index.  For example, if you are reading just the Mud rules (E3.6), you will not know that they have an affect on SMOKE.  To learn that mud negatively affects SMOKE, you need to look in the rules for Deep Snow (E3.734):what:  Also, if you look up Mud in the index, it is silent about its interaction with SMOKE.

(anyone conversant enough with the ASL rules will likely be able to point out that the rules for SMOKE in chapter A do contain this information, however, when I am preparing for a scenario with Mud EC, I generally read the Mud EC rules, not the entirety of chapter A).

title: Wire and pillbox questions
question:
How does the wire work? If it is in a terrain with a pillbox do I pay the movement factors to move into the hex with the wire and place the unit on top of the wire. Then if I want to enter the pillbox I need to roll a die and have more MF than the roll to move into the location?

What if wire is in an open ground hex? Can I spend 1 MF to move into the hex and then stay onto of the wire and pay the COT for the next hex entered without dealing with the wire?
author: happyloaf
consensus_answer:
I'll provide even more detail because wire and PBs are kind of silly, for precisely the interpretations stated above - they are counterintuitive and not the way you assume they should be played. Getting through the wire and INTO the PB is as described above, but getting out is goofed up - to leave the PB, you get placed back ON the wire (I know - it's b*llsh*t to me too). This essentially comes down to B26.4 ('...to enter a Wire Location...') and B30.1 (A pillbox is a separate non-vertical-level Location inside its hex...'). So, when you leave the PB Location, you are entering the Wire Location anew for the purposes of B26.4. Even if you immediately try to reenter the PB, you still have to go through the wire; dumb, stupid, absurd mechanic, but thems the rules. 

It gets worse when you consider the placement of DCs vs the wired PB. The unit placing the DC gets to do so without (i) paying the wire dr or (ii) paying the +1 MF for PB entry). So, to defend your PBs well with wire, you need to have the wire one hex out to catch the DC placers and not impede your PB boys from leaving. Of course, a bunker will let you get out without taking the wire dr (B27.54).

Wow Brent Pollock! I just found some old scenarios I had called BP#. I was asking myself, where did I get these and what is BP? I found my answer latter that day. Write any scenarios lately?

Additional remark :

Units which set up offboard are concealed.

When they enter the board they only loose concealment when in the LOS of a Good Order enemy unit (and if not using Assault Move in non open ground).

This can be usefulls, even for vehicles, if the latter can approach the battleline without being seen by the enemy : it keeps him in doubt about the nature of the vehicles...

...and since no one else mentioned it, I'll add the reminder that OB-given "?" must be placed on the top of the stack to prevent double-dipping of post-set-up "?".

Interseting. You know, I have never played it that way.  For instance, if I have a squad that I want to make look like it has a SW, I sometimes place a OB ? counter in the stack and then place the non-OB ? counter on top..

Playing it the way you suggest, I would, in effect, have to place two OB ? counters on the squad.

Not saying you are wrong, but I don't see where it says you have to place the ob ? on the top of the stack.

A12.11 ...thus giving the mistaken impression of a stack of real counters beneath a "?" but a single such counter cannot be placed beneath unconcealed units

A12.12 ...[EXC: only one non-OB-designated "?" can be placed per stack of units and not on top of any previously placed "?"].

So I think you can place a couple of Dummies at the bottom of a stack... But you won't have the option of Concealing that stack normally if out of LOS.
Remember that good order enemy units cause loss of Concealment and that unbroken enemy units prevent gain of Concealment

Another thing that should be pointed out is that OB given ? can be used as the small or large concealment. 

A great tactic if the defense only has one vehicle is to put two large concealment in concealment terrain so your arriving opponent does not know which one is the real vehicle and which is just two large ? counters.

Very useful for those German OB's with a lone Tiger or Panther.

title: DRMs ... Have I got it right?
question:
This is the situation:

Playing Le Herission ... I have my CE assault gun (SIG I) start up, move up the road 2 hexes, changed VCA 1 point and stop (so i used up 4 MPs out of 12 MPs) then fire at a stack of concealed frenchies in a stone building during the Advancing Fire Phase. What are the DRMs here?

I have +2 (advancing fire phase fire), +4 (changed VCA 1 hex point for NT gun), +2 (concealed units) and +3 (stone building TEM)= +11....which makes it impossible to hit but i get to put an acquired -1 counter on the target. Is that right?

Assuming the target did not get out of the way, i will now have the following DRM for Defensive fire during the French player turn : +2 (concealed), +3 (Stone building TEM) and -1 (acquired -1) = +4 total. Hope i've got it right. Can someone clarify please?

Assuming i get a hit, does the target still get the +3 DRM for TEM? Of course, the concealed status will not count any more and they lose concealment status.

Tactically, should I use area fire in the above case? ..and if so, which column of the IFT should be used if a hit is achieved?
author: Lamskiy
consensus_answer:
I think Binko has the right DRMs; Ben makes a good point re ATT and acquisition.

Area fire attacks at half the FP. So the only time you would want to use Area Fire is probably at long range when the To Hit chance is much better. 

Normally I'd agree but the sIG IB is a gnarly beast, with a 150mm MA.  Even at halved firepower it still hits on the 12 column.  Let's look at your chances either way, in the upcoming DFPh:

Infantry Target Type:  Base 8 To Hit, with +2 DRM for Concealment and a further +3 for Stone Building TEM - you need to roll a three or less (8.3%); success brings a roll on the 30 column with no DRMs, where any result is a 1MC or better.  So, overall you have an 8.3% chance of inflicting a result.

Area Target Type:  Base 7 To Hit, with -1 DRM for Acquisition, +2 for Concealment, and no TEM DRM for an ATT shot - you need to roll a six or less (41.7%); success brings a roll on the 12 column where the +3 TEM DRM now applies - you have a 41.7% chance of an NMC or better (58.3% chance of a PTC or better).  Here you have an overall chance of 17.4% of inflicting at least a normal morale check.

So, you have an interesting choice - ITT allows you to bring the pain in  a serious way (KIAs on the 30 column up to 5) but the ATT doubles your chance of a meaningful result.  The sIG IB has a circled B9 Ammo Depletion number, meaning it won't be around long - you need to make every shot count.  In this case you might forgo the 30 column jackpot in exchange for a much better chance of making the French roll a morale check.  

Thanks to all who clarified. Learnt something new here. The big surprise for me was acquisition cannot be earned against concealed targets (gotta check the ASLRB).

All the while, i suspected that using ATT would give me better chances of doing some damage, or to wait for concealment to be stripped from targets before blasting them; i.e. using infantry to fire at them first and then the SIGs if they lose concealment.

I am normally conservative with vehicles and support them with infantry close by to ensure that them no good frenchies don't pop up and CC them while in urban areas.

Cheers
-Lamskiy-

Two more points outside the scope of Lamskiy's initial post, relevant to the sIG IB and Le Hérisson:

- With a circled B9 ammo depletion number I'm reluctant to fire acquisition shots in the AFPh.

- I think these critters are best used as smoke platforms supporting the infantry attack.  If they get too aggressive some saucy Frenchmen are going to pop out and burn them down to the roadwheels (CC modifiers: -1 Street Fighting/-1 No MGs/-2 OT Vehicle).  That CVP cap could soon loom large.

JR

Thanks to all who clarified. Learnt something new here. The big surprise for me was acquisition cannot be earned against concealed targets (gotta check the ASLRB).

Not quite - as Ben says, Infantry and Vehicle Target Type acquisition can't be earned versus concealed targets, but Area Target Type acq can be.

JR

Also remember that you cannot get normal Acquisition against a Concealed target; You can only get Area Acquisition.  So if you fire ITT, you can't place an Acquisition counter at all.

That's one reason to use Area Target Type against Concealed targets.

title: the "X1" overlay
question:
Hope i can receive some clarification on this overlay.

I was playing (solitaire) the Taking of Takrouna which uses the "X1" overlay. According to F12.43, the location is subject to +4 DRM. Does a unit in this location enjoy additional HA DRM?

Does firing a mortar from this location be penalised since firing from this location is halved as area fire? (I assumed no).

cheers
-Lamskiy-
author: Lamskiy
consensus_answer:
Isn't X1 stone buildings? As such, no, you wouldn't be able to fire a MTR out of it, nor would it get +1 for HA, which is never cumulative with any +TEM in that Location.

title: Route Phase Prisoner Question
question:
If a unit can be interdicted 3 MF into a route and it starts the route next to an enemy unit must it surrender (assuming it is capable of surrendering during the Route Phase)? Or can it attempt to low crawl or route and risk interdiction? Last, if a broken DM unit is adjacent to 2 enemy units that are on either side and it has no way to route even with low crawl is it eliminated or captured (I'm assuming eliminated?)?

Once again,

Thanks!
author: happyloaf
consensus_answer:
Definitely hooped. The silver lining in usually having your troops get shredded by KIAs and Ks is that you don't have to remember these rules ;-)

I suppose another way is to be a good player and always have a rout route, but where's the fun in that?!

Can always count on J.R. to get it right. Lesson number one - don't trust someone who has mainly been playing VotG for the past year plus to remember when units Surrender. The only way to get Prisoners in that game is to nab them in CC.

From ASLRBv2:

20.21 RtPh: Any broken Infantry unit during its RtPh that is both ADJACENT to Known, Good Order, armed enemy Infantry/Cavalry and unable to rout away from it or only able to rout while being subject to Interdiction or resorting to Low Crawl (regardless of how it actually routs or if the possible unconcealed Interdictor is Known to it), will surrender to that enemy unit as its prisoner instead...

Sounds like the unit Surrenders even if the interdiction occurs after the first hex of the rout path.

JR

Kind words, Ben, but I'll have to disagree - I get the rules wrong more often than I'd care to admit.  I learn something new about this game almost every week.  

OP-Ben, don't take *anyone's* rules knowledge for granted - if something feels wrong, check it out yourself. It's a luxury to have a more experienced player to get you up to speed - it's by far the best way to learn - but we all get something wrong once in a while!

The way I've been laying it for decades is that only the first Location entered matters for determining the Surrender enforcement. So, it sounds like the unit in question may rout and choose to stop just before having to take Interdiction. This is much the same mechanic as the direction the routing unit moves being based on the current Location rather than Locations along the foreseen path; hence you may start routing towards an unknown enemy unit, only to have that rout route stopped once the unit becomes known.

title: Concealment and Prisoners... Who uses 'em?
question: As the subject. Concealment and Prisoners, how often does everyone use these rules? Every time? Dependent upon scenario? Never? I've only been playing ASL for about a year and a half now, and infrequently at best (Less than 50 games under my belt), and I very rarely use these. Perhaps it has something to do with the fact that I mainly play with players I'm teaching (or rather, learning along side of), but they usually choose to play "no quarter" and whenever I mention prisoners, I'm met with rolling eyes and long sighs. Pro's? Con's?
author: StAtiC9
consensus_answer: I know the question is from years ago, but it's there so others like me can find answers about a game they've grown to love. This is my opinion, having played far fewer games than the person asking and always playing solo: concealment is essential. You can't enjoy being a defender without it. The attacker will know everything about you and will simply make you look like a fool. As an attacker, not using concealment is advantageous (you'll most likely win), but you won't feel the uncertainty or the doubt of sending your men to their deaths, you won't think about how and where to attack, you won't enjoy trying to WIN. You'll be a no-brainer. The axis of attack, the main effort, thinking... all pointless. Just put all your forces on this point (the least defended) and roll the dice... you'll be playing a kill-or-be-killed game (if so, Warhammer 40,000 is better; the miniatures are bigger and cooler), and since you choose where, you'll kill more and better. Regarding POWs, I'm only giving an approximation due to lack of experience. I don't play with this rule either. It took me quite a while to feel comfortable with the rest of the rules, and I was overwhelmed by the number of pieces on the board to even be interested in it. However, despite having enjoyed it a lot, I feel that in some games one side won or lost simply because of the absence of this rule. That's how it is; the scenarios assume you'll use this rule, and that's why they give you more or less AFV, MMC, or fill it with HT or trucks. CVP, POW... the scenario was tested that way. If you don't use this rule, you'll enjoy it as much as I did at the beginning, without getting a headache from so many pieces on the board or even more doubts about the rules. But now I feel comfortable with the rules, and I think I've played some great scenarios without really perceiving all their nuances. That my victories and defeats were faked. I wonder if it was all just like a fool looking at a Velázquez painting and saying, "What a beautiful painting, I wouldn't mind putting it in my living room." Now I want to learn that rule and replay those same scenarios in all their glory. Something tells me that what I took for granted as the winning tactic for that scenario for one side or the other—or what I assumed would inevitably be the winner—will be put to the test. In short, use concealment ASAP, use POW when you can play by new rules without having a nervous breakdown.

Between Concealment and Prisoners, Concealment is certainly the more central rule. While it's not critical in every scenario, you definitely want to take that ? when you can. And in some scenarios, most obviously ones with dummies in the OOB, concealment is a huge part of the game. Prisoners similarly depend on the scenario. Many VC's make taking Prisoners a much better proposition. Also, Prisoners often gain value in longer scenarios. In a typical short, 5-6 turn scenario where you declare NQ in the 2nd or 3rd turn, there will probably be few opportunities for the enemy to effectively regroup, so calling NQ and letting them rout might not hurt much. But over the course of a longer scenario, taking Prisoners can easily get an extra 2-3 enemy squads out of play.

In any event, I agree with Steve's comment that someone who rolls their eyes at an ASL rule might be playing the wrong game. Knowing what the rules say and seeing how to put them to work for you is central to what ASL is. I love it when an opponent pulls out an obscure rule that saves his hide, because that opponent just taught me a new trick I can use in the future. And certainly Concealment and Prisoners are nowhere close to being obscure - those are just basic things you've got to know to play ASL well.

As an expansion on this, rather than think of a particular section as something you don't play, have it be something you don't play yet. When I started playing I thought concealment was silly and was sloppy about gaining and keeping it. I learned fairly quickly that concealment is very powerful. It has great impact on the game.

Prisoners, on the other hand, are lower priority to overall play. If you are still struggling with concealment or your options for Defensive First Fire, you can skip over Prisoners until you have a better grasp of more important rules. Another example, Gun Duels (just popped into my mind; no other significance). Opportunities for Gun Duels are relatively rare. You could ignore those rules for quite a while and have it matter not at all. But once in a while understanding how Gun Duels work will win you a game. Your quality in this game can grow for years. I am just starting to pay attention for opportunities to use WP grenades with my Americans. Smoke grenades are more likely and to date have been my preference, but WP grenades strip concealment and potentially can break targets. I have played for years without trying for WP grenades, but I am now adding them to my repertoire.

As this question seems to be geared towards new players, I'll have to disagree with the fellow who recommended campaign games and PTO scenarios.  Not exactly beginner friendly stuff.  

The MMP website has a great old General article that gives a list of great beginner scenarios.  The best part is that the author lists the rules that you will need to know to play each one.  This is the best intro to ASL that I am aware of, as it lets a new player know exactly what he needs to know from the RB as he goes along...instead of slogging through armor rules before you ever play an infantry scenario, for example.

The only problem is that a lot of the scenarios in the article are from Paratrooper which is OOP forever.  They are later in the series, however, so you can get started playing the BV scenarios and then decide whether or not you want to pay eBay prices for Paratrooper or wait for the re-issue of Yanks (which is rumored to include the Paratrooper scenarios/board).

Either way, I've found it a great way to get started in ASL...after playing all of the SK's of course.

Concealment is an absolute must.  The scenarios were written assuming that the players would be using concealment whenever possible, so omitting it would likely create some serious balance issues.  This is one of that major reasons that SK scenarios don't port well over to full ASL and vice-versa.

On top of that, it's not like the concealment rules are all that hard.  If you can play ASL at all concealment should be a breeze.

Prisoners, on the other hand, are up to the individual player.  But there are really good reasons to use Prisioners in some scenarios, some really good reasons not to in others.  Remember that prisoners are worth double CVP's, so if the scenario you're playing calls for maximum CVP's (as opposed to building objectives, for example) omitting the possibility of taking prisoners is a case where laziness might actually equal cheating!

You won't get far into the ASL ouvre without finding a scenario in which taking prisoners is an integral part of winning the scenario.  I'm thinking here of Mila 18...scenario 2.

Concealment is a very important rule to use : why not try to make your units less vulnerable and introduce some fog of war (even playing with your opponent's faltering memory) ?
Nothing more rewarding than to advance concealed in CC and have that nasty -2 ambush drm in your favor !
Not speaking of HIP for emplaced Guns which keeps your opponent in permanent doubt about his manoeuvres...
If you skip concealment rules, your opponent will beat you most of the time - especially if you are the Defender, as ASL rewards the Attacker.

About prisonners, No Quarter is not allways the best way to go.
If the victory conditions ask for controlling a geographical objective, better reap prisoners than invoke NQ that will allow some brokies to rout away and come back into play...
Prisonners don't come back into the game, most of the time.
Sure, you could consider that dispatching a HS to guard a bunch of them can fragilize your OB, but the deal is often beneficial.

Lee,

If you are getting lots of prisoners in your games I think you might want to check the rules again.  They should not be that common.  And remember PW's do not turn on their guards until the location is in Melee.  The first round of CC does not qualify because the units are not in Melee until that initial round of CC is resolved.

I know! I don't think we're playing any rules wrong - we've looked up prisoners frequently. We are playing infantry-only scenarios (since I'm new) and a number have had Conscripts who will surrender if you look at them funny. I think it's just one of those things. In our current game I caught one of his reinforcements. He made a bad gamble on LOS and I stripped his concealment and broke him on the board edge. I moved adjacent on my turn and instant prisoners.

Good to know, all. After this late night post I got to thinking about it and realized that for the most part, we HAVE been using concealment on almost all non-starter kit scenarios. The few games that I have been playing lately have mostly been with new players and have mainly been starter kit scenarios. Probably why we haven't been using concealment lately!:laugh: I think that new players tend to find the concealment to be a tad fiddly, and as I am desperate for F2F players, I do whatever I can to accomidate them and keep them playing (and wanting more!) But as far as prisoners go, I think that I only ever used them once. Perhaps it's time to review those rules again and give them another shot. Or maybe I can just talk one of them into a Valor of the Guards CG.

Don’t forget that prisoners can be interrogated and potentially give up information. I actually play to capture prisoners because I find that fun and potentially useful.
Prisoner Interrogations is a chapter E rule, and as such it is optional. Unless it is invoked by SSR or the players so agree, it is not in play.
In addition as was mentioned, giving units that would usually surrender a way to route can make it more difficult to win. Deploying squads as guards is also another tactical problem to solve that I find interesting. I also like the “role playing” element when playing the good guys: they’re not going to just mow down guys who would surrender. 
Invoking No Quarter is a downside. Having Prisoners is the only way to let Soviets deploy.

Concealment is absolutely critical to the game.  It effects firepower, ambush, close combat, To Hit DR directly to name some and effects tons of other things indirectly.

Do not declare NQ if you do not have to.  It is easier to eliminate units for Failure to Rout if you have not declared NQ.  It is tons easier to wipe out units by cutting rout paths then just blasting away at them.

Lee,

If you are getting lots of prisoners in your games I think you might want to check the rules again.  They should not be that common.  And remember PW's do not turn on their guards until the location is in Melee.  The first round of CC does not qualify because the units are not in Melee until that initial round of CC is resolved.

Brad

Even if designers are lame and don’t activate the optional chapter E rules, I actually play to capture prisoners because I find that fun and potentially useful to capture units that might survive to rally. In addition as was mentioned, giving units that would usually surrender a way to route can make it more difficult to win. Deploying squads as guards is also another tactical problem to solve that I find interesting. I also like the “role playing” element when playing the good guys: they’re not going to just mow down guys who would surrender.

I've just started playing ASL. I've been playing weekly for about 3 months. Concealment has been in every game and I can't imagine where it wouldn't be important.

We've had prisoners come up nearly every game, although every time it does my partner (who's played since Squad Leader days) says "this doesn't usually come up" We've had several scenarios where prisoners were taken but the guards got jumped in close combat. Then you have to worry about all the escape attempt rules. Other than the escape attempts (which you don't have to worry about unless the guards get jumped) the prisoner rules are pretty simple.

If the people you are teaching are rolling their eyes at Prisoners then it's unlikely they will become committed ASL players. :)

Generally speaking it's better to take prisoners when you are attacking, particularly if the victory conditions are to do with building control. It allows you to "mop up" (a specific prep fire action, not just a general term) - otherwise a broken squad can rout upstairs and deny you control just as that turn clock runs out.

Usually on the defense, it's better to mow them down. There's a higher chance that the guarding unit will get broken and it'll come to tears.

I came across a situation recently where taking prisoners was a bad thing, but I had little choice.  My British AA Gun "chaff cutter" had broken an adjacent German squad.  When the squad surrendered, the Crew manning the AA Gun were forced to Guard;  And because the prisoners had a higher unit size # than the Crew, I could no longer fire!

If it had not been the first scenario of a 6-game campaign, I would have declared NQ.

Once, my friend took  my HS prisoner and they ended up beating up their guard, taking their weapon and bringing up the rear.

It was one of those moments that really makes me love that game.

I don't really see anything in Chapters A-D as being optional. I actually don't think of anything in the rules as optional, but players have been know to forget rules and play without them. :)

Always;  I've never met a player who doesn't try to play by the full rules.  The exception is players who choose to use the optional IIFT. 

If the people you are teaching are rolling their eyes at Prisoners then it's unlikely they will become committed ASL players. :)

...or stick with scenarios that have No Quarter in place, such as Red Barricades, VotG, East Front SS and most of the PTO after some date in '42 or somesuch.

And I'll boost what others posted - Concealment: learn to use it or you'll die a horrible cardboard death.

I was bluffed last weekend by a concealed 7-0. Concealment should be banned!

Nothing better than having exit VC and a couple prisoners in your back pocket ready to go.
And remember PW's do not turn on their guards until the location is in Melee.... and the guards must be broken (IIRC, NRBH).

title: One more route question
question:
As I read the rules if a unit is broken in a building hex must it route? I am assuming it doesn't have to since it is not in the open ground (it is in a building) however it is in LOS of an enemy unit (the one that fired and broke it initially). Must this unit leave the building if a single hex or can it stay there? I know it can route upstairs or to another hex if it is a multihex building and then continue to route up levels or down levels but can it choose to stay in its current location?

I have looked at the excellent tutorial and it mentions that the unit cannot route in place but I cannot find a basis for this in the rules. Thanks for the continued help for a newbie.
author: happyloaf
consensus_answer: A broken unit need not rout if in a building UNLESS it is adjacent to a Known Enemy Unit. LOS and range (greater than 1) do not matter.

replies.body: A broken unit need not rout if in a building UNLESS it is adjacent to a Known Enemy Unit. LOS and range (greater than 1) do not matter.
That's what I thought but the tutorial mentioned you can't rout in place but it seemed like in some situations you can.
Note, though, that a broken unit in range and LOS to an enemy will likely stay DM for quite a while.

title: SW and Defensive First Fire question
question: If a unit moves and spend 2 MF's and is in LOS of a defending unit that also has a LMG can the LMG fire twice at full strength if it maintains ROF on the first shot? I know the infantry that possesses the SW can fire a 2nd shot using subsequent first fire at half FP but can the machine gun fire at full strength for the 2nd MF shot and if that retains ROF can it fire at other units that move in its LOS until ROF is lost and RF is left at that site?
author: happyloaf
consensus_answer:
Now, a question: 

Why did I italicize the last phrase in the MMG/HMG rule (which is A9.21 IIRC)?

MMG/HMG that hold Rate of Fire and are firing from a woods, rubble or building hex would not be able to fire outside the covered arc established by their first shot for the remainder of that phase.

Remember, Defensive First Fire takes place during the Movement Phase, is a DIFFERENT phase than the Defensive Fire Phase, which occurs after the Movement Phase is completed. (See A3.3 and A 3.4)

So what does that mean? Since I can only fire at units MOVING using First Fire and Subsequent First Fire in the Movement phase, what happens to my unused rate of fire if everyone has finished moving?

IF I still have ROF with my LMG/MMG/HMG, I can wait for Def. Final Fire Phase, and since I had ROF, my MG is NOT marked with a First Fire, so I can NOW fire again - and this time, at ANYONE in my LOS, because the covered arc goes away at the end of the Movement phase! 

(There is an exception for pinned units, but that's a different learning moment!) 

Hope this is helping! If it is confusing, just ignore me!

    ---Russ

a) and use the MG in addition to its Inherent FP, the LMG fires at half FP (with sustained fire breakdown penalities). Both are marked with a "Final Fire" counter.

In both cases, the squad and its MG only can Final Protective Fire afterwards - and the MG MUST be used.

title: Concealed Units
question:
1.  Does a concealed unit prevent an enemy unit from gaining concealment?

2.  If a concealed unit moves in LOS of a concealed enemy unit does it   lose concealment?

3.  Can a unit gain concealment if in LOS of a concealed enemy unit?

The way I look at it, a concealed unit is not a known unit and may contain only Dummy counters. So in order to prevent or cause an enemy unit to lose its concealment it would have to reveal at least one of its concealed units (perhaps by random selection if more than one concealed unit in the stack). If this is the case, does the unit that just revealed itself return to its concealed state or remain unconcealed?
author: grahamj
consensus_answer:
1. Yes. This is one reason to keep your dummies alive and hunt down the opponent's dummies.

See the Example in A12.121. It specifically mentions a Dummy stack.

2. Only if it is a non-dummy unit, which must be momentarily revealed to force loss of concealment (most guys I've played with just need a verbal, 'yup, it's real'). The enemy unit retains its "?" after this momentary revelation. The one that gets revealed is the owner's choice. However, machanics are different when you try to enter a Location with a "?" or Hidden enemy unit.

See A12.14. Middle of paragraph before the Example.

As Steve mentioned, the Chapter A table is the final answer to all the exceptions and is actually more comprehensive than the rulebook.

I think I'm starting to understand concealment now that I've re-read through the rules and looked at Table A12.121.

Concealment Lost depends on LOS to good order enemy units and non-Dummy concealed units

Concealment Gain depends on LOS to unbroken enemy units or concealed units that may contain Dummy units or not

A concealed unit that moves into open ground in LOS of a concealed enemy unit also loses its concealment provided the enemy concealed unit is not a Dummy unit (Defender temporarily reveals one unit or player can use the Honor System instead)

Concealment is also lost if an enemy unit attempts to enter its location during the Mph (provided it is not a concealed Dummy unit). Attacker reveals one of his units first to prove they are not Dummy counters

Hidden units may become concealed instead in order to prevent an enemy unit in its LOS from gaining concealment

The concealment chart - on the Infantry rules divider - is a real help.
Concealment rules are not among the most easy ones to master...

title: Point Attack
question: Does an aircraft continue to fire at its initial target every time it moves into a hex towards it (sort of like Strafing except shooting at the same target) and then once it reaches the initial target hex it may no longer attack (targets outside the initial target hex I suppose)?
author: grahamj
consensus_answer:
Does an aircraft continue to fire at its initial target every time it moves into a hex towards it (sort of like Strafing except shooting at the same target) and then once it reaches the initial target hex it may no longer attack (targets outside the initial target hex I suppose)?

Yes, but you only get two attacks versus the Point target:

7.402 POINT ATTACKS: A FB makes a Point Attack in the same manner as a Strafing Run with the following differences. After a FB has made its initial attack from four hexes away and has moved toward that target to the next hex along the predesignated Hex Grain, it may attack the same target hex again. Moreover, because it is now attacking from only three hexes away (six-hex Aerial Range), any To Hit DR is based on the 0-6 column of the To Hit Table instead of the 7-12 column. After this second attack, the FB must still attempt to continue moving along the predesignated Hex Grain until it occupies its target hex for purposes of receiving Light AA fire, but cannot make any additional attacks during that Player Turn.

Hope this helps,

JR

title: Just grabbed ASL from AH, not the MMP 2nd edtion, will I miss much.
question:
Just grabbed a complete (I think) Avalon Hill ASL 1st edition rulebook (could not pass on it for $5).
Is this obsolete at this point (with 2nd edition MMP???)
Thanks
Tim
author: timrichter9
consensus_answer:
Great buy !

First thing to do is assess which errata is in your book. Look through the chapters. I assume you have A,B, C, D, and J? Looking at the bottom of the pages, some of them SHOULD have superscripts next to them like A7^87, A13^87,B7^87, C3^89, D9^89 etc. D1^91 was later, 

That will tell you which pages were updated. (If you got it "new" chances are it was a later printing, and the 87 and 89 errata pages were incorporated into the book. (You can also check the last page of the A or B chapter (don't remember which now) to see if the original 'errata page coupons are in it. If they are, and they are not stamped already used. then you have a very first edition, first printing. But most of the books, even ones coming off shelves for the first time, will have the '87 updates to A&B, and some have the 89 updates for C&D. 

If you are a first time player, this is all fine. MOST of the 87 and 89 errata were important as it cleaned up original ideas and made them much clearer, or cleaner. Often, the later errata can be like fine tuning, where a word is changed, since with the MANY MANY users, it became very important to have an EXACT understanding of what was being attempted. But until you decide to get REALLY deep into this, you are cool. Now, if you have some counters, you are set to go. 

(And you can use this link to get started!)

http://www.russgifford.net/asl_training.htm

Plus there are MANY other fine training pieces all over the web and BGG. Enjoy!

        ---Russ

The Squad Leader boards are identical to the ASL boards and can be used without any problems (note that the newest ASL boards have been redone with new art and are thinner, but they are functionally identical to the Squad Leader boards).

The Squad Leader counters are different than the ASL counters. You might be able to, with some difficulty, play ASL using the SL infantry, leader, and support weapon counters... but I'm not sure if it would be worth the trouble you'd encounter.

If you want to skip the ASLSKs completely and learn ASL right from the start, then you might want to look for a cheap used copy of Paratrooper. With the ASL Rulebook, the Squad Leader boards, and Paratrooper you would have everything you need to start playing ASL.

If you are certain that ASL is the game for you, then getting the current version of Beyond Valor is a better choice: it has lots of mapboards, lots of scenarios, the counters that are necessary for every other ASL product (other than Paratrooper), and these counters have slightly better printing & more legibility than the ones found in old Avalon Hill products like Paratrooper.

Trying to play ASLSK scenarios with the ASL rulebook is a bad idea, because the Starter Kits will be missing many needed counters, such as snipers, concealment, berserk, and rubble, etc. (none of which are used in the ASLSK rules).

And I agree with the other posters that the 1st edition rules will work fine for learning the game.

Obsolete no.  However the 2nd edition book is much improved.  It has much of the errata incorporated and several of the confusing sections reworded.  It also has parts not included in the 1st edition.  The 1st edition is fully playable as is though.  If you decide you enjoy the the game I'd spring for a 2nd edition rule book, you'll appreciate the upgrade.  You can get for ~$65 online.

From MMPs website:
"Not only are the Rules back in full color, but the 2nd Edition also benefits from all the fine-tuning accumulated over the past 15 years. The 2nd Edition also contains material not previously included in the basic Rules, such as: more examples of play throughout, the advanced rules of Chapter E (night, weather, boats, planes, skis, convoys, etc.), the beginner's Training Manual in Chapter K, an expanded Index, and widely-acclaimed playing aids such as the Offboard Artillery Player's Aid and the Overrun Flowchart.Each chapter is in a larger font for ease of reading.

And all without changing how this great game is played.  The fruits of 15 years of "playtesting" can be seen here in the ASL RULES 2nd Edition which incorporates all previous errata and questions & answers. Great care has been taken to clear up ambiguities in the rules while keeping the game the same."

Oh my gosh.  I dug into the Infantry chapter of ASL.  How does ANYONE remember all of the 100s of possible rules that effect a chit as it acts??  I may have gotten in WAY over my memory's capacity here....

Tim,

Recently I wiped 20+ years of dust off my first edition (never really devoted the necessary time originally) rulebook.  I've been very casually reading ASL for a couple weeks now and I agree with what's already been stated; because everything is so intuitive it really isn't that difficult.

1) To start, don't worry about anything other than Chapters A and B.
2) Skim everything.  Look at all the dividers, charts, index, etc.  Read every heading and subheading.  Look at all pictures and read the captions.
3) Then go through at whatever pace you want.  I started pretty casually but as the abbreviations become second nature I'm starting to get excited about playing and I notice I'm reading more and more each time.
4) If you already haven't, I highly recommend listening to Russ' excellent video tutorials at http://www.russgifford.net/asl_training.htm.

(And I like the nice 'clean up and zoom in' on the new SK counters.)

But as you saw, I lean toward the new BV anyway. 

Also Tim - Jay has a FABULOUS set of tutorials - you'll want to check them out!

4) If you already haven't, I highly recommend listening to Russ' excellent video tutorials at http://www.russgifford.net/asl_training.htm.

I'll second that. The tutorials were very helpful. Also Jay's tutorial for the starter kits is great: ASLSK Tutorial

Keep in mind that ASL has rules for everything that could ever happen anywhere. A lot of the rules are rare. The problem with the rulebook is that it's not clear which parts are the everyday core rules and which are the unusual situation ones. For a lot of things you just need to remember that something can happen and have a rough idea of what triggers it. Then you can look it up if you need to.

I also use a 1st ed. rulebook (although the 2nd edition is shipping to me right now) and my partner uses 2nd edition. There haven't been any rules issues at all. It does help that he's been playing for over 20 years. Try and find an experienced player in your area if you can. It's a huge help. You can focus on the basics and he can make sure you aren't missing things and let you know when something unusual happens.

Now, what are you going to use for counters?

If you are 'already sold' the easy answer is the newest version of Beyond Valor has a TON of stuff at about $89. (Price may fluxuate - I saw it for $84 at my local store.)

The new edition has tons of Germans and Russians, the original boards 20-23, and now it includes original SL boards as well, plus TONS of GREAT scenarios. A GREAT buy. 

Or - you can purchase ASL Starter kit 1, ignore the rules, and use the boards and scenarios that come with it. Around $25 most places.

title: ASL Rule Question
question:
Hi!
n
I hope this is the right forum for my question.

A week ago I played my first ASL scenario with tanks, and in 3h we only played 30min becouse we allways had problems with the rules.

To be precise, only with the rules about tanks in motion.

I hope someone can help me here.

1. Are tanks allowed to Defensiv First Fire?

2. What if a defending tank is under a motion counter? What panaltys do count during DFF?

Thx for your help

Sve
author: SvenPatrick
consensus_answer:
1. yes, tanks can First Fire.  Note that their MG are not Infantry and the tanks may not Subsequent Fire Fire or Final Protective Fire their MG.  However, they can Subsequent First Fire their MA (which may result in Intensive Fire or normal SFF if IFE).

2. Motion requires all MG/IFE to fire at half FP.  And a tank's MA firing when in Motion gets gets the +2 (Case B), +1 or +2 for restricted(C1) or limited(C2) aim, and finally +2 for T/ST and +3 for NT (+1 if stabalized) for Case C.  And finally the lower dr is x2.

And if the AFV is BU, that is afurther +1 (Case I).

So a normal CE "tank" has a turreted main weapon, which results in a total of +5 DRM with and the lower dr is doubled.  An SP has NT and would be +6.

Examples:
Assume a Motion CE AFV with turreted MA.

DR: 4, 2 results in double lower dr to 4 which is a total of 8 +5 is a Final TH of 13.

DR: 1, 2 results in double lower dr to 2 which is a total of 4 +5 is a Final TH of 9

You're reading it wrong; check your Close Combat Table and you'll see it's 'vs broken unit (A11.16)'.  A11.16 isn't crystal clear, saying 'A broken unit...is subject to a -2 DRM to the CC DR.' title: Mortars Firing on Open Top Halftracks Transporting Troops?
question:
First it is not AF added up to 4, just having ALL AF being less than 4.  Same is true for the +1 DRM.

Yes, even large AFV can be destroyed by mortars.  But only the big ones.

I agree it is strange that mortars aren't allowed to target passengers of a half-track from a reality point of view.  But this ain't reality.  It's ASL.

Everything else looks good.

For your "Why can't a mortar get a direct hit and wipe out the passenger squad" question, look at rule C3.7, Critical Hits.  That blows up the whole thing.

Also remember that a halftrack with a BU counter is quite vulnerable to CC.  It will be OT and have no usable MG.  And the passengers can not participate.

Mortars are strange things.  They either do great things or nothing.  The following mantra is quite common, "Hit, rate.  No effect.  Hit, rate.  No effect.  Hit, rate.  No effect."
consensus_answer:
David, I agree with you that the attack is resolved using C1.55 which references C7.345 which details the attack resolution. I also agree with you that it seems logically that there SHOULD be a -1 DRM for OT. But I can't find it.  

I'm really working hard to get this portion of the rules clear in my mind and if you can cite the specific rule that gives a -1 DRM for a mortar attack on an OT AFV I'd really appreciate it. This doesn't only apply to Halftracks but would also affect stuff like OT Tank Destroyers. 

C7.22B provides an additional -1 DRM for Aerial attacks or MOL/DC attacks from a higher elevation against OT vehicles. D6.61 provides for attack even against BU passengers in an OT Armored Halftrack if the firer has an elevation advantage. But I can't find anything that provides a -1 DRM for being OT when Armored Halftracks come under regular mortar fire. 

Logically there should not be a penalty for an OT vehicle being fired on by a mortar. Unless the mortar round lands inside the vehicle (which is handled by the critical hits, I believe) then the mortar bomb is landing at ground level outside of the vehicle and the armored sides of the halftrack provide protection to the crew and passengers.

The other cases (elevation advantage or air attacks) involve direct fire against the passengers and crew that bypasses the protective side armor of the half track or other OT vehicle. Likewise the DC/MOL are being tossed down into the vehicle

replies.body:
From a reality point of view, why would anyone in their right mind target a vehicle of any kind with a mortar?  There is no WAY one would ever hit a moving vehicle directly with a mortar attack!  You're basically guessing where a vehicle would go to hit it...no f-ing way to do it...

Not to put a damper on your rule question...ASL is like that with the rule-checking.  And, rarely, reality loses to the rules.

If the passengers are CE then they are, by definition, exposed to the blast effects of a large explosion (a 120mm mortar has more exposive power than a similar-sized artillery round.)

If they are hunkered down inside the HT then only a direct hit on the vehicle will (and should) affect them. 

I don't see anything unrealistic or unexpected by these results.
Two quick thoughts you may have had, but I couldn't tell.  Guessing the normal German halftrack (SPW/251/1) was involved, there is a +1 TH for small target, and an additional -1 for OT on the TK.

                               OT   -1    Here it is

To sum up things.

To Hit

Mortar uses Area Target Type.
The ht is moving, so it is the only unit that can be affected by Def First Fire.
Minimal TH DRM : +2 moving (but if restricted aim, can be higher) and +1 for small size.

Effects :
You don't use the 60mm column, but the 12 IFT column (which is the half of the 24 column corresponding to 120 mm : one does not halve the calibre, but the original IFT value for Area Fire).

A CH (if original 2 TH DR) is resolved on the 36FP table and, as 48 is 12FP higher than 36, the heavy payload rule (C.7 "In addition, any CH that generates FP in excess of 36 FP is resolved on the 36+ column of the IFT with a -1 bonus DRM for each whole multiple of eight FP in excess of 36.") will allow a supplemental -1 DRM for the resolution of the hit.

To kill the ht, you have -2 DRM (all AF less than 4 and OT) : see result on the IFT table (less than K# - i.e. a final 3 or less = elim, = K# (or 1 higher than K#) : Immob if hull hit, Shock if upper structure hit).
All is on the AFV destruction table.

If the ht is not destroyed, all vulnerable PRC suffer general collateral attack, using the TK DR (and +2 CE DRM).

That is how I believe things are resolved.

title: Field Promotion Question
question:
First off I would like to say this is my first time posting anything to this website although I have been visiting for over a year.
I am unsure on the exact workings of field promotions so I will give ya'll way too much info.  I have Russian 9-2, 8-1, and 2 4-4-7's in Melee with a German 8-3-8.  The German player is the attacker.  The Russian leader are attacking each with a different squad but are combing the roll into 1 on 1 odds down 2 and the german squad is attacking the 9-2, 4-4-7 at 3 to 2 odds.  The german rolls a 6 which is a possible casualty reduction and the Russian stack rolls an Original DR of 2.  This is where I get stuck I am unsure if the Russian squads are eligiable for field promotion if attacking with leaders. I rolled out two different outcomes
1.) No field promotion is allowed, and the resulting random selection chooses the 9-2 which then fails his would dr. 
2.) Field promotion occurs and the squad that is stacked with the 9-2 is selceted via Random selection and the final DR for field promotion results in the creation of a 7-0 leader, thus changing the German result to noeffect as the odds are now 1 on 1.
I just want to know which outcome is correct as it has a significant effect on the game.
Cheers.
author: j23flo
consensus_answer:
I don't believer there is any Random Selection.  It doesn't matter which squad created the leader in this case.  It is just created.  The rule does not mention RS, so it should not be used.  (In other words, you couldn't have created 2 leaders.)

In this case I suppose you would decide which squad the new leader is defending with after he is created.

I think your #2 is correct minus the Random Selection plus allowing you to dictate which squad the new leader is defending with.

I agree with Jeff's basic point (you assign the leader to the MMC with which you wish it to defend) but another issue popped into my head:  what if you had a 458 and a 447 instead of two 447s?  The morale of the 'spawning' unit contributes a drm to the Leader Creation die roll if it's 8 or better (or 6 or less), so it matters if the base unit is the Elite unit or the 1st Liner.  I suggest in this case you would randomly determine the morale of the originator, with no possibility of multiple new leaders.  That's just a a guess, and I have nothing from the ASLRB to substantiate it.

JR

consensus_answer:
It's not that players think the game is perfect and cannot be improved; there's just a strong desire to have everyone playing by the same exact set of rules.I think this would be the major motive for not tweaking the rules too much.
The size of the rulebook has also an impact on the situation : learning it already takes a lot of time - not speaking of mastering most of it ¨
Imagine that any guys comes around and wants to change this or that detail (among hundreds of them)...
It easily would generate into a global mess.

And there is the real risk that the proposed variant does not take in count many effects on other rules : that impact can reveal itself as disastrous - but only after some months or years.
How can one go back, if such a modification has been adopted ?

There was the case of the bridge -1 TEM, additional to the FFMO one.
The erratum (which tried to be consistent with the Terrain chart), created such a mess among the community, that it had to be annulated by a subsequent erratum.

For the veteran ASL players maybe this is simply a reaction to the "bad old days" of Squad Leader, where all of the rules published in the three SL expansions were optional rules. Just imagine trying to play ASL if most of the rules could be used only if both players agreed to use them!I agree.
The simple size of the Rulebook speaks about the risks of major modifications.

it might make a fine SSR for a particular situation, if the scenario designer could provide any sort of verifiable historical justification for it.I agree. An SSR is the best way to go.

ASL is a game, which is by definition an approximation - and thus uses abstractions.
ASL is not reality, nor a very precise simulation (although, among wargames, it is among the most detailed ones). So trying to "change" it to something "more realistic" is an illusion that leads nowhere.

title: Next n00b question -- where does defensive fire occur?
question:
This is an issue we keep going back to the rules on (using ASL SK 2), and we keep getting flummoxed. 

A unit is in a hex, say, A002 or whatever.It is moving to, I dunno, B003. The attacker announces "I am moving this unit from this hex to that hex, expending 2 MF to do so". The defender says "I am using Defensive First Fire on that unit."

Does the fire "land" in the hex the unit was IN, or the hex the unit is moving TO? If the unit breaks, does it stop moving in A002 or is it in B003?

For any other "You expend MF (placing a DC, using smoke, etc), I shoot" scenario, does the shooting take place BEFORE or AFTER the effect of expending the MF? Is the smoke placed no matter what, in other words, or can firing on the unit cancel the smoke placement attempt (by breaking or eliminating the unit)?
author: LizardSF
consensus_answer:
Fire always takes place AFTER the MF are expended. So you would fire after the smoke is placed. Using the AFTER reasoning, you see that the fire is directed at the new hex. A unit moving from a5 to a6 is fired on at a6, because it is after the MF is spent that they may be fired on.

Note p.10 of the SK2 rulebook, 1st column: "Units expend MF based on the terrain that is entered...whenever a player moves a unit he states out loud the MF expended by that unit in entering that hex..." And also on p. 10, line 8 of 3.3.1: "Any time a unit or stack expends MF in the LOS of a Good Order Defender unit, the DEFENDER has the option to temporarily halt movement while he fires at it..."

Basically, you haven't moved unless you've spent MF, you haven't spent MF unless you've entered a new hex (or placed smoke, etc.), and the defender can't fire unless you've spent MF.

The defender cannot prevent movement into a hex or cancel smoke placement by defensive firing. If a unit breaks, they are broken in the new hex.

As noted above, but when placing a DC the MF cost is based on the 'target' hex, but they are expended in your current hex. So, although you are not moving into a new hex you are considered moving, and any DFF attacks against that unit uses TEM, FFNAM and FFMO modifiers (if applicable) based on the hex you are placing the DC from.

The other exception to the general rule is that the DFF against a unit placing a DC can cancel the (successfulness of the) action.
if you are in a hex and haven't moved, then you move to another hex, the defensive first fire takes place in the hex you move into.

title: N00b question -- fire groups with different DRMs
question:
So, I'm still learning this using ASL SK 2. A question came up in the last game we couldn't figure out.

If you have two units form a fire group, and one's LOS passes through two grain hexes, and one passes through one, how do you handle the different DRM for the combined group? (Or any other situation where one group has one DRM and another has another, but you're combining firepower.)
author: LizardSF
consensus_answer:
Actually, it comes down to being the worst of all possible worlds.

In a multi-hex fire group:
Use the worst possible TEM (generally caused by a wall or hedge).
Use the worst possible Hindrance
Use the worst applied leadership modifier.
If any one unit is CX, apply the +1 for that.

There's probably a few other individual modifiers, but you get the idea. And you take all of those components individually, and add them up. So, if you have two squads in a multi-hex firegroup, and one unit is firing through two hexes of grain (+2 Hindrance), and the other is firing through one hex of grain, but is CX (+1 Hindrance, +1 CX), you add the +2 Hind to the +1 CX for a +3 DRM.

title: OBA questions
question:
My friend and I are playing our first scenario with OBA, and I have a couple questions.  

The Germans get one 80+mm module of HE.  It is the beginning of the German prep fire phase.  FFE:2 is on the board.

First, does each OBA attempt begin with a Radio Contact check, regardless of Battery Access being previously established?

Second, if my FFE:2 is not in position to do any damage, I will correct it.  But after reading the rules it seems to me that with an FFE, as opposed to a SR, I cannot correct AND attack in the same phase.  Is this true?  If it is, will it convert to FFE:C at the end of the phase, or will I get another chance to use the FFE:2 next turn?

Thanks in advance for the help, folks!
author: paulus22
consensus_answer:
From FFE:C there are three different paths you can follow but they all require you pull another chit for Battery Access.
With a FFE:C on the map, here's the short version of your three options (assuming that you maintain contact and draw a black chit for a new fire mission):

(A) Place an AR anywhere on the map, which will be subject to normal extent of error, to place a new SR.

(B) Place an AR within 18 hexes of the FFE:C, with the extent of error limited by the distance from the FFE:C, to place a new SR.

(C) Leave the FFE:C in place, convert to FFE:1, resolve, and then convert to FFE:2.

All of these options, of course, have various restrictions/requirements.

What you *can't* do with a FFE:C is correct your aim and continue firing; you either continue firing at the same location, or you correct your aim and go back to just a SR on the map.

Hi there ,

title: Concealment loss
question:
In the advance phase, can a concealed squad advance into a non-open ground hex, in LOS of good order enemy with out loosing concealment?
Yes.

My confusion comes from the concealment loss/gain table.  Case A says yes for using non-assault movement while case B says no because I didn't advance into an open ground hex.
I'm not certain you're reading the chart correctly. You're asking whether ? is lost. So you're looking at the red values in the Infantry row. So if the Infantry does any of A, B, C, or D they lose concealment. You're not using non-assault movement (that's only in the MPh, not the APh), so A is OK. You're not advancing into OG, so B is OK. C and D are irrelevant. So you're good.
consensus_answer:
You can also usually assault move into a non-open ground hex without losing concealment.

Note that if you advance into terrain that could not have assault moved into (for example, terrain that takes more than 3MP for a squad without a leader) you will lose concealment too.

Or into a space that takes three MPs and you're green/conscript, you lose it. Basically, if it takes your normal full MP to move into a space (not advance) then you lose concealment. 

One trick on the defense is to alternate a guy moving forward and backwards during your MPh/AdvPh, so the enemy doesn't get a shot at him during DfPh. This is called "skulking". To elaborate this, have two units to do this. One moves back and gains concealment, while the other one, which gained concealment last round, moves forward during AdvPh to start the dance again.

Remember that this is a maneuver game more than a fire game...I know. I know. You don't believe me, but you will... :D

I always thought you had to Assault Move in order to keep your concealment. I figured there was a difference between Advance and Assault move.There is a clear difference :
- Advance occurs during the Advance Phase
- Assault Move occurs during the Movement Phase

So, advancing in concealment terrain during APh, even if you spend MF that would not allow Assault Move during MPh, does not make you loose concealment.
Even an Advance into Difficult terrain (which puts your Infantry under CX) will not make you loose concealment, if the terrain is concealed.

author: hank__hill
consensus_answer:
I have a question regarding the example on page A12, top left corner. The example shows a level one obstacle on a level one hill (I3). It shows H2 as a blind hex on a level one hill, but is measured 2 hexes away on a level two hill (J4).
J4 is a level 3 hill, not a level 2 hill.

Since J4 is equal to the level of the obstacle in I3, shouldn't H2 be visible?
As above, J4 is level 3, thus it's higher than the obstacle in I3. If it were equal, then none of the level 1 hexes would be visible at all. You have to be higher than the obstacle to see over it, regardless of how the blind hexes work out otherwise. And, as Devon said, all "real" obstacles (i.e. not just crestlines) always cast at least a single blind.

J4 is actually higher than the obstacle in I3, but it doesn't matter.  The number of blind hexes cannot be reduced below one (unless you're dealing with non-cliff crestlines)(A6.42).

title: Rule 4.51, CX...when do they come off?
question:
Okay it says "A unit's CX counter is removed...as soon as it:...or moves."

CX come off at the start of the Mph though, so how would it end up moving with a CX marker if it comes off at the start of the Mph? Moving comes after the start of the Mph, where the CX is removed.

I can't see how a unit would have a CX DURING the Mph since the CX comes off at the START of the Mph.

ASLO:

It says that the CX comes off at the end of it's next Mph. The very next sentence says it comes off at the start of the Mph. 

Which is it?
author: myndreach
consensus_answer:
Okay it says "A unit's CX counter is removed...as soon as it:...or moves."
I don't see the contradiction here. Moving is one of many triggers for removing a CX counter.

CX come off at the start of the Mph though, so how would it end up moving with a CX marker if it comes off at the start of the Mph? Moving comes after the start of the Mph, where the CX is removed.
If you're going to be very precise about it, no - this is not the correct formulation. Refer to the Extended Sequence of Play on the red binder divider. The "Beginning of THE MPh" is extremely limited and includes actions for only a few rare cases. CX status will be removed when the unit moves during ITS MPh. So, as you say, a unit will never move with CX the turn after it gained it.

I can't see how a unit would have a CX DURING the Mph since the CX comes off at the START of the Mph.
Because the unit could have declared Late Double Time - see the EXC to A4.5.

It says that the CX comes off at the end of it's next Mph.
Read the whole sentence - that's the fallback case for a whole list of possibilities. The CX is removed whenever any of them occur. So if you Prep Fire a CX unit, the CX is removed. If you decline Prep and move, the CX is removed then. If you decline Prep and also decline to move (maybe because another Prep didn't work out), then the CX is removed at the end of the MPh. 

The very next sentence says it comes off at the start of the Mph.
Actually, it says "a Mph", which is different. The CX counter is removed (if the unit moves) at the beginning of ITS MPh, and thus does not affect the unit during that MPh.

title: Hexgrains?
question:
I'm relatively new, and am looking for lots of good examples of hexgrains and alternate hexgrains, with graphics to show explanations. I'm mainly looking for help with Firelanes and Human Waves.

Thanks!
author: myndreach
consensus_answer:
In this case.

At the risk of over-explaining:

The particular point is that a hexgrain is just that. A... grain (see definition 6).

When you look at a hex grid, you can see straight rows of hexes going in three directions.

If you look at any particular hex in the above illustrations, as you move through any particular side to an adjacent hex and keep going in that direction, you are following a hex grain. So, in this case the hexgrains go up-down, upper left-bottom right, and lower left-upper right, and any particular hex will have these three grains passing through it.

To preserve players' sanity, the firelane rules generally just allow you to follow the hex grain when setting one up. This makes siting of MG especially important on the defense.

However, the FL rules also allow for 'alternate' hexgrain use. This is based off of the six hexspines radiating out from a hex (these are the same lines that separate the six adjacent hexes from each other). See the Covered Arc discussion in chapter C for a better idea of what is meant.

So here, you're allowed to fire down the junction of two adjacent hexes to set up your FL. Past that, you go to another hex, and then down the next hexspine, and so on. So, obviously the actual hexes are affected by the FL, but what happens in between? (On the hexspines?) There, you have to choose one side or the other to be affected by the FL. Pick a hex in the above illustration, and pretend you have a good amount of flat clear ground to work in. You can set up an alternate hexgrain FL firing directly to the left or right, but for the alternate hexes (where you're firing along the hexspine), you have to choose whether you're affecting the hexes above or below the spine. You get to make this choice once, when you set up the FL, and the entire FL follows that choice. You can't affect the adjacent hex above the hexspine, and then affect the hex below the hexspine 3 hexes away.

title: Vehicle gun questions........
question:
Hi all

 I just need a quick dbl-check of a few rules

1: you can only Intensive Fire at an adjacent or same hex target?

2: Tanks can get ROF during BFF or AFPH , but for only 1 extra shot?

3: for a roll of 12 , that malfunctions the MA but the attack still occurs

4: A tank only gets recalled if it tries to repair and breaks all its weapons ( MA, BMG CMG AAMG)

5: During the AFPH or MPH, a tank does not get any acquisition counters?

thats it for now, cheers

(I hope I got at least 3 of the 5 correct!)
author: dude163
consensus_answer:
NRBH but...
1) You can only Intensive fire at an adjacent target during the Defensive Final Fire phase - in the Movement phase you can Intensive fire further away.
2) You can have multiple ROF during BFF, not just 1 extra shot. You can never have ROF in the AFPh for vehicles.
3) Yes
4) No. Main armament only, MG's are irrelevant unless they are the MA. Things like Grants with two MA's - 37mm in a turret, and 75* in a side turret have to break both. 
5) You get acquisition in the AFPh but not in the Mph - its a tradeoff - ROF or acquisition - although you don't get acq if you are not stopped, unless gyrostabalized.

title: Mortar Spotter
question:
A mortar spotter is predesignated during the PFph/DFph and marked with an appropriate fire counter for having used a SW during that phase.

Do I place a PF or Final Fire marker on my spotter?
Can my spotter still use his Inherent FP if he's a MMC because a MMC can use 1 Sw + its Inherent FP.

Confused
author: grahamj
consensus_answer:
He could benefit from his leadership as well?
No. See C9.3 and note the "no leadership" triangle in the parenthesis after "can be a Spotter".

A leader can, however, direct the mortar crew itself, giving his bonus on their TH roll, even for spotted fire.

Huh, cool. I didn't know that, however, my good leaders usually have other things to do. :angry:

I usually put the nugget up in a building, with the other HS running the mortar or sometimes full squad running two mortars in an adjacent woods or such. Also, I believe that spotting is NOT a concealment loss activity. NRBH. Therefore setting up HIP or concealed, especially if the spotter could be in several adjacent locations or levels is sneaky.

So, it's a good tactic and adds a bit to an already great game.

title: Desperation Morale
question:
When a unit has a DM counter on it it must add a +4 DRM when it attempts to rally for the first time right? According to the phase sequence removal of DM counters happens after the rally attempt.
So I suppose the next turn the DM counter is no longer there and the unit may attempt to rally without the +4 DRM penalty right?
author: grahamj
consensus_answer:
Yes, the negative effect of desperation morale is considered once, and then removed (although there are some circumstances in which the counter may remain). 

Note: you may also either have to or want to keep DM on a guy. The first is the case if you didn't get to rally terrain (ie. low crawl or the terrain was too far away). The second case is (if allowed) is if you want to continue routing (ie. to a safer place or farther away or to a key space to end in).

Keep in mind that keeping your opponent's brokies under continual DM by sending a little fire their way on subsequent turns can be a path to success. :devil:

Which might be a reason to keep them running, if feasible.

 It is more difficult to rally the units immediately after than they have broken, but it gets easier after they have found some cover and changed their underwear.

title: EC process - Noob is confused
question:
My friend and I are taking the leap into full ASL after learning the basics from the starter kits, and I still can't quite figure out the process of dealing with Environmental Conditions and wind.  We are about to start Scenario 1 from BV, and need to figure it out so the blazes work properly. 

SO...

During Rally Phase, what exactly happens with regards to EC?  I've read the rules multiple times, but I can't quite conceptualize (a common problem in attempting to visualize the rules) what happens.

I know that a DR is made, and on a 2 the wind changes, and on a 12 there are gusts, and on other rolls various other things happen.  My major question is, with regards to the EC set at scenario start, is there a roll to see if THIS changes?  For example, if it starts moderate and dry, can it ever start raining?

Thanks for the help, oh masters of the squads!
author: paulus22
consensus_answer:
So, according to you, the ECs stay the same throughout the scenario, but the wind changes during the rally phase check.
I think that about the only time that EC can change *during* a scenario is if you have Overcast conditions, in which case rain (or snow) could start (or stop) falling during the scenario itself. When rain starts falling for the first time, EC changes to "Wet" for the remainder of the scenario; falling snow creates Mist. (See E3.5, 3.51, E3.71)

replies.body:
The EC are set by the scenario.  The only time you would roll for the EC is in a DYO (design your own) scenario.

Scenario 1 has the unfortunate problem of having EC of Wind with Blazes already on board.  It's not a very good introductory scenario.

Do you have BV 3rd edition?  I'm sure there are better introductory scenarios such as Commando Shenke, The Czerniakow Bridgehead or The Commissar's House, which are all infantry only scenarios.  (And 2 of those are in all editions of BV.)

But to answer your question.  No, you do not roll at the beginning of the scenario.  You roll at the beginning of the Rally Phase.  If it's a 2 or a 12, something happens.  Otherwise nothing happens (in this particular scenario anyway).

If you roll a 2, the strength or direction of the wind may change.  If you roll a 12, Gusts remove all Smoke.  But Scenario 1 also requires you to remember to check for blaze/flame spread in each Advancing Fire Phase.  It's just one more thing to remember that you'll forget.  Skip #1 and go to one of the ones mentioned above, or another all infantry scenario with, "EC are moderate, there is no wind at start".  You still may get wind if you roll a 2 on the Wind Change DR, but it won't be as crazy as good ol' scenario 1.

title: Defending AFVs First and Final Fire?
question:
Hi, as I am not that long playing ASL I have a question you may help me with.

When using your AFV in your own MPf you use BF. That is all clear to me. But when using an AFV in your opponents MPf for defence you use its MA like an ordinary gun. As long it does not loose ROF it can still fire multiple shots of Final Fire in its own DFPf (C.2.241), everything right so far?

But how are its VMGs used in this situation?

In my MPf I have to use them together with my MA or do not use them at all. And if I use them with the MA together I won't be able to fire my ROF MA in my AFPf, right?
author: Periplaneta
consensus_answer:
For the last part, right. If you use any armament on a vehicle, any other armament has to be used in the same fire phase, be that Prep, Movement or Advancing Fire. Do note that as the DEFENDER, MPh and DFPh are considered all one fire phase.

Generally speaking, an MA is not marked with a First/Final Fire counter until it looses ROF (and therefore can keep firing without penalty such as IF).

title: Learning Concealment
question:
My friend and I have worked through ASLSK1-3, and now are learning the full ASL system.  The second scenario we are attempting is Scenario B from the 'Classic' batch of scenarios that originally were for Squad Leader.  This one brings up some questions about concealment, since I don't fully comprehend how this all works yet.

My questions are:

When a unit sets up under concealment, it remains concealed until it moves/fires/etc, regardless of being in LOS of enemy units, right?

After all the ? counters are placed from the scenario card, any other units out of LOS of any enemy revealed, Good Order unit get a free ? counter, right?

Concealed units DO force Loss of Concealment for enemy concealed units that move in the open, fire, etc, right?

I think I've answered most of these questions by discussing with my friend and repeatedly re-reading the concealment rules, but I'd like some clarification from all-y'all.  Thanks!
author: paulus22
consensus_answer:
But I think I figured out that a ? unit is NOT a good order unit, but DOES still have an effect on concealment.
Well, not exactly. A Dummy unit/stack (multiple ?'s) is not Good Order. A (real) unit under a ? counter is Good Order. However, you must momentarily reveal it (lift up the ? counter) in order to strip enemy concealment. This is primarily a matter of verification - since ASL's rules attempt to be rigorous enough for tournaments, you can't simply say that a concealed unit is real without proving it. However, there are also some gameplay ramifications here as well. It's sometimes a better idea not to momentarily reveal your own unit and let the enemy keep his concealment in order to keep him in the dark about where your own real units are. What you choose depends on how valuable that knowledge would be in that situation.

Because the rule about momentary reveals is primarily a verification issue, some people consider it "gamey" and house-rule it in friendly play. A number of players I've met will "show a boot" without revealing the exact stats of the unit. A few will simply go by one another's word without any verification at all. However, the rules as written are quite clear that the unit must be completely (though only momentarily) revealed.
