The rules for infantry smoke are in A24.  The relevant parts say that during a mild breeze, smoke cannot be placed into the three adjacent hexes in an upwind direction (A24.1).  A24.11 states that infantry smoke is never dispersed or subject to drift, and cannot be placed in Heavy-Winds.

The reason you can't find a rules reference is because there is no such rule.  Gusts have absolutely zero effect on SMOKE grenades; nor is there any effect on firing new SMOKE from ordnance/FFE.

Gusts (B25.651) have an effect twice in the Player Turn: the RPh and the AFPh.  There are two effects: firstly, in both phases, the strength of SMOKE counters currently on the board is reduced.  Secondly, in the AFPh, blazes can spread more easily.

SMOKE grenades are placed during, and only have an effect in, the MPh.  Gusts have no effect in the MPh.  (Gusts also have no effect in the PFPh or the DFPh, when new SMOKE counters may be placed on board.)

Now, there COULD have been a rule saying that you can't use SMOKE grenades in a player turn where Gusts are in effect.  It's not difficult to conceptualise.  However, there is no such rule, so it isn't true.

Don't invent rules; there are plenty of them in the rulebook already.

Are you sure guys about infantry smoke grenades being possible during wind gusts?

Absolutely.

My question is, is wind gust *stronger* wind than heavy wind?

No.  It's not a question of "strength".  In real life, gusts represent intermittent "bursts" of strong wind.  "Heavy wind" just doesn't stop, it keeps on blowing (strongly).  Thus, in the game, "Heavy wind" is a continual effect, while "gusts" are an occasional effect.  It's just that the artificial nature of the structure of the game turn makes those "occasional" effects completely predictable.

title: Wall/Hedge LOS question
question:
B9.2 states:

"A wall/hedge lying lengthwise (on a hexspine) exactly along a LOS is a Half-Level LOS obstacle only if ... touching one of the viewing/target hexes and the vertex opposite of the viewing/target hex has walls/hedges on all of its three hexspines." (Emphasis in Original).

I'm struggling with the precise definition of the word "one" as used in the above sentence. 

Does "one" mean:
A. At least one; or
B. One and only one.

It makes difference if the wall/hedge lies along a hexspine that connects both the viewing and target hex.  Look at page B9 for an example.  If the rule means "at least one," there would not be an LOS between P4 and Q6 on the examples in the right hand column, because at least one of the viewing/target hexes is touching the hedge, and the opposite vertex has hedges on all three hexspines.

But, if one means "one and only one," then there would be an LOS between P4 and Q6, because the hegde is adjacent to both the viewing and target hexes; it is not merely adjacent to only ONE of them, it is adjacent to TWO of them, therefore LOS would not be blocked.

I admit, that the "one and only one" definition makes less sense.  For that reason my gut tells me that "one," as used in B9.2, means "at least one."  But I'm usually wrong on these things, so I thought I'd put it out there.  It doesn't help that the rule decided to put the word "one" in italics, which lead me to consider that perhaps "one" means "one and only one."
author: Devon Harmon
consensus_answer:
It means one and only one - the LOS is clear between P4 and Q6 in the examples. I agree that the wording of the hedge/wall LOS rules is initially confusing. But once you get it, it does make sense. Rather than try to pick apart the wording, consider this smashing ASCII art...

   /
X--|   Y
   \

Should X's LOS to Y be blocked? Well, certainly the above diagram should be no less restrictive than this one...

   /
X  |    Y
   \

And that's clearly blocked, so the first diagram's LOS should also be blocked. Now try rereading the passage with those diagrams in mind and hopefully the restrictions make more sense.

title: MG Fire Lanes: Can manning Infantry use SFF/FPF?
question:
So I have been going over the rules for Fire Lanes, and I think I have found a contradiction. 

A9.223 states " A MG may cancel its Fire Lane in order to gain freedom to fire elsewhere (/its manning Infantry may use Subsequent-First-Fire/FPF after establishing the Fire Lane) only if a TPBF/CC-Reaction situation occurs..." 

The way I read this is that the only way an MG can fire again is if a TPBF/CC-Reaction situation occurs. Since the part about manning Infantry is in parenthesis, this limitation does not apply to them, and they may use SFF/FPF freely after establishing a Fire Lane. 

But then I read the comprehensive Fire Lane example on the next page (A22). In the example, a 4-6-7 unit uses an MG to set up a Fire Lane. Later, an enemy unit moves into the Fire Lane and is attacked by the residual FP of the Fire Lane. The example then states "but the 4-6-7 cannot Subsequent First Fire against it (9.223)" 

???? 

Doesn't 9.223 say the 4-6-7 can use SFF after establishing a fire lane? Am I misinterpreting 9.233?
author: Devon Harmon
consensus_answer:
I think I see now.  Is it that little slash just inside the parenthesis that makes the limitation also apply to the part inside the parenthesis?

I'm no english major, but it seems a poor way to convey that thought.  Although admittedly, I am not properly informed on the correct grammatical usage of the "/".

So the rule really says: "A MG may cancel its Fire Lane in order to gain freedom to fire elsewhere only if a TPBF/CC-Reaction situation occurs.  Likewise, its manning infantry may only use SFF/FPF in the same situation.  In this case, the Fire Lane must be cancelled, even if the unit entering the MG's hex does so across the hexside of the Fire Lane."

All the more reason to assign my MGs to Half-Squads.

title: C1.23 Field Phones
question:
Admittedly, I often times make things more complex than they need to be.  I try to give some meaning to each and every word the designer uses.  I figure if the words are there, somebody put them there for a reason.

Anyway...C1.23 states "A Field Phone and its Observer may always set up using HIP (if otherwise able to)."  Emphasis mine.

It seems pretty simple, but it is the part in parenthsis that I have trouble with.

Does this mean:
1.  A Field Phone and Observer can always set up HIP unless an SSR says they can't.

or

2.  A Field Phone and Observer can set up HIP if that side is allowed to set up some units HIP (SSR, Night Defender, Japanese, etc...)

I'm leaning towards number 2 (which means that 1 is correct), as I personally feel it carries out the "if otherwise able to" language.  But then the rule says they can "always" set up HIP.  

If the intent is that they can always set up HIP, unless an SSR says they can't, I feel the rule is poorly worded.  If the intent is that they can set up HIP if allowed to by other rules (otherwise able to), then I also feel the rule is poorly worded because of the use of the word "always."

Thoughts?
author: Devon Harmon
consensus_answer:
Damon,

     I've always played it that you can set up an observer HIP if in concealment terrain. And all the long time experienced players I've played with seem to agree...
 
    still the wording does seem open to interpretation...

   As you can't move an observer and their field phone though, if they weren't HIP they wouldn't be very effective. The enemy could stay out of LOS or just blatt the observer.

   There may be a perry sez or errata on the subject. It might be worth posting on the gamesquad forums...there's some mighty city slick rules lawyers on there.

replies.body:
Damon,

     I've always played it that you can set up an observer HIP if in concealment terrain. And all the long time experienced players I've played with seem to agree...
 
    still the wording does seem open to interpretation...

   As you can't move an observer and their field phone though, if they weren't HIP they wouldn't be very effective. The enemy could stay out of LOS or just blatt the observer.

   There may be a perry sez or errata on the subject. It might be worth posting on the gamesquad forums...there's some mighty city slick rules lawyers on there.

IIRC: There are some places (open ground in LOS of an enemy unit) where you are generally not able to setup concealed. HIP is really just a special form of concealment. The parenthetical clause is telling you that you can't set up your observer HIP in a place where he would be barred from setting up concealed normally, so you can't use this rule to override the normal concealment rules (which normally, it would, having a higher number).

I believe the "if otherwise able to do so" is referring to the terrain in the hex, any SSR saying you can't, etc.

This is one of the parenthetical clauses in the ASLRB which probably shouldn't be there. 

But then again, those are just my thoughts.

I have re-written my rulebook to read "A Field Phone and its Observer may always set up using the rules for HIP." 

It just makes more sense to me that way.

title: What constitutes a leader action?
question:
As detailed as the rules to this game are, I'm having dificulty locating a specific list of things that constitute an action taken by a leader.

When I was taught the game, I was told that generally a leader can only do one thing per phase.

Some of the rules bear this out.  For example, A3.1 clearly states "RALLY PHASE (RPh): Both players may attempt to repair weapons, rally broken units, etc. Each unit may attempt only one type of action in a RPh."

So, during the RPh, can a leader attempt to recover a SW from a broken squad (A4.44), and then attempt to rally the broken squad?

Clearly the leader attempting recovery is an action for the leader, but is the act of rallying the unit an action for the leader, or is it just an action for that unit?  A10.71 makes reference to leaders attempting to rally broken units.  Put in those words, it makes it seem like the leader is trying to get the units to rally, and it would therefore be an action on the leader's part.  That being said, A10.6 states that "Broken units of both sides may attempt to rally during any RPh if a Good Order friendly leader is present in the same Location."  This seems to imply that it doesn't matter whether the leader has acted in the Rally Phase or not, pointing to the conclusion that it is not an action for the leader.

So I ask again, does using a leader to rally troops in the same Location constitute an action for that leader, such that it would preclude him from attemping recovery or repair in that same RPh.

As a corollary question, would attempting to deploy good order squad(s)during the RPh count as an action for a leader?  Would recombining constitute an action for a leader?
author: Devon Harmon
consensus_answer:
So I ask again, does using a leader to rally troops in the same Location constitute an action for that leader, such that it would preclude him from attemping recovery or repair in that same RPh.
Yes. This is implied in the example in A3.1, though I'm not sure it's spelled out anywhere.

As a corollary question, would attempting to deploy good order squad(s)during the RPh count as an action for a leader?

title: Self-rally without the ability...
question: I was reading in a strategy forum today that "the attacking player may self-rally one MMC during the rally phase, even if it doesn't have self-rally capability." Is this true? If so, can anyone quote section in the book that this rule is contained in?
author: StAtiC9
consensus_answer:
Yes
In your half player turn, as the FIRST rally attempt of the rally phase, you may attempt to self rally one unit not capable of typical self rally.  Its called Field Promotion (18, pg A37 in RBV2).

From the RBV2:

18. FIELD PROMOTIONS
18.1 Leader creation during play may occur in either of two ways.

18.11 SELF-RALLY: The first MMC Rally attempt of a player’s own
RPh may be performed as Self-Rally regardless of Self-Rally capability
(10.63) in an attempt to rally that MMC, provided there is no Good Order
leader in that Location and the broken unit is not Disrupted (19.12). If this Self-Rally attempt results in an Original 2 DR, the MMC is rallied and, in addition, the ATTACKER may roll on the Leader Creation Table with a +1 drm for having been broken prior to the Self-Rally 2 DR. Any Original DR other than 2 during the Self-Rally attempt is handled as a normal Self-Rally attempt, so the broken unit can still rally without a Field Promotiontaking place even if it is not normally capable of Self-Rally.

title: 1987 and 89 Upgrades to ASL 1st Edition...?
question:
Hi,

   Can anyone tell me if the 1987 and 89 upgrades to the first edition effectively update it to second edition?  If not, what changed from 1st to 2nd?  Are the second edition rules a must have to play today, or is the first edition w/ '87 & '89 compatible?

Bruce
author: Ellowen-Deeowen
consensus_answer:
One of the Journals does have a writeup from MMP that states the changes and additions to the RB.
It is in ASL Journal #3: "First Do No Harm – Designer's Notes on the 2nd Edition" by Perry Cocke.

The Wall Advantage, Hedge/Bocage, and Human Wave rules apparently had the most major changes, but off-hand I couldn't say exactly how much difference there is between the 1st edition and 2nd edition versions of these rules. One example that I can give is that the 2nd edition added a step to the Advanced Sequence of Play (ASOP) for declaring Wall Advantage that was not present in the 1st edition ASOP.

The changes to the rest of the rules were primarily incorporating existing errata and Q&A's, and some wording changes for better clarity in some areas.

Are the second edition rules a must have to play today, or is the first edition w/ '87 & '89 compatible?
The 1st edition rules, even with all of the published errata for them, are not equivalent to the 2nd edition rules... and the 1st edition is no longer being supported with errata. But the 1st edition rules are still quite usable: the vast majority of the rules work exactly the same way in both editions.

The 2nd edition rulebook is a much-improved rulebook in many ways, and a recommended purchase if you can afford it, but, unless you are planning to compete seriously in the top tournaments, it is not required. The 1st edition rules will still work fine for casual gaming with friends, and for beginners looking to move to ASL from the Starter Kits.

The leader DRM is mandatory only for morale checks. The owner may choose to use it for a fire attack. If the units in a hex spit their firepower between several attacks against different targets, the leader can be used for only one of these. 

When a firegroup fires, it will get the leader modifier from the hex with the worst leader modifier in that attack. title: Snipers
question: Does any one have a blow by blow example of how snipers work?  I understand when they are activated, but how do they determine their target, etc.
author: Warhammer
consensus_answer:
without going to far into the rules...

1. At the start of the game each player places the sniper counter within 6 hexes of 6 enemy occupied hexes.....5 occupied hexes...4 occupied hexes....

2. On activation a die is rolled, 1 or 2 indicates a possible hit.
   

3. Target hex dr like a spotting round to determine target.
   Sniper counter moves to target hex.

4. sniper selects target if multiple targets or an alternate 
   target closest to  initial hex.

5. to resolve attack roll a die, roll of 1 breaks MMC or eliminates SMC
   roll of 2 pins MMC or wounds SMC. 3-6 no effect.

It's all in rules section A14

Very close, but  no extra dr is needed as stated in #5. 

When sniper is activated and you roll the 1 or 2 for a possible hit (meaning eligible targets are available), resolution of the attack takes place when you roll the first 1 or 2.  You don't roll again.  

i.e.  you don't need to roll the DR = SAN then roll a dr=1,2 and again a dr=1,2  (ASLese) Just DR then dr...and determine via #3

Yeah, that's a pretty huge difference in terms of game effect as well there, basically accidentally requiring another roll with only 33% odds to do anything.

One of those things that ASL does; it took us awhile to be comfortable we were getting the spotting round movement part right (I think those rules are very oddly written for such a simple concept).  Would have been nice if rather than cross-referencing to Chapter C, they would have just said in the sniper rules something like roll one die for direction, another die for number of hexes.

title: [Fun] Rules for making coffee in ASL
question: That is beautiful.
consensus_answer:
Excellent!

The corollary to this in  is:

E78. Making Coffee

"One lump or two?"

- Bugs Bunny

When this event occurs, the receiving player must determine a Random Hex [1.8]. That player may select one unit in or adjacent to that hex and have it try to make coffee. The player then makes a Making Coffee Roll [O20.2.4].

If the Making Coffee Roll exceeds the Coffee/Tea Rating for that nation and year then coffee is made. If the unit is broken, unbreak it. If the unit is suppressed, remove the suppression marker. If the unit already has a veteran marker on it, take no further action. Otherwise, place a Veteran marker on it.

If the Making Coffee Roll equals the Coffee/Tea Rating for that nation and year, then it becomes Suppressed, unless the unit is British, in which case it becomes Broken.

If the Making Coffee Roll equals the Coffee/Tea Rating for that nation and year, then it becomes Broken.

If an unmodified 12 is rolled, then the game ends and whoever was the acting player wins.

title: Difference between SMOKE and WP placement?
question:
Hi,

Under the rules section A24.SMOKE it states:"Units attempting to place
SMOKE grenades must specify the hex they wish to place them in before rolling the placement dr, but are otherwise free to observe the placement attempts of previous moving units before designating their own
placement attempts."

Whats the sense of the underlined phrase. It seems logical that one unit after the other makes a move. Or does this phrase count for a stack of units?

And so the next question comes up; under A24.3 WP it states:"The rules for placement of WP grenades are identical to those of conventional smoke except that such use must be announced prior to the Placement Attempt dr."
But where is the exception in that. I see no difference between SMOKE and WP Placement.
Maybe it could count for a stack of units, but nothing seem to indicate
that. 
I hope you know what I mean and can answer my questions.
Thanks in advance.

Greetings,
Chris
author: konsum24
consensus_answer:
Forget my question, now it's clear.
I was a little bit confused.
:) actually, it turns out that you're not the only one that has been confused by this...

I decided to look into this matter further. I could not find any "Perry sez" or 2nd ed. Q&A/errata for this, but I did find a debate between Ole Boe and Bruce Probst – both well-respected rules experts – from Aug 2005 on ConsimWorld:

A24.1 says quite clearly "Units attempting to place SMOKE grenades must specify the hex they wish to place them in before rolling the placement dr, but are otherwise free to observe the placement attempts of previous moving units before designating their own placement attempts."
Yes, and "previous moving units" are units that moved previously, but have now finished their MPh, i.e. units that are not part of the moving stack.
In other words, it's legal to say of a stack consisting of two squads moving together: "Squads A & B will both attempt to place SMOKE in adjacent hexes. Squad A wants to try for hex 1." (Rolls die) "OK, since that worked, Squad B wants to try for hex 2." (Rolls die)
No, because A is not a previously moving unit when moving stacked with B. This is clear from A4.2 which says: "Units moving as a stack ... must designate at the same time all actions for the same MF." So you can clearly not designate the placement hex of squad B after having seen the result of squad A.
If this were not true, the "otherwise free to observe" clause would be so trivial as to be pointless (of course you observe the activities of units that moved previously!). (There was an old unofficial 1st ed. Q&A which did exactly support what you wrote above, but clearly the current 2nd ed. text of A24.1 overrules it.)
I checked this, and the text of the 1st ed. A24.1 uses the same wording, so Bruce's claim that the 2nd ed. text overrules the 1st ed. Q&A has no logical basis: the text didn't change!

I agree that the sentence in question is so trivial as to be pointless. That doesn't allow you to act as if it means something else than it actually says though
This was the end of their discussion. I don't think Ole managed to change Bruce's mind on this, but apparently neither one felt strongly enough about it to ask for a ruling from MMP (a "Perry sez").

I agree with Ole here, and disagree with Bruce: The "otherwise free to observe" part of A24.1 does not constitute an exception to units moving as a stack, which is ALWAYS simultaneous. This is exactly what the rules say, and the 1st ed. Q&A is powerful evidence that this is the correct interpretation. 

But, given that two rules experts couldn't agree on what this rule is saying, perhaps someone really should ask Perry for a ruling...

If you tried for normal smoke you succeed, if you try for WP you fail because your smoke exponent is one lower after declaring WP.

Hi,

First I had a problem with the term "SMOKE". I don't note that when it's
spelled completely in CAPITAL letters, it refers to both "smoke" and "WP".

So I was confused about the phrase under A24.3WP:"The rules for placement....except that such use must be announced prior to the Placement Attempt dr."
And of course, a use of WP must be announced.:shake:
Now it seems so simple.

So the only problem was the phrase under A24.1"....,but are otherwise free to observe the placement attempts of previous moving units before designating their own placement attempts."

I decided to handle this rule as follows:
Lets say a stack of two units, A and B move together. 
First I announce that I want to place smoke (with both units A and B) in an adjacent hex.
At this time they don't have to designate the hexes, but they designate at the same time all actions for the same MF, and the "actions" in this case are placing smoke in an adjacent hex. 
At this point I haven't to say in which particular hex the units want to place smoke (lets say the units only prepare their smoke grenades). 
Then I decide that unit A want to place smoke in an adjacent hex1 and make a placement dr.

Prisoners are never armed: (A20.5) "... a white unarmed counter..."

An additional question that i think pertinent: 
In A20 seems that we talk of "Prisoners eliminated in an escape attempt" but not prisoners captured in an escape attempt. 
This means that in CC against prisoners attempting to escape you can't try to re-capture them.
Once they escaped successfully, they become unarmed (or Green if re-armed) and they can be captured again (with -1 DRM modifier).

This means that in CC against prisoners attempting to escape you can't try to re-capture them. ...

Above statement is correct?

No.  CC against escaping prisoners uses regular CC rules (other than the special cases such as it being non-simultaneous) and so capture via CC remains a valid option ... and unarmed units are always treated as inexperienced and so the -1 in capture attempts is still applicable.

The more important issue is, what else is going on?  If there are non-prisoner enemy units involved in the same CC then re-capturing prisoners isn't going to do you any good as the prisoners will just keep on escaping while a Melee is in effect ... indeed it is actually detrimental for the guards because escaping prisoners (including non-prisoners participating in the same attack) always attack first ....

Of course, if the only reason the prisoners are able to escape is the fact that their guards are broken, and there are no other units involved, then re-capture of the prisoners before the CC finishes simply isn't going to be an option.  The guards don't get to run away and rally!

Captured Prisoners are alwais considered Unarmed units, they don't become Unarmed units only once succesfully escaped {A20.5 "A Personnel unit is captured as (i.e., exchanged for) a  white (1)-0-6 unarmed counter of the appropriate size..."}.

Just a curiosity... Being Prisoners also Unarmed enemy units, this means a guard is alwais in LOS of his "unbroken enemy ground (unarmed) unit" prisoner and can't gain concealment? :whistle:

Just a curiosity... Being Prisoners also Unarmed enemy units, this means a guard is alwais in LOS of his "unbroken enemy ground (unarmed) unit" prisoner and can't gain concealment? :whistle:

No.  The game distinguishes between prisoners and unarmed units.

Prisoners are unarmed, but they are not unarmed units.  They aren't any type of unit (check the Index definition of "unit".  Prisoners are not capable of independent movement).

Conversely unarmed units are units (it's right there in the name) but to be an unarmed unit you cannot be a prisoner.

To dive further into the rabbit hole, there are even two types of unarmed units: those who used to be prisoners and those who have never been prisoners.  The latter can be fired on with no particular consequences; firing on the former may provoke a Massacre.

And diving even deeper, you have the question of unarmed units that are in possession of a functioning SW/Gun.  They are "armed unarmed units". :)

title: Snipers?
question: Any rules governing snipers in ASL?  If so, how do they work?
author: puck4604
consensus_answer: A14.22  NON-TARGETS: Only [...] prisoners [...] are ineligible Sniper targets.

replies.body:
Yes there are, but they're very abstracted.

Basically each side has a sniper counter that goes somewhere on the map, then whenever the opposing player rolls a certain number (Determined by the scenario) whenever they're rolling the dice, there's a possibility that the sniper will be triggered. So if the German's SAN (Sniper Activation Number) is a 4, whenever the British player rolls a 4 when resolving fire attacks or morale checks, the sniper could be activated.

If it is, two dice are rolled to move it around, where it then attacks the nearest enemy. Depending on the number rolled to activate it, it will either kill or wound and SMC, or pin or break a squad.

There are rules for snipers shooting each other, or squads trying to shoot the sniper, but these hardly ever come up.

The main thing is that a sniper isn't a unit, and cannot really be controlled by the player. It's main purpose is to cut down the number of dice rolled, if one player has a high SAN, then the other player may want to reduce the number of low odds attacks he makes, because he's more likely to trigger the sniper than damage the enemy.

Snipers are abstracted, but they work well. Each side has a sniper number (SAN) 2 to 7. This is a type of scenario balance, since the closer to 7 the number is the more likely a result will be. Basically, as stated before if your opponent rolls that magic "Sniper number", then the sniper may be activated (subsequent 1 or 2, so 1/3 chance).

People can discount the Sniper, until he kills your 10-3 leader or breaks the squad guarding prisoners or manning that critical MG. The cool thing about it is that you don't control him. So, it can have an effect from nada to full blown chaos. If the number is high, it can limit the amount of extraneous 2 +1 shots taken.

In my opinion, as with most of the ASL rules, they really come into play during a Campaign Game (CG). Sometimes you get two snipers and adjustable SANs. In CGs and some scenarios, sniper hunting (as opposed to snipe hunting...:surprise: ) is worth doing. Basically, use an attacked stack who hasn't done anything to do a sniper check. This can "pin" the sniper for the turn or reduce it's number. Get it below 2 and it's gone. (A big deal for a CG.)

So, it is an elegant and fun system.
Do snipers target prisoners in random selection?
A14.22  NON-TARGETS: Only [...] prisoners [...] are ineligible Sniper targets.

The ASL Sniper rule is an improvement over the original SL SMC sniper counters.
You don't control when those guys fire - which is exactly what happens on the field.
As you don't need to hide them (they are simulated by a marker that moves on the board), and as they work "by themselves", they are also well adapted to solitaire play.

I have lost some nice leaders, who were hiding from all enemy units (e.g. crawling up a hill via a gully) to sniper fire.

There are sniper check mechanics and snipers can attack one another (thus reducing the sniper activation number or 'pinning' a sniper during a Player Turn).

Sniper activation numbers (SAN) do play a role in balancing a scenario - typically a defender has a higher SAN than the attacker.

Note, too, that Sniper rules 'simulate' more than Sniper fire : they can also be considered as simulating other elements of fate on the battle field (including friendly fire - especially at night, where SAN are automatically increased to depict that type of misfortune).

When I started to play ASL, I shied away from the Sniper rules... But when I did try them, I never more refrained from using them : they add to the numerous "surprises" that an ASL play offers.

author: konsum24
consensus_answer:
No, there is no need to expend 1 more MF to cross the wall at the D4-E4-D5 [edit: D4-E4-E5] vertex (this is just like the 4.3 example discusses at the other vertex). Think of the unit as being slightly inside hex D4 and so it can move along the open ground into E5 going around the wall rather than crossing it.

To clarify a bit more, the reason you need to pay 1 MF to cross the wall into D5 is that moving directly from D4 to D5 requires crossing the wall. Moving directly from D4 to E5 does not require crossing a wall.

title: Terrain Question
question:
It's been a while since playing ASL and now I'm getting back into it.  Unfortunately, I left my rulebook in another state!  Yeah, I need to get that back here ASAP.

Meanwhile, a question came up.  I'm playing against some Finns in the snow and I think we're doing the IFT modifiers incorrectly.  We're combining all the modifiers and it gets pretty crazy.

For example, let's say I'm firing at the following hex:

- a Finn (in a snow smock) +1
- up a hill +1
- in a foxhole +2
- in woods +1
- through a LOS hindrance +1

Should this really be a +6 attack???  Are all of these items cumulative?  I'm guessing we're doing this wrong and some items are not cumulative.  Please let me know!

Thanks,
Jason
author: kypros
consensus_answer:
1) Foxholes are not cumulative with any terrain in the hex such as woods, shellholes, walls, etc...
Correct, see B27.3

2) Height advantage is also not cumulative with any positive modifier in the hex.
Correct, see B10.31

3) Hinderances will always add a modifier. I thought so on this one...it certainly makes sense.
Correct. A6.7 is the rule, although it does not contain any completely explicit statement saying that LOS Hindrances ALWAYS apply... but the key point is that it does not provide any exceptions in which a LOS Hindrance would not apply.

Note, however, that the Hindrance must be between the firing unit and the target in order to apply; Hindrance terrain in the firing unit's hex, and/or in the target unit's hex, never adds a modifier to a shot.

4) Snow smocks will always count unless specifically mentioned as an exception (I believe the rules note that they don't get the +1 in a building, for instance).
Hmmm... the Winter Camouflage rule, E3.712, doesn't exactly say this.

If the Winter Camouflage rules apply (that is, if the "snow smocks" are not a SSR applicable only to that scenario), and if snow is present (of course), then the Finnish infantry will receive a +1 LV (low visibility) Hindrance DRM if:

* the shot is at a range greater than 8 hexes, and

* there is no positive TEM other than SMOKE

(I think the main advantage of Winter Camouflage, for infantry, is that it allows you to Assault Move or advance into open ground and still retain concealment.)

In your example, the foxhole TEM would prevent you from claiming the Winter Camouflage LV Hindrance DRM.

So the shot would be a +3: +2 for the foxhole, and +1 for the LOS Hindrance.
